en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Disciples in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
(First Part) Discourse on the Commencement of the Book:
To the Lord of Great Compassion, who has gone to the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known;
I pay homage to the one who teaches the skillful, profound, and diverse methods.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, by which people are led out from the world.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, endowed with the virtues of morality and the rest, who stands firm in the paths and fruits— the unsurpassed field of merit.
Whatever merit is produced by this homage to the Triple Gem, [may it be for the welfare of all beings].
Having become one whose obstacles have been removed everywhere through his splendor,
I shall [recite] those verses spoken by the Elder Subhūti and others— those who had fulfilled their duties and were such-like—
as well as those spoken by the Elder Nuns, which are free from worldly motives.
By way of the method of inspired utterances (udāna), they are profound, subtle, and beautiful;
connected with emptiness (suññatā) and illuminating the noble Dhamma.
Known by the name *Theragāthā* and likewise *Therīgāthā*, they belong to those who are such [noble ones].
Although the commentary on the meaning of those [texts] which the great seers compiled within the *Khuddakanikāya* is difficult for me to compose—
because they must be fathomed by means of profound knowledge— [I shall nevertheless undertake it].
Since this concise commentary upholds the Teacher’s dispensation,
and the exposition of the former master-lions remains intact,
therefore, relying upon it and diving into all five [collections], [one should proceed].
Relying upon the Nikāyas and the method of the ancient commentaries—
pure, unadulterated, and precise in its determination of meaning—
I shall follow the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins without contradiction.
For those passages whose meaning is difficult to discern and which lack a sequential narrative,
I shall provide a beautiful commentary on their meaning, elucidating them by analyzing both the text and its significance according to my ability, while illuminating the definitive interpretation.
With care, for the sake of those who desire the long endurance of the true Dhamma, listen, O virtuous ones,
as I analyze the verses of the Elders and the verses of the Elder Nuns.
What, then, are these *Theragāthā* and *Therīgāthā*, and how did they come to be? Granted, this matter has already been stated within the verses themselves;
nevertheless, it is stated again here for the sake of clarification. In that regard, first, the *Theragāthā* were spoken by the Elder Subhūti and others.
For they, having reflected upon the bliss of the path and its fruition as they had personally attained it, uttered certain verses by way of spontaneous exclamation (*udāna*).

Some spoke by way of reviewing their own dwellings in meditative attainments (*samāpatti-vihāra*), some by way of questions, and some at the time of their final *parinibbāna* by way of elucidating the liberative nature of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
All of these were compiled together at the time of the Council (*saṅgīti*) and recited by the compilers of the Dhamma under the title "Theragāthā.
The *Therīgāthā*, however, consists of verses taught specifically for the sake of the Elder Nuns (*therī*).
Furthermore, among the three Piṭakas—the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—it is included within the Sutta Piṭaka.
Among the five Nikāyas—the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included within the Khuddaka Nikāya.
It consists of: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, and so forth.
The *Itivuttaka*, the *Jātaka*, the *Abbhutadhamma*, and the *Vedalla*—these are included within the category of verse (*gāthā*) among the nine factors of the Dispensation (*sāsanaṅga*).
As it is said: "I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks, and eighty-four thousand are those doctrines that have been transmitted to me."
Thus, among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma acknowledged by the Dhamma-treasurer, some have been included in this collection.
Therein, the *Theragāthā* begins with the first chapter (*nipāta*) and proceeds by increments of one up to fourteen chapters;

it consists of the fourteen-chapter section, the sixteen-chapter section, the twenty-chapter section, the thirty-chapter section, the forty-chapter section, the fifty-chapter section, and the sixty-chapter section.

The *Sattatinipāta* (Seventy Chapter) consists of a collection of twenty-one chapters (*nipāta*). A "chapter" (*nipāta*) is so called because it is a placing down (*nipātana*) or a setting forth (*nikkhipana*).

Since there is a single placement or setting forth of verses in each instance, it is called the "Single Chapter" (*ekanipāta*). In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining [chapters] as well.

In that regard, there are twelve sections (*vaga*) in the Single Chapter. By taking ten verses in each section, there are one hundred and twenty elders (*thera*), and an equal number of verses. For it is said:
“One hundred and twenty elders, who had fulfilled their duties and were free from taints, well-chanted [this] in the Single Chapter by those great seers.
In the Chapter of Twos, there are forty-nine elders and ninety-eight verses; in the Chapter of Threes, sixteen elders and forty-eight [verses].
The Gāthā: in the Catukkanipāta there are thirteen elders and fifty-two verses; in the Pañcakanipāta there are twelve elders and sixty verses;
in the Chakkanipāta there are fourteen elders and eighty-four verses; in the Sattakanipāta there are five elders and thirty-five verses;
in the Aṭṭhakanipāta there are three elders and twenty-four verses; in the Navakanipāta there is one elder.
In the ninth [nipāta], there are seven elders and seventy verses; in the eleventh [nipāta], one elder and eleven verses;
in the twelfth [nipāta], two elders and twenty-four verses; in the thirteenth [nipāta], one elder and thirteen verses;
in the fourteenth [nipāta], two elders and twenty-eight verses; there is no fifteenth [nipāta]; in the sixteenth [nipāta]...
In the [Dvaya]nipāta, there are two elders and thirty-two verses; in the Vīsatinipāta, ten elders and two hundred and forty-five verses;
in the Tiṃsanipāta, three elders and one hundred and five verses; in the Cattālīsanipāta, one elder and forty-two verses;
in the Paññāsanipāta, one elder and fifty-five verses; in the Saṭṭhinipāta, one elder and sixty-eight [verses].
Verses: In the Sattatinipāta there is one elder and seventy-one verses.
When added together, however, there are two hundred and sixty-four elders and one thousand three hundred and sixty verses. And this has been said:
“There are one thousand verses, And three hundred and sixty.”
"And two hundred and sixty elders have been proclaimed.
As for the *Therīgāthā*, there are nine sections— from the first section (*ekanipāta*) up to the ninth section (*navanipāta*)— and then the eleventh section,
the twelfth section, the sixteenth section, the twentieth section, the thirtieth section, the fortieth section, and the great section (*mahānipāta*).
The collection consists of sixteen nipātas. Therein, in the Ekanipāta there are eighteen therīs and eighteen verses;
in the Dukanipāta, ten therīs and twenty verses; in the Tikanipāta, eight therīs and twenty-four verses;
in the Catukkanipāta, one therī and four verses; in the Pañcakanipāta, twelve therīs and sixty verses; in the Chakkanipāta...
Eight elder nuns [have] forty-eight verses; in the Satta-nipāta, three elder nuns [have] twenty-one verses;
from the Aṭṭha-nipāta up to the Soḷasa-nipāta, one elder nun [has] as many verses as the measure of that respective nipāta;
in the Vīsati-nipāta, five elder nuns [have] one hundred and eighty verses; in the Tiṃsa-nipāta, one elder nun [has] thirty-four verses; in the Cattālīsa-nipāta...
There is one elder nun with forty-eight verses; in the Mahānipāta as well, there is one elder nun with seventy-five verses.
Thus, the measure of the nipātas, the verse-chapters, and the individual verses herein should be understood.
Commentary on the Nidāna Verses.
Thus, these *Theragāthā* (Verses of the Elders) are of a limited extent. Even therein it is said:
“Listen to the verses leading to the meaning of those who have developed themselves, like roaring lions with fangs within mountain caves.”
This is the first verse spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council for the purpose of praising those elders.
Therein, the word *sīha* (lion) occurs in the sense of the king of beasts in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, the lion is the king of beasts.
It occurs in the sense of a designation in such passages as, "Then Sīha the general approached the Blessed One. "Sīha" [means...]
“Monks, this is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” and so forth—this refers to the Tathāgata.
In that context, just as [the term] was used for the Tathāgata by way of a metaphorical identification (*sadisa-kappanā*), so too here it should be understood by way of a metaphorical identification.
Therefore, *sīhānaṃ va* means “like lions. The elision of the vowel occurs by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), as in the case of *evaṃsa te* and so on. In that regard:
*iva* is a particle (*nipāta*). *Suṇātha* is a verb (*ākhyāta*). The others are nouns (*nāman*). In the phrase *sīhānaṃ va*, the genitive case is used in the sense of connection (*sambandha*).
Although the related term is not expressed here by way of its form (*sarūpato*), it is nevertheless expressed by way of its meaning (*atthato*).
For just as when it is said, "The face of this one is like that of an elephant," it means "his face is like the face of an elephant."
This meaning is already expressed; likewise here, when "of lions" (*sīhānaṃ*) is stated, the meaning "like the roar of lions" is already expressed.
If it is argued that in that case there is the presence of the word "sound" (*mukha*), here too [the meaning is established] because of the presence of the word "roaring" (*nadantānaṃ*).
Therefore, "of lions" is an illustrative statement (*nidassanavacanaṃ*), while "roaring" shows the connection with that which is to be illustrated.
“Of the fanged ones” (*dāṭhīnaṃ*) is an epithet for them. “In the mountain clefts” (*girigabbhare*) indicates their place of activity. “Listen! (*suṇātha*) is an exhortation to hear.
“Of those with developed minds” (*bhāvitattānaṃ*) shows the source of what is to be heard. “Verses” (*gāthā*) shows the subject matter to be heard.

“Leading to the meaning” (*atthupanāyikā*) is an epithet for that [subject matter]. And here, although it is in the masculine gender—as in “of the roaring lions, the fanged ones”—it is used as a collective.
The meaning should also be understood according to the feminine gender by changing the grammatical gender (*liṅga*) of the word *āgataṃ* to “of lionsess” (*sīhīnaṃ*) and so forth.

Alternatively, by the principle of singular remainder (*ekasesa*), “lions” (*sīhā*) refers to both lions and lionesses; thus, these three introductory verses (*nidānagāthā*) are common to both the *Theragāthā* and the *Therīgāthā*.

In this context, he is a lion because of his endurance and his slaying. For just as there is no such thing as danger for the lion, the king of beasts, due to his possession of superior strength—even from creatures such as the sarabha deer or excellent wild elephants—he endures even dangers such as wind and heat;
and when setting out on his hunt, by virtue of his fiery majesty, he fearlessly and undauntedly overcomes those such as rutting scent-elephants and forest buffaloes that may encounter him.
And they dwell in comfort, having overcome and indeed slain [their enemies] there,

having eaten their tender flesh; even so these great elders, through their possession of the excellence of noble powers, endure all perils, having overcome and slain— that is, having abandoned— the power of defilements such as lust,
and being fearless and undaunted toward anything due to the intensity of their fiery energy, they dwell in the bliss of jhāna and the like.
They "dwell" (viharanti) like lions because of their endurance and their slaying; thus they are "lions" (sīha).

As for the meaning of the word, just as *takka* is said in the sense of "churning" (*kantana*) through a transposition of its initial and final letters, so too should the lion (*sīha*) be understood in the sense of "slaying" (*hiṃsana*). Likewise, it is understood in the sense of "endurance" (*sahana*).
However, when explained according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) by means of the *pisodarādi* class of compounds, there is nothing further that needs to be said.

Alternatively, just as the lion, the king of beasts, dwells alone because of his own majestic power and does not expect any companion, so too these [monks] are "lions" in the sense of solitary wandering because of their majestic power and their delight in seclusion;
thus the Blessed One said: "The lion, the elephant who wanders alone."
Alternatively, they are called "lions" because they possess distinctions such as fearlessness, speed, and prowess, just like lions; these are the great elders. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, these two do not tremble when a thunderbolt strikes: which two? A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted and the lion, the king of beasts.
The speed of the lion is not shared by others, nor is its prowess; for indeed, it can leap over even a hundred bulls.

He falls upon the forest, the non-violent, and so forth; even while still a cub, he shatters the likeness of even the finest rutting elephants in their state of intoxication and devours them like a mere shoot of ivory.

However, their speed of the Noble Path and their speed of supernormal power (*iddhi*) are not shared by others, and their exertion through right effort (*sammappadhāna*) is unsurpassed. Therefore, "like lions" means like those who resemble lions.

...as it were. In this context, the lion should be understood as a simile for something inferior, because the meaning of "enduring" (*sahanādi*) and so forth is found only in the Elders (*thera*), who are exceedingly distinguished.

"Roaring" (*nadantānaṃ*) means "shouting. For just as lions, when they are hungry, when exerting themselves in their range, or at times of satisfaction, emerge from their lairs, stretch themselves, and let out a lion’s roar—a fearless cry—so too do these [Elders] at times of reflecting on the internal objects of the senses, during the recitation of the *Udāna*, and so forth.
They uttered this fearless roar. Therefore it is said: “Like roaring lions. *Dāṭhīnaṃ* means “of those possessing tusks.
The meaning is either “of those with prominent tusks” or “of those with excellent tusks.
For just as lions, by the strength of their four exceedingly firm and sharp tusks, overcome their adversaries and bring their own desires to fulfillment, so too...

In this way, by the power of the four noble paths as their fangs, they overcame the adversaries that had never before been overcome throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), and brought their own aspirations to their ultimate fulfillment.
Here too, the meaning should be understood through the metaphorical application of "fangs" (*dāṭhā*), as if they were like actual fangs.
"In a mountain cleft" (*girigabbhare*) means in a mountain cave; the locative case is used in the sense of proximity. Some read it as "in a mountain thicket" (*girigavhare*).
"In mountain thickets" means in forest groves. This, moreover, shows both their place of shining and the ground suitable for the lion’s roar. The construction is: "roaring in the mountain recesses.
For just as lions, dwelling mostly in mountain recesses—places secluded from people due to being difficult for others to approach—by their very sight...
Just as lions roar while roaming their domain in order to ward off the terror of small animals that might arise,
so too do these [arahants], dwelling in empty huts that resemble the inaccessible mountain recesses difficult for others to approach,
utter the fearless roar known as the forthcoming verses, in order to avoid the craving, views, and petty hopes of the inferior worldlings (puthujjana).
They roared. Therefore it was said: “Like roaring lions, fanged [beasts] within mountain caves.

“Listen! is a command to hear; by this, he generates a desire to hear in the assembled assembly for the verses that are about to be spoken, producing respect and great esteem while instilling enthusiasm for listening.

Or else, the meaning of the words beginning with "of lions" (sīhānam) should be understood according to their primary sense alone, without resorting to a figurative application. Therefore, because they possess fangs that are praised for their extreme sharpness and firmness,
and because they roar like the lion’s roar of the lions— the kings of beasts— who roar within mountain caves, their fearless cries are similar to those [of the lions].

"Listen to the verses" is the meaning. This is what is intended: "Just as the lion-roars of lions, the kings of beasts, being free from fear from any quarter, are fearless cries that cause terror to other animals, even so, listen to these verses which are like the lion-roars of the elders who have developed their minds through heedfulness;
for they are fearless cries—since all causes of fear have been thoroughly abandoned—and they cause terror to heedless people."

"Bhāvitattānaṃ" means those who have developed their minds. For the mind is called "self" in such passages as, "The self, it is said, is difficult to tame; he indeed who has established his self is straight like a shuttle," and "the right disposition of the self.

Therefore, [it refers to] those who have reached the culmination of the cultivation of serenity and insight through the practice of higher consciousness (adhicitta), and who stand having attained that pinnacle.

*Attha*: meaning. Alternatively, *bhāvitattānaṃ* means "of those whose intrinsic nature has been cultivated," that is, of those who have cultivated such things as virtue (*sīla*) which constitute their very nature.
It is called a *gāthā* because it is sung; it is a four-footed or six-footed utterance set forth by sages in the *anuṭṭhubha* meter and so forth.
Others are also called such because they resemble them. They lead one toward the meanings distinguished as "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) and so on.
Or, "they lead toward" means they lead toward the goal (*atthūpanāyikā*).

Alternatively, "of those who have cultivated themselves" (*bhāvitattānaṃ*) refers to those who have cultivated the state of selfhood (*bhāvitattabhāvānaṃ*); for the "self" (*attā*) is so called because the conceit "I" (*ahaṃ-māna*) is placed (*āhita*) therein;
and that [self] has been properly cultivated by them through the cultivation of diligence and the cultivation of blamelessness.

He was made to immerse himself in the fragrance of virtue. By this, he shows the fulfillment of all four kinds of development (*bhāvanā*): the development of the body, the development of virtue, the development of the mind, and the development of wisdom.
Here, "development" refers to the path leading to full enlightenment (*sambodhi*). That which is the actualization of truth (*saccasambodhi*) is twofold:
by way of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) and by way of its meaning (*tadattha*). Furthermore, enlightenment (*sambodhi*) is threefold.

[There are] perfect enlightenment, solitary enlightenment, and disciple-enlightenment. Therein, it is "perfect enlightenment" because of awakening to and awakening others to all phenomena rightly and by oneself.
Path-knowledge, which has omniscience as its proximate cause, and omniscience, which has path-knowledge as its proximate cause, is called "perfect enlightenment. Therefore he said:

“‘Buddha’ refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (*sayambhū*), teacherless, and who by himself fully awakened to the truths among doctrines unheard before; therein he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers (*bala*).
For mastery over the powers is for the purpose of awakening those capable of being awakened. ‘Paccekabodhi’ means individual self-awakening;

the meaning is the realization of the truths by one’s own self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) without having previously been awakened [to them]. For it is through the state of self-born knowledge that those who are perfectly enlightened (*sammāsambuddha*) [attain their status].”

Even though the realization of truth (*saccābhisamaya*) occurs spontaneously by itself, it is "awakened along with" (*sānubuddha*), because it serves as the cause for the realization of truth for immeasurable beings;
yet it does not serve as the cause for the realization of truth for even a single being among these [beings].

They are called "disciples" (*sāvaka*) because they are born at the conclusion of hearing the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma. The realization of truth by those disciples is "disciple-enlightenment" (*sāvakasambodhi*).

This threefold [realization] should be understood as the fulfillment of the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, through reaching the culmination of the respective paths leading to the three types of Bodhisattvas; for the other types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) are inseparable from it.
Indeed, there is no clear realization of cultivation without the clear realization of direct experience (*sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya*).

When there is the realization through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*), the realization through abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) and the realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) are necessarily established.

For when the Great Bodhisatta, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment and performed his preliminary duties in his final existence, ascends the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and resolves:
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints (*āsava*) through non-clinging."
Having made his promise, while seated upon the invincible throne, he shattered the army of Māra even before the time of twilight had arrived;
in the first watch of the night, by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, he recollected the aggregates in their manifold modes and locations in which he had previously dwelt;
in the middle watch, through the purification of the divine eye, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings and the knowledge of the future; and in the last watch...
“Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, namely aging and death.
Having thus applied insight (*vipassanā*) by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) starting from aging and death, he sat upon the stone slab to cut through the great thicket of ignorance.
Like one brandishing an axe to cut through the thicket of defilements, the Lord of the World wielded the axe of knowledge;
and because the perfection of causes for Buddhahood had reached maturity, he conceived the embryo of insight (*vipassanā*) for the attainment of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*),
entering various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) from time to time, and applying the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as they had been defined.
Contemplating formations of manifold modes and bases by way of insight into phenomena according to their occurrence (*anupādā-dhamma-vipassanā*),
one expands the section on contemplation through three hundred and sixty million methods; when, while that insight-knowledge— known as the Great Diamond Knowledge— is proceeding with its sharp, keen,
and clear state as the factor leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-gāminī*), one joins it with the Path, then [it occurs] according to the sequence of the Path.
At the moment of the supreme path, one is said to "attain" full enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) by casting off the one thousand five hundred defilements;

from the moment of the supreme fruit onwards, it is said to have been "attained. Since the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and so forth, also come into his possession at that time through his state of being a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha), this is first of all the way to full enlightenment by way of clear realization (abhisamaya). As for its meaning:

However, from the time of the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra) until his rebirth in the Tusita heaven, the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) that took place during this interval is as follows:
whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been explained in full detail in the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka, complete in all its aspects;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method set forth therein.
The Paccekabodhisattas, having made the aspiration for Pacceka-bodhi and having gradually accumulated the requisites for individual enlightenment,
when they reached their final existence at such a time, took hold of the sign of spiritual urgency that appeared through the ripening of their knowledge.

Having seen with particular clarity the disadvantage in states of existence and so forth, they— by means of self-arisen knowledge— [realized] the process of existence, its cause, and the cessation [of that process].
Having delimited the cause of cessation, and cultivating the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths according to the method set forth in the passage beginning, "He attends wisely,
'This is suffering,'" they thoroughly rub away at mental formations in accordance with their own initial aspiration.
Gradually bringing insight to its peak and attaining the supreme path through the sequence of the paths, they realize the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.

They are said to "fully awaken" because, from the moment of attaining the fruit of the highest path, they become Paccekabuddhas and thus become the most worthy recipients of offerings in the world including its devas.
As for the disciples, however, having heard the discourse on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths from the Teacher or their fellow celibate companions, at that very [moment]...
Whether at that very moment or at a later time, by practicing the appropriate course of training, striving, and exerting themselves, they cause insight to reach its peak;

then, either through the progressive development of the path or by penetrating the Truths, they attain the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakasambodhi) either on the level of a chief disciple (aggasāvaka)—which is the success corresponding to their own specific resolve—or simply at the moment of the supreme path (aggamagga). Beyond that, they are known as disciple-buddhas (sāvakabuddhas).

They become the foremost recipients of offerings in the world with its devas. Thus, first of all, should individual enlightenment (paccekabodhi) and disciple-enlightenment (sāvakabodhi) be understood from the perspective of direct realization (abhisamaya).
As for their meaning, however, just as for the Great Bodhisattvas the minimum limit is four incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya),...
The accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment should be undertaken for one hundred thousand eons according to the middle measure— namely,
eight *asaṅkhyeyya* periods plus one hundred thousand eons— or for sixteen *asaṅkhyeyya* periods plus one hundred thousand eons according to the superior measure;
and these distinctions are to be understood by way of those who are preeminent in wisdom, preeminent in faith, and preeminent in energy.

For those in whom wisdom (*paññā*) predominates, faith (*saddhā*) is weak and wisdom is sharp; consequently, through the clarity and proficiency of their skill in means (*upāyakosalla*), the perfections (*pāramitā*) reach fulfillment before long. For those in whom faith predominates, wisdom is middling;
thus, for them, the perfections reach fulfillment neither too quickly nor too slowly. However, for those in whom energy (*vīriya*) predominates, wisdom is weak.
Thus, for them, the perfections reach fulfillment only after a long time. It is not so for the Pacceka-bodhisattvas.
For although they possess a preponderance of wisdom, they must still accumulate the requisites for enlightenment for two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, and not less than that.
Even those with a preponderance of faith or energy [reach their goal] only after a few more [aeons] beyond the aforementioned limit.
Having thus passed through two asaṅkhyeyyas, they awaken to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, but not during a third asaṅkhyeyya.

However, for those Disciple-Bodhisattvas who have made the aspiration for the state of a Chief Disciple (Aggasāvaka), the accumulation of the requisites must be undertaken for one asaṅkhyeyya and a hundred thousand kappas. For those [who aspire] to the state of a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka)...
For those [conditions], there are exactly one hundred thousand eons for a Buddha, as well as for his mother, father, attendant, and son.
In this regard, it is said: “Human birth, possession of male gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher, Going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite service, and zeal;”
“When the eight qualities are brought together, the aspiration succeeds. When this was said,
from the time of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) of the Great Bodhisattvas who had made their vow after bringing those eight qualities together,
they applied themselves with particular diligence to giving and the other perfections, performing great acts of charity day by day, such as the Vessantara-giving.

Even for those accumulating all the qualities of the perfections, such as virtue appropriate to their respective stages, there is no attaining the state of Buddhahood in the interim without reaching the aforementioned limit of time. Why? Because their knowledge has not yet reached full maturity.
For the Buddha-knowledge, like a crop harvested at its predetermined time, arises only according to that fixed period.
"Reaching growth, increase, and abundance, the embryo is conceived and proceeds toward maturity"—
thus it is said: "Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender,
freedom from taints, vision, exertion, and zeal— these are the causes for the formal resolve."

For those Pacceka-bodhisattvas who have combined these five qualities and made their resolution, and for those Śrāvaka-bodhisattvas who have made their aspiration through an aspiration endowed with two factors—
namely, "merit" (*adhikāra*) and "zeal" (*chandatā*)— if they do not reach the specific time limit stated for each case but instead attain, in the interim,
either the enlightenment of a Pacceka-Buddha or the aforementioned enlightenment of a Śrāvaka, [they are called *antarā-parinibbāyī*].
And there is no realization [of the fruits]. Why? Because their knowledge has not reached maturity.

For just as the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*)—which is nurtured by the perfections of giving and so forth in the case of the Great Bodhisattvas—gradually takes on an embryo and, reaching full maturity, fulfills the Buddha-knowledge;
even so, [the wisdom of these others] is nurtured by giving and so forth, gradually taking on an embryo according to what is appropriate.
As they reach maturity, they fulfill the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) and the knowledge of disciple-enlightenment (sāvakabodhi).
Through their practice of giving, in various states of existence, they possess an inclination toward non-greed;

thus, with minds unattached everywhere and hearts free from longing, and through their practice of virtue, they maintain well-restrained body and speech, possessing utterly pure bodily and verbal actions and a pure livelihood.
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties and being moderate in eating, they concentrate the mind through devotion to wakefulness.
This devotion to wakefulness of theirs should be understood by way of the practice of going and returning.
For those practicing in this manner, by virtue of the perfection of their preliminary application, the eight attainments and the five direct knowledges arise without difficulty.
The six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) become the foundation, and preliminary insight (*pubbabhāgavipassanā*) is already within one's grasp.

Furthermore, energy (*vīriya*) and the other [faculties] are indeed included therein. For that exertion in the accumulation of merit through giving and so forth for the sake of *paccekabodhi* or *sāvakabodhi* is energy;
that endurance which does not obstruct it is patience (*khanti*); and that non-deception in undertaking giving, virtue, and so forth—
This is the truth. This resolve, which consists in unwavering concentration at all times, is the *adhiṭṭhāna*.

That which is the desire for the welfare of those beings who are the objects of one’s practice of giving, virtue, and so forth, is *mettā*. That which is the equanimity toward the wrongdoings committed by beings is *upekkhā*.
Thus, while giving, virtue, and meditation, as well as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, are being perfected, energy (*vīriya*) and the other [factors] [are likewise accomplished].

They indeed become perfected ones (*siddha*). That very same path of practice consisting of giving and so forth, for the sake of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) and *sāvakabodhi* (disciple-enlightenment), is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) because it is cultivated and thoroughly developed within the mental continuum (*santāna*) of those bodhisattvas.

Specifically, it refers to the path of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) proceeding within a continuum specially conditioned by giving, morality, and other virtues; through which those bodhisattvas become endowed with the attainment of the preliminary practices (*pubbayoga*).
They exist. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one who practices the preliminary yoga. What are the five?
Here, Ānanda, one who practices the preliminary yoga attains final knowledge early in this very life; if he does not attain final knowledge early in this very life..."
“Then, at the time of death, he propitiates another; then, being a son of the gods, he propitiates another;
then, in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct knowledge; then, in his final existence, he becomes a paccekabuddha.
Thus, through the development of serenity and insight, which is the preliminary practice permeated by the perfections and constitutes the path leading to cessation—

The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, whose personal beings have been cultivated through the cultivation of the path known as clear realization (*abhisamaya*), are called "those of cultivated being" (*bhāvitatta*).
Among them, it is the disciples of the Buddha who are intended here.
Furthermore, by the phrase "like lions," the Elder demonstrates that his own conduct is similar to that of a lion, thereby [showing] his adversaries...
By the phrase "unconquerability," he shows that these [teachings] cannot be overcome by opposing doctrines, and that they proceed having overcome them.

By the verse beginning, "Like lions roaring... and so forth, through the demonstration that the verses of the Elder are like the lion's roar, he shows their unconquerability by opposing doctrines and that they proceed having overcome them.
By the phrase "of those with developed minds," he indicates the cause for both of these.
He causes them to be manifested. By virtue of having cultivated their own being, the elders are here said to be like lions; their verses, too, are like the lion’s roar.
By the phrase "leading to the goal" (*atthūpanāyikā*), he shows the purpose for overcoming. In this context, the "adversary" of the elders is the defiled state (*saṃkilesadhamma*);

its overcoming consists of its abandonment through the modes of abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), together with its abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
When that [cessation] exists, both abandonment as subsiding and abandonment as escape are necessarily established;

for this reason they are called "those by whom [the path] has been developed. Indeed, at the moment of the Path, the Noble Ones are said to be "developing the development of diligence," but it is from the moment of the highest fruit (aggaphala) onwards that they are truly said to be "those by whom [it] has been developed. This is the meaning stated here.

Among these, the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) is shown by abandoning through the factor of substitution (*tadaṅgappahāna*); the perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*) by abandoning through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*);
the perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*) by abandoning through eradication (*samucchedappahāna*); and by the remaining [abandoning], their fruit is shown.

Furthermore, by means of virtue, the excellence at the beginning of their practice (*paṭipatti*) is shown, according to the passage: "And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is perfectly purified."

Because of the statements, “Being established in virtue” and “The non-doing of all evil,” virtue is indeed good in the beginning of the practice, as it brings about qualities such as freedom from remorse.
The state of being good in the middle is shown by means of concentration;

because of the statements, “Developing the mind” and “The undertaking of what is wholesome,” the practice of concentration is indeed good in the middle, as it brings about qualities such as the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).
The excellence of the conclusion through wisdom is demonstrated by the statements, “the purification of one’s own mind,” and “develop wisdom.

Wisdom itself is the conclusion of the practice; since it is the culmination of all wholesome states, it is truly excellent because it brings about equanimity toward the desirable and the undesirable.
“As a solid block of stone is not moved by the wind,
so the wise do not waver amidst blame and praise.
Thus it was said.

Likewise, the state of possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*) is shown by means of the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*); for it is by relying on the perfection of virtue that one attains the three knowledges.

The state of possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) is shown by means of the perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*); for it is by relying on the perfection of concentration that one attains the six direct knowledges.

The state of possessing the analytical knowledges (*pabhinnapaṭisambhidā*) is shown by means of the perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*); for it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that one attains the four analytical knowledges.

They attain [these]. By this, it should be understood that the meaning shown is that among those elders, some were possessors of the three knowledges (*tevijjā*), some were possessors of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and some had attained the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).
Likewise, through their perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*), he shows their avoidance of the extreme consisting in devotion to sensual pleasure.

By means of the perfection of concentration, he shows the cultivation of the middle way, which is characterized by the avoidance of self-mortification; by means of the perfection of wisdom, he shows the cultivation of that same middle way.

Likewise, by means of the perfection of virtue, he shows the abandoning of those defilements through the non-transgression [of precepts]. By means of the perfection of concentration, he shows the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*);

by means of the perfection of wisdom, he shows the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Or alternatively, by means of the perfection of virtue, he shows the purification of the defilement of misconduct.
It shows the purification of the defilement of craving through the perfection of concentration, and the purification of the defilement of views through the perfection of wisdom.
Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of abandonment as a factor (tadaṅgappahāna), their transcendence of the states of woe is shown;

by means of suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna), the transcendence of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) is shown; and by means of eradication (samucchedappahāna), the transcendence of all states of existence (bhava) is shown.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by one who has developed himself," three kinds of development should be understood here: development of virtue, development of mind, and development of wisdom;
for the development of the body is included within them. And the development of virtue is the beginning of practice, and so forth—all as explained previously.
Just as other herds of deer cannot endure the lion’s roar, much less overcome it, but rather...
Just as the lion’s roar overcomes [all other sounds], even so the doctrines of the other sectarians cannot withstand the doctrine of the Elders; how much less can they overcome it?
Rather, it is the doctrine of the Elders alone that overcomes them. Why is that? Because it proceeds by way of the formula:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are non-self," and also by way of the "element of Nibbāna."
Indeed, no one can alter things otherwise than they are by their very nature (*dhammatā*), because such a reversal is impossible.
Whatever is to be said regarding this matter will be clarified further on. Thus, the exposition of the meaning of the first verse should be understood in brief.
As for the second verse, however, this is the exposition of its meaning by way of showing the connection (*sambandha*). In that regard, of those elders...
Desiring to announce the verses, he spoke the words beginning with "according to name" (*yathānāma*) in order to proclaim them by way of their common names, clans, and qualities.
However, their specific [individual] characteristics will be revealed in the various verses themselves.

In that context, "according to name" (*yathānāma*) means those who are known by whatever names they have, such as Subhūti, Mahākoṭṭhika, and so forth, according to the method of their designations. "According to clan" (*yathāgotta*)...
"By whatever clan" means by whichever lineage they were known in each respective birth, according to the method beginning with "Gotama" or "Kassapa.
"Dwellers in accordance with the Dhamma" (yathādhammavihārino) means dwellers in such-and-such a state of the Dhamma;

that is, instead of remaining at the level of mere study (pariyatti), they dwelt having entered into meditative attainments (samāpatti) as was appropriate. Alternatively, "dwellers in accordance with the Dhamma" means...
"Abiding according to the Dhamma" means those who frequently dwell in such states as the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*), and whose qualities—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—are of such a kind;

that is the meaning. "According to their inclination" (*yathādhimuttā*) means those who have such an inclination among faith-inclination, wisdom-inclination, and so on, or those who are inclined toward emptiness (*suññatā*) and the like;
or alternatively, those who are inclined toward Nibbāna in whatever way—that is "according to their inclination."
“For those intent upon Nibbāna, the taints come to an end. This should be understood as referring to both [aspects] by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
For the aforementioned resolution occurs only prior to the attainment of Arahantship, not after it. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“The person who is faithless, ungrateful, and a destroyer of the bond,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the reading is *yathāvimuttā*, meaning "according to their respective deliverance" among the three types:

wisdom-deliverance (*paññāvimutti*), both-sided deliverance (*ubhatobhāgavimutti*), and so forth. *Sappaññā* means "possessing wisdom," being endowed with the threefold wisdom: the wisdom of rebirth with three roots (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*), the wisdom of maintenance (*pārihārika-paññā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-paññā*). *Vihariṃsu* means that by virtue of that very possession of wisdom, they dwelt in the comfortable abiding (*phāsuvihāra*) as it was obtained.
They dwelt. "Untiring" means not lazy; the meaning is that they were diligent according to their strength in the practice for their own welfare and in the practice for the welfare of others.
And here, by mentioning their names and clans, he shows that those elders were well-known for their manifest wisdom. By mentioning their dwelling in the Dhamma...

By the phrase "endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampada*), he shows the perfection of virtue; by "endowed with concentration" (*samādhisampada*), he shows the perfection of concentration. By the phrase "possessing wisdom according to their inclinations" (*yathādhimuttā sappaññā*), he shows the perfection of wisdom.

By the word "unwearied" (*atanditā*), he shows the perfection of energy (*vīriyasampada*), which is the cause for the perfections of virtue and the others. By the phrase "according to their names" (*yathānāmā*), he shows that they are made known by their respective names.

By the phrase "according to their clans" (*yathāgottā*), he shows the attainment of the noble lineage of those who follow through faith (*saddhānusārī*) and those who follow through the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).

By the phrase “dwelling in accordance with the Dhamma” and so forth, he shows the attainment of the perfections consisting of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
by the word “unwearied,” he shows the practice for the benefit of others on the part of those established in such perfection for their own benefit.
Alternatively, “according to their names” is a demonstration of the names given to those elders by their teachers, mentioned merely as a conventional designation.
“According to their lineage”: this is a demonstration of their status as sons of noble family (*kulaputta*), by way of praising their family background.

By this, he shows that they have gone forth out of faith (*saddhā-pabbajita*). “Dwelling according to the Dhamma”: this is a demonstration of the perfection of their conduct (*caraṇa-sampatti*), because it illuminates their possession of the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so forth.

“Resolute according to their inclination and possessed of wisdom”: this is a demonstration of their perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā-sampatti*), culminating in the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).

Because it demonstrates the attainment through the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Unwearied" (*atanditā*) shows the means for attaining the perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*).

Or, by the phrase "according to their names," he shows that they are indeed made manifest by their respective names. By the phrase "according to their clans" (*yathāgotta*), however, he shows the perfection of the latter two wheels [of the Dhamma].
For one who has not previously performed merit and whose self is not rightly directed, this is not possible.
The attainment of excellence in lineage is possible for those who follow by faith (*saddhānusārī*) and those who follow by Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).

By the phrase "dwelling according to the Dhamma," he shows their possession of the two preceding wheels; for such specific qualities cannot arise in one living in an unsuitable place or lacking the support of virtuous friends (*sappurisa*).
By the phrase "according to their inclination," he shows their association with the perfection of hearing the true Dhamma.
[The Blessed One] shows this. For without the voice of another, the penetration of the Truths by disciples is not possible.
By the phrase "wise and untiring," he shows the infallible cause for the aforementioned distinction of qualities, because it demonstrates the undertaking of the method (*ñāya*).

Another interpretation: by the mention of their lineage in the phrase "according to their clan" (*yathāgotta*), [the Blessed One] indicates the perfection of those elders' systematic attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
This shows that for one endowed with the lineage as previously described, proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is possible.

By the phrase "dwelling in accordance with the Dhamma" (*yathādhammavihārino*), the inclusion of "dwelling in the Dhamma" indicates perfection in hearing the True Dhamma (*saddhammasavana*), because such dwelling cannot exist without hearing the True Dhamma.
By the term "according to their inclination" (*yathādhimuttā*), he shows the practice of the Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipadā*) that has reached its culmination.
By the term "possessing wisdom" (*sappaññā*), he indicates that they act with full awareness in all circumstances.

By the term "unwearied" (*atanditā*), he shows that those who, having fulfilled their own welfare according to the method already described, remain untiring in their practice for bringing about the welfare and happiness of others.

Likewise, by the phrase "according to their lineage" (*yathāgottā*), their perfection in going for refuge is shown, since this refers to the lineage of those who follow through faith (*saddhānusārī*).

By the phrase “dwelling in accordance with the Dhamma,” the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), preceded by the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), is shown. By the phrase “resolute and possessed of wisdom,” the aggregate of wisdom (paññakkhandha) and the others are shown.
Furthermore, going for refuge is the beginning of the qualities of a disciple; concentration is the middle;
and wisdom is the end. Thus, by showing the beginning, the middle, and the end, all the qualities of a disciple are shown.
However, in order to show that right practice by which such an abundance of qualities was attained by them, it is said: "Having practiced insight here and there," and so forth.
"There and there" means in those various secluded dwellings, such as forests, the foot of trees, mountains, and so on.
Alternatively, "there and there" means at each respective occasion for uttering inspired exhortations (*udāna*) and the like. "Having practiced insight" means having clearly perceived.
Having accomplished purification of view and purification by overcoming doubt through the discernment of mind-and-body and the grasping of conditions;
having attained the fifth purification by means of the sequence beginning with the comprehension of aggregates;
and having intensified insight by reaching the culmination of purification by knowledge and vision of the way—having touched it, that is, having reached and realized it. The Immortal...
They call it *nibbāna*. For because it is itself subject to no decay and because it is the cause for the non-decay of those who have attained it, there is no passing away (*cuti*) therein;

thus it is "the undecaying" (*accuta*). Because it is unmixed with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) and because it is to be practiced by those seeking its goal, it is called the "footing" (*pada*).
"The end of what is made" (*kata-anta*) means the end of the conditioned. For that Noble Path which has been attained by them—

Because it has been produced by its own conditions, it is called "made" (*kata*). However, what is intended here is that its fruit, which constitutes its culmination, is "the end of what is made" (*katanta*).
That "end of what is made" is the supreme fruit. Alternatively, conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) are called "made" because they are produced and brought forth by conditions;
Nibbāna is the "end of what is made" because it is the state of escape from them. It is that "end of what is made" [which they] contemplate. "Contemplating" means...
“Indeed, through the attainment of the Noble Path, this Noble Fruit has been attained by me;
the unconditioned element has been attained”—thus one contemplates the practice by means of the knowledge and vision of liberation regarding the Noble Fruits and Nibbāna.

Alternatively, because the sixteenfold duties—such as full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth—which are to be performed by a Noble One have been accomplished by one established in the highest fruit, [one contemplates the practice] by way of the penetration of the Truths.
Because it has been brought to completion, it is called "done"; thus, those who reflect upon what has been done have demonstrated the reflection on the defilements abandoned by this [method].
However, according to the previous method, the other reflections are also shown; thus, nineteen reflections are demonstrated.
Regarding the phrase "this meaning": here, "this" refers to the entire meaning of the verses of the Elders and Elderesses, both for oneself and for others therein.
This was said because [the meaning] was close and evident due to revolving within the minds of the Great Elders who had assembled as the compilers of the Dhamma.

"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning expressed by such verses as "My hut is thatched," which relates to oneself, relates to others, and is connected with both the mundane and the supramundane. "They proclaimed" means they proclaimed it by way of composing it into verse.
The construction is as follows: "Listen now to those verses being spoken by me, which illuminate that [teaching] and are self-referential (attūpanāyika) to those of developed mind.

And those great elders, speaking thus, through verses that manifest their own correct practice and demonstrate the absolute nature of the Dispensation as leading to liberation, urge others as well toward that same correct practice.
It should be understood that the Venerable Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika illuminates this matter;

and while illuminating it, he shows that the praise of those [Buddhas] by means of these verses, as well as the placement of those [verses] as the introductory cause for their words, is indeed appropriate to the context.
The commentary on the introductory verses is finished.
1. Ekakanipāta 1.
Paṭhamavagga 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Subhūti
Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the Elder’s Verses that proceed according to the method beginning with "My little hut is thatched.
Since this commentary becomes clear and easy to understand when it is spoken by setting forth the occasion for each respective verse,
we shall therefore provide the commentary on the meaning while setting forth the occasion for each instance.
Regarding that, what is the origin of the verse beginning with "My little hut is thatched"? It is said:

Long ago, it is told, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons before the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Lord of the World, a son was born to a certain wealthy brahmin in the city named Haṃsavatī. They gave him the name Nanda-māṇava. When he reached maturity—
Having mastered the three Vedas and finding no essence therein, he went with his retinue of forty-four thousand young brahmins to the foot of a mountain and took up the ascetic life of an *isi*.
There he attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
He also explained a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to his pupils, and they too, before long, became attainers of *jhāna*.
And at that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having appeared in the world and dwelling in dependence upon the city of Haṃsavatī,
one day at the hour of dawn, surveying the world, perceived the potential for Arahantship in the matted-hair ascetics who were disciples of the ascetic Nanda,
as well as the potential for the status of a disciple in the ascetic Nanda himself, who was endowed with two factors.
Having seen his aspiration, he performed his bodily care early in the morning; then, at the time of the morning meal,
taking his bowl and robe and without informing anyone else, like a lion walking alone while Nanda the ascetic’s disciples had gone out for fruit,
he descended from the sky onto the earth right before Nanda the ascetic’s very eyes, thinking, "May he know my state as a Buddha."
He stood there. Having seen both the majesty of the Buddha and the perfection of his marks, the ascetic Nanda contemplated the manual of marks and thought:
"One endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home, becomes a wheel-turning monarch;
if he goes forth, he becomes an omniscient Buddha who has lifted the veil from the world. This noble being is undoubtedly..."
Knowing him to be the Buddha, he went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The ascetic Nanda also took a seat suitable for himself and sat to one side.
At that time, forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics arrived, carrying various excellent and nutritious fruits.

Having arrived in the presence of the teacher, they looked at the seats occupied by both the Buddhas and the teacher and said, "Teacher, we used to wander about thinking, 'In this world there is no one greater than you,' yet we think this man is even greater than you.
The ascetic Nanda replied, "Sons, what are you saying? [He is] like a mustard seed..."
“If you wish to compare Sineru, which rises sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas high, to something else, do not compare it to me, but rather to the Omniscient Buddha,” he said.
Then those ascetics, thinking, “If this man were insignificant, our teacher would not have brought such a comparison;
how great indeed is this noble being! fell at his feet and paid homage with their heads.
Then their teacher said: "Sons, we have no gift worthy of our Buddhas;
yet the Blessed One has arrived here at the time for the alms-round. Therefore, we shall give whatever gifts we can afford according to our means.
Bring forth each of you whatever choice fruits you have brought. Having spoken thus, he had them brought, and having washed his hands, he said:
He himself placed it into the bowl of the Tathāgata. As soon as the Teacher had accepted the various fruits, the deities added divine food.
The ascetic himself filtered the water and gave it [to the Teacher].
Then, when the Teacher had finished his meal and was seated, he summoned all his pupils and, in the presence of the Teacher, recited the *Sāraṇīya* [Dhamma].
He sat there speaking thus. The Teacher thought, "Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus come.
The bhikkhus, perceiving the Teacher's mind, arrived—numbering about one hundred thousand, all of them with taints destroyed—and having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side.
The ascetic Nanda addressed his pupils: "Sirs, even the seat upon which Buddhas sit is low; for a hundred thousand recluses..."
“There is no seat; it is fitting for you today to perform a sublime honor for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Fetch flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain. Because the domain of psychic power is inconceivable, he fetched flowers endowed with color and fragrance in a mere moment and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddhas measuring a league in extent.
They prepared the seats. For the two chief disciples, it was three *gāvutas*; for the rest of the monks, it consisted of various sizes such as half a *yojana* and so forth;

for the youngest member of the Saṅgha, it was the measure of a *usabha*. When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Nanda stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined in reverence and said, "Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend this flower-seat."
He said: "The Blessed One sat upon the flower-seat. When the Teacher was thus seated, the monks, perceiving the Teacher's gesture, sat each upon his own assigned seat.
The ascetic Nanda stood holding a large flower-parasol over the head of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher, thinking, 'May this honor shown to the ascetics bear great fruit,' entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)."
He entered [the attainment]. Knowing that the Teacher had entered it, the monks also entered it.

While the Tathāgata remained seated for seven days having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), when the time for alms-round arrived, the resident disciples would partake of forest roots and fruits, and at other times they would stand with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddhas. However, the ascetic Nanda [did not even go on] alms-round.
Without leaving, he spent seven days in a state of joy and happiness while holding the flower-parasol.

The Teacher, having emerged from cessation, commanded a disciple endowed with two qualities—the quality of dwelling in non-conflict (*araṇavihāra*) and the quality of being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*)—saying, "Offer words of appreciation for the flower-seats to the company of seers. He [the disciple], like a wheel-turning monarch...

Having received a great gain from his presence, he—like a great warrior whose mind was filled with joy—remained in his own domain, contemplated the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas, and offered words of thanksgiving.
At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher himself taught the Dhamma.
At the end of that teaching, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained Arahatship. The Teacher...
“Come, monks,” he said, extending his hand. At that very moment, their hair and beards vanished.
The eight requisites appeared already fastened upon their bodies, and they surrounded the Teacher like elders of sixty years’ standing.

But the ascetic Nanda, because his mind was distracted, did not attain any distinction. It is said that for him, [the mind of] the elder Araṇavihārin— [...was not established.]** *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)*

From the moment he began to listen to the Dhamma in the presence [of the Buddha], the thought arose in him: "O, may I too, in the future, receive the same burden that this disciple has received under the teaching of the Buddha who is to arise!
However, because of that reflection, he was unable to realize the path and its fruition. Then, having paid homage to the Tathāgata and standing before him, he said:
“Venerable sir, what is the name of this monk among your dispensation who offered the expression of appreciation for the flower-seats to the company of seers?
“This monk has attained the foremost rank in the factors of dwelling in the forest and in the factors of being worthy of offerings.
“Venerable sir, by virtue of the honor I performed for seven days while holding a flower-parasol, I do not seek anything else...”
"I aspire for prosperity; moreover, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I become a disciple endowed with two qualities just like this elder," he thus made his aspiration.
The Teacher, wondering, "Will this ascetic's aspiration be fulfilled? sent forth his knowledge of the future.
Looking into the future, he saw that it would be fulfilled after the passing of one hundred thousand eons, and said to the ascetic Nanda:

"This aspiration of yours shall not be in vain; after the passing of one hundred thousand eons in the future, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and it will be fulfilled in his presence. Having spoken thus, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.

Surrounded by the community of monks, he leapt into the air. The ascetic Nanda stood with palms joined in reverence toward the Teacher and the community of monks until they had passed beyond the range of his vision. At a later time, he approached the Teacher from time to time and listened to the Dhamma.
Without falling away from his meditative absorption, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world. From there—
Furthermore, after passing away from there, he went forth for another five hundred births and became a forest-dweller.
During the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa as well, he went forth and, being a forest-dweller, fulfilled the practice of "going and returning" (*gatapaccāgatavatta*).
Indeed, it is said that there are none who reach the status of a Great Disciple without fulfilling this practice. Regarding the practice of "going and returning," however, in the *Aṭṭhakathās*...

This should be understood according to the method already stated. Having fulfilled the practice of going forth and returning for twenty thousand years, he passed away and was reborn in the Kāmāvacara deva-world, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. For this is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Nisabha;”
“My hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully laid out.
At that time, I lived alone and without a companion on Mount Nisabha— a matted-hair ascetic named Kosiya, practicing rigorous austerities.”
“At that time, I did not eat fruits, roots, or leaves;
I lived only on what was naturally provided.
Even while renouncing my very life, I did not disturb my livelihood.”
I satisfy my own mind and avoid wrong livelihood.
Whenever a mind associated with lust arises in me,
I examine it myself and, being one-pointed, I subdue it.
“You lust after what is lustful, and you hate what is hateful;
you are deluded by what is delusive. Depart from this forest!
This is the dwelling place of those who are pure, stainless, and ascetic.”
"Do not defile that which is pure; depart from this forest.
Having become a householder, when you have obtained a son, do not fail both of them; depart from this forest."
“Just as a log with a firebrand in it is incapable of performing any function anywhere—neither in the village nor in the forest—for it is not considered a log; so you are like a log with a firebrand:
neither a householder nor one who is self-restrained.”
“Today you are free from both sides; depart from this forest.
‘Could this indeed be for you?
Who knows this of you—that you bear the yoke of faith for me, who am so full of indolence?’”
“The wise will loathe you, just as a city-dweller loathes filth;
having dragged you forth, the seers will constantly reproach you.
The wise will speak ill of you, saying that you have transgressed the teaching.”
"If you do not find companionship, how will you live?
"A powerful elephant, approaching a sixty-year-old Mātaṅga elephant that has split apart in three ways,
draws that tusker out from the herd."
“Having strayed from the herd, he finds neither ease nor comfort;
distressed and dejected, he broods and trembles.
In the same way, those with matted hair will likewise drive that fool away.”
Being separated from them, you will find no happiness or well-being.
Whether by day or by night, pierced by the arrow of sorrow,
you will burn with feverish anguish like an elephant who has strayed from the herd.
“Just as a counterfeit piece of gold does not shine anywhere,
so you, being devoid of virtue, will not shine anywhere.
Even while living in a house, how will you live?”
“Neither paternal wealth nor maternal wealth—no inherited fortune do you have.
By performing work yourself and shedding sweat from your limbs, in this way you shall live at home;
it would be good for you, yet that does not please you.”
“In that way I restrained there the mind that had fallen into defilement;
by giving various discourses on the Dhamma, I turned the mind away from evil.
As I dwelt thus, abiding in heedfulness,”
Thirty thousand years passed for me in the forest.
Seeing me delighting in heedfulness and seeking the supreme goal,
the Sambuddha Padumuttara came into my presence.
“Shining with the hue of a timbarūsaka flower, immeasurable and incomparable,
the Buddha, peerless in form, was then walking in the sky.
Like a king of sāl trees in full bloom, like lightning amidst thick clouds.”
The Buddha, peerless in wisdom, then walked back and forth in the sky.
Like a fearless lion king, like a proud elephant king,
and like a joyful tiger king, he then walked back and forth in the sky.
“Resplendent with the color of a lion’s mane, resembling embers of acacia wood;
like a wish-fulfilling jewel, he then walked back and forth in the sky.
Resembling a pure white lotus, like the full moon on the fifteenth day.”
At that time, like the sun at midday, he was walking back and forth in the sky.
Seeing him walking in the heavens, I then thought:
"Is this being a god, or is it perhaps a human?"
“Neither have I heard of nor seen such a man upon this earth;
yet there exists even a single verse of a mantra that says, ‘This one shall be the Teacher.
Having reflected thus, I gladdened my own heart.”
I then gathered together various flowers and fragrances.
Having prepared a beautiful and delightful seat of flowers for that one of excellent mind,
the foremost among those who are charioteers of men, I spoke these words:
“O Hero, this seat is prepared for you, worthy of you;
gladdening my heart, please sit upon this flower-strewn seat.
Thereupon the Blessed One sat down, fearless like a lion.
For seven days and nights, the Buddha remained upon that excellent seat of flowers.
For seven days and nights, I stood there paying homage.
Then, having arisen from that meditative absorption, the Teacher, the unsurpassed one in the world, [spoke].
Proclaiming his own deed, he spoke these words:
“Cultivate the recollection of the Buddha, the unsurpassed among all meditations;
having cultivated this mindfulness, you will fulfill your heart’s desire.”
“For thirty thousand eons you will delight in the world of the gods;
eighty times you will exercise divine sovereignty as lord of the gods;
and a thousand times you will be a wheel-turning monarch, a king over a realm.”
“You will experience all that— a vast regional sovereignty, beyond counting—
which is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.
Wandering through successive births, you will obtain great wealth.”
There is no deficiency in your enjoyments; this is the fruit of recollecting the Buddha.
"In a hundred thousand eons, one born of the Okkāka clan, named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world."
“Having abandoned eighty crores [of wealth], along with many slaves and laborers,
you shall go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Gotama.
Having gratified the Perfectly Awakened One, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas,”
“By the name Subhūti, you shall become a disciple of the Teacher.
Seated within the community of monks, you will establish yourself as foremost in two respects:
in the quality of being worthy of offerings and in dwelling in the forest.”
Having spoken this, the Fully Awakened One, whose name is the Supreme among those born from the water,
the Hero, ascended into the sky like a king of swans in the air.
Instructed by the Lord of the World, and having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he departed.
Always, with joy, I cultivated the supreme recollection of the Buddha.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned my human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“Eighty times I exercised the sovereignty of the gods as Lord of Devas;
a thousand times I was a universal monarch, a wheel-turning king.
My regional kingdoms were vast and beyond counting.”
I experience this excellent attainment, the fruit of recollecting the Buddha.
“As I transmigrate through various states of existence, I obtain great wealth;
there is no deficiency in my riches—this is the fruit of recollecting the Buddha.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons past, whatever deed I performed then, I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit of recollecting the Buddha.
The four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations—”
"The six higher knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the Venerable Elder Subhūti speak these verses.
In this way, having experienced celestial splendor by being reborn again and again in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he—
Passing away from there, he was born in the world of humans and, having become a universal monarch and a regional king on many hundreds of occasions, experienced sublime human prosperity.
Then, in the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika in the house of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi; his name was Subhūti.
At that time, our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually went to Rājagaha.
There, performing a service for the world by accepting the Veḷuvana Grove and other acts, he dwelt in dependence on Rājagaha in the Sītavana.
Then, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, taking merchandise for trade, departed from Sāvatthī.
Having gone to the house of his friend, the merchant of Rājagaha, and having heard of the appearance of a Buddha,
he approached the Teacher while He was dwelling in the Sītavana forest; at that very first sight, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*),
requested the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī, and then, along the forty-five *yojanas* of the road, gave a gift of one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at every *yojana*.
Having established a monastery, he purchased Prince Jeta’s park—measuring eight *karīsas* by royal measure—in Sāvatthī for a price of ten million pieces of gold.
Having built a monastery there for the Blessed One, he presented it to him.
On the day the monastery was formally dedicated, this householder Subhūti went together with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and, while listening to the Dhamma, developed faith.

Having received it, he went forth. After his full ordination, he made the two *mātikās* proficient, requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and while practicing the duty of a recluse in the forest, he developed insight based on the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and attained Arahantship.
When he taught the Dhamma, he did so by making it non-specific (*anodissaka*), following the method established by the Teacher.

Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who dwell in a state free from conflict (*araṇavihārī*). While wandering for alms, he would enter the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettājhāna*) in every house;
having emerged, he would receive the alms-food, thinking, "In this way, it will be of great fruit for the donors.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). Thus the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus..."
“Subhūti, they are those who dwell in the forest; Subhūti, they are those who are worthy of offerings.
Thus, having established himself in Arahatship and reached the pinnacle of the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled, this Great Elder became renowned and distinguished throughout the world.
Wandering through the countryside for the welfare of many people, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
When King Bimbisāra heard that the Elder had arrived, he approached him, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, please stay right here.
Having said, “I shall prepare a dwelling place for you,” he departed and forgot about it. Since the Elder could not find a lodging, he spent his time in the open air.
By the power of the Elder, the rain did not fall. The people, distressed by the lack of rain, [reported this] to the king.
They raised a cry at the door of the residence. The king, wondering, "For what reason indeed does the rain not fall?
and thinking, "I suppose it is because of the Elder’s dwelling in the open air," had a leaf-hut built for him.
Having said, "Venerable sir, dwell in this leaf-hut," he paid homage and departed. The Elder entered the hut.
He sat cross-legged upon a grass mat. At that time, however, the rain fell only in light drizzles and did not pour down in a steady stream.
Then the Elder, wishing to dispel the world’s fear of drought and demonstrating the absence of any danger—both internal and external—to himself, declared:
“My little hut is thatched, comfortable, and sheltered from the wind; rain, O god, as you please!
My mind is well-concentrated and liberated; I dwell ardent, O god—rain as you please!
Thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, the word *channa* (covered) first appears in the sense of "suitability," as in: "That girl is suitable for this boy" and "It is not unsuitable, it is not improper.
It appears in the sense of a specific number distinguished by its verbal form, as in: "There are, Phagguna, six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*).
It appears in the sense of "covering" or "concealing," as in: "The rain pours through what is covered; it does not pour through what is open. [And] "What shall I say to you..."

In such passages as "Even though covered, I shall do [it]," it refers to the lower and upper robes (*nivāsana-pārupana*). In such passages as "The Venerable Channa is practicing improper conduct," it refers to the formal rule (*paññatti*).
In such passages as "Completely covered, completely enclosed; the hut is covered, the fire is placed within," it refers to covering with grass and the like.
Here too, it should be understood as covering with grass and the like; therefore, [it means] by means of grass or leaves...
"Or covered" means that just as when it is covered rain does not fall, there is no falling of rainwater, and it does not pour down; thus the meaning is "properly covered.
The word *me* occurs in the sense of the agent (*karaṇe*) in such passages as "It was attained with difficulty by me; now it is fitting to proclaim it," where the meaning is "by me.
In such passages as "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to me in brief," it occurs in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāne*), meaning "to me."

The meaning [of *me*] is as follows: in such passages as, “Bhikkhus, even before my full enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened,” it occurs in the sense of a possessor (*sāmī*).
Here too, it should be understood in the sense of a possessor; the meaning is “mine.

Although for those whose taints are exhausted there is nothing whatsoever that can be called “mine” because they are unsullied by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), it is nevertheless used according to worldly convention.
Yet even for them, there is the mere conventional expression, "I" and "mine. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"How may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma, and not heirs to material things?
Furthermore, the term *kuṭikā* refers to the mother's womb, the body composed of the four elements, and also to a dwelling sheltered by grass and so forth. For it is said thus:
"In 'You call the mother a hut, the wife a nest,
the children the lineage, and craving my bond'—
in such passages as these, the mother's womb is called a 'hut.'"
“In this skeleton hut, bound together with flesh and sinews;
fie on this foul-smelling corpse, a mass of filth, which you regard as ‘mine’!”—in such passages, the "body born of karma" refers to the collection of hair and so forth.
[And: “The hut of the Blessed One Kassapa’s sister is leaking.”
In such passages as “A hut (kuṭi) means one that is plastered inside or plastered outside,” it refers to a grass-thatched dwelling.
