Here too, that same meaning should be understood, because a leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā) is intended. For a hut (kuṭi) itself is a small hut (kuṭikā); thus, a less well-known type of hut is called a “kuṭikā.
Furthermore, the word *sukha* (pleasure/happiness) occurs in such passages as: “Having turned away from pleasure and pain, and previously from joy and grief... and so forth.

It occurs [in the sense of] "feeling" in the phrase, "He has come to pleasant feeling. It occurs in the sense of the "root of pleasure" in such passages as, "The arising of Buddhas is pleasant; the teaching of the True Dhamma is pleasant.
It occurs in the sense of the "cause of pleasure" in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, this is a designation for merit, namely 'pleasures'.
It occurs in the sense of the "object of pleasure" in such passages as, "For form, Mahāli, is pleasant, followed by pleasure, and immersed in pleasure."
In such passages as, “These, Cunda, are dwellings in happiness in this very life in the discipline of the Noble One,” it refers to non-affliction (*abyāpajja*).

In such passages as, “Nirvana is the supreme happiness,” it refers to Nirvana. In such passages as, “To such an extent, monks, is it not easy to reach by mere description how happy are the heavenly realms,” it refers to the state that is a condition for happiness.
In such passages as, “[Karma] leading to heaven, having a happy result, conducive to heaven,” it refers to... [the heavenly realm].
“Desirable and pleasing” means what is agreeable. Here too, it should be understood as a desirable condition for happiness.
For that hut, having been made agreeable both inside and out, is called “pleasant” because of the comfort of dwelling there;
likewise, because of its possession of a favorable climate—being neither too cold nor too hot—it serves as a condition for physical and mental happiness.
“Windless” (*nivātā*) means without the danger of wind, because the windows are closed with fitted shutters;
this is a description of the pleasant nature of that little hut. For in a lodging with wind, one does not obtain a favorable climate, but in a windless place, one does.
“Rain” (*vassa*) means: rain down, pour forth the stream well. “O God” (*deva*): this word *deva*—these... [text fragment]

In passages such as, “Your Majesty, those eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī—here, Your Majesty, conceive a desire for life,” it refers to conventional deities who are kṣatriyas.
In passages such as, “The gods of the Four Great Kings are beautiful and abound in happiness,” it refers to deities by birth.
In passages such as, “The teaching of that God beyond gods, the All-Seeing One,” it refers to... [the Buddha].
Regarding "among the pure deities" (*visuddhidevesu*): when the Blessed One’s status as the supreme deity among the pure deities is stated, his status among others is already implied.

In such phrases as "when the cloudless, cloud-free sky [is clear]," it refers to the atmosphere (*ākāsa*). In such phrases as "and the deity does not, from time to time, send down rain properly," it refers to a cloud or the rain-god Pajjunna.
Here too, it should be understood as referring to a cloud or Pajjunna. "Rain" (*vassa*)...
Indeed, the Elder addresses him thus while giving his command. "Yathāsukham" means according to one's pleasure.
He speaks thus out of favoring the state of being sustained by rain, saying: "Since there is no external danger for me because of your raining, rain as you wish.
Now, demonstrating the absence of internal dangers, he says "cittam," etc. Therein, "cittam me susamāhitam" means: My mind is well-composed.
My mind has been established upon the object with perfect, extreme, and complete one-pointedness.
And this is not merely by way of suppressing the hindrances and so forth;
rather, it is liberated—specifically liberated from all fetters included within the lower and higher categories, and from all defiled phenomena by means of their utter eradication.
The meaning is: "Having abandoned those by way of both subsiding and abandoning, he remains. "Ardent" means possessing energy.

Having become one who has initiated energy for the sake of attaining the fruition-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*) and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*), I dwell;

I maintain my personal existence through divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*) and so forth, but not for the sake of abandoning the defilements (*kilesa*), since that which is to be abandoned [has already been abandoned].

The intention is "due to the absence [of danger]. Furthermore, showing that "just as you, O King, were urged by me to rain because of the absence of external dangers, so too [you may rain] because of the absence of internal dangers," he said again, "Rain, O King.
Another method: *channā* means covered, concealed, or shut off. *Kuṭikā* refers to the personal body (*attabhāva*). For that [body] is a collection of many constituent parts...
In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, for a person hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has come to be, as well as name-and-form externally," it appears as "body" (kāya).
In such passages as, "Empty this boat, bhikkhu; when emptied, it will go lightly for you," it appears as "boat" (nāvā).
And in the passage, "O builder of the house, you are seen; the peak of the house is dismantled."

In such instances as these, it is derived from *āgata* (“come”). In such instances as “A being, covered by many [defilements], stands in a cave, a man plunged into delusion,” it is derived from *guhā* (“cave”).
In such instances as “The chariot has flawless wheels, a white canopy, and it rolls with a single axle,” it is derived from *ratha* (“chariot”).
In such instances as “You shall not build a house again,” it is derived from *geha* (“house”). In such instances as “The hut is open; the fire is extinguished,” it is derived from *kuṭī* (“hut”).

Therefore, here too it is called a "hut" (*kuṭikā*). For this personal existence (*attabhāva*), which is obtained in dependence upon the earth element and so forth—designated as bones and the like—and upon contact and the like, is called a "hut" because it is obtained in dependence upon them, just as a hut named after its house is obtained in dependence upon timber and the like;
and also because it is the dwelling place of the monkey of the mind. As it has been said:
“With a skeleton for its thatched roof, it is called ‘the monkey’s dwelling’;
the monkey, having entered the hut with five doors,
wanders about from door to door, knocking again and again.”

Furthermore, this hut of the personal existence (attabhāva-kuṭikā) of the Elder is called "covered" because it has been properly closed by means of wisdom, having restrained the leakage of lust and other defilements that would otherwise break through the three, six, and eight doors of non-restraint.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "I call it the restraint of the streams; by wisdom these are covered. According to the method thus stated...
They are "happy" because they have attained happiness through the very absence of the suffering of defilements and by being endowed with spiritual (nirāmisa) bliss;
for that very reason, they are "sheltered," meaning they live in seclusion due to having struck down pride, intoxication, rigidity, and agitation.
And this method is not accomplished merely by the restraint of my own defiled states, but rather by the supreme concentration of the highest path (*aggamagga-samādhi*). Thus...
Showing that his mind was liberated from all fetters both through the state of concentrated mind and through the wisdom of the supreme path, he said: "My mind is well-concentrated and liberated.
Having become such, he did not remain idle, thinking, "Now I have done what was to be done," but rather he dwelt with ardor in promoting the welfare and happiness of the world including its devas.
Filled with such enthusiasm, even during my alms-round, I dwell from house to house solely in the sublime abodes (brahmavihāra).
Therefore, O King Pajjuna, whether out of a desire to do what is pleasing to me or out of compassion for the beings who depend on rain for their livelihood, please grant us a proper downpour of rain;
this is how the meaning here should be understood.

And here, by the words “My little hut is thatched, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind,” the Elder shows his training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), which is divided into mundane and supramundane.
By “My mind is well-concentrated,” he shows the training in higher consciousness (*adhicitta-sikkhā*). By “It is liberated,” he shows the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*).
By “I dwell ardent,” he shows the dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*). Alternatively, [the same may be understood as follows:]...

By the words, “My hut is covered, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind,” he shows the dwelling in the signless (animitta-vihāra), because it illustrates the removal of signs such as permanence by way of closing the door against the rain of defilements.
By the words, “My mind is well-concentrated,” he shows the dwelling in the desireless (appaṇihita-vihāra).
By the word, “Liberated,” he shows the dwelling in the empty (suññata-vihāra). By the words, “I dwell ardent,” he [shows] those three dwellings...
The means for realization. Alternatively, by the first [verse] the abandoning of hatred is shown; by the second, the abandoning of lust; and by the third, the abandoning of delusion.
Likewise, by the second [verse], or by the first and second together, he shows the success in dwelling in the Dhamma; by the third, the success in liberation.
By the phrase "I dwell ardent," it should be understood that he shows his state of being untiring in the practice for the welfare of others.

Thus, because the dwellings in the Dhamma and so forth mentioned in the verse beginning with "according to their names" have been shown by this verse, the phrase beginning with "It is said thus" was spoken in order to show the names and clans that were not shown there. For those elders who are well-known by name alone are mentioned by name;
those who are well-known by clan alone are mentioned by clan; and those who are well-known by both are mentioned by both.
"...he will see. Now, this elder was distinguished by his name rather than by his clan; therefore, it is said, "Thus indeed the Venerable Subhūti.
In that context, *itthaṃ* means "this manner," with the sense of "in this way.
*Sudaṃ* is *su* + *idaṃ*, with the elision of the vowel *i* due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*). Furthermore, *sū* is merely a particle. The construction is: "This is the verse. *Āyasmā* means...
This is a term of endearment; it is a term expressing deep respect and reverence. "Subhūti" is the proclamation of his name.

For he was beautiful and pleasing to behold both by virtue of his physical perfection and his perfection of qualities. Thus, because he was endowed with the splendor of beautiful bodily limbs and the splendor of the perfection of virtue and other such qualities, he was known as "Subhūti.
Because of his possession of firm qualities such as the essence of virtue, the Elder was so designated. He spoke.

He spoke. But why did these great elders manifest their own virtues? It was because, having reflected upon the supramundane Dhamma—which they themselves had attained, which had never before been attained by them in this long course of time, and which is supremely profound, exceedingly peaceful, and sublime—they were moved by a surge of joy and inspired by a sense of noble exultation;
and furthermore, it was for the purpose of demonstrating the world-transcending nature of the Dispensation, even though they were themselves possessed of supreme fewness-of-wishes.
Noble ones proclaim their own virtues, just as the Lord of the World proclaims his own virtues— saying, for instance, "Monks,
the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers and is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence"— according to the inclinations of those to be enlightened; in this same way,
this verse constitutes the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Subhūti in the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the sub-commentary on the *Theragāthā*, is completed. 2.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika.
"Upasanta" is the verse of the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika Thera. What was his origin?
This elder, too, having been born into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, reached maturity;
after his parents passed away, he established a household and lived the life of a householder. One day, [he heard] of the Blessed One Padumuttara...
At the time of the preaching of the Dhamma, seeing the inhabitants of Haṃsavatī city approaching with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings— moving toward the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, inclining, leaning, and tending in their direction— the Teacher, having arrived together with the great multitude,
saw him being placed by the Master in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and [thought]: "It is said that this..."
Thinking, "In this dispensation, he is the foremost of those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);

oh, would that I too might become the foremost of those who have attained the analytical knowledges in the dispensation of a single Buddha," he approached the Blessed One after the assembly had risen at the conclusion of the Teacher's teaching and invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow."
The Teacher consented. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he went to his own residence.
Throughout the entire night, he adorned the sitting and standing areas for the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with fragrant garlands, flower wreaths, and other ornaments;
he had exquisite hard and soft foods prepared, and at the end of that night, in his own residence—

Having fed the Blessed One— who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus— with various kinds of rice gruel and solid foods, along with meals of various flavors, soups, condiments, and fragrant jasmine rice,
he thought at the conclusion of the meal: “I aspire to a great position,
yet it is not fitting for me to attain that position by giving an offering on only a single day.”
“I shall make my aspiration after giving alms in successive order for seven days. Following that very method, he gave great alms for seven days;

at the conclusion of his meal duties, he had the storehouse of cloth opened, placed the finest fine cloth sufficient for a triple robe at the feet of the Buddha, and [did the same] for the hundred thousand monks.
Having given the three robes to the Tathāgata and approached him, he said, "Venerable Sir, may I too, like that bhikkhu whom you have placed among the foremost from this seventh day hence,
go forth in the dispensation of a Buddha who will arise in the future and become the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)," and having spoken thus,
he prostrated at the feet of the Teacher and made his aspiration.

He made this aspiration. Seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, the Teacher prophesied: "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world; within his dispensation, your aspiration shall be fulfilled.
This is also stated in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the Sage who knows all the world,
appeared as one possessed of vision one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
He was the instructor, the enlightener, and the deliverer of all living beings.”
The Buddha, skilled in teaching, delivered many people across [the flood].
Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all breathing things,
he established all the heretics who arrived there in the five precepts.
“Thus it was free from turmoil and empty of non-Buddhist sectarians,
yet variegated with Arahants who had attained mastery and were ‘such-like’ (tādī).
That Great Sage rose up fifty ratanas high.”
Resembling a priceless golden image and endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks,
his lifespan lasted for a hundred thousand years;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people across [to liberation].
“Then, in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas;
having approached the Supreme One in all the world, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma.
At that time, the Hero addressed a disciple whose range of intelligence was fully developed.”
“He who was skilled in the meanings, the Dhamma, the terminology, and inspired speech—
having heard that the Best of Victors, together with his disciples, had placed him at the foremost rank, I was filled with joy; I then provided food for seven days.”
“Having covered the ocean of wisdom along with his disciples with my wings, I prostrated at the soles of his feet and aspired for that very state.
Then the Foremost One in the World said: ‘Behold this supreme among birds!’”
“Bowing at my feet, which possess the luster of the interior of a lotus, she said:
‘This woman aspires to the state of a monk, the most excellent of Buddhas;
by virtue of her faith, generosity, and hearing of the True Dhamma.’”
“Having been happy in every state, wandering through various existences,
you shall obtain this heart’s desire in a future time.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, born into the Okkāka clan...”
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma,
will be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Koṭṭhika."
“Having heard that, being joyful, I then served the Jina for as long as life lasted,
with a mind of loving-kindness, mindful, wise, and concentrated.
By the ripening of that karma, and by my volitions and aspirations...”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
For three hundred times I exercised sovereignty over the gods,
and for five hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
“A vast regional sovereignty, beyond counting, I enjoyed;
everywhere I was happy by the power of that deed.
For two existences I transmigrated: among the gods and then among humans.”
"I go not to another destination; this is the fruit of well-performed deeds.
I am reborn into two kinds of families: among kṣatriyas or among brahmins.
I am not born into a low family; this is the fruit of well-performed deeds."
“When my final existence was reached, I became a kinsman of Brahmā;
I was reborn in Sāvatthī into a wealthy brahmin family.
My mother’s name was Candavatī, and my father was Assalāyana.”
When the Buddha disciplined my father through complete purification, I,
full of faith in the Sugata, went forth into the homeless life;
Moggallāna was my teacher, and Sārisambhava was my preceptor.
"While my head was being cut away, my view was severed along with its root.
While wearing the saffron robe, I attained arahantship.
My mind is now intent upon the meaning, the Dhamma, the etymologies, and inspired eloquence."
Because of that, the Chief of the World, having distinguished me, placed me in this foremost position:
"When questioned by Upatissa, I explained what was not yet seen;
therefore, among those possessing the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), I am foremost in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a nāga who has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
It was indeed a blessing for me to come into the presence of the Buddha.”
The three true insights have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“The four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations have been realized;
the six direct knowledges have been verified; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Thus, accumulating the equipment of merit and knowledge in various states of existence and wandering from one life to another among gods and humans, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī into a family of great brahmin landowners.
They gave him the name Koṭṭhika. When he reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas and attained perfection in the brahminical arts, one day—
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he acquired faith;
having gone forth and from the time of his full ordination onward, applying himself to the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having gained mastery over the analytical knowledges, even when he approached various well-known great elders to ask questions, he [beheld] the One of Ten Powers.
Even when approaching to ask a question, he asked questions concerning only the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Thus, because of his prior application there and his mastery over them, this elder became the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges.
Then the Teacher, taking the *Mahāvedalla-sutta* as the occasion, established him in the position of being the foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges.
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), namely Mahākoṭṭhika.
At a later time, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*):
“Peaceful, restrained, measured in speech, and unflustered;”
"He shakes off evil states, just as the wind shakes off the leaves from a tree.
Thus indeed did the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika Thera speak this verse.
Therein, "calmed" means by the calming of the six faculties, including the mind, through making them free from worldly involvement.
"Peaceful. "Restraint" means withdrawn and abstained from all evil-doing. "Measured in speech": *manta* is said to mean wisdom (*paññā*);
one who speaks after having investigated with that [wisdom] is "measured in speech"—the meaning is that he speaks without relinquishing such qualities as speaking at the proper time.
Alternatively, he is "measured in speech" because he speaks by way of measured speech; [this refers to his] freedom from ill-spoken words.
The meaning is that, by way of speaking, he speaks only what is well-spoken, being endowed with the four factors.
He is "unagitated" (anuddhata) because he does not exalt himself through birth and so forth;

or alternatively, he is "calm" (upasanta) by the subsiding of the three types of bodily misconduct through abstention from them, and "restrained" (uparata) by the cessation and abandoning of the three types of mental misconduct.
He is measured in speech because of the non-occurrence of the four types of verbal misconduct and his habit of speaking with deliberation.

He is undisturbed because of the absence of restlessness, which arises from the threefold misconduct. Thus, established in pure virtue through the abandonment of the threefold misconduct, composed through the abandonment of restlessness, and having made that very concentration the foundation, he increases insight.
By means of the sequence of the paths, one shakes off evil states;
in the sense of being loathsome, one shakes off all evil defilements and abandons them by way of their total eradication. How so?
Like the wind shaking a tree leaf: just as the wind, the Māluta, shakes a leaf from a tree—a withered, pale leaf—shaking it loose from its attachment and carrying it away.
Thus, one established in the practice as described removes evil qualities from one's own continuum;
in this way, it should be understood that this verse is also the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*), expressed by means of the term "final knowledge" (*aññā*) itself.
And here, by the mention of abandoning misconduct of body and speech, he shows purity of application (*payoga-suddhi*); by the mention of abandoning mental misconduct, [he shows purity of intention].

Purity of disposition (*āsaya-suddhi*). Thus, for one whose application and disposition are pure, by this statement of the absence of restlessness—“unrestless” (*anuddhata*)—he shows the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) through their association with that [restlessness]. Among these, by purity of application, the perfection of virtue (*sīla-sampatti*) is elucidated;

by purity of disposition, the grasping of those factors conducive to the development of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*); and by the abandonment of the hindrances, the development of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*).
By the phrase “he shakes off evil states,” the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*) is elucidated.

Thus, the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*), the Dispensation which is good in three ways, the three abandonments beginning with abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*),
the practice of the Middle Way through the avoidance of the two extremes, and the means for transcending the states of deprivation, existence, and so forth, are all explained.
Having determined [the meaning] as appropriate, it should be applied. By this method, the application of the meaning in the remaining verses should also be understood as appropriate.
However, we shall explain only the specific points not previously mentioned here and there.
"Thus indeed the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika" is a term of honor, just as it is in the case of Mahāmoggallāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata:
"Behold this wisdom," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Kaṅkhārevata. What is his origin? This elder [also] [arose] from the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara...
In due time, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great brahmin nobles.
One day, at the time of the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dhamma, he went to the monastery together with the great multitude in the manner described above.

Standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost place among those who delight in jhāna. [Seeing this, he thought: “By me too...”

Thinking, "In the future, it is fitting that I become like this," at the conclusion of the teaching, he invited the Teacher, performed great honors according to the manner described above, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, by means of this meritorious deed, I do not aspire for any other prosperity;
rather, just as that bhikkhu was [treated] by you seven days from now..."
Having been established in the foremost place among meditators, he made this aspiration: "In the future, may I also become the foremost among meditators in the dispensation of a certain Buddha.
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that it would indeed come to pass, said:
"At the end of one hundred thousand future aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; in his dispensation, you..."
Having prophesied, "You shall become the foremost among those who practice meditation," he departed.

Having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, and having wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, he was reborn during the time of our Blessed One in a family of great wealth in the city of Sāvatthī; and after his meal, for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma—
Accompanied by a great multitude of people, he went to the monastery and stood at the edge of the assembly.
Having heard the Dhamma discourse of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, faith was born in him; he went forth, received full ordination, and requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

While performing the preliminary work for jhāna, he became an attainer of jhāna. Taking jhāna as his foundation, he reached Arahantship. For the most part, [he served] the One Possessed of Ten Powers...
While entering the meditative attainments that were to be entered, he became one who had mastered mastery over the jhānas day and night.
Then the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among meditators, saying: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are meditators, namely Kaṅkhārevata.
And this is also said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye of all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
With a jaw like a lion’s, a voice like Brahmā, and a sound like a swan or a drum.”
Moving with the stride of a nāga, with a radiance exceeding that of the moon and sun:
“O one of great wisdom, great hero, great meditator, and of great power;
the protector of great compassion, who dispels the great darkness.”

“Then once, the Fully Enlightened One, the Sage who knows the hundreds of mental dispositions of beings, the Foremost in the Three Worlds, taught the Dhamma for the sake of training many who were ready to be disciplined.
[He taught it] to the Hero, who delights in meditation, who is absorbed in jhāna, peaceful, and undisturbed.”
Praising the assembly, the Victor gladdened the people:
“At that time, in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin who had mastered the Vedas.
Having heard the Dhamma, I was delighted and aspired for that state.”
Then the Conqueror, the Guide, in the midst of the Saṅgha, declared:
"Be joyful, O Brahmā! You shall obtain that heart’s desire.
In a hundred thousand aeons from now, you will be born in the family of Okkāka."
"One named Gotama by clan will become a Teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma,
shall be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Revata."
“By that well-performed kamma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
And now, in this final existence, I was born in the city of the Koliyans.”
Born into a noble Kṣatriya family, prosperous, flourishing, and possessing great wealth,
when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in Kapilavatthu,
I, having placed my faith in the Sugata, went forth into the homeless life.
“I had many doubts here and there concerning what is and is not the True Dharma;
the Buddha dispelled them all by teaching the supreme Dharma.
Thereupon, having crossed over the cycle of existence, I then delighted in the bliss of meditative absorption.”
Then, while dwelling as a Buddha, I saw him and said this:
“Whatever doubts there may be here or in the world beyond, whether experienced by oneself or experienced through another—
all those, the meditators abandon them all, being ardent as they lead the holy life.”
“Karma performed a hundred thousand eons ago has shown its fruit here to me;
like an arrow released from a bow, I have been completely liberated and have consumed my defilements.
Then, seeing me devoted to meditation, the Buddha, the Sage who has reached the end of the world,”
The Greatly Wise One, the foremost among meditating monks, declared:
“The defilements have been incinerated by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a nāga who has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.”
“Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of the Buddha;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.
The four analytical insights and these eight liberations—”
"The sixfold direct knowledge has been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having thus fulfilled his task, the Great Elder reflected upon how his mind had long been clouded by doubt in the past and how it was now entirely free from doubt, and he thought: "Oh, how great indeed is the power of my Teacher’s teaching!"

Thinking, "Now he has become one who is thus free from doubt and whose mind is inwardly calmed," and having conceived great reverence while praising the Blessed One’s wisdom, he spoke this verse: "Behold this wisdom.

(3) In this context, *paññā* means that which knows in various ways (*pakāre jānāti*) and that which makes known by way of various modes (*pakārehi ñāpeti*). It refers to the various modes [of the disciples], such as their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), conduct (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*).

The meaning is that he knows the categories of phenomena—such as the wholesome and so forth, and the aggregates and so forth—in the manner they are to be taught; he penetrates them according to their true nature, and makes them known through those very modes.
For it is the Teacher’s knowledge of teaching that is intended here; thus he said, "this.

Having grasped that [knowledge], which stands before him as if directly perceived by virtue of the power of teaching established within himself, through his mastery of the guiding principles (nayaggāha),...

"‘These’ was what was said. Or rather, at the very moment the Teacher’s knowledge of the teaching is grasped by the disciples through its method (*naya*), at that same moment their own penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) regarding their own domain is likewise grasped through that method. Therefore, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said:
‘Furthermore, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me. "Behold!"—having attained a state of wonder, he addresses [the Buddha] without specifying [who he is]. It refers to himself alone.
Or [it refers to] the mind, as the Blessed One declared while uttering an *udāna*: “Behold this world, overcome by manifold ignorance, delighting in what has become, not yet freed from becoming.
“Of the Tathāgatas”: they are called *tathāgatas* in the sense of having come (*āgama*) and so forth in such a way (*tathā*).
For he is a *tathāgata* because he has come in such a way; he is a *tathāgata* because he has gone in such a way; he is a *tathāgata* because he has come to the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*).
He is the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of phenomena as they really are;

he is the Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they are; he is the Tathāgata because of his speaking things as they are; he is the Tathāgata because of his acting in accordance with what he has seen; and he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming. Thus, for these eight reasons, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata because he has come from suchness (tathatā); he is the Tathāgata because he has gone to suchness; [he is the Tathāgata] because of the characteristic of suchness.
He is a *Tathāgata* because he has gone (*gata*) [to that state]; he is a *Tathāgata* because he has come (*āgata*) in such a way; he is a *Tathāgata* because he is of such a kind (*tathāvidha*);

he is a *Tathāgata* because he has proceeded (*pavattita*) in such a way; he is a *Tathāgata* because he has come from those who are thus (*tathehi āgata*); and he is a *Tathāgata* by virtue of having gone in such a way (*tathā gatabhāvena*).
This, in brief, is how the Blessed One is a *Tathāgata* through these eight reasons. For the detailed explanation, however, one should consult the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
This should be understood according to the method explained in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā and the Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā.
Now, in order to show the unique distinction of that wisdom, the passage beginning with “Just as a fire” was spoken. “Just as a fire” is the word of the simile (*upamā*).
“Just as” (*yathā*) shows its status as a simile. “Blazing” (*pajjalito*) shows the connection with the thing being illustrated (*upameyya*).
“Nisītha” indicates the time for performing the task. This is the meaning here:

just as when the fourfold darkness of night has set in, a blazing fire standing on a high place remains in that spot dispelling the gloom, even so this knowledge of the teaching belonging to the Tathāgatas is in every respect—
One sees wisdom dispelling the deepest doubts of those who are ready to be trained (*veneyya*).

Because it gives the light consisting of knowledge to beings through the elegance of its teaching, it is called "the giver of light" (*ālokadā*). Because it gives the eye consisting of wisdom itself, it is called "the giver of the eye" (*cakkhudadā*).
Showing that both of these have as their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) the removal of doubt, he said: "Those who remove the doubt of those who have come [to them]."

Those Tathāgatas, through the power of their teaching, completely dispel, scatter, and destroy the doubt and uncertainty— consisting of sixteen bases that arise in the manner of "Did I exist in the past? and so forth, directed toward those who have come to them and approached them as those to be trained,
as well as that consisting of eight bases which arises in the manner of "He doubts the Buddha, he doubts the Dhamma," and so forth.
Furthermore, doubts consisting of remorse regarding the discipline (*vinaya-kukkucca*) are removed by that very discipline itself.

Another method: Just as a fire blazing at the dead of night, with its intensified flames, dispels darkness and reveals the level and uneven ground merely by providing light to those standing on a high seat, thus being a giver of illumination; so too...
Furthermore, for those standing nearby, it makes that [object] very clear; because it performs the function of the eye, it is called "the giver of sight.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, having dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom for those who stand far off and have not performed meritorious deeds, and having distinguished the irregularities of the body and so forth from what is regular, becomes a "giver of light" for those nearby.
Furthermore, for those who have stood firm and performed their duties, they are "givers of vision" because they cause the Dhamma-eye to arise.

One should behold the wisdom and the preeminent knowledge of those Tathāgatas—who, being such as these, dispel and scatter the doubts even of those like me who have come within the range of their speech and are full of uncertainty—by means of the arising of the Noble Path. Thus, this [is the meaning] for the Elder.

There is also a verse of declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇagāthā*) by means of his own manifestation of the overcoming of doubt. For this elder, while still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), was scrupulous even regarding what is permissible;
due to his abundance of doubt, he was known as "Kaṅkhārevata," and even later, at the time when his taints were destroyed, he was addressed by that same name.
Therefore it is said: "Thus indeed the venerable Kaṅkhārevata spoke this verse. The meaning of that is exactly as stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇa:
"One should associate only with the virtuous," these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. What is their origin? It is said that this [Elder] was formerly... of Padumuttara [Buddha].
Even before the arising of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a prominent brahmin family.

Having gradually attained maturity, on one day when the Teacher had appeared in the world, he went to the monastery with the great multitude at the time of the Buddha’s Dhamma teaching. Sitting at the edge of the assembly, he listened to the Dhamma.
Hearing this and seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who preach the Dhamma,
he thought, "In the future, it is fitting that I too should become like this. At the conclusion of the teaching, when the assembly had risen,
he approached the Teacher, invited him [to his home], and having performed a great honor in the manner described above, he spoke thus to the Blessed One:
— “Venerable sir, by this meritorious deed I do not seek any other prosperity. However,
just as that bhikkhu was established in the foremost position among preachers of the Dhamma seven days from now, may I too, in the future,
become the foremost among the bhikkhus who preach the Dhamma in the dispensation of a certain Buddha,” he thus made his aspiration.
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied:
"In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; having gone forth in his dispensation, you shall become the foremost among those who preach the Dhamma."
Thus, having practiced the wholesome Dhamma there for as long as life lasted, when he passed away from that state,
he wandered through the realms of gods and humans for one hundred thousand eons while accumulating the requisites of merit and knowledge. Then, in the time of our Blessed One,
in a brahmin village named Doṇavatthu not far from the city of Kapilavatthu, he was born into a prominent brahmin family as the elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña.
He was reborn as [the Buddha’s] nephew. On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Puṇṇa.
After the Teacher had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually went to Rājagaha and dwelt there.
Puṇṇa went forth in the presence of the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña, and having received full ordination, he performed all the preliminary duties.
Having applied himself to his exertion and brought the duties of one gone forth to their ultimate fulfillment, he thought, "I shall go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
However, instead of going into the Teacher's presence together with the Elder Mātula, he remained behind right in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu.
There, applying himself to wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), he soon brought his insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak and attained *arahantship*.
He attained it. And this is also said in the Apadāna:
“A reciter of the scriptures, a bearer of the mantras, one who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas—I, surrounded by my disciples, approached the Supreme among Men.”
“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
the Great Sage briefly proclaimed my deed.
Having heard that Dhamma from him and having paid homage to the Teacher, I— ”
Having raised my hands in reverential salutation, I departed facing the south.
Having heard [the teaching] in brief, I expounded it in detail;
all my disciples were delighted upon hearing me speak.
“Having dispelled their own views, they gained confidence in the Buddha’s mind.
I shall teach them both in brief and likewise in detail.
I am one who knows the method of the Abhidhamma for the purification of the points of discourse.”
Having made it known to all, I dwell free from taints.
"Five hundred kappas from now, there were four excellent illuminators;
endowed with the seven treasures, they were lords over the four continents."
“The four analytical knowledges... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Now, five hundred sons of noble family who had gone forth under the Elder Puṇṇa were there.
Because the Elder himself had attained the ten topics of discourse, he instructed them in those same ten topics of discourse. Abiding by his instruction, they all—
They had attained arahantship. Knowing that their own duty as renunciants had reached its culmination, they approached their preceptor and said:
"Venerable sir, our task has reached its peak; we have mastered the ten bases of discourse.
It is now time for us to see the One of Ten Powers. Having heard their words, the Elder thought: "My...
The Teacher knew that those monks had attained the ten bases of discourse. He thought, "When I teach the Dhamma, I do so without ever abandoning the ten bases of discourse;
when I go, all these monks will follow and surround me.
But it is not fitting for me to go in such a crowd and see the One of Ten Powers; let them go first and see him. Thus he addressed those monks.
He said: "Friends, you go on ahead and see the Tathāgata; pay homage at his feet in my name, and I too shall follow along the path you have taken.

All those elders—residents of the kingdom that was the birthplace of the One of Ten Powers, all of whom were free from taints (khīṇāsava) and had attained mastery of the ten topics of discourse—accepted the exhortation of their own preceptor.
Having paid homage to the Elder, they traveled by stages on their journey, covering a road of sixty yojanas.
Upon reaching the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana in Rājagaha, they prostrated at the feet of the One of Ten Powers and sat down to one side.
Now, it is the custom for the Blessed Buddhas to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
The Blessed One, having exchanged pleasant greetings with them in the manner beginning, “Is it tolerable, monks?
asked, “And from where have you come, monks? When they replied, “From the birthplace,” he asked, “Now who, monks, among the monks of the birthplace who are fellow-celibates in the birthplace—”

"Thus, being himself moderate in his wishes, he is one who speaks to the bhikkhus on the subject of moderation in wishes"—with these words, he asked about a bhikkhu who had attained the ten bases of discourse.
They replied, "Venerable sir, it is the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.
Upon hearing this account, the venerable Sāriputta desired to see the elder. Then the Teacher [departed] from Rājagaha...

He went to Sāvatthī. The Elder Puṇṇa, having heard that the One of Ten Powers had arrived there, thought, "I shall see the Teacher," and having gone, he reached the Tathāgata right inside the Fragrant Chamber. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, the Elder went to the Blind Men’s Grove for the sake of seclusion.
He sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
The Elder Sāriputta, having heard of his arrival, went along looking back toward him;
finding a suitable spot, he approached the one sitting at the foot of the tree, exchanged greetings with the elder, and [discussed] that sequence of the seven purifications.
He questioned him. As the Elder answered each of his questions, he won over the king’s mind with the parable of the chariot-horses;
they both rejoiced in one another’s well-spoken words. Later, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Teacher declared of the Elder:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are preachers of the Dhamma."
Namely, Puṇṇa. Thus he placed him in the foremost position among preachers of the Dhamma. One day, reflecting upon his own attainment of liberation, he thought:
“Relying on the Teacher, both I and many other beings have been freed from the suffering of *saṃsāra*;
indeed, association with true persons is of great benefit! Filled with rapture and joy, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), released by the force of his gladness:
He spoke the verse: “One should associate only with the virtuous.
In this context, “only with the virtuous” means with true persons (*sappurisa*). Here, “the peaceful ones” (*santa*) refers to the Noble Ones (*ariya*), beginning with the Buddhas.
For they have abandoned the qualities of the unvirtuous without exception, and because they have reached the pinnacle of the True Dharma, they are preeminently worthy of praise.
And specifically, they are called "peaceful, true persons. "One should dwell together" (samāsetha) means one should dwell equally, that is, live together with them. The meaning is:
by attending upon them, by desiring to hear from them, and by following their example in view, one should come to dwell in common with them.
"By the wise who see with their own hands" is a praise of them. "Wisdom" (paṇḍā) is said to be *paññā* (understanding); it has arisen in these [persons].
They are wise (*paṇḍita*). Precisely because they see the goal (*attha*)—divided into one's own welfare and so forth—without error, they are "seers of the goal" (*atthadassin*).
One should associate with those wise ones who are seers of the goal. Why? Because they are peaceful and wise;

or, because by properly serving them, one finds the goal through the knowledge of the path and so forth, as they are exclusively beneficial and worthy of being sought after due to their great virtues and peaceful nature.
And it is great; it is profound because of its unfathomable nature and because it is the domain of profound knowledge;

it is difficult to see because it cannot be seen by those with inferior aspirations and so forth, and because it is hard for others to perceive; it is subtle because it is difficult to see, because its intrinsic nature is delicate and refined, and because it is the domain of refined knowledge;
and it is atomic because of that very subtlety of its intrinsic nature—this is Nibbāna in the sense of being non-perverted.
Or, it is "meaning" (*attha*) because it is the ultimate intrinsic nature; it is "great" (*mahanta*) because it produces the state of an Arahant and is a sign of greatness;
it is "profound" (*gambhīra*) because its intrinsic nature is not superficial; it is "hard to see" (*duddasa*) because it cannot be seen easily but must be seen with difficulty;

and it is both "profound" and "hard to see" because of its profundity and its being hard to see—thus is the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, the Truth of Cessation is especially subtle and minute. Thus it is.
The wise attain the Four Truths through their perfection of wisdom; having exerted themselves in the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Truths, the wise attain them correctly.
"Diligent" means fulfilling the practice of heedfulness by never being separated from mindfulness in all circumstances.
"Discerning" means being clever and skillful in the cultivation of insight (vipassanā). Therefore, one should associate only with the wise.
The construction [is as follows]. Or, *paṇḍitehatthadassibhi* is an ablative expression (*nissakkavacana*).

Because wise men (*dhīrā*), who are diligent (*appamattā*) and discerning (*vicakkhaṇā*), attain an aim (*attha*) characterized by greatness and other such qualities when they associate with those who have become a collective of wise men who see the goal (*atthadassī*), therefore the connection is:
"One should dwell only with such virtuous ones. Thus, this [verse] serves to illustrate the Elder’s realization.
There was also a verse of the declaration of final knowledge.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇa is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Dabba.
"Yo duddamiyo" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dabba. What is its origin? He too was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha.

Having reached maturity, while listening to the teaching of the Dhamma according to the manner described below, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among those who assign lodgings. [Thereupon,] he performed a work of merit...

Having attained that position and aspired for it, he was prophesied by the Teacher; and having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until the time when the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was declining.
At that time, seven bhikkhus—including himself and six others—became single-minded and, seeing others showing disrespect toward the Teaching, thought: "Here..."
"What shall we do? Having practiced the duty of a recluse in solitude, we shall bring an end to suffering.
Having said this, they fastened a ladder and climbed to the high summit of the mountain. Then, saying, "Those who know the strength of their own minds, let them descend the ladder;
those who still cling to life, let them come down, lest you be filled with regret later," they all became single-minded and [climbed down] the ladder.
Having prostrated themselves and exhorted one another, saying, “Be diligent, friends,” they sat down in places according to their preference and began to practice the duty of a recluse.
There, one elder attained Arahantship on the fifth day and thought, “My task is accomplished; I am in this...”
"What shall I do in this situation? he thought. Then, by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said, "Friend, eat this almsfood;
let the duty of wandering for alms be mine alone, while you perform your own work.
[The others replied,] "Friend, did we say anything like this as we were setting up the ladder: 'Whoever first [attains] the Dhamma..."?
“Let him realize [the goal]; let that monk bring back almsfood, and the rest of us, having consumed what he brings, shall practice the duty of a recluse.
“There is no such person, friend,” they replied. “You have obtained this through your own past causes; we too, being able, shall bring an end to the cycle of existence. You may go then.
Unable to convince them, the Elder [continued] his alms-round in a suitable place.

Having partaken [of the food], he departed. Another elder, having attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) on the seventh day, passed away from there and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma-world.
The other elders, passing away from there, wandered among gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*), and were subsequently reborn in various families.
One was reborn in the royal palace in the city of Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra; another in the kingdom of Majjhimantika...
One was reborn in the womb of a female wanderer; one was reborn in the house of a householder in the kingdom of Bāhiya; and one was born in a nunnery.
This Elder Dabba, however, took conception in the house of a Mallan king in the city of Anupiya in the kingdom of the Mallas.
His mother passed away while he was still in the throes of childbirth. Her corpse was carried to the cemetery and placed upon a wooden pyre.
They set fire to it. The surface of her belly, heated by the force of the flames, split in two.
By the power of his own merit, the boy leaped up and landed upon a wooden pillar. Taking the boy, they gave him to his grandmother.
As she was choosing a name for him, she fell upon that wooden pillar; because he had regained his life after falling there, she gave him the name "Dabba. Of him—
And when he was seven years old, the Teacher, accompanied by the community of monks, while wandering on tour through the kingdom of the Mallas, was staying in the Anupiya Mango Grove.
Prince Dabba, upon seeing the Teacher, felt faith at the very sight;
desiring to go forth, he asked his grandmother, "I shall go forth in the presence of the One of Ten Powers. She replied, "Very well, dear child," [and gave her consent]. Prince Dabba—
Having taken him and gone into the presence of the Teacher, he said, "Venerable Sir, please grant this boy the going-forth.
The Teacher gave a sign to a certain bhikkhu, saying, "Bhikkhu, let this boy go forth.

Hearing the Teacher's word, that elder, while granting the going-forth to Prince Dabba, explained the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*). [The prince], being endowed with past roots of merit...
Having made his resolution, the being established himself in the fruit of stream-entry at the moment of shaving off the first coil of hair;
in the fruit of once-returning while the second coil was being shaved; in the fruit of non-returning with the third;
and the shaving of all the hair and the realization of the fruit of arahantship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after. The Teacher [was staying] in the kingdom of the Mallas.
Having dwelt there as long as he pleased, he went to Rājagaha and took up residence in the Bamboo Grove.
There, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having gone into seclusion and reflected upon the completion of his own duties, desiring to apply himself to performing services for the Saṅgha, thought:
"What if I were now to assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and [distribute] the meals?"
"And you should assign the meal. He went into the presence of the Teacher and reported his own reflection.
The Teacher gave him his approval and accepted his appointment as the assigner of lodgings and the designator of meals.
Then, thinking, "This Dabba, though still young, stands in a great position," he ordained him into full membership at the age of only seven years.
From the time of his full ordination, the Elder Dabba Mallaputta lived in dependence on Rājagaha;
he assigned lodgings for all the monks residing there and distributed their alms-food. His reputation as a distributor of lodgings became famous in all directions:
"It is said that Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings in one place for monks who are of like character and standing."
“He prepares lodgings; he prepares lodgings both nearby and far away; and for those unable to go, he leads them there by means of psychic power.
Then, at all times—whether it was the right time or not—the monks would direct him to prepare lodgings, saying, “Friend, prepare lodgings for us in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove;
for us in the Deer Park at Maddakucchi,” while they watched his psychic power.
They depart. He too, having fashioned mind-made bodies by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), gives one such monk identical to himself to each elder;

then, walking ahead with his finger glowing, he says, "This is the bed, this is the chair," and so forth, prepares the lodgings, and returns once more to his own dwelling place. This is the summary here.
This story, however, has been related in detail in the Pāḷi itself.

Taking this very incident as the occasion for a teaching (aṭṭhuppatti), the Teacher, seated later on in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, established the Elder in the position of being foremost among those who arrange lodgings, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who arrange lodgings, namely Dabba."
“...the son of a merchant. And this is also said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the Sage who knows all the world, the Eyeful One, arose one hundred thousand aeons ago from here.”
“The Buddha is the advisor, the one who makes things known, the savior of all living beings;
skilled in teaching, he has delivered many people.
Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all living beings.”
He established all the heretics who arrived there in the five precepts.
Thus it became free from turmoil and empty of heretics,
yet variegated with Arahants— those self-controlled ones who have attained the state of the Tādi.
“With fifty-eight precious qualities, that Great Sage is exalted;
resembling a priceless golden ornament, he possesses the thirty-two excellent marks.
His lifespan lasts for as long as one hundred thousand years.”
Remaining for that long, he brought many people across.
At that time, in Haṃsavatī, I was the son of a wealthy merchant of great renown;
having approached the Light of the World, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma.
“Hearing the words of him who was praising the Teacher together with his disciples as they were assigning lodgings for the monks, I was filled with joy.
Having performed a service for that Great Sage and for the Saṅgha...”
Bowing my head at his feet, I aspired for that very state.
Then that Great Hero, proclaiming my deed, said:
"He who fed the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha for seven days."
“This one with eyes like lotus petals, a lion-like neck, and golden skin,
has fallen at my feet, aspiring for the supreme state.
In a hundred thousand aeons from now, he will be born in the lineage of the Okkākas.”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
A disciple of that Buddha, renowned by the name Dabba,
will then be the foremost in the assignment of lodgings.”
“By that well-performed kamma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
For three hundred times, I exercised sovereignty over the gods.”
Five times over, I was a wheel-turning monarch.
Through the power of that karma, I enjoyed extensive regional sovereignty, beyond all counting, and was happy in every respect.
“Ninety-one aeons ago, a leader named Vipassī arose,
beautiful to behold and possessing insight into all phenomena.
With a corrupted mind, I reviled a disciple of that Neutral One.”
Knowing him to be pure, with all taints utterly destroyed,
I took a voting ticket and offered milk-rice to that hero among men, the Great Seer, and his disciples.
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great renown, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan, arose as the best among those who speak.
Having illuminated the Teaching and having overcome the false teachers,”
Having disciplined those who were to be disciplined, he has attained Nibbāna along with his disciples.
When the Protector, together with his disciples, had attained Nibbāna and the Teaching was coming to its end,
the gods, deeply moved, wailed with tears streaming down their faces and weeping countenances.
“The Destroyer of the Dhamma will pass away; we shall not see the Subhadda;
we shall not hear the True Dhamma—alas for our meager merit!
Then this entire earth, though normally immovable, will tremble and shake.”
And Sāgara, as if filled with grief, uttered a piteous cry.
Celestial drums resounded in the four directions,
and terrifying thunderbolts struck on every side.
“Meteors fell from the sky, and a comet was seen;
flaming circles of smoke trailed behind them, and the deer cried out piteously.
Having seen these dreadful portents, which signal the destruction of the Teaching,”
The seven monks were deeply moved, and we then reflected:
“Without the Teaching, our lives are of no use to us;
having entered the great forest, let us apply ourselves to the Conqueror’s Dispensation.”
“Then we saw in the forest an exalted, towering rock;
having climbed it by means of a ladder, we caused that ladder to fall away.
Then the Elder admonished us: ‘The arising of a Buddha is very difficult to encounter.’”
Faith, once gained, is extremely difficult to find, and the teaching remains for only a short time.
Those who miss this moment fall into the boundless ocean of suffering;
therefore, one must apply oneself while the Sage’s doctrine still endures.
“That elder was an Arahant, and his follower was a Non-returner;
the others, being well-disciplined and diligent, went to the world of the gods.
He, having crossed over saṃsāra, attained Nibbāna alone in the Pure Abodes.”
I and Pakkusāti, Sabhiya and likewise Bāhiya,
as well as Kumārakassapa— we have all gone to those various places,
liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra, having been shown compassion by Gotama.
“In Malla Kusinārā, while I was still in the womb, my mother died and ascended the funeral pyre;
from there I fell down. I fell upon a heap of *dabba* grass, and thus I became known as Dabba.”
“By the power of my celibacy, I was liberated at the age of seven.
By the power of the milk-rice, I attained the five factors;
yet, though I was one whose taints were exhausted, I was much reviled by the wicked.”
“Both merit and evil have I now transcended;
having attained supreme peace, I dwell free from taints.
Having made the recluse laugh, I prepared his lodging.”
The Conqueror, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position:
“The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.”
“Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical insights... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

But while he was in such a state, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka— urged on by that very scrap of karma for which they had previously cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years due to a wicked deed committed by way of slandering a single elder whose taints were destroyed— thought:
"We have been alienated from this householder who provides excellent almsfood."
They accused him of an unfounded offense involving a *pārājika* rule because he had grasped the teaching incorrectly.

When that legal dispute had been settled by the Saṅgha through the procedure of *sativinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness), this elder, out of compassion for the world and manifesting his own virtues, spoke this verse: "He who is difficult to tame..."
5. Therein, "he who" (*yo*) is an indefinite designation; its definite nature is to be understood by means of the word "that one" (*so*).
By both [terms], having treated it as if it were something else, he speaks of himself alone. "Difficult to tame" (*duddamiyo*) means one who is hard to subdue, impossible to tame.
And this was the agitation of the mind—adorned with the pride of defilements, full of deceptive displays of speculative views—at the time when he was still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Having reflected upon the lack of tranquility of the faculties, he speaks thus. "By taming" means by the supreme and foremost taming of the Path;
for one who has been tamed by that is worthy of being called "tamed," because there is no further need to tame him, and not by any other means.
Alternatively, "by taming" means tamed by the Tamer, the Charioteer of Men to be Tamed. "Dabbo" means *drabyo*, which signifies "capable. Thus he said:
The Blessed One, referring to this very elder, said: “Dabba, Dabbas do not evade in such a manner.

“Contented” means satisfied with the contentment regarding requisites as they are obtained, with the contentment regarding meditative attainments, and with the contentment regarding the paths and fruits.
“One who has crossed over doubt” means that because the sixteen-based and eight-based doubts have been eradicated by the first path itself.

"Free from doubt. "The Victor" (*vijitāvī*): he is a Victor because he has conquered and dispelled everything belonging to the side of defilement that must be conquered by a noble person (*purisājānīya*).
"With fear departed": because all twenty-five kinds of fears have completely departed, his fears are gone and he is stilled in fearlessness.
Again, "the Elephant" (*dabba*) is a designation of his name. "Parinibbūta": there are two kinds of *parinibbāna*.
There is the nibbāna of defilements, which is the element of nibbāna with residue remaining; and the nibbāna of the aggregates, which is the element of nibbāna without residue remaining.
Of these, it is the nibbāna of defilements that is intended here. Therefore, the meaning is:

"one who has attained nibbāna through the nibbāna of defilements" because the states to be abandoned have been entirely abandoned by means of the Path. "Steadfast" (ṭhitatta) means having a stable nature, immovable.

He is unshakable by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) due to having attained the state of one who is "such-like" (tādi) regarding desirable things and the rest. The particle *hi* is a nipāta used in the sense of a reason;

therefore, because he—who previously remained difficult to tame—was tamed by the Teacher with the supreme taming due to his steadfastness, and because he is contented, has crossed over doubt, is victorious, and is free from fear, he is thus Dabba, the Parinibbuta, and for that very reason, the one whose self is established (ṭhitatta).

When that state had thus come to pass, the Elder— out of compassion for beings whose intellects are led by others and who might mistake mere confidence for something else— declared his final knowledge (*aññā*), saying that only such clarity of mind should be cultivated, not a different kind of confidence.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dabba is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sītavaniya The verse beginning with “Yo sītavanaṃ” belongs to the Venerable Sambhūta Thera. What is its origin?

It is said that more than eighteen hundred aeons ago, the Fully Enlightened One named Atthadassī appeared in the world and, from the great flood of saṃsāra, [delivered] the world together with its devas.
One day, while crossing over together with a great community of monks, he arrived at the bank of the Ganges.
At that time, a man who had been reborn in a household there saw the Blessed One;
with a mind full of serene faith, he approached, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, do you wish to go to the other side? The Blessed One replied, "We shall go."
Thus, having immediately prepared and brought a boat, the Teacher, out of compassion for him, boarded the boat together with the community of monks.

He himself also boarded, and having safely brought them to the opposite shore, he provided a great almsgiving on the following day, escorted the Blessed One and the community of monks for some distance, and then, with a devout heart, paid homage and returned. By that—
Having transmigrated among gods and humans by means of meritorious deeds, he was reborn at the end of more than thirteen hundred kappas ago in a kṣatriya family and became a wheel-turning monarch,
a righteous king who ruled according to the Dhamma. Having established beings on the path to a happy destination,
he passed away from there and, during the ninety-first kappa, went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī, undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutadhammas).

Living in a charnel ground, he practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth in his dispensation together with three companions;

having practiced the duty of a recluse for twenty thousand years and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for one interval between Buddhas, he was now born in this arising of a Buddha as the son of a great brahmin family in Rājagaha.
He was born. They gave him the name Sambhūta. When he reached maturity, he attained proficiency in the brahminical arts.
Together with three companions—Bhūmija, Jeyyasena, and Abhiradhana—he went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth. It is with reference to these that it was said:
“Bhūmija, Jeyyasena, Sambhūta, and Abhirādhana—
these have directly realized the Dhamma in the teaching of the One who is Supreme.
Then Sambhūta, having received the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body from the Blessed One, dwelt constantly in the Sītavana grove.
He dwelt there; for that reason, the Venerable One became known as “Sītavaniya.

Now at that time, the Great King Vessavaṇa, while traveling through the air toward the southern region of Jambudīpa on some business, saw the Elder sitting in the open air, attending to his meditation subject. Descending from his celestial palace, he paid homage to the Elder.
“‘When the Elder emerges from concentration, inform me of his arrival and provide him with protection,’ he commanded two *yakkhas* and departed.
Standing near the Elder, they informed him when he had withdrawn his attention and sat down.
Upon hearing this, the Elder said, ‘Tell the Great King Vessavaṇa in my name:’”
"The Blessed One has established what is called 'protection by mindfulness' for those who abide in his teaching; that very protection protects one such as me.
You need not concern yourself with that matter; for those who abide in the Blessed One’s instruction, there is no further need for such protection.
Having dismissed them with these words, he immediately intensified his insight (vipassanā) and realized the threefold clear knowledge (vijjā). Then—
Vessavaṇa, returning and having reached the Elder’s presence, recognized by the mere look on his face that his task was accomplished.
He went to Sāvatthī, informed the Blessed One, and in the presence of the Teacher, praised the Elder:
“Endowed with the protection of mindfulness, steadfast, and concentrated through energy;”
“Born after the Teacher, arisen from him, a possessor of the three knowledges, one who has gone beyond death”—with this verse he praised the Elder’s virtues. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men...”
Honored by his disciples, he approached the bank of the Ganges.
"The Ganges was level with its banks and as deep as a crow’s drink, difficult to cross;
yet I ferried across the Saṅgha of monks and the Buddha, the supreme among bipeds."
“In eighteen hundred kappas, because of the deed I performed then, I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit of my crossing over.
In thirteen hundred kappas, there were five existences as a universal monarch.”
“Possessing the seven treasures, powerful universal monarchs.
And in this final existence, I was born into a brahmin family;
together with three companions, I went forth into the teaching of the Teacher.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Then, seeing the bhikkhus going to see the Blessed One, the Venerable Sambhūta said, “Friends, pay homage with your heads at the feet of the Blessed One in my name, and speak thus,” and he entrusted his legal case to his Teacher.
Proclaiming a state of non-harming, he spoke the verse beginning, “He who [dwells] in the Cool Grove.

Those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and while conveying the message of the Elder Sambhūta, said, “Venerable sir, the Venerable Sambhūta pays homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and speaks thus,” and they recited that verse. Having heard it, the Blessed One—
“Monks, the wise monk Sambhūta has practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and does not trouble me with legal matters concerning the Dhamma.
Vessavaṇa informed me of his welfare,” he said.
Furthermore, those monks reported to the Teacher the verse spoken by the elder Sambhūta: “He who [dwells] in Sītavana... and so forth.
Therein, "Sītavana" refers to a large and terrifying charnel ground forest near Rājagaha bearing that name.
"Upaga" means he approached it by way of making it his dwelling place; by this, he shows the dwelling place appropriate for one who has gone forth, as authorized by the Blessed One.
"Bhikkhu" is so called because he looks with fear upon *saṃsāra* and because he has shattered the defilements (*bhinnakilesatā*). "Eko" means alone, without a second.

By this, he shows physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). "Contented" (*santuṭṭho*) means satisfied; by this, he shows the noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*) characterized by contentment with the four requisites.
"With a concentrated mind" (*samāhitatto*) means one whose mind is concentrated through concentration distinguished as access and absorption;

by this, he shows the noble lineage that delights in meditation (*bhāvanārāma*) by way of the cultivation of mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). "Victorious" (*vijitāvī*) refers to one who practices correctly within the Teaching.
Having conquered the multitude of defilements that must be conquered, he stands firm; by this, he shows seclusion from the substrates of existence (*upadhiviveka*).

Because the defilements, which are the causes of fear, have departed, he is "one whose hair does not stand on end" (*apetalomahaṃsa*); by this, he shows the fruit of right practice. "He guards, guarding":
*kāyagatāsatiṃ* means mindfulness having the body as its object; he does not relinquish the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body by way of its cultivation.
“Steadfast and wise” (dhitimā dhīro) refers to the demonstration of practice based on his state of concentration or his manifestation of victory over the unconquered.
This is the summary of the meaning here: that bhikkhu, out of indifference toward the pleasure of seclusion, went alone to the Cool Grove;
having gone there, being content due to the absence of fickleness, steadfast, and developing the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body, he [realized] what was thus attained.
Having made *jhāna* the foundation, having brought his insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak, and having become concentrated and victorious through the attainment of the supreme path,
he became one whose hair stands on end no more because all causes of fear have been entirely removed due to the completion of what was to be done.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sītavaniya is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhalliya "Whoever has dispelled..."—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bhalliya. What is its origin?
It is said that in the thirty-first aeon ago, before a Buddha had appeared, he offered various fruits with a devout heart to a Paccekabuddha named Sumanas and was reborn in the happy realms.
Thus wandering through saṃsāra, he was reborn at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī in a brahmin family in the city of Aruṇavatī.

Having heard that "Ujita and Ojita, the two sons of caravan leaders, were the first to give alms-food to the Blessed One Sikhī when he had first attained full enlightenment," he approached the Blessed One together with his own companion.
Having paid homage, invited [the Buddha] for the following day, and offered a great almsgiving, they made this aspiration:
"Venerable Sir, may we both, in the future, be the first to offer food to a Buddha such as you.
Having performed meritorious deeds here and there, they wandered through the realms of gods and humans during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
They were reborn as brothers who were the sons of the merchant Gopālaka. For many years, they served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with milk-rice offerings.
However, in the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn as brothers who were the sons of a caravan leader in the city of Pokkharavatī.
Among them, the elder was named Taphussa and the younger was named Bhalliya; they were about five [in number].
Hundreds of carts, filled with merchandise and traveling for trade, passed along the great highway not far from the Rājāyatana tree at a time when the Blessed One—
having spent the first seven days after his initial enlightenment reviewing the bliss of liberation and the Dhamma,
and then spending the eighth week dwelling at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree— was present there; and at that time, even though the ground was level...
On that stretch of ground, because there was no mud or water, the wagons could not proceed.

As they wondered, "What indeed is the cause of this?", an ancient blood-relative deity, manifesting herself amidst the branches of a tree, said: "Friends, this Blessed One has recently attained full enlightenment;
for seven days he has been without food, experiencing the bliss of liberation, and is now at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree."
“While he is seated, serve him with food; that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.

Having heard this, they experienced sublime joy and gladness. Thinking, “The preparation of food is a mere distraction,” they gave the Lord both the stirred drink and the honey-cake, went for refuge by the two formulas, and received the hair-relics.
They arrived; for they were the first to become lay followers (*upāsaka*).
Then, when the Blessed One had gone to Bārāṇasī, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, and was staying at Rājagaha in due course, Tapussa and Bhallika approached Rājagaha.
Having approached the Blessed One and paid homage, they sat down to one side. The Blessed One taught them the Dhamma. Among them, Tapussa...

Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, he remained a lay follower (*upāsaka*). But Bhalliya, having gone forth, became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Sambuddha named Sumana then dwelt in Takkarā;”
Having taken a vallikāra fruit, I gave it to the Self-Awakened One.
