"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that fruit I gave then, I do not know any state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Then one day, Māra, for the purpose of terrifying the Elder Bhalliya, displayed a fearsome form. The Elder, proclaiming his own transcendence of all fear, recited the verse beginning with “He who has driven away...
(yopānudī). 7. In this context, *yopānudī* means he who drove away, cast off, abandoned, or destroyed. *Maccurājassa* refers to Death (Māra).
Death is the dissolution of the aggregates (*khandhā*). Because it brings living beings under its own control, it is the "King" (*rājā*) in the sense of sovereignty;

thus, it is the "King of Death" (*maccurājā*). His "army" (*senā*) consists of old age, disease, and so forth. For these serve as the constituent parts for its exercise of power, and are therefore called an "army.
It is for this reason that he is called "Mahāsena" (He of the Great Army), because of that great, manifold, and vast [host]. As it has been said: "For..."
“One should not enter into battle with that Death, the Great Army. Alternatively, in the sense of slaying virtues, “Death” here refers to Māra the son of a deity;
and because they accompany him, sensual pleasures and the like constitute his army. Thus it is said:
“Sensual pleasures are your first army; the second is called discontent;”
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is called craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor for you; the sixth is called fear.
The seventh is doubt for you; the eighth is conceit and hypocrisy.
The construction is as follows: "Like a reed-bridge, very weak"—because it is devoid of essence, the army of defilements is like a reed-bridge, being exceedingly feeble;
and because of the great power of the nine supramundane states, the "great flood" is like the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
He who has driven it away by means of that [path], the victor, free from fear, the tamed one—he is "parinibbuted, established in self."
Having heard this, Māra thought, "The ascetic knows me," and vanished right then and there.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhalliya is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vīra.
"Yo duddamiyo" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vīra. What is its origin?
It is said that in the ninety-first aeon ago, he tended to the dwelling place of the Blessed One Vipassī.
One day, having taken *nigguṇṭhi* flowers resembling *sindhuvāra* blossoms, he made an offering to the Blessed One. By that meritorious deed, he [reappeared] among gods and humans.
Wandering through existence, thirty-five eons ago, he was reborn into a kṣatriya family and became a wheel-turning monarch named Mahāpatāpa.
Ruling his kingdom with righteousness and justice, he established sentient beings on the path to heaven.
Furthermore, in this present eon, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a very wealthy merchant and [provided for] the poor, the destitute, and others.

While giving alms, he gave milk-rice to the Saṅgha. Thus, accumulating the equipment of merit consisting of giving here and there, and gathering the other equipment for the sake of Nibbāna, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in the city of Sāvatthī in a minister’s family belonging to King Pasenadi; they gave him the name Vīra. He—
Having reached maturity and being endowed with qualities such as strength and speed that were consistent with his name, he became a hero in battle.
Although his parents, out of persistence, arranged for him to take a wife, he obtained only one son.

Then, urged by past causes, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and in *saṃsāra*, and filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he went forth into homelessness; and by striving and exerting himself, before long—
He became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I was a monastery attendant for the Blessed One Vipassī;
having taken a nigguṇṭhi flower, I offered it to the Buddha.”
“Ninety-one aeons ago, because I offered this flower in worship, I have not known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Twenty-five aeons from now, I shall be a sole lord of men.”
“By the name Mahāpatāpa, I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus, while the Elder was spending his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition after reaching Arahantship, his former wife—”
Desiring to cause him to fall away from the religious life, she strove to seduce him by various means at intervals;
one day, having gone to his place for the midday rest, she began to display feminine gestures and the like. Then the Venerable Vīra thought:
"This woman is indeed as foolish as one who wishes to move Mount Sineru with the wind from a gnat's wing while desiring to seduce me"—thus he perceived the futility of her actions.
Illuminating this, he spoke the verse beginning with “He who is difficult to tame. 8.
Herein, the meaning of the words beginning with “yo duddamiyo” has already been explained above. This, however, is merely the application [of the terms] here:
he who was previously "difficult to tame" (duddamiyo) because his defilements were untamed, or because he could not be tamed or conquered by enemies in the forefront of battle;
But now, he is tamed by the highest taming; he is a hero through the perfection of the energy of the fourfold right exertion;
he is contented in the manner already described; he has crossed over doubt, is victorious, and is free from horripilation;

he is a hero, one who bears the name of a hero, and is completely extinguished (parinibbuto) by the total extinction of the defilements; for that very reason, his nature is established, such that even a hundred or a thousand like him could not [disturb it].
“‘He is to be winnowed out. Having heard this, that woman thought, ‘When my husband has behaved in such a manner, what use have I for the household life?
Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she went forth among the bhikkhunīs and, before long, became one possessed of the three knowledges (*tevijjā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vīra is finished.”

9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Pilindavaccha "Welcome," is the verse of the Venerable Elder Pilindavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī;
as described in the manner stated below, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
While listening, he saw the Teacher place a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among the deities for his being dear and pleasing to them.

Having aspired to that very status and performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed away from there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in the human world during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, [he went] to the Teacher’s stupa...

Having performed worship for the Saṅgha and distributed a great almsgiving, he passed away from there and, wandering only among gods and humans, became a wheel-turning monarch during the time when no Buddha had appeared. Having established the great multitude in the five precepts, he made them destined for heaven.
Even before our Blessed One had appeared, he was reborn in Sāvatthī in the household of a brahmin; his name was Pilinda.
They gave him a name; his clan name was Vaccha. Consequently, he later became known as Pilindavaccha.
However, due to a great sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) within *saṃsāra*, he had gone forth as a wandering ascetic (*paribbājaka*).

Having mastered the spell known as Cūḷagandhāra, he traveled through the air by means of that spell and, becoming a knower of others' minds, lived in Rājagaha having attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame.

Then, when our Blessed One had attained full enlightenment and gradually arrived at Rājagaha, from that time on, through the power of the Buddha, that spell of his no longer succeeded and it did not accomplish its purpose.
He thought: "I have indeed heard this from my teachers and their teachers as they spoke: 'Wherever the Mahāgandhāra spell...'"
“‘It holds; however, the Cūḷagandhārī spell does not succeed there.
But ever since the arrival of the ascetic Gotama, this spell of mine has not succeeded.
Without a doubt, the ascetic Gotama knows the Mahāgandhārī spell. What if I were to attend upon him and learn that spell from his presence?”
So he approached the Blessed One and said this: “Great Ascetic, I wish to master a certain branch of knowledge in your presence;
please grant me the opportunity. The Blessed One said, “In that case, go forth [into homelessness].

Thinking, “Going forth is the preliminary practice for the acquisition of knowledge,” he went forth. After the Blessed One had taught him the Dhamma in accordance with his temperament, [he continued:]
He gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he soon developed insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*.

As for the deity who, having followed his advice in a previous birth, was reborn in the heavenly realms—it was out of gratitude toward him that she developed great reverence and would go to attend upon the Elder morning and evening. Therefore, the Elder [was known] to the deities...
He attained preeminence in being beloved and pleasing. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Protector of the World, Sumedha, the Supreme Person, had passed away into Nibbāna, with a clear heart and a joyful mind, I performed an offering at his stupa.”
“And those whose taints were destroyed there, possessing the sixfold direct knowledge and great psychic power—
to them I brought together there and provided a communal meal for the Saṅgha.
At that time, I was the attendant of the Blessed One Sumedha.”
At that time, he named Sumedha expressed his appreciation:
"By that clarity of mind, I was reborn in a celestial mansion;
eighty-six thousand nymphs delighted me."
“They always follow me alone with all their desires;
I surpass other devas—this is the fruit of meritorious karma.
In the twenty-fifth aeon, there was a kshatriya named Varuṇa.”
“I was a Wheel-turning Monarch at that time, one whose food was pure.
Seeds were not sown, nor were plows led forth;
humans enjoyed rice that ripened without being tilled.”
“Having exercised sovereignty there, I went once more to the realm of the gods;
even then, such a perfection of wealth was produced for me.
Neither friends nor enemies, nor any living beings at all, could harm me.”
I am dear to everyone; this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.
Because I gave gifts back then during thirty thousand eons, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of anointing with fragrant scents.
“In this auspicious aeon, I was once a lord of men;
a king of great majesty, a wheel-turning monarch of mighty power.
Having established many people in the five moral precepts, I—”
"Having led [beings] only to a happy destination, I became dear to the deities.
'The defilements are burnt up by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus, because he was exceedingly beloved by the deities, the Blessed One [addressed] this elder by way of his being dear and pleasing to the deities."
He placed him in the foremost position, saying: “This is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples, O bhikkhus, who are dear and pleasing to the deities, namely Pilindavaccha.

One day, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he reflected upon his own virtues and, praising the arrival at the Blessed One’s presence for the sake of the knowledge that was the cause of those virtues, said: “Welcome!”
He spoke this verse: "It has not departed.
In this context, *svāgataṃ* means a beautiful arrival; the connection is "this is mine. Alternatively, *svāgataṃ* means well-arrived;
the case ending must be transformed to [the dative] *mayā*. *Nāpagataṃ* means it has not departed from the increase of welfare.
"Not departed. "This was not ill-spoken by me" means: "What I have spoken or what I have investigated here is not poorly said or poorly examined.
This is what is meant: my coming into the presence of the Blessed One, or my having arrived there, is a welcome arrival;
because it is a welcome arrival, it is not an ill-arrived one. As for the Dhamma [heard] in the presence of the Blessed One...
"Having heard what was thought, spoken, uttered, and declared by me, or even what was investigated by my mind, this too is not ill-thought.
Now, showing the reason for that, he said "In those well-analyzed," and so forth. "Well-analyzed" means analyzed in various ways.
"In phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means in knowable phenomena (*ñeyya-dhamma*) or in the phenomena of tranquility (*samatha-dhamma*), [as opposed to] those of the various non-Buddhist sects.

Among the teachings spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones after having analyzed them according to their nature and so forth, or according to suffering and so forth—“I approached that which is supreme therein”:
I approached that which is supreme among those, namely the Dhamma of the Four Truths, or the teaching of the Dispensation that makes it known;
I approached it, thinking, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya. By the Perfectly Enlightened Ones...

Or rather, among the phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) which have been analyzed according to their true nature by way of the wholesome and so forth, and by way of the aggregates and so forth—whatever therein is the best, the highest, the most excellent—that is the dhamma of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna;
I approached it, I attained it through personal direct experience, and I realized it. Therefore, the construction is: "Welcome to me, not unwelcome; well-considered, not ill-considered."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pilindavaccha is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa:
“He dwells without longing” (vihari apekkhaṃ). These are the verses of the venerable Elder Puṇṇamāsa. What is their origin? It is said that he was a follower of Vipassi Buddha.

In the time of the Blessed One, having been reborn in the womb of a ruddy sheldrake, he saw the Blessed One walking by and, with a mind full of faith, took a *sāla* flower with his own beak and made an offering.

By that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he became a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*) eight times during this very seventeenth aeon. Now, in this [present life]...
In the aeon of the Blessed One Kassapa, when the Dispensation was declining, he was reborn in a family of householders.

Having gone forth and practiced the duty of a recluse, he passed away from there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha as the son of a brahmin named Samiddhi in the city of Sāvatthī. On the day of his birth, in that house, all...
The empty jars became filled with gold coins; therefore, they gave him the name Puṇṇamāsa.

When he reached maturity, having attained proficiency in the brahminical sciences, he performed the marriage ceremony. Having obtained a son and being endowed with the necessary spiritual predispositions (*upanissaya*), he came to loathe the household life.
Approaching the Blessed One and hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and...
Having received full ordination and fulfilled the preliminary duties, he applied himself to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths;
by intensifying his insight, he attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the river Sindhū, I was then a ruddy goose;”
Subsisting on a diet of pure moss, I was well-restrained among evildoers.
I saw the stainless Buddha walking along the path of the wind;
grasping a sal tree with my trunk, I offered it to Vipassi.
“He whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established—
by that clarity of mind, he does not go to an evil destination.
‘How welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Best of Buddhas!’”
“By me, while living as a bird, a good seed was planted.
Because I offered that flower ninety-one eons ago, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“Sucārudassanā by name—these eight of one name—were wheel-turning monarchs of great power during the seventeenth aeon.
‘The defilements have been burnt up by me... [the rest as above] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Then his former wife, desiring to seduce him, approached him together with their son, beautifully adorned and prepared, and began to perform what is called the "act of revealing her feelings" through affectionate conversation and other such means.
Seeing her purpose, the Elder, demonstrating that he was unattached to anything whatsoever, spoke the verse: “Dwell free from longing.”
10. *Tattha viharī* means he specifically took away, removed, or led away. *Apekkhanti* refers to craving (*taṇhā*).
*Idha* means in this world or in this present personal existence (*attabhāva*). *Huranti* means in another, future personal existence.

Alternatively, *idha* refers to the internal sense bases (*ajjhattika-āyatana*), while *huranti* refers to the external ones. The word *vā* has the sense of conjunction, as in [the phrase] "whether footless or two-footed," and so forth.

"Like" (viya): he shows himself as if he were another. "A master of knowledge" (vedagu): one who has gone by means of knowledge—that is, one who has gone to or attained Nibbāna by means of the knowledge of the Path;
or one who stands having fully realized the Four Truths by way of their full understanding, abandoning, realization, and cultivation.
"Self-controlled" (yatatta): one whose nature is restrained by the restraint of the Path, or one whose nature is restrained by right effort.
"Unstained by all phenomena" means unstained by any phenomena as objects through the smearing of craving and views;

by this, he shows the transcendence of worldly conditions such as gain and so forth. "Of the world" refers to the five aggregates of clinging, for they are called the "world" (*loka*) in the sense of breaking apart and disintegrating.
"Having known" (*jaññā*) means having understood. "And both arising and passing away" (*udayabbayañca*) means both origination and dissolution.
By this, he shows the preliminary practice for the qualities as previously described. This, however, is the meaning here:

one who, having understood through fifty-four modes the arising and passing away of the entire world consisting of the aggregates and so forth, is a master of knowledge (vedagū), self-controlled, and untainted by anything;
such a person, having removed all expectations, is contented and is not affected by any such adverse occurrences.
“He conceives [of them as his own]; therefore, you foolish woman, go back by the very path by which you came.
Then that woman thought, “This ascetic has no regard for me or my children; it is impossible to seduce him,” and she departed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter of the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the sub-commentary on the *Theragāthā*, is completed. 2.
The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cūḷavaccha "Abounding in gladness":
these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Cūḷavaccha. What is their origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a poor family and, making his living by working for others, [saw] the Blessed One...
Having seen the elder named Sujāta seeking a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), he approached him with a devout mind, gave him a cloth, and paid homage by prostrating himself at the five points.
By that meritorious deed, he exercised sovereignty over the gods thirty-three times;
he was a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) seventy-seven times; and many times he was a regional king. Thus, among gods and humans...
While wandering in saṃsāra, during the period when the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was declining, he went forth into homelessness and practiced the duty of a recluse.

Passing from one existence to another among the destinies of gods and humans for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, he was reborn at the time of our own Blessed One in a brahmin family in Kosambī.
His name was Cūḷavaccha. Having reached maturity, he [studied] the brahminical arts...
Having heard of the perfection of the Buddha’s qualities, he approached the Blessed One with a serene mind;

the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to him. Having gained faith, he went forth, received full ordination, and having performed the preliminary duties, he took a meditation subject suitable for his temperament and dwelt practicing it.
At that time, the monks of Kosambī had fallen into a state of quarreling.

They existed. At that time, the Elder Cūḷa-Vaccha, without adopting the views of either group of monks, stood by the instruction given by the Blessed One, cultivated insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The disciple named Sujāta was a follower of the Blessed One Padumuttara.”
Seeking discarded rags, he was then wandering among the refuse heaps.
"In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was once a servant for others;
having given him half a garment, I paid homage with my head bowed low."
“By that well-performed karma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-Three.
Thirty-three times I served as the Lord of the Gods, exercising sovereignty over the devas.”
And seventy-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
Through the gift of half a cloth, I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter, having enjoyed extensive regional sovereignty that is beyond counting.
“If I so desired today, I could cover this earth with its forests and mountains in linen cloth—
this is the fruit of that half-piece of cloth.
Because of the gift I gave back then, a hundred thousand aeons ago, [I have attained this].”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of a harvest well-reaped.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then, having attained arahantship, the Elder Cūḷavaccha [reflected] upon the ruin of his own welfare caused by those monks’ delight in quarreling.

Having seen this, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*); reflecting upon the distinction he had attained for himself, he uttered the verse beginning with "abounding in gladness" (*pāmojjabahulo*) out of joy and happiness.

11. In that context, "abounding in gladness" means that due to the state of perfectly pure virtue (*suparisuddhasīlatā*), there is an absence of remorse regarding higher wholesome states (*adhikusala-dhamma*).
Because of his delight, he is full of joy. For this very reason, it says: "In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha.
Therein, "Dhamma" refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) or the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*).

Indeed, because it was revealed through the self-exalting teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, it is preeminently called "proclaimed by the Buddha. Furthermore, because it is the means for its realization—
The Dhamma of the teaching is indeed obtainable here as well. He speaks with reference to Nibbāna as "the peaceful state" (*santaṃ padaṃ*).

For such a bhikkhu attains and finds Nibbāna—the peaceful state, the peaceful constituent, the subsiding of all formations due to its nature as tranquility, and bliss because of its supreme happiness. Indeed, a bhikkhu who is pure in virtue...
By means of the absence of remorse, one who is full of gladness and devotedly engaged with the True Dhamma attains all perfections culminating in liberation.
As it is said: “Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose;
non-remorse has gladness as its purpose,” and so forth. Alternatively, “full of gladness” refers to the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One, and the well-expounded Dhamma.
"‘The Saṅgha is well-practiced’—this refers to the Triple Gem, and one who possesses great joy therein asks:

‘What does that person, full of joy, do? To this he says: ‘In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha,’ and so forth. For one endowed with faith, the association with true persons, the hearing of the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma arise with ease;
thus, successions of attainments are as if already held in the hand. As it is said: ‘One who has conceived faith approaches [the teacher]...’"
“Approaching, he pays homage,” and so forth.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷa-Vaccha is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahā-Vaccha.
“Paññābalī” (The Power of Wisdom) is the verse of the Venerable Mahāvaccha Thera. What is its origin?

It is said that he gave a gift of drinking water to the Blessed One Padumuttara and his community of monks. Later, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, having become a lay follower, he performed much meritorious karma conducive to the turning away from rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). By means of those meritorious deeds, in various places...

Wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in the kingdom of Magadha, in the village of Nāḷaka, as the son of a brahmin named Samiddhi. His name was Mahāvaccha.
When he reached maturity, having heard that the Venerable Sāriputta was a disciple of the Blessed One, [he thought], "He too is indeed of great wisdom; his discipleship..."
“Having approached him, he is, I believe, the foremost person in this world.

Having thus conceived faith in the Blessed One, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and, applying himself to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), before long attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the peerless Saṅgha of Bhikkhus under the Buddha Padumuttara;”
With a clear mind and a joyful heart, I filled a water jar.
"Whether on a mountain peak, in a difficult path, in the sky, or upon the earth—
whenever I desire water, it appears for me instantly."
“In a hundred thousand aeons past, the gift that I gave then— I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving water.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... all states of existence have been uprooted.”
"The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having thus attained arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he spoke this verse beginning with "One endowed with the power of wisdom" in order to inspire his fellow celibates by demonstrating the world-transcending nature of the Dispensation.

Regarding that, "one endowed with the power of wisdom" refers to one who, by means of both functional wisdom (*pārihāriya-paññā*) and insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), frequently and pre-eminently...

Endowed with the power of wisdom (*paññābala*). "Established in virtue and vows" means established and endowed with the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*) in its highest excellence, as well as with the vows known as the ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*).
"Concentrated" means concentrated by means of concentration (*samādhi*) distinguished as access and absorption.

"Delighting in jhāna" means delighting in—and constantly devoted to—the contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) arising from that very state.
He is mindful by virtue of never being separated from mindfulness at all times. "Yadatthiyaṃ" means that which is not devoid of purpose (*attha*);

that which has a purpose is "yadatthiyaṃ. Just as the consumption of requisites is purposeful for one who uses them, so too is the eating of food [purposeful] when he eats it. For it is purposeful through the enjoyment of ownership, that is, through the enjoyment of inheritance.
Or, the phrase "not otherwise than food" should be regarded as a mere illustration. It is called *bhojana* because it is eaten or consumed;
that is, the four requisites. Alternatively, there is the reading *yadatthika*.

For whatever purpose—for which purpose the requisites were permitted by the Teacher—namely for the sake of the maintenance of the body and so forth, and for the sake of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*).
Therefore, one who consumes food as a requisite for the sake of final nibbāna without clinging should, for that very reason, be anxious about the time;
he should await the time of his own final nibbāna without clinging. "In this" means in this teaching (*sāsana*).
The intention is that this [state] does not exist for an outsider who is free from passion for sense-pleasures (*kāma*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāvaccha is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vanavaccha:
"With the color of a dark cloud," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Vanavaccha. What is his origin? It is said that he [was a disciple] of Atthadassin.
In the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn in the womb of a tortoise and lived by a river named Vinatā. His body was the size of a small boat.

It is said that one day, seeing the Blessed One standing on the bank of the river, he thought, "The Blessed One likely wishes to go to the other side," and desiring to carry him there, he lay down at the Blessed One's feet, offering his back for him to mount. The Blessed One...
Knowing his intention and feeling compassion for him, the Blessed One mounted [the boat].

Filled with joy and gladness, he brought him safely to the opposite shore in that very moment, like an arrow shot with speed from a bowstring as it cuts through the air. Having explained to him the fruit of that merit and the excellence of his rebirth resulting from it, the Blessed One departed.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through many hundreds of births, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic on numerous occasions.

Later, during the time of Buddha Kassapa, he was reborn in the womb of a pigeon; there, seeing a certain bhikkhu dwelling in the forest who lived in loving-kindness (*mettā*), his heart was filled with serene confidence.

Then, passing away from there, he was reborn in a noble family in Bārāṇasī. Upon reaching maturity, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he went forth into homelessness and accumulated much meritorious karma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Thus, after wandering through various realms among gods and humans, at this present arising of a Buddha, he took conception in the home of a brahmin named Vacchagotta in the city of Kapilavatthu.
He took her. Her mother, whose pregnancy was mature and who had developed a longing to see the forest, entered the forest and wandered about;
at that very moment, the winds born of karma agitated her womb, and they enclosed her within a barrier.
She gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit. He became a playmate, playing in the dust together with the Bodhisatta. His name was Vaccha.

He came to be known as Vanavaccha because of his delight in the forest. Later, when the Great Being had gone forth on the Great Renunciation and was exerting himself in the Great Struggle, [Vanavaccha] thought, "I too shall dwell in the forest together with Prince Siddhattha.
Having gone forth and taken up the ascetic life, while dwelling in the Himalayas, he heard of the state of the Buddha's full enlightenment.
Having approached the Blessed One, gone forth, and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he dwelt in the forest.
Before long, having brought insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak, he realized *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-Existent One, the Leader of the World;”
The Tathāgata approached the bank of the Vinatā river.
Having emerged from the water, the turtle who feeds upon the depths said:
“Desiring to ferry the Buddha across, I have come to the Leader of the World.”
“May the Buddha, the Great Sage Atthadassī, mount me!
I shall carry you across; you are the one who brings an end to suffering.
Understanding my intention, the highly renowned Atthadassī—
Having mounted upon my back, the Leader of the World stood there.
"Since I can remember myself, since I have attained the age of discretion,
I have never known such happiness as that which I feel when my soles are touched."
Having crossed over, the Fully Awakened One, Atthadassī of great renown,
stood upon the riverbank and spoke these verses:
“As far as the mind extends, so far do I cross the flow of the Ganges.”
"And this wise tortoise-king ferried me across.
By virtue of this act of crossing over for the sake of awakening and through his state of loving-kindness,
he will delight in the world of the gods for eighteen hundred aeons."
“Having come here from the world of the gods, urged on by the root of his wholesome merit,
he will sit upon a single seat and cross over the river of doubt.
Just as even a small seed sown in a fertile field,”
When the right provisions are bestowed, the fruit satisfies the farmer.
"In the same way, this field of the Buddha, taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One—
when the right provisions are bestowed, its fruit will satisfy me."
“I am dedicated to the exertion, peaceful and free from acquisitions;
having fully understood all taints, I dwell without taints.
That deed which I performed back in eighteen hundred eons—”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of my crossing over.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Kapilavatthu, he went there to the Teacher.
Having paid homage and come together with the bhikkhus, he was asked as a matter of greeting, "Friend, have you found a comfortable dwelling in the forest?
Being thus questioned, he praised the mountain where he himself had resided, saying, "The mountains in the forest are delightful, friend," and recited the verse beginning with "Blue-cloud-colored.
Regarding that: "Blue-cloud-colored" means having the appearance of blue clouds and being shaped like blue clouds. "Delightful" means by way of beauty.
“Possessing rays and luminous. “Cool water” means cool water. “Pure-bearing” (sucindharā):

it is called pure-bearing either because its ground-portion is clean and pure, or because it is a dwelling place for noble ones (ariya) whose minds are pure; for the nasalization was added for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.
There is also the reading “sītavārisucindharā,” meaning “bearing cool and pure water,” that is, possessing a reservoir of cool and stainless water.
The meaning is as follows: "Covered with *indagopaka* insects" means covered by red insects the color of coral named *indagopaka*;
he spoke thus because of the rainy season. Some, however, say that *indagopaka* refers to red grasses; others say they are *kaṇikāra* trees.
"Rocks" (*selā*) means mountains made of stone, not sand-mountains; therefore he said: "Just as..."
"A mountain of rock. They delight me; they cause me to rejoice, nourishing my delight in seclusion.
Thus, while announcing his own long-cultivated delight in the forest, the Elder illustrates the threefold delight in seclusion.
In this context, it is precisely by means of the seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*) that the declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*) is illustrated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vanavaccha is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the novice Sīvaka.
"The Preceptor" refers to the verses of the novice Sīvaka. What is their origin? It is said that in the thirty-first aeon ago, [he was born] during the time of Vessabhu...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he one day entered the forest for some business.
There, seeing the Blessed One Vessabhū seated among the mountains, his heart was filled with faith;
he approached, paid homage, and stood with palms joined in reverence. Then, seeing beautiful *kāsumārika* fruits there, he took them.
Having taken them, he offered them to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One accepted them out of compassion.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he went forth into homelessness together with his maternal uncle when the latter had gone forth under the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having accumulated much wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), during this current appearance of a Buddha, [he became] the Elder Vanavaccha.
Having been reborn as a nephew, his name was Sīvaka.

His mother, having gone forth in the religious life under her own elder brother Vanavaccha and having brought her duties as a nun to completion while he was dwelling in the forest, heard of that news and said to her son:
"Dear Sīvaka, go forth in the presence of the Elder and attend upon him."

"He is now an elderly elder. At his mother's single word, and because of the service he had previously rendered her, he went into the presence of the Elder Mātula, received the going-forth, and lived in the forest while attending upon him.
One day, having gone to the vicinity of a village on some business, a severe illness arose in him. Among the people...
Even while they were administering medicine, his illness did not subside. As he was lingering there for a long time, the Elder thought, "The novice is taking a long time;
what could be the reason? He went there, saw that he was ill, and spent the day attending to him with whatever care was appropriate for his condition.
Then, during the night, at the time of the powerful dawn, he said: "Sīvaka, no..."
“From the time I went forth, I have never before lived in a village; let us go from here to the forest alone.
Hearing this, Sivaka said, “Venerable sir, although my body is now situated in the village, my mind is in the forest;
therefore, even as I lie down, I shall go to the forest alone. Having heard this, the Elder took him by the arm and [led him] to the forest itself.
Having led him there, he gave him exhortation. Abiding by the elder’s exhortation and practicing insight (vipassanā), he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I saw the stainless Buddha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower as he sat amidst the mountains.”
“With a clear heart and joyful mind, having joined my palms in reverence,
I took a *kāsumāri* fruit and gave it to the Best of Buddhas.
Thirty-one eons ago, that fruit which I then offered— ”
“I do not know an evil rebirth; this is the fruit of giving the fruit [of my gift].
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc.]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship, he compared the meaning spoken by his preceptor with what he himself had said, and proclaiming his own delight in seclusion and the completion of his task, he recited the verse beginning, ‘My preceptor spoke to me.’”

14. Therein, "preceptor" (*upajjhāya*): he is called a preceptor because he reflects upon what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and having established a desire for their welfare, he gazes [upon them] with the eye of knowledge.
"Māṇava" is a term for oneself. "Spoke" (*avaca*) means he said. "Sīvaka, let us go from here"—this indicates the manner of speaking;
that is to say, "Sīvaka, come, let us go from this village boundary to the forest region itself; that alone is for us."

The intention is that they are "fit for clothing. When Sivaka was thus addressed by his preceptor, he became stirred with a sense of urgency like a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip; and wishing to go to the forest itself, he declared:
"My body dwells in the village, but my mind has gone to the forest."
"Even though I am lying down, I shall go; for one who understands, there is no attachment," he said.

The meaning of this is: since now, although this body of mine remains in the village, my inclination has gone to the forest alone, therefore—even while lying down—I shall go, because of the inability to stand, sit, or walk due to illness.
Slithering along like a reptile in this manner of lying down, he said: "Come, venerable sir, let us go to the forest itself.

Why? Because there is no attachment for one who understands. Since there is no attachment anywhere for one who knows, as they truly are, the danger in sensual pleasures and in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and the benefit in renunciation and *nibbāna*, therefore, with a single word—
Thinking, "The preceptor’s command has not been fulfilled," he gave an answer on that pretext.
The commentary on the verses of the novice Sivaka is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna.
"Cut off five, abandon five"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kuṇḍadhāna. What is its origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having reached maturity, he approached the Blessed One in the manner described below and listened to the Dhamma; then the Teacher [prophesied] one bhikkhu as the foremost...
Seeing him being placed in the foremost position among those receiving voting sticks, he aspired to that rank and wandered about performing merit accordingly.
One day, when the Blessed One Padumuttara had emerged from the attainment of cessation and was seated, he offered him a large betel-leaf tray, yellowish-red with powdered mana-shilā stone. That—
The Blessed One accepted it and consumed it. By that meritorious deed, he exercised sovereignty among the gods eleven times.

Twenty-four times he was a universal monarch (*cakkavattī*). Thus, having repeatedly performed meritorious deeds and wandering from one state to another among gods and humans, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity. And of those Buddhas who possessed long lifespans...
Indeed, there was not a Uposatha every half-month. For instance, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassi, the Uposatha occurred every six years.
However, the Great Sage Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha every sixth month.
At the time of that recitation of the Pātimokkha, two monks who were friends living in different regions [approached] for the Uposatha...
"Let us go," they said, and they departed.
Then this earth-deity thought: "The friendship between these two monks is exceedingly firm;
would it be broken if a divisive person were present, or would it not be broken? Observing their opportunity, she remained not far from them.
He went on his way. Then a certain elder, having placed his bowl and robes in the hand of another, went to a convenient place by the water for the purpose of washing his body;
and having washed his hands and feet, he emerged from the vicinity of the thicket.
A terrestrial deity followed behind that elder, appearing as a woman of supreme beauty, and as if shaking out her hair and arranging it, she [stood] upon his back.
Acting as if wiping away dust and as if arranging her garment to put it on, she followed step by step behind the Elder and emerged from the thicket.
Standing to one side, the Elder friend, seeing that occurrence, was overcome with grief and thought:
"Now my long-standing affection for this monk is lost; if I were to [reveal] such a state..."
Thinking, "I would know [this]; for so long a time I would not have placed my trust in him," he said to the monk as he was still approaching, "Here, friend, take your bowl and robe;
I will not travel the same road with such an evil person. Upon hearing those words, the heart of that modest monk was pierced by a sharp spear.
It appeared as if he were so. Then he said to him: "Friend, what is this you say? For all this time I have not known even a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
Yet today you call me 'evil'; what have you seen? "What need is there for anything else to be seen?
What did you do being in one place with such a woman, beautifully adorned and prepared?"
“He has departed. “This is not possible, friend; I do not see such a woman,” he replied.
Although the other spoke thus up to three times, the elder did not believe him;
instead, taking only what he himself had seen as the truth, he did not go by the same path as the other, but went by another path into the presence of the Teacher.
He departed. The other monk also went to the presence of the Teacher by another path.
Then, at the time when the Saṅgha of monks was entering the Uposatha hall, that monk recognized the other monk in the Uposatha hall and said:
"In this Uposatha hall there is such a wicked monk; I will not [perform the Uposatha] with him."
Thinking, "I shall observe the Uposatha," he went out and stood outside.

Then a terrestrial deity, thinking, "A grave deed has been done by me," approached him in the guise of an elderly lay follower and asked, "Venerable sir, why is the noble one standing in this place? "Lay follower, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall."
“I did not perform the Uposatha with him; I remained outside,” he said. “Venerable sir, do not think so.
This bhikkhu is pure in virtue. I am merely a woman seen by you;
I was here for the purpose of testing you, observing whether the friendship of these elders was firm or not. Thus she spoke while looking for signs of their integrity.
“That deed has been done. “But who are you, good man?

“I am a terrestrial deity, venerable sir,” said the son of the gods, standing there by means of his divine power. He prostrated at the elder’s feet and entreated him, saying, “Venerable sir, forgive me;
the elder did not know this fault. Let us perform the Uposatha. Thus he requested the elder in the Uposatha hall.
He admitted him [into the Saṅgha]. That elder first observed the Uposatha together with him in one place; however, because of their former friendship, he did not remain in one place with him again.
No formal legal procedure (kamma) is recounted regarding this elder, but the elder who had been accused attained Arahatship while repeatedly applying himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā).
Due to the outflow of that karma, as a terrestrial deity, he was not released from the fear of the states of misery for the duration of one interval between Buddhas.
However, whenever he returned to the human state at any time, whatever harm was done by anyone else would fall upon him alone.
During the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a brahmin family; his name was Dhāna-māṇava.
They gave him a name. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas;
later in life, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth.
From the day of his full ordination, a woman beautifully adorned and prepared would enter the village together with him whenever he entered, and leave whenever he left.
When he enters the monastery, she enters with him; when he stands, she stands too—thus she is seen as a constant companion.
The Elder does not see her. Yet, through the residual force of his past karma, she appears before others.
When women in the village give conjey and almsfood, they say: "Venerable sir, this one bowl of conjey is for you; this one is for her."
“Of our companion,” they said, joking. This caused the elder great distress.
Even when he went to the monastery, the novices and young bhikkhus surrounded him and mocked him, saying, “A *koṇḍa* has been born!
Because of that very reason, the name Kuṇḍadhāna Thera arose for him. Rising up again and again, by them...
Unable to endure the play being performed, he fell into a state of madness and said, "You are Koṇḍas! Your preceptor is a Koṇḍa!

Your teacher is a Koṇḍa! Then they reported this to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, Kuṇḍadhāna speaks such harsh words together with the young novices. The Teacher summoned him and asked, "Is it true, Dhāna?"
Having said, "You speak harsh words to the novices," when the other replied, "It is true, Blessed One," he asked, "Why do you speak thus?
He answered, "Venerable sir, unable to endure constant harassment, I speak this way.
The Buddha said, "You cannot digest the karma you have committed in the past until this very day; do not again speak such harsh words to the monks. Having said this, he spoke further:
“Do not speak harshly to anyone; when spoken to, they may retort.
For contentious speech is painful, and retaliatory blows may strike you back.
If you keep yourself unruffled, like a gong that has been struck,”
“You have attained Nibbāna; no agitation exists within you.
Furthermore, they reported this matter of the elder’s wandering about with a woman to the King of Kosala.
The King sent messengers, saying, “Go, men, investigate,” and he himself, with a small retinue, [approached] the elder.
Having gone to the dwelling place, he stood to one side observing.
At that moment, the Elder was sitting performing needlework, and that woman appeared as if standing in a spot not far away.
Seeing this, the king thought, "There must be a reason for this," and went to the place where she was standing. As he approached, she [disappeared] from the Elder’s leaf-hut.
She appeared as if she had entered [the leaf-hut]. The king also, having entered that very leaf-hut with her and searching everywhere, not seeing her, formed the perception:
"This is no woman; it is a single result of the Elder’s karma.
Although he first went near the Elder, he did not pay him homage; then, realizing the truth of the matter, he returned and approached the Elder.
Having paid homage, he sat to one side and asked, "Venerable sir, I hope you are not distressed for lack of almsfood?
The Elder replied, "It is sufficient, Great King. "Venerable sir, I know well the situation of the noble ones;
who indeed would have faith in you while living with such defilement? From now on, you must no longer go anywhere..."
“There is no need for you to do so; I shall attend upon you with the four requisites.
You must not neglect wise attention,” he said, and established a regular supply of almsfood.

Having obtained this support from the king, the Elder, with his mind unified through food that was conducive to his health, developed insight and attained Arahatship. From that time on, the woman disappeared.
At that time, while Mahāsubhaddā was living in the city of Ugganagara in a family of wrong views, she resolved upon the Uposatha, thinking, "May the Teacher have compassion for me.

Having become free from the scent of raw flesh, she stood on the upper terrace of her palace and said, "May these flowers, without remaining in between, stand as a canopy over the head of the One of Ten Powers; may the One of Ten Powers [know] by this sign tomorrow..."
"May he accept alms from me together with five hundred bhikkhus," she said, and having made this declaration of truth (*saccakiriya*), she scattered eight handfuls of *sumana* flowers.
The flowers went forth and, at the time of the Teacher's preaching of the Dhamma, they remained suspended as a canopy over the Teacher’s head.
Seeing that canopy of *sumana* flowers, the Teacher [knew] Subhaddā by means of his own mind.
Having accepted the alms-food, when dawn had risen on the following day, he said to the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, today we shall go for alms as far as a long distance; do not give voting tickets to worldlings, but give them only to the Noble Ones.
The Elder announced this to the monks: "Friends, the Teacher will go for alms as far as a long distance today; [do not give tickets] to worldlings..."
"Do not take them; let only the Noble Ones take the voting tickets. Elder Kuṇḍadhāna said, "Bring it, friend, bring the ticket," and extended his hand first.
Ānanda, having formed the thought, "The Teacher does not cause such bhikkhus as these to receive the ticket;
he causes only the Noble Ones to receive it," went and reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "To him who requests it..."
"Give me a voting ticket," he said. The Elder thought: "If it is not proper for me to give a voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna, then the Teacher will surely prevent me;
there must be a reason for this. Thinking, "I shall give a voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna," he set out on his journey.
Even before Kuṇḍadhāna arrived, [the Elder] had already attained the fourth jhāna, the basis for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having entered into meditative attainment and stood in the air by means of psychic power, he stretched out his hand and took the voting ticket, saying: "Bring it, friend Ānanda; the Teacher knows me;
the Teacher does not forbid a monk such as I from taking the first voting ticket.
On account of this incident, the Teacher made [this] the occasion for [proclaiming] the Elder as the foremost among those who take the first voting ticket in this Dispensation.

He placed him in the foremost position. Since this Elder, having obtained the King as a supporter and through the acquisition of suitable food, attained a concentrated mind and performed the work of insight (vipassanā), became possessed of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) due to his excellence of spiritual potential (upanissaya).
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“For seven days I attended upon the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person,
the Best of Buddhas, with a clear mind and a joyful heart while he was in seclusion.
Knowing that it was time for him to emerge, I served the Great Sage Padumuttara.”
Taking a large plantain leaf, I approached him.
Having accepted it, the Blessed One, the omniscient leader of the world,
the Great Sage, consumed it while gladdening my heart.
Having partaken [of the meal], the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed leader of the caravan,
sat upon his own seat and spoke these verses:
“And those pacifying *yakkhas* who are present on this mountain;”
"O beings of the past and future in the forest, listen to my words:
'I shall praise him who attended upon the Buddha, like a lion, the king of beasts; listen as I speak.'"
“Eleven times he will be a king of the gods;
twenty-four times he will be a wheel-turning monarch.
In a hundred thousand aeons, born into the Okkāka clan,”
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
"By reviling virtuous ascetics who are free from taints,
through the ripening of that evil karma, he shall receive this name."
“He will be a true heir to my Dhamma, born from my mouth, fashioned by the Dhamma;
he will be a disciple known by the name Kuṇḍadhāna.
Devoted to solitude, a meditator delighting in jhāna, I shall be.”
Having gladdened the Teacher, I dwell free from taints.
Surrounded by disciples and honored by the community of monks,
the Jina sat within the assembly of monks and caused the voting sticks to be distributed.
“Having arranged my robe over one shoulder and having paid homage to the Leader of the World,
I first took hold [of the bowl] in the presence of the Best of Speakers.
By that deed, O Blessed One, you who cause the ten-thousandfold world-system to tremble...”
Having sat within the community of bhikkhus, he placed me in the foremost position:
"My energy is the yoke-bearer, carrying me to the security from bondage;
I bear my final body in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Even though this elder was such as this, those ordinary monks who did not know his virtues then wondered at the first distribution of voting tickets, “What indeed is this? To dispel their doubt, the elder—
Having ascended into the sky and displayed a miracle of psychic power, he spoke the verse beginning with "Cut the five" while answering the question through another means.
Therein, "cut the five" refers to the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) which produce rebirth in the states of misery.
Just as a man might cut and abandon the binding rope on his foot with a knife by means of the lower three paths,

so too, "he abandons five" means that a man should, by means of the path of Arahatship, abandon and cut the five higher fetters (*pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojana*) which are the causes for rebirth in the upper deva worlds, just like the binding rope on one's neck. Five.

"One should cultivate them further" means that for the sake of abandoning those very higher fetters (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*), one should cultivate the five faculties beginning with faith even further—above the attainment of the path of non-returning—and increase them by way of attaining the supreme path.

"One who has transcended the five attachments" means that, having become thus, one has transcended the five attachments through their overcoming and abandonment: namely, attachment to lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views.
"Having offered [the sacrifice]. A bhikkhu is called 'one who has crossed the flood' (oghatiṇṇa)": because he has completely shattered the defilements, he is a bhikkhu;
and the meaning is that, having crossed over the floods of sensual desire, existence, views, and ignorance, he is said to be established in Nibbāna, which is the further shore of those floods.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa "Even as a noble thoroughbred horse...
These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa. What is their origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a family home; having approached the Blessed One, he heard the Dhamma.

Having heard [the teaching], he gained faith and went forth; yet, while practicing the duties of a recluse, he was unable to produce any distinction because he lacked the perfection of the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).

However, having accumulated much wholesome merit conducive to the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he saw the Blessed One Vessabhū thirty-one aeons ago and, with a devout mind, offered a *mātuluṅga* fruit.
He gave it away. By that meritorious deed, having been reborn among the devas and performing further acts of merit, he proceeded from a happy destination to a happy destination.
During this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī;
even before the Blessed One’s full enlightenment, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic in the presence of Uruvelakassapa.
While tending the fire at the hermitage of Uruvela-Kassapa, he attained arahantship together with a thousand former matted-hair ascetics through the teaching on the discourse concerning the burning.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower, like the full moon on the fifteenth day;”
I saw the Leader of the World, like a tree ablaze with light.
Having taken a mātuluṅga fruit, I offered it to the Teacher,
the Hero worthy of offerings, with my own hands in full faith.
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I gave that fruit back then, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Thus, on one occasion, after emerging from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), this elder—the preceptor of the Venerable Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika, who had attained the noble fruit—reflected upon that peaceful, sublime, non-material bliss and his own former practice.
Through the force of his rapture, he uttered the verse: "Just as a noble thoroughbred horse... and so forth.
16. *Tattha* (therein): *yathāpi* is a particle used for the purpose of introducing a simile. *Bhadra* means beautiful, endowed with strength, power, capacity, speed, prowess, and so forth.

*Ājañña* means a thoroughbred (*ājānīya*), one of noble birth who understands what is to be done and what is not to be done. There are three kinds: the bull-thoroughbred, the horse-thoroughbred, and the elephant-thoroughbred.
Among these, the bull-thoroughbred is intended here. Furthermore, he is appointed to the task of plowing.
Therefore he said, “*naṅgalāvattanī*. It means that which turns the plough—the share—back and forth, or that which ploughs the field by turning the plough hither and thither.
Alternatively, *naṅgalāvatta* is that where the plough turns; it is the path of the plough in the field, and [the word refers to] that *naṅgalāvatta*.
Here, for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhattha*), it is stated with the long vowel as "*vattanī*. "Sikhī" (the Crested One).
Because it stands upon the head and resembles a crest, it is a "crest" (sikhā), meaning a horn. One who possesses that is a "Sikhī" (the Crested One).
Others, however, say that "kakudha" (the hump) is intended here by the word "sikhā. In either case, this is a description of his preeminent physical characteristics as "Sikhī.
"Without difficulty" means without fatigue. "Night and day" means nights and days; thus, for me...
The construction is: "they go with little difficulty. This is what is meant:

just as a noble bull, when yoked to plowing, goes with little difficulty, turning here and there while disregarding even thick grass, roots, and the like on the furrow-path, until he displays weariness from the plowing of the grass;
so too, for me, even the nights and days pass with little difficulty.

“They go, they transcend. Regarding this, he states the reason: “When non-sensual happiness has been obtained. The meaning is: because the peaceful and sublime happiness of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), which is unmixed with the bait of sensual desires (kāmāmisā), the bait of the world (lokāmisā), and the bait of the round of existence (vaṭṭāmisā), has been obtained;

therefore [they transcend]. This locative case is used in the sense of identity (paccatte), as in the examples “in the forest thickets” (vanappagumbe) and “then indeed, O friend, it should be said” (tena vata re vattabbe). Alternatively, it means from that point onward.
Reflecting that "days and nights pass away without difficulty," he said: "When worldly-free happiness is attained.
The meaning is: when worldly-free happiness has been attained, from the very moment it was attained.
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa is finished.
7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dāsaka “*Middhī yadā*... is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dāsaka. What is its origin?
It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, when no Tathāgata had yet appeared, [the Elder] descended from Mount Gandhamādana to the realm of men during the time of the Paccekabuddha named Ajita.
While he was wandering for alms in a certain village, [a woman] gave him delightful mango fruits.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, he went forth into the teaching during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa and performed much merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
Thus, being devoted to wholesome karma, as he proceeded from a happy destination to a happy destination, in this [life]...
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī. His name was Dāsakokkisa.
He was appointed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika to the task of maintaining the monastery;
while diligently looking after the monastery, he gained faith through frequent visits to the Buddha and listening to the Dhamma, and subsequently went forth. Some, however, say:
“During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, this man was born into a noble family.
When he reached maturity, while attending upon a certain elder who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*), he desired to have some work performed for him and gave orders to the elder.

Because of that deed, during the time of our own Blessed One, he was reborn in Sāvatthī from the womb of Anāthapiṇḍika’s slave-woman. Upon reaching maturity, he was employed by the merchant in the maintenance of the monastery.”
He was established [in the faith] exactly according to the method already described and attained confidence.
Having understood his virtuous conduct, behavior, and disposition, the Great Merchant made him a free man and said, "Go forth as you please. The monks then ordained him.
From the time of his ordination, however, he became indolent and lacking in energy; he performed no part of the duties or observances.
“Where is his ascetic practice? Having eaten as much as he desires, he dwells mostly in sleep.
Even at the time for hearing the Dhamma, he enters a corner and, sitting on the edge of the assembly, sleeps while snoring loudly.
Then the Blessed One, considering his past predispositions, in order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency, said: “When one is slothful and gluttonous...”
...and he spoke this verse: "17.
Therein, 'middhī' means one overcome by *thīna-middha* (sloth and torpor); for whatever *middha* one overcomes, one necessarily overcomes *thīna* as well.

'Yadā' means at which time. 'Mahagghaso' means one who eats much; [this refers to] those who eat from the hand, those who eat until their clothes are soaked, those who eat until they are full, those who eat until they vomit, and those who eat like crows."

"Like a certain [person]. "One who sleeps" means one whose nature is to sleep. "Turning over as he lies" shows that by repeatedly turning over while lying down, he is devoted to both the pleasure of the bed, the pleasure of the side, and the pleasure of torpor.
"Fed on fodder" means nourished and filled with the food of pigs, such as broken rice and the like; for a domestic pig is thus raised from its very childhood.
When his body was stout, being unable to go outside the house, he would simply lie down, turning over and over on his bed and so forth.

This is what is meant: when a man is drowsy and gluttonous—like a great boar filled with fodder—and being unable to maintain himself through any other posture, he is habitually prone to sleep and lies rolling about.
At that time, he was unable to attend to the three characteristics—“impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Due to his failure to attend to them, being of dull wisdom, he entered the womb again and again and was not liberated from dwelling in the womb.
Upon hearing this, the Elder Dāsaka was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; he established insight meditation and before long realized Arhatship.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Fully Enlightened One named Ajita then dwelt in the Himalayas;
the Sage was perfected in conduct and skilled in meditative concentration.”
“To the golden-hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings,
as he was entering the street, I gave a mango fruit.
In the ninety-first aeon from now, because I gave that fruit then— ”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

Having attained arahantship, the Elder recited that very verse, saying, “The Blessed One instructed me with this verse; it has become my goad,” and thus his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*) was accomplished by means of repeating the words of another.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dāsaka is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Siṅgālakapitu:
"There was an heir of the Buddha... These are the verses of the Elder Siṅgālakapitu. What is their origin? It is said that he lived ninety-four [aeons] ago from now.
In that eon, having seen the Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsi wandering for alms, he paid homage with a devout mind and gave him a palm fruit from his own hand.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas;
performing further merits and wandering through successive happy realms, he was eventually reborn in the human womb during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having gained faith in the Teaching, he went forth and cultivated the perception of the skeleton (*aṭṭhikasaññā*).
Later, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, he took a wife, obtained a son, and gave him the name Siṅgālaka;
thus, he was addressed as "Siṅgālaka’s father. At a later time, he...
Having abandoned the bonds of home, he went forth into the Teaching. The Blessed One, observing his inclination, gave him the meditation subject of the perception of the skeleton.
Having taken that up, he dwelt among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
Then, a deity dwelling in that forest, for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in him, said: "The fruit of your cultivation will soon be within your grasp."
Clarifying this matter by means of a different designation, she spoke the verse beginning, “There was an heir of the Buddha.
(18) Therein, *ahu* means “was”; this is a word for the past tense used in the sense of the present. *Buddhassa* means “of the omniscient Buddha.
*Dāyādo* means “an heir,” specifically an heir to the Dhamma, through one’s own correct practice of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
*Ādāyako* means one who takes or seizes. Alternatively, *ahū* means "there was.
The intention is that some obstacle to his status as an heir to such a Buddha will arise right now. Therefore he said: "I think that he will soon carry away [his] lust for sensual pleasures.
Regarding *Bhesakaḷāvana*: it is so called because it was obtained and taken possession of by a *yakkha* named Bhesaka; or else, because of the *bhesakaḷas*.
In the forest named Bhesakaḷāvana, so called because of its abundance of wood and other such things;
speaking of the reason for that bhikkhu’s status as a true heir of the Buddha, he said: “With the perception of bones alone, he overspread this earth.
Therein, *kevalaṃ* means entirely and without exception. *Aṭṭhisaññāya* means by the meditation on the nature of bones. *Apharī* means [he overspread], thinking “bones.”
He expanded [the meditation] by way of resolute conviction. "Earth" refers to the earth that is one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*).
For here, "personal existence" is called "earth," as in such passages as, "Who shall destroy this earth? He thinks: "I think.
The reading *maññāhaṃ* is also found. "He"—that is, that bhikkhu—will quickly, before long, abandon and relinquish sensual lust.
I think so. Why? Because the perception of the skeleton is the direct antidote to sensual lust. This is what is meant:

a bhikkhu who, having obtained the perception of the skeleton in one part, stands pervading his own entire body or the bodies of all beings as nothing but bones—he, making that jhāna on the skeleton his basis and practicing insight, will before long [attain deliverance].
"By means of the path of non-returning, he will abandon craving— which, in the sense of 'desiring,' is called 'kāma,' and in the sense of 'delighting,' is called 'rāga'—
by means of the supreme path. Having heard this verse, that elder, thinking,
"This deity has spoken thus for the purpose of generating effort in me," resolved upon unyielding energy and developed insight (vipassanā).
He attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Sataraṃsī, the self-become, the unconquered;
having arisen from seclusion, went forth for alms.”
“Holding fruit in my hand, I saw the Bull among Men and approached him;
with a clear heart and joyful mind, I gave him a palm fruit.
For ninety-four aeons from that time, because of the fruit I then gave, [the results have ripened].”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

Having attained arahantship, he recited that very verse as an inspired utterance (udāna) in response to the words spoken by that deity. That itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Siṅgālapitā is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kula:
“For one leading away water,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kula. What is their origin? It is said that this elder was already [a practitioner] in the past.
Having accumulated a great deal of wholesome merit as a support for the turning away from saṃsāra, he was endowed with spiritual excellence.
Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī traveling through the air, he stood there with a devout mind, desiring to offer a coconut fruit.
The Teacher, knowing his intention, descended and accepted it. With an exceedingly clear mind, by virtue of that very acquisition of faith, he—
Having approached the Teacher, he requested the going-forth; the Teacher commanded a certain bhikkhu, "Ordain this man.

Having been ordained and received full admission, and having practiced the duty of a recluse, when he passed away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans for six intervals between Buddhas.
Then, during the arising of this present Buddha, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
He was reborn, and his name was Kulotissa. When he reached maturity, having gained faith in the Dispensation, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One;
however, due to his great restlessness, he was unable to achieve any distinction.
Then one day, while entering a village for alms, he dug the earth along the way and constructed a water channel so that water would flow to wherever he desired.
Having seen a man and observed him, he entered a village; there he saw a fletcher inserting an arrow-shaft into a reed-stand and straightening it by looking at it with the corner of his eye.
Having observed that as well, as he was going along, he went further ahead and saw carpenters fashioning parts of a chariot wheel, such as the rim, the nave, and so forth.

Having observed that as well, he entered the monastery; after finishing his meal and putting away his bowl and robes, while sitting in the daytime dwelling, he took the signs he had seen as metaphors and applied them to the taming of his own mind, thinking:
"Even insentient water, people lead wherever they wish; likewise, even an insentient, crooked reed-stalk—"
“By means of skillful methods, people straighten what is crooked; likewise, carpenters straighten and bend wood, logs, and the like by means of lathe-axes and other tools.

So why should I not straighten my own mind? Having thought thus, he established insight meditation and, striving and exerting himself, attained Arahatship before long. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a monastery attendant.
I saw the stainless Buddha traveling along the wind-swept path.
Taking a coconut fruit, I gave it to the Supreme Buddha.”
Standing in the sky, the one of great renown accepted it.
"Producing joy for me and bringing happiness in this very life,
having given the fruit to the Buddha with a serene mind."
“At that time I attained rapture and vast, supreme bliss;
for wherever it was produced, a jewel indeed arose.
In the ninety-first aeon hence, that fruit which I then gave—”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
My divine eye is purified, I am skilled in concentration, and I have reached perfection in the higher knowledges; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Thus, having taken those signs as goads and having developed insight, he reached Arahantship. Combining his own taming of the mind with those [signs], he spoke the verse beginning, “For water-carriers lead the water,” while declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*).
19. Regarding that, in the phrase “water indeed” (*udakaṃ hi*), the word *hi* is a mere particle. “They lead” (*nayanti*) means they direct it from place to place on the earth.
Having dug out low-lying places, having filled them, or having made channels or set up wooden troughs, they lead the water to whatever place they desire.
Because they lead it thus, they are called "channel-makers" (*nettikā*). "The shaft" (*tejana*) means an arrow. This is what is meant:
channel-makers lead water to whatever place they wish according to their own preference; fletchers also, having heated it, bend the shaft straight.
They fashion [it]. By means of bending, carpenters, when planing wood for the sake of rims and so forth, bend it according to their own preference, making it either straight or curved.

In the same way, having made this much their object, those of good vows, possessing beautiful conduct through the morality and other qualities they have undertaken, and being wise, tame themselves by generating the path of stream-entry and so forth, [attaining] arahantship.
But among those who have attained [the goal], they are called "exclusively tamed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kula is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Ajita.
The verse of the Venerable Elder Ajita begins: "I have no fear of death. What is its origin?
It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, he offered a wood-apple fruit with a mind full of faith.
Thereafter, performing various meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, even before our own [Buddha] had appeared in this aeon, he...
In Sāvatthī, he was reborn as the son of a brahmin who was the chief court priest to the Great King of Kosala;

his name was Ajita. At that time, a brahmin named Bāvari, a resident of Sāvatthī, who possessed the three marks of a great man and had mastered the three Vedas, departed from Sāvatthī and went forth into the ascetic life.
Having gone forth, he dwelt in the Kapittha Monastery on the banks of the Godhāvarī River.
Then Ajita, who had gone forth in his presence, was sent by Bāvari—having been urged by a deity desiring his welfare—to the presence of the Teacher.
Together with Tissa Metteyya and others, he approached the Blessed One; having asked his questions mentally, and when those [questions] were answered, his mind became filled with faith.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, taken up a meditation subject, and developed insight, he attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Sambuddha, golden-hued, the recipient of offerings;”
As I was traveling along the road, I gave a wood-apple fruit.
Because I gave that fruit ninety-one eons ago, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he uttered this verse while letting out a lion’s roar: “In death there is no fear for me.
Herein, “in death” means on account of death, with death as the cause. “For me” means for myself; “there is no fear” because the root of existence has been severed.

Because birth has been completely exhausted. For those whose root of existence (*bhava*) is not severed, there might be fear of death, thinking, "What will my future rebirth be like? "Attachment" (*nikanti*) means longing or craving;

that does not exist [for me], because the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), having their formations thoroughly crushed, manifest clearly as being essentially nothing but suffering and devoid of core substance. And being such as this, I cross over the doubt...
