“I shall lay down, I shall cast off, my own body—that which is reckoned as a body, this burden of suffering. And while laying it down, thinking:

“What was to be accomplished with this body has been accomplished; now it must certainly be discarded,” I shall lay it down, being fully aware through the attainment of abundance of wisdom, and clearly mindful through the attainment of abundance of mindfulness. This—
Having spoken this verse, the Elder entered into jhāna and immediately thereafter attained final nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ajita is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. Third Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nigrodha.
"I do not fear fear," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Nigrodha. What is their origin? It is said that this...

Eighteen hundred kappas ago, having been reborn in a family of great brahmin householders, he reached maturity and, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, abandoned the bonds of home and entered a forest region.
There, having built a leaf-hut in a certain sāl grove, he went forth as an ascetic and lived subsisting on forest roots and fruits. By him—

At that time, the Sammasambuddha named Piyadassi, having appeared in the world, was extinguishing the heat of the defilements for the world including its devas with the rain of the nectar of the Dhamma.
One day, out of compassion for the ascetics, he entered that Sāla grove and attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
While the ascetic was going to gather forest roots and fruits, he saw the Blessed One and, with a mind full of faith, [approached] the blossoming trunks and branches of the Sāla trees.
Having taken [the flowers] and fashioned a *sāla*-bower, he completely covered it with *sāla* blossoms.
After paying homage to the Blessed One, he stood there offering worship, moved by joy and gladness, and did not even go for the sake of food.
The Teacher, having emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), thought out of compassion for him, "Let the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) come," and [considered] "In the community of monks..."
“...he will clarify his mind. At that very moment, the community of monks arrived. Seeing the community of monks as well, he paid homage with a serene mind and stood with palms joined in reverence.

The Teacher, under the pretext of manifesting a smile, spoke the Dhamma, revealing the man’s future prosperity, and then departed together with the community of monks. By means of that meritorious deed, he—
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he accumulated a vast amount of wholesome merit as a basis for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
During this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a prominent brahmin family; his name was Nigrodha.

On the day the Jeta Grove was accepted [as a monastery], he conceived faith upon seeing the majesty of the Buddha, went forth into homelessness, and having begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), before long—
He became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having plunged into a grove of *sāla* trees, my well-prepared hermitage was there;
covered with *sāla* blossoms, I dwelt then in that forest."
“The Blessed One Piyadassī, the self-become, the supreme person,
the Sambuddha who desires solitude, approached the Sāla grove.
Having departed from my hermitage, I went to the forest.”
Seeking roots and fruits, I was then wandering in the forest.
There I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One, lovely to behold and of great renown,
seated in perfect composure, shining brilliantly in the great forest.
“Having erected four pillars and constructed a well-made pavilion above the Buddha, I covered it with *sāla* flowers.
Having maintained that *sāla*-covered pavilion for seven days,”
Having gladdened my mind there, I paid homage to the Best of Buddhas:
“At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen from his meditative absorption,
sat down— the Supreme among Men— gazing a yoke’s length ahead.”
“A disciple named Varuṇa approached the Teacher Piyadassī,
the Guide, together with one hundred thousand seers.
And the Blessed One Piyadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men— ”
Seated within the community of bhikkhus, the Jina manifested a smile.
Anuruddha was the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassi;
having arranged his robe over one shoulder, he questioned the Great Sage.
“What indeed, Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher’s smile?
Since there is a reason present, the Teacher has manifested a smile.
‘The young brahmin who bore my sal-tree canopy for seven days—’”
Recalling that deed, I broke into a smile:
"I see no place where merit ripens—whether in the world of the gods or among humans; there is simply no room for it."
“For one who dwells in the world of the gods, endowed with meritorious deeds,
his assembly shall be as vast as a forest of *sāla* trees.
There, amidst divine dances, songs, and instrumental music,”
The virtuous one, established in meritorious deeds, will always obtain it.
"As long as his assembly remains, so long will he be fragrant with scent,
and a rain of *sāla* flowers shall fall."
“Having passed away from there, this person will return to the human realm;
here too, the canopy of *sāla* trees shall endure for all time.
Here, dancing and singing, accompanied by the rhythmic beat of drums, shall prevail.”
“They will always attend upon me; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
And as the sun rises, a shower falls from the *sāla* tree;
joined with meritorious karma, it rains at all times.
“In eighteen hundred kappas,
one born of the Okkāka clan, named Gotama, will become a Teacher in the world.
A true heir to his Dhamma, a son born from his own breast, fashioned by the Dhamma;”
“Having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
For one who penetrates the Dhamma, there will be a canopy of *sāla* trees;
for one being cremated on the pyre, that shall serve as a covering there.”
Having proclaimed the result of his own kamma, the Great Sage Piyadassī taught the Dhamma to the assembly, gladdening them with a rain of Dhamma.
For thirty eons, he exercised sovereignty among the devas.
Sixty-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
Having come here from the world of the gods, I obtain abundant happiness;
even here, this *sāla*-canopy is the fruit of that pavilion.
“This is my last, my final existence now proceeds;
here too, the Sāla-tree canopy shall be mine for all time.
Having satisfied the Great Sage Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas,”
I have reached the immovable state, having abandoned both victory and defeat.
Because I worshipped the Buddha during eighteen hundred eons, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been incinerated by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a nāga who has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
Truly, it was a blessing for me to come into the presence of the Supreme Buddha.”
The three types of higher knowledge have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“The four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations;
the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Having thus become one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijña*), and while spending his time in the bliss of the fruit [of liberation], he spoke this verse beginning with “I do not fear fear” by way of declaring his final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*), in order to demonstrate the nature of the Dispensation as leading to liberation.
21. In this context, it is called *bhaya* (fear) because they fear it; that is, birth, aging, and so forth.

*Bhayassa* is a genitive case used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*); the meaning is: “I do not fear from fear,” that is, from the cause consisting of birth, aging, death, and so on, which is the object to be feared. Therein...
He states the reason: "Our Teacher is skilled in the Deathless. Our Teacher is proficient in the Deathless; he is expert in bestowing the Deathless upon those who are to be trained.
"Wherein fear does not abide" means that in Nibbāna, as previously described, fear finds no footing and gains no opportunity.
"From there" means from that Nibbāna. "They go" means they proceed precisely to the state of fearlessness.
For Nibbāna is indeed called the state of fearlessness. But by what means do they go there? To this he says: "The bhikkhus go by way of the path.
This means that the bhikkhus—who carry out the Teacher’s instruction—go by means of the Noble Eightfold Path, as they are those who look upon the fear within saṃsāra.
Or, the word *yattha* (where) refers to that cause (*nimitta*), namely, the Noble Path, by reason of the attainment of which self-reproach and so forth [cease].
"Even the twenty-five kinds of fear do not remain; they find no foothold.
For that reason, the bhikkhus in the Teacher’s dispensation go by means of that noble path to the state of fearlessness. By that same path I too have gone;
therefore, I am not afraid of fear. Thus the Elder declared his realization.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nigrodha is finished.
2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cittaka:
"Nīlāsugīva" refers to the verses of the Venerable Elder Cittaka. What is his origin? It is said that from the time of Padumuttara Buddha...
From that time onward, accumulating wholesome merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), he was reborn in the human womb ninety-one aeons ago.

Having attained maturity and seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of flowers, paid homage, and resolved upon the Teacher and Nibbāna, thinking: "There must surely be a state of peace here."
Having passed away from there due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Performing further merits and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin, by name Cittaka.
When the Blessed One went to Rājagaha and stayed at the Veḷuvana grove...
While dwelling [there], he approached the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith.
Having gone forth and taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suited to his temperament, he entered a forest region.
Devoted to meditation, he attained jhāna, and by developing insight based on that jhāna, he reached Arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I saw the stainless Buddha Vipassī, the leader of the world, sitting amidst the mountains, radiant like a *kaṇikāra* flower.
Having plucked three *kiṅkaṇī* flowers, I offered them to him.”
Having paid homage to the Fully Awakened One, I departed facing the south.
By that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I made offerings to a Buddha, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula] ...the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship, he went to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher.

There, when asked by the bhikkhus, "Friend, did you dwell diligently in the forest?", he answered with a declaration of his own diligent dwelling by reciting the verse beginning, "The blue-necked one."
22. Therein, "nīlāsugīvā" means those with blue and beautiful necks; here, the vowel is lengthened for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukha*).
The meaning is: "endowed with a beautiful neck characterized by a patterned design. They are mostly "blue" because of their blue color.

They are "beautiful-necked" (*sugīvā*) because of the elegance of their throats. "Sikhino" (crested) means they possess a crest (*sikhā*) growing on their heads that is radiant. "Morā" means peacocks.
*Kārambiyanti* means "in the *kāramba* trees. Or else, *kārambiyanti* is the name of that forest; therefore, the meaning is "in the forest named *kāramba*.

*Abhinadanti* means that, having heard the thundering of the clouds during the rainy season, they utter their *kekā* cries and, with voices perfected by the excellence of the season, they cry out as if surpassing the swans and other birds. *Te* refers to those peacocks.
“Sporting in the cool breeze” means sporting, as it were, with the cool wind from the clouds, raining down sweet showers.
“Slept” means lying down for the sake of dispelling the drowsiness caused by food, or sleeping at the permitted time for the purpose of allaying physical fatigue.
“Meditate” means those whose nature is to meditate through the jhānas of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), being devoted to spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*). “Awakened” means—
They awaken [others] with the thought: "Even these people, not succumbing to sleep but remaining awake, perform what ought to be done by themselves; how much more so should I?
Thus, the intention is that they rouse one from lying down by generating clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cittaka is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gosāla “Indeed, in the bamboo grove... This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Gosāla. What is its origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) here and there, during the ninety-first aeon ago...

On a certain mountain, seeing the rag-robe of a Paccekabuddha hanging from the branch of a tree, he thought with a devout heart, "This is indeed the banner of an Arahant," and worshipped it with flowers.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. From then on, wandering only among gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
In the kingdom of Magadha, he was born into a wealthy clan (ibbha-kula) and was known by the name Gosāla.

However, because he had previously been acquainted with Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa, when he heard that the latter had gone forth, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*sañjāta-saṃvega*), thinking: "If even one of such great wealth has gone forth, why should I not do so?
Having thus gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) suited to his temperament, he [sought] what was appropriate...
Seeking a place to dwell, he lived on a certain mountain ridge not far from his own birthplace.
His mother gave him almsfood every day. Then one day, when he had entered the village for alms, his mother gave him rice porridge prepared with honey and sugar.
Taking that, he went into the shade of a bamboo thicket on that mountain.
Having sat down at the foot [of the tree] and partaken of his meal, he washed his bowl and hands and began insight meditation (*vipassanā*).

Through the attainment of suitable food, his body and mind became healthy; thus, being concentrated, as the knowledges of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and the others grew sharp, courageous, and powerful, he easily brought insight to its peak and, following the sequence of the paths, reached the culmination of his development together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
He realized arhatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa;
there I saw a rag-robe hanging upon the branch of a tree.”
“Having then plucked three kiṅkaṇī flowers,
with a heart uplifted from below, I worshipped the rag-robe.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations...”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
"In the ninety-first aeon from now, because of the deed I performed then—
having honored the banner of the Arhat— I have not known a miserable rebirth."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahatship, desiring to go to the mountain peak itself for the sake of dwelling in the happiness of the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra), he spoke this verse, “I, indeed, in the bamboo thicket,” while proclaiming his own practice: “Having eaten the honeyed milk-rice...

Regarding that, “in the bamboo thicket” (veḷugumbasmiṃ) means in the vicinity of a bamboo grove, in its shade. “Having eaten the honeyed milk-rice” (bhutvāna madhupāyasaṃ)... [the verse continues]... “I am going to the mountain peak. (Note: The provided text fragment ends here.)
Having eaten the milk-rice mixed with honey, "clockwise" means by way of grasping what is favorable, that is, by correctly receiving the Teacher’s instruction—this is the meaning.
"Contemplating the arising and passing away of the aggregates" means contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging;
even though his task is now accomplished, he nevertheless enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
The intention is: "I shall establish insight. "I will go to the mountain peak" means: I will go specifically toward that very mountain peak where I previously dwelt.
"Cultivating seclusion" means: cultivating both the seclusion of subsided defilements (*paṭipassaddhiviveka*) and the bodily seclusion of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*);
or, I will go for the sake of cultivating that [seclusion]. Having spoken thus, the Elder remained right there.
He has gone; this indeed was the verse of the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gosāla is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sugandha.
"Having gone forth every year" refers to the verse of the Venerable Sugandha Thera. What is its origin?
It is said that ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Tissa, he was reborn in the human womb;
having reached maturity, he wandered in the forest as a hunter. Out of compassion for him, the Teacher showed him a footpath.

He went there. Having seen the Teacher’s footprint-shrines, and because he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he thought, "These are the footprints of the Supreme Person in the world with its devas," and filled with joy and gladness, he took *koraṇḍaka* flowers, made an offering, and gladdened his heart.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; having passed away from there, he [was reborn] again and again.
Having performed meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he became a householder during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.

Having offered a great almsgiving to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and having ground highly precious yellow sandalwood to plaster the interior of the Gandhakuṭī, he made this aspiration: “In whatever place I am reborn, may I...”

"May my body be thus fragrant. Having performed many meritorious deeds in various states of existence in this manner, and wandering only among the happy realms, he was reborn during the present arising of a Buddha in the home of a wealthy brahmin in Sāvatthī.
From the time he entered his mother’s womb until after his birth, his mother—
His entire body emitted a fragrant scent; on the day of his birth, however, it was especially supremely sweet-smelling, and this fragrance wafted even into the houses of his neighbors.
His parents, thinking, "Our son has come having taken his own name for himself," gave him the name Sugandha.
As he gradually reached maturity, he saw the Elder Mahāsela.
Having heard the Dhamma in his presence, he went forth and, while practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship* within seven days.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the past, I was a forest worker; my father and mother had passed away.”
“I live by slaughtering animals; no wholesome merit exists for me.
Yet, near my dwelling, the Leader of the World, the Three-Eyed One, out of compassion, showed three footprints.”
“Having seen the footprint of the Teacher named Tissa,
with a joyful heart I gladdened my mind in that footprint.
Having seen the *koraṇḍa* tree in full bloom, growing from the earth...”
Having taken whatever cloth I had, I honored the Best of Men.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned this human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
“Whichever womb I was reborn into, whether among the gods or among humans,
I had skin like the *koraṇḍaka* flower and I was exceedingly radiant.
Because of that deed which I performed ninety-two eons ago, [I have attained this result].”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of worshipping the footprint.

Having attained arahantship and declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*), he spoke this verse: “I went forth every year,” and so forth. “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. It was after attaining arahantship that he spoke this verse while declaring his final knowledge: “I went forth every year.”
24. Therein, "anuvassika" means one who has followed (*anugata*) or approached (*upagata*) the rains; thus it is "anuvassa. One who is "anuvassika" is simply one who has entered the rains.
"Pabbajita" means one who has approached the going-forth (*pabbajjā*); the meaning is that one who, having gone forth, has merely entered the rains for one year is "ekavassika.
Alternatively, "anuvassa" refers to the rains that have followed, come after, or departed; one who possesses that is "anuvassika. Of whom...
Because the year of one who has gone forth is not yet complete, it does not count; thus, when he is addressed in this way, it is said that he is "not yet a full year" (*avassika*).

"Behold the excellence of the Dhamma" (*passa dhammasudhammata*): behold the state of being well-expounded, the state of being perfectly proclaimed, and the quality of leading exclusively to liberation of the Dhamma of your Teacher, wherein you were ordained for less than a year.
[The knowledge of] past lives and the knowledge of the divine eye.
"Knowledge of the destruction of the taints": the three types of higher knowledge have been attained and realized by you;
for that very reason, "the teaching of the Buddha"—that is, the instruction and admonition of the Perfectly Enlightened One—"has been practiced.
Based on this fulfillment of what was to be done, the Elder, filled with joy and gladness, speaks of himself as if he were another person.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sugandha is finished.
5. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nandiya.
"A radiance has arisen"—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Nandiya. What is its origin? It is said that he [was born] during the time of Padumuttara...
When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna during the time of the Blessed One, he had a railing made of sandalwood for the shrine and performed a magnificent offering and act of reverence.
From that time forth, being endowed with noble aspiration, he accumulated much meritorious karma conducive to the realization of liberation in various places;
and as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
He was reborn in Kapilavatthu in the royal Sakyan clan. Because his birth brought joy to his parents, they gave him the name Nandiya.
When he reached maturity, after Anuruddha and others had gone forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher, he too went forth.
Performing the work of insight meditation, he attained Arahantship before long due to his prior merit. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eldest in the world, the bull among men—
having blazed like a mass of fire, the Sambuddha has attained final Nibbāna.
And when the Great Hero had attained Nibbāna, his stupa became widespread.”
Even from afar they pay homage at the most excellent house of the relics.
With a clear heart and a joyful mind, he constructed a railing of sandalwood;
at that time, the trunk of the stupa appeared, worthy of the stupa.
“As I was being reborn in existence, whether as a god or a human, I did not see anything deficient in myself; this is the fruit of my former karma.
Fifteen hundred eons ago, there were eight people from here.”
"All those named Samatta were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
Having attained arahantship, while dwelling together with the Elder Anuruddha and others in the Pācīnavaṃsa Migadāya, [he spoke] this... [verse]. In this [context]:
On one occasion, Māra the Evil One, desiring to terrify him, displayed a fearsome form. The Elder, recognizing it as "this is Māra," said:
"O Evil One, what can your machinations do to those who have transcended the realm of Māra?
On the contrary, because of this, you yourself will meet with distress and misfortune. Thus showing this, he spoke: "The light has arisen..."
He recited the verse beginning with “phalagaṃ.
Therein, “obhāsajātaṃ” means that light has arisen through the light of knowledge (*ñāṇobhāsa*), because the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*) has been attained.
By that, the meaning is that it is exceedingly radiant due to the total destruction and dispersal of the darkness of the defilements (*kilesa-andhakāra*).
“Phalaganti” means having reached the fruit, having arrived at it; the intention is that it is accompanied by the knowledge of the highest fruit (*aggaphala*).
“Cittaṃ” refers generally to the mind of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). Therefore he said, “frequently.

For because those whose taints are destroyed constantly enter the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship throughout all time due to their inclination toward cessation, that mind deserves to be called “accompanied by the fruit.”
*Tādisaṃ* means "of such a kind," that is to say, an *arahant*. *Āsajja* means having assailed or having overcome.
*Kaṇha* is an address to Māra; for he is called "Kaṇha" because of his dark deeds and his dark birth.
*Dukkhaṃ nigacchasi* means you will undergo suffering—here, suffering consisting of useless physical exhaustion such as entering into foul places, and [suffering] in the future world...
"And you shall incur, you shall reach, the suffering of the states of misery for which there is no remedy. Having heard this, Māra thought, "The ascetic knows me," and vanished right then and there.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nandiya is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya "Having heard well-spoken words," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Abhaya. What is their origin?
It is said that he went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara and became a preacher of the Dhamma. At the time of preaching the Dhamma, first, by means of four...
Having praised the Blessed One with verses, he afterwards preached the Dhamma.
By the power of that meritorious deed, for a hundred thousand aeons, there was no rebirth for him in the states of misery. Thus it is said:
“Having praised the Self-Existent Abhaya, the Victor Padumuttara, with a devout heart...”
“Possessing sublime faith, he shall not go to the plane of misery for hundreds of thousands of eons.

Due to the excellence of his field [of merit] and the like, and because of the exceedingly sublime nature of his preceding and succeeding volitions of final determination, such was that immeasurable outflow of merit, that outflow of the wholesome. “For those who have faith in the inconceivable, the result—”
For it is said: “It is inconceivable. In various states of existence, the merit he had accumulated served as a support for him.
Thus, he made an offering of *ketaka* flowers to the Blessed One Vipassī.
By means of such sublime and distinguished merits, wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn in this current arising of a Buddha as the son of King Bimbisāra.
His name was Abhayatissa. His origin will be made clear later.

Having been instructed by the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta in a dilemma consisting of two opposing points, and being dispatched with the command, "Having asked this question, refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama," he approached the Blessed One, asked that question, and [regarding] that question—

When the Blessed One had declared that the matter was not to be answered categorically, the Nigaṇṭhas were defeated; and having recognized the Teacher’s state as a Perfectly Enlightened One, he professed himself a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

Then, after King Bimbisāra passed away, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went forth into the Dispensation, and having become a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) through the teaching of the *Tālacchiggaḷūpama-sutta*, he again applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
He realized arhatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the Vinatā River, the Supreme Person dwelt;
I saw the stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-composed.”
“With a flower of honey-scented *ketaka*, I then,
with a clear heart and joyful mind, worshipped the Best of Buddhas.
In the ninety-first aeon from now, because I worshipped that flower...”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Having attained arahantship, he then spoke the verse beginning with “Having heard well-spoken words,” declaring his own realization by extolling his own practice. Thus he said: “*Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsanan*. (The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then, having attained arahantship, he declared his own realization (*aññā*) by extolling his own practice, speaking the verse: “*Sutvā subhāsitaṃ vācan*. (Having heard well-spoken words...)
26. Therein, "having heard" means having lent the ear and having investigated by way of the door of the ear.

"Well-spoken" means spoken well, spoken correctly; it refers to a discourse on the Dhamma that reveals the Four Truths, which has been spoken—by virtue of being the Perfectly Enlightened One and out of great compassion—without contradicting anything, but as the absolute means for establishing the intended meaning.
For there is no teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One that is devoid of truth.
"Of the Buddha" means of the omniscient Buddha. "Kinsman of the Sun": because he was born in the lineage of the sun, the sun is his kinsman;
thus he is the Kinsman of the Sun, the Blessed One. Or, the Blessed One is the Kinsman of the Sun; thus he is the Kinsman of the Sun. Of that Blessed One.
Because he was his own legitimate son. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“He who, in the darkness and gloom, is the maker of light, the radiant one with a circular halo and fierce splendor—O Rāhu, do not swallow him as he moves through the sky! O Rāhu, release my offspring, the Sun!”
"Paccabyadhiṃ" means I penetrated. "Hī" is a mere particle. "Nipuṇaṃ" means subtle, extremely refined;
it refers to the truth of cessation, or indeed to the four truths themselves. Alternatively, "hī" is a particle used in the sense of a cause. The meaning is:
because I have penetrated the subtle four truths, there is now nothing further to be penetrated. As for how he penetrated them:

He said: "As with the tip of a hair by means of an arrow. The construction is as follows: just as a well-trained, skilled archer, hitting his mark without missing, might pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with an arrow, even so did he penetrate the subtle Noble Truths.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Abhaya is finished.
7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya "Grass and Kuśa" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Lomasakaṅgiya. What is its origin?
It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī and with a mind full of faith, he worshipped him with various flowers; by that meritorious deed...
Having been reborn in the world of the devas, he performed further merits again and again and continued to wander only through the happy realms.
Then, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he practiced the duties of a recluse.
At that time, when the Teacher had spoken on the practice of the "One Fortunate Night," a certain bhikkhu engaged him in a discussion based on the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*. He [the former]—

He did not understand. Not understanding, he made a resolution, thinking, "May I in the future be capable of preaching the *Bhaddekaratta* to you," while the other [the monk] resolved, "May he ask me.
Of these two, the first wandered among gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, and was reborn at the time of our Blessed One in the Sākyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. To him...
Because of his delicate nature, fine hairs grew on the soles of his feet like those of Soṇa; therefore, he was named Lomasakaṅgiya.
The other, having been reborn in the world of the gods, became known as Candana.
When Anuruddha and the other Sakyan princes went forth into homelessness, Lomasakaṅgiya did not wish to go forth. Then, in order to stir him with a sense of urgency, the deva-son Candana—
Having approached him, he asked about the *Bhaddekaratta*. The other replied, "I do not know.
Again, the devaputta rebuked him, saying, "Then why did you make a pact with me, saying, 'Let us speak of the *Bhaddekaratta*,' yet now you do not even know its name?
The other, together with him, approached the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, it seems that previously I [made a pact] with this one..."

“I made a promise, saying, ‘I shall preach the *Bhaddekaratta* discourse. The Blessed One said, “Yes, noble son, you did indeed make such a promise at the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. This matter should be understood in detail according to the method found in the *Uparipaṇṇāsa*.
Then Lomasakaṅgiya said, “In that case, venerable sir, please grant me the going-forth. The Blessed One said, “No...”
He refused, saying, "The Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.
He went to his mother and said, "Mother, give me permission to go forth; I shall go forth.
When his mother said, "Dear one, you are so delicate; how will you go forth? he, demonstrating his capacity to endure hardships...
He recited the verse: “*Dabbaṃ kusaṃ poṭakilan*.
(27) Therein, *dabba* refers to the *dabba* grass, which is also called *saddula*. *Kusa* refers to the *kusa* grass, which is called *kāsa*.
*Poṭakila* refers to a shrub, both thorny and thornless; however, in this context, it refers specifically to the thorny variety.

This is what is intended. *Usīra* and the others are easy to understand. As for the *dabba* grasses and other such weeds, they cause pain even when stepped upon by the feet and create obstacles to walking;
yet I shall push them aside with my chest and remove them with my chest.
Pushing them away in this manner, enduring that painful sensation, I shall enter the interior of a thicket in the forest region.
"I shall be able to practice the duty of a recluse"—this shows that there is no need even to mention being trodden upon by feet.
"Cultivating seclusion" means cultivating bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).
For one who has abandoned the company of crowds and cultivates bodily seclusion, and who concentrates the mind on any one of the thirty-eight meditation objects, [the hindrances do not arise].

There is seclusion of mind for one who does not delight in company; there is attainment of seclusion from the substrates (upadhiviveka) through the wearing away of the defilements by one who is concentrated, performing the work of insight and yoking serenity and insight together, but not for one who is unconcentrated.
Therefore it is said: "They cultivate seclusion," meaning they cultivate bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrates.
When the son had spoken thus, his mother said, "In that case, dear one, go forth," and gave her permission. He approached the Blessed One and requested the going-forth.

The Teacher granted him the going-forth. Having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject and was entering the forest when the monks said to him, "Friend, you are so delicate; how will you be able [to endure it]?"

"Let us dwell in the forest. Having spoken that same verse to them as well, he entered the forest and, applying himself to meditation, before long became one possessed of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"To the golden-hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings..."
As he was setting out on the road, I honored him with various flowers.
“For ninety-one eons, because of the flower I offered in worship, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping a Buddha.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, the Elder spoke that very same verse as his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya is finished.
8. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Jambugāmiyaputta "Is it not that you are intent on clothing?"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Jambugāmiyaputta. What is its origin?
It is said that he, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated there wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, one day, having seen *kiṃsuka* flowers, he took those flowers and, recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, offered them in honor of the Blessed One by tossing them into the air as an act of worship.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Thereafter, performing further meritorious deeds, he passed from state to state among gods and humans.
While wandering in saṃsāra, during this dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in Campā as the son of a lay follower named Jambugāmiya.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Thereafter, performing further meritorious deeds and wandering successively through the realms of gods and humans, during this same dispensation of a Buddha, in Campā, [he was born] as the son of a lay follower named Jambugāmiya.

He was reborn there, and thus he received the name Jambugāmiyaputta. When he reached maturity, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and lived in the Añjana Forest at Sāketa.
Then his father thought, "Does my son indeed dwell with delight in the Teaching?"
In order to investigate whether or not this was so, he wrote the verse beginning with “I hope you are not addicted to clothing” and sent it.

Having read it, [the son] was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, “My father suspects me of living in negligence, and even now I have not transcended the plane of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Striving and exerting himself, before long he attained the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Having seen a *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom, and raising my hands in añjali,
I recollected the Best of Buddhas and worshipped him in the sky.
By that well-performed deed, and by my intention and aspiration...”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Thirty-one eons ago, from this time, because of the deed I performed then, I have never known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of making an offering to a Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he went to the city where his kinsmen lived and, demonstrating the liberating nature of the Teaching, displayed a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).
Upon seeing this, his kinsmen became clear-minded in faith and constructed many monasteries for the Saṅgha.
The Elder, too, taking the verse sent by his own father as a goad, exerted himself with diligence and realized *arahantship*.
Even while declaring his higher knowledge (*aññā*), he recited that very same verse—“Is he not addicted to clothing?”—for the sake of honoring his father. 28.
Therein, *kacci* is a particle used for inquiry; *no* is a particle of negation; *vatthapasuto* means one who is addicted to clothing.

“Addicted to clothing,” meaning one who delights in the adornment of robes. This is mentioned merely as an illustration, as it is intended to include the prohibition against the frivolity of adorning one’s bowl and other such items.
There is also a reading, “Kacci na vatthapasuto” (Is he not addicted to clothing?), which has the same meaning.

“Delighting in adornment” means one who is fond of and takes pleasure in the beautification of the physical person—just like certain people who, even after going forth, remain fickle and obsessed with bodily strength regarding requisites such as robes and the like.
They are fit for the purpose of adorning and beautifying one’s own body.

"Why then were you not devoted to requisites and fond of ornaments?"—this is the meaning of both these phrases here. "The fragrance consisting of virtue" refers to the fourfold virtue that is perfectly purified by being made free from breach and so forth;
regarding this, [it is said]: "And he who is born into a family of those possessing virtue..."
The other [kind of person] is a family of immoral people; because of their immorality, they emit the foul odor consisting of immorality. Thus, the meaning is:
"Without emitting such a foul odor, do you perhaps emit the fragrance consisting of virtue? Alternatively, "na itarā pajā" means "not the other kind of family," i.e., not a family of immoral people.
By asking, "Is that not the case, since you emit the fragrance consisting of virtue? he clarifies, through contrast (*vyatireka*), precisely the emission of the fragrance of virtue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jambugāmiyaputta is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Hārita:
"One should uplift oneself... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Hārita. What is his origin? It is said that he [lived] during the time of previous Buddhas...

Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated the equipment of merit that serves as the necessary condition for liberation in various places, he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sudassana thirty-one aeons ago;
with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of *kuṭaja* flowers.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering only through the happy destinies, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha in the city of Sāvatthī.

He was reborn in a great brahmin family. His name was Hāritotissa. When he reached maturity, his parents brought him home a young brahmin girl as a wife, one who was suitable for him in terms of lineage, beauty, and other qualities.
While he was enjoying the pleasures of wealth with her, one day, observing the excellence of their own physical forms and being impelled by the natural law of things, he reflected:
He attained a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, “Such a form as this will soon be crushed by old age and death.
After only a few days had passed, a black snake bit his wife and killed her.
Having become even more intensely stirred by that event, he went into the presence of the Teacher; having heard the Dhamma and severed the bonds of the household life, he went forth.
While he was dwelling there having taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to his temperament, that meditation subject did not succeed and his mind did not become straight.
Having entered a village for alms, he saw a fletcher inserting an arrow-shaft into a lathe and making it straight. Seeing this, [he thought]:
"These people can indeed make even an insentient thing straight; why then should I not [make my] mind..."
Thinking, "I will not act uprightly," he turned back from that very spot and, sitting in his daytime resting place, began the practice of insight (vipassanā).
Then the Blessed One, sitting in the sky above him, spoke the verse beginning with "Lift up yourself" while giving him instruction.
It is also said that this elder himself spoke it, as if instructing himself as if he were another.

29. Therein, "they lift up" (*samunnamayanti*) means lifting up correctly; that is to say, not allowing oneself to fall into the side of indolence by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), but rather drawing oneself up from there and applying evenness of energy (*vīriyasamata*).
"The self" (*attan*) refers to the mind; alternatively, "lift up" means lift up from the side of indolence.
The letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhi*). Because of your inferior energy, your mind [does not enter] the path of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
If it does not proceed [straight], straighten it properly by means of exerting energy; the intention is: "make it neither bent nor crooked.
Acting thus, like a fletcher straightening an arrow, having made the mind straight, shatter ignorance, O Hārita!
Just as a fletcher, while piercing a shaft that is even slightly bent or crooked, [hits] the target...

"Just as one straightens a bent bow for the purpose of breaking it, so too, having straightened the mind by piercing it with absorption (appanā) through protecting it from falling into sloth and torpor and preventing it from falling into agitation, and having thus concentrated the mind and intensified insight,
break and cleave through ignorance quickly with the knowledge of the supreme path. Having heard this, the Elder increased his insight.
Before long, he became an arahant. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Vasala;
a Buddha named Sudassana dwells within that mountain range."
“Having taken a *hemavanta* flower, I went through the air;
there I saw the Perfectly Awakened One, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints.
Then, taking a *kuṭaja* flower and placing it upon my head, I—”
I offered them to the Buddha, the Self-Existent One, the Great Sage.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I made this offering of flowers, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of that flower-offering."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he also spoke this very same verse while declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Hārita is finished.
10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya "An affliction has arisen for me"—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Uttiya. What is their origin?

It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) here and there; thus, ninety-four aeons ago from now...
In the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn as a large crocodile in the river Candabhāgā.
Seeing the Blessed One approaching the bank of the river intending to cross to the other side, he became inspired with faith and, desiring to carry him across, lay down near the shore.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One placed his foot upon his back; he, thrilled and elated, [carried him across].
With his courage doubled by the force of the drink, he cut across the current and, with swift speed, brought the Blessed One to the opposite shore.
The Blessed One, observing the clarity of his mind, prophesied: "After passing away from here, he will be reborn in the world of the gods;
from that point on, wandering only through happy destinies, he will attain the Deathless ninety-four aeons hence. Having thus spoken, he departed.
Thus, wandering through happy destinies alone, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin, by name Uttiya.
Upon reaching maturity, thinking, "I shall seek the Deathless," he wandered about as a renunciant.
One day, having approached the Blessed One and heard the Dhamma, he went forth into the teaching.
Being unable to produce spiritual distinction because his virtue and other qualities were not purified, he saw other bhikkhus who, having produced distinction, were declaring their own realization.
He approached the Teacher and requested a brief exhortation.
The Teacher gave him a brief exhortation beginning with: "Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the beginning."
Thus, abiding by his advice, he began insight meditation (*vipassanā*). While he was engaged in insight meditation, an illness arose.

When the illness had arisen, he became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); making the exertion of energy his foundation, he performed the work of insight meditation, and having brought insight to its peak, he attained *arahantship*. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“At that time, I was a crocodile on the bank of the Candabhāgā River.
Having gone down to my feeding ground, I went to the river-ford.
At that moment, Siddhattha, the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person, [was there].”
Desiring to cross the river, he approached the river-ford.
When the Fully Awakened One had arrived there, I too went to that place;
having approached the Fully Awakened One, I uttered these words:
“Ascend, O Great Hero; I shall carry you across.
Have compassion for me, O Great Sage, and enter my ancestral domain.
Hearing my cry, the Great Sage ascended.
With a joyful heart, I gladdened the Leader of the World.
“On the far bank of the river stands Siddhattha, the Leader of the World;
there he comforted me, saying, ‘You shall attain the Deathless.’”
“Having passed away from that body, I went to the world of the gods;
there I experienced divine bliss, honored by celestial nymphs.
And seven times I exercised sovereignty over the gods as Lord of Devas.”
Three times I was a wheel-turning monarch, the lord of the earth.
Now, devoted to solitude, wise and well-restrained,
I bear my final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“Ninety-four aeons ago, I helped cross that Bull among Men;
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state—this is the fruit of that act of crossing.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Having attained arahantship, he declared his full knowledge (*aññā*) by way of manifesting the perfection of his own right practice, and uttered the verse beginning, "When affliction had arisen for me.

30. Therein, "when affliction had arisen for me" (*ābādhe me samuppanne*): when a disease—known as "affliction" because it afflicts the body and caused by an imbalance of the primary elements (*visabhāga-dhātu*)—had arisen in me;
[then] mindfulness arose for me (*sati me udapajjatha*). [The thought occurred: "Affliction has indeed arisen for me; however, it is possible that..."

"It may happen that this illness will increase. As long as this illness does not increase, let me now arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
Thus, mindfulness—which serves as the basis for the arousal of energy—belongs to one who is oppressed by painful feeling on account of that very illness.
This occurred to me. Therefore he said: "Awakening has arisen for me; it is time for me not to be negligent.
For it was by making mindfulness that had thus arisen his goad that this elder attained arahantship.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttiya is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gahvaratīriya.
"Let him bite when touched": this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Gahvaratīriya. What is its origin?

It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, while wandering in the forest as a deer-hunter, he saw the Blessed One Sikhi teaching the Dhamma to gods, nāgas, and yakṣas at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen this, with a mind full of serene confidence, he grasped the sign in his memory, thinking, "This is what is called Dhamma.

By virtue of that mental clarity, he was reborn in the world of the gods; subsequently, wandering from one happy destination to another, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the arising of this Buddha.
Having attained the name Aggidatta and reached maturity, [he witnessed] the Blessed One’s Twin Miracle.
Having seen [this], he conceived faith in the Teaching, went forth, and after receiving a meditation subject, lived in a forest place named Gahvaratīra.
Because of this, he became known by the name Gahvaratīra. Having developed insight, he attained Arahatship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the past, I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
there I saw the stainless Buddha, honored by the hosts of gods.
He was proclaiming the Four Truths, teaching the state of deathlessness.”
I heard the sweet Dhamma from Sikhin, the Kinsman of the World.
My mind was gladdened by the sound of that Peerless One;
having gladdened my mind therein, I crossed over further existence, so difficult to cross.
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, the perception I then acquired— I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of the perception of sound.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Having attained arahantship, he paid homage to the Blessed One and went to Sāvatthī.
Upon hearing that he had arrived, his kinsmen approached him and offered a great almsgiving. After staying for a few days, he desired to go back to the forest.
His kinsmen said to him, "Venerable sir, the forest is indeed full of many dangers, such as gadflies and mosquitoes."
“Dwell right here,” they said. Having heard this, the Elder thought, “The forest life alone is pleasing to me.
Praising his delight in seclusion, he answered them with the verse beginning, “Touched by gadflies and mosquitoes.
(31) Therein, “touched by gadflies and mosquitoes” refers to the *andhakamakkhikā* (dark flies), which are given the name “gadflies” (*daṃsa*) because of their habit of biting.

The meaning is that he was stung and bitten by those known as *makasanaññita*, whose hands have needle-like mouths. "In the forest" (*araññe*) means in a wilderness, because it possesses the characteristics of a forest as stated in the rule: "five hundred bow-lengths from the boundary.
"In the great forest" (*brahāvane*) means in a vast woodland (*araññāniya*) due to its density of large trees and thickets.
"Like an elephant accustomed to the front of battle" (*saṅgāmasīseva nāgo*) means like a war-elephant stationed at the head of the battlefield.

Regarding the clash with hostile armies: having developed enthusiasm, thinking, "Dwelling in the forest has been praised and extolled by the Buddha and others," one should—being mindful and possessed of clear comprehension—endure, endure, and tolerate whatever arises there in that forest, or whatever contact with gadflies and the like occurs.
The meaning is that one should not abandon the forest dwelling on account of [the thought], "Gadflies and such are afflicting me."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gahvaratīriya is finished.
2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Suppiya:
"By one who grows old while aging... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Suppiya. What is their origin? It is said that he [was a disciple] of Padumuttara...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he went forth as a forest ascetic and lived in a wilderness region.
There, having seen the Blessed One, he offered various fruits with a devout mind, as did he for the Saṅgha of monks.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born into a kṣatriya family during the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Having been reborn and gradually attained the state of full maturity, he experienced a sense of spiritual urgency through reliance on a virtuous friend and went forth in the Dispensation, becoming one of great learning.
However, he lived exalting himself with pride in his birth and pride in his learning, while disparaging others.
Due to the outflow of that karma, during this arising of a Buddha, he was born in Sāvatthī in a despised form.

He was reborn in a family of cemetery-keepers; his name was Suppiya. Later, having reached the age of discretion, he approached his own friend, the Elder Sopāka, and having heard the Dhamma in his presence, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of right conduct, he recited the verse beginning, "By one who is aging while surrounded by the unaging..."
32. Therein, "ageless" (*ajara*) means free from aging; this is said with reference to Nibbāna. For because it is unborn, there is no aging therein;
or, because when it is attained, aging no longer exists for the person, it is called "ageless" by virtue of being the cause for the absence of aging.

"By that which is aging" (*jīramānena*) means by that which is decaying, reaching decay moment by moment. "By that which is burning" (*tappamānena*) means by that which is being tormented by lust and the other [defilements].
"By one being burned by the eleven fires. "Nibbāna": that which has the nature of being extinguished (nibbuta) due to the absence of the aforementioned torments.

"I would exchange": I would trade for it or cause it to be procured. "The supreme peace": the highest tranquility, because its nature is the subsiding of the fever of all defilements (kilesa) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra).
"Security from bondage": because it is not followed by the four bonds (yoga). "Of anyone superior to oneself": [of anyone] more excellent than oneself.
"Because of its non-existence, it is unsurpassed. This is the concise meaning here: because it is being overcome by aging moment by moment, it is "decaying";
likewise, because it is being tormented by the fires of passion and so forth, it has gone thus—being impermanent, suffering, coreless, entirely of an unpeaceful nature, and beset by calamity.
Because it is the opposite of that, it is "undecaying," having become the supreme peace.
"Having exchanged it for the unsurpassed Nibbāna, which is free from all affliction, [I would think]: 'Truly great is my gain!

Truly great is my prosperity, now come into my hand! For just as people, when exchanging any kind of goods, feel great respect for what is being taken by one who is free from attachment, so too this elder, dwelling with resolute effort, was free from attachment toward his own body and life."
Proclaiming that his mind was directed toward Nibbāna, he said: “The supreme peace, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Developing that very practice and intensifying his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship.
Thus it is stated in the Apadāna:
“A brahmin named Varuṇa, a master of the mantras,
having abandoned his ten sons, then entered the forest.
Having constructed a well-made hermitage, beautifully divided and delightful,”
Having built a leaf-hut, I lived in the forest. Padumuttara,
the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings—
desiring to uplift me, he came to my hermitage.
“To the extent that there was a vast radiance within the forest grove,
the woods then blazed forth through the power of the Buddha.
Having seen that miracle of the Tathāgata, the supreme Buddha,”
Taking a leaf-basket, I honored him with fruit.
Having approached the Fully Enlightened One, I gave him a khāri-measure of grain.
Out of compassion for me, the Buddha spoke these words:
“Take a khāri-load and follow behind me;
when the Saṅgha has partaken, merit will accrue to you.
Taking that basket, I gave it to the community of monks.”
Having gladdened my mind there, I was reborn in Tusita. There,
through my meritorious deeds, I always experienced happiness accompanied by divine dances, songs, and instrumental music.
“Whichever womb I am reborn into, whether among the gods or among humans, there is no deficiency in my wealth;
this is the fruit of giving fruit.
As far as the four continents extend, together with their oceans and mountains...”
Having given fruit to the Buddha, I exercised lordship.
"Whatever flocks of birds fly in the sky, they all come under my control;
this is the fruit of giving fruit."
“Whatever yakkhas, bhūtas, and rakkhasas there are within the forest grove,
as well as kumbhaṇḍas and garuḷas, they all come to attend upon me.
Turtles, jackals, honey-bees, gadflies, and mosquitoes— both kinds— [attend upon me].”
Even the gods come under my control; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
Even the birds known as supaṇṇas, born of the feathered race and possessed of great strength, go to me for refuge; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“Even those long-lived nāgas, possessing psychic power and great fame—even they come under my control;
this is the fruit of giving alms. Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, and jackals...”
The forest deities attend upon me; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The herbs, the grass-dwellers, and those who dwell in the sky—all go to me for refuge; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“Having touched that which is very hard to see, most subtle, profound, and well-expounded, I dwell [in peace]; this is the fruit of the giving of fruit.
Having attained the eight liberations, I dwell free from taints.”
“I am ardent and wise; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
Those sons of the Buddha who have attained the fruits, whose faults are exhausted and whose fame is great—I am one among them;
this is the fruit of giving fruit.”
“Having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, urged on by the root of my wholesome merit,
and having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
These sons of the Buddha, of great renown, possess the threefold knowledge and have attained supernormal powers.”
Having attained the divine ear, I am one among them:
“In the hundred-thousandth aeon, the fruit that I gave back then— I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Even after attaining Arahantship, he recited that very same verse as his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Suppiya is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Sopāka "Even as toward an only son... is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sopāka. What is its origin?

It is said that he, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) here and there, [served] Kakusandha...

In the time of the Blessed One, having been reborn as the son of a certain householder, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a mind full of faith, offered *bījapūra* fruits to the Teacher. Out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted them.
Having also gained deep confidence in the community of monks, he established a system of providing meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) for the sake of the Saṅgha.
He gave milk-rice to three monks for as long as he lived.
Through those meritorious deeds, experiencing successive success in the realms of gods and humans, he was once reborn in the human womb and gave milk-rice to a Paccekabuddha.
Thus, having performed merits here and there and wandering only through happy destinies, in this [life]...
Due to the outflow of past karma during the arising of a Buddha, he took rebirth in the womb of a certain poor woman in Sāvatthī.
His mother carried him in her womb for ten months, and when the fetus was fully matured and it was time for birth, she was unable to give birth;
she fell into a swoon and lay for a long time as if dead. Her relatives, thinking, "She is dead,"...
Having led him to the charnel ground and placed him upon the funeral pyre, they departed without applying fire, as a wind and rainstorm arose through the power of a deity.
Because the boy was destined for his final existence, he emerged from his mother's womb healthy and unharmed through the power of that deity;
however, the mother passed away. The deity took the child and, appearing in human form, placed him in the house of the cemetery keeper.
For some time he nourished him with suitable food; thereafter, the cemetery keeper raised him as his own son.
As he grew up in this way, he would wander about playing with a boy named Supiya, who was the keeper's son.
Because he had been born and raised in the cemetery, he became known by the name Sopāka.

Then one day, at the hour of dawn, the Blessed One spread out the net of his knowledge and, surveying those to be trained as if they were his own kinsmen, saw that the boy was caught within that net of knowledge; he then went to the cemetery.
Urged on by his past causes, the boy approached the Teacher with a devout mind, paid homage to him, and stood before him. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to him.
Having heard this Dhamma and requested ordination, when asked, "Have you been permitted by your father? he led his father into the presence of the Teacher.
His father approached the Teacher, paid homage, and gave his permission, saying, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this boy.
The Teacher ordained him and directed him to the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*). Having taken up the meditation subject of loving-kindness, he...
While dwelling in the charnel ground, after a long time he produced the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*);
taking that *jhāna* as his foundation, he developed insight (*vipassanā*) and realized *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Kakusandha, the Great Hero, who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena...”
Having withdrawn from the community, he went into the depths of the forest.
"Taking some seed-pulp, I strung it upon a creeper;
at that time, the Blessed One was meditating in the mountain cleft."
“Having seen the God of Gods with a serene mind,
I gave seed-pulp to that Hero worthy of offerings.
Because I gave that pulp back in this very aeon, [the fruit has ripened].”
“I do not recognize an unfortunate rebirth; this is the fruit of the seed of *miñja*.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having become an Arahant, he then spoke the verse beginning with ‘Just as toward an only son’ to demonstrate the method for the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) to other monks who dwell in charnel grounds.”

33. In this context, *yathā* is a particle used in the sense of a simile (*opamma*). Regarding the term *ekaputtasmiṃ*: one who purifies (*punāti*) and protects (*tāyati*) the family lineage is a son (*putta*);
a son includes various types such as those born of one’s own loins (*atraja*) and so forth. One who is the only son is an "only son" (*ekaputta*); the phrase refers to that only son.

This locative case (*bhummavacana*) is used here in the sense of an object (*visaya*). Regarding the word *piyasmim*: it is [so called] because of being beloved (*piyāyitabbatā*), because of being an only son, and because of his physical form, character, conduct, and so forth.
And [it refers to those] who are objects of love. "Virtuous" (*kusalī*): "wholesome" (*kusala*) is said to mean safety and well-being;

one who possesses that which is to be obtained is "virtuous," meaning one who seeks the welfare of beings and has a disposition of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Toward all living beings" means toward all sentient beings.
"Everywhere" means in all directions, or in all states of existence, or in all conditions. This is what is meant:
It is as follows: just as parents would be skilled, wishing solely for the welfare of a beloved and dear only son, so too one should be skilled, wishing solely for the welfare of all beings—
be they situated in any of the directions such as the east and so forth, in any of the realms of existence such as the sense-sphere existence and so forth,
or in any of the stages of life such as childhood and so forth— regardless of whether they are friends, neutrals, or enemies.
"Without establishing a boundary, one should cultivate loving-kindness that is of a single flavor everywhere by means of breaking down all boundaries.

Having spoken this verse, he gave this instruction: "Venerable sirs, if you should devote yourselves to the cultivation of loving-kindness in this way, you will certainly partake in those eleven benefits of loving-kindness which were spoken of by the Blessed One, beginning with 'one sleeps happily.'"
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sopāka is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Posiya “Those who do not dwell near” is a verse of the Venerable Elder Posiya. What is its origin? It is said that in previous Buddhas...
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated much wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) here and there, he wandered only among the happy realms.
Ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Tissa, he was wandering in the forest as a deer-hunter.
Then, the Blessed One went to the forest to favor him and appeared within the range of his vision.
Thus, having seen the Blessed One, with a mind full of serene confidence, he laid aside his weapon, approached, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One indicated that He wished to sit down. At once, he took handfuls of grass, carefully spread them upon a level patch of ground, and offered them.
Out of compassion, the Blessed One sat there. And when He was seated...
Experiencing no small measure of joy and gladness toward the Blessed One, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This much is sufficient for this man’s seed of merit," rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the Blessed One had left, Sīha, the king of beasts, killed him. Having passed away, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Thinking, "If he does not approach the Blessed One, he will be killed by a lion and reborn in hell," the Blessed One approached him for the purpose of ensuring his rebirth in a happy destination and for the purpose of planting the seeds of wholesome merit.
Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from that heavenly world and, wandering only among happy destinations, [arrived] in this...
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, in Sāvatthī, a son was born to a certain very wealthy merchant as the younger brother of the Elder Saṅgāmajita.
His name was Posiya. When he reached maturity, he took a wife, and having obtained a son, he was urged by the natural law of one in his final existence to renounce birth and the rest.

Having developed a sense of spiritual urgency, he went forth into homelessness, entered the forest, and, dwelling in seclusion, devoted himself to the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.
Before long, having brought insight to its peak, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Lambaka;”
Right there, the Sambuddha Tissa was walking in the open air.
At that time, I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
having seen that God of Gods, I offered him a handful of grass.
“Having given a seat for the Buddha, I gladdened my heart;
having paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, I departed facing north.
Not long after I had gone, the king of beasts tore it apart.”
“From the Soṇa monastery, I, being virtuous, passed away there.
Because I had performed meritorious deeds in the presence of the Supreme Buddha,
free from taints, I went to the world of the gods like an arrow released with great force.”
“There stood there a beautiful sacrificial post, fashioned by meritorious deeds;
it had a thousand shafts and a hundred cross-pieces, adorned with banners and made of gold.
Its radiance shone forth like the risen sun with its hundred rays.”
Surrounded by celestial maidens, I rejoiced here, pursuing my desires.
Having fallen from the world of the gods, impelled by the root of my wholesome merit,
I came to human existence and attained the destruction of the taints.
“In the ninety-fourth aeon, I gave a sitting mat;
I do not know a state of woe—this is the fruit of that handful of grass.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Having attained arahantship, he came to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One; out of compassion for his kinsmen, he went to the house of his relatives.
There, his former wife paid him homage and, like a laywoman, first showed him the proper conduct by offering a seat and other courtesies.
However, not understanding the Elder’s disposition, she subsequently desired to seduce him with feminine gestures and the like.
The Elder thought, "Alas! These blind fools act in such a manner even toward one like me," and without saying anything, he rose from his seat and went straight to the forest.
When the forest-dwelling monks asked him, "Friend, why have you returned so quickly? Were you not seen by your kinsmen?
the Elder, explaining what had occurred there, recited the verse: "These women are not easy to approach."
34. Therein, "women who are not near" (*anāsannavarā*) means these women are neither close nor approached;

rather, they remain at a distance, being excellent (*varā*)—that is, supreme—and bringing benefit to a man, and that indeed constantly, at all times, not only by night but also by day, and even during private moments.
"By one who knows" (*vijānatā*) means by one who understands. There is also a textual reading, "not others who are near" (*anāsannaparā*), which has the same meaning.
This is the intended meaning here: wild elephants, horses, buffaloes, lions, tigers, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas are better when they do not approach humans; they do not bring about harm.

But if they were to approach, they would cause harm only in this present life. Women, however, having approached, cause harm both in this present life and in the future life, and even that which pertains to liberation.
Having destroyed their welfare, they bring about great misfortune; therefore, these women are always best when not near, for they are ever discerning.
Now, making this matter personal, he says "From the village," and so forth. Therein, "from the village" (*gāmā*) means "to the village. This is an ablative form used in the sense of the accusative.
"Having come from the forest" (*araññamāgamma*) means having arrived from the forest. The letter *m* is a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
This is the accusative case used in the sense of the ablative. "From there" means from the bed.
"Without taking leave" means without speaking to his former wife, even not saying so much as "Be heedful. "I am the one to be supported" (posiya): he speaks of himself as if he were another.
As for those who read "departed" (pakkāmi), their construction is: "I, the one to be supported, departed. As for those [who say] "that woman [addressed] the Elder..."

Having fed him who had come to her house, she became desirous of seducing him. Seeing this, the Elder immediately departed from the house, went to the monastery, and sat down upon his couch in his own dwelling place.
Then that woman, having adorned herself after the meal, approached the Elder’s dwelling place in the monastery.
Seeing her, the Elder said nothing at all; he simply rose and went to the daytime quarters.
When they say, "He has gone," the meaning of the verse line, "Having come from the village to the forest," is taken according to the literal sense alone.
For here, "vihāra" (monastery) is intended by the term "arañña" (forest).
The commentary on the verses of Thera Posiya is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sāmaññakāni "Seeking happiness through happiness"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sāmaññakāni. What is its origin?

It is said that he, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots in various states of existence, [was reborn] ninety-one aeons ago during the time of Vipassī Buddha.
In the time of the Blessed One, having been reborn among human beings, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī and, with a mind full of faith, offered him a couch.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha as the son of a certain wanderer;
his name was Sāmaññakānīti. When he reached the age of discretion—

Having seen the Teacher’s Twin Miracle, his mind became serene; he went forth into the Dispensation, took up a meditation subject suitable to his temperament, and having attained jhāna, he used that jhāna as a basis to develop insight and reached Arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the Blessed One Vipassī, the World’s Elder, the Neutral One,
I gave a single couch with my own hands, out of faith. Through that,
I attained elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and celestial vehicles.”
By that gift of a couch, I have attained the destruction of the taints.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because I gave a couch at that time, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of the gift of a couch."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Now, the wanderer named Kātiyāna, who had been a householder friend of the Elder, had from the time of the Buddha’s appearance failed to receive even enough food and clothing due to the loss of gain and honor among the sectarians; having fallen into a state of destitution, he approached the Elder.
“You Sākiyaputtiyas,” he asked, “are indeed those who have attained great gain and the highest heaven, living in happiness; we, however, are suffering and live in hardship.
How, then, for one practicing what way do happiness pertaining both to this present life and to future lives come to be?
Then the Elder said to him: “In the ultimate sense, that which is called ‘happiness’ is exclusively supramundane happiness.”
And he spoke the verse, "The seeker of happiness finds happiness when practicing accordingly," thereby explaining by way of a sequence his own state of having attained that [happiness] for him. 35.
Therein, "happiness" (sukha) refers here to non-material happiness; and that consists of both the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) and Nibbāna.
For it has been said: "This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future," and "Nirvana is supreme happiness.
"Seeking happiness" means having happiness as one's purpose; that is, one who desires the aforementioned happiness. "Obtains" means reaches.
This happiness belongs only to the seeker, not to anyone else. But who is the seeker? To this he says: "One who practices it."
Practicing for that purpose means practicing by means of whatever practice [is required]; this is the sense.
