Not only does one who practices in that way obtain happiness, but he also attains fame—namely, fame spread abroad in the presence of others through such statements as, "Thus he is virtuous, with perfectly pure bodily and verbal action, with perfectly pure livelihood, a meditator devoted to meditation," and so forth.
"His fame increases" means that his fame—consisting of the praise of his virtues in his presence and the perfection of his retinue—causes him to flourish.
Now, in order to show the meaning previously stated in general terms as "practice that," by way of its specific form, it says:
"He who develops the noble, eightfold, straight, and direct path for the attainment of the Deathless. This is its meaning.
That person who, by being far removed from defilements, is noble in the sense of being completely pure;

which is "eightfold" because it is the collection of the eight factors beginning with right view; which is "straight" in the sense of being non-crooked due to its nature as the middle way free from the two extremes;
which is "direct" through the abandonment of bodily crookedness and so forth; and which is to be "traversed" by those seeking Nibbāna—this is the Path.

By slaying the defilements and in the sense of proceeding, one cultivates, produces within one’s own continuum, and increases the practice leading to the cessation of suffering— which has received the name "path"— for the sake of attaining and reaching the deathless,
unconditioned element. This is called, in the primary sense, "the pursuit of happiness," and therefore one obtains the aforementioned happiness.
Having heard this, the wanderer, with a mind full of faith, went forth and practiced rightly. Before long, having increased his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship*.
This itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāmaññakāni is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Kumāputta "Excellent is learning"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kumāputta. What is its origin?
It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; ninety-one aeons ago, having become an ascetic clad in deerskin, he lived in the royal park at the city of Bandhumatī.
Vasanta, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī with a mind full of faith, offered oil for anointing the feet.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

From then on, wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka in the kingdom of Avantī, into a householder’s family. His name was Nanda.
They did so. His mother’s name was Kumā, and therefore he became known as Kumāputta.

Having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta, he gained faith and went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties, while practicing the ascetic life on the slopes of a mountain range, he was unable to achieve any distinction; thus, he approached the Blessed One and [listened to] the Dhamma.
Having heard the meditation subject and purified it, while dwelling in a suitable location and increasing his insight, he realized arhatship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I dwelt in the royal garden;”
At that time I was a Cammavāsī, carrying a water-pot.
I saw the stainless Buddha, the self-become, the unconquered;
I dwelt with him who was resolute in striving, absorbed in meditation, delighting in jhāna.
“Seeing him who had accomplished all desires, who had crossed the flood,
and was free from taints, I gave him anointing oil with a clear and joyful mind.
Ninety-one eons ago, I gave him that anointing oil.”
“I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of anointing oil.

Having attained arahantship, seeing monks in the forest who were preoccupied with physical strength, he spoke the verse beginning, “Excellent is what is heard, excellent is conduct,” while exhorting them and clarifying the world-transcending nature of the Buddha’s teaching: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s message has been accomplished.”
36. In this context, *sādhu* means "excellent. *Suta* means "hearing.

Furthermore, what is intended here is specifically the hearing of the ten bases of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*), which is based on turning away from worldly existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissita*) and is associated with qualities such as fewness of desires (*appicchatā*).
*Sādhucaritakaṃ* refers to that very practice of fewness of desires and so forth being performed; for it is precisely excellent conduct that is called "conduct" (*caritaka*). By both these two terms—

He shows that learning and the corresponding practice are "beautiful. "Always" means at all times—whether during the stages of being a novice, a middle-ranking monk, or an elder—or in every moment of the postures.
"Living without a home": in the sense of being a place where defilements dwell, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "homes," or else the six worldly objects of the senses.
As it is said: "The sign of form is a home, a distraction, and a bond..."
“Householder, he is called ‘one who wanders from abode to abode’,” and so forth. The practice for the sake of abandoning those abodes is dwelling without an abode (*aniketavihāra*).

Regarding the inquiry into the meaning: it is the questioning of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) by one desiring to understand that [practice], concerning the distinctions of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate truth, or concerning the meaning of wholesome states and so forth, or the nature of phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*), such as: “Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What...”

The inquiry, beginning with “What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? and so forth, is the inquiry into the meaning (*atthapucchana*). As for “acting in a clockwise manner” (*padakkhiṇakamma*):
having made that inquiry, it is the resolution upon his instruction and the practice of right conduct by way of grasping [the teaching] in a clockwise manner.

Here too, the word “well” (*sādhu*) should be brought in and connected. “This is the state of a recluse” (*etaṃ sāmaññaṃ*) refers to what was stated in the passage beginning with “Well heard” (*sādhu sutaṃ*).

That which is learning, that which is conduct, that which is dwelling without a home, that which is inquiry into the meaning, and that which is respectful service—this is the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*), this is the condition of being a recluse (*samaṇabhāva*).

Since the state of a recluse exists only through this very practice and not otherwise, therefore "the state of a recluse" (*sāmañña*) is, in its primary sense, a designation for the Path and its Fruit. Or rather, this is the unerring practice (*apaṇṇakapaṭipadā*) leading to it.
To show for what kind of person this asceticism (sāmañña) is possible, it is said: "of one who possesses nothing" (akiñcanassa).
This means: of one who does not have a possessor, that is, one who is devoid of the grasping and possession of fields, land, gold, silver, female and male slaves, and so forth.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kumāputta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Kumāputtasahāya "Going to various countries...
is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kumāputtasahāya. What is its origin?

It is said that he, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) here and there, [passed away] from this world...
In the ninety-fourth aeon, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn into a noble family.
Upon reaching maturity, he entered the forest, cut many tree trunks, fashioned them into walking sticks, and gave them to the Saṅgha.
Having performed other meritorious deeds according to his means, he was reborn among the devas; from that point onward, he continued to be reborn only in the happy realms.
Revolving through the cycle of rebirths, he was born into a prosperous family in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka during this current dispensation of a Buddha.
His name was Sudanta; some say it was Vāsula.
While wandering about as a dear companion to Kumāputta, having heard that "Kumāputta has gone forth," he thought, "Surely that Dhamma and Vinaya cannot be inferior, since Kumāputta..."
Thinking, “He has gone forth,” he himself, desiring to go forth as well by following his example, approached the Teacher.

The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. With an even greater inclination for the life of renunciation, he went forth and dwelt on the Pariyanta Mountain together with Kumāputta, devoted to the practice of meditation. And at that time...
Many bhikkhus, while wandering on a tour through various districts, whether going or returning, arrived at that place.
Because of this, there was a great clamor there. Seeing this, the Elder Sudanta thought:
"These bhikkhus, having gone forth in the Dispensation that leads to liberation, are following thoughts of the countryside and are failing in mental concentration."
Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and making that very urgency a goad for the taming of his own mind,
he spoke the verse beginning,
"Going to various countries. (37) Therein, "various countries" (*nānājanapada*) means distinct and diverse regions, such as the many kingdoms of Kāsi, Kosala, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: "They go" means they travel. "Wandering about" means wandering on tours of the countryside by way of such thoughts as, "That district has abundant food and alms are easily obtained; that one is secure and free from disease," and so forth.

"Unrestrained" means being uncontrolled in mind due to the non-abandonment of those very thoughts regarding the countryside. "And they fail in concentration" refers to all superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
They fail in the concentration that is the foundation [of all], which is divided into access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*). The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of "it is possible.

By wandering through other lands, they fail because they do not attain the concentration they have not yet attained due to the lack of opportunity for meditation, and they fail because they let what they have attained waste away by failing to bring it to mastery.
The phrase "what will wandering through the country accomplish? is merely an exclamation. For those who have become thus...
"Roaming through kingdoms and wandering through the countryside—what will that accomplish? What purpose indeed will it achieve?

It is useless," he says while censuring [the practice]. "Therefore" means: because such wandering to foreign lands does not bring benefit to a bhikkhu, but rather brings harm due to the loss of attainments; therefore. "Having subdued contentiousness" refers to the place of residence.
Having guided away and pacified the agitation of the mind that has arisen through resentment by means of a corresponding reflection, one should meditate.

One should meditate by means of both kinds of meditation: meditation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and meditation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). "Not preceded" means not preceded by wrong thoughts or by craving and so forth; [it refers to] those...
The meaning is that, without falling under its influence, one should attend only to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having spoken thus, the Elder took that very sense of urgency as a goad, increased his insight (*vipassanā*), and attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Having entered the forest grove and cut down a bamboo stalk at that time...”
Having made it my object of focus, I gave much to the Saṅgha.
With that serene state of mind, having paid homage to the virtuous ones and given a walking staff as a support, I departed facing north.
“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that staff at that time, I have never known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving a staff.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as before]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
However, having kept in mind that very purpose for which he had used the goad to attain arahantship, even though he had already attained arahantship, the Elder recited this very verse:
"They go to various countries. Therefore, that itself became his declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kumāputtasahāya is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gavampati:
"Who by psychic power [crossed] the Sarabhū... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Gavampati. What was his origin? It is said that in previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duty, in this thirty-first aeon he beheld the Blessed One Sikhi and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of flowers.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; performing further merits, he had a parasol and a railing constructed for the stupa of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana.
Furthermore, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, at a certain...
He was reborn in a noble family. In that family, there were many herds of cattle, which cowherds guarded.
He wandered about there from time to time, supervising their various tasks.
One day, he saw an elder whose taints were exhausted (khīṇāsavathera) walking for alms in the village and, after returning outside the village, daily performing his meal-ritual at a certain spot.
Thinking, "The venerable one will suffer from the heat of the sun," he raised four *sirīsa* poles, placed *sirīsa* branches over them, and having constructed a bower of branches, he gave it to him.
Some say that he planted a *sirīsa* tree near the bower. Out of compassion for him, the Elder sat there every day. By that meritorious deed, he—
Then, passing away from there, he was reborn among the Cātumahārājika devas.

As an indicator of his past deeds, a great *sirīsa* grove appeared at the gate of his celestial mansion (*vimāna*), which was adorned at all times by other flowers endowed with exquisite color and fragrance;
because of this, that mansion became known as "Serīsaka. That son of the gods remained among the devas for the duration of one *buddhantara*.
Having wandered through births among humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he became one named Gavampati among the four lay companions of the Venerable Yasa.

Upon hearing that the Venerable Yasa had gone forth, he went into the presence of the Blessed One together with his own companions. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma; at the conclusion of the teaching, together with his companions...
Together, he was established in Arahatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“In former times I was a deer-hunter, wandering through the forest;
there I saw the stainless Buddha, who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena.”
“Toward that Greatly Compassionate One, who delights in the welfare of all beings,
I, with a clear heart and joyful mind, offered a *nela* flower.
Thirty-one eons ago, that flower which I offered— ”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard verse]... the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, the elder, experiencing the bliss of liberation, dwelt at Añjana Grove in Sāketa.
At that time, the Blessed One, having gone to Sāketa together with a great community of monks, was staying in the Añjana Grove.
There was no sufficient lodging. Many monks lay down on the sandy banks of the river Sarabhū near the monastery.
Then, at the hour of midnight, as a flood of water came down from the river, the novices and others raised a loud and great clamor.
The Blessed One, having understood this, commanded the Venerable Gavampati: “Go, Gavampati, and by stopping the torrential flood, provide a comfortable dwelling for the bhikkhus.
The Elder replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and by the power of his psychic potency (iddhi), he stopped the river’s current;
it stood still from afar like a mountain peak. From that time forth, [it was known] of the Elder...
The Elder’s spiritual power became manifest in the world. Then one day, the Teacher,

seeing the Elder preaching the Dhamma while seated in the midst of a great assembly of deities, spoke the verse beginning with “He who by psychic power [crossed] the Sarabhū,” praising him in order to reveal his virtues out of compassion for the world.

38. Therein, "by means of psychic power" (iddhiyā) means by means of the psychic power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāniddhiyā). "The Sarabhū" refers to the river of that name, which is called "Sarabhū" in the world.
"He stopped" means he prevented it from flowing, turned back its current, and established it as a great mass of water like a mountain peak.
"Unbound" (asita) means not bound; one who is free from the support of craving and views, [and from] those things reckoned as fetters...
Or, because all fetters have been utterly severed, he is unbound by any bond; for that very reason, due to the absence of the defilements known as "agitation" (*ejā*), he is "undisturbed" (*aneja*).
O Gavampati, he has "transcended all attachments" (*sabbasaṅgātigata*) because he stands having transcended all attachments such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views.

He is a "great sage" (*mahāmuni*) because of his state as one beyond training (*asekha*). For that very reason, [he is free] from the various types of existence, such as existence through sensual desire (*kāma-bhava*) and existence through karma (*kamma-bhava*).
"Because he has gone to Nibbāna, the further shore of all existence, he is 'one who has gone beyond existence' (bhavassa pāraguṃ).
'The gods pay him homage' means that even the gods pay homage to him, let alone other beings.

At the conclusion of this verse, a great multitude of people attained penetration of the Dhamma. As the Elder was declaring his own realization, he spoke this very verse, thinking, "I shall honor the Teacher."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gavampati is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa:
"As if struck by a sword" refers to the verses of the Venerable Elder Tissa. What is their origin? It is said that he, too, [attained realization] under previous Buddhas.
Having performed his duties and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences,
he cleared away the withered leaves at the foot of the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Tissa and purified it. By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans,
he was reborn in this appearance of a Buddha in the city of Kapilavatthu as the son of the Blessed One’s paternal aunt.
He was named Tissa by name. Having followed the Blessed One into the homeless life and received full ordination, he dwelt in a forest region;
yet, giving rise to pride on account of his birth, he wandered about full of anger and distress, and full of complaints, making no effort toward the duties of a recluse.
Then one day, the Teacher [saw him] at his daytime resting place with his mouth wide open.
Beholding him sleeping with his divine eye, he traveled through the air from Sāvatthī, stood right above him in the sky, and having radiated light,
he awakened him by means of that light, aroused his mindfulness, and while giving him exhortation,
spoke the verse beginning, "As if struck by a sword."
39. In this context, "with a spear" (*sattiyā*) is merely a heading for the teaching; the meaning is "with a weapon such as a single-edged blade" (*ekatodhārādi*).
"Struck" (*omaṭṭho*) means "hit. For there are four kinds of strikes: *omaṭṭha*, *ummaṭṭha*, *maṭṭha*, and *vimaṭṭha*.
Among these, a strike delivered from above with the face downward is called *omaṭṭha*; a strike delivered from below with the face upward is *ummaṭṭha*.
That which has pierced through like a nail-point is called *maṭṭha*; all the rest is called *vimaṭṭha*.
However, in this context, *omaṭṭha* is intended. For that is most cruel, a wound with an arrow difficult to extract, hard to treat, and internally corrupt;
it is filled with pus and blood, which, without flowing out, surrounds the opening of the wound.
He remains. Those wishing to extract the pus and blood must tie him to a bed and place him with his head downward;
thus they encounter death or suffering amounting to death. "Being burned" means being consumed by fire.
"On the crown" means on the head. This is what is meant: just as a man struck by a spear [requires] the extraction of the dart and the treatment of the wound...
He exerts energy, applies such effort, and strives for the sake of this goal;
just as a man whose head is on fire would exert energy, apply such effort, and strive to extinguish that fire, even so, bhikkhu,
you should dwell with mindfulness and diligence, generating extraordinary enthusiasm for the abandoning of sensual lust.

Thus the Blessed One, while giving exhortation to that elder for the purpose of pacifying the underlying tendency to anger, concluded the teaching by focusing on the abandonment of sensual lust, as it is closely related to that goal.
Having heard this verse, the elder dwelt with a heart moved by spiritual urgency, applying himself to insight meditation.
Knowing his inclination, the Teacher taught the Tissatthera Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. At the conclusion of that teaching, he—
He established himself in arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having enjoyed both kinds of glory—among gods and among humans—at the end he attained the auspicious, unsurpassed Nibbāna.”
“Whatever person generates merit by dedicating it to the Fully Enlightened One, or to the Bodhi tree of that Teacher—
what indeed is difficult for such a person to obtain?
Regarding the Path, the Fruit, and the future, as well as the qualities of the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges— ”
Having become superior to others, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
"In the past, having joyfully cast aside my claim to the Bodhi tree,
I have now become endowed in every way with these twenty factors."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, the Elder spoke this very same verse in order to honor the Teacher while declaring his own higher knowledge.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tissa is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Vaḍḍhamāna "Struck as if by a spear" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vaḍḍhamāna. What is its origin?
It is said that this venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa ninety-two aeons ago.
Having reached the age of discretion, he saw the Blessed One wandering for alms and, with a mind full of faith, offered mango fruits that were perfectly ripe and detached from their stalks.
Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas;
accumulating further meritorious deeds in succession, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance into a Licchavi royal family in Vesālī.

His name was Vaḍḍhamāna. When he reached maturity, being faithful, confident, generous, delighting in giving, a doer of good deeds, and an attendant of the Saṅgha, he was—as if scorched by fire—when the Teacher performed the act of overturning his bowl for such an offense.
Having asked the Saṅgha for forgiveness and having had the disciplinary act suspended, he became filled with spiritual urgency and went forth into homelessness.
But having gone forth, he lived overcome by sloth and torpor. The Teacher, wishing to stir him up, recited the verse: "As if struck down by a spear.

(40) In this context, "for the abandoning of craving for existence" means for the sake of abandoning craving for existence—that is, craving for the fine-material realm and craving for the immaterial realm.
Although there is no such thing as abandoning external fetters without first abandoning internal fetters, [the phrase is used] because they do not exist simultaneously.
However, by the mention of the abandoning of the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), the abandoning of the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) is also already stated.
Or rather, because for some noble ones (*ariya*) who have completely severed the lower fetters,

the higher fetters are difficult to abandon, the Blessed One, showing that which is easy to abandon as contrasted with that which is difficult to abandon, [speaks] under the heading of the abandoning of lust for existence (*bhavarāga*).
He speaks of the abandonment of all the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). Or rather, this was stated thus according to the specific inclination of the Elder.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vaḍḍhamāna is concluded.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Fifth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirivaḍḍha.
"Lightnings follow the rift"—this is a verse of the Venerable Sirivaḍḍha Thera. What is its origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome karma conducive to the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) here and there, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī ninety-one aeons ago. Having reached maturity, he [saw] Vipassī...
Having seen the Blessed One and made an offering of *kiṅkaṇī* flowers, he was reborn in the world of the gods by virtue of that meritorious deed.
Performing further merits and wandering through successive happy destinies, he was born during this current appearance of a Buddha in the house of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha;
his name was Sirivaḍḍha. When he reached maturity, at the time of Bimbisāra’s accession...
Having conceived faith in the Teacher and the True Dhamma, he went forth due to his possession of the necessary causes.
Having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, he dwelt in a mountain cave in a certain forest retreat not far from the Vebhāra and Paṇḍava mountains, devoted to his meditation subject.
At that time, a great unseasonable cloud arose; streaks of lightning entered the mountain clefts.
They moved about as if [in play]. For the Elder, who was overcome by the fever of the heat, the fever was allayed by the breezes from the clouds within the mountain caves.
Through obtaining a favorable season, his mind became one-pointed. With a concentrated mind, he intensified his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Resembling a golden casket, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the World;
that Supreme Person bathed after plunging into the water.
Grasping a *kiṅkaṇī* flower, I offered it to Vipassi.”
With an uplifted mind and joyful heart, [I offered this] to the Tathāgata, the Lord of Bipeds:
“In the ninety-first aeon, because I offered this flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“In the twenty-seventh aeon, there was a king named Bhīmaratha;
endowed with the seven treasures, he was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [the rest as in the standard formula] … the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, however, while expressing a spontaneous utterance (*udāna*) based on himself under the guise of addressing others, he spoke the verse beginning, "Lightnings follow the rift.
(41) In this context, *vivaraṃ* means the intermediate space or the middle. *Anupatanti* means they fall or proceed in accordance with that [space];
the meaning is that they flash forth. For the flashing forth itself is what is called the movement of the lightning streaks. This is due to the connection with the prefix *anu*.
And here there is the use of the accusative case, as in “shining along the tree. *Vijjutā* means lightning.
The construction is: “following the gap between Vebhāra and Paṇḍava,” that is, between Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava.
“Having gone into the mountain gap” means having approached the mountain cave (*pabbataguha*). “He meditates” means by means of contemplation directed toward the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).
He meditates by means of contemplation on the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and develops [the practice] while striving for serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

He is the legitimate son (*orasaputta*) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is "the peerless one, the such-like" (*tādi*); that is, he is the son of the Buddha who is peerless and beyond comparison due to his perfection of the body of Dhamma—beginning with the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)—and his perfection of the physical body, and who is "such-like" (*tādi*) due to his possession of the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇa*) toward the desirable and undesirable, and so forth. By the very word "son,"...
And here, it should be understood that full realization (*aññā*) was declared by the Elder through his demonstration of having been born after the Teacher.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirivaḍḍha is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Khadiravaniya.
"Cāle upacāleti" is a verse by the Venerable Elder Revata of the Khadiravana. What is its origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of ferrymen at a landing place.
While performing the work of a ferryman at the Payāga ford on the Great Ganges, one day he [saw] the Blessed One together with his community of disciples on the bank of the Ganges.

Seeing that he had arrived, with a mind full of faith, he prepared a boat and, having brought him to the opposite shore with great honor and hospitality, saw a certain bhikkhu being designated by the Teacher as the foremost among those who dwell in the forest.
Having made a resolution for that purpose, he offered a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The Blessed One—
And he declared that his aspiration would never fail.
From then on, performing wholesome deeds that served as the necessary conditions for renunciation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) here and there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.

During this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in the village of Nālaka in the kingdom of Magadha, in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī. When he had reached maturity, his parents [bound him] with the ties of domestic life.
He became desirous of being ordained. Having heard that the Elder Sāriputta had gone forth, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking:
"My elder brother, the noble Upatissa, has abandoned this wealth and gone forth;

how could I swallow later what he has already spat out like a globule of spittle? Like a deer that does not approach a snare, he deceived his kinsmen and, through the perfection of his causal conditions, [went forth].
Being thus urged, he went into the presence of the monks, announced that he was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, and declared his desire for the going-forth.
The monks ordained him, and having conferred full admission upon him when he had reached twenty years of age, they assigned him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having taken up the meditation subject, he entered a *khadira* wood and [resolved]: "Arahatship..."

“Having reached [the Buddha], I shall see the Blessed One and the General of the Dhamma. Thus striving and exerting himself, because his knowledge had reached full maturity, he became a possessor of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña) before long. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Ganges, named Bhāgīrathī, flows forth from the Himalayas;”
In a certain place, I was a boatman, and I ferried people across to the other shore.
“The Leader named Padumuttara, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds,
arrived at the bank of the Ganges together with one hundred thousand masters.”
“Having brought many boats, well-constructed by carpenters,
and having made a covering for the boat, I invited the Bull among Men.
And the Sambuddha, having arrived, boarded that boat.”
Standing in the midst of the water, the Teacher spoke these verses:
“He who has ferried across the Fully Awakened One and the stainless Saṅgha,
by that clarity of mind, he shall rejoice in the world of the devas.”
“A celestial mansion will arise for you, well-constructed and not like an ordinary ship;
it will have a canopy of flowers and shall support you forever in the sky.
In the forty-eighth aeon, there will be a kshatriya king named Tāraka.”
“He will be a wheel-turning monarch, victorious over the four quarters.
In the fifty-seventh aeon, a kṣatriya named Cammaka,
arising like the sun, shall shine with great power.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the family name Gotama, will become a Teacher in the world.
Having passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he will go to the human state.”
One named Revata by name will become a nominal Brahmin.
Having gone forth from the home, urged on by his white roots of merit,
he will go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Gotama.
“Thus, having gone forth later on, devoted to practice and possessing insight,
by fully understanding all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Energy is my yoke-bearer, carrying me toward the security from bondage.”
I bear my final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The karma performed during one hundred thousand [aeons] has shown its fruit here to me;
like an arrow released from a bowstring, it has utterly liberated me and consumed my defilements.
“Then, seeing me delighting in the forest, the Sage who has reached the end of the world designated me as the foremost of the forest-dwelling bhikkhus, O Greatly Wise One.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having become possessed of the six supernormal powers, the Elder, after tidying his lodging and taking his bowl and robes, set out and eventually reached Sāvatthī. Entering Jetavana, he paid homage to the Teacher and the Dhamma-Senāpati, and dwelt for some days in Jetavana.
Then, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of Noble Ones, [he spoke] regarding those who dwell in the forest...
He placed him in the foremost position among the monks, saying: "Monks, this is the foremost among my monk disciples who are forest-dwellers, namely Revata of the Acacia Grove.
Later, having gone to his own birthplace, he [addressed] the three sons of his sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—by the names "Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā."
Having brought his three nephews and ordained them, he assigned them to their respective meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). They dwelt devotedly engaged in those meditation subjects.

At that time, a certain ailment arose in the Elder. Hearing of this, the Elder Sāriputta approached Revata with the thought, "I shall inquire after his illness and inquire about his spiritual attainments. The Elder Revata—
Seeing the Dhammasenāpati approaching from afar, he spoke the verse beginning with "Cāle upacāle" as an exhortation to arouse mindfulness in those novices.
In that context, "Cāle, Upacāle, Sīsūpacāle" is an address to them; [it means] "O Cālā, O Upacālā, O Sīsūpacālā."
Indeed, those three children, who had received their names based on feminine gender characteristics, were still addressed in that way even after they had gone forth into homelessness.

And it is said: "Their names were Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā. Demonstrating the purpose for which he addressed them with the words "Cālā," etc., he said, "Dwell mindful, indeed," and stated the reason for this: "He has come..."
“He is like a hair-splitter. *Patissatā* means mindful. *Kho* is used for emphasis.
*Āgato* means he has come. *Vo* means “to you. *Vālaṃ viya vedhī* means “like a hair-splitter”; this is the concise meaning here:
“The venerable Mātula, who is like the Teacher because of his sharp, swift, and penetrating wisdom, has come as a hair-splitter; therefore, having established the perception of him as a recluse...”
“Dwell always endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension; be diligent in the state you have attained.
Having heard this, those novices performed the duties of welcoming and so forth for the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
At the time of greeting the two maternal uncles, the elders, they entered into meditative concentration not too far away and sat down. The General of the Dhamma, together with the elder Revata—
Having exchanged greetings with them, he rose from his seat and approached those novices.
Because they had already set a time limit for themselves, they rose, paid homage, and stood still as the Elder was approaching.
The Elder asked, "In which various dwellings do you reside? When they replied, "In such-and-such a one," he said, "Even children are being trained in this way by me..."
"Truly, this brother has practiced in accordance with the Dhamma," he said, praising the Elder, and then departed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khadiravaniya is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumaṅgala.
"Sumuttiko" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sumaṅgala. What is its origin?

Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn as a tree deity.
One day, seeing the Teacher standing in a single robe after having bathed, he—

Filled with joy, he clapped his hands. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through births among gods and humans, he was reborn during the present arising of a Buddha in a certain village not far from Sāvatthī, in a poor family, due to the ripening of that same karma.
His name was Sumaṅgala. When he reached maturity, he possessed only the tools of a hunchbacked laborer: a coughing-stick, a plow, and a hoe.

Having offered [the oblation], he lived by means of agriculture. One day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was distributing a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he arrived carrying a jar of curd along with people who were bringing provisions for the gift.
Seeing the honor and respect shown to the bhikkhus, he thought, "These recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, are well-dressed in fine garments..."
Having eaten fine food and dwelling in dwellings sheltered from the wind, he thought, “What if I were to go forth?

Having approached a certain great elder and informed him of his intention to go forth, the elder, feeling compassion for him, ordained him and assigned him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). While dwelling in the forest, he became weary of living alone.

Becoming dissatisfied and desiring to leave the monastic life, he was traveling toward his native village when, on the way, he saw farmers who had bound their hair-tufts, were plowing a field, were dressed in soiled garments, had bodies covered in dust, and were being scorched by the wind and sun.
Seeing them, he was moved with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: "Alas, these beings experience great suffering for the sake of their livelihood!"
He attained it. Because his knowledge had reached full maturity, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) appeared to him exactly as he had grasped it.

Approaching the foot of a certain tree, having gained seclusion and applying wise attention, he increased his insight and, following the sequence of the paths, reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Atthadassī, the supreme Victor, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
having gone forth from his dwelling, approached a pond.
Having bathed and drunk, the Sambuddha, having emerged and wearing only a single robe,”
The Blessed One stood there, surveying every direction.
"I was seated within my dwelling when I saw the Leader of the World;
with a joyful heart, I clapped my hands in delight."
“Shining like a four-rayed sun, gleaming like refined gold;
I was devoted to dance and song, and to the fivefold musical instruments.
Whichever womb I entered—whether that of a deity or a human—”
I overcome all beings; my glory is vast.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
Having satisfied yourself, O Sage, you have satisfied others.
“Having sat upon a rug, having smiled at the Subhadda,
and having attended upon the Sambuddha, I was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
For sixteen hundred kappas, and two, nine, and one [kappa] of *cintita*...”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, powerful wheel-turning monarchs—my defilements have been burnt away... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) while praising his own excellence and liberation from suffering, beginning with the words, “I am well-freed.”
43. Therein, "well-liberated" (*sumuttika*) means one for whom there is beautiful liberation (*mutti*) that is final and free from renewed existence (*apunarbhava*).
However, because of the excellence and wonder of that liberation, he clapped his hands and said, "Well-liberated!
Furthermore, demonstrating the firmness of his own confidence in that liberation, he said, "It is well; I am well-liberated."
He said: “It means ‘Well done! We are truly well-liberated. But from what does this state of being well-liberated come?
Granted, this elder was indeed completely liberated from all the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*);

however, pointing out the suffering that had arisen for him which was exceedingly undesirable, he spoke the words beginning with “by three hunchbacks. In that context, “by hunchbacks” means by those having the nature of hunchbacks.
Or by means of three crooked things. This is an ablative construction in relation to the word *mutta*.
For even though a farmer is not himself hunchbacked, he displays himself as hunchbacked in three ways: in reaping, in plowing, and in the work of digging.

Indeed, those tools such as the sickle with which the farmer performs the reaping and so forth are also called "crooked" because of their curved shape; thus it is said, "by means of three crooked things."
Now, showing those [implements] according to their specific forms, he said: "By me with sickles, by me with ploughs, by me with small spades.
Therein, "by me with sickles" means "I was released by means of sickles"; this is the locative case used in the sense of the instrumental.
The same principle applies to the others as well. Others, however, explain: "'By me with sickles' means I was bent over by means of sickles acting as instruments."
They say this. According to their opinion, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental or the causal.

The expression “naṅgalāsu” is stated by means of a change of gender; the meaning is “by means of ploughs,” that is, by means of those who plough with ploughs. Because of the smallness of the hoe used by oneself, or because of its being used [only] occasionally, it is called “khuddakuddālāsu”;
there is also a textual reading “kuṇṭhakuddālāsu. It is [so called] precisely because of its being used [only occasionally].

"Atikhiṇakhaṇittesu" means "with very sharp spades. In the phrase "idhameva," the letter *m* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). Alternatively, the particle *vā* in "atha vā" is merely an expletive.
Because they were located in the village, although those sickles and other tools were indeed right here, in my very presence, nevertheless, the meaning is that they were quite sufficient.
This repetition is due to a sense of urgency. "Jhāyāti" refers to meditating by way of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the fruits [of the path].
"Meditate for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, by way of the divine abodes and so forth. He addresses himself as "Sumaṅgala.

The repetition (*āmeḍita*) is used here to show his earnestness regarding meditation. "Dwell heedful": because you have attained the full expansion of mindfulness and wisdom, you are indeed heedful in every respect;
therefore, dwell now in happiness, Sumaṅgala. Some, however, [explain it differently].

“They say that even before attaining Arahantship, while the Elder was proceeding along the path of insight (vipassanā) and had developed a deep delight in the Teaching, he spoke this verse out of loathing for the suffering of household life as experienced by himself; subsequently, having further developed insight, he reached Arahantship.
According to their opinion, the meaning of the words “Meditate, dwell with diligence” is as follows:
It is indeed appropriate even from the perspective of the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sumaṅgala is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sānu.
"The mother weeps," is the verse of the Venerable Sānu Thera. What is its origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [once] offered water for the purpose of washing the hands and feet and rinsing the mouth of the Blessed One Siddhattha ninety-four aeons ago.
He brought it forward. For at the time of the meal, the Teacher desired to wash his hands and feet; observing the Teacher’s intention, he brought water.
After the Blessed One had washed his hands and feet and eaten, he desired to rinse his mouth;
knowing that as well, he brought water for rinsing the mouth. The Teacher rinsed his mouth and completed the task of cleansing it.
Thus, out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted the service being performed by him.

Having been reborn in the world of the gods through that meritorious deed, and having performed further merits as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, he took conception in the home of a certain lay devotee in Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha. While he was still in the womb...
The father had gone abroad, and after ten months had passed, the female lay devotee gave birth to a son and gave him the name Sānu.

As he gradually grew up, when he was only seven years old, she had him ordained in the presence of the monks, thinking, "In this way, he will grow up without obstacles and partake in ultimate happiness. Thus, he became known as the novice Sānu.

Being wise, perfected in his duties, learned, a preacher of the Dhamma, and possessing a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, he became dear and pleasing to gods and humans—all this is to be understood according to the method set forth in the Sānu Sutta.
In a previous birth, his mother was reborn in the womb of a yakkha. The yakkhas [recognized her], saying, "This is the mother of the Elder Sānu."
Having become full of great respect, they honored him.

As time passed in this way, as if manifesting the danger of the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), one day, due to a lack of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) and emerging through unwise means, a thought of wishing to disrobe arose in Sānu.
The mother of that *yakkhinī*, knowing this, informed the human mother.
—“Sānu, your son conceived the thought, ‘I shall disrobe.
Therefore, you should say to Sānu when he has awakened: ‘This is the word of the yakkhas:
Do not commit an evil deed, whether in public or in private.’”
“If you commit an evil deed, or if you are committing one, there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you were to fly up and flee.
Having spoken thus, the mother-yakkhinī vanished right then and there. But the human mother—
Upon hearing this, she was overcome with lamentation and grief, and became possessed by mental anguish.
Then, in the morning, the novice Anusāma dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and approached his mother; seeing her weeping, he asked, "Mother, on account of what do you weep?
When she replied, "On account of him," he said to his mother, "Mother, people weep for one who is dead."
He recited this verse: "Or he who, though living, is not seen.
(44) Its meaning is as follows: "Mother, it is indeed relatives or friends who weep on account of a deceased relative or friend who has gone to the other world;
or [they weep] for a relative or friend who, while still living, has gone to another country."
"Because he has departed, he is not seen; or perhaps they weep on his account. Neither of these reasons exists in my case.
This being so, as you see me standing here before you, alive and well, why do you weep, mother?
There is simply no reason for you to weep on my account."
Hearing this, his mother—showing that in the Noble One’s discipline, falling away from the training and returning to the lower life is death—recited a verse in accordance with the words of the Sutta:
“They weep for one who is dead, or for one who is alive but not seen;
yet they weep even more for him who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, returns here again.”
“They weep for that son as well, for though he was once alive, he is now dead.
My dear, having been pulled out from the fiery pit, you wish to fall back into the fiery pit.
Thus he spoke these two verses.
In this context, "having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having relinquished objective sensual pleasures through an inclination toward renunciation;
this should be understood as the abandonment of the defilement of sensual desire by way of its specific factor (tadaṅga). Here, "renunciation" is intended as the forsaking of sensual pleasures.
"Returns here again" means he returns once more to this home; he speaks with reference to returning to the lower life. "Or that [person]" refers to whoever...
Having gone forth, he falls away from the religious life; even for such a person, they weep as if for one who is dead. Why is that?
Because one who has fallen away is, in effect, already dead through the death of his virtues, even though he is still living after that falling away.
Now, in order to produce in him an especially intense sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), it is said: "From the burning pit," and so forth. Its meaning is: "Day and night it is ablaze..."
“Because it resembles the Kukkuḷa hell in its nature as something burning, it has been lifted up—drawn out—from the state of a householder by me, who have compassion for you, dear Sānu.
Do you wish to fall into the Kukkuḷa? You are desirous of falling.
Upon hearing this, the novice Sānu was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega); he established insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Seeing the ascetic eating, his mind serene and undisturbed,
I took water in a jar and gave it to Siddhattha.
Today I am stainless, pure, and my doubts are destroyed.”
For one being reborn into existence, a beautiful fruit is produced.
Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave water to Yama;
I do not recall ever falling into an evil state—this is the fruit of giving water.
“In the sixty-first aeon, there was but one Vimala;
he was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [the rest as above] … the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, however, the Elder, by way of this verse, thought, "The commencement of my insight and the attainment of arahantship have occurred," and he recited that very same verse as an utterance of joy (*udāna*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sānu is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin.
"Even as a noble thoroughbred horse"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ramaṇīyavihāri. What is its origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit here and there, saw the Blessed One Vipassī ninety-one aeons ago;
with a mind full of faith, he prostrated himself on his five limbs and offered worship with *koraṇḍa* flowers.
He performed that meritorious deed. Having been reborn among the devas by virtue of that merit and performing further merits, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans.
In this present dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a certain merchant.
Overcome by the intoxication of youth, he lived infatuated with sensual pleasures. One day, he [encountered] a certain adulterer...
Seeing various punishments being inflicted by the king’s men, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he went forth.

Once gone forth, because of his temperament characterized by passion (*rāgacarita*), he always kept his cell well-swept, his water for drinking and washing well-set out, and his bed and chair well-arranged. Because of this, he became known as "the one who dwells in delightful lodgings" (*ramaṇīyavihārī*).
Thus, due to being overwhelmed by lust, he applied his mind inappropriately and committed the offense of intentional emission of semen.

Becoming remorseful, thinking, "Shame on me! How can one such as I consume what has been given in faith?", he set out with the intention, "I shall disrobe," and sat down at the foot of a tree along the way. While carts were passing along that same road, one [person]...
A bullock harnessed to a cart, exhausted and stumbling on uneven ground, fell down;
the carters released him from the yoke, gave him grass and water, relieved his fatigue, and having re-harnessed him to the pole once more, they departed. Seeing this, the Elder thought:
"Just as this bullock, though he stumbled once, rose up and bore the yoke again, so too must I, by means of the defilements..."
"Even if one has once stumbled, it is appropriate to rise again and practice the duty of a recluse.

Emerging with such wise reflection, he turned back, explained his situation to the Elder Upāli, and having emerged from the offense according to the method prescribed by him, restored his virtue to its natural state.
Having established insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having seen the footprint marked with the ornament of the wheel,
following step by step upon the path of the Great Seer Vipassi,
and seeing the flowering koraṇḍa tree worshipped by me along with its roots;”
Joyful with a joyful heart, I paid homage to the supreme state.
“For ninety-one eons, because I offered that flower in worship, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“In the fifty-seventh aeon, I was one who was free from stain;
endowed with the seven treasures, I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he spoke this verse—“Just as a noble thoroughbred, having stumbled, stands firm”—to illustrate his own attainment of the Noble Dhamma along with his prior practice.
(45) Therein, *khalitvā* means having stumbled. *Patitiṭṭhati* means he stands firm; he stands once again in his original place.
*Evaṃ* means just as a noble bull, while carrying a burden, reaches a state of exhaustion upon reaching uneven ground...
Having approached once and slipped and fallen, he does not abandon his burden on that account alone;
rather, because he is endowed with steadfastness, speed, and perseverance, even though he has stumbled and fallen, he stands up again, and remaining in his own true nature, he carries the load.
In the same way, one who has encountered the exhaustion of the defilements and stumbled through a failure in action restores that stumble by means of the attainment of steadfastness and vigor.
"Consider me, and take note of me, as one endowed with vision through right view of the Path;

as a disciple born into the noble birth by virtue of having heard [the Dhamma] from the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One; and as his own legitimate son (orasa-putta) by virtue of the nobility produced through effort in his breast, because my function is like that of a well-bred thoroughbred (ājānīya). This is the meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rāmaṇīyavihāri is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Samiddhi:
"Out of faith I went forth"—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Samiddhi. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
In the exercise of his agency as a doer, accumulating merits here and there, he saw the Blessed One Siddhattha ninety-four aeons ago;
with a mind full of faith, he took flower buds bound together with their stalks and offered them in worship.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and by performing further merits, he continued to revolve through the happy destinies alone.
During this dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn into a noble family in Rājagaha. From the time of his birth, that family increased in wealth, grain, and other assets;
and as for his own person, it was handsome, beautiful to behold, and endowed with virtues.

Thus, through both the excellence of his prosperity and the excellence of his virtues, he became known simply as "Samiddhi. At the meeting with King Bimbisāra, he [witnessed] the majesty of the Buddha.
Having seen this, he gained faith, went forth, and dwelt devotedly engaged in meditation. While the Blessed One was staying at Tapodārāma, on one occasion he thought thus:
"It is indeed a gain for me that my Teacher is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One;
I have gone forth in the well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya; and my fellow-celibates are virtuous and of lovely character."

As he was thinking thus, a sublime rapture and joy arose within him. Unable to endure it, Māra the Evil One produced a great, terrifying sound not far from the Elder, as if the very earth were being rent asunder.
The Elder reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “Māra intends to cause you to lose your vision; go there, bhikkhu.”
“Dwell without reflecting,” he said. Having gone there and dwelling, the Elder soon brought his insight (vipassanā) to its peak and attained Arahatship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Seated amidst the mountains, shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower...”
To Siddhattha, the charioteer of men, who was illuminating all directions,
I then made my bow straight, fixed an arrow,
and having plucked a flower with its stalk, I offered it to the Buddha.
“In ninety-four aeons ago, because I offered this flower, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In fifty-one aeons ago, I was once Jutindhara.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
[He then recited: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
But while the Elder remained right there after attaining arahantship, one who did not know his state of having destroyed the taints [approached him] in the same manner as before.

Māra let out a great, terrifying sound. Hearing it, the Elder remained fearless and undaunted, thinking, "Even a hundred or a thousand Māras like this would not make even a single hair on my body quiver.
Declaring his own realization, he spoke the verse: "With faith I went forth.
(46) Therein, "with faith" means with both the faith in the fruit of karma arising from the desire for the Dhamma, and the faith in the Triple Gem.
“Ca” (and) indicates that he refers to himself. “Pabbajito” means one who has gone forth. “Agārasmā” means from the house or from the household life.

“Anagāriyaṃ” means the state of homelessness; for that which is beneficial to the house—namely, any work such as farming or trade—is called “agāriya,” and because of the absence of that, it is called “anagāriya.
“Sati paññā ca me vuḍḍhā” means that my mindfulness and wisdom have increased; they are characterized by the act of remembering.

"Mindfulness exists" and "wisdom has the characteristic of clear comprehension"—these states have increased and grown for me from the moment of insight meditation through the sequence of the paths up to Arahantship;
now they need no further growth, as mindfulness and wisdom have reached full maturity.
This shows that "the mind is well-concentrated" by way of both the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and supramundane concentration (*lokuttara-samādhi*).
"And my mind is well-composed; there is nothing further for it to be composed. This shows that my concentration has reached full maturity.
Therefore, 'O Evil One, do as you wish with forms'—do whatever various distortions you please directed toward me;
yet you shall not afflict me with them, nor even cause the slightest trembling of my body."
“You will not be able [to do so]; how could there be any change in your mind? Therefore, your action, like an unaccepted gift, achieves no purpose at all;
it results in nothing but mere mental distress for you. Thus the Elder rebuked Māra.
Upon hearing this, Māra thought, “The ascetic knows me,” and vanished right then and there.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Samiddhi is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ujjaya:
"Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero! These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Ujjaya. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties by making meritorious deeds in various states of existence, he beheld the Blessed One Tissa ninety-two aeons ago and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of *kaṇikāra* flowers. By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
and having performed further merits and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
In Rājagaha, he was reborn as the son of a certain Sottiya Brahmin; his name was Ujjaya.
When he reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas, he saw no essence therein and, urged by his spiritual predispositions, went to Veḷuvana.
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, and—
Having taken up a meditation subject suitable to his temperament and dwelling in the forest, he increased his insight and before long attained Arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Seeing a *kaṇikāra* tree in full bloom, I then plucked its flowers;”
I offered [a flower] to Tissa, the Tathāgata who had crossed over the flood.
"In ninety-two aeons from now, because I offered that flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha."
“In the thirty-fifth aeon from now, renowned as Aruṇapāṇi, I shall be a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahatship, he went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Expressing his realization in the manner of praising the Blessed One, he recited the verse:
“Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero! (47). In this context, *nama* is an expression of salutation. *Te* is an expression of the recipient of that act of salutation;

the meaning is “to you. *Buddha vīra* is an address to the Blessed One. For the Blessed One is [the one who has] understood, according to the classification of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth.
He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to the Dhamma in its entirety through his self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), by way of the categories such as "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*).
Likewise, he is called "Hero" (*vīra*) because he is endowed with great energy (*vīriya*) while striving to utterly crush the five Māras.
"Atthu" means "let it be"; its connection is with the word "namo. "Vippamuttosi sabbadhī" means...
You are completely liberated and dissociated from all defilements and from the entire realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);

there is nothing whatsoever that remains unliberated by you. Therefore, "dwelling in your *apadāna*, I dwell free from taints (*anāsava*)"—meaning, dwelling in your *apadāna*, that is, in your instruction and the path you have traversed, I am practicing according to my capacity and strength.
"Because all four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, have been thoroughly abandoned, I dwell without taints; homage to you, such a Buddha, O Hero!
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ujjaya is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sañjaya.
"Since I... is a verse of the Venerable Sañjaya Thera. What is its origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) here and there, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, gathered materials through the distribution of alms among a great multitude and performed meritorious acts dedicated to the Triple Gem; he himself...
Having become poor, he was occupied with performing meritorious deeds for those groups and others.
From time to time, he would approach the Blessed One, pay homage, and with a devout mind perform various services for the monks.
By virtue of that meritorious karma, he was reborn in the world of the devas; having performed further merits and wandering through the happy realms, in this [life]...
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy Brahmin named Sañjaya by name.
When he reached maturity, seeing renowned Brahmins such as Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti who were deeply devoted to the Teaching, he conceived faith and approached the Teacher.
The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. He [listened to] the Dhamma...

Having heard [the teaching], he became a stream-enterer. Later, he went forth into homelessness. At the very moment of his going forth, while still holding the razor, he attained the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā).
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“There was a great multitude of monks for the Blessed One Vipassī;”
I was a servant, busying myself with all kinds of tasks.
"I have no gift to offer the Sugata, the Great Seer," [I thought];
yet, with a mind full of serene confidence, I paid homage at the feet of the Teacher.
“Ninety-one aeons ago, I performed services;
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state—this is the fruit of service.
And eight aeons ago from now, I was a king named Sucintita.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [etc. …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the six direct knowledges, he then spoke the verse beginning ‘Since I went forth’ as his declaration of final knowledge.”
48. In this context, "since I went forth" means from which time, from which starting point, I went forth.

From the time of my going forth, I do not recall any intention that was ignoble and associated with hatred—that is, associated with the defilements of lust and so forth—and for that very reason, ignoble and base;
or, because it is not to be resorted to by the noble ones (*ariya*) and is to be resorted to by the ignoble ones (*anariya*), it is ignoble and evil.
“I do not recall having given rise to wrong thoughts such as sensual thought (kāmavitakka), which are named ‘thoughts’ because they imagine unreal qualities and so forth in an object;
rather, I declared my higher knowledge (aññā) thus: ‘I attained Arahatship at the very tip of the razor.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sañjaya is finished.
9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka "Resounding with the *cihacihā* [of birds]," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka. What is his origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having been reborn and attained the state of full consciousness, he saw the Blessed One and, with a mind full of serene faith, made an offering of flowers.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; performing further acts of merit and wandering through the happy realms, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in Sāvatthī within a clan of outcasts. Upon reaching maturity, during the acceptance of the Jeta Grove...
Having conceived faith, he went forth into homelessness, took up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament, and dwelt in the forest.
Because of his personal excellence and his inspiring conduct, which was worthy of one who had gone forth, he became known by the name Rāmaṇeyyaka (“The Delightful One”).
Then one day, Māra, desiring to terrify the Elder, let out a terrifying sound. That—
Having heard this, the Elder, being of firm character, was not disturbed by it;
knowing, "This is Māra," he spoke the verse beginning with “*Cihacihābhinadite*” to show his disregard for him.
Regarding that, “*Cihacihābhinadite*”: because of the state of constantly producing the sound “*cihacihā*,” it is called “*cihacihā*.”
The meaning is: for the sake of the sound of the cries of the birds known as *vaṭṭaka*, that is, on account of their screaming.
And "by the warbling of the *sippika* birds": *sippika* refers to the *devaka* birds, also called *paranāmaka*, which are tree-dwelling animals resembling hungry children due to illness.

Some call them "great *kalandaka*"; [the phrase means] by the warbling, the great screams, of the *sippikas*. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause; thus, it means "on account of that."
The meaning is this: "My mind does not tremble" means my mind neither quivers nor wavers. This is what is intended:
"O Evil One, because of your shouting in this forest—just as [birds] might cry out for the sake of food or the chirping of small birds—my mind does not fall away from its meditation subject.
He states the reason for this: "For I delight in unity."

The word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Because my mind, having abandoned association with the crowd, delights in and is devoted to solitude (*ekatta*), or to one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) by abandoning outward distraction, or to Nibbāna which is of a single nature (*ekasabhāva*), therefore it does not waver or fall away from its meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
While reciting this verse, it is said, the Elder attained insight (*vipassanā*).
Having increased [his merit], he attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One, golden-hued, with a hundred rays, full of majesty, the Lion of the Śākyas, with a mind of loving-kindness, had ascended the walkway.”
"With a clear mind and joyful heart, having paid homage to the Supreme Knower,
I took a *minela* flower and offered it to the Buddha.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that flower which I offered in worship..."
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In the twenty-ninth aeon, I was named Sumeghaghana, a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
This was the very verse by which the Elder proclaimed his final knowledge (aññā).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vimala.
The verses beginning with "He waters the earth and it blows" are the verses of the venerable Elder Vimala. What is their origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Vipassi...
Having been reborn in a family of conch-blowers at Kāla, he reached maturity and attained proficiency in that craft.
One day, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, his mind was filled with serene faith;

he made an offering by blowing his conch and from then on, from time to time, attended upon the Teacher. By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and from there to other realms...
Having performed meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he thought, "In the future,
may my body be stainless and pure," and so he bathed the Bodhi tree with scented water,
had the seats in the courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree washed, and also had the monks wash their soiled monastic requisites.
Having passed away from there, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in Rājagaha into a clan of outcasts (*ibbha*).
While dwelling in his mother’s womb and when emerging from it, his body was undefiled by bile, phlegm, and other impurities;
like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, it remained unstained, just like that of a Bodhisattva in his final existence.
He became perfectly pure, and therefore they gave him the name Vimala.

When he reached maturity, having seen the majesty of the Buddha upon his entry into Rājagaha, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and after receiving a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he dwelt in a mountain cave in the kingdom of Kosala.
Then one day, a great cloud that rained over the four continents [sent] rain throughout the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Having spread out, it rained. It is said that such rain falls only during the lifetime of Buddhas and Cakkavattins when they stand in the open air.
Through the subsiding of the fever of heat and by obtaining a favorable climate, the Elder’s mind became concentrated and one-pointed.
With his mind thus concentrated, he immediately exerted himself in insight (vipassanā) and, following the sequence of the paths, [attained the fruit of Arhatship].
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“I was a conch-blower for the Blessed One Vipassī;
I was ever devoted to the service of the Sugata, the Great Seer.”
“Behold the fruit of my service to the Protector of the World, the Tathāgata:
sixty thousand musicians always attend upon me.
For ninety-one eons, I served the Great Sage.”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of my attendance.
Twenty-four aeons hence, there will be sixteen kings named Mahānigghosa, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, with a mind gladdened by the completion of his task, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), reciting the verse: “The earth is moistened and the wind blows.
(50) Therein, *dharaṇī* means the earth; for it is called “the bearer” (*dharaṇī*) because it supports the entire world-system (*dharādhara*).
"It sprinkles" means that it sprinkles with the torrents of rain from a great cloud that rains down, filling the sky on all sides.
"The breeze blows" means that a cool wind blows, mixed with droplets of water.
"Lightning flashes in the sky" means that bright flashes, issuing from the great cloud here and there with thundering and rumbling sounds, move to and fro across the atmosphere.

And they wander about. "Thoughts are stilled" means that through the attainment of serenity and insight accomplished by means of a suitable climate, all nine great thoughts—beginning with sensual thought—having been stilled in the preliminary stage by way of their partial abandonment (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, are stilled by the attainment of the Noble Path;
they are cut off without remainder. Because it is in proximity to what is currently occurring, the moment of the Noble Path is referred to as "present."
He speaks having made [this statement]. Or rather, this is a word for the present used in the sense of the past.

"My mind is well-concentrated"—thereby, because of that very supramundane concentration (*lokuttara-samādhi*), the Elder declared his final knowledge (*aññā*), meaning: "My mind is thoroughly concentrated; now there is nothing further to be done for its concentration."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vimala is finished.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
6. The Sixth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Four Elders beginning with Godhika.
The four verses beginning with “The god rains” are the verses of these four elders: Godhika, Subāhu, Valliya, and Uttiya.
What is their origin? These too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, [arose] in various states of existence.
Accumulating merit, they were reborn in noble families during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha ninety-four aeons ago.
Having reached maturity, they lived as companions to one another.
Among them, one saw the Blessed One Siddhattha wandering for alms and gave him a spoonful of food. The second, with a mind full of faith, prostrated himself in the fivefold manner.
Having paid homage, he held up his hands in *añjali*. The third, with a mind full of faith, worshipped the Blessed One with a handful of flowers.
The fourth made an offering with *sumana* flowers. Having thus inspired confidence in their hearts toward the Teacher, they were reborn in the world of the gods by virtue of that meritorious deed.
Continuing to perform further acts of merit, they wandered through successive births among gods and humans.
Having been born into noble families during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa and having become companions, they went forth into the teaching and practiced the duties of a recluse.
During the time of our own Blessed One, they were reborn in Pāvā as the sons of four Mallan kings.
They were given the names Godhika, Subāhu, Valliya, and Uttiya, and they became dear friends to one another.
They went to Kapilavatthu on some business.
At that time, the Teacher had gone to Kapilavatthu and, while residing in the Nigrodha Monastery, had displayed the Twin Miracle and subdued the Sakyan kings headed by Suddhodana.
Then those four Mallan princes, having seen the miracle and gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), they attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"The Supremely Enlightened One, golden-hued, the recipient of offerings, The most excellent one who had gone forth from the forest and come to the state beyond suffering (nibbāna)."
“I offered a spoonful of alms-food to Siddhattha, the Great Sage,
the one who is peaceful through wisdom, the Great Hero, the Neutral One.
Following his footstep by footstep, he was extinguishing the great multitude of people.”
A sublime joy has arisen in me toward the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
That gift which I gave ninety-four eons ago—I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of giving alms to a monk.
“In the seventy-eighth aeon ago, there were seven wheel-turning monarchs named Mahāreṇu, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as above]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Thera Godhika:
“The Sambuddha, golden-hued like a bull of noble breed,
like a three-fold rutting elephant, a Mātaṅga, a great Sage.”
