“I did not see the Eldest of the World entering the street— He who illuminates all directions like the full moon.
Having clarified my mind in wisdom and raising my hands in reverent salutation, I paid homage.”
With a serene heart and joyful mind, I paid homage to Siddhattha.
"The deed that I performed back in the ninety-fourth aeon—
I do not know a state of misery, for this is the fruit of that perception of wisdom."
“In the seventy-third aeon, there were sixteen supreme among men;
they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
The Elder Subāhu said:
“At that time, I was a florist living in Tivarā;
I saw the stainless Buddha Siddhattha, who is honored by the world.”
"With a clear heart and a joyful mind, I offered a handful of flowers.
Wherever I was reborn, by the power of that deed,
I experienced the desirable fruit of my own well-performed merit in the past."
Encircled by beautiful garlands—this is the fruit of offering flowers.
“For ninety-four eons since I offered that flower, I have not known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of the flower-worship.”
“Excluding the present one, there were four hundred and ninety-nine kings there whose names were identical to my own.
My defilements have been incinerated... [and so forth]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Thera Valliya said:
“I offered birth-flowers to the Blessed One Siddhattha;
seven flowers were scattered by me in jest upon his feet.”
“By that deed, today I surpass both men and gods;
I bear my final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Ninety-four aeons ago, the flower that I offered—”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of offering flowers.
In the thirteenth aeon ago, there were thirteen universal monarchs named Samantagandha, lords of men over the four quarters.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus spoke the Elder Uttiya.
Having attained arahantship, these four elders became renowned and famous throughout the world among kings, royal ministers, and high officials.
Being honored and revered, they dwelt together in the forest.
Then one day, when those four elders had arrived at Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra approached them, paid homage, and invited them to spend the three-month rains retreat.
He had separate huts built for each of them, but through a lapse of mindfulness, he did not roof them. While the elders were in these unroofed huts,
They were dwelling there. During the rainy season, the rain did not fall. The king, wondering, "What indeed is the reason the rain does not fall?

and having understood that reason, had those huts roofed over, and after having them plastered with clay and decorated with paintings, he held a festival for the huts and gave alms to a great community of monks. Out of compassion for the king, the elders...
Having entered their huts, they attained the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness (*mettā-samāpatti*).
Then, a great cloud arose from the northeastern direction and began to rain at the very moment the elders emerged from their absorption.
Among them, the elder Godhika emerged from his absorption and, together with the thundering of the clouds—
“The god rains as if well-sung; my little hut is thatched, pleasant, and sheltered from the wind;
my mind is well-composed. So, O god, rain if you so desire!”—thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, "it rains" means it sprinkles and pours down a stream of rain. "The god" refers to the cloud.

The intention is that it thunders like a beautiful song (*sugīta*). For at the time of raining, the cloud shines as it rises up with hundreds and thousands of layers, thundering and emitting flashes of lightning, and not alone. Therefore, its sound is smooth, sweet, and deep.
“‘The god rains’ indicates that it is raining. By this, he says that [the hut] is not oppressed by sound: ‘My little hut is covered, pleasant, and windless.
Just as the god does not rain, so this little hut of mine is covered with grass and other materials; thus he says it is not oppressed by that rainy weather.
It is ‘pleasant’ because of the presence of the comfort of use and the comfort of a suitable climate. It is [windless] due to the doors being shut and the windows being closed.”
"Free from the affliction of wind. By both [phrases], he speaks of being unoppressed by way of the suitability of the dwelling.
"And my mind is well-concentrated": my mind is thoroughly concentrated by means of the supreme concentration, well-fixed upon the object of Nibbāna;
by this, he shows the state of having little concern due to the absence of internal afflictions. "If you then desire": then.
"If you now aspire—if you so desire—rain down; pour forth water; let a stream of rain flow.
He addresses the cloud as "O Deva.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Godhika is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Subāhu (52).
There is a distinction only in the third word of the verses spoken by the others.

In that regard, in the verse spoken by Subāhu, the phrase "my mind is well-composed and my body" means that my mind is thoroughly composed within the physical body (*karajakāya*) by means of the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).

It was rightly applied. For this elder, having taken as a basis the jhāna obtained through the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), and having developed insight, attained arahantship. With reference to him, it is said: "The mind is well-concentrated upon the body.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Subāhu is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Valliya (Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) 53.
Regarding the verse from the Elder Valliya’s collection, "In that [hut] I dwell heedful":

because he has brought his practice of heedfulness to its ultimate perfection within that small hut, he is "heedful" by means of a mode of conduct associated with noble dwelling, divine dwelling, and so forth, as well as the dwelling in the postures.
"I dwell; I maintain my personal existence"—this is what is meant.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Valliya is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttiya.
54. In the verse spoken by the Elder Uttiya, "without a second" means without a companion; that is to say, one who is devoid of the company of defilements and the company of social groups.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttiya is finished.
The commentary on the verses of the four elders is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Añjanavaniya "Having made a small hut with a throne...
These are the verses of the venerable elder Añjanavaniya. What is their origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a florist named Sudassana, and with *sumana* flowers, he [honored] the Blessed One...
Having performed worship and created much merit in various places, he wandered among gods and humans;
then, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he practiced the duties of a recluse.
Now, during this arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in Vesālī into the Vajjī royal family, and when he reached maturity, there arose in the Vajjī kingdom the fear of drought and the fear of disease.
Regarding "fear of non-human beings," three kinds of fear arose. All of that should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Ratana Sutta*.

However, when the Blessed One had entered Vesālī, the fears had subsided, and many gods and humans had attained penetration of the Dhamma through the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, this prince [perceived] the majesty of the Buddha.
Having seen this, he gained faith and went forth. Just as he did, so too did the four persons who are about to be mentioned immediately after him.
For they were also Licchavi princes who had been his companions, and they likewise went forth in this very same manner.
Even in the time of the Sambuddha Kassapa, having been his companions, they went forth together with him and practiced the duty of a recluse; and so too in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
"They planted the seeds of wholesome merit at the feet [of the Buddha].

Thereupon, having performed his preliminary duties, while staying in the Añjana Forest cemetery at Sāketa, he obtained an old chair discarded by people as the time for the commencement of the rains approached;
having placed it upon four stones, covered it above and around with grass and other materials, and secured a door, [he lived there].
Having entered the rains retreat, he attained *arahantship* while still striving and exerting himself during the very first month. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“By the name Sudassana, I was a garland-maker at that time;
I saw the stainless Buddha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men.”
“Having taken a *jāti* flower, I worshipped Padumuttara;
with pure vision and a joyful mind, I attained the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Through this offering of flowers and through the aspirations of my heart,”
For a hundred thousand aeons, I did not fall into an unhappy destination.
Sixteen kings named Devuttara reigned;
thirty-six aeons ago, they were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s instruction has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he emerged from his meditative attainment, reflected upon the prosperity he had obtained, and, moved by a surge of joy, uttered this verse of exultation:
“Having fashioned a small throne out of a chair... (55). In this context, “āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā” means that an *āsandi* is a four-legged seat with long legs; it is elongated.
The four-legged chair is also indeed permissible; having constructed a small hut for the purpose of dwelling— where one can sit but not lie down—
in the manner described below, and having built the hut so that one who sits therein can easily practice the Dhamma of a recluse due to the absence of seasonal dangers,
by this [phrase] the most excellent type of lodging is indicated.
This demonstrates his own fewness of wishes and contentment. And this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“For one sitting cross-legged, the knees are drenched with rain;
Yet that is sufficient for the comfort of a bhikkhu who is resolute.”
Others, citing the reading "āsandikuṭikaṃ," explain the meaning as "having built a small hut the size of a chair (āsandī).
Still others, however, explain the meaning as: "A 'chair' (āsandī) is a hut built over a bedstead for the purpose of people sitting on chairs and such;
having built that chair-hut. *Oggayha* means having plunged into or entered.

"Añjanavana" is a forest of that name; for because the creepers there have flowers the color of collyrium (*añjana*), they are called "añjanā," and due to the abundance of these, that forest received the name "Añjanavana. Others, however, say that "añjanā" refers to a certain kind of great shrub.
Having descended into that Añjanavana and constructed a small hut on a tripod stand, he attained the threefold knowledge (*tisso vijjā*). Thus it was done.

The construction is to be understood through the ellipsis of the words "I am dwelling in the teaching of the Buddha. And this very [verse] was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Añjanavaniya is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kuṭivihārin.
"Ko kuṭikāyaṃ" is a verse of the Venerable Kuṭivihāri Thera. What is its origin?

It is said that when the Blessed One Padumuttara was traveling through the air, [the thera], thinking "I shall give a gift of water," took cool water and, filled with joy and gladness, threw it upward with his face turned upwards.
The Teacher, knowing his intention, for the sake of increasing his faith, [appeared] in the sky...
Standing still, he accepted it. Because of that, he experienced no small measure of rapture and joy.
The rest is exactly as told in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. This, however, is the distinction:

having gone forth in the manner described and performed the preliminary duties, while he was applying himself to insight meditation, he was walking near a field in the evening when it began to rain; [he took shelter] with the field-guardian’s...
Seeing a grass hut, he entered it and sat down upon a grass mat there.
As soon as he was seated, having found a climate conducive to his needs, he exerted himself in insight meditation and attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Golden-Hued Sambuddha, walking along the path of the wind;”
Like a blazing cauldron, like a kindled sacrificial fire.
“Taking water in my hand, I threw it up into the air;
the Great Hero, the compassionate Buddha, the Seer, received it.”
“Standing in the sky, the Teacher named Padumuttara,
knowing my intention, spoke these verses:
‘By this gift of water and by the arising of joy;’”
Even for a hundred thousand eons, he does not fall into an evil rebirth.
By that karma, O Lord of Bipeds, Supreme One in the World, Bull among Men,
I have attained the unshakable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.
“By the name Sahassarāja, you were three universal monarchs;
for five hundred and sixty aeons, you were lords of men over the four quarters.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained arahantship, while the elder was sitting there, a field-guard came and asked, "Who is in the hut?
Upon hearing this, the elder said, "A bhikkhu is in the hut," and so forth. Taking these words of the field-guard and the elder together, it is said:
"Who is in the hut? A bhikkhu is in the hut, One free from lust, with a well-composed mind."
"Know this, friend: your hut has not been made in vain.
Thus it was included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti).
In that context, "Who is in the hut? is the question posed by the field-guard.

“Bhikkhu, in that hut” was the elder’s reply. Then, having caused him to express appreciation for the use of that hut because of his own status as the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*anuttara-dakkhiṇeyya*), and in order to establish that very same merit on a magnificent scale, the words beginning with “free from lust” (*vītarāgo*) were spoken.
Their meaning is as follows: A certain bhikkhu, whose defilements are destroyed, is sitting in that hut; therefore, by means of the supreme path...

Because he has completely severed passion, he is one free from passion; because he has made Nibbāna his object by means of unsurpassed concentration, he is one whose mind is well-composed through the state of being well-concentrated.
And regarding this matter, friend Khettapāla, know it as I say it, believe it, and resolve upon it:
your little hut has not been built in vain; the hut built by you is fruitful and not barren.
"It is fruitful and sweet, because it has been consumed by an Arhat whose taints are exhausted.
If you rejoice in this, it will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Having heard this, the field-guardian thought, "What a gain for me! What a great blessing for me, that such a one [has eaten] in my hut!"
“Noble sir, having entered, he sits down,” he stood there with a clear mind,
offering his words of appreciation. The Blessed One, having heard this conversation between them with his divine ear-element and having understood his expression of thanks,
spoke these verses to the field-guardian, illustrating the excellence inherent in that very state:
“The bhikkhu dwelt in a hut, his mind peaceful and free from taints;
by the ripening of that kamma, you shall become a lord of the gods.
Thirty-six times as lord of the gods, you shall exercise divine sovereignty.”
“Thirty-four times you will be a wheel-turning monarch, a king over the realm;
then, free from passion, you will become a Paccekabuddha named Ratanakuṭi.

Because he had attained distinction while staying in a hut, from that time forth the Elder became known by the name Kuṭivihāri (Hut-Dweller). This very verse also served as the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kuṭivihāri is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the second Elder Kuṭivihāri:
“This they call ancient,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kuṭivihāri. What is their origin? It is said that he [was a disciple] of Padumuttara...
With a mind full of faith toward the Blessed One, he gave him a fan fashioned from reeds and *vilīva* grass during a time of fever.
The Teacher gladdened him with a verse of thanksgiving. Whatever else remains to be said here is exactly as told in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya.
This, however, is the distinction: it is said that after he had gone forth in the manner described, in a certain old hut...
While dwelling there, he failed to reflect upon the duties of a recluse and, thinking, "This hut is dilapidated;

it is necessary to build another," he gave rise to thoughts regarding new construction work. A deity desiring his welfare, in order to produce a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in him, spoke this verse beginning with "This they say" (*ayamāhu*), which has a profound meaning behind its superficial appearance.
57. In this context, *ayaṃ* is a term denoting proximity and direct perception. *Āhu* means "it was" (*ahosi*);
it is stated with a long vowel for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse. *Purāṇiyā* means ancient or long-standing.
Regarding the phrase "you desire another new hut": because of the oldness and decay of this hut, you now desire another hut to be constructed, which is new.
You have desired, you desire, and you aspire. But completely cast out every hope regarding the hut, as if it were an old one;
in this new hut as well, cast out hope, craving, and longing. Be entirely dispassionate toward it.
Why? Because, O monk, a new hut that is now being constructed is suffering.

Because it brings suffering, it is "suffering"; therefore, not producing any new suffering, you should do what must be done by yourself while remaining in this very old hut as it has been constructed. This is the intended meaning here:
"O Bhikkhu, thinking 'this old grass-hut is dilapidated,' you wish to build another new grass-hut, but not the duty of a recluse."
However, one who desires in this way but does not apply himself to meditation fails to transcend the production of renewed existence;
thus, he is indeed one who merely wishes to construct a future hut for his own selfhood.

Yet that hut is as fragile as a new grass hut, and because it is constructed with difficulty and is further permeated by the suffering of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so forth, it is itself suffering.
"Therefore, like a grass hut, completely dispel all attachment and hope for this hut of the self;

let your mind be utterly detached from it, and thus the suffering of the round of existence shall not be yours. Having heard the words of the deity, the Elder was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Applying himself with diligence and exertion, he established insight meditation and, before long, became established in Arhatship. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Of Padumuttara Buddha, the World’s Elder, the Neutral One,
who sat upon a bed of grass, peaceful and neutral—
taking a reed-bundle and binding it into a fan, I [offered it].”
I offered it to the Buddha, the Lord of bipeds, the Tathāgata.
Having accepted the fan, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the World,
understanding my intention, spoke this verse:
“Just as my body has been extinguished and no fever remains,
so too may your mind be liberated from the three fires.
May all the gods, whoever they may be who dwell in the forest, assemble here.”
We shall hear the word of the Buddha as it brings joy to the donor.
Seated there, the Blessed One, honored by the assembly of devas,
spoke these verses while gladdening the donor:
“By means of this seed as a cause, and through the aspirations of his mind,
he who is named Subbata shall become a wheel-turning monarch.
Urged on by that remaining karma and by the root of merit, he shall attain his goal.”
One named Māluta by name will become a wheel-turning monarch.
"By means of this seed-offering and through such vast merit,
for a hundred thousand eons he shall not fall into an evil rebirth."
“In the thirty thousand kappas [ago], there were thirty-eight named Subbatā;
in the twenty-nine thousand, eight named Māluta.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having established himself in Arahatship, he recited that very same verse, thinking, "This was the goad for my attainment of Arahatship.

That verse itself became the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*). Because he had gained distinction through the exhortation regarding the hut, his conventional name became "Kuṭivihāri" (the Hut-dweller).
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of the second Elder, Kuṭivihāri.
8. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika "Delightful is my little hut"—this is the verse of the venerable elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika. What is its origin?
It is said that he too, having planted seeds of merit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, [arrived here] from this world...
At the end of one hundred and eighteen aeons, during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, he was reborn in a noble family.
Upon reaching maturity, he offered a seat worthy of a Buddha to the Blessed One.

Having honored the Blessed One with flowers, prostrated himself in the fivefold manner, and circumambulated him, he departed. The rest is exactly as described in the account of the Elder Añjanavaniya.

But this is the distinction: it is said that after he had gone forth in the manner described and performed his preliminary duties, he was dwelling in a small hut at a certain village monastery in the Vajji country.
That hut was beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing; its walls and floors were well-finished, and it was endowed with the charm of a garden, a lotus pond, and so forth.
The ground around it was strewn with sand like a net of pearls, for the Elder.
And because it was well-swept and its grounds were thoroughly maintained due to his perfection in the observance of duties, it remained even more exceedingly delightful.
While dwelling there, he established insight (vipassanā) and before long was established in Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having entered a forest grove, quiet and undisturbed..."
I gave the lion throne to the Tathāgata Atthadassi.
Taking a garland in my hand and circumambulating him,
I attended upon the Teacher and departed facing northward.
“By that deed, O Lord of Bipeds, Supreme One in the World, Bull among Men, I have brought myself to final extinction;
all states of existence have been utterly uprooted.
Regarding the gift I gave back then during eighteen hundred aeons—”
“I do not recall ever being born in a state of misery; this is the fruit of the lion throne.
Seven hundred eons from now, there will be a kshatriya who brings about peace;
endowed with the seven treasures, he will be a powerful wheel-turning monarch.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

However, after he had attained Arahantship and was living there with the elders, people who were looking for a monastery came from various directions to see the hut because of its delightful state. Then one day, several women of a dissolute nature—
Having gone there and seen the delightful nature of the hut, they said with the intention, "If this ascetic dwells here, his heart might be drawn toward us":
"Venerable sir, your dwelling place is delightful; we too are of a delightful appearance, being in the prime of youth.
Having said this, they began to display feminine gestures and the like. The Elder—
Manifesting his own state of being free from lust (*vītarāga*), he spoke this verse: “Delightful is my little hut, a gift of faith, enchanting.
(58) Therein, “Delightful is my little hut”: that which you said, “Venerable sir, your little hut is delightful,” is true.
This little hut where I dwell is delightful and pleasing to the eye; moreover, it is a gift of faith—of such a kind as this...

Because they are to be given with faith and a desire for the Dhamma—after making them pleasing and giving them to those who have gone forth, thinking, “This is the fruit of such an action”—they are called *saddhādeyya* (gifts of faith).

They are not produced by mere wealth. Furthermore, they are called *manorama* (delightful) because they delight the mind of both those who see them being given in such a way and those who consume them. Because they are gifts of faith...
For indeed, it is delightful that noble persons, having carefully prepared the gift to be given with faith and other virtues, give it;
and while enjoying what has been given out of faith, they possess both the practice and the disposition for the sake of not deceiving the donor.
The intention is that you are not deficient in practice and disposition in the manner you have conceived, unlike [those who say], "I have no need for maidens. Because... [of this].
"My mind has completely turned away from sensual pleasures; therefore, I have no need for maidens.
For even by way of the work of a servant, there is no purpose for those like me in women, let alone out of passion; thus, I have no need for maidens.
And here, the mention of "maidens" should be understood as an illustration. In the presence of one such as I...

"Practice in this way" means: showing that this action would shine before those of similar disposition—even before those who have offended you and who act improperly—he said, "O women, go there to those who need you.
In this context, "those who" refers to those who are not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures. "Need" means purpose. "There" means to them, in their presence. "Women" refers to—
He addressed them. Upon hearing this, the women became abashed, hung their heads, and departed by the same way they had come.
In this context, it should be understood that by the Elder’s very statement of his lack of interest in sensual pleasures—“I have no need for maidens”—he declared his attainment of Arahatship.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kosala-vihārin "Out of faith I went forth"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kosala-vihārin. What is its origin?
It is said that he too, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, planted seeds of merit and performed various meritorious deeds. The rest...
It is exactly like the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. This, however, is the distinction:

it is said that after he had gone forth in the manner described and performed the preliminary duties, he lived in a forest near a certain village in the kingdom of Kosala, depending on a family of lay devotees.
Seeing him dwelling at the foot of a tree, that lay devotee had a small hut built and gave it to him. The elder dwelt in that hut.
Having attained concentration through a favorable dwelling and having intensified his insight (vipassanā), he reached Arahantship before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himālaya, I dwelt upon a bed of leaves;”
I was then possessed by greed for food, being of superior virtue.
Having dug up khaṇantālu and kalamba, as well as biḷāli and takkala,
and having brought kola, bhallātaka, and billa, it was prepared [for me].
“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
having understood my intention, came into my presence.
To that great Naga who had approached— the God of Gods, the Bull among Men— ”
Having taken hold of a cat, I sprinkled it into my alms-bowl.
The Great Hero then consumed it, pleasing me at that time;
having finished eating, the All-Knowing One spoke this verse:
“Having gladdened my own heart, you gave me a *biḷāli* flower;
for a hundred thousand eons, you shall not fall into an evil rebirth.
My final existence is now unfolding; all states of becoming have been utterly uprooted.”
“I bear my final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
In the fifty-fourth aeon, O Sumekhaliya, I was known by that name;
endowed with the seven treasures, I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, he uttered this verse, “Out of faith I went forth,” expressing his inspired utterance (*udāna*) through the surge of joy arising from the experience of the bliss of liberation.
59. Therein, “out of faith” refers to having seen the majesty of the Blessed One upon his arrival at Vesālī, [thinking], “It is exclusively leading to deliverance...”
"This is the teaching; therefore, by means of this practice, I shall surely be liberated from aging and death"—with such arisen faith he went forth and entered the homeless life.
"A hut has been made for me in the forest": a hut was built for me while I dwell in the forest in accordance with that going-forth;
having become a forest-dweller suited to the life of renunciation, I live withdrawn in seclusion.

He shows this by saying: “Diligent, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful. By means of physical seclusion attained through dwelling in the forest, one who devotes himself to wakefulness is *appamatta* (diligent) due to the non-departure of mindfulness from that state; he is *ātāpī* (ardent) due to the exertion of energy;
and by increasing insight through the fulfillment of preliminary mindfulness and clear comprehension, he attains the fullness of wisdom and mindfulness upon reaching Arahantship.

The meaning is: "I dwell being perfectly mindful and clearly comprehending. This very declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*) occurred during the recital of his state of heedfulness and other qualities;
however, because he had resided for a long time in the kingdom of Kosala, the designation "Kosalavihārī" arose.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kosalavihāri is finished.
10. The Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Sīvali "Those intentions of mine were fulfilled"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sīvali. What is its origin?
He too, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, went to the monastery in the manner described above and, standing at the edge of the assembly, listened to the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher place a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who receive gains, [the man] thought, "In the future, it is fitting that I too become like this.

He then invited the One of Ten Powers, gave a great almsgiving for seven days to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and said, "Bhagavā, by means of this meritorious deed, I do not aspire to any other prosperity; rather, in the future..."

He made this aspiration: "May I also, under the dispensation of a single Buddha, become the foremost among those who receive gains, just like that bhikkhu whom you have placed at the head of this list.
Seeing that there would be no obstacle, the Teacher declared:
"This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future in the presence of Gotama Buddha," and then he departed. That clansman, too, for as long as he lived...
Having performed wholesome deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in a certain village not far from the city of Bandhumatī during the time of Vipassī Buddha.

At that time, the inhabitants of the city of Bandhumatī, having consulted with the king, were giving alms to the One Possessed of Ten Powers. On one occasion, they all gathered together and gave alms as one.
“Is there perhaps nothing for us in the way of offerings? they wondered, and so they did not see any honey or jaggery curd.
Thinking, “We shall bring it from somewhere,” they stationed a man on the road leading into the city from the countryside.
At that time, this son of good family, taking a vessel of jaggery curd from his own village, was going toward the city thinking, “I will bring something [as an offering].”
Thinking, "I shall enter after washing my face and rinsing my hands and feet," he looked about for a convenient spot.
Seeing a honeycomb the size of a plowshare that was free of flies, he thought, "This has arisen for me through merit," and taking it, he entered the city.
A man appointed by the citizens saw him and asked, "Sir, for whom are you carrying this? He replied, "For no one."
“Master, I have brought this for sale. “In that case, sir, take this kārṣāpaṇa and give me this honey and the sugar-curd.
He thought, “This is not of great value, yet he gives much all at once; it is right to test him.
Then he said to him, “I will not give it for a single kārṣāpaṇa.”
“If that is so, take two and give them to me. “I will not give even two,” he replied. By this means, increasing [the number], it reached one thousand.
He thought: “It is not right for it to increase too much; let it be for now. I shall ask him what work must be done with this.
Then he said to him: “This is not of great value, yet you give much; for what purpose do you take this?”

“Sir, here the city-dwellers, having come into conflict with the king, are seeking these two things while giving alms to the Seer Vipassī, not seeing them at the gateway for the distribution of gifts.
If they do not obtain these two things, the defeat of the citizens will occur;
therefore, I shall take them by making a wager of a thousand pieces. “But is this permissible only for the citizens?”
"It is not permitted to give them to others. "There is no prohibition against giving them to anyone at all.
"But is there anyone among the citizens who gives a thousand [pieces of gold] on a single day? "No, noble lady.
"Do you know that these two are worth a thousand each? "Yes, I know it. "In that case, go and inform the citizens."
‘One man here does not give these two for their price, wishing instead to give them with his own hand;
you should therefore be free from anxiety regarding these two. But as for you, you shall be the bodily witness to my preeminence in this act of giving.
Having taken five pungent spices with the māsaka he had received for his travel expenses, he ground them into powder and [mixed them] with curd.
Having taken sour gruel, squeezed a honeycomb into it, mixed it with the powder of the five pungent spices, and placed it in a lotus leaf, he prepared it and took it with him.
Sitting not far from the One of Ten Powers, close to the honors being offered by the great multitude, he waited for his turn to receive the bowl, watching for an opportunity;
and having discerned the right moment, he approached the presence of the Teacher.
Having arrived, he said, "Lord, this is a gift from one who has fallen into misfortune; please accept it out of compassion for me.

Out of compassion for him, the Teacher accepted it with a stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings, and he made a resolution such that it would not be exhausted even as it was being served to the six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.
When the noble son had finished his meal duties, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, standing to one side, said:
“Blessed One, today I have seen the residents of the city of Bandhumatī bringing offerings to you.
By the result of this deed, may I too, in each successive birth, attain the highest gain and the summit of glory. The Teacher—
Saying, “So be it, noble sons,” he gave a blessing for the meal to him and the city-dwellers and departed.

That noble son, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, took rebirth in the womb of Princess Suppavāsā during this dispensation of the Buddha. From the moment of conception, [the fetus]...
In the evening and in the morning, hundreds of offerings were brought on carts and presented to Suppavāsā.
Then, in order to test her merit, they had her touch a basket of seeds with her hand; from each single seed, a hundred or even a thousand stalks emerged.
In each field of a karīsa’s measure, fifty or sixty cartloads of grain arose. Even when the time came to fill the granary—
They touched the storehouse door with their hands. By the merit of the princess, every place they took from was filled again as soon as it was taken.

Even when giving to anyone from a full food-vessel while saying, "By the merit of the princess," the rice was not exhausted until they had finished serving. Thus, even while the child was still in her womb, seven years passed by.
When her pregnancy had matured, she experienced great suffering for seven days.
Addressing her husband, she said, "Before I die, while I am still alive, I shall give alms. She then sent him to the Teacher with these instructions:
"Go, report this situation to the Teacher and invite him; whatever the Teacher says, take that to heart and remember it well."
“Go and tell me when you have returned. He went and reported her message to the Blessed One.
The Teacher said, “May Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter be happy and healthy; may she give birth to a healthy son.
When the king heard this, he paid homage to the Blessed One and set out toward his own village. Even before he had arrived, from the womb of Suppavāsā—
The fetus emerged like water from a water-pot; the people sitting around began to laugh with tearful faces, and the great multitude, thrilled and overjoyed, went to announce the news to the king.
Upon seeing their arrival, the king thought, "I suppose the discourse delivered by the One of Ten Powers must have reached its conclusion."
He thought thus. Having returned, he delivered the Teacher’s message to the princess.
The princess said, "The meal you have been invited to provide will indeed be a meal of blessing, a meal for life itself; go and invite the One of Ten Powers for seven days. The king did so.
For seven days, they offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. The boy—
Because he was born cooling the hearts of all his kinsmen who had been consumed by grief, they gave him the name Sīvali-dāraka.
Since he had dwelt in the womb for seven years, from the time of his birth he was capable of performing all kinds of work.
On the seventh day, the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, engaged in a conversation with him. The Teacher also recited a verse from the *Dhammapada*:
“He who has transcended this mire, this difficult path, this cycle of existence and delusion;
who has crossed over, reached the further shore, is a meditator, unshaken and free from doubt;
who, through non-clinging, has attained Nibbāna—him I call a brahmin.”
Then the Elder said to him, "But why is it not fitting for you to go forth after having experienced such a mass of suffering?

"I would go forth, venerable sir, if I were permitted," he replied. Suppavāsā, seeing her son conversing with the Elder, thought, "What is my son talking about with the General of the Dhamma? and approached the Elder.

He asked, "Venerable sir, what is my son saying to you? [The Elder replied,] "Having related the suffering of dwelling in the womb that he himself experienced, he says, 'With your permission, I shall go forth. [The father said,] "Excellent, venerable sir;
let him go forth. The Elder led him to the monastery, gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*), and—
As he was ordaining her, [the Elder] said, "Sīvalī, there is no need for you to have any other instruction; simply reflect upon the suffering you experienced for seven years.
She replied, "Venerable Sir, it is your burden alone to ordain me; as for what I am capable of doing, I shall know that myself.
At the very moment she removed her first coil of hair, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
At the moment of the second recitation, he was established in the fruit of a once-returner; at the third, in the fruit of a non-returner.
Furthermore, the shaving of all his hair and the realization of Arahatship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after.
From the day of his going forth, the four requisites for the Saṅgha of monks arose for them as much as they desired. Thus did this story originate here.
Later on, the Teacher went to Sāvatthī. The Elder paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, I wish to test my merit;
please give me five hundred bhikkhus. "Take them, Sīvalī," he replied.
Taking the five hundred bhikkhus, he set out toward the Himālaya and traveled along a forest path. First, for him—
The deity dwelling in the banyan tree gave alms for seven days. Thus he [recited]:
"First he saw the Banyan tree, secondly Mount Paṇḍava;
thirdly at the Aciravatī river, and fourthly the excellent ocean."
“He went to Himavanta as the fifth, to Chaddanta as the sixth, to Gandhamādana as the seventh, and then to Revata as the eighth.
At all these places, they gave gifts for exactly seven days each. However, on Mount Gandhamādana, King Nāgadatta the deity...
On one of those seven days, she gave an offering of milk; on another day, an offering of ghee.
The community of bhikkhus said: "Your Majesty, neither milch cows being milked nor the churning of curds are seen here; from where, O King, does this come to you? [He replied:
"Venerable sirs, this is the result of giving a meal with a ticket for milk during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa."

"His fruit," said the King of Devas. Later, the Teacher, taking the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana as the occasion for a discourse, placed that elder in the foremost position among those who have attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory within his own dispensation.
Now, regarding the attainment of Arahantship by this elder who had thus reached the pinnacle of gain and glory, some teachers say...
They speak thus: "When the Dhamma-Senapati had given his exhortation in the manner previously described, [the Bodhisatta] thought, 'I shall know what I am able to do.
Having gone forth and taken up the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna), he saw on that very day a certain secluded hut;
having entered it, he recalled the seven years he had spent within his mother's womb."
“Having recollected suffering and, following that, observing the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze throughout the past and future, his knowledge reached maturity;
he entered the path of insight and, immediately thereafter, exhausting all the taints through the sequence of the paths, attained Arahatship.
Thus, in both cases, it was indeed the attainment of Arahatship by the Elder.
[The Dhamma] was proclaimed. But the Elder had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and possessed the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā). Therefore it is said in his Apadāna:
“At that time I was the king of the gods named Varuṇa;
I attended upon the Perfectly Enlightened One, together with my chariots, forces, and mounts.”
“When Atthadassī, the supreme among men, the Protector of the World, had attained Nibbāna,
I took all the musical instruments and went to the supreme Bodhi tree.
Accompanied by instrumental music, dancing, and the rhythmic beating of drums, I was absorbed in that performance.”
I attended upon the Supreme Bodhi tree as if it were the Fully Enlightened One standing before my eyes.
Having attended upon that Bodhi, a tree grown from the earth,
I sat cross-legged and passed away right there.
“Delighted by my own deeds and full of faith in the supreme Awakening,
through that clarity of mind I was reborn in the realm of the gods.
Sixty thousand celestial musicians always attend upon me.”
“Among humans and among devas, wandering through existence after existence, the three fires have been extinguished within me;
all states of becoming have been utterly eradicated.
I bear my final body in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Thirty-four generations ago, there were thirty-four kṣatriyas known by the name Subāhu;
they were endowed with the seven treasures five hundred kalpas from now.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, he uttered the verse, "Those intentions of mine have been fulfilled," expressing his exultation through the surge of joy experienced upon realizing the bliss of liberation.

Regarding this, "those intentions of mine have been fulfilled" refers to those very intentions of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth—which were previously sought by him as the means for the total eradication of sensual intentions (*kāma-saṅkappa*) and the rest—that now result in the attainment of true knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti*). As for "for which purpose I entered the hut": it was for that very purpose. "They realize true knowledge and liberation" means that those [intentions] bring about the realization of true knowledge and liberation.
“O when indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?”—
with this intention of liberation, aiming at liberation, his resolves and aspirations were constant,
diligent, and directed toward that purpose, for that motive, and for the accomplishment of that end, so that he might contemplate the empty hut.
"I entered [the path] while reviewing and seeking the three knowledges and the liberation through fruition;

those [goals] were accomplished for me, and now they have all been accomplished and fulfilled for me. This means that my wholesome intentions have reached completion and my desires have been fulfilled.
To demonstrate their successful attainment, it is said: "Abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit" (*mānānusaya*). For, by abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit—
The construction is: "They abandoned, they utterly cut off; therefore those intentions of mine were fulfilled.
For when the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) is abandoned, there is no underlying tendency left unabandoned, and Arahantship is indeed attained.
Thus, the abandonment of the underlying tendency to conceit is stated by making it the cause for the success of the aforementioned intentions.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sīvali is finished.
The commentary on the Sixth Chapter is finished.
7. The Seventh Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vappa The verse beginning with "He sees, he sees" belongs to the venerable Elder Vappa. What is its origin?

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and having reached the age of discretion, [he thought], "Such-and-such a person and such-and-such..."
Having heard the praise, "And the Elder was one of the first to receive the Dhamma from the Teacher," he approached the Blessed One and made this aspiration:
"May I too, Blessed One, in the future become one of the first to receive the Dhamma from such a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
And in the presence of the Teacher, he declared his taking of refuge.

Thus, having performed meritorious deeds for as long as life lasted, he passed away from there and, wandering only among gods and humans, was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Kapilavatthu as the son of a brahmin named Vāseṭṭha; his name was Vappa.
He had been prophesied by the seer Asita, who declared, "Prince Siddhattha will become omniscient," along with Koṇḍañña and others.
Having abandoned the household life together with the sons of brahmins and gone forth as ascetic wanderers, thinking, "When he has attained omniscience,
we shall hear the Dhamma in his presence and reach the Deathless," they attended upon the Great Being while he was dwelling at Uruvelā and exerting himself in striving for six years;
then, becoming disillusioned with the consumption of substantial food, [they went] to Isipatana.
He had gone [to the Buddha]. Having attained full enlightenment, the Teacher spent seven weeks and then went to Isipatana;

when the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*) he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), and on the fifth day of the fortnight, together with Aññā Koṇḍañña and others, he reached arahantship.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“A battle between the two kings of the gods had arisen;
it was arrayed for combat, and a great clamor broke out.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings—”
Standing in the sky, the Teacher inspired the great multitude:
“All the gods, their minds delighted, having laid aside their armor and weapons,
paid homage to the Fully Awakened One and remained there with one-pointed attention.”
“Knowing my intention, he uttered a lion’s roar of speech;
the compassionate Knower of the World brought peace to the great multitude.
A man with a corrupted mind, while harming even a single living being...”
Through that corruption of mind, one is reborn in a state of misery.
Like an elephant at the head of battle, harassing many living beings, pacify your own mind; do not be slain again and again.
“The army of both the kings of the *yakkhas* was struck with wonder;
they went for refuge to the Eldest of the World, who is compassionate toward his children.
Having instructed the people, the Visionary One raised his foot.”
Beholding him like a god, he departed facing northward:
"I went for refuge first to the Tathāgata, the Lord of bipeds;
for a hundred thousand eons, I did not fall into an evil rebirth."
“There were sixteen bull-like chariot-warriors named Mahādundubhi;
thirty thousand eons ago, they were all wheel-turning monarchs.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [pe] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, however, and reflecting upon the greatness of the Teacher’s virtues by way of reviewing the excellence he himself had obtained, he uttered the verse beginning with “The seer sees,” demonstrating:
“Alas! How such a Teacher as this was treated by us with words such as ‘one who indulges in luxuries’;
oh, how the state of a worldling (puthujjana) is blinding and sightless, while only the noble state (ariyabhāva) brings vision!”
61. Therein, "passati" means he sees; "passo" means one who sees, for by right view he knows phenomena without error and awakens—thus he is a noble one endowed with vision.

He sees with the eye of wisdom that one who sees, who possesses non-erroneous vision, thinking, "This one is one who sees without error," knowing phenomena and non-phenomena according to their true nature. It is not only the one who sees [that he sees].
Furthermore, one who sees what is not seen— that is, one who, being devoid of the eye of wisdom, does not see phenomena as they truly are—
sees with his own eye of wisdom that ordinary person (puthujjana) who likewise does not see, thinking, "Truly, this venerable one is blind,
lacking eyes. Thus, "not seeing, he does not see the one who does not see, nor does he see the one who sees" means that he does not see because he lacks the eye of wisdom.
Just as a blind fool does not see, nor perceive, another such blind fool because he does not see the nature of what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma,
so too, with his own eye of wisdom, he neither sees nor knows a wise person who perceives the nature of what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma as it truly is,
thinking, "This one is of such a kind. Therefore, I too, in the past...
Although he had previously failed to see the Blessed One— who, devoid of any lack of vision, perceives the entirety of the knowable as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand—

and had likewise failed to see Pūraṇa and others according to their true nature, he now shows his own unerring practice regarding what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, thinking: "But now, endowed through the power of the Buddha, I see both of them according to their true nature."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vappa is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjiputta.
"We are alone in the forest," etc., are the verses of the venerable Elder Vajjiputta. What is their origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī ninety-one aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, he made an offering with a devout mind using *nāgapuṣpa* filaments. By that meritorious deed...
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a family of ministers;
his name was Vajjiputta. Having seen the majesty of the Buddha during the Blessed One’s journey to Vesālī, he gained faith and went forth.
Having performed the preliminary duties and received a meditation subject, he dwelt in a certain grove not far from Vesālī.
And at that time, there was a festival in Vesālī. Here and there, dancing, singing, and instrumental music were being performed;
the great multitude, joyful and delighted, was enjoying the excellence of the festival.
Hearing of this, that bhikkhu—emerging improperly, shunning seclusion, and abandoning his meditation subject—proclaimed his own lack of delight:
“We dwell alone in the forest like a discarded log in the woods;
on such a night as this, who indeed could be more wretched than we?”—thus he spoke this verse.
Hearing it, the deity dwelling in that forest grove, out of compassion for the bhikkhu, said: “Even though you, bhikkhu...”
Showing this meaning by saying, "You speak while despising forest-dwelling, yet the wise who desire seclusion surely hold it in high esteem," [the Buddha said]:
"You dwell alone in the forest like a discarded log in the woods;
many envy you, as those bound for hell envy those going to heaven."

Having spoken this verse, she rebuked him, stirring him with a sense of urgency, saying: "How is it, monk, that having gone forth in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One, which leads to liberation, you would entertain thoughts that do not lead to liberation?
Thus stirred by that deity, like a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, that monk entered the path of insight and, before long, [attained realization].
Having made insight (vipassanā) his primary pursuit, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Golden-hued Sambuddha, like the sun with its hundred rays, illuminating all directions, like the full moon, the king of stars.”
“Surrounded by his disciples, like Mount Meru by the oceans,
I took up the elephant Reṇu and offered it to Vipassi.
For ninety-one eons from now, because I offered that elephant Reṇu...”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In the forty-fifth aeon hence, you will be a kshatriya named Reṇu, a powerful universal monarch endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, however, he combined the manner in which he himself and his deity had spoken—“This has become my goad for attaining Arahantship”—and said:
“We dwell alone in the forest, like a discarded log in the woods;”
"Many envy me, as those bound for hell envy one going to heaven"—thus he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is: although we are alone, each by ourselves, like a piece of wood cast away in the forest due to our state of detachment...
"We dwell in this forest without companions. Yet, while I dwell thus, many people envy me;

many sons of noble family who desire my welfare aspire to me, thinking, "O, would that we too might abandon the bonds of the household and dwell in the forest like the Elder Vajjiputta! How so? Like those in hell longing for one bound for heaven.

The meaning is as follows: just as those beings born in hell through their own evil karma long for those who go to heaven and reach heaven, thinking, "Oh, would that we too, having abandoned the suffering of hell, might experience the happiness of heaven," so it is in this case.
And here, because the use of the plural form for the first person (*attan*) is required.
Regarding the phrase “we dwell alone,” the singular usage in “of that mine” (*tassa me*) is employed with reference to the singularity of that state.
Both “of that mine” (*tassa me*) and “going to heaven” (*saggagāminan*) should be understood as dative cases used in the sense of the accusative, in view of the word “desiring” (*pihayanti*).
And “desiring that” means desiring such qualities as dwelling in the forest and so forth.
It was said thus, taking it to mean "they are called [by that name]. The intended meaning is either "to him" or "in my presence, he possesses virtues.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjiputta is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Pakkha.
"Cutā patanti" (They fall when cut) is the verse of the Venerable Pakkha Thera. What is its origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences after having made a commitment under previous Buddhas, became a general of the yakṣas ninety-one aeons ago.
Having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of divine cloth. By that meritorious deed, among gods and humans...
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn during this dispensation of a Buddha in the Sakyan royal family at the village of Devadaha among the Sakyans;
his name was Sammoda Kumāra. Later, in his childhood, his feet could not move due to a wind-disease (vātaroga).

For some time he moved about like a cripple on a wooden frame; therefore, the designation "Pakkha" (the Cripple) arose for him. Even later, when he was free from illness, they continued to recognize him by that same name.
Having witnessed the miracle at the assembly of the Blessed One’s kinsmen, he gained faith and went forth into homelessness.
Having performed the preliminary duties and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he dwelt in the forest.
Then one day, while going to enter a village for alms, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree along the way. At that time, a hawk was carrying a piece of meat...
Taking it, he went through the air; many hawks pursued him and made him drop it.
One hawk seized the fallen piece of meat, but another snatched it away from him and took it. Seeing this, the Elder thought:

"Just as this piece of meat, so too are sensual pleasures (kāmā) shared by many, fraught with much suffering, and full of much despair"—and thus [he reflected] upon the danger in sensual pleasures and the excellence of renunciation (nekkhamma).
Having reflected upon the benefits and established insight, he attended to the objects as "impermanent" and so forth;
then, having wandered for alms and finished his meal, he sat in his daytime resting place, deepened his insight, and attained Arahatship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Vipassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
entered Bandhumatī at that time together with sixty-eight thousand [monks].
Having departed from the city, he went to the Dīpa Cetiya.”
I saw the stainless Buddha, the recipient of offerings.
Eighty-four thousand yakkhas attend upon me with great care,
just as the hosts of the Thirty-three gods attend upon Indra.
“Having emerged from my meditation, I then took up a cloth and paid homage with my head; I offered it to the Great Sage.
‘Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the excellence of our Teacher!’”
Through the power of the Buddha, the earth trembled.
Having seen that marvel, so wonderful and hair-raising,
I set my mind upon faith in the Buddha, the Lord of bipeds, the Tathāgata.
“Having gladdened my heart and offered cloth to the Teacher,
I went for refuge along with my ministers and my retinue.
That deed which I performed then, ninety-one aeons ago— ”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Fifteen aeons from now, there will be sixteen kings named Suvāhana, mighty universal monarchs endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, he spoke the verse beginning with “Falling away, falling down” (*cutā patantī*) as a declaration of his final knowledge (*aññā*), by way of summarizing that very object of spiritual urgency which he had used as a goad to develop insight and thereby reach that realization.

In this context: “fallen away” (*cutā*) means having fallen from [the state of a trainee]. “Falling down” (*patantī*) means they are following after [the lower realms]. “Fallen” (*patitā*) means having fallen to the ground by way of passing away.
Or they have fallen by flying through the air. "Greedily" means having fallen into greed. "Returning again" means having approached once more.
The word *ca* (and) should be construed with every term. This is what is meant: here the hawks fall and swoop down;
and the piece of flesh, having fallen from the other’s mouth, has also fallen upon the ground; and being greedy, they fall into greed.

All the hawks have fallen and have returned once more. Just as these hawks [behave], so too do beings wandering in *saṃsāra* who have fallen away from wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*): they fall into the hells and other realms.

Having thus fallen, even when established in a state of prosperity, they are greedy—through their pursuit of sensual pleasure in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*), and through their attachment to existence in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpadhātu* and *arūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, because they have not been liberated from that very karma leading to various states of existence (*bhava*), these beings have indeed arrived at the suffering designated as "existence" (*bhava*).
As for me, however, the task to be done—the sixteenfold task consisting of the divisions such as full comprehension (*pariññā*)—has been completed;
there is nothing further to be done now. This is the delight, the joy, the state to be rejoiced in by the Noble Ones, which has escaped from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).

Nirvana is delightful, greatly enjoyed, and charming. "Attained by that happiness" means that it is followed by, or has approached, the happiness of the attainment of the fruit—the ultimate happiness of Nirvana;

or alternatively, the meaning should be understood as the happiness of the fruit and the happiness of Nirvana being followed by the happiness of insight and the happiness of the path, which serve as the means for attaining happiness.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pakkha is finished.
4. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña.
"Arisen at Dumavhayā" refers to the verses of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences,
he was reborn ninety-one aeons ago during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a family endowed with great wealth. Having reached maturity, one day,
seeing the Blessed One Vipassī surrounded by a vast assembly teaching the Dhamma, his mind became filled with serene confidence.

He honored [the Buddha] with four golden flowers. For the sake of increasing his faith, the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*) that a golden radiance overspread that entire area. Seeing this, his mind became even more filled with serene confidence;
having paid homage to the Blessed One and taken that as a sign, he went to his own home.
Without relinquishing the joy inspired by the Buddha as his object, he passed away from a certain illness and was reborn among the Tusita devas.

Having performed further meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took conception in the womb of Ambapālī, dependent upon King Bimbisāra, at the time of this Buddha’s appearance.
For King Bimbisāra, in his youth, had [been captivated] by Ambapālī’s perfection of form.
Having heard this, his desire arose; accompanied by a few attendants and disguised as a stranger, he went to Vesālī and spent one night in her company.
At that time, she conceived a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) within her womb.
She informed him of the fact that the embryo had been established. The king, having made himself known and given what was appropriate to be given, departed.
When her pregnancy had reached maturity, she gave birth to a son; his name was Vimala, and later he became known as Vimalakoṇḍañña.
Upon reaching maturity, having seen the majesty of the Buddha during the Blessed One’s visit to Vesālī, he went forth with a devout mind.
Having performed the preliminary duties and established insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Vipassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
sat down and taught the deathless state to the multitude of people.
Having heard his Dhamma— the Dhamma of that Tathāgata, the best of bipeds— ”
I offered four golden flowers to the Buddha.
At that time, as far as the assembly extended, there was a golden canopy;
both the radiance of the Buddha and the golden light were vast and pervasive.
“With a joyful heart and a happy mind, filled with rapture and palms joined in reverence,
he brought them gladness and bestowed the happiness of the present life.
Having entreated the Fully Awakened One and paid homage to him of noble vows,”
Having given rise to joy, I returned to my own abode.
Seated within my palace, I recollected the Supreme Buddha;
through that clarity of mind, I was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
“In the ninety-first aeon, because I offered that flower, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
There were sixteen kings named Nemisammata.”
“In the forty-fourth aeon from now, there were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*) by way of another designation, reciting the verse beginning with ‘Dumavhayā’.”
64. Therein, "Dumavhayā" means she who is to be called by the name of a tree (*duma*), namely the mango (*amba*); the meaning is "Ambapālī.
This locative case is used here in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*). "Uppanno" refers to one who has arisen or is arising within her womb.
"Jāto paṇḍaraketunā" means he was born with King Bimbisāra as the cause—the king who was known as "Paṇḍaraketu" because of his white garments and white banner.

The meaning is: "born dependent upon that. Alternatively, "arisen" (*uppanno*) indicates the initial manifestation [of birth], while "born from that" (*tato hi jāto*) indicates the specific mode of birth (*abhijāti*).
For in the world, the conventional usage of "born" begins from the time of delivery.

And here, by the phrase "arisen from the one called a tree," he avoids the state of self-exaltation and demonstrates the possibility of attaining distinction even for those with many different mothers.
He illuminates [the meaning]. By the phrase “Born with the white banner” (*jāto paṇḍaraketunā*), he removes the disparagement of others by showing the joy of one who has understood.
“With the banner” (*ketuhā*) means one who has abandoned conceit. For conceit is called a “banner” because it has the characteristic of puffing up, like a banner;

thus it is said that conceit “manifests as a desire for being a banner. “By the banner alone” (*ketunāyeva*) means by wisdom (*paññā*) alone. For wisdom, in the sense of rising pre-eminently among blameless states, is the crusher of Māra’s army.
And in the sense of being the precursor, it is called the banner (*dhaja*) of the Noble Ones (*ariya*). Therefore he said: "The Dhamma is indeed the banner of the sages.

"He shattered the great ensign" (*mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī*): Because its scope is vast, it is "great"; and because it consists of many types of conceit—such as pride in one's family, birth, and so forth—as well as other defiled states (*kilesadhamma*), it is an "ensign" (*ketu*) in the sense of being raised high.
Thus, Māra the Evil One is the "Great Ensign" (*mahāketu*). He [the Buddha] shattered him by means of the destruction of his power and the transcending of his domain.

"He overcame him who was free from deceit" means: by saying "He destroyed Mahāketu," he declared his attainment of Arahatship under the guise of another, presenting himself as if he were someone else.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha Regarding "Ukkhepakatavaccha":
these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha. What is their origin?
It is said that he too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various births, [attained his goal].
In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn in a noble family and reached maturity.
When a guild of merchants was building a pavilion for the Teacher but could not find a single pillar, he provided a pillar and performed the duty of a friend.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and subsequently performed further acts of merit.
Having performed [meritorious deeds], he wandered among gods and humans and was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin;
"Vaccha" was his name derived from his clan. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and went forth.
While dwelling in a village monastery in the kingdom of Kosala, for the monks who arrived one after another...
He mastered the Dhamma in its presence, yet he did not know the divisions, thinking, "This is the Vinaya, this is the Sutta, this is the Abhidhamma.
Then one day, having questioned the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, he discerned everything according to their respective divisions.
Even prior to the Council of Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgīti), the designations such as "Piṭaka" were already established within the true Dhamma of the scriptures.
Thus it was, for that is the conventional designation used by the monks, such as "one who masters the Vinaya" and so forth.

While learning and thoroughly inquiring into the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, he observed the material and immaterial phenomena described therein; having established insight and practiced its synthesis, he attained Arahatship before long.
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“For the Blessed One Siddhattha, there was a great multitude of a large company;
they had gone for refuge to the Buddha and placed their faith in the Tathāgata.
Having all come together and consulted one another, they built a pavilion for the Teacher.”
Not finding a single pillar, they searched throughout the Great Forest.
Having seen them there in the wilderness, I then approached that group;
raising my hands in reverent salutation, I questioned the assembly.
“When questioned by me, those virtuous lay followers replied:
‘We wish to build a gabled hall, but a single pillar cannot be found.
‘Give me a single pillar,’ [he said], ‘and I shall give it to the Teacher.’”
“I shall fetch the pillar; let them be free from anxiety.
They, with serene and joyful minds, gave me the pillar;
then, having turned back, they went to their own homes.
“Not long after the assembly had departed, I then offered a pillar;
joyful with a joyful heart, I raised it up first.
By that clarity of mind, I was reborn in a celestial mansion.”
My palace was lofty, rising seven stories high.
While the drums were being beaten, I always enjoyed my pleasures.
In the fifty-fifth aeon, I was King Yasodhara.
“Even there, my dwelling rose seven stories high, equipped with excellent gabled chambers,
supported by a single pillar, and enchanting to the mind.
In the twenty-first aeon, there was a kshatriya named Udena.”
Even there, my dwelling rose up seven stories high.
"In whatever womb I am reborn—whether among the gods or among humans—I experience every happiness;
this is the fruit of that single pillar."
“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that pillar back then, I have never known a state of misery.
This is the fruit of that single pillar.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as usual]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained Arahantship and being established in tirelessness because his task was accomplished,
he taught the Dhamma after examining the Buddha-word contained in the Three Piṭakas, out of compassion for the householders and renunciants who approached him. And while teaching, on one occasion,
he demonstrated himself as if he were another, saying:
“Of the child who was suspended, the total across many years— that he proclaims to householders, well-seated and with sublime joy. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “of the child who was suspended” means of the monk for whose sake the suspension (ukkhepa) had been performed; [he speaks] in the presence of each individual...

The meaning is: having cast the sections of the Vinaya, the Sutta, and the Abhidhamma that were mastered back upon the very Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma according to their respective limits—having fixed them right there by way of recitation like a calf tied to its mother.
This genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; "calculated over many years" means for many successive years.
It was placed in the heart by way of synthesis. There is also a reading “saṅkhalitaṃ”;
it means made like a chain, or brought forth from the mouth as a single connected whole. The remainder of the phrase is “that which is the word of the Buddha.
“Tañ” means he speaks or recites that Dhamma of the scriptures. “Of householders” is stated because they constitute the majority. “Well-established” refers to that Dhamma.
The meaning is that he sits perfectly still, not expecting gain, honor, and so forth, but speaks while standing solely upon the foundation of the sphere of liberation.

Therefore it is said, "exceedingly joyful," meaning that he has attained an exceeding joy arising both from the bliss of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*) and from the occasion of teaching the Dhamma. For this has been said:
“Just as, friends, in whatever way a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, exactly as he has heard it and mastered it,
in that very way he gains knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*) regarding that Dhamma, gains knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammaveda*), and gains joy connected with the Dhamma,” and so forth.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Meghiya "The Great Hero gave instruction": these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Meghiya. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and sowing seeds of wholesome karma in various states of existence, [was reborn] ninety-one aeons ago during the time of Vipassi Buddha...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached the age of discretion.
At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī, having reached the conclusion of his Buddha-activities, relinquished the life-force.
Consequently, when earthquakes and other portents occurred, the great multitude became terrified and alarmed. Then, the Great King Vessavaṇa explained the matter to him and reassured him.

Upon hearing this, the great multitude was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Therein, this son of noble family, having heard of the Buddha’s majesty, conceived profound reverence and esteem for the Teacher and experienced a sublime joy and gladness.
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during the present arising of a Buddha in the royal Sakyan clan at Kapilavatthu.
His name was Meghiya. Having reached maturity, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and attended upon the Blessed One.
While the Blessed One was staying at Jālikā, Meghiya saw a delightful mango grove on the bank of the Kimikālā River and desired to dwell there.
Although he was refused twice by the Blessed One, on the third occasion he was granted permission, and so he went there.
Having gone there, while being devoured by the flies of wrong thoughts, he failed to attain concentration of mind. Returning to the presence of the Teacher, he reported the matter to him.

Then the Blessed One gave him this instruction, beginning with: "Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, five things lead to its maturation. Standing upon that instruction, he [applied] insight...
Having increased [his spiritual faculties], he attained Arahatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“When Vipassī, the Chief of the World, relinquished the life-force, the earth trembled, this land girt by the oceans.”
“My finely adorned crest-ornament was stretched out and spread wide;
even my palace shook at the time of the Buddha’s passing away.
When my palace trembled, a great terror arose within me.”
“For what purpose has this vast radiance arisen?
“Vessavaṇa has come here and brought peace to the great multitude;
there is no fear for living beings. Be one-pointed and self-restrained.”
“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the perfection of our Teacher!
At whose arising the earth trembles.
Having praised the majesty of the Buddha, may I rejoice in heaven for an eon.”
In the remaining aeons, I practiced wholesome conduct.
That perception of the Buddha which I obtained ninety-one aeons ago—I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit of that perception of the Buddha.
“In this fourteenth aeon, I was a king of great majesty;
by name Samita, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship and received instruction in the presence of the Teacher, declaring his full understanding thus:
“The Great Hero, who has gone beyond all phenomena, gave me his guidance;
having heard his Dhamma, I dwelt near him, mindful.”
“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “he instructed” means that he exhorted and gave guidance by saying, “Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, five things lead to its maturation,” and so forth.
“The Great Hero” means one who has great prowess, through the perfection of the perfection of energy and by means of the resolve on energy endowed with four factors.
The meaning is that he is one of great energy due to his possession of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*) which is not shared by others.
