"One who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammānaṃ pāragū*): having reached and attained the further shore—the limit—of all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) by means of the movement of knowledge, he is one who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena;
the meaning is "the Omniscient One" (*sabbaññū*). Or alternatively, [he is so called] because he has become the further shore of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhamma*).
"Having gone to and attained Nibbāna by means of self-awakened knowledge, he has reached the further shore of all phenomena (*sabbadhammāna pāragū*).
"Having heard his Dhamma" means having heard that Dhamma of the Four Truths, which is preeminent, from that Buddha, the Blessed One.
"I dwelt in his presence" means that, being harassed by wrong thoughts in the Mango Grove, I went to the Cālikā Monastery and dwelt in the very vicinity of the Teacher.
“Satō” means being mindful; the meaning is that one is diligent in the cultivation of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Regarding the word “ahaṃ” (I):

just as in the phrase “anusāsī” (you have instructed), the word “maṃ” (me) is understood, so here in the phrase “vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ” (knowledge has been attained, the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished), it should be construed as “mayā” (by me).
Furthermore, by the phrase “kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ,” the aforementioned attainment of the threefold knowledge itself is shown to be the fulfillment of the Teacher’s instruction.
He explains it by way of another method. For indeed, the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth is precisely what constitutes acting upon the Teacher’s instruction.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Meghiya is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Ekadhammasavanīya.
"The defilements have been burnt away by me": this is the verse of the Venerable Ekadhammasavanīya Thera. What is its origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a tree deity.
Seeing several monks wandering lost in a great forest, he descended from his abode out of compassion and comforted them.

Having fed him, he brought him to his intended destination. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in the world during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa;
and when the Buddha had performed his duties and attained final Nibbāna, at that time there was a king of Bārāṇasī named Kikī. When he passed away, his son was a king named Puthuvinda. His son—
There was one named Susāma. His son, becoming known as Kikī Brahmadatta, ruled the kingdom;
when the Dispensation had disappeared and he could not find anyone to hear the Dhamma, he caused a proclamation to be made: "I shall give a thousand [pieces of gold] to whoever teaches the Dhamma.
Finding not even a single preacher of the Dhamma, he thought: "In the time of my father, grandfather, and their predecessors, the Dhamma was prevalent..."
“Preachers of the Dhamma were easy to find in the past; but now, one who can speak even a single four-line verse is rare.
Before my perception of the Dhamma perishes, I shall go forth into homelessness.
As he was thus abandoning his kingdom and departing for the Himalayas, Sakka, the king of the gods, approached and taught him the Dhamma with the verse: “Impermanent indeed are conditioned things.”

Having spoken thus, he turned back. Having returned and performed much merit, as he wandered among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a merchant’s family in the city of Setavyā.
Upon reaching maturity, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Siṃsapā Grove near the city of Setavyā, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. To him, the Teacher—
Having observed his underlying disposition, he taught the Dhamma with this verse: “Impermanent indeed are all conditioned things.
Because of the spiritual work he had previously performed there, the perception of impermanence became more manifest to him as it was established;
moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he went forth, applied himself to the contemplation of the Dhamma, and attended to the perception of suffering and the perception of non-self.
Having made insight (vipassanā) his primary pursuit, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The disciples of Buddha Padumuttara were forest-dwellers;
lost in the vast wilderness, they wandered about like the blind.”
“Having recollected the Fully Awakened One, Padumuttara the Leader—
I am the son of that Sage, lost in the great forest.
Descending from my celestial abode, I went into the presence of the monks.”
I pointed out the path to them and gave them food.
By that kamma, O Lord of Bipeds, Foremost in the World, Bull among Men,
I attained arahantship at the age of seven.
“Twelve universal monarchs named Sacakkhu by name, endowed with the seven treasures, [will appear] five hundred kappas from now.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Because his task was accomplished through the hearing of a single teaching, he received the designation "Ekadhammasavanīya" (One Who Has Heard a Single Teaching). Having become an arahant, while declaring his realization, he recited this verse:
"The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
The cycle of birth has been exhausted; there is now no further becoming."
In this context, "defilements" (*kilesa*) refers to lust and the rest; they are called defilements because they defile, afflict, and torment the continuum (*santāna*) in which they have arisen.
"Burnt up" means that, like trees and shrubs by the fire of Indra, they have been consumed root and branch by the fire of the noble path’s knowledge (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*).

"By me" means by myself, or within my own continuum. "All states of existence" (*bhava*) refers to the existence of sensual desire (*kāma-bhava*), the existence of formative action (*kamma-bhava*), and so forth. These have all been utterly eradicated.
All states of existence have been eradicated because the defilements have been burnt away. For as long as the cycle of defilements exists, there must necessarily be a cycle of kamma.

And precisely because the cycles of kamma and becoming have been destroyed, the states of rebirth (upapatti-bhava) have likewise been destroyed, having been brought to a state where they are no longer subject to arising.
"The wandering in birth is exhausted" refers to birth and so forth—
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
Saṃsāra, defined by this characteristic, has been specifically exhausted; therefore, there is now no further becoming. Because of this in the future...
There is no further becoming; therefore, the wandering in birth is exhausted. And because there is no further becoming, it should be stated by way of reversal:
"because all states of existence have been uprooted. Alternatively, one should connect it thus: "the wandering in birth is exhausted;
for that very reason, there is now no further becoming."
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Ekadhammasavanīya is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Ekudāniya:
"Heedfulness for one of lofty mind," is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ekudāniya. What is its origin? This [Elder] also, during previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn as a general of the *yakkhas* during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he fell into lamentation and grief, thinking: "Alas, it is my misfortune!
Alas, it is my ill-gotten luck! For I did not obtain the opportunity to perform meritorious deeds such as giving while the Teacher was still living."
Then a disciple of the Teacher named Sāgara, having dispelled his grief, exhorted him toward the worship of the Teacher’s stupa.
Having worshipped the stupa for five years, he passed away from there;

through that merit, wandering only among gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, and upon reaching maturity, he [served] the Teacher from time to time.
He approached the Teacher. At that time, the Teacher was frequently exhorting his disciples with the verse beginning, “One whose mind is exalted.
Having heard this, he conceived faith and went forth. After going forth, he recited that very same verse over and over again.
While practicing the duties of a recluse there for twenty thousand years, because his knowledge was not yet fully matured, he remained [unliberated].

He was unable to produce any distinction [in his spiritual progress]. Then, passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods and, wandering successively through happy destinies alone, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha at Sāvatthī as the son of a wealthy brahmin.
Upon reaching maturity, having seen the majesty of the Buddha at the time of the acceptance of the Jetavana, he acquired faith.
Having gone forth and performed his preliminary duties, he dwelt in the forest and approached the presence of the Teacher.
At that time, the Teacher saw the Venerable Sāriputta practicing higher consciousness not far from him and uttered this inspired utterance:
"Of exalted mind. Having heard this, although he had been dwelling in the forest for a long time in meditation, at that moment—
He recited that very verse at the appropriate time; therefore, the designation *Ekudānī* (One-Giver) arose for him.
Then, one day, having attained one-pointedness of mind and developed insight, he reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Immediately after the Sugata Atthadassi had passed away into Nibbāna...”
I was reborn in the womb of a yakkha, and at that time I attained great renown.
"Alas, it was a poor gain for me; my dawn was ill-fated and my life poorly established, since while wealth still remained for me, the One with Vision passed into final nibbāna."
“Knowing my intention, a disciple named Sāgara, desiring to rescue me, came into my presence.
‘Why do you grieve? Do not fear; practice the Dhamma, O wise one.’”
The perfection of seeds for all beings has been bestowed by the Buddha.
Whether one should fill the Fully Awakened One, the Leader of the World, while he is still present,
or whether one should honor even a relic the size of a mustard seed after he has passed into Nibbāna— [the merit is equal].
“In equal clarity of mind, the merit is equally sublime;
therefore, having built a stupa, worship the relics of the Victor.
Having heard Sāgara’s words, I had a Buddha-stupa constructed.
For five years I attended upon the supreme stupa of the Sage.
By that kamma, O Lord of Bipeds, Supreme One in the World, Bull among Men,
having experienced prosperity, I attained Arahatship.
“With vast wisdom, four of them were wheel-turning monarchs of great power, endowed with the seven treasures, during seven hundred aeons from now.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [pe] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

But having attained arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one day, when requested by the Venerable Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika to test his inspired eloquence with the words, "Friend, recite the Dhamma for me," he— because of his long-standing familiarity with it—
recited: "For the sage of exalted mind who is diligent, training in the paths of sagehood,
For such a one who is tranquil and ever mindful, sorrows do not come to pass."
He spoke this very verse.
In that context, *adhicetasa* means "possessing higher consciousness"; the meaning is: one endowed with the fruit-of-Arahantship consciousness, which is superior to all states of consciousness.
*Appamajjato* means "not being negligent"; it refers to one who, through diligence (*appamāda*), is possessed of constant application toward blameless qualities.

It has been said: "He who understands both worlds is therefore called a muni. Thus, either by virtue of understanding both worlds, or because he possesses *mona*—where *mona* is said to mean knowledge (*ñāṇa*)—and thus is endowed with that *mona* consisting of the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship, one whose taints are destroyed is called a muni;
[the phrase refers to] "of that muni. "Training in the paths of *mona*" means training in that which is reckoned as the knowledge of arahantship.
It refers to one who trains in the paths of the sage—that is, in the means and methods consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment—or in the three trainings.
This is stated by way of taking up the preliminary practice. For the Arahant has already completed his training;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "the Sage" (muni) because he has attained the state of a sage through this very training while thus training.
Since this is so, therefore the meaning of these words is indeed appropriate as follows: one is "of lofty mind" (*adhicetaso*) by virtue of the lower paths and fruits;

"diligent" (*appamajjato*) by virtue of the practice of the awakening to the Four Truths through heedfulness; and a "sage" (*munino*) by virtue of being endowed with the knowledge of the supreme path.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the causes for striving (*padhāna*) are declared by the phrase "being diligent in training" (*appamajjato sikkhato*).
Therefore, the meaning is "with a superior mind" because of heedfulness and because of training.
"Sorrow does not exist for such a one" means that within such a sage whose taints are destroyed, sorrows—which are mental torments based on causes such as separation from the beloved—do not arise.
Alternatively, it means that sorrows do not exist for the Asekha Sage who has attained the characteristic of "suchness."

"Of one who is tranquil" means of one who is tranquil through the absolute pacification of lust and the other defilements. "Always mindful" means of one who is never devoid of mindfulness at any time due to having attained the fullness of mindfulness.

And here, by the term "of one with higher mind," the training in higher consciousness (adhicitta-sikkhā) is indicated; by the term "of one who is heedful," the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is indicated.
It should be understood that by the words “of the sage training in the paths of sagehood,” the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is indicated;

or rather, by the word “of the sage” (munino), the training in higher wisdom is shown, while by the phrase “training in the paths of sagehood,” the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) for those supramundane trainings is shown.
Furthermore, by the words “sorrows do not arise” and so forth, the benefits resulting from the fulfillment of the trainings are made manifest—this indeed is the [intention] of the Elder.
There was a verse of the declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa-gāthā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ekudāniya is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Channa.
"Having heard the Dhamma, which is of great flavor from the Great One"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Channa. What is its origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Upon reaching maturity, one day he [saw] Siddhattha...
Seeing the Blessed One approaching the foot of a certain tree, he, with a clear mind, spread out a mat of leaves of soft texture and offered it to him.
Having scattered flowers all around, he performed an act of worship.
Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; and having again performed further merits, he continued to dwell only in the happy realms.
While wandering in saṃsāra, during the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the womb of a slave woman in the household of King Suddhodana;
his name was Channa, and he was born at the same time as the Bodhisattva. Having gained faith upon meeting the Teacher’s kinsmen, he went forth into homelessness out of affection for the Blessed One;
yet, giving rise to the sense of possessiveness, thinking, "He is our Buddha, our Dhamma," [he fell away].

Unable to sever his affection and failing to practice the duties of a recluse, he was terrified by the "Brahma-punishment" (brahmadaṇḍa) prescribed by the Teacher according to the rules He had laid down for when the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna.
Having become deeply moved by spiritual urgency, he severed his attachment and, practicing insight meditation, attained Arahatship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the Blessed One Siddhattha, I gave a spread of leaves;
I also offered an oblation all around and scattered flowers over him.
Because of that virtuous deed, I now enjoy this delightful and most precious celestial palace.”
And costly flowers shower down upon my bed.
“I lie down upon a bed variegated with a spread of flowers;
even as I lie there, a rain of flowers falls upon the bed.”
“Ninety-four eons ago, I gave a leaf-mat as a spread;
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state—this is the fruit of that matting.
These seven wheel-turning monarchs were known as ‘those who used grass mats.’”
“In this fifth aeon, these lords of men appeared. Having attained arahantship and being satiated with the bliss of liberation, he uttered this inspired exclamation, overflowing with the surge of joy:
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus, having reached arahantship and being gratified by the happiness of liberation, he uttered this *udāna*, released through the force of his joy.
“Having heard the Dhamma of great flavor from the Great One,
taught by the supreme knowledge of omniscience,
I have entered the path for the attainment of the Deathless.”
Thus he spoke this verse: “One who is skilled in the path to security from bondage.
Therein, *sutvāna* means having heard, having grasped with the ear, having applied the ear, and having reflected by way of the gateway of the ear.
*Dhammaṃ* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Mahato* refers to the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). For the Blessed One is great through his most sublime qualities.

Because he is endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and because he is especially worthy of honor by the world including the devas, he is called "Great" (*mahā*), which gave rise to his designation as the "Great Ascetic" (*Mahāsamaṇa*).
This is an ablative expression: "having heard the Dhamma from the Great One.

It is of "great flavor" (*mahārasa*) because it bestows the flavor of liberation (*vimuttirasa*); that is, it possesses a sublime flavor through the excellence of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"Desitaṃ" means: one who knows all is "sabbaññū"; the state of being such is "sabbaññutā.
Knowledge itself is the supreme, or among knowledges it is supreme, thus it is "ñāṇavaraṃ. He whose supreme knowledge is the state of omniscience is "sabbaññutaññāṇavaro," the Blessed One.
By that—by means of which the supreme knowledge known as omniscience functions as the instrument—the Dhamma was taught and spoken.

"Having heard" (*sutvāna*)—this is the construction. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Itivuttaka-vaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Itivuttaka) in the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
"The path" (*maggaṃ*) means the Noble Eightfold Path. "I set out upon" (*papañjin*) means I practiced.
"For the attainment of the Deathless" (*amatassa pattiyā*)—the construction is: "I set out upon that which serves as the means for the realization of Nibbāna. "He" (*so*) refers to him.
The Blessed One. "Skilled in the path to security from bondage" means he is skilled and well-versed in that path which leads to Nibbāna, which is free from the four bonds.
This is the meaning here: having heard the Blessed One’s teaching on the Four Noble Truths, I have practiced the path that is the means for attaining the Deathless;
the path of practice has been undertaken by me, and it is precisely that [which is meant].
But the Blessed One is skilled in every way in the path to security from bondage, and he is expert regarding other beings' mental continuums or the mental constituents of others;
it is by relying on his arrangement that I too shall enter upon the path. And this very verse was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Channa is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Puṇṇa "Virtue alone...
This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. What is its origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [lived] ninety-one aeons ago during a period when the world was devoid of a Buddha.
Having been reborn in the world in a brahmin family, he reached maturity and attained proficiency in the brahminical arts.
Seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. He constructed a leaf-hut in a region of the Himalayas and made his dwelling there.
Not far from his place of residence, on a certain mountain slope, dwelt a Paccekabuddha.
Having become afflicted with illness, he attained final nibbāna; at the time of his final nibbāna, there was a great radiance.
Seeing this, and wondering, "How indeed has this radiance arisen?", he wandered here and there in search of its cause.
Then, seeing a paccekabuddha who had attained final nibbāna in a mountain cave, he gathered fragrant wood, cremated the body, and [anointed] it with scented water.
He poured it out. Then a certain son of the gods, standing in the sky, said this: “Excellent, excellent, worthy man!
You have produced and fulfilled much merit that leads to a happy destination;
by this you will be reborn only among the happy destinations, and your name shall be ‘Puṇṇa. Through that meritorious deed, he [passed] among gods and humans.
Wandering through successive births, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a householder’s family in the city of Suppāraka in the country of Sunāparanta;
his name was Puṇṇa. When he reached maturity, he traveled to Sāvatthī with a great caravan for the purpose of trade.
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī. Then, together with the residents of Sāvatthī...
Having gone to the monastery with the lay followers, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher;
having gained faith, he went forth and lived pleasing his preceptor and teacher through the performance of duties and services.

One day, he approached the Teacher and said, "It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would exhort me with a brief instruction, which I may hear and [practice] in the Sunāparanta country."

“May I dwell [there],” he said. To him the Blessed One gave this exhortation, beginning with, “Puṇṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye,” and having caused him to let out a lion’s roar, He dismissed him.
He paid homage to the Blessed One, went to the Sunāparanta country, and while dwelling at the port of Suppāraka, he applied himself to serenity and insight, thereby realizing the threefold knowledge.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Dependent on the peak of Pabbhāra, the Self-Existent One,
the Unconquered, that Buddha, being afflicted by illness, dwelt within the mountain range.”
“Until that very moment, there was a clamor all around my hermitage;
but as the Buddha was attaining Nibbāna, a light arose.
As far as the forest grove extended—wherever the bears, cuckoos, and hyenas dwelt—”
Then all the tigers and lions let out a great roar.
Having seen that omen, I went to a mountain slope;
there I saw the Fully Awakened One, extinguished and unconquered.
“Like a blossoming king of *sāla* trees, like the risen thousand-rayed sun,
like a charcoal fire whose flames have subsided— thus was the Unconquered One extinguished.
Having filled the funeral pyre with grass and wood, I caused it to be set there.”
Having prepared a well-constructed funeral pyre, I cremated the body.
After the body had been cremated, I sprinkled it with scented water;
then a *yakkha* standing in the sky immediately called out my name.
“The duty that was fulfilled by you for the Self-Existent Great Seer—
O Sage, may you always be known by the name Puṇṇaka.
Having passed away from that body, I went to the world of the gods.”
There, a divine fragrance rained down from the sky.
Even then, my name was Puṇṇaka;
whether as a god or as a human, I fulfill every intention.
“This is my last birth; my final existence now proceeds.
Even here, the name ‘Puṇṇaka’ is proclaimed.
Having satisfied the Perfectly Awakened One, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyas;”
“Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
That deed which I performed ninety-one eons ago—
I do not recognize any bad destination as the result of that minor act.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, the Elder inspired great faith in the Dispensation among many people;
consequently, about five hundred men declared themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*), and about five hundred women declared themselves female lay followers (*upāsikā*). There he—
Having had a fragrant cell named Candanamāḷa constructed with red sandalwood,

he invited the Blessed One by means of a messenger bearing flowers, saying, "May the Teacher, together with five hundred bhikkhus, accept the Māḷa. And the Blessed One, by his power of psychic majesty,
went there together with that many bhikkhus, accepted the Candanamāḷa, and [did so] even before the dawn had risen.
He returned. Later, at the time of his final passing away (parinibbāna), the Elder, making his declaration of enlightenment (aññā-byākaraṇa), spoke this verse:
“Virtue alone is supreme here; but one possessed of wisdom is the highest.
Among humans and gods alike, victory comes through virtue and wisdom.”
In this context, "virtue" (*sīla*) means virtue in the sense of "gliding" (*sīlana*); it also carries the meanings of "establishment" and "concentration.
For virtue is the foundation of all wholesome qualities; thus it is said: "A wise man, established in virtue...
It also means that one concentrates and makes one's body and speech undistracted. And this very virtue is the foremost of all qualities because it serves as their root.
And because it is the foremost state. As it is said: "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify yourself in regard to wholesome states.
And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is perfectly pure," and so forth;
and also: "The Pātimokkha is its mouth, it is its foremost. The word *idha* is a mere particle. *Paññavā* means endowed with knowledge. He is the highest, the best.
By means of the verse that defines the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā gāthā*), he demonstrates the preeminence of wisdom alone.
For wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme leader. Now, he shows the reason for that status of morality and wisdom as the highest and most excellent, saying:

"Among humans and gods, victory comes from morality and wisdom. The meaning is that, by means of the cause of morality and wisdom, there is victory over opposing factors and victory over sensual desires and defilements.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇa is finished.
The commentary on the Seventh Chapter is finished.
8. The Eighth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Vacchapāla.
"O you who perceive the extremely subtle and refined meaning"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vacchapāla. What is its origin?
This venerable one also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
In the ninety-first aeon from now, having been reborn in a brahmin family and attained proficiency in the brahminical arts, he was once tending the sacrificial fire.
One day, taking milk-rice in a large bronze bowl and seeking out a worthy recipient for his offering, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking in the air;
struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, he [approached] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he showed his desire to give it. Out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted it.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin;
his name was Vacchapāla. At the meeting with Bimbisāra, by means of the Elder Uruvelakassapa—
Having displayed a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), when the Teacher had performed the supreme act of prostration, he saw this and gained faith.
Having gone forth, even seven days after his ordination, he developed insight (*vipassanā*) and became one possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Fully Enlightened One, golden-hued, Possessing the thirty-two excellent marks;”
Pavana has gone forth, preceded by the community of monks.
Desiring to offer a sacrifice, I increased the milk-rice with a great bronze platter and presented it as an offering.
“At that time, the Blessed One, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
had ascended the walking-path in the sky, the realm of the wind.
And having seen that marvel, that wonder that makes the hair stand on end...”
Setting aside the bronze bowl, I paid homage to Vipassī:
"You are the God, the All-Knowing One, among gods and humans alike;
out of compassion, O Great Sage, please accept [this]."
“The Blessed One, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the World, the Teacher,
the Great Sage in the world, accepted [the offering], having understood my intention.
That gift which I gave back in the ninety-first aeon— ”
I do not recall ever being born in a state of misery; this is the fruit of that milk-rice offering.
"In the forty-first aeon, there was a kshatriya named Buddha;
endowed with the seven treasures, he was a mighty wheel-turning monarch."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so on] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he then clearly demonstrated the fact that he had personally realized Nibbāna with ease:
“By one who sees the exceedingly subtle and profound meaning, skilled in intellect, and humble in conduct;”
"By one who has well cultivated the virtue of the Buddhas, nibbāna is indeed not difficult to attain"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "by one who sees the meaning that is extremely subtle and refined": it is "subtle" in the sense of being exceedingly difficult to see, and "refined" in the sense of being delicate.
One who sees the meaning of truth, dependent origination, and so forth, by setting aside [notions of] impermanence and the like, is one who sees the extremely subtle and refined meaning;
it is by means of such a person. "Skilled in intelligence" (*matikusala*) means skilled and clever in intelligence—that is, in wisdom (*paññā*).

It refers to one who is skilled in generating the wisdom of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga*), knowing: "When proceeding in this way, wisdom increases; when proceeding in that way, it does not increase."
"Of humble conduct" means one whose character is humble and lowly toward fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*), and who behaves appropriately toward both elders and juniors.
"One who has cultivated the virtue of the elders" means that the virtue of the elders has been cultivated—that is, practiced—by him;
he is thus "one who has cultivated the virtue of the elders. Alternatively, it means one by whom those possessing the virtue of the elders have been cultivated, that is, attended upon.

"By him who has cultivated the virtue of honoring the elders"—the word *hīti* here signifies a cause. Because he is humble in conduct, has cultivated the virtue of honoring the elders, is skilled in wisdom, and perceives meanings that are extremely subtle and refined, therefore Nibbāna is not difficult for him to attain; this is the meaning.
For by virtue of his humility and his cultivation of the virtue of honoring the elders, the wise [should] advise and instruct him.
They think thus, and by abiding in their instruction, through his own skill in intellect and his ability to perceive extremely subtle and refined meanings,
he performs the work of insight (vipassanā) and before long attains Nibbāna;
this indeed was the verse of the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vacchapāla is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ātumā:
"Just as a bamboo shoot with its tip growing rapidly... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Ātumā. What is their origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having fulfilled his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation in various states of existence, he was reborn in a noble family ninety-one aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking along a street and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of scented water and fragrant powder. By that meritorious deed...
Having been reborn in the world of the gods and wandering from one happy destination to another, he went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and practiced the duty of a recluse;
however, because his knowledge was not yet fully ripened, he was unable to attain any distinction.
Then, during this current arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a merchant, and Ātumā was his name.
When he had reached maturity, his mother consulted with her kinsmen, saying, "I shall bring a wife for my son.
Having considered this, and being urged by the perfection of his causal conditions, he thought, "What use have I for the household life? I shall go forth right now!
He went into the presence of the monks and was ordained. Even though he had been ordained, his mother, desiring to make him disrobe, [approached him] in various ways.
He enticed her. Without giving her an opportunity, revealing his own intention, he said:

"Just as a bamboo shoot, when its tip has grown and its sheaths have formed, is difficult to extract, so too, now that you have been brought here as my wife, I have obtained your permission and am going forth into homelessness."
He spoke this verse. In it, *kaḷīra* means a sprout; here, however, the bamboo sprout (*vaṃsaṅkura*) is intended. *Susū* means young. *Vaḍḍhitagga* means having grown branches.
Alternatively, *susuvaḍḍhitagga* means having well-grown branches—that is, having branches with leaves produced. *Dunnikkhamo* means difficult to exit.
It would be impossible to extract or pull it out from the bamboo thicket. "Born with branches" means having branches already grown;
even on those branches, further offshoots have arisen at every node.

"In this way, I am brought by my wife"—just as a bamboo with its top grown tall, with its branches and offshoots intertwined among the other bamboos, becomes difficult to remove from the bamboo thicket, so too am I [brought] by my wife.
Once I have been brought here, my lineage will increase through sons, daughters, and so forth, and due to this attachment, it would become difficult to withdraw from the household life.

However, just as a bamboo shoot that has not yet developed branches and leaves is easy to pull out from the bamboo thicket, even so, I too shall be easy to withdraw, being one who has not yet developed bonds such as children and wife; therefore, [I must leave] while still unbrought.
“Having obtained my wife’s permission, and having had her give me her own consent, I have now gone forth.
Thus he manifested his own delight in renunciation, thinking, “Now that I have gone forth, it is well, it is excellent”;
or alternatively, he says to his mother, “Having obtained her permission, I have now gone forth. This is the meaning here: even if she did not previously give her consent, [he speaks thus].
"But now I have gone forth; therefore, grant me your permission to remain in the state of a recluse. I am not to be turned back by you.

While speaking thus, even as he stood there, he increased his insight (*vipassanā*), exhausted the defilements through the sequence of the paths, and became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Seated in the excellent palace, I beheld Vipassi, the Conqueror;
the All-Knowing One, free from craving, shining like Mount Kakudha.
And not far from the palace, the Leader of the World was walking.”
His radiance streamed forth like that of the thousand-rayed sun.
Taking scented water, I sprinkled it over the Best of Buddhas;
through that clarity of mind, I passed away there.
“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I sprinkled scented water [over the Buddha], I did not experience a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshiping a Buddha.
Thirty-one aeons from now, there will be a kshatriya named Sugandha.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge, he took leave of his mother and, even as she was looking on, departed through the air. Even after reaching Arahantship, from time to time he recited that very same verse.”

In this context, by means of the expression “I have gone forth,” this too became a verse of the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa-gāthā*), because it illustrates the state of having gone forth from the stains of passion and so forth within his own continuum.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Having caused the stain within himself to go forth, for that reason he is called ‘one who has gone forth’ (*pabbajita*).”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ātuma is finished.
3. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Māṇava:
"Having seen one who is old, and one who is suffering from illness... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Māṇava. What is their origin?

This person also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family ninety-one aeons ago.

Having become a master of the marks (*lakkhaṇadhara*), he examined the marks at the birth of the Blessed One Vipassī, proclaimed the preliminary signs, and declared with certainty: "This one shall surely become a Buddha."
Having thus prophesied, he praised him with various methods, paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the happy realms alone, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the house of a wealthy brahmin in Sāvatthī.
Having grown up within the inner quarters until the age of seven, in his seventh year—
Having been led to the park for the purpose of his initiation, he saw an old man, a sick man, and a corpse along the way;

because these had never been seen by him before, he questioned his attendants and, upon hearing of the inherent nature of aging, sickness, and death, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Without turning back from there, he went to the monastery, heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, obtained permission from his mother and father, went forth, and [applied himself to] insight (*vipassanā*).
Having established [the practice], he attained arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When Vipassi was being born, I interpreted the signs:
‘The Buddha will arise in the world and bring peace to the people.’”
“When he was being born, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled;
that Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, now teaches the Dhamma.
When he was being born, a vast radiance appeared.”
Thus now the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, teaches the Dhamma:
"In whose birth the flowing rivers did not flow,
he is now the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, who teaches the Dhamma."
“When he was born, the fires of Avīci did not blaze;
that Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, now teaches the Dhamma.
When he was born, the flocks of birds did not stir.”
Thus now the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, teaches the Dhamma.
"At whose birth no whirlwind blew,
he is now the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, who teaches the Dhamma."
“At the moment he was born, all the jewels shone forth;
that Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, now teaches the Dhamma.
At the moment he was born, beings were able to take steps.”
Thus now the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Visionary, teaches the Dhamma:
"As soon as he was born, the Fully Awakened One surveyed all directions and let out a lion’s roar;
this is the natural law of the Buddhas."
“Having stirred the people to spiritual urgency and having praised the Leader of the World,
I paid homage to the Fully Awakened One and departed facing toward the north.
For ninety-one eons, because I extolled that Buddha...”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of my praise.
Ninety aeons ago, I was a powerful wheel-turning monarch named Sammukhāthavika, endowed with the seven treasures.”
“Pathavīdundubhi by name, from ninety-one [aeons] ago,
was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
From eighty-eight aeons ago, there was a kshatriya named Obhāsa.”
Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
Eighty-seven aeons ago, he was known as Saritacchedana;
endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
“In the eighty-sixth aeon, he was named Agginibbāpana,
a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
In the eighty-fifth aeon, he was named Gatipacchedana.”
Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
A king named Vātasama, for eighty-four eons,
was endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
“Ratanapajjala by name, in the eighty-third aeon,
was a mighty wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures.
Padavikkamana by name, in the eighty-second aeon...”
Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
A king named Vilokana, for eighty-one eons,
was endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
“In the eightieth aeon, there was a kshatriya named Girasāra;
he was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

But when the monks had attained their rest from the journey and asked him, “Friend, with what sense of urgency did you go forth while still so very young? he answered them by declaring the occasion for his own going-forth:
“Having seen one aged and one afflicted by disease, and having seen one dead whose life-span was exhausted, I then went out and went forth, abandoning delightful sensual pleasures.”
He spoke this verse.
In it, "old" (*jiṇṇa*) means overcome by old age, being possessed of such things as broken teeth, graying hair, and wrinkled skin.
"Suffering" (*dukkhita*) means having reached suffering. "Afflicted" (*byādhitā*) means sick. And here, even when "afflicted" is stated, the state of having reached suffering is implied.
The word "suffering" (dukkhita) is used for the purpose of illustrating his state of severe illness. "Dead" means one who has passed away;
since one who has passed away is said to have reached the exhaustion, decline, and dissolution of life, it is therefore stated as "gone to the exhaustion of the life-span.
Thus, because he has seen those who are aged, sick, and dead, [he realizes]: "These things called aging and so forth do not belong to these individuals alone, but rather are common to all."
"Therefore, I too have not transcended old age and the rest"—this was said because of his agitation. *Nikkhamitūnā* means having gone forth; or rather, this is the reading itself:
having departed from the household with the intention of going forth (*pabbajjā*). *Pabbajim* means he entered the going-forth in the Teacher’s dispensation.

*Pahāya kāmāni manoramāni* means "having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures"; they are called "delightful" because they gladden the minds of those who are not free from lust due to their quality of being desirable and pleasing.

The meaning is: having abandoned delightful sensual objects, and having discarded them by means of a state of indifference through the total eradication of the desire and lust bound to them by means of the Noble Path.
And this was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*) by way of praising the abandonment of sensual pleasures.
Because he went forth while still a young brahmin student (*māṇava*), this Elder acquired the name "Māṇava" (the Student).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Māṇava is finished.
4. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Suyāma:
"Sensual desire and ill will... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Suyāma. What is their origin? He, too, [attained his realization] under previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various existences, ninety-one aeons ago during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in the city of Dhaññavatī into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in the brahminical arts and taught the brahmin mantras. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī was accompanied by a great community of monks.

Together with [the Buddha], he entered the city of Dhaññavatī for alms. Seeing him, the brahmin, with a clear and faithful heart, led him to his own home, prepared a seat, spread a floral carpet upon it, and offered it to him.
When the Teacher was seated there, he satisfied him with exquisite food; and when he had finished eating, he honored him with flowers and perfumes.
The Teacher, having delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, departed. By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

and after performing further meritorious acts and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha as the son of a certain brahmin in Vesālī, and his name was Suyāman.
Having reached maturity, he [became proficient] in the three...
Having become a master of the Vedas and one endowed with supreme detachment, he felt loathing for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures among householders.
Inclined toward meditative absorption (jhāna), he gained faith upon the Blessed One’s visit to Vesālī, went forth into homelessness, and attained Arahantship on the very day his hair was cut.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“At that time, in the city of Dhaññavatī, I was a brahmin learned in the characteristics [of kings], in the Itihāsa, and in the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha;
I was a master of the Padapāṭha and grammar, and skilled in the science of omens.”
I taught the mantras to my pupils and became a master of the three Vedas.
When my father and mother were reunited, desiring to offer a sacrifice, I placed five handfuls of blue lotuses upon my back.
“Then the Blessed One Vipassī, the Bull among Men, preceded by the community of monks, arrived illuminating all directions.
Having prepared a seat and invited the Great Sage, [he sat down].”
Having arranged that flower, I brought it to my own home.
Whatever food was prepared in my own house,
with a mind full of faith, I gave it to the Buddha with my own hands.
“Having known that he had finished eating, I offered him a handful of flowers.
Having expressed his appreciation, the All-Knowing One departed facing northward.
In the ninety-first aeon from now, because I gave those flowers at that time—”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of giving flowers.
In the kalpa immediately following this one, I was a king named Varadassana, a powerful universal monarch (cakravartin) endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so on] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his realization by way of praising the abandonment of the hindrances:
“Sensual desire and ill will, sloth and torpor for a bhikkhu;”
“Restlessness and doubt do not exist at all”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, *kāmacchanda* means desire for sense pleasures; it is called *kāmacchanda* because it is both desire (*kāma*) and longing (*chanda*), that is, sensual lust.
However, here every kind of greed is intended by the term *kāmacchanda*, since even that which is to be abandoned by the supreme path is included; therefore he said, "at all."
"...is not found. For all phenomena of the three planes are "sensual pleasures" (kāma) in the sense of being desirable; the lust that operates therein is sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

Therefore the Blessed One said: "In the formless realm, dependent upon the hindrance of sensual desire, there arise the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor, the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance.
The mind becomes corrupted and reaches a state of putrefaction.
By this [term], ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is meant: resentment proceeding in the manner of "He has done me harm," and so forth.
Sloth (*thīna*) is the mind's lack of fitness, its lack of vigor and fortitude; torpor (*middha*) is the body's lack of fitness, its loss of strength.

Both of these together—sloth and torpor—are called *thinamiddha*; they are spoken of as one because of the unity of their function and their nutriment. Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the state of being agitated.
Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is that state by which the mind becomes excited and unpeaceful; it is the mental distraction (*cetaso vikkhepa*).
It should be understood that by the inclusion of restlessness itself, remorse (*kukkucca*) is also included here, because they are identical in their function, nutriment, and opposites.
Its characteristic is subsequent regret. For it is the remorse that has as its basis wholesome or unwholesome deeds done or left undone.
That is remorse (*kukkucca*). Doubt (*vicikicchā*) means one falls into uncertainty, thinking, "Is it thus, or is it not thus?

Alternatively, it is called doubt because, while investigating the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), one is troubled and exhausted by it; it is doubt having the Buddha and others as its object.
"In every way" (*sabbaso*) means without remainder. "Is not found" (*na vijjati*) means it does not exist; because it has been eradicated by the Path, it is no longer perceived. And these two terms—
Each term should be applied individually; this is the application here:

"That bhikkhu for whom sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt do not exist at all because they have been utterly eradicated by this or that noble path—nothing further remains for him to do, nor is there any need for the accumulation of what has already been done"—thus he explains one thing by means of another under the guise of "final knowledge" (aññā).
For when the five hindrances have been completely eradicated by the Path, all defilements are likewise eradicated because they are associated with them.
Therefore he said: "All these Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances, the defilements of the mind.
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Suyāma is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Susāradatta "Excellent is the sight of those well-disciplined"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Susāradatta. What is its origin?
It is said that he was reborn into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; having attained mastery in the various branches of knowledge, [he later became a monk].
Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic.
Having established a hermitage in a forest region of the Himalayas, he dwelt there. Then the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring to favor him, approached him at the time for alms-round.
Seeing him from afar, with a mind full of serene faith, he went out to meet him, took his bowl, and [offered] sweet...
Having placed the fruits inside, he gave them [to the Blessed One]. The Blessed One accepted them, offered words of thanksgiving, and departed.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha into a family of brahmins who were kinsmen of the Dhamma-Senāpati.
Because of his dull wit, he was given the name Susārada; later, in the presence of the Dhamma-Senāpati...
Having heard the Dhamma, he acquired faith, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight, attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“A reciter, a bearer of mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas;”
Not far from the Himalayas, I dwell in a hermitage.
I have an *agnihotra* fire and white lotus fruits;
having placed them in a leaf-cup, I have hung it upon a tree branch.
“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
came to me while wandering for alms, desiring to uplift me.
With a clear heart and a joyful mind, I gave a fruit to the Buddha.”
“Producing joy for me and bringing happiness in this very life,
the Golden-hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings,
the Teacher standing in the sky, spoke this verse:”
“By this gift of fruit, and by your volition and aspiration,
for a hundred thousand eons you shall not fall into an unhappy destination.
By that very same root of merit, having experienced prosperity, [you shall attain further success].”
I have reached the immovable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.
Seven hundred eons from now, I was King Sumaṅgala,
a powerful wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he then declared his realization by way of praising the benefits of relying upon a true person:
“Good is the sight of those well-disciplined; doubt is cut away and wisdom increases.”
“They make even a fool wise; therefore, meeting with the virtuous is good.
Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “good” (sādhu) means beautiful or auspicious. “The sight of those well-disciplined” (suvihitānaṃ dassanaṃ) means the seeing of those who are well-trained.
The elision of the *anusvāra* has been made for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhatthaṃ*). The construction is as follows:

"It is good to see the Noble Ones (*ariya*), whose personal existence (*attabhāva*) is well-ordered through virtues such as morality, and who have well-established the teaching of the Dhamma out of compassion for others.
The term "seeing" (*dassana*) should be regarded as merely illustrative, since hearing and other such acts are also of great benefit. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Those monks, bhikkhus, who are perfected in virtue, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation;

who are instructors, informers, revealers, inciters, inspirers, and encouragers, and who are capable of expounding the true Dhamma—even the sight of such monks, bhikkhus, I say is of great benefit; hearing them... [and so forth].”

“I say, monks, that approaching them... [and so on] ...waiting upon them... [and so on] ...recalling them... [and so on] ...even following them into the homeless life is of great benefit to those bhikkhus.
Or rather, because the others are rooted in seeing, only “seeing” is mentioned here; as for the phrase “doubt is cut off,” and so forth, that refers to that [seeing].

This is the statement of the reason. For when such spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta) are seen, a wise clansman who desires his own welfare approaches them and attends upon them, asking questions such as, "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?
They dispel his doubts regarding the many points that give rise to uncertainty; therefore it is said, "doubt..."

"...is destroyed. And because, by dispelling their doubt through the teaching of the Dhamma, you cause them to generate right view regarding the courses of kamma and right view regarding insight (vipassanā) in the preliminary stage, therefore their intelligence increases.
But when they, having increased their insight, penetrate the Truths, then the doubt based on the sixteen grounds and the eight grounds [is abandoned].
It is cut off, it is utterly severed; by way of the non-figurative sense, wisdom and intelligence increase.
Because they have transcended folly, they are wise. He increases their intelligence; thus they make even a fool wise. Therefore, etc., is the conclusion:
because, in the manner already stated, seeing the virtuous cuts off doubt and increases intelligence, they...

They make the fool wise; therefore, for that reason, it is good and beautiful that there is association with the virtuous, the true persons, and the Noble Ones—the meaning is that it is a harmonious union and right growth with them.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Susāradatta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Piyañjaha.
These verses belong to the Venerable Elder Piyañjaha. What is his origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the realization of liberation throughout various existences, [lived] ninety-one aeons ago from now.
In the time of the Blessed One Vipassi, during the kappa, this person was a tree deity dwelling in a mountain cleft in the Himalayas.
At assemblies of deities, because of his lack of great power, he stood at the edge of the assembly and listened to the Dhamma.
Having gained faith in the Teacher, one day, seeing a very pure and delightful stretch of sand on the Ganges, he recollected the virtues of the Teacher.
Thinking, "Even more than this, the virtues of the Teacher are perfectly pure, infinite, and immeasurable," he thus gladdened his heart by taking refuge in the virtues of the Teacher.
Through that meritorious deed, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the Licchavi royal family at Vesālī.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a warrior eager for battle, undefeated in combat, and one who brought about the destruction of his enemies' beloved possessions.
Piyañjaha became known by that name. Having gained faith upon the Teacher’s visit to Vesālī, he went forth into homelessness.
Dwelling in the forest, he developed insight and attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“I dwelt on a mountain, in the midst of the Himalayas.”
Seeing the beautiful sandbank, I recollected the Supreme Buddha:
"There is no comparison for his knowledge; there is no conditioned phenomenon equal to the Teacher.
Having directly known all phenomena, he is liberated through wisdom."
"Homage to you, O noble among men; homage to you, O supreme among men!
There is no one equal to you in knowledge, as far as the highest knowledge extends.
Having placed my mind in confidence in your knowledge, may I rejoice in heaven for an eon."
In the remaining aeons, I practiced wholesome conduct.
Since I attained that perception ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of the perception of knowledge.
“In this seventieth aeon, there was one Pulinapupphiya;
endowed with the seven treasures, he was a mighty wheel-turning monarch.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, however, in order to declare his higher knowledge (*aññā*) by way of demonstrating the meaning: "The practice of the noble ones is contrary to the practice of blind worldlings," he spoke this verse:
"Fall when they rise up; rise up when they fall;
dwell among those who do not dwell; do not delight among those who delight."
In this context, "rising up" means becoming puffed up; it refers to beings who do not remain humble due to self-exaltation through pride, restlessness, rigidity, aggression, and so forth.
"He should cause them to descend" means he should bow down; that is, by avoiding those very same evil qualities, he should become modest in conduct.
"Descending" means becoming bowed down; it refers to those who are falling away from virtue due to inferior inclinations and laziness.
One should cause them to arise and uplift them; through the inclination toward what is sublime and the exertion of energy, one should strive for excellence.
Alternatively, "while they are arising" means while the defilements are rising up, lifting their heads by way of obsession.
One should cause them to fall back through the power of reflection, so that they do not arise again, by means of appropriate contemplation.
One should both suppress and eradicate them. "While they are falling" means while they are collapsing;

that is, when improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) occurs, or when the states of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā-dhamma) that have been undertaken begin to decline due to a deficiency in the application of energy (vīriya-payoga).
One should cause them to arise, establish, produce, and increase them by means of proper attention (yoniso-manasikāra) and the perfection of the exertion of energy.
"Living while others do not live": when beings are not living the life of the path, the holy life (*brahmacariya*), or the noble dwelling (*ariyavāsa*), one should oneself live that dwelling;
or, when the noble ones are not living the dwelling of the defilements—the second kind of dwelling—by which they are said to be "not living," one should oneself dwell in such a way.
"Not delighting while others delight": when beings delight in the pleasures of the sense-qualities (*kāmaguṇa*) or in the delight of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Among those who delight [in worldly things], he himself likewise does not delight; nor should he delight in him. The meaning is: among the Noble Ones (ariya) who delight in the non-material joy of meditative absorption (jhāna) and so forth, he himself likewise delights;
but otherwise, at any other time, he never delights nor finds pleasure.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Piyañjahatthera is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hatthārohaputta “This mind formerly wandered on its wanderings” is the verse of the venerable elder Hatthārohaputta. What is its origin?

It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and in various states of existence, he accumulated merit conducive to the turning away from the round of rebirth (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī and having attained maturity, one day he saw the Teacher departing from the monastery surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

With a mind full of faith, he made an offering of flowers, prostrated himself with the five limbs touching the ground, and after circumambulating him to the right, he departed. By that meritorious deed, he [passed] through the realms of gods and humans...
Wandering through saṃsāra, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance in Sāvatthī into a family of elephant trainers.
Having reached maturity, he attained perfection in the art of training elephants. One day, while training an elephant on a riverbank, being impelled by the excellence of his past causes, he thought:
"What use have I for this taming of elephants? The taming of oneself alone is better."
Having reflected thus, he approached the Blessed One; having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, he went forth into homelessness.
Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to his temperament, he applied himself to the work of insight (vipassanā).

With long-standing practice, like a skilled elephant trainer using a hook to restrain a fierce, rutting, noble elephant, he used the hook of reflective discernment (paṭisaṅkhāna) to turn back his mind which was wandering away from the meditation subject.
Restraining it, he spoke this verse: "In former times, this mind wandered on its wanderings.
(77) Therein, the word "this" (*idaṃ*) is spoken because the mind being described is directly perceived by oneself.

"In former times" (*pure*) means prior to the time of restraint. "Wandered" (*acāri*) means it roamed; due to its lack of stability, it circled among various objects. "Its wanderings" (*cārikaṃ*) refers to conduct according to its own whims.
Therefore he said: “Wherever one wishes, wherever one desires, as one pleases. “That” refers to that mind. “Today” means now. “I shall restrain” means I will subdue it;
I will make it free from its habitual tendencies. “By means of method” means by way of skillful means.
How so? Like the hook’s grip upon a rutting elephant. This is what is meant: previously, this mind of mine...
In regard to objects such as forms, according to whatever he wished to delight in—
that being "according to his desire" (yenicchakaṃ)— and wherever his inclination lay— that being "wherever desired" (yatthakāmaṃ)—
he traveled for a long time as he pleased, wandering in such a way that it brought him happiness; today, I [have subdued] that elephant whose pride and intoxication were broken.
"I shall restrain him with systematic attention as if with a goad, just as a skilled elephant trainer known as a *hatthācariya* restrains [an elephant] with a goad;
I will not allow him to transgress. While speaking thus, the Elder increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and realized *arahantship*.
Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Golden-Hued Sambuddha, Vipassī, worthy of offerings,
Departed from the monastery, preceded by his disciples.
Having seen that Best of Buddhas, the All-Knowing One, free from craving,”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I offered a *gaṇṭhi* flower.
Through that clarity of mind toward the Tathāgata, the Lord of Bipeds, the Neutral One, I,
with a joyful heart, bowed again to the Tathāgata.
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I offered that flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Forty-one eons ago, there was a kṣatriya named Caraṇa...”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so on] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
This indeed was the verse of the Elder’s proclamation of final knowledge.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Hatthārohaputta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Meṇḍasira "Through many a round of births...
These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Meṇḍasira. What is his origin? It is said that he, too, [was born] during the time of previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties by performing meritorious deeds conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, he was reborn in a brahmin family ninety-one aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic (*isipabbajjā*).
While dwelling in the Himalayas with a great company of seers, he saw the Teacher; with a mind full of serene faith, together with the company of seers, [he offered] lotuses.
Having had flowers brought and performed a flower-offering to the Teacher, and having exhorted the disciples to practice with diligence, he passed away and was reborn in the world of the devas.
Wandering on from one state to another, during the arising of this Buddha, he was born into a householder family in Sāketa;
because his head resembled that of a ram, he received the name Meṇḍasīra. While the Blessed One was at Sāketa in the Añjana Grove...

While dwelling there, he approached the Teacher, gained faith, and having gone forth, applied himself to serenity and insight until he became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Gotama;”
Covered with various trees, it was the abode of great hosts of beings.
And in its midst there was a hermitage that had been fashioned;
honored by my disciples, I dwelt in that hermitage.
“Let my circle of disciples come; let them bring me a lotus.
I shall perform an offering to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Lord of bipeds.
Having assented, saying “So be it,” they brought me a lotus.
Having made such a sign, I offered it to the Buddha.
Then, having gathered my disciples together, I instructed them thoroughly:
"Do not be negligent; diligence brings happiness."
“Having thus instructed those disciples who were patient with my words,
I then passed away while devoted to the virtue of diligence.
In the ninety-first aeon, that flower which I offered— ”
“I do not recall being born in an evil state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In the fifty-first aeon, I was a king named Jaluttama, a powerful wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus, recollecting his own past lives:
“Through many cycles of birth and wandering, I ran on, seeking without finding.”
“For me, born into suffering, a mass of suffering has come upon me”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “the wandering through the round of many births” refers to this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*) numbering many hundreds of thousands of births;

because it intends a long duration, the singular number is used in the sense of absolute connection. “They have wandered” means they have transmigrated, by way of passing away and being reborn again and again.

I wandered about. "Not finding" means not obtaining or not attaining the knowledge that turns one back from that [saṃsāra]. "Of mine" (*tassa me*) refers to me as I was thus wandering through cyclic existence.
"Born of suffering" (*dukkhajātassa*) means having suffering arisen by way of birth and so forth, or having the nature of suffering by way of the three types of suffering (*dukkhatā*).
"The mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandho*) is a heap of suffering consisting of the rounds of kamma, defilements, and their results.
"Aparaddho" means that from the moment he attained the path of Arahatship, he has departed and passed away; he will not be reborn.
Alternatively, the reading is "aparaṭṭho," which means "departed" because his prosperity has vanished due to the complete eradication of its causes.
And this very statement was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Meṇḍasira is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rakkhita:
"All lust has been abandoned by me"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Rakkhita. What is its origin? It is said that he [attained his realization] under Padumuttara Buddha...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, he one day heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching;
with a mind full of faith, he offered praise concerning the knowledge of the teaching. The Teacher, observing his clarity of mind, said:
"In the past, one hundred thousand kappas ago, this person was Rakkhita under the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama."
“He will become a disciple named [Rakkhita],” he prophesied. Having heard this, his mind became even more filled with serene faith;

performing further meritorious deeds, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during the arising of this present Buddha, he was reborn in the Sākiya royal family in the village of Devadaha, where his name was Rakkhita.
He was one of those whom the Sākiya and Koliya kings provided for the purpose of attending upon the Blessed One.
Five hundred royal princes were given [to him] and they went forth; he was one among them.

However, because those royal princes had gone forth not out of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) but because they were overcome by world-weariness (*ukkaṇṭhā*), when the Teacher led them to the banks of the Kuṇāla Lake and, by teaching the Kuṇāla Jātaka and explaining the faults of women, revealed the peril of sensual pleasures and directed them toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), then this one too—
Devoting himself to his meditation subject, he developed insight and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, was teaching the deathless state to a great multitude of people.”
“Having heard his words, uttered with the voice of a bull,
I then stood with one-pointed mind, having raised my hands in reverential salutation.
Just as the ocean is the chief among bodies of water, and Mount Neru is the most excellent mountain peak;”
In the same way, those who act under the sway of their own minds do not approach even a fraction of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Having established the method of the Dhamma, the compassionate Seer, the Buddha,
sat amidst the community of monks and spoke these verses.
“He who praised the knowledge of the Buddha, the Leader of the World,
will not go to an evil destination for a hundred thousand eons.
Having incinerated the defilements, one-pointed and well-composed— ”
"One named Sobhita shall be a disciple of the Teacher.
For fifty-five thousand aeons, seven will be glorious and exalted;
endowed with the seven treasures, they will be mighty wheel-turning monarchs."
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [etc.]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, however, while reviewing the defilements he had abandoned, he spoke the verse beginning with “All lust.

79. Therein, “all lust” refers to every kind of lust, including the various types such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and so forth. “Abandoned” means through the cultivation of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

"All ill will has been abandoned" means it has been abandoned by way of its total eradication. "All ill will" refers to every instance of malice, divided into many categories such as the bases for resentment and so forth.
"It has been uprooted" means it has been completely destroyed by the Path.

"All delusion has departed from me" refers to all delusion—whether it be the eightfold division according to its bases, such as "ignorance regarding suffering," or its manifold divisions according to the classification of the bases of defilement.
"Delusion has departed from me because it has been shattered by the Path. I have become cool; I am extinguished.

Thus, through the abandonment of the root defilements, all associated corruptions were thoroughly stilled. Because of the absence of the distress and fever of defilements without remainder, he attained a state of coolness.
For that very reason, he declared his final knowledge: "I am one who has attained Parinibbāna through the complete extinction of all defilements."
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rakkhita is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Ugga:
"Whatever karma was performed by me... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Ugga. What is their origin? He too, during the time of previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and cultivating merits in various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, thirty-one aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One Sikhi one day and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of *ketaka* flowers.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and from there on, in successive lives...
Wandering only through happy realms, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha as the son of a merchant in the town of Ugga in the kingdom of Kosala;

his name was indeed Ugga. Having reached maturity, when the Blessed One was staying at the Bhaddārāma in that same town, he went to the monastery, heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Teacher, and having gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
Practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“On the bank of the Vinatā River, there was a fruit-bearing *pilakkhu* tree.
While searching for that tree, I saw the Leader of the World.”
“Having seen a ketaka flower in bloom,
I then cut it from its stalk and offered it to the Buddha Sikhin, the Kinsman of the World.
By means of that knowledge, you attained the state that is imperishable and deathless.”
I revere that knowledge, O Supreme Buddha, Great Sage.
Having performed worship to knowledge, I saw a *pilakkhu* tree;
I have attained that wisdom—this is the fruit of the worship of knowledge.
“Thirty-one eons ago, when I offered that flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of an offering of knowledge.
Thirteen eons from now, twelve [beings] shall emerge as Arhats.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his own full knowledge (aññā) by demonstrating the severance of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭūpaccheda):
“Whatever karma has been performed by me, whether it be little or much—all that is now completely exhausted;
there is no further existence now. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “whatever karma has been performed by me” refers to whatever karma [was done] through the three doors of action and the six doors of rebirth.

Whatever ripening karma has been done, accumulated, produced, or brought forth by me throughout the beginningless cycle of existence— in manifold ways, through the eight doors of non-restraint and the eight doors of restraint, and by way of evil deeds such as killing or meritorious deeds such as giving—
whether it be little or much: that [karma] is "little" because of the weakness of its basis, intention, application, defilements, and so forth.
Or, because of their strength and their constant occurrence, it is "much.
"All this has been utterly exhausted" means that all this karma has reached total exhaustion because the supreme path that brings about the destruction of karma has been attained;

for by the abandoning of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the cycle of karma (*kammavaṭṭa*) is indeed abandoned, since the cycle of results (*vipākavaṭṭa*) is no longer produced. Therefore he said: "Now there is no further becoming."
The meaning is: "There is no further production of renewed existence for me in the future. There is also a reading, "sabbampetaṃ," which is analyzed as the phrase "all this.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uggata is finished.
The commentary on the eighth chapter is finished.
9. The Ninth Chapter. 1.

The Explanation of the Verses of the Venerable Elder Samitigutta. “Whatever evil was done by me”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Samitigutta. What is its origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
