Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various existences, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Blessed One and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of *jātisumana* flowers.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, in whatever existence he was reborn, he possessed excellence of lineage, physical form, and retinue.

He stood there having overcome other beings. However, on one occasion, seeing a certain Paccekabuddha wandering for alms, he thought, "This bald man is surely a leper; that is why he goes about covered up," and spitting upon him, he departed.
Because of that deed, he was boiled in hell for a long time, and then [during the time of] the Blessed One Kassapa...
Having been reborn in the human world at a later time, he entered the wandering life of a paribbājaka.
Seeing a lay follower endowed with virtue and good conduct, he became inwardly resentful and reviled him, saying, "May you become a leper!
Furthermore, he defiled the bath-powders placed by people at a bathing ford. Due to that kamma, he was reborn again in hell for many years.
Having experienced suffering, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin;

his name was Samitigutta. Upon reaching maturity, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and dwelt with perfectly purified virtue. Due to the outflow of his past karma...
A skin disease arose; because of it, his bodily limbs were for the most part cut and broken, and they were oozing.

He was staying in the infirmary. Then one day, the General of the Dhamma went to inquire after the sick, and while asking after the monks who were ill here and there, he saw that monk and said, "Friend, as long as the continuity of the aggregates persists..."

"Indeed, all feeling is nothing but suffering; however, when the aggregates do not exist, there is no suffering. Having thus taught the meditation subject of the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*), he departed.
Abiding by the elder’s instruction and increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he realized the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
This is stated in the *Apadāna*:
“At the birth of Vipassi, a vast radiance appeared;
the earth, together with its oceans and mountains, trembled.
And the omens were interpreted: ‘A Buddha shall arise in the world.’”
The foremost among all beings, he will uplift the world.
Having heard the signs from the soothsayers, I performed a birth-offering;
there is no such honoring as this birth-offering.
“Having performed wholesome deeds, I gladdened my own mind;
having offered a birth-ceremony, I passed away there.
Whichever womb I was reborn into—whether among the gods or among humans—”
“I overcome all beings—this is the fruit of honoring at birth.
My nurses attend to me, following the power of my mind;
they are unable to provoke my anger—this is the fruit of honoring at birth.”
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I made that offering, I did not experience an unfortunate rebirth;
this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha at birth.
There were thirty-four kings named Supāricariya.”
“In this third aeon, I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
My defilements have been burnt away... [etc.]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), by reflecting upon the defilements he had abandoned, he recalled the evil kamma he had committed in previous births according to the diseases he was currently experiencing; then, demonstrating that those [defilements] were now entirely abandoned, he said:
“Whatever evil I have committed in the past, in other births, that is to be experienced right here;
no other basis for it exists”—thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, “evil” (pāpa) refers to unwholesome karma (*akusala-kamma*). For that is called “evil” in the sense of being base or contemptible. “In the past” (*pubbe*) means formerly.
"In other births" means in births other than this one, in other personal existences (*attabhāva*). This is the meaning here:
"Even though no such evil was committed by me in this present existence, there is now no possibility for that [result] to arise;
however, whatever was committed in other births than this one is to be experienced right here, for that indeed [ripens] right here."
The fruit that is to be felt and experienced in this very selfhood—why is this? Because no other basis exists;
there is no other continuity of aggregates (*khandhappabandha*) that could serve as the occasion for the ripening of that karma.

However, these aggregates, because all clinging (*upādāna*) has been abandoned, are like a fire without fuel; through the cessation of the final consciousness, they are without rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*).
"They cease"—thus he answered another.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Samitigutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kassapa.
"Wherever there is good almsfood"—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Kassapa. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family and attained mastery in the three Vedas and other brahminical arts.
One day, upon seeing the Blessed One, he made an offering with *sumana* flowers with a devout mind. While making it...
He also scattered handfuls of flowers over and all around the Teacher. By the power of the Buddha, the flowers remained in the form of flower-seats for seven days.
Having seen that marvel, his mind became even more filled with serene confidence.
Performing meritorious deeds again and again, and wandering through the happy realms for a hundred thousand eons, he was born in Sāvatthī during this present dispensation of a Buddha.
He was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin from the northern regions, and his name was Kassapa.
While still in his childhood, his father passed away. His mother raised him.

One day, having gone to Jetavana and heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he—due to his possession of the necessary roots of merit—became a stream-enterer on that very seat, and [then informed] his mother...

Having gone into her presence and obtained her permission, he went forth. When the Teacher had completed the rains retreat and the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), and had departed on a journey through the countryside, the monk, desiring to go along with the Teacher, went to his mother’s presence to take leave of her.
As she was dismissing him, she gave him this exhortation:
“Go wherever there is good alms-food, safety, and fearlessness;
go there, my son, do not be overcome by grief. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “yena yena” means “wherever. This instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative; that is, in whichever [place].
"Disābhāge" means in the various directions. "Subhikkhāni" means where alms-food is easily obtained; the intended meaning is "countries. "Sivāni" means secure, healthy, and free from disease.

"Abhayāni" means fearless regarding dangers such as thieves; however, the dangers of disease and famine are already included by the two preceding terms, "subhikkhāni" and "sivāni. "Tena" means there, in those respective directions.
“Puttaka” (little son)—she addresses him out of compassion. “Mā” is a particle used in the sense of prohibition; “do not be struck by grief” means:
having gone to kingdoms devoid of the qualities mentioned [in the previous verse], do not be afflicted by the sorrow born of famine, fear, and so forth.
Having heard this, the Elder thought: “My mother wishes for me to go to a place free from sorrow; well then, let us—altogether...”

Thinking, "It is right to attain a state that is entirely free from sorrow," he became filled with enthusiasm, applied himself to insight (vipassanā), and before long reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"A reciter of the scriptures, a bearer of the mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas;..."
Standing in the open air, I beheld the Leader of the World—
like a forest-dwelling lion, like a fearless king of tigers,
like a great elephant with temples split in three, so was the Great Seer.
“Having taken Sereyaka, I tossed him into the air;
by the power of the Buddha, they surrounded him on all sides.
The Great Hero, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, performed an act of resolve.”
They covered the bull among men from all sides with a canopy of flowers.
Then that floral mantle— its stalks within and its surface without—
formed a covering for seven days and thereafter vanished.
“Having seen that marvel, so extraordinary and hair-raising,
I gained serene confidence in the Buddha, the Sugata, the Leader of the World.
Impelled by that serene confidence and by the root of merit, I was urged on.”
For a hundred thousand eons, I did not fall into an unhappy state.
For fifteen thousand eons and twenty-five [thousand],
I was wheel-turning monarchs named Vītamalāsana, possessing great power.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he recited that same verse again, thinking, “This very word of my mother became a goad for my attainment of Arahantship.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kassapa is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Sīha "Living with lion-like diligence"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sīha. What is its origin?
It is said that he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; then, eighteen hundred kappas ago, during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, at the Candabhāgā River...

Having been reborn on the bank of a river in the womb of a *kiṃnara*, living there subsisting on flowers and clothed in flowers, he saw the Blessed One Atthadassi traveling through the air. With a mind full of faith and desiring to pay homage, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One, knowing his intention, descended from the sky and went to the foot of a certain tree.
He sat down cross-legged. The kinnara, having ground the heartwood of sandalwood, performed an offering with the sandalwood fragrance and flowers;

he paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into the royal family of the Mallas, and his name was Sīha. He [approached] the Blessed One...
Seeing him, he paid homage with a serene mind and sat down to one side. The Teacher, observing his disposition, preached the Dhamma to him.
Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and, having received a meditation subject, lived in the forest.
However, his mind wandered among various objects and was not one-pointed; thus, he was unable to accomplish his own purpose.
He was unable to do so. Seeing him, the Teacher stood in the air and said:
“Dwell with lion-like heedfulness, untiring by day and night;
develop wholesome states and quickly cast off this heap of suffering.”
He exhorted him with a verse. At the conclusion of that verse, he increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“At that time, on the banks of the Candabhāgā River, I was a *kinnara*;
I fed on flowers and likewise wore garments of flowers.”
“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men, went forth from the edge of the forest like a king of swans into the sky.
Homage to you, O noble steed of a man! Your mind is perfectly purified.”
“Your facial complexion is serene, and your faculties are perfectly clear.
Having descended from the sky, the one of vast wisdom and great intelligence spread out his outer robe and sat down cross-legged.”
“Having taken some melted sandalwood paste, I went to the presence of the Conqueror;
with a clear heart and a joyful mind, I offered it to the Buddha.
Having paid homage to the Fully Awakened One, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,”
Having generated joy, I departed facing northward.
"In eighteen hundred aeons, because I worshipped with sandalwood, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“Fourteen hundred eons ago, there were those three, named Rohaṇī by name, mighty wheel-turning monarchs.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
As for the verse beginning with "Be diligent like a lion," which was spoken by the Blessed One as an exhortation: therein, "O Lion" is an address to that elder.
"Dwell diligent" means: dwell free from negligence through the non-abandonment of mindfulness, remaining endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all postures.
Now, this dwelling in diligence, together with its fruit, is briefly [described]:
In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “day and night” was spoken. Its meaning is as follows:

by means of the four right efforts (*catusammappadhāna*), according to the method stated—“he purifies his mind from obstructive states while walking and sitting”—he is untiring, not indolent, and possessed of aroused energy, [cultivating] both the wholesome states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) as well as supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*).
"Develop, produce, and increase [these qualities]. Having developed them thus, quickly abandon this accumulation, your personal existence (attabhāva).
First, by abandoning the desire and lust bound to it, abandon it quickly and without delay.
Being thus, you will later abandon it entirely through the cessation of the final consciousness. This is Arahantship.
But having attained [the goal], the Elder, declaring his own realization, recited that very same verse in response.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sīha is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nīta.
"Having slept all night"—this is the verse of the Venerable Nītatthera. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there was a brahmin named Sunanda who, while teaching the mantras to many hundreds of brahmins, performed a sacrifice called the Vājapeyya.
Out of compassion for that brahmin, the Blessed One went to the place of sacrifice and walked back and forth in the air.
Seeing the Teacher, the brahmin, with a mind full of faith, had his disciples bring flowers;
he scattered them into the air and made an offering. Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, that spot and the entire city became covered as if by a canopy of flower garlands.
The great multitude experienced sublime joy and gladness toward the Teacher. The brahmin Sunanda—

By that root of merit, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha at Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin; his name was Nīta. When he reached maturity, he thought:
"These recluses, sons of the Sakyan, live with pleasant conduct and pleasant behavior, eating fine food and dwelling in dwellings sheltered from the wind."
Thinking, “Having gone forth among these [monks], it will be possible to dwell in comfort,” he went forth out of a desire for happiness.

Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, he attended to it for only a few days; then, discarding that, he ate as much as he desired until his belly was full, and during the day he spent his time delighting in company and engaging in worldly talk, while at night he was overcome by sloth and torpor.
He sleeps all night long. The Teacher, observing the ripening of his causal conditions, spoke this verse while giving him exhortation:
“Sleeping all night and delighting in social company by day—when indeed will this dull-witted one make an end of suffering?”
In that context, *sabbarattiṃ* means throughout the entire night. *Supitvāna* means having slept;

the meaning is that, without applying oneself to wakefulness as described in such passages as, "During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting," but rather simply falling asleep during all three watches of the night. *Divā* means during the day.
The meaning is "the entire portion of the day. "In company" (*saṅgaṇika*) refers to sitting together with those who engage in frivolous talk and individuals who are physically robust;
one who delights in that, is fond of it, and whose desire for it has not departed is called "delighting in company" (*saṅgaṇike rato*).
The reading *saṅgaṇikārato* is also found in the text. "Kudāssu nāma" means "when indeed. *Assu* is merely a particle; in what [time]...?
The meaning is "at what time. *Dummedho* means "one devoid of wisdom. *Dukkhassa* refers to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
*Antam* means the end or conclusion. When indeed will he bring about the absolute non-arising [of suffering]?

The meaning is that for one such as this, there is no making an end to suffering. There is also a textual variant: “*Dummedha dukkhassantaṃ karissasi*” (O witless one, will you make an end to suffering?).

When the Teacher had thus spoken this verse, the Elder was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); he applied himself to insight (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“A brahmin named Sunanda, a master of the mantras, a reciter devoted to making offerings, performed the Vājapeyya sacrifice.”
“Padumuttara, the knower of the world, the supreme, compassionate seer,
then walked back and forth in the sky out of compassion for the people. Having walked back and forth,
the perfectly enlightened one, the omniscient leader of the world— ”
“He pervaded beings with loving-kindness, immeasurable and free from attachment.
Having cut the stems of the flowers, the brahmin, a master of the mantras,
gathered all his pupils together and caused them to throw them into the air.”
“For as long as there was a covering of flowers over the city,
by the power of the Buddha, it did not disappear for seven days.
By that very root of merit, having experienced prosperity,”
Having fully understood all taints, he has crossed over the world’s attachment.
“In the eleventh century of eons, there were thirty-five kshatriyas named Ambaṃsa;
they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, the Elder recited that very same verse as his declaration of final knowledge (aññā).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nīta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sunāga "Skilled in the mental sign" refers to the verses of the Venerable Elder Sunāga. What is his origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [reached this state] thirty-one aeons ago.
In the era of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he became a master of the three Vedas and, while dwelling in a hermitage in a forest retreat, he taught the mantras to three thousand brahmins.
Then one day, having seen the Teacher and observed his physical marks, as he was reflecting upon the mantras concerning those marks, [he thought]: "By such [marks]..."
Thinking, “One endowed with the marks will become a Buddha, a Conqueror of the infinite, possessed of infinite knowledge,” a sublime faith arose in him regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
By virtue of that mental clarity, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
wandering on from one state to another among gods and humans, he was now reborn in this present age of a Buddha as the son of a certain brahmin in the village of Nālakā.
His name was Sunāgotissa. He was a lay friend of the Dhammasenāpati;
having gone into the presence of the Elder and heard the Dhamma, he established himself on the plane of vision (*dassanabhūmi*), went forth, applied insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship*.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himālaya mountains is a mountain named Vasabha;
at the foot of that mountain, a hermitage had been established.
At that time, a brahmin was teaching three thousand students."
Having gathered my students together, I sat down to one side.
Sitting there to one side, a brahmin who had mastered the mantras,
seeking the Veda of the Buddha, set his mind upon wisdom with serene confidence.
“Having gained confidence in my mind there, I sat upon a bed of leaves;
having folded my legs crosswise in the full lotus posture, I passed away right then and there.
Thirty-one eons ago, that perception which I attained back then—”
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of my perception of knowledge.
In the twenty-seventh aeon, there was a king named Siridhara, a powerful universal monarch (cakravartin) endowed with the seven treasures.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge under the pretext of teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus:
“Skilled in the sign of the mind, having understood the flavor of seclusion;”
"Meditating, wise and mindful, one may attain spiritual happiness"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "skilled in the sign of the mind" means being proficient in grasping the sign of the mind in cultivation; "at this time... [the rest follows].
“He should exert the mind; it should be gladdened in this [state];
it should be looked upon with equanimity in this [state]”—thus he is skillful in grasping the sign of the mind that is fit for exertion and so forth.

“He should know the flavor of seclusion” means having recognized the flavor of mental seclusion, which has been developed through physical seclusion; the meaning is that he should experience the bliss of seclusion. “The flavor of seclusion...”

For it is said: “Having drunk. They meditate; they meditate both by means of the contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) at first, and subsequently by means of the contemplation of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).

“Clever” (*nipaka*) means skillful in maintaining the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). “Mindful” (*patissata*) means one whose mindfulness is established. “He would attain bliss that is non-material” (*adhigaccheyya sukhaṃ nirāmisaṃ*):
having thus become established in the bliss of mental seclusion (*cittavivekasukha*) obtainable through proficiency in the signs of serenity (*samatha*) and so forth.

The meaning is: being mindful and clearly comprehending, meditating by means of insight-meditation (*vipassanā-jhāna*) itself, one would attain and reach the non-material bliss of Nibbāna and the bliss of the fruit, because of its being unmixed with the bait of sensual desires or the bait of worldly existence.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sunāga is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nāgita "Those outside here, the many who speak other doctrines"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Nāgita. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a brahmin named Nārada; one day, while sitting in a threshing-floor...
Seeing the Blessed One proceeding, preceded by the community of monks, he, with a mind full of serene confidence, praised him with three verses.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods; having performed further merits and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was now reborn in this appearance of a Buddha in the Sakya royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu, and his name was Nāgita.
This was his name. While the Blessed One was dwelling in Kapilavatthu, he heard the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta;
having gained faith, he went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Seated in a spacious hall, I saw the Leader of the World;”
To him whose taints are destroyed, who has attained power, and who is honored by the community of monks—
“A hundred thousand masters of the three knowledges, possessing the six super-knowledges and great psychic powers,
attend upon the Perfectly Awakened One; who, seeing this, would not have faith?”
“Who, having seen the Perfectly Awakened One of infinite knowledge— before whom no comparison for knowledge exists in the world with its devas—
would not have faith? Who, seeing him proclaiming the Body of Dhamma, that sole mine of jewels, would not have faith?”
They were unable to divert their minds; who, seeing this, would not be filled with faith?
Having praised the Sambuddha Padumuttara, the unconquered one, with these three verses—Nārada, who was compassionate toward his kinsmen—[he attained the fruit].
“By that clarity of mind and by my devotion to the Buddha,
for a hundred thousand eons, I did not fall into an evil rebirth.
Thirty eons ago from now, there was a kshatriya named Sumitta.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [etc. …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship, however, relying on the Teacher’s teaching that is not otherwise and the fact that the Dhamma leads to liberation, he—filled with joy and gladness born thereof—uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) as it burst forth from the force of his rapture:”
“This is the path leading to Nibbāna, unlike that of the various other teachers outside [this fold];
thus indeed does the Blessed One instruct the Saṅgha, the Teacher himself showing it as if in the palm of his hand.”—
Thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, "outside of this" means outside of this Buddha’s teaching, in other systems;
therefore he said, "those who profess various other doctrines," meaning those belonging to various non-Buddhist sects. "The path does not lead to Nibbāna as this one does":
just as this Noble Eightfold Path goes exclusively toward Nibbāna—thus being "leading to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagamo*) or "going to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagāmī*)—so too is the path leading to Nibbāna.

In the doctrine of the sectarians (titthiya), there is no [true ascetic], because the teaching of other sectarians has not been proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One (asammāsambuddha). Therefore the Blessed One said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic;
right here is the second ascetic; right here is the third ascetic; right here is the fourth ascetic; empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics.
“Iti” means “thus. “Assu” is merely a particle. “Saṅghaṃ” refers to the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha); this is an expression used in its highest sense, just as...
“The Teacher of gods and humans. Or, “the Saṅgha” means a multitude; the intended meaning is the class of those to be trained (*veneyyajanā*).

“The Blessed One” (*Bhagavā*) is so called due to reasons such as possessing good fortune (*bhāgyavantatā*); this is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Itivuttaka-vaṇṇanā* within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
“Teacher” (*Satthā*) [is so called] by way of the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
He instructs according to what is appropriate; thus he is the Teacher (*satthā*). They lie down (*sayanti*) by themselves. This is the meaning here:

"Just as the Noble Eightfold Path leading to Nibbāna—which comprises the three aggregates of virtue and so forth and consists of the eight factors beginning with right view—exists in my teaching, so there is no such thing as a 'path' in the systems of outsiders. Thus he roared his lion’s roar to us.
The Teacher, the Blessed One— having himself known through his own self-arisen knowledge, or having been moved by great compassion—

teaches and exhorts the community of monks and those people ready to be trained, displaying [the truth] as clearly as an amalaka fruit on the palm of one's hand through the excellence of his skill in teaching.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nāgita is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paviṭṭha:
"The aggregates have been seen as they really are. These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Paviṭṭha. What is their origin? He too—

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and, throughout various existences, cultivating merit that served as the necessary condition for the turning away from saṃsāra, he became an ascetic named Kesava during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.

One day, having approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and with a mind full of serene confidence, he paid homage, raised his joined palms, circumambulated the Teacher three times, and departed. By that—
Having been reborn in the world of the gods through meritorious deeds, and having performed further acts of merit, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha;
gradually attaining maturity, and with a disposition inclined toward renunciation, he went forth as a wandering ascetic and trained there in whatever was to be learned.
While wandering about, having heard that Upatissa and Kolita had gone forth in the Buddha’s dispensation, he thought, “Those two were indeed of great wisdom;
it would surely be better for me to go forth as well. He went into the presence of the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth.
The Teacher instructed him in insight meditation (*vipassanā*). Having begun insight meditation, before long he attained *arahantship*.
He realized the truth. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
"My name is Nārada, and I am known as Kesava;
having examined what is wholesome and unwholesome, I went into the presence of the Buddha."
“With a mind of loving-kindness, compassionate, seeing the welfare [of others], the Great Sage, the Visionary,
teaches the Dhamma while consoling all beings.
Having gladdened his own heart and placing his hands in añjali upon his head,”
Having paid homage to the Teacher, I departed facing toward the north.
Seventeen hundred eons ago, there was a king,
a lord of the earth named Amittatāpana, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his final knowledge:
“The aggregates have been seen as they truly are; all states of existence have been shattered.”
“The wandering in birth is exhausted; now there is no further becoming”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “aggregates” (*khandhā*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*).

For these are to be seen with insight (*vipassitabbā*) by way of full understanding—such as the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*)—through the discernment of insight and the common characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*). “Seen as they really are” means [seen] by means of wisdom accompanied by insight.
By means of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), [existence] has been seen without error as "this is suffering," and so forth.

"All existences have been shattered" means that all *kāmabhava* and other types of existence—both *kammabhava* (existence as karma) and *upapattibhava* (existence as rebirth)—have been split and destroyed by the sword of path-knowledge.

For it is precisely through the shattering of the defilements (*kilesa*) that *kamma*-existence and rebirth-existence are said to be shattered. Therefore he said: "The cycle of birth is exhausted; there is now no more."
"Rebirth. Its meaning has already been explained above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Paviṭṭha is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajjuna.
"Indeed, I was able [to overcome] myself"—this is the verse of the Venerable Ajjuṇa Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence throughout various births, was reborn in the womb of a lion during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
One day in the forest, at the foot of a certain tree, he saw the Teacher seated there.

Seeing him, he thought, "This is indeed the most excellent of men at this time, a lion among men," and with a mind full of faith, he broke off a branch of a blossoming *sāla* tree and offered it to the Teacher.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha into a merchant family in Sāvatthī. His name was Ajjuṇa. When he reached the age of discretion—
Having become well-acquainted with the Nigaṇṭhas, Paṭṭa thought, "In this way I shall attain the Deathless.
With a mind inclined toward liberation (*vivaṭṭajjhāsayatā*), he went forth among the Nigaṇṭhas at a very young age.

Finding no essence there, and having gained faith upon seeing the Teacher’s Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), he went forth in the Dispensation. Beginning insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he became an Arahant before long.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“At that time I was the king of beasts, a noble lion with beautiful manes;
while searching for a mountain fastness, I saw the Leader of the World.”
“This Great Hero indeed brings peace to the great multitude;
what if I were now to attend upon this God of Gods, the Bull among Men?
Having broken off a branch of a sal tree, I brought it along with its sheath and its flowers.
Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One, I offered him a most excellent flower.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because I offered that flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of the gift of flowers."
“In this ninth aeon, there were three kings named Virocana, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained arahantship, uttering an inspired exclamation through the surge of joy born from the attainment of unsurpassed bliss, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, I was able to lift myself out of the water onto dry land;
like one being swept away by a great flood, I have penetrated the Truths.”
In this context, *asakkhiṃ* means "I was able. *Vata* is a particle used for expressing wonder; for this penetration of truth is indeed most wonderful. Therefore he said:
"What do you think, monks, which is more difficult or more hard to accomplish—to pierce from end to end the tip of a hair split sevenfold? and so forth.
By *attānaṃ*, he speaks with reference to one's own internal self (*niyakajjhatta*); for that which is not another is the self. *Uddhātuṃ*... [meaning "to lift up"].

"To lift up" (*uddharituṃ*); there is also a reading, "lifted up" (*uddhaṭaṃ*). "Water" (*udaka*) refers to the water known as the great flood of *saṃsāra*. "Dry land" (*thala*) refers to the dry land of *nibbāna*.
"Being swept away by the great flood" means being swept away, as it were, in the great ocean. This is what is meant:
just as a man being swiftly swept away by a great flood of water that is deep, vast, and without a foothold, might be [rescued] by someone...
Just as one who has obtained a sturdy ship, well-equipped with oars and rudders and brought by one desiring their welfare,
would be able to rescue themselves from it with ease and reach the further shore; even so, I, being swept away in the great flood of *saṃsāra* by the force of defilements and volitional formations,
having obtained the ship of the Noble Path endowed with serenity and insight brought by the Teacher, [rescue] myself from it...
“Alas! I was unable to lift myself up and reach the dry land of Nibbāna. To show how he did succeed, he said, “I penetrated the Truths.

Because I penetrated the four Noble Truths—suffering and the rest—by means of the penetration of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing, and because I knew them through the knowledge of the Noble Path, therefore the construction is:
“Indeed, I was able to lift myself up from the water to the dry land.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ajjuna is finished.
9. (First) Commentary on the verses of the Venerable Elder Devasabha:
“I have crossed over the mire and the swamp,” these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Devasabha. What is his origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in the form of a pigeon during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
One day, upon seeing the Teacher, he offered a *piyāla* fruit with a mind full of faith.
The Teacher consumed it in order to increase his faith; through that act, his heart became exceedingly serene.
Having offered oblations from time to time, he would approach [the Teacher], pay homage, and gladden his heart. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
performing further merits, as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, he was now reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha as the son of a certain provincial king.
While still in his youth, he was established in the kingdom and enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty.
An elder approached the Teacher, and the Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency;
renouncing his kingdom, he went forth and, applying himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship* before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“At that time I was a pigeon, not causing any disturbance;
I made my bed upon a mountain slope, not far from the Teacher with the Crested Hair.
Morning and evening I beheld the Buddha, the Leader of the World.”
“I have no gift to offer the Tathāgata, the Lord of Bipeds.
Taking a priyāla fruit, I went into the presence of the Buddha;
the Blessed One, the elder of the world, the bull among men, accepted it.
“From that time onwards, having served the Guide without fail,
through that clarity of mind, I passed away there.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, as for the fruit that I gave— ”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of giving a gift.
“Fifteen aeons ago, there were three kings named Piyālī;
endowed with the seven treasures, they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, reflecting upon the defilements he had abandoned, he felt joy and uttered this inspired utterance:
“We have crossed over the mire and the quagmire; we have avoided the abyss.”
“Freed from floods and bonds, all conceits have been shattered”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, *uttiṇṇā* means crossed over or transcended. *Paṅkapalipā* refers to both mud (*paṅka*) and mire (*palipa*). Mud is called natural swamp.
"Mire" (*palipa*) is a deep, wide, great swamp. But here, it is called "mud" (*paṅka*) because it is like mud.
Sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) is so called because it smears the mind by causing it to become impure. It is like a morass (*palipa*);
it is a dense craving and lust directed toward children, wives, and so forth, which, according to the method already stated, thoroughly smears and is difficult to cross over.

He said, "I have crossed over the mud and the morass," meaning that I have completely transcended those by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). They are called *pātālā* because they cause one to fall (*pātāyālanti*); [they are located] in the great ocean.

"Lower regions. Some, however, call the abode of the Nāgas "Pātāla. Here, however, they are called "Pātālā" because, like the Pātāla [abyss], they are unfathomable, difficult to grasp, and hard to cross.
These are the views (*diṭṭhiyo*). And these have been entirely avoided and eradicated by me through the attainment of the first path;
thus he said, "Pātālā have been avoided. He is "freed from the floods and the ties," meaning from the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*) and the others.

The meaning is that he is liberated and completely freed from the fetters such as the bodily fetter of covetousness by means of the respective paths; furthermore, he has transcended them by way of no longer scattering [the mind] toward them and being unfettered.

"All conceits are shattered" means that all nine kinds of conceit have been specifically brought to destruction and eradicated through the attainment of the supreme path. Some read "mānavidhā hatā," which means the divisions of conceit.
The meaning is as follows: others say it means "mānavisā," but in that case, the meaning should be understood as "mānavisā" [in the sense of] "due to the fruit of the suffering of a māna-visa.
(First) The commentary on the verses of the Elder Devasabha is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāmidatta.
"The five aggregates have been fully understood": this is the verse of the Venerable Sāmidatta Thera. What is its origin?
This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.

Having reached maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he made an offering of flowers by fashioning a "parasol above a parasol" (chattātichatta) over his stupa. By that meritorious deed...
Having been reborn in the world of the gods and performing further meritorious deeds, he wandered through successive births among gods and humans.
During this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin in Rājagaha; his name was Sāmidatta.
Having gradually attained maturity and heard of the majesty of the Buddha, he went to the monastery together with lay devotees.
Seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, he sat down to one side with a serene mind.
The Teacher, observing his disposition, taught the Dhamma in such a way that he gained faith and a sense of spiritual urgency regarding *saṃsāra*.
Having gained faith and become filled with urgency, he went forth into homelessness; however, because his knowledge was not yet fully matured, he remained for some time largely indolent. Again—

Encouraged by the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he took up a subject for meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) for insight (vipassanā) and, dwelling there with diligent application, he attained Arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Blessed One, the supreme Atthadassī, had attained final Nibbāna;”
Having had a multi-tiered parasol made, I offered it upon the stupa.
Coming there from time to time, I paid homage to the Leader of the World;
having fashioned a canopy of flowers, I offered it upon the parasol.
“For seventeen hundred eons, I exercised sovereignty over the devas;
I do not go to the human state—this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa.
My defilements have been incinerated; all states of existence have been uprooted.”
“Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Later on, when asked by the monks, "Friend, have you attained any superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)?", he—proclaiming to them both the deliverance of the Dispensation and his own practice in accordance with the Dhamma—uttered this verse as his declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa):
"The five aggregates are fully understood; they stand with their roots cut off.
The wandering in birth is exhausted; there is now no further becoming."

In this context, "the five aggregates have been fully understood" means that these five aggregates of clinging have been delimited by me through the three kinds of full understanding as "this is suffering;
this is the extent of suffering; there is nothing beyond this," and thus they have been known, understood, and penetrated.
"They stand with their root cut off" means that precisely because they have been so fully understood, the root, which is the origin [of suffering], has been entirely...
Because they have been abandoned, they now remain with their roots cut off until the cessation of the final consciousness;

however, with the cessation of the final consciousness, they cease without any further rebirth-linking. Therefore it was said: "The wandering in birth is exhausted; there is now no more renewed existence.
The meaning of this has already been explained above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāmidatta is finished.
The commentary on the ninth chapter is finished.
10. The tenth chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paripuṇṇaka "Death is not so esteemed as the hundred flavors... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Paripuṇṇaka. What is his origin?
This one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Dhammadassi and attained maturity.
When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he performed a magnificent worship with flowers and other offerings at the Teacher’s shrine.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas; and after performing further merits, wandering through the happy destinies alone, he was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha in the Sakyan royal family at Kapilavatthu.
Having reached maturity, because of his complete prosperity, he was known as Paripuṇṇaka.
It was known. Because he possessed great wealth, he was always consuming food called "one hundred flavors.

Upon hearing that the Teacher partook of mixed food, he thought: "Even though the Blessed One is so delicately nurtured, he maintains himself by whatever means necessary out of regard for the bliss of Nibbāna;
why then should we, being greedy for food, become obsessed with the purity of food? Only the bliss of Nibbāna..."
"But we must seek it for ourselves. Thus, having conceived a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding *saṃsāra*, he abandoned the household life and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
Directed by the Blessed One to the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), he established himself therein.

Taking the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) attained there as his foundation, he applied himself to the work of insight (*vipassanā*). Having developed insight, he reached Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“When the Protector of the World, Dhammadassī, the bull among men, had entered Nibbāna,
I raised a flagstaff at the stupa of that Best of Buddhas.
Having constructed a ladder, I ascended that most excellent stupa.”
Having taken a jasmine flower, I offered it at the stupa:
“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the excellence of our Teacher!
I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of my worship at the stupa.”
“Ninety-four aeons ago, there were sixteen kings named Thūpasīkha, universal monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship, however, out of deep reverence and esteem for the Dhamma, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) released by the force of his joy, reciting the verse:

“Not so is the hundred-flavored food, nor even ambrosia, as that which I have partaken of today. (91) Therein, “not so is the hundred-flavored food, nor even ambrosia, as that which I have partaken of today”:
*tathā* means in that manner; *mataṃ* means what is esteemed; *satarasaṃ* refers to food of a hundred flavors—“food of a hundred flavors.”

They say it is "food prepared with hundredfold-matured ghee" and so forth. Alternatively, the word *sata* has many meanings, as in expressions such as "by the hundreds" (*sataso*) or "by the thousands" (*sahassaso*).
Therefore, that food which possesses many soups and many condiments is called "hundred-flavored" (*satarasa*) because of its manifold tastes;
the meaning is "food of various flavors. *Sudhā-anna* means "ambrosia-food" (*sudhābhojana*).
It is the food of the gods. "That which has been enjoyed by me today" means that which has been experienced by me today.
And this phrase "that which has been enjoyed by me" should also be connected with the words "the hundred-flavored divine ambrosia. This is what is meant:

that which has been enjoyed by me today, at this very moment, by way of entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and by way of entering the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), [is such that] absolutely...

While enjoying the peaceful, sublime bliss of Nibbāna, it did not seem desirable, nor agreeable, nor esteemed to me—just as the hundred-flavored food enjoyed by me during my time as a king, or the celestial ambrosia enjoyed in my state as a deva, were neither desirable nor agreeable. Why?
Because this [bliss] is practiced by the Noble Ones, is non-material, and is a groundless state for the defilements.
But that which is frequented by worldlings, carnal, and the basis for the defilements—does not approach even a fraction, a part, or a portion of this [teaching].
Now, teaching the Dhamma mentioned in the words "that which I have enjoyed today," he said:

"The Dhamma well-taught by Gotama, the Buddha, who sees the immeasurable. Its meaning is as follows: it is immeasurable (*aparimita*), that is, unlimited, because it is devoid of arising and passing away.
He saw the peaceful, unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu) through his self-born knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa); he was a seer of the immeasurable, infinite, and unfathomable range of the knowable.
Thus, by that Perfectly Enlightened One of the Gotama clan, who sees the immeasurable, it has been well proclaimed:
“The destruction [of craving], dispassion, the deathless, the sublime,” and “the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the stilling of all conditioned phenomena,” and so forth.
The connection is: "The Dhamma has been taught; today I have partaken of Nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Paripuṇṇaka is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vijaya.
"Whose taints are utterly destroyed"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vijaya. What is its origin?
This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassi.
Having reached maturity, after the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, he had a railing inlaid with jewels constructed for his stupa and there offered a magnificent...
I had a railing constructed. By that meritorious deed, he wandered through many hundreds of existences with the radiance of a jewel.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī;
his name was Vijaya. Having reached maturity and attained perfection in the brahminical sciences, he went forth as an ascetic.
Having gone forth and dwelling in a forest region as one who had attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna), he heard of the appearance of a Buddha.
With faith having arisen, he approached the Teacher, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma, he went forth, established insight (vipassanā), and before long attained arahantship.
He attained [the fruit]. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Protector of the World, Piyadassī, the supreme among men, had attained Nibbāna, with a clear and joyful heart, I offered this pearl.”
“Having surrounded it with jewels, I constructed a most excellent altar;
having made a great offering at that altar, I passed away there.
Whichever womb I was reborn in—whether among the gods or among humans—”
They carry jewels in the sky; this is the fruit of meritorious karma.
For sixteen hundred eons, thirty-six kings named Maṇippabhāsa were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge (aññā) by reciting the verse: “He whose taints are utterly destroyed. 92.
In this context, “he whose taints are utterly destroyed” refers to that supreme person whose four taints—beginning with the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava)—have been completely exhausted.

"Completely exhausted" means they have been worn away by the Noble Path. "Not dependent on nutriment" refers to one who is not dependent on, nor attached to, nor obsessed by craving or views regarding nutriment;
this is merely an illustration, for it should be understood that all four conditions are included here under the heading of "nutriment.
Alternatively, the word "nutriment" (*āhāra*) should be understood here as a synonym for "condition" (*paccaya*). "Emptiness, signless..."
And here, the "and" (cā) includes the wishless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha) as well; for these three are indeed names for Nibbāna itself.
For Nibbāna is the "emptiness liberation" (suññatā-vimokkha) because it is empty due to the absence of lust and the other defilements, and it is liberated from them.

Likewise, it is the "signless liberation" (animitta-vimokkha) because it is signless due to the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, and the absence of the signs of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), and it is liberated from them. [It is also the desireless liberation] because of the absence of the desires (paṇidhi) for lust and the rest...
Because it is without existence (*abhāva*), it is wishless (*appaṇihita*); and because it is liberated from those [characteristics], it is called the "wishless liberation" (*appaṇihito vimokkho*).
For one who dwells having made that object of focus by means of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), this threefold liberation is his domain;
"his track is hard to trace, like that of birds in the sky. Just as for birds traveling through the sky, [one cannot say] "at this place they stood with their feet..."
Just as it is impossible to know whether [a bird] has gone by stepping on this spot, or by striking this spot with its breast, or by its head,
or by its wings; even so, it is impossible to make known that such a bhikkhu has gone by this particular word among the "words for hell" and so forth.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vijaya is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Eraka:
“Pleasures are painful, like *eraka* grass,” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Eraka. What is its origin? This [Elder] also, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher;

with a mind full of faith, but finding nothing suitable to give the Teacher, he thought, "Well then, I shall perform a merit that is the very essence of my body," and [stood] on the path where the Teacher was traveling.
Having cleared it, he made it level. The Teacher set out upon the path prepared in that manner. Seeing the Blessed One there, he paid homage with a serene mind;
raising his joined palms, with a heart full of faith and never abandoning the joy inspired by the Buddha as long as he remained within the range of sight, he stood there.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, passing from one state to another.
Having performed meritorious deeds and wandering only among the happy destinies, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a reputable householder.

His name was Eraka; he was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and possessed of the highest proficiency in all duties that ought to be performed. His parents, by virtue of their lineage and physical form...
Having brought a maiden who was suitable in conduct, age, and skill, they performed the marriage ceremony.
While living with her in his home, because he was in his final existence, his mind became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) toward *saṃsāra* due to some particular cause;
he went into the presence of the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, having acquired faith, he went forth. Of him—
The Teacher gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Having received the meditation subject, after the passing of a few days, he lived overcome by dissatisfaction.
Then the Teacher, knowing the movement of his mind, spoke this verse as an exhortation: "Pleasures are painful like *eraka* grass.
Upon hearing it, he thought: "I have acted improperly, I who am in the presence of such a Teacher..."
Having taken up a meditation subject, he lived full of wrong thoughts while letting it go.
Then, overcome by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he applied himself to insight (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having crossed the river, the one with vision went into the forest;”
I beheld the Fully Enlightened One, Siddhattha, endowed with the excellent marks.
Taking my spade and basket and leveling that path,
I paid homage to the Teacher and gladdened my own heart.
“Ninety-four aeons ago, the deed that I performed then— I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of giving a path.
In the fifty-seventh aeon, I was a sole lord of men.”
“By name he was Suppabuddha, the Leader, the Lord of Men.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus become an Arahant, he declared his final knowledge.”
“Sensual pleasures are suffering, Eraka; sensual pleasures are not happiness, Eraka.
He who desires sensual pleasures, Eraka, desires suffering;
he who does not desire sensual pleasures, Eraka, does not desire suffering.”
He repeated back that very verse spoken by the Blessed One.

Therein, "Sensual pleasures are suffering": these sensual pleasures of the object (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures of the defilement (*kilesakāma*) are suffering because they are the basis for suffering, and because their intrinsic nature consists of the suffering of change and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
They are "suffering, miserable, and productive of suffering. For this has been said: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair..."
"The danger here is even greater," and so forth. With the word "eraka" (grass), the Blessed One first addressed him;
later, however, the Elder spoke of himself by name. "Sensual pleasures are not pleasant":

these sensual pleasures are not pleasant to one who understands them, yet they appear as pleasant to one who does not understand them. As it is said: "He who saw pleasure as suffering, and saw suffering as..."

"From the dart," and so forth. "He who desires sensual pleasures, he desires suffering": whatever being desires objective sensual pleasures through the desire of defilement (*kilesakāma*), that desiring is suffering because it is presently accompanied by feverish distress, and because it is the cause of the suffering of the states of woe in the future, as well as the cause of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Objective sensual pleasures, moreover, are the basis for suffering. Thus, he [desires] that which has the nature of suffering.
It is said that he "desires the sign of suffering and the basis of suffering. The other [verse] was spoken by way of its opposite to make that same meaning known;
therefore, its meaning should be understood as the reverse of what was stated [above].
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Eraka is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mettajit.
"Salutation indeed to that Blessed One"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Mettajit. What is its origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi, he was reborn into a noble family; having reached maturity, he became deeply devoted to the Teaching and [approached] the Bodhi tree.
Having constructed a railing with bricks, he had it finished with plaster. The Teacher offered him a blessing of thanksgiving.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods; passing from one state to another, performing further acts of merit as he transmigrated among gods and humans, he was now born in this era of a Buddha as the son of a certain brahmin in the kingdom of Magadha.
He was reborn, and his name was Mettajīti. When he reached maturity, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic.
While living in the wilderness, hearing of the appearance of a Buddha and urged on by his past causes, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having asked a question concerning the ways of worldly involvement and renunciation, and once the Teacher had answered the question, he gained faith.
Having gone forth and established insight, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I made a Bodhi-mound for the Sage Anomadassī;
having given a lump of lime, I performed the work of plastering.”
Having seen that well-performed deed, Anomadassi, the supreme among men,
the Teacher standing before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses:
“By this good deed, and by his volition and aspiration...”
Having experienced prosperity, he will bring an end to suffering.
“My facial complexion is serene; I am one-pointed and well-concentrated.
I bear my final body within the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“In this hundredth aeon, when it was complete and lacking nothing, I was a king named Sabbaghana, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship, however, he praised the Teacher, reciting this verse:
"Homage indeed to that Blessed One, the glorious son of the Sakyas;
by him, having reached the summit, this supreme Dhamma has been well-taught."
In this context, *taṃ* means "to him. *Naṃ* is an honorific particle. *Hi* is a mere expletive.
*Tassa* refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
he is the "Son of the Sakyas" (*Sakyaputta*) because he was the son of the Sakyan king. Furthermore, he is honored for his unique attainment of merit and for the supreme glory of his physical form.
Because he is endowed with the glory of the Dhamma-body, he is "glorious" (*sirīmā*). "Homage be to that glorious Blessed One, the Son of the Sakyas"—the meaning is:
"I pay homage to him. "By him" means by that Blessed One. "This" refers to that Dhamma, which he speaks of because it is directly realized by himself.
"Having reached the summit" means having attained omniscience (*sabbaññutā*), or the state of supremacy through all qualities.
"By one who has attained the state of excellence. "The supreme Dhamma" means that the foremost, most excellent, ninefold supramundane Dhamma has been well taught and proclaimed without error.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mettajī is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Cakkhupāla.
"I am blind, my eyes have been destroyed"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Cakkhupāla. What is its origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds throughout various existences after making a resolution under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Upon reaching maturity, when the stupa festival was being held for the Blessed One who had attained final Nibbāna, he offered an *umā* flower.
Having taken it, he made an offering to the stupa. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

passing from one state to another, performing further acts of merit, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa. They gave him the name Pāla. His mother, having run toward him...
While they were wandering about after having run away, she conceived another son. His parents gave him the name Cūḷapāla, and they referred to the other as Mahāpāla.
When they reached maturity, they bound them with the ties of marriage.
At that time, the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana. There, Mahāpāla—by those going to Jetavana—
Having gone to the monastery with the lay followers and heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith.
Placing the burden of his household upon his younger brother, he himself went forth.

Having received full ordination and lived for five years in the presence of his preceptor and teacher, he completed the rains retreat, performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, and received a meditation subject from the Teacher.

Having obtained about sixty companion monks and seeking a dwelling place conducive to meditation with them, he stayed in a leaf-hut in a forest glade that had been built and offered by lay devotees residing in a certain frontier village;
while performing the duties of a recluse there, he was afflicted by a disease of the eyes. A physician [prescribed] medicine.
Having prepared it, he gave it to him. However, the man did not follow the treatment prescribed by the physician. Consequently, his disease increased.

Thinking, "The pacification of the disease of the defilements is far better for me than the pacification of this eye disease," he disregarded the eye ailment and applied himself exclusively to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
As he was exerting himself in that cultivation, before long—without any interval between them—[he attained realization].
Both his eyes and his mental defilements were shattered. He became an arahant through dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka). Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the World-Honored One, the recipient of offerings, had attained Parinibbāna—the Blessed One Siddhattha—there was a great festival for the Mahāthūpa.”
“When the festival was taking place for the Great Seer Siddhattha,
I took an *umā* flower and offered it upon the stupa.
For ninety-four aeons from now, because of that flower I offered, [the result has been...]”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping a stupa.
Furthermore, nine aeons ago, there were eighty-five kings named Somadeva, who were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then, when the Elder had returned to the monastery after vomiting his eyes and the monks had gone into the village for alms, the lay devotees asked, “Why has the Elder not come?
Upon hearing the reason, they were overcome with grief; they brought almsfood and said, “Venerable sir, ...”
"Do not worry at all; we ourselves will now bring almsfood and attend to you," they said, and did so accordingly.
The monks, abiding by the elder's advice, attained Arahatship before long.

Having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they said, "Venerable sir, we shall go to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher. The elder replied, "I am weak and sightless..."
"The road is fraught with danger; there will be peril for you who travel with me.
You should go on first. Having gone, pay homage in my name to the Teacher and the Great Elders.
After telling Cūḷapāla of my condition, send back some man," he said. They, having entreated him once more, set out on their journey.
Not obtaining [permission], they replied, “Very well,” and after putting their lodgings in order and taking leave of the lay devotees, they proceeded by stages to Jeta’s Grove.
There they paid homage to the Teacher and the Great Elders.
On the following day, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, they related that news to Cūḷapāla, who said, “Venerable sir, this is my nephew.”
When it was said, "There is one named Pālita; I shall send him," they replied, "The road is dangerous; it is not possible for a householder to go alone.
Therefore, he must be ordained. Having thus ordained him, they sent him off. He proceeded by stages until he reached the presence of the Elder.
Having informed the Elder of his identity and taking him with him, as he was returning along the way, at a certain village...
The neighbors, having heard the sound of a woman gathering firewood singing in a forest clearing, became infatuated with her.
Releasing the tip of their staffs, they said, "Wait a moment, venerable sir, until we return," and went into her presence, where they fell into a failure of virtue.
The elder thought, "Just now I heard the sound of a woman's song."
The Elder thought, "The novice is taking a long time; surely he must have fallen into a failure of virtue.
When the novice returned, he said, "Let us go, venerable sir. The Elder asked, "Have you become a wicked man? The novice remained silent, and even when questioned again, he did not speak.
The Elder said, "I have no need for a staff from one such as you who has committed such evil."
Having said, "Go," when he replied again, "The road is full of many dangers and you are blind; how will you go?

[the Elder] spoke this, demonstrating the following point: "Fool, even if I were to lie down right here and die, or were to turn over from side to side, there would still be no such thing as 'going' for me."
“I am blind, my eyes destroyed; I have plunged into the midst of a wilderness journey.
Even lying down, I would go on, but not with an evil companion”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "blind" means deprived of sight. "With eyes destroyed" means one whose vision is ruined; by this, [he says] "on account of the failure of my effort."
“Blind because his eyes have been destroyed, not blind by birth”—this distinguishes the state of blindness as it has been described above.
Alternatively, the term “blind” (*andha*) here indicates a deficiency of the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), as in such passages as “he supports his blind and aged parents”;
it does not refer to the kind of blindness found in such passages as “all these wanderers are blind and sightless,” or “the one-eyed man, the two-eyed man, and the blind man.”
The phrase "I am one whose eyes are destroyed" is said to demonstrate the deficiency of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*); by this, he shows his blindness in its primary sense.

"One who has set out on the road through the wilderness" means he has entered a long path in a desolate wilderness, not that he has entered the dense wilderness of birth and so forth—the journey of *saṃsāra*. For it was such a wilderness journey that this Elder had transcended.
“Standing” means even while lying down; even while reclining, as my feet drag along and I roll and turn upon the ground with my chest and knees, I would go on.
“Not with a wicked companion” means they will not go together with such a wicked person acting as a companion—this is the construction.
Having heard that, the other was filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought: “Alas, what a grave and reckless deed I have committed!”
Saying this, he raised his arms and, weeping, rushed into the forest thicket.
Then, by the power of the Elder’s virtue, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat manifested a state of heat.
Sakka, perceiving the reason for this, approached the Elder and, identifying himself as a man from the village of Sāvatthī, took hold of the tip of the Elder’s staff and shortened the path.
On that very day at evening, having led the Elder to Sāvatthī, he had him sit on a wooden plank in a leaf-hut built by Cūḷapālita in the Jeta Grove.
After informing the Elder of his arrival through the guise of a friend, he departed;
and Cūḷapālita attended upon him with great care for as long as he lived.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cakkhupāla is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Khaṇḍasumana:
"Having offered a single flower... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Khaṇḍasumana. What is their origin? It is said that he...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and having attained maturity,
he performed a great act of worship by surrounding the stupa of that Teacher— who had since passed into parinibbāna—
with a sandalwood railing. By virtue of that meritorious deed, while experiencing sublime prosperity among gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa...
Born into a family of householders, when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna and the King was making an offering of flowers for the golden stupa, he could not obtain any flowers.

Seeing a single withered *sumana* flower, he purchased it for a high price and, taking it to the shrine, performed an offering and gave rise to sublime joy and gladness. By that meritorious deed, he...
Having been reborn in the world of the gods and enjoyed celestial bliss for eighty crores of years, he was reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance into a royal family of Mallas in Pāvā.
At the time of his birth, pieces of sugar and jasmine flowers appeared in his house;
therefore, they gave him the name Khaṇḍasumana. When he reached the age of discretion, [he encountered] the Blessed One...
While staying at Cunda’s Mango Grove in Pāvā, [he] approached [the Buddha], and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith.
Having gone forth, he applied himself to insight meditation and before long became one possessed of the six super-knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men;”
Having blazed like a mass of fire, the Perfectly Enlightened One has attained final Nibbāna.
When the Great Hero had attained Nibbāna, his stupa became widespread;
from afar they pay homage at that most excellent, supreme shrine for the relics.
With a clear mind and joyful heart, he fashioned a sandalwood railing;
at that time, the trunk of the stupa appeared, perfectly suited to the monument.
Whether being reborn in existence as a deity or as a human—
"I see no fault in myself; this is the fruit of my former karma.
Fifteen hundred eons ago, there were eight men;
all of them were named Samata, universal monarchs of great power."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship and recollecting his own previous birth, he saw that his offering of a *sumana* flower there was the cause for his attainment of heaven and a supportive condition (*upanissaya*) for Nibbāna. Thus, proclaiming this matter by way of a spontaneous utterance (*udāna*), he said:
“Having given a single flower, for eighty crores of years...”
“Having enjoyed the celestial realms, I have attained Nibbāna with what remained,” he spoke this verse.
In that regard, *ekapupphaṃ* means a single flower; here, however, it refers specifically to a jasmine (*sumana*) flower.

*Cajitvāna* means having relinquished by way of performing an offering at the Teacher’s stupa, on account of that act of giving. *Asīti vassakoṭiyo* refers to eighty crores of years according to human reckoning.
"Eighty koṭis of rains"—this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to being reborn again and again in the second of the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure (*kāmasagga*). Therefore, "in the heavens" (*saggesu*) refers to the heavenly world known as the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*);
here the plural number is used because of the process of arising there repeatedly. "Having enjoyed" (*paricāretvā*) [refers to] forms and so forth.
Having enjoyed pleasures by indulging the sense-faculties in their objects, or having entertained and served himself with celestial nymphs;

"I am quenched by what remains"—this refers to that which, among the wholesome volitions proceeding from the offering of flowers, serves as the supporting condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) remaining over and above the kamma that bestows worldly success. Much...
For in that case, volition proceeds according to the sequence of what precedes and what follows.

Or, by the phrase "by the remainder," it means: while that very result of karma was not yet exhausted, I have attained Nibbāna through the exhaustion of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*); I am fully extinguished.
By this, it is shown that even the final existence (*carimattabhāva*) in which one stands and realizes Arahantship belongs to that [same category].
This shows that it is the result of kamma. It refers to the same kind [of kamma] with reference to which it is stated elsewhere: "by the remainder of the ripening of that very kamma.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khaṇḍasumana is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa.
The verses of the Venerable Elder Tissa, who abandoned a hundred-pala bronze vessel. What is their origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a family of carriage-makers.
Having reached maturity, one day, upon seeing the Blessed One, he became inspired with a serene mind; he fashioned a plank from a piece of sandalwood and offered it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One consumed it. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
having performed further merits and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance into a royal family in the city of Roruva.
Upon reaching maturity, when his father passed away, he was established in the kingdom. Having become an unseen companion to King Bimbisāra, he—
He sent him gifts such as jewels, pearls, and garments. King Bimbisāra, having heard of his merit, sent a return gift:
he had the life of the Buddha painted on a cloth and the principle of dependent origination inscribed on a golden plate, and sent them.
Upon seeing these, because of his past service rendered under previous Buddhas and because this was his final existence...

Having observed the life of the Buddha depicted on a cloth painting, having read the sequence of dependent origination inscribed upon a golden plate, and having discerned the processes of arising and ceasing while fixing the order of the Dispensation in his heart, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and thought:
"I have seen the appearance of the Blessed One, and the sequence of the Dispensation is known to me in its essential outline; sensual pleasures bring much suffering and much despair."
"What use have I now for household life? Abandoning his kingdom, shaving off his hair and beard, and donning saffron robes, he went forth under the Blessed One.
Taking an earthen bowl, King Pukkusāti departed from the city while the great multitude was still lamenting; traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha. There, he...
Having approached the Blessed One who was dwelling at Sappasoṇḍika Crag, he paid homage and sat down to one side.

The Teacher taught the Dhamma. Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, he took up the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā), and dwelling with diligent application, he brought his insight to its culmination and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the past, I was a cartwright, well-trained in woodworking;
