having fashioned a sandalwood plank, I gave it to the Kinsman of the World.
This celestial mansion, beautifully constructed of gold, shines forth.”
Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and celestial vehicles appeared before me.
"Palaces and palanquins arise according to my wish;
this is the fruit of the unshakable jewel for me—this is the fruit of the plank."
“Ninety-one eons ago, I gave a wooden plank;
I do not know a state of misery—that is the fruit of that plank.
In the fifty-seventh eon, there were four named Nimmita.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he spoke of his own practice by way of a spontaneous utterance (udāna):”
“Having abandoned a bronze vessel weighing a hundred *pala*, adorned with a hundred royal ornaments, he took up a clay bowl—this was his second consecration. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “having abandoned” (*hitvā*) means having relinquished. “Weighing a hundred *pala*” (*satapala*) refers to that which has a hundred *pala* [of weight]; it is measured at one hundred *pala*.
*Kaṃsa* means a platter. *Sovaṇṇa* means made of gold. *Satarājika* means endowed with many lines due to the variegated decoration of its surface and the various patterns of its designs.

Regarding the phrase "I took up a clay bowl": having previously eaten from such a magnificent vessel while following the exhortation of the Buddhas, [the Buddha thought], "Now, having discarded that, I have taken up a bowl made of clay; oh!"

"Excellent! I have performed the noble vow; it has been fulfilled," he says, expressing his approval of both the renunciation of the kingdom and the undertaking of the going-forth under the guise of praising the vessel.

Therefore he said: "This is the second consecration. Taking the first consecration to the kingship as the basis, this undertaking of the going-forth is my second consecration; for by means of that, [he was consecrated] from passion and the other [defilements].

Action that is defiled, accompanied by apprehension and fear, leading to harm, bound up with suffering, and base—this, however, by contrast, is "excellent" and "refined"; this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tissa is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya "Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Abhaya. What is its origin?

He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Sumedha...
Having been reborn in a noble family at the proper time and having reached maturity, he one day saw the Blessed One Sumedha and, with a devout heart, made an offering of *saḷala* flowers.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas; performing further acts of merit and wandering through the happy realms, he was now reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
Named Abhaya, having reached the age of discretion and being urged on by the perfection of his causes, he went one day to the monastery.
Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and after performing the preliminary duties, dwelt practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
Then, one day, as he had entered a village for alms, [he saw] a woman fully adorned and prepared...
Upon seeing a woman, through the influence of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) arose toward her form.
Having entered his dwelling, he thought, "While I was looking with my mindfulness abandoned, a defilement (*kilesa*) has arisen in me regarding the object of form;
this is unbecoming of me. Thus restraining his own mind, he immediately intensified his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*.
He attained it. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Self-Existent One, unconquered, named Sumedha, Cultivating seclusion, plunged into the great forest.”
“Having seen a flowering *saḷala* tree,
I fashioned a garland and offered it before the Buddha, the Leader of the World.
For thirty thousand eons, because of that flower which I offered...”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
For one hundred and nineteen eons, there were sixteen Sunimmita kings, possessors of the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”
“The defilements have been burnt up by me… [and so on] … the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship, he demonstrated the non-arising of defilements within himself, showing: “For one who follows after defilements, there is no lifting up of the head from the suffering of the round of existence. But I do not follow after them,” as he said:
“Having seen a form, mindfulness was lost, As I attended to a pleasing sign;”
"One whose mind is impassioned experiences [it], and he remains clinging to it;
his taints increase, leading him toward the root of existence"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) that is provocative of passion; however, in this context, it specifically intends the form of a woman. "Having seen" (*disvā*)...
"Having seen with the eye" means having grasped it by way of observing the primary and secondary characteristics (nimitta-anubyañjana) following upon the door of the eye;
the meaning is "because of that very grasping of it. "Mindfulness is lost" means that mindfulness—which occurs as "the foul" regarding the body whose intrinsic nature is foul—is destroyed.
To show how mindfulness is lost after seeing a form, he said: "while attending to a pleasing sign."

The construction is as follows: when one attends to the object as it presents itself through improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra), taking it as a sign of endearment—thinking, for instance, "it is beautiful" or "it is pleasant"—mindfulness is lost. Thus, being truly possessed by passion, he feels;
that is, having become thoroughly impassioned, he experiences and delights in that objective form. And while delighting in it, he persists in clinging to it.
Having become attached to that object—having swallowed it and finalized it—one continues in that state;

and for one who has become thus, the taints (āsava) that lead to the root of existence increase. Thus, the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, which by their very nature approach the state of being the root and the cause of existence—that is, of *saṃsāra*—increase further and further for that person and do not diminish.
However, for me, having stood firm in reflection and increased insight, as I penetrated the Truths through the sequence of the paths,
those four taints were abandoned and utterly exhausted without remainder— this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Abhaya is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya "Having heard a sound, mindfulness was lost"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Uttiya. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Sumedha...
Having been reborn in a noble family at the appropriate time and having reached maturity, he one day saw the Teacher.
With a mind full of faith, he prepared and offered a couch worthy of a Buddha—spread with woolen blankets and other coverings and provided with a canopy—in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī).
By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born here in Kapilavatthu during this arising of a Buddha.

He was reborn in the Sakyan royal family, and his name was Uttiya. When he reached maturity, having witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during a gathering of the Teacher’s kinsmen, he gained faith and went forth.

While practicing the duties of a recluse, one day, having entered for alms, he heard the sound of a woman singing on the road; through the influence of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), he...
When desire and lust arose therein, he suppressed them by the power of reflection.
Having entered the monastery and sat in the daytime resting place with a sense of spiritual urgency born within him, he immediately intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the Blessed One Sumedha, the Elder of the World, the Neutral One,
I indeed gave a couch provided with a canopy and an over-awning.
At that time, that couch was endowed with the seven precious gems.”
Knowing my intention, it always arises for me.
"In the thirty thousand kappas [ago], I then gave a couch;
I do not know a state of misery—that is the fruit of the couch."
“Twenty thousand eons ago, three persons with golden radiance, endowed with the seven treasures, were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

But having attained Arahantship, in order to demonstrate the arising of defilements within himself and to show: "For one who does not feel disgust for defilements, there is no turning away from the suffering of the round; however, I do indeed feel such disgust," he said:
"Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost by one who attends to a pleasing sign;
with a mind full of passion, he experiences it and remains clinging to it."
“His taints increase, leading him toward saṃsāra”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “sound” refers to a sound-object that incites passion. Regarding the phrase “leading toward saṃsāra”:
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases;”

“The process that has been cut off, yet continues to flow, is called ‘saṃsāra’”—thus they are called *saṃsāra-upagāmino* because they approach [existence] as the cause for the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra as thus described; or alternatively, the reading is *saṃsārūpagāmino*. The rest is exactly according to the method explained in the immediately preceding verse.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttiya is finished.
10. (Second) Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Devasabha:
“Endowed with Right Exertion” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Devasabha. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Sikhī...

Having been reborn in a noble family at the appropriate time and having reached the age of discretion, he one day saw the Blessed One Sikhi and, with a mind full of faith, made an offering of bandhujīvaka flowers.

Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present dispensation of the Buddha in the Sakya royal family at Kapilavatthu; his name was Devasabha.
Thus, having reached maturity, when the Teacher arrived to quell a quarrel over a spittoon, he saw the power of the Buddha and, with a mind full of faith, established himself in the refuges.
Later, while the Teacher was dwelling in the Nigrodha Monastery, he approached the Teacher;
having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness. Having performed the preliminary duties and applying himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā), before long—
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Like the moon, stainless, pure, serene and untroubled;
with delight and becoming utterly exhausted, he has crossed over the attachment to the world.”
“The excellent Sage, who extinguishes the people, who has crossed over and carries others across,
meditating in the forest, one-pointed and well-composed.
Having fastened bandhujīvaka flowers together with a thread, I— ”
I offered it to the Buddha Sikhin, the Kinsman of the World.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that deed I performed then, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“In this seventh aeon, O Lord of Men, there was one of great renown named Samantacakkhu, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained arahantship, relying on the bliss of liberation he had realized,

and filled with joy and gladness, he uttered this inspired verse: “Endowed with the right efforts, having mindfulness as his domain, Covered with the flowers of liberation, the taintless one shall attain final Nibbāna.”
In this context, "endowed with right exertion" means one who has perfected the fourfold right exertion;

the meaning is that he stands having accomplished the task to be done by them. "Having the foundations of mindfulness as his domain" means that the foundations of mindfulness—namely, the contemplation of the body and so forth—are his domain, his sphere of activity; thus he is "one whose mind is established in the four foundations of mindfulness."
The meaning is as follows: Liberation itself is the flowers, supremely fragrant through the splendor of its qualities;
being completely, perfectly, and thoroughly covered and adorned by them, it is called "covered with the flowers of liberation. "He will attain final Nibbāna, free from taints":

a bhikkhu practicing rightly in this manner will, before long, having become free from taints, attain final Nibbāna in both the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining.
This was the meaning. And this itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
(Second) The commentary on the verses of the Elder Devasabha is finished.
The commentary on the tenth chapter is finished.
11. The Eleventh Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhānika.
The verses beginning with "Having abandoned the state of a householder, because of not being satisfied" belong to the Venerable Elder Belaṭṭhānika. What is their origin?
This person, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, he was reborn into a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained perfection in the brahminical arts; then, abandoning the household life, he went forth as an ascetic.
While wandering about surrounded by other seers, one day, upon seeing the Blessed One Vessabhu, he was filled with rapture and joy.
With a mind full of faith, he made an offering of flowers dedicated to the Teacher’s wisdom.
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
Having reached maturity under the name Belaṭṭhānika, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and attained faith.
Having gone forth and taken up a meditation subject, while dwelling in the forest of the Kosala kingdom, he was lazy, prone to physical lethargy, and harsh in speech;
he did not give rise to the mind intent on the duty of a recluse. Then the Blessed One, observing the ripening of his knowledge, said:
"Having abandoned the household life, yet not having reached the goal, with a plow-mouthed face, gluttonous and indolent..."
"Like a great boar fattened on fodder, the fool enters the womb again and again.
With this illuminating verse he stirred him to spiritual urgency. Seeing the Teacher as if sitting right before him and hearing that verse, he was seized by a sense of urgency;
and because his knowledge had reached maturity, he established insight and, before long, attained Arahantship.
He attained it. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Seated amidst the mountains, shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower, illuminating all directions like the star Osadhī.”
“There were three young men, well-trained in their own craft;
taking a load of a khārī measure, they followed behind me.
Into a basket, seven flowers had been placed by that ascetic.”
Having taken them, I offered them to Vessabhu within my knowledge:
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered this flower, I have not known a bad rebirth;
this is the fruit of the offering of knowledge."
“In the twenty-ninth aeon, one named Vipulābha, endowed with the seven treasures, will be a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship, however, honoring the Teacher’s instruction and declaring his own realization (*aññā*) by way of contrast, he recited that very same verse in response.
In this context, "having abandoned the state of a householder" means having renounced the condition of a layperson and gone forth into homelessness.

"Because of not having reached the goal" means because of not having reached the appropriate goal—that is, because of not having completed the full comprehension and other qualities appropriate for one who has gone forth in the Dispensation for its specific purpose.
The meaning of "apariyositabhāvo" is "one who has not performed what was to be done. Alternatively, "anavositatto" means having a nature that is not fully settled;

it refers to one who has not completed the dwelling that ought to be dwelt in according to the successive stages of the purifications and the paths, and thus has not dwelt in the ten dwellings of the noble ones (ariyavāsa).
One who possesses a plough (naṅgala) in the sense of a mouth is called "mukhanaṅgalī. By means of the plough...
The meaning is that by the employment of harsh speech toward others, one digs a pit for oneself as if digging the earth.
"Gourmand" (*odariya*) means one who is intent on the belly, devoted solely to nourishing the stomach. "Lax" (*kusīta*) means indolent, one who does not apply himself to meditation.
Showing the result of one who is thus, he said: "Like a great boar fattened on fodder, the dull-witted one enters the womb again and again. Its meaning is as follows:

This has already been stated below. Furthermore, it should be understood that he explained "knowledge" (aññā) by way of contrast: whereas a dull-witted person, having gone forth, enters the womb again and again due to a nature characterized by non-fulfillment and so forth, one such as I—a wise person—does not do so;
rather, because his nature is the opposite and he has reached the pinnacle of right practice, he attains final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhānika is finished.
2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Setuccha:
"Deceived by conceit," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Setuccha. What is his origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...

Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Tissa.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, having seen the Blessed One Tissa, he offered with a devout mind a very sweet jackfruit and prepared coconut salad. By that meritorious deed...

Having been reborn in the world of the gods and wandering from one state to another among gods and humans, he was reborn during this current arising of a Buddha as the son of a certain provincial king; his name was Setucchoti.
When his father died, he was established in the kingdom, but due to a lack of energy and skill, he failed in his royal duties and lost the kingdom to the hands of others.
Having become stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) upon encountering suffering, he saw the Blessed One wandering on tour through the countryside;
having approached him and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and while performing the preliminary practices, attained *arahantship* that very day.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In former times, I gave fruit to the Blessed One Tissa;
I also offered a coconut, a highly esteemed snack.
Having given that to the Buddha, to Tissa the Great Seer,”
Desiring pleasures, I enjoyed whatever I wished for as I was reborn.
Ninety-two aeons ago, when I gave that gift, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving the fruit.
“In this thirteenth aeon, there was a king equal to Indra;
endowed with the seven treasures, he was a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained arahantship, reproaching the defilements,
he spoke this verse: “Deceived by conceit, becoming defiled amidst conditioned phenomena,
Agitated by gain and loss, they do not attain concentration.”

Therein, "deceived by conceit" means they are utterly deluded by the theft of the merchandise of the wholesome through conceit—such as the mode of proceeding beginning with "I am superior"—which leads to self-exaltation and disparagement of others.

"Becoming defiled amidst formations" means becoming defiled amidst internal and external conditioned phenomena, such as the eye and so forth, and visible forms and so forth, [thinking]: "This is mine; this I am."
“This is my self”—thus they fall into defilement by way of grasping through craving for that sign.

“Shaken by gain and loss” means they are shaken, crushed, and overcome by the attraction and repulsion arising because of the gain of robes, bowls, and so forth, as well as cloth and other such things, and by the lack of gain of those very same things.
And this is merely an illustration; the remaining worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) are also included here.

The inclusion [of these types] should be understood. "They do not attain concentration" means that such persons never find, obtain, or reach one-pointedness of mind (*cittakaggatā*) by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), because of the absence of those qualities conducive to concentration and the presence of their opposites.
Here too, they are like those who are ignorant and overcome by pride and so forth.
They do not attain concentration; those who possess such knowledge do not [fail]. However, those like me, being unconquered by them, certainly do attain concentration.
This should be understood as an explanation of what is otherwise through the method of contrast (*vyatireka*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Setucchattha is finished.
3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bandhura "I have no need for this"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bandhura. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was a cowherd in the royal palace of a certain king.

One day, seeing the Blessed One walking through the royal courtyard with his retinue, he, with a mind full of faith, took *kaṇavera* flowers and honored the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
passing from one happy destination to another, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha as the son of a merchant in the city of Sīlavatī.
His name was Bandhula. When he reached the age of discretion, he went to Sāvatthī on some business;
having gone to the monastery with the lay devotees, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma. Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness.
Through the ripening of his knowledge, he established insight and, before long, attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Siddhattha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men—
honored by his disciples, he entered the city.
I was a highly esteemed cowherd in the king’s inner palace.”
Seated upon my palace, I beheld the Leader of the World.
Having taken a kaṇavera flower, I scattered it over the Saṅgha of monks;
setting the Buddha aside, I then scattered even more.
“In ninety-four aeons ago, because I offered this flower in worship, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In eighty-seven aeons ago, there were four [disciples] of great psychic power...”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, powerful universal monarchs [have passed away].
‘The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and standing in gratitude, he sought to repay the favor of the king who had assisted him.”
Having gone to the city of Sīlavatī, while teaching the Dhamma to the king, he proclaimed the Truths (*saccāni*).
At the conclusion of the Truths, the king became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*); he then had a great monastery named Sudassana built in his own city and dedicated it to the Elder.
There was great gain and honor for him. The Elder, having dedicated both the monastery and all the gain and honor to the Saṅgha, [departed].
Having himself wandered for alms according to his former practice and subsisting on that, he stayed there for a few days and then desired to go to Sāvatthī.
The bhikkhus said, "Venerable sir, please stay right here; if you lack any requisites, we shall provide them for you.
The Elder replied, "Friends, I have no need for superior requisites."
Showing: "I exist; I subsist by various conditions; thus am I satisfied by the flavor of the Dhamma," he said:
"I have no need for this; I am happy, satiated by the flavor of the Dhamma.
Having drunk the most excellent of flavors, I shall not cultivate intimacy with poison."
He spoke this verse.

Regarding that: "I have no need for this" means that I have no need for this material gain—the essence of which is the requisites—which you, desiring to satisfy me, say you will fulfill; I have no purpose with it. Contentment—
"Supreme happiness" means that one sustains oneself by means of various conditions [of food]. Now, showing the primary reason for having no desire for such things, he says:

"Happy, satiated with the essence of the Dhamma. This means that he is happy—satisfied with the highest bliss—being satiated and gladdened by the essence of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) and by the essence of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*).

The meaning is as follows: "Having drunk the supreme essence of flavors" means having stood after drinking that aforementioned flavor of the Dhamma, which is the foremost, the best, and for that very reason the most excellent among all flavors;
thus he said: "The flavor of the Dhamma overcomes every other flavor. And:
"I will not cultivate intimacy with poison"—having stood after drinking such a supreme flavor, the flavor of the Dhamma, one does not cultivate intimacy with poison, that which is like poison.
"I shall not form intimacy or association with the flow [of defilements]; there is no reason for acting in such a way"—this is the meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bandhura is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Khitaka.
"Light indeed is my body"—this was the verse of the Venerable Khitaka Thera. What is its origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn as a commander of the yakkhas during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
One day, while sitting in an assembly of yakkhas, he saw the Teacher at a certain place...
Seeing him sitting at the foot of a tree, he approached, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, experiencing a sublime sense of rapture and joy, he rose while clapping his hands, paid homage to the Teacher, circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and departed. By that meritorious deed, among gods and humans...
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; his name was Khitakaṭṭha.
Having reached the age of discretion, upon hearing of the great psychic power of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, he was impelled by past causes and resolved, "I shall become one possessed of psychic power.
Having gone forth and received a meditation subject from the Blessed One, he...
Practicing calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), he became a possessor of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men, named Paduma, the Visionary One, having gone forth from the forest, teaches the Dhamma.”
“It was the time of the yakkhas, not far from the Great Seer;
whatever business they had come for, they were waiting there at that moment.
Having understood the Buddha’s speech and his teaching of the Deathless,”
With a clear mind and joyful heart, I stood there clapping my hands.
"Behold the fruit of well-performed deeds:
because I attended upon the Teacher, for thirty thousand aeons I did not fall into an unhappy rebirth."
“In twenty-seven hundred kappas, one named Samalaṅkata, endowed with the seven treasures and possessing great power, will be a wheel-turning monarch.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained arahantship, he dwells experiencing various kinds of supernormal power through his mastery over the higher powers with particular distinction,
and he benefits sentient beings by means of the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of instruction.
When asked by the bhikkhus, "Friend, how do you exercise your supernormal power?", he explained the matter as follows:
“Light indeed is my body, touched by abundant rapture and bliss;
like cotton blown by the wind, my body seems to float”—thus he spoke this verse.
Some say it was spoken “by way of an inspired utterance” (*udāna*).

In this context, "my body is indeed light" means: by the suppression of the hindrances and so forth, by the fourteenfold taming of the mind, and by having thoroughly mastered the cultivation of the four bases of psychic power, my material body is indeed very light;
the intention is that I can, through the power of the mind, transform even this physical body—which is composed of the great primary elements and is inherently sluggish—according to my will.
"And touched by abundant rapture and bliss" means: "My body is touched by a vast, sublime, and great bliss accompanied by rapture that pervades everywhere"—this is the construction.
And this is stated for the purpose of showing how the body became light;
for the arising of the perception of lightness occurs simultaneously with the arising of the perception of bliss. And here, the "pervasion" of bliss refers to—
It should be understood by way of the material form originated by that [consciousness].
But how can there be a pervasion of rapture and bliss for one possessing the fourth jhāna, when that state has transcended rapture and bliss? This is true;

however, this was not stated according to the defining characteristics of the fourth jhāna itself, but rather by way of its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*). Furthermore, the phrase "with rapture and bliss" refers to a bliss accompanied by or similar to rapture.
For here, equanimity (upekkhā) is intended as "pleasure" because of its peaceful nature and its association with a specific excellence of knowledge.

Thus it is said: "He enters upon and attains the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness. He enters, penetrates, touches, and reaches the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness that is co-nascent with the supernormal consciousness (iddhicitta), which has either the foundational jhāna or the material body as its object.
This is also the meaning here. Thus it is said in the Commentary: "The perception of pleasure is the perception associated with equanimity.

For equanimity is called 'peaceful pleasure,' and that very perception should also be understood as a 'light perception' because it is liberated from the hindrances and from opposing factors such as applied thought.
Furthermore, for one who has entered into that state, even the body born of karma becomes like a tuft of cotton."

He becomes as light as a shuttle. Thus, with a body that appears as light as a tuft of cotton blown by the wind, he goes to the Brahma-world. Therefore he said: "Like cotton tossed by the wind, my body seems to float.
The meaning of this is: whenever I desire to go to the Brahma-world or elsewhere by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), then, by means of the wind called *mālu*...
"My mind is stirred; my body seems as if it were leaping through the air like a tuft of cotton.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khitaka is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Malitavamha.
"Distressed" (*ukkaṇṭhito*) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Malitavambha. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a bird in a certain lake not far from the Himalayas.
The Blessed One Padumuttara, wishing to favor him, went there and walked back and forth on the shore of that lake. The bird—
Having seen the Blessed One with a mind full of faith, he took blue lotuses from the lake and offered them to the Blessed One.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the city of Kurukaccha as the son of a certain brahmin;
his name was Malitavambha. When he reached the age of discretion...
Having approached the Elder Mahāpacchābhūma and heard the Dhamma in his presence, he gained faith and went forth.
He dwelt performing the work of insight meditation. Now, this was his nature:
wherever food suitable for him was difficult to obtain and other things were easy to find, he would not depart from there; but wherever food suitable for him was easy to find and other things...

It was difficult to find, and he did not dwell there but departed. While dwelling in this manner, because of his perfection of causes and his noble birth as a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), he soon increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himalayas, there was a great natural lake."
Covered with red and blue lotuses, and strewn with white lotuses—
there, at that time, I was a bird named Kukuttha,
virtuous, endowed with wisdom, and skilled in discerning merit and demerit.
“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
the Great Sage, was walking not far from the Jātassara Lake.
Having plucked a water-born lily, I offered it to the Great Seer.”
Knowing my intention, the Great Sage accepted it.
And having given that gift, impelled by the root of merit,
I did not fall into an unhappy state for a hundred thousand eons.
“Sixteen hundred eons ago, there were eight lords of men named Varuṇa, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship and reviewing his own practice, he uttered this verse in exultation:
“Though one be weary, one should not stay; though one be delighted, one should depart.
A wise person should never dwell in a residence that leads to harm.”

Regarding that: "Even if one is dissatisfied, one should not dwell"—meaning, even if while dwelling in a certain residence dissatisfaction and lack of delight arise toward higher wholesome states due to not obtaining suitable food, one should still dwell there;
because of obtaining other suitable things, one neither departs nor does one depart. Here, the word "departs" (*pakkamati*) should also be connected with the negative particle *na*.
"Even while enjoying myself, I shall depart from whichever residence where, due to the deficiency of the necessary requisites for my dwelling, there is no weariness, but rather I find delight;
even while thus enjoying myself, should I fail to obtain the remaining suitable conditions, I shall depart from there and not remain.
Practicing in this way, I shall before long accomplish my own welfare. And herein is this...
This is the application [of the verse] regarding the reflection on one’s own practice. However, in the case of giving advice to another, it should be applied by way of an injunction:

"One should abide, not depart. As for the line, "But the wise man should dwell where it is not conducive to harm," this refers to a residence where requisites are easily obtained but the ascetic practice (*samaṇadhamma*) does not reach fulfillment; and as for the residence where [requisites are...]
Even the duty of a recluse does not reach fulfillment; such a residence is here called "conducive to harm" because it is associated with lack of progress.
A wise person of discerning nature who desires to fulfill his own welfare should certainly not dwell in such a place.
However, where a residence endowed with five factors is found, as well as the seven suitable [qualities]...
The meaning is: "They are obtainable; one should dwell right there.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Malitavambha is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Suhemanta.
"Of the meaning possessing seven characteristics": this is the verse of the Venerable Suheṇanta Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, lived as a forest-dweller in a grove during the time of the Blessed One Tissa ninety-two aeons ago. To favor him, the Blessed One—
Having entered the forest, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree in a place near [the Blessed One].
Upon seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, he gathered fragrant *punnāga* flowers and offered them to the Blessed One.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods; and having performed further merits, he wandered through successive births among gods and humans.
During this appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in the border regions;

his name was Suḥemanta. Having reached the age of discretion, he approached the Blessed One while he was dwelling in the Deer Park at Saṅkassanagara, and having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and became a master of the Three Piṭakas.

Having established insight meditation (*vipassanā*), before long he became one possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*) and attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Having entered a forest grove, I lived there as a hunter;
seeing a *punnāga* tree in full bloom, I recollected the Best of Buddhas.”
“Having plucked that fragrant, scented, and beautiful flower,
I fashioned a stupa on the sand and offered it to the Buddha.
Ninety-two aeons ago from now, that flower which I worshipped— ”
“I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
In a single ninety-first aeon, I was once a dispeller of darkness, a mighty wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he thought: “I have indeed attained whatever can be attained by a disciple;
what if I were now to provide assistance to the bhikkhus? Having thought thus, because of his mastery over the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he—
And out of tirelessness, he dwelt advising and instructing the monks who approached him as was appropriate,
cutting through their doubts, preaching the Dhamma, and explaining the meditation subject so that it became free from thicket and tangle.
Then one day, while explaining the distinction between the monks who had approached him and other wise individuals—

“He who sees but a single limb is dull-witted regarding a meaning that has a hundred limbs and bears a hundred characteristics, while he who sees all [limbs] is wise”—thus he spoke this verse. In this context, "having a hundred limbs" (*sataliṅga*):
they are called "limbs" (*liṅga*) because they lead one toward a hidden meaning; they are the grounds for the occurrence of a word with respect to its meanings.
Because it has hundreds of manifold characteristics (*liṅga*), it is called "possessing hundreds of characteristics" (*sataliṅga*). Here, the word *sata* has many meanings;

as in the expression "a hundred thousand" (*sataṃ sahassaṃ*) and so forth, its meaning is not restricted to a specific number. Regarding the phrase "of the object" (*atthassa*): this refers to the knowable (*ñeyya*).

For the knowable is called "the object" (*attha*) because it is to be reached (*araṇīya*) by means of knowledge. And although that [knowable] is one, it possesses manifold characteristics, as follows:

Regarding the expressions “Sakka, Purindada, Maghavā,” and “wisdom (paññā), knowledge (vijjā), intelligence (medhā), understanding (ñāṇa”), the word *inda* applies to the Lord of the Thirty-three by virtue of a particular characteristic or ground for application;
yet the words *sakka* and so forth do not apply to him there by that same [characteristic], but rather by another.
Likewise, the word *paññā* applies to right view by virtue of a particular characteristic, but the words *vijjā* and so forth do not apply to it by that same [characteristic]. Therefore...
It is said: "Of the meaning possessing a hundred characteristics.
"Possessing a hundred characteristics" means having many characteristics. A characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is that by which something is characterized;

it is the state of being a condition belonging to a meaning that arises from conditions, in dependence upon its own fruit. For by means of that, this [meaning] is characterized as "this is the cause of that."
And since many different varieties of a single meaning are found, he said, "possessing hundreds of characteristics.

Alternatively, they are called "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāni*) because they are characterized; these are specific modes such as the conditioned nature of various meanings, which should be understood as specific states in terms of their actual meaning. Furthermore, these constitute their common characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), such as impermanence and so forth.
They are called "marks" (*liṅga*) because they mark or make known. These are its aspects (*ākāra*), since many [aspects] are found even for a single meaning.
Therefore it was said: "Of the meaning which has a hundred marks, which bears a hundred characteristics. Thus the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said:
"All phenomena in all their modes come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One."

"One who sees but a single part is dull-witted": thus, regarding a matter that possesses many characteristics and many marks, one who sees only a single part—due to a lack of broad wisdom—sees merely a single characteristic and a single mark;
having become dogmatically attached (*abhinivissa*) to what he himself has seen, thinking "this alone is the truth," he rejects the other as "vain," like a blind man who has been shown an elephant.
The dull-witted one of poor wisdom is a "grasper of a single aspect" because he fails to understand the various specific modes existing therein and because he adheres erroneously to them.
The wise man, however, is a "seer of a hundredfold," for with the eye of his own wisdom he perceives all the many modes existing therein in their entirety;
or rather, he perceives with the eye of wisdom the many modes obtainable therein.
"He sees for himself, he shows it to others, and he proclaims it; he is indeed wise, discerning, and skilled in matters of meaning.
In this way, the Elder revealed to the monks the excellence of his own attainment of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Suhemanta is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhammasava "Having weighed [the matter], I went forth"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dhammasava. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a brahmin named Suvaccha, who had mastered the three Vedas.
Having seen the faults of household life, he went forth as an ascetic;
having established a hermitage in a mountain retreat within a forest region, he dwelt there together with many ascetics.

Then the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring to plant the seed of merit within him, stood in the sky near the hermitage and displayed a miracle of supernormal power. Upon seeing this, his mind became filled with serene faith.
Desiring to make an offering, he had *nāgapuṣpa* flowers gathered. The Teacher, thinking, "This is sufficient for this ascetic as a seed of merit," departed.
Taking the flowers, he scattered them along the path by which the Teacher was going and stood with palms joined in reverence, his heart full of faith.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and thereafter he continued to be reborn only in the happy realms.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha.

Having attained the name Dhammasava and reached the age of discretion, urged on by the perfection of his causal conditions, he perceived the danger in the household life and the benefits of going forth.
He approached the Blessed One, who was dwelling at Dakkhiṇāgiri, and having heard the Dhamma, [he went forth].
Having gained faith, he went forth and, applying himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā), attained arahantship before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The brahmin named Suvaccha, a master of the mantras;”
Honored by his disciples, he dwelt within the mountain range.
The Victor named Padumuttara, the recipient of offerings,
desiring to uplift me, came into my presence.
“He walked back and forth in the air, and likewise emitted smoke and blazed with fire;
having perceived my laughter, he departed facing the east.
Having seen that marvel, that extraordinary and hair-raising sight...”
Having taken a *nāgapuṣpa* flower, I scattered it upon the path he had traveled.
"In a hundred thousand aeons from now, because of that flower which I scattered,
and through that clarity of mind, I did not fall into an evil rebirth."
“Thirty-one hundred eons ago, there was a king named Mahāraha;
he was a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he was filled with joy and uttered this verse by way of an inspired utterance:
“Having weighed [the matter], I went forth from the home to the homeless life;
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

In this context, "I went forth after weighing [the matter]" means that I investigated and examined, by means of wisdom that had reached a state of balance, the danger in household life through such passages as "Household life is cramped, a path of dust," and the danger in sensual pleasures through such passages as "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair," as well as the benefit in renunciation as their opposite.
The rest is exactly as explained below. This very...
And thus there was the Elder’s proclamation of final knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammasava is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammasavapitu.
This is the verse of the Venerable Dhammasavaṇīputta Thera, who lived for one hundred and twenty years. What is its origin?
This [Thera] too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family when the world was empty of Buddhas.
Having reached maturity, he saw a Paccekabuddha dwelling on a mountain named Bhūtagaṇa; with a mind full of faith, he made an offering of grass, spikes, and flowers. He...
By virtue of that meritorious deed, having been reborn in the world of the devas and wandering from one happy destination to another,
he was now reborn in this era of a Buddha’s appearance in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha.
Upon reaching maturity, he took a wife, obtained a son named Dhammasava, and after that son had gone forth into homelessness, he himself reached the age of one hundred and twenty years.
“My son has gone forth while still so young; why then should I not go forth as well?
With this sense of spiritual urgency born within him, he went into the presence of the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gone forth, established insight (vipassanā).
Before long, he realized arhatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himālaya mountains is a mountain named Bhūtagaṇa;
there dwells a single Conqueror, a self-become one who has transcended the world.
Taking a blade of grass, I offered it to the Buddha.”
For ninety-nine thousand aeons, I was not subject to rebirth in the lower realms.
Eleven aeons ago, I was Dharaṇīruha,
a wheel-turning monarch of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s dispensation has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he, filled with joy, uttered this inspired utterance:
“He who was two hundred years old went forth into homelessness;”
“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “he who was one hundred and twenty years old” means he who was one hundred and twenty years of age; that is, I, being one hundred and twenty years from birth.
“I went forth” means I entered the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). The rest is exactly as previously stated. And this [verse] belongs to this elder.
The declaration of final knowledge was made.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammasavaṇīputta is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
"Surely this one is not compassionate for our supreme welfare"—this is a verse of the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita Thera. What is its origin?
He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family ninety-four aeons ago.
Having reached maturity, one day he saw seven Paccekabuddhas dwelling at the foot of a mountain.
Having seen him, with a mind full of faith, he took kadamba flowers and offered them in worship. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas;

and after performing further merits and wandering through successive happy destinies, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born in Sāvatthī into a family of outcasts (ibbha), and his name was Saṅgharakkhita. When he reached the age of discretion—
Having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness, took up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and dwelt in the forest with a certain bhikkhu as his companion.
Not far from the elder’s dwelling place, in a thicket of woods, a doe gave birth;
while protecting her young fawn, she did not go far away for food even though she was famished, out of affection for her offspring. And nearby...
He grew weary from the lack of grass and water. Seeing him, the Elder thought, "Alas! This world, bound by the fetters of craving, experiences great suffering and is unable to sever it.
Stricken with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he took that very [suffering] as his goad, developed insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Not far from the Himālaya is a mountain named Kukkuṭa;
at the foot of that mountain, those seven Buddhas dwell.
Having seen a kadamba tree in full bloom, rising up like the king of lamps,”
Taking them with both hands, I scattered them over seven Buddhas.
"In the ninety-four aeons since I offered that flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“Ninety-two aeons ago, there were beings named Puppha;
they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so forth]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having attained Arahantship and knowing that his own companion bhikkhu was dwelling with an abundance of wrong thoughts, he used that very same doe as a simile and exhorted him:
"Surely this one, who is supremely compassionate for our welfare, does not contemplate the Teaching when retired in solitude;
for thus he dwells with unrestrained faculties, like a young doe in the forest."
He spoke this verse.
In that context, *na* is a particle used for negation in the phrase *na nūnāyanti*. *Nūna* is used in the sense of reflection (*parivitakka*). The word division is *nūna ayanti*.

"Extremely compassionate for the supreme welfare" means one whose nature is to have compassion for sentient beings through what is supreme—that is, exceedingly—or through the supreme, unsurpassed welfare.
Of the Blessed One. "Secluded" (*raho-gata*) means having gone to a private place; the meaning is that he had gone to an empty dwelling and was engaged in physical seclusion.
"Reflects upon" (*anuvigaṇeti*): here, the two words "surely not" (*na nūna*) should be brought in and connected as "surely not reflects upon" (*nānuvigaṇeti nūna*);

the meaning is: "I think he does not contemplate," or "I conjecture he does not apply himself. "The teaching" (*sāsana*) refers to the teaching of practice, namely, the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "For thus" (*tathā hi*) means for that very reason; specifically, because of not applying oneself to the Teacher’s dispensation.

"This one" (*ayaṃ*) refers to this bhikkhu. "With loose faculties" (*pākatindriyo*) means having faculties—namely the six, with the mind as the sixth—that are released toward their respective objects, being possessed of their natural state [of distraction];
the sense is that his eye-door and so forth are unrestrained. Because of the non-severance of that fetter of craving (*taṇhāsaṅga*),...
That bhikkhu dwells with his faculties unguarded; showing a simile for him, [the Blessed One] said:

"As a young doe in the forest. Just as this young doe, because her affection for her fawn is not severed, experiences suffering in the forest and cannot transcend it, even so this bhikkhu, because his attachment is not severed, has his faculties unguarded.

The intention is that while dwelling [in such a state], one does not transcend the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Alternatively, there is the reading “*taruṇavijātikā*,” meaning a young cow with a newborn calf.
Having heard that, the bhikkhu was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); he developed insight (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship*.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Usabha "Mountains well-grown upon the mountain peaks"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Usabha. What was his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds conducive to liberation throughout various existences during previous Buddha-eras, [was reborn] thirty-one aeons ago from now...
During the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn as a son of the gods. One day, upon seeing the Teacher, he made an offering with celestial flowers with a mind full of faith.
That flower-offering remained for seven days in the form of a pavilion of flowers. A great assembly of gods and humans gathered there.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he [was reborn] during this current appearance of a Buddha.
He was reborn in a wealthy clan in the kingdom of Kosala, and his name was Usabha. Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher at the time of the acceptance of the Jeta Grove;
having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, he dwelt in a forest at the foot of a mountain.
At that time, when the clouds of the rainy season had poured down, the mountain peaks were thick with trees, shrubs, creepers, and dense foliage.
Thus it was. Then one day, the Elder emerged from his cave and, beholding the beauty of that forest and the beauty of the mountain, reflected with wise attention:
"Even these trees and other things, though insentient, attain growth through the perfection of the seasons;
why then, having obtained favorable conditions for the seasons, shall I not attain growth in virtues? Thinking thus—
“Mountains well-grown upon mountain peaks, watered by fresh, rising clouds;
they produce even greater strength in the bull who desires solitude and perceives the forest”—
thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, *nāgā* means trees; some say it means "elephants" (*nāgā*), in which case the meaning is "elephant-trees. *Nagaggesu* means on the mountain peaks.
*Susaṃvirūḷhā* means having grown roots well all around, and having properly produced branches, sprouts, and twigs both on the perimeter and above.
*Udaggameghena navena sittā* means sprinkled by a newly arisen, magnificent, and great rain-cloud.
"Rained upon. "Desiring seclusion" means: for one who desires the seclusion of the mind—which is secluded from defilements;

for one who, having already attained physical seclusion through dwelling in the forest, now seeks the seclusion of the mind which serves as the support for attaining seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*);
for one who is devoted to wakefulness—this is the meaning. Therefore he said, "perceiving the forest."
"Dwelling in the forest" is praised and extolled by the Teacher; and that is for the sake of the complete fulfillment of the development of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Therefore, thinking "I must bring this [fulfillment] into my own hands," one who perceives the forest in this way and abounds in the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*)—this is the meaning.
"Produces" means they cause to arise; for while this word is singular, it refers to a plurality. Some, however, read it as "janenti."
*Bhiyyo* means "further and further. *Usabhassa*—he speaks of himself as if he were another.

*Kalyatam* means the state of being fit (*kalya-bhāvam*), the workability (*kammaññatam*) of the mind, its fitness for cultivation (*bhāvanā-yogyatam*). This very meaning has already been explained above.
While the Elder was speaking this verse, he intensified his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“I was a son of the gods, and being such, I worshipped the Leader Sikhī;
with mandārava flowers, I offered them to the Buddha.
For seven days, that divine garland remained as a canopy over the Tathāgata.”
All the people gathered together and paid homage to the Tathāgata:
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered this flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“In this tenth aeon, I was a king named Jutindharo;
endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verses follow] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
And this indeed was the verse of the Elder’s proclamation of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Usabha is finished.
The commentary on the eleventh chapter is finished.
12. The Twelfth Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jenta.
“Difficult indeed is the going forth, difficult are households to dwell in”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Jenta. What is their origin? This one, too...

Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, he was reborn as a son of the gods during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
One day, upon seeing the Teacher, he made an offering with *kiṅkirāta* flowers with a devout heart.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this [life]...
During the time of a Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn as the son of a local chieftain in the village of Jenta in the kingdom of Magadha;
his name was Jenta. When he reached maturity, even in his youth, being impelled by the perfection of his causal conditions, his mind became inclined toward the renunciate life.
He then reflected: "Renunciation is indeed difficult, and the household life is hard to dwell in."
"The Dhamma is profound, and wealth is difficult to acquire; what indeed should be done? Thinking thus, he wandered about full of reflection.
One day, having gone into the presence of the Teacher, he heard the Dhamma. From the moment he heard it, he became intent on the going-forth;
having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he developed insight (*vipassanā*).
By means of the pleasant practice leading to swift direct knowledge, he realized arhatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“I was a son of the gods, and being virtuous, I worshipped the Leader Sikhin;
having taken a *kakkāru* flower, I offered it to the Buddha.”
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered that flower, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
And in the ninth aeon from now, I was King Sattuttama.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so on] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, however, while reviewing his own practice, he thought: “Truly, I was able from the beginning for me…”
Thinking, "I shall cut off arisen thoughts," he became joyful and, demonstrating both the manner in which thoughts arise and their complete eradication, said:
"Difficult indeed is the going forth, difficult is the life at home; the Dhamma is profound, and wealth is hard to acquire."
"Difficult is our livelihood by means of this or that other [method]; it is fitting to constantly contemplate impermanence"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "difficult to go forth" means having abandoned both a small or great mass of wealth as well as one's circle of kinsmen.
In this teaching, because going forth by giving one’s breast [in sacrifice] is difficult, going forth is painful;
thus it is "difficult to go forth" (*duppabbajja*). *Vā* is a mere particle, or it has the sense of emphasis: "Going forth is painful.
If one were to dwell in a household, households are difficult to dwell in, because for one dwelling in a household, there is the duty of a king for a king, and the duty of a lord for a lord.
A householder must perform the duties of a householder; he must maintain his dependents as well as the ascetics and brahmins.
Even while performing those various tasks that ought to be done, the household life is as difficult to fill as a leaking jar or the great ocean.
Therefore, considering these homes to be painful and difficult to endure, they are said to be "hard to dwell in."

"It is difficult to dwell [in solitude]. If I were to persist in the going-forth, the Dhamma is profound—that true Dhamma of realization for the sake of which one goes forth must be attained by one who has gone forth;
it is profound because it is the domain of profound knowledge, difficult to see, and difficult to penetrate due to the profundity of the Dhamma.
If I were to dwell at home, wealth would be difficult to acquire."
Those possessions without which it is impossible to dwell at home are difficult to acquire because they must be obtained with pain and great effort.

This being so, one might abandon the household life and devote oneself solely to the going-forth; yet even so, our livelihood would be one of hardship rather than ease, for here in this teaching of the Buddha, we would have to subsist on requisites as they are obtained rather than by choice.

"Living is a hardship, a suffering; because household life is difficult to endure and wealth is difficult to acquire, our livelihood must be maintained at home with various means of subsistence—our way of life is indeed arduous and laborious.
What, then, ought we to do in this regard? It is proper to contemplate the entirety of impermanence throughout the whole day, as well as during the first and last watches of the night.

The entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes is impermanent; because it possesses arising and passing away, because it has a beginning and an end, and because it is merely temporary, it is not permanent—it is "impermanent.
It is appropriate to contemplate and to see with insight (vipassanā) in this way.

Since the other contemplations are easily accomplished once the contemplation of impermanence is established, only the contemplation of impermanence is mentioned here; for within the impermanent, there is suffering and non-self.
Because it is non-deviant and because it is easy for one following the Teaching to grasp; therefore he said: "What is impermanent, that is suffering;
what is suffering, that is non-self," and "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation," and "Formations are subject to vanishing.
Thus, by way of mutual opposition, these arise one after another.
This shows that after restraining discursive thought (*vitakka*) and commencing insight (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence (*aniccatā*), he has now become one who has accomplished his task.
Therefore it was said: "His own practice," and so forth. This itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jenta is finished.
2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vacchagotta "I am a possessor of the three knowledges, a great meditator"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vacchagotta. What is its origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was planting the seeds of wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various states of existence. Under Vipassi [Buddha]...

Having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, he one day performed an offering to the Buddha together with the king and the citizens.

Thereafter, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn at the time of this current Buddha’s appearance in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin; because of his lineage, he was known as Vacchagotta.
His name was Vacchagotta. Having reached maturity, he attained perfection in the brahminical sciences;
yet, seeking liberation and seeing no essence therein, he went forth as a wandering ascetic.
While wandering about, he approached the Teacher, asked a question, and when it was answered, with a mind full of faith, he remained in the presence of the Teacher.
Having gone forth, while practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he became a possessor of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Like the rising sun, like the sun with its golden rays, like the moon on the fifteenth day—thus I saw the Leader of the World departing.”
“Sixty-eight thousand [monks], all of them with taints destroyed,
surrounded the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men.
Having swept that street, as the Leader of the World was departing— ”
There, with a serene mind, I raised up a banner.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because I offered that banner, I have not known a bad rebirth;
this is the fruit of the gift of the banner."
“In this fourth aeon, I was a king of great power, endowed with every excellence, renowned as Sudhaja.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges and having reflected upon his own practice, he was filled with joy and uttered this verse as an inspired utterance:
“I am a possessor of the threefold knowledge, a great meditator, skilled in mental tranquility;
my own goal has been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

In this context, regarding the phrase "those who possess the threefold knowledge": although they previously perceived me as a "brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge" because I had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, that was merely a conventional designation, since the function of true knowledge (*vijjā*) is absent in those [Vedic] texts.

But now, because I have attained the three types of knowledge consisting of the knowledge of past lives and so forth, I am a "possessor of the threefold knowledge" in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), [having realized] the great and complete...

He is a "great meditator" (*mahājhāyī*) because he burns away the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination, and because he meditates upon the great, sublime, and excellent Nibbāna by means of the great path, fruit, and jhānas.

He is "skilled in mental tranquility" (*cetosamathakovida*) because he is adept at concentrating the mind through the subsiding of those defiled states that cause agitation of the mind. By this, he states the cause for his possession of the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*).

Indeed, the state of possessing the three knowledges (*tevijjatā*) is due to the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) accompanied by skill in concentration, not by it alone. "One's own goal" (*sadattha*) means one's own purpose;
here, the letter *ka* has been changed to *da*, as in such expressions as "one who has attained his own goal" (*anuppatta-sadattha*).

Furthermore, "one's own goal" should be understood as Arahatship; for that is, in the sense of being bound to oneself, in the sense of not abandoning oneself, and in the sense of being the ultimate aim of oneself.
Because it is one's own welfare, it is called "one's own purpose" (*sakattha*). This very purpose of my own has been reached and attained by me.
By this, he shows that he has brought the aforementioned state of being a great meditator to its ultimate perfection. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Vacchagotta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vanavaccha.
"Acchodikā puthusilā" (The clear-watered, broad-stoned [lake]) is the verse of the venerable Elder Vanavaccha. What is its origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was planting the seeds of wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence. Under Vipassi...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached maturity and lived by performing work for others.
Having committed an offense against someone, he was threatened by the fear of death; while fleeing, he saw a Bodhi tree along the way.
With a mind full of serene faith, he swept the base of that tree, made an offering with *piṇḍibandha* *asoka* flowers, and having paid homage, stood facing the Bodhi tree.
While paying homage and sitting cross-legged, seeing his adversaries who had come to kill him, he did not let his mind become agitated toward them;
instead, focusing his attention solely on the Bodhi tree, he leapt into a precipice a hundred fathoms deep.

By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and after performing further acts of merit and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, during this present dispensation of a Buddha, he was born into a family of great wealth in Rājagaha.
He was reborn as the son of a brahmin, and his name was Vaccha.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained faith upon meeting Bimbisāra, went forth into homelessness, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Engaged in the service of others, I committed an offense;”
Driven by fear and enmity, I ran toward the edge of the forest.
Seeing a flowering tree with well-formed clusters of blossoms,
I took a copper-colored flower and scattered it over the Bodhi tree.
“Having swept that Bodhi tree, the supreme *pāṭali* among trees,
I sat down at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having folded my legs in the cross-legged posture.
Those who were searching for the path I had taken came into my presence.”
Having seen them there, I directed my attention toward the supreme Bodhi tree.
Having paid homage to the Bodhi tree with a mind full of serene confidence,
I leaped across many palm trees in that terrifying mountain pass.
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I offered that flower, I did not experience a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Bodhi tree.
And in the third eon before this, I was King Susaññata.”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [and so forth] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he dwelt only in the forest out of delight in seclusion; therefore, the designation ‘Forest-Fosterling’ (Vanavaccha) arose for him.”
Then, on one occasion, the Elder went to Rājagaha for the sake of favoring his kinsmen.

While staying there for a few days, being attended upon by his relatives, he indicated his intention to depart. His kinsmen entreated him, saying, "Venerable sir, please stay at our own monastery out of favor to us;
we shall attend upon you. The Elder, under the pretext of describing the delightful beauty of that mountain retreat, said:
Declaring his delight in seclusion,
he spoke this verse: “With clear waters, many rocks, frequented by cattle, monkeys, and deer, and covered with water-moss— those mountains bring me joy.”
In this context, "clear-watered" (*acchodikā*) means that because the water in these [pools] is clear, not turbid, and subtle, it should have been called "clear-water" (*acchodaka*);
however, by a change of gender, it is stated as "clear-watered" (*acchodikā*). By this, he shows their excellence regarding water.

"Broad-stone" (*puthusilā*) means that because there are broad, extensive, soft, and pleasant-to-the-touch stones in these [pools], they are "broad-stone. By this, he shows the excellence of the places for sitting.
It shows [this]. Those that have "tails" (*naṅgula*) like those of oxen are *gonaṅgulā*; they are black monkeys, though some indeed call them "ordinary monkeys.
Because it is filled—that is, mixed—with *gonaṅgula* monkeys and deer such as the *pasada*, wandering here and there, it is called *gonaṅgulamigāyuta*.
By this, its possession of the characteristics of a forest is shown through its being a haunt of non-human beings (*amanussa*).
[The Blessed One] shows this. "Covered with water-moss" means that because of constant oozing from their springs, they are covered here and there with *udaka-sevāla* (aquatic moss).
"Those rocks delight me" means: those such rocks and mountains where I dwell delight me in my fondness for seclusion;
therefore, the intention is that I shall go right there. And this very...
The Elder’s declaration of final knowledge was accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vanavaccha is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Adhimutta.
"Veneration for bodily integrity": this is the verse of the Venerable Adhimutta Thera. What is its origin?
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family;
having reached maturity and attained proficiency in the brahminical sciences, he saw the peril in sensual pleasures, abandoned the household life, and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic.
Having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, he approached the human realm;
seeing the Teacher proceeding surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with a mind full of faith, he spread his own bark garment at the feet of the Teacher.
The Teacher, knowing his intention, stood upon it. Having honored the Blessed One, who was standing there, with the fragrance of black aloe-wood, [he said]: "Lift me up..."

He praised him with ten verses beginning with "The world... The Teacher, having prophesied, "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, after going forth in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, he will become one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges," departed.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and from then until the present arising of this Buddha—
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī.
Having attained the name Adhimutta and reached the age of discretion, he achieved mastery in the brahminical sciences;
yet, seeing no essence therein, and because it was his final existence, he sought liberation. He witnessed the power of the Buddha during the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery.
Having seen [this], he gained faith and went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Having established insight (*vipassanā*), before long he attained *arahantship*.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Like a *kaṇikāra* tree in full bloom, like a lamp-tree blazing bright;”
Shining like a medicinal herb, or like lightning in the sky;
fearless and undaunted, like the maned king of beasts;
illuminating the light of knowledge, he crushes the hosts of the sectarians.
“I saw the Leader of the World, lifting up this world, cutting through all doubts, roaring like the king of beasts.
I was one wearing matted hair and deerskin, tall, upright, and majestic.”
Having taken a bark garment, I spread it at the soles of his feet.
Having taken black aloe-wood, I anointed the Tathāgata;
having anointed the Perfectly Enlightened One, I praised the Leader of the World.
“O Great Sage who has crossed the flood, you have rescued this world;
with the light of knowledge, you illuminate the supreme wisdom that was not previously known.
You set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion and trample down the followers of other sects.”
The Bull, victor in battle, has caused this earth to tremble.
Just as waves in the great ocean break upon the shore,
even so do all views shatter within your wisdom.
"Just as when birds have flown into a fine-meshed net,
those creatures caught within the net are immediately oppressed;
even so are the sectarians in the world who rely on various heretical doctrines."
O Noble One, within your supreme knowledge, O Blessed One, all things revolve.
You are the firm foundation for those swept away by the flood;
you are indeed the protector of the friendless, the refuge for those trembling in fear, and the ultimate resort for those seeking liberation.
“A solitary hero without equal, an accumulation of loving-kindness and compassion;
peerless, perfectly equanimous, and peaceful, a master, such a one who has conquered what was to be conquered.
Wise, free from delusion, unmoving, and beyond doubt.”
"You are contented, having cast off the tusita-pleasures; stainless, self-restrained, and pure.
You have transcended attachments, destroyed pride, and attained the threefold knowledge; you have gone beyond the three realms of existence.
You have passed beyond all boundaries, are reverent for the Dhamma, have reached your goal, and are a marvelous source of welfare."
“You are a savior like a boat, a provider of treasure for those who seek it;
