you are as fearless as a lion, and as majestic as a lordly elephant.
Having praised the one of great renown, Padumuttara, with these ten verses,”
Having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, I then stood silent. Padumuttara,
the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings,
the Teacher standing amidst the community of bhikkhus, spoke these verses:
“He who praised my virtue, my knowledge, and the true Dhamma—him I shall extol; listen as I speak.
For sixty thousand eons, he will delight in the world of the gods.”
Having overcome other gods, he will exercise lordship.
Later, having gone forth and being urged on by the root of his wholesome merit,
he will go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Gotama.
“Having gone forth, having avoided evil deeds with the body,
and having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Just as a thundering cloud satisfies this earth with its moisture,”
In that very same way, O Great Hero, you have satisfied me with the Dhamma.
Having praised the Leader of the World for his virtue, wisdom, and Dhamma,
I have attained supreme peace— Nirvana, the deathless state.
“Oh, may that Blessed One, the Visionary, indeed remain for a long time!
May they come to know what is yet unknown, and may they touch the deathless state.
This is my final birth; all states of existence have been utterly eradicated.”
Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
Because I praised the Buddha a hundred thousand aeons ago, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that eulogy.
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, while exhorting the monks who lived with him and were burdened with physical sluggishness, he said:
“For those heavy with bodily slothfulness, while life is wasting away...”
“For one greedy for bodily pleasure, how can there be the excellence of a recluse?”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “one who prizes bodily coarseness”: *duṭṭhulla* means unfitness for the beautiful; the coarseness of the body is *kāyaduṭṭhulla*;
one for whom that bodily coarseness is held dear and esteemed is “one who prizes bodily coarseness,” being one whose wisdom lacks the means of escape.
"Devoted to nourishing the body" means being full of physical heaviness; [the text says] "for one heavy with bodily coarseness.
"While life is wasting away" means while the formations of life are quickly diminishing, like the water in small streams.

"Greedily attached to bodily comfort" means having fallen into a craving for the ease of one's own body through choice foods and the like. "Whence can there be goodness in a recluse?"—for one of such a kind...
From what cause and by what means could there be goodness or the state of being a true ascetic for a person?
The intended meaning is that the goodness of an ascetic belongs only to one who is entirely indifferent toward both body and life, who is content with whatever may come, and who has aroused energy.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Adhimutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahānāma:
"This one is indeed honored as if by a mountain. These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Mahānāma. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.

Having been reborn and attained proficiency in the brahminical sciences, he abandoned the life of a householder and, having established a hermitage on the bank of a certain river, lived there teaching the mantras to many brahmins.
Then one day, the Blessed One approached that hermitage in order to favor him. Upon seeing the Blessed One, his heart was filled with faith, and [he offered] a seat...
Having prepared it, he gave it to him. When the Blessed One was seated, he offered him very sweet honey.
After the Blessed One had consumed it, he departed, having prophesied the future in the same manner as was related below in the account of the Elder Adhimutta.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods and, wandering from one happy destination to another, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
Having been reborn in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī and having attained the name Mahānāma, he reached the age of discretion and approached the Blessed One.
Having heard the Dhamma, he acquired faith, went forth, and took up a meditation subject.
While dwelling on the mountain named Nesādaka, being unable to suppress the obsession of the defilements, he thought: "What..."

“Of what use is this life of mine with such a defiled mind? Thus, feeling revulsion for his own existence, he climbed to the high peak of a mountain and, identifying himself as if he were another, said:
“Here you shall fall from the mountain, covered with many thickets and porcupine quills!”
“By the mountain Nesāda, the illustrious Paricchada,” he spoke this verse.
Therein, “this one is being left behind” means: O Mahānāma, you are being left behind; you are falling away.
“By the mountain” means by this mountain which serves as his dwelling place. “Abounding in *kuṭaja* trees, *indasāla* trees, and *sallakī* plants” [is the description of that mountain].
"Endowed with *indasāla* trees. "By one named Nesādaka. "A mountain (*giri*)" means a rocky peak (*sela*).

For it is called a "mountain" (*pabbata*) because it stands with joints known as ridges; and it is called a "mountain" (*giri*) because it swallows (*giraṇa*) water by way of flowing forth and so on, and because it swallows (*giraṇa*) substances such as medicinal herbs that constitute its essence.
Since both meanings are possible here, [it is referred to as "mountain"].
Having said "by a mountain," it is further stated as "by a hill. "Yasassinā" means renowned and celebrated for all its virtues.
"Paricchadena" means surrounded on all sides by various kinds of trees, shrubs, and creepers; or, because it serves as a dwelling place, it is "that which constitutes a covering for you.
This is the intended meaning here: O Mahānāma, if [you] were to abandon the meditation subject...
"You are full of discursive thoughts; thus, by this Nesādaka mountain—which is endowed with shade and water, favorable, and serves as a dwelling place—you are wasting away.
Now, having cast you down from here, I shall kill you. Therefore, it is not possible for you to remain under the sway of discursive thoughts.
Thus, while reproaching himself, the Elder intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship.
He attained [it]. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the river Sindhū, my hermitage was well-prepared;
there I taught my students the Itihāsa together with its characteristics.”
“Those who love the Dhamma, disciplined, and desirous of hearing the excellent teaching,
who have reached perfection in the six factors— they dwell on the banks of the Sindhu.
Skilled indeed in the movements of portents and in the marks [of excellence],”
“Seeking the supreme goal, they were dwelling in the forest at that time.
Then a Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha appeared in the world;
out of compassion for us, the Guide approached.”
“Having prepared a grass mat for the Great Hero, the Wise One, the Leader of the World, who had arrived, I gave it to the Eldest in the World.
Taking honey from the forest, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas.”
Having partaken [of it], the Fully Awakened One spoke these words:
“I shall praise him who gave me that honey with his own hands, full of faith; listen as I speak.
“By this gift of honey and by the straw mat,
he shall rejoice in the world of the gods for thirty thousand eons.
After those thirty thousand eons, born into the Okkāka clan...”
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His heir in the Dhammas, his own legitimate son, fashioned from the Dhamma,
having fully understood all taints, will attain Nibbāna, free from taints."
“Having come here from the world of the gods, when he had entered his mother’s womb,
he rained down a shower of honey, covering the earth with honey.
As soon as he had issued forth from her womb, the ocean, so difficult to cross, [receded].”
Even there, honey-rain falls for me, raining at all times.
Having gone forth from the home into homelessness,
I am a recipient of food, drink, and gifts of honey— this is the fruit of that.
“Having become one who has all desires fulfilled among gods and humans,
it was by that very gift of honey that I attained the destruction of the taints.
When the rain had fallen and the grass was four inches high, when the earth was covered with flowering trees;”
In an empty house, under a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, I dwell always happy and free from taints.
Having transcended all existence—both the great and the low—I have today exhausted my taints; there is now no further becoming.
“In the thirty thousand aeons past, whatever gift I gave at that time, I have never known a bad rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving honey.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as follows] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
And this indeed was the Elder’s verse of declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahānāma is concluded.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya.
"Having abandoned the six bases of contact"—this is the verse of the Venerable Pārāpariya Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in the womb of a *nesāda* (hunter) during the time of the Blessed One Piyaḍassī.
When that Blessed One had attained full maturity, while wandering in a certain forest grove at the place where he used to roam, Piyaḍassī...
The Blessed One, desiring to favor him, entered the attainment of cessation and sat down. Seeking deer, the man arrived at that place;
seeing the Teacher, his heart was filled with serene faith. Making the Blessed One the center, he constructed a bower of branches and covered it in the shape of a gabled house with lotus flowers.
Experiencing sublime joy and gladness, he remained there for seven days.
He stood there paying homage. Day after day, he removed the withered flowers and covered [the shrine] with fresh ones.
At the end of seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and called to mind the community of monks.
Immediately, about eighty thousand monks surrounded the Teacher, thinking, "We shall hear the sweet discourse on the Dhamma."

The deities assembled, and there was a great gathering. The Teacher, offering words of appreciation, prophesied his future prosperity among gods and humans, as well as his attainment of the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi) during this current appearance of a Buddha, and then departed.
Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Rājagaha.
Having reached maturity and become a master of the three Vedas, he received the title Pārāpariya on account of his lineage on both sides.
While teaching many brahmins the mantras, he witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural power during the Teacher’s journey to Rājagaha; having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness.
Performing the work of insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Piyadassī, the self-become leader of the world;
the perfectly enlightened one, desiring solitude, a sage skilled in concentration.
Having entered the forest grove, the great sage Piyadassī—”
Having spread out a rag-robe, the Supreme Person sat down.
“In the past, I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
seeking the pasada deer, I used to roam about at that time.”
“There I beheld the Fully Enlightened One, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints;
like a blossoming king of sāl trees, or like the risen sun with its thousand rays.
Having seen the God of Gods, the one of lovely appearance and great glory,”
Having gathered from Lake Jātassara, I then brought a lotus.
Having brought that beautiful hundred-petaled lotus and having fashioned it into a gabled chamber, I covered [the Buddha] with that lotus.
“Compassionate, merciful, lovely to behold, the Great Sage;
for seven days and nights the Buddha, the Conqueror, dwelt in the gabled chamber.
Having discarded the old, I covered it with new.”
Having raised my hands in reverential salutation (*añjali*), I stood there for some time.
Having emerged from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Great Sage Piyadassī,
the Leader of the World, sat down while surveying the directions.
“At that time, there was an attendant named Sudassana, possessed of great psychic power.
Having understood the mind of the Buddha, the Teacher Piyadassī,
he was surrounded by eighty thousand bhikkhus.”
He approached the Leader of the World as he sat happily at the edge of the forest.
"All the deities dwelling within the grove,
having understood the Buddha's mind, then gathered together."
“When the yakkhas had assembled, along with the kumbhaṇḍas and rakkhasas,
and the community of bhikkhus had arrived, the Jina uttered these verses:
‘He honored me for seven days and built a dwelling for me.’”
I shall praise it; listen as I speak.
"Extremely difficult to see, most subtle, profound, and well-expounded—I shall praise it with wisdom; listen as I speak."
“For fourteen eons he shall exercise divine sovereignty;
a great gabled hall, covered with lotus flowers,
he shall maintain suspended in the sky— this is the fruit of his work of offering flowers.”
For four hundred and twenty-four eons, he will wander through the cycle of existence.
There, he will maintain a celestial mansion made of flowers in the sky,
just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
“Just so, in his knowledge, the defilements do not adhere;
having turned away from the five hindrances with his mind,
he will generate a mind set on renunciation and go forth from the home.”
Then he will emerge carrying a palace made of flowers.
"For one who dwells at the foot of a tree, being vigilant and mindful,
there a palace made of flowers shall be borne above his head."
“Having given robes, almsfood, requisites,
and lodgings to the Saṅgha of monks, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Having lived in a gabled house, I went forth into homelessness.”
Even while dwelling at the foot of a tree, a gabled mansion is provided for me.
"I have no intention regarding robes or almsfood;
endowed with meritorious deeds, I receive what is already prepared."
“Counted by number, many millions of eons— incalculable— have passed for me,
empty of those who were liberated, the Leaders of the World.
In the eighteenth century of eons, Piyadassī was the Guide.”
Having attended upon him, I have come to this womb.
Here I see the Sambuddha, the one named Anoma, the possessor of vision;
having approached him, I went forth into the homeless life.
“The Buddha, the Conqueror, who brings an end to suffering, has shown me the path;
having heard his Dhamma, I have attained the unshakable state.
Having satisfied the Fully Awakened One, Gotama, the bull among the Sakyans,”
“Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
Because I worshipped the Buddha during eighteen hundred eons, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he became filled with joy and, as an inspired utterance, said:
“Having abandoned the six bases of contact, guarding the doors, and well-restrained;”
"Having vomited up the root of evil, I have attained the destruction of the taints"—thus he spoke this verse.

Therein, "having abandoned the six bases of contact" (*chaphassāyatana*) refers to the six internal sense-bases, such as the eye and so forth, which have received the name "bases of contact" because they are the locations for the arising of the six types of contact, beginning with visual contact; [this is said] by way of abandoning the defilements bound up with them.

"Having abandoned. "With guarded doors, well-restrained": because the doors of the eye and so forth are thus guarded, and because they are well-shuttered by the door-bolt of mindfulness through preventing the entry of evil states such as covetousness that arise therein, he is "one with guarded doors, well-restrained.
Alternatively, he is "one with guarded doors" because the six doors, including the mind, have been protected in the manner described.
The meaning here should be understood as follows: "well-restrained" (*susaṃvuta*) means being thoroughly restrained by means of the body and so forth.

"Having vomited up the root of misery" (*aghamūlaṃ vamitvāna*) means having ejected, that is, cast out from one's continuum, by means of the medicinal potion of the application of the Noble Path, the fault known as ignorance and craving—which constitutes the root of misery, namely the suffering of the round of existence—or indeed all the faults of the defilements; and for the sake of having cast them out.

"Or: 'I have attained the destruction of the taints' (*āsavakkhaya*)—the taints such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth are destroyed herein, or it is to be attained through their destruction;

thus, 'the destruction of the taints' refers to Nibbāna and Arahantship. Having attained and realized that destruction of the taints, he declared his full knowledge (*aññā*) by way of a spontaneous utterance (*udāna*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pārāpariya is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Yasa "Well-anointed, well-dressed"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Yasa. What is its origin?

This [Elder] as well had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; accumulating in various births the merits that serve as the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), under Sumedha...
In the time of the Blessed One, having been a Naga king of great power, he led the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha to his own abode and offered a great almsgiving.

He clothed the Blessed One in a most costly set of three robes (ticīvara), and he clothed each individual bhikkhu in a pair of costly separate garments and with all the requisites for a recluse. He...

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born as the son of a merchant and honored the Great Seat of Enlightenment with the seven kinds of jewels. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth into homelessness under his teaching and practiced the duties of a recluse.
Thus wandering only among happy destinies, during the time of our own Blessed One—
He was reborn in Benares as the son of a very wealthy merchant, named Yasa by name, who was exceedingly delicate.
"He had three palaces"—all this is to be understood according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka.
Urged on by his past causes, he observed the disorder of his attendants while they were overcome by sleep during the night-watch.
Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, as if wearing golden sandals, he departed from his home;
having emerged through a city gate opened by a deity, he went to the vicinity of Isipatana and cried out, "Alas, it is afflicted! Alas, it is overwhelmed!
At that time, the Blessed One, while dwelling at Isipatana, was walking back and forth in the open air for the sake of favoring him, and said, "Come, friend."
When he was told, "Yasa, this is untroubled; this is unafflicted," he became joyful, thinking, "So there is indeed that which is untroubled and unafflicted.
Taking off his golden sandals, he approached the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
After the Teacher had delivered a progressive discourse and given a teaching on the Truths, at the conclusion of the Truths, Yasa became a stream-enterer.
When his father, who had come seeking him, was being taught the Truth by the Blessed One, he realized Arhatship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having plunged into the great ocean, my abode was well-constructed;”
A lotus pond created by the gods, resounding with the cries of ruddy geese;
covered with mandārava flowers and with pink and blue lotuses;
and there a river flows, with beautiful landing places and enchanting to the mind.
“Covered with fish and turtles, teeming with various birds;
resounding with the cries of peacocks and herons, and the sweet songs of cuckoos and other warblers.
Pigeons, ravens, swans, and ruddy geese frequenting the rivers;”
There were dindibha birds and sālika birds, pammas and jīvajīvaka birds.
Swans and krauñca cranes cried out, and there were many kosiya and piṅgala birds.
It was endowed with the seven treasures, and its sands consisted of jewels and pearls.
“The trees are made entirely of gold, wafting various fragrances;
they illuminate the palace day and night at all times.
Sixty thousand musical instruments resound morning and evening.”
Sixteen thousand nymphs always attend upon me.
Having gone forth from my celestial abode, with a clear heart and joyful mind, I paid homage to Sumedha, the Leader of the World, who possesses great glory.
“Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, I invited him along with the Saṅgha;
that wise one, the Leader of the World, Sumedha, accepted my invitation.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to me, the Great Sage dismissed me.”
Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, I returned to my own abode.
I addressed my attendants: "All of you, assemble!
At the time of forenoon, the Buddha will come to my abode."
“It is a gain for us, it is well-acquired by us, that we dwell in your presence;
we too shall perform an offering for the Teacher, the Supreme Buddha.
Having prepared food and drink, I announced the time.
Accompanied by one hundred thousand seers, the Leader of the World approached.
I went out to meet him with music consisting of five types of instruments;
that Supreme among Men sat down upon a throne made entirely of gold.
“At that time, there was a canopy made entirely of gold;
fans were fanning within the community of monks.
With abundant food and drink, I satisfied the community of monks.”
I gave a pair of fine robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Seated within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he who is called Sumedha— the recipient of the world’s offerings— spoke these verses.
“I shall proclaim his praise—he who satisfied all these people with food and drink; listen as I speak.
For eighteen hundred eons, he will delight in the world of the gods.”
A thousand times he will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch.
Whatever womb he enters— whether that of a deity or a human—
he will always wear a covering made entirely of gold.
“In thirty thousand aeons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world.
His heir in the Dhammas, his own legitimate son, fashioned from the Dhamma— ”
Having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Sitting amidst the community of bhikkhus, he will roar the lion’s roar:
"They hold a parasol over the funeral pyre; you shall be consumed beneath that parasol."
“I have attained the state of a recluse; my defilements have been incinerated by me.
Whether in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree, no distress exists for me.
That gift which I gave back then, thirty thousand aeons ago—”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of all my giving.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then the Blessed One, stretching out his right arm to the venerable Yasa, said, “Come, monk. Immediately upon these words,
With hair and beard only two finger-breadths long and wearing the eight requisites, he appeared like an elder of sixty years.
Reflecting upon his own practice and uttering a spontaneous exclamation (*udāna*) based on his former state, from the time he attained the status of an "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*), he said:
"Splendidly anointed, splendidly dressed, adorned with all ornaments;..."
"I have attained the threefold knowledge; the Buddha’s teaching is accomplished"—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, "well-anointed" means having his body anointed with the beautiful ointment of saffron and sandalwood. "Well-dressed" means well-clad in garments of highly valuable Kāsī cloth.
"Adorned with all ornaments" means [adorned] with all ornaments, beginning with those for the head.
"Adorned. "I attained" means I reached. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Yasa is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kimila.
"Only the Bodhisatta falls [from heaven]"—this is the verse of the Venerable Kimila Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha.
Having reached the age of discretion, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he offered *saḷala* garlands in honor of the Teacher’s relics.
He performed an offering by means of a pavilion. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;

passing from there to there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance in the city of Kapilavatthu within the royal Sākiya clan, and his name was Kimila.
When he reached maturity, he lived endowed with an abundance of wealth. As for him, the ripening of his knowledge—

Having seen this, while staying at Anupiya for the purpose of inspiring a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), the Teacher manifested a beautiful woman’s form standing in the prime of youth and showed her before him;
then, he caused her to appear successively as if overcome by old age, disease, and misfortune. Seeing her, Prince Kimila, manifesting an extreme sense of spiritual urgency, said:
“Age falls upon even a Bodhisatta; form remains just as it was, yet appearing as if different.
Though he himself is present and has not departed, I remember him as if he were another,” thus he spoke this verse.
In this context, *abhisatto* means as if instructed or commanded by the devas, saying, "Go quickly, do not stay!
There is also a reading *abhisaṭṭho*, which means as if urged on by someone saying, "Go swiftly!
*Nipatati* means he rushes forward, runs toward [it], and does not stop; the meaning is that moment by moment he reaches destruction and passing away.
“Vaya” refers to a particular stage of the body, such as childhood, youth, and so forth. Here, however, it is youth that is intended;
for that [youth] appears to him as something rushing away and wasting away. “Rūpa” means the perfection of form;
he says this, but “rūpa” here refers to the body, which is “space enclosed by bone, sinew, and flesh.”
[This is] as in such passages as, "It is simply form that comes to be reckoned [as such]. Regarding the phrase "existing just like something else":
the intention is that this form, being of such a nature, exists and is present in that very same way, yet it appears to me as if it were something other.
Some read it as "tadeva santaṃ" (existing as that very thing). "Tasseva sato" means while that very thing is existing for me, being identical and not otherwise.

"Avippavasato" means for one who does not live apart; for when one has lived away for a long time, even that which is not other appears as if it were other, thinking "this too is not here"—this is the intended meaning.
"Aññasseva sarāmi attānan" means: "I remember my own self as if it were the self of another being";
the sense is that I recall, consider, and perceive it thus. As he attends to its impermanence in this way...
An even stronger sense of spiritual urgency arose within him. Having become filled with that urgency, he approached the Teacher, and after hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith.
Having gone forth and established insight, he attained Arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When Kakusandha had attained Nibbāna, while the brahmin was living the holy life;”
Having taken a *saḷala* flower garland, I had a pavilion constructed.
Having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, I obtained a supreme palace;
I outshine the other gods—this is the fruit of my meritorious deed.
“Whether by day or by night, while walking or standing,
I am covered with *saḷala* flowers— this is the fruit of meritorious karma.
Because I honored the Buddha in this very aeon,”
“I do not recognize a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Having attained arahantship, the elder, explaining his own previous mental application to impermanence, recited that very same verse. Thus, this also became the elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kimila is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjiputta:
"Having approached the thicket at the foot of a tree," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Vajjiputta. What is their origin? He too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
he saw a Paccekabuddha going for alms ninety-four aeons ago and, with a devout mind, gave him plantains.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and through successive acts of merit...
Having performed [meritorious deeds], he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a Licchavi king in Vesālī.
Because he was the son of a Vajji king, his conventional name became "Vajjiputta.
While still young, even at the time of training in elephant-lore and other skills, because he was endowed with the necessary causes, he lived always inclined toward renunciation.
Having gone to the monastery at the time of the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he sat on the edge of the assembly and, having heard the Dhamma, gained faith.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he applied himself to insight meditation and before long became a possessor of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One, the thousand-rayed one, the self-become, the unconquered,
having arisen from seclusion, went forth for his almsround.
Seeing him with fruit in hand, I approached that bull among men.”
With a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave a *avaṭa* fruit.
Because I gave that fruit back in the ninety-fourth aeon, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving that fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge, at a later time, not long after the Teacher had passed into final Nibbāna, he made an appointment to recite the Dhamma.
While the Great Elders were dwelling here and there, one day, while the Venerable Ānanda was still merely a trainee (sekha)...
Seeing him surrounded by a great assembly teaching the Dhamma, [the deity] inspired him with the resolve to attain the higher paths, saying:
“Having entered the thicket at the foot of a tree, having set Nibbāna in your heart, meditate, Gotama, and do not be negligent! What will that rattling sound do for you?”
He spoke this verse.

In that context, "the thicket of the foot of a tree" means a thicket that is the root of a tree. For there is a thicket that is not the root of a tree, and there is the root of a tree that is not a thicket;
among these, by the mention of "the root of a tree," [it is indicated] because the location is endowed with shade.

It shows the absence of the perils of wind and heat. By the mention of "thicket," it shows the absence of the peril of wind due to being sheltered from the wind, as well as the absence of crowding by people;
and by both of these, it shows suitability for meditation (*bhāvanā*). "Having approached" (*pasakkiya*) means having gone near.
"Having placed Nibbāna in the heart" (*opiyā*) means [fixing] the state of peace (*nibbuti*) with the thought: "In this way, having practiced, Nibbāna is to be attained by me."
"Having placed [the mind] in the heart and having fixed it in the consciousness. "Meditate" means meditate by means of characteristic-contemplation (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*);
cultivate the cultivation of the Path together with the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā*). "Gotama"—this is how he addresses the Dharma-treasurer by his clan-name.

"And do not be negligent" means do not fall into negligence regarding the higher wholesome states. Now, as for the kind of negligence the Elder might have, [the text follows] by way of its prohibition:
Showing this, he said: “What will your *biḷibiḷikā* do? In this context, *biḷibiḷikā* refers to the act of *viḷiviḷikiyā*;
just as the sound *biḷibiḷī* is a meaningless occurrence, so too is the designation of a person (*janapaññatti*) similar to *biḷibiḷikā*. What will it do for you?
What kind of purpose does it accomplish for you? Therefore, having abandoned the designation of a person, one should be intent upon one’s own true goal.
He gave this exhortation: "It shall be so.

Having heard it, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) at the words spoken by others regarding the smelling of the stench of excrement. Spending most of the night walking back and forth (*caṅkama*), he intensified his insight (*vipassanā*).
Upon entering his lodging and lying down upon his bed, he attained *arahantship* the very moment he reclined.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjiputta is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Isidatta:
"The five aggregates have been fully understood"—this is a verse of the venerable Elder Isidatta. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Blessed One walking along the road, he offered a sweet mango fruit with a devout mind. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Having performed various meritorious deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in the village of Vaḍḍha in the kingdom of Avantī as the son of a certain caravan leader; his name was Isidatta.
Upon reaching maturity, he became an unseen companion to the householder Citta in Macchikāsaṇḍa, and by him [he was introduced to] the qualities of the Buddha.
Having received the message sent by letter, he conceived faith in the Teaching.

Having gone forth in the presence of the Elder Mahākaccāna and begun the practice of insight (vipassanā), before long he became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Golden-Hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings;”
To one traveling on the road, I gave a fruit that brought joy and delight.
“In the ninety-first aeon, because I gave that fruit at that time, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, he thought, “I shall go to attend upon the Buddha.
After taking leave of the Elder, he traveled by stages to the Middle Country, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. [The Teacher asked: “Is it well with you?”
When the Teacher had thus exchanged greetings with him, saying, "Bhikkhu, is it endurable? Is it sustainable?

and so forth, [the bhikkhu] declared his own realization (aññā) by way of replying and announcing: "Venerable Sir, from the time you entered upon your teaching, all my suffering has departed and every danger has been stilled."
“The five aggregates have been fully understood; they stand with their roots cut off.
The destruction of suffering has been reached; the destruction of the taints has been attained by me. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “the five aggregates have been fully understood” means that all five of my aggregates of clinging have been fully understood by means of wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
Through the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*), suffering has been fully delimited and known as "this is suffering; this is the extent of suffering; there is nothing more than this.
The intention is that among those [factors], there is nothing further to be fully understood (*pariññātabba*).
They "stand with their roots cut" because their roots—namely ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), and so forth—have been completely understood, severed, and abandoned by the Noble Path.

They remain until the cessation of the final consciousness. "The destruction of suffering has been attained" means that, precisely because its root has been severed, the exhaustion and complete destruction of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) has been reached, and Nibbāna has been realized.

"I have attained the destruction of the taints" refers to the "destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*) in the sense that it is to be fully realized at the end of the destruction of all taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire.
The meaning is: "arahantship has been attained" (*pattaṃ*) means it has been acquired (*paṭiladdhaṃ*), having received its name.

Some, however, read: "this is my final body" (*antimāyaṃ samussayo*). Because of the very attainment of Nibbāna, this final body (*samussayo*), which is my personal existence (*attabhāvo*), is the last of all;
there is now no further becoming—this is the meaning. As for whatever was not stated here and there, that is self-evident because of the method already explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Isidatta is finished.
The commentary on the Twelfth Chapter is finished.
And thus ends the commentary on the *Theragāthā* within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
The Exegesis of the First Chapter, Adorned with One Hundred and Twenty Verses by Elders.
2. The Second Chapter (Dukanipāta)
1. First Chapter: 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara.
The verses of the Venerable Elder Uttara, beginning with "In the world of existence there is nothing permanent," are found in the Second Book (Dukanipāta). What is their origin?
This person also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences,
became a master of occult sciences (*vidyādhara*) during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha and traveled through the air. At that time, for the sake of favoring him,
the Teacher sat at the foot of a certain tree within a forest, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha.

While scattering them, he was traveling through the air; seeing the Blessed One, his heart filled with serene faith, he descended from the sky and honored the Blessed One with vast, perfectly pure *kaṇikāra* flowers.
By the supernatural power of the Buddha, the flowers remained suspended above the Teacher in the shape of a parasol. With even greater intensity of faith, at a later time...
Having passed away and been reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, he experienced sublime divine prosperity.
Remaining there for the full span of his lifespan, when he passed away from that state, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.

During this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin; his name was Uttara. Upon reaching maturity, he attained perfection in the brahminical sciences.
Having returned, he became highly esteemed by the world for his birth, physical appearance, learning, age, and virtuous conduct.
Seeing his success, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, desiring to give him his own daughter, made his intention known.
Out of a disposition toward renunciation, [the Elder] rejected that proposal, and from time to time [he visited] the Dhammasenāpati.
While attending upon him, he heard the Dhamma in his presence and, having gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
Being perfected in his duties, he attended upon the Elder.
At that time, a certain illness arose in the Elder, and for the sake of medicine for it, the novice Uttara—
Early in the morning, having taken his bowl and robe, he departed from the monastery. On the way, he placed his bowl on the bank of a pond, went near the water, and washed his face.
Then a certain house-thief, pursued by guards, fled out through the main gate of the city; while fleeing, he dropped the bundle of jewels he had carried onto the novice’s bowl.
Having placed it in his bowl, he fled. The novice approached the vicinity of the bowl. King’s men pursuing the thief saw the bundle in the novice’s bowl and, saying, "This is the thief;
the theft was committed by him," they bound the novice with his hands behind his back and presented him to the brahmin Vassakāra. At that time, Vassakāra was appointed to the king’s court of justice.
Having offered the sacrifice, he gave instructions for the execution by cutting and splitting [the victim].
Thinking, "Previously he did not obey my word and went forth among the pure heretics," and being bound by malice, he impaled him alive upon a stake without even purifying his karma.

Then the Blessed One, observing the ripening of his wisdom, went to that place; with the rays of light from the jewels on his outstretched hand-nails piercing through the mass of white clouds, [he appeared].
Placing his hand— whose soft, tender, long fingers were enveloped in flames like a stream of liquid gold and vermilion trickling down—
upon Uttara’s head, he said, “Uttara, this fruit of your past karma has arisen;
you must endure it with the power of reflective contemplation,” and then he taught the Dhamma according to Uttara’s disposition.
Uttara, having attained sublime rapture and gladness through the thrill of joy born from the touch of the Teacher’s hand—
which was like an anointment with the Deathless— ascended the path of insight as he had previously cultivated it;
and because his knowledge had reached maturity and due to the excellence of the Teacher’s teaching, he instantly exhausted all defilements according to the sequence of the paths.
He became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Fully Enlightened One named Sumedha, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks, the Blessed One desiring solitude, went to the Himalayas.”
“Having plunged into the Himalayas, the foremost compassionate Sage,
the supreme among assemblies, sat down after folding his legs crosswise.
At that time, I was a Vidyadhara, a wanderer through the sky.”
Taking up my trident, I then went through the air toward the Sugata.
Like a fire upon a mountain peak, like the moon on the full-moon day,
the Buddha illuminated the forest like a blossoming king of *sāla* trees.
“Having emerged from the forest thicket, I ran toward the Buddha’s rays, which resembled the color of the tips of reeds;
seeing them, my mind was filled with serene confidence.
I saw a flower being gathered, a *kaṇikāra* flower with the fragrance of a deity.”
Taking three flowers, I worshipped the Best of Buddhas.
By the power of the Buddha, those three flowers at that time had their stalks turned upward and their petals downward, casting shade for the Teacher.
“By that well-performed kamma, and through my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned my human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
There, a well-constructed mansion of mine came to be known as ‘Kaṇikāra’.”
Sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width,
with a thousand joints and a hundred segments, adorned with banners and made of gold,
with a hundred thousand spires— it appeared to me in the sky.
“Thrones made of gold, made of gems, and even made of rubies;
and crystal thrones, too, as one desires and as one wishes.
And costly couches, provided with cotton mattresses and various ornaments.”
And [a bed] with hair turned upward on one side, provided with a pillow.
"Having departed from existence, wandering on a journey through the realms of the gods,
may I go wherever I desire, honored by the hosts of deities."
“I stand beneath the flower; it is my canopy above.
For a hundred leagues all around, it is covered with *kaṇikāra* blossoms.
Sixty thousand musical instruments attend me morning and evening.”
“They constantly attend upon me, unwearied by day and night.
There, with dances, songs, cymbals, and instrumental music, I delight in play and pleasure; I rejoice, seeking after my desires.”
“Having eaten and drunk there, I rejoiced then among the Thirty-three gods;
accompanied by throngs of women, I rejoiced in that most excellent palace.
And five hundred times I exercised sovereignty over the devas.”
Three times among the Sata [deities], I was a wheel-turning monarch;
my regional sovereignty was vast and beyond counting.
Wandering from birth to birth, I obtained great wealth in every existence.
"I have no deficiency in enjoyments; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
I transmigrate through two states of existence—among the gods and among humans;
I know no other destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“I am born into two classes: among the Khattiyas and the Brāhmaṇas.
I am never born into a lowly family; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, palanquins, and chariots.”
I obtain all of this; it is the fruit of this worship of the Buddha.
A multitude of female slaves, a multitude of male slaves, and women beautifully adorned—I obtain all of this;
it is the fruit of this worship of the Buddha.
“Silk garments and woolen blankets, as well as linen and cotton cloths—I obtain all of this;
this is the fruit of my worship of the Buddha.
Fresh clothing, fresh fruits, and food of the finest flavors—”
“I obtain all of this; it is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
‘Eat this, consume this, sleep upon this bed;
I obtain all of this; it is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.’”
“I am honored everywhere, my fame has risen high;
I always have a great following and a never-divided assembly;
I am the foremost among my kinsmen—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”
“I know neither cold nor heat; no fever exists within me.
Furthermore, no mental suffering exists in my heart.
Having become golden-hued, I wander through existence after existence.”
"I do not know the cause of this change in my complexion; it is the fruit of this worship of the Buddha.
Having passed away from the world of the gods, impelled by the root of my wholesome merit, I was born in the city of Sāvatthī into a very wealthy family of great sāl-tree merchants."
“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, I went forth into homelessness;
at seven years of age, I attained arahantship.
Recognizing my virtues, the Buddha, the Visionary One, ordained me.”
“I am young and worthy of honor; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
My divine eye is purified, I am skilled in meditative concentration, and I have reached perfection in the higher knowledges; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.”
“Having attained the analytical knowledges, skilled in the bases of psychic power,
and having reached perfection in all phenomena— this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
Because I worshipped the Buddha thirty thousand aeons ago,”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.
Having thus become one possessed of the six higher knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijña*), he rose up from the stake and, standing in the air out of compassion for others, displayed a miracle.
The great multitude was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement. At that very moment, his wound healed completely.
When asked by the bhikkhus, "Friend, while experiencing such suffering, how were you able to apply yourself to insight (vipassanā)?
he replied, "Friends, long ago I had already clearly seen the peril in saṃsāra and the true nature of conditioned phenomena; it was thus that I..."
Showing that even while experiencing such suffering, he was able to increase his insight and attain distinction, he said:
“There is no state of existence that is permanent, nor are conditioned phenomena eternal;
those aggregates arise and pass away again and again.”
“Having understood this danger, I have no desire for existence;
having emerged from all sensual desires, I have attained the destruction of the taints.”—
he spoke these two verses.

In that regard, there is no state whatsoever that is permanent; for existence is divided into such categories as: kamma-existence, rebirth-existence, sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, and five-constituent existence.
Even therein, it is further distinguished as inferior, intermediate, superior, long-lived, abundant in happiness, or mixed with both happiness and suffering.
Thus, there is no such thing whatsoever that is permanent, stable, steadfast, or of an indestructible nature, because it has arisen dependent upon this or that cause.
And since this is so, the construction is: "even conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are not eternal.

For the five aggregates, which have received the name "conditioned phenomena" because they are constructed by conditions, are designated as "existence" (*bhava*) based upon them. These are indeed only conditioned phenomena.
Having arisen from what has been sacrificed [into the fire of conditions], they undergo transformation through aging and death; thus they are impermanent and subject to change.
For this reason, they are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*). Therefore it was said: "Those aggregates arise and pass away one after another.
These five aggregates, spoken of by way of the succession of existence (*bhava*) and the succession of formations (*saṅkhāra*), proceed one after another according to their respective conditions.
They arise; and having arisen, being oppressed by aging, they pass away and break apart—this is the meaning.
By this, he shows that the five aggregates, which receive the conventional designations "existence" (bhava) and "formations" (saṅkhārā), have the nature of arising and passing away.
For when one contemplates formations after applying the three characteristics, even the three types of existence appear as if ablaze, and the danger in what is conditioned becomes apparent.

Having first understood the fault through the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā), the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) seen through the characteristics of impermanence appear even more clearly as suffering and non-self.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: “What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self.
For when one contemplates the conditioned phenomena by applying the three characteristics, the three realms of existence (bhava) appear like a house on fire.
They appear as terrifying; therefore he said, "I am one who has no need for existence.

But for one who has thus completely turned away from all forms of existence, not even a trace of longing for sense pleasures can arise; therefore he said, "I have escaped from all sense pleasures," with "I am" to be supplied.
This means: my mind has turned away from divine sense pleasures just as it has from human ones.

The meaning is as follows: "I have attained the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)"—because I have thus thoroughly polished away my mental formations, clearly seen the danger in states of existence, and my mind is free from attachment to sensual pleasures, therefore even while sitting upon a stake, I have attained the destruction of the taints, which is Nibbāna and Arhatship.
And for others who are fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*) who have not yet attained this state of mind, there is an effort toward its attainment.
"Obligatory duties"—thus he gave this exhortation to the bhikkhus.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttara is concluded.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja.
"‘Not by this way... and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Elder Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja. What is their origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the womb of a lion and lived in a mountain cave.
When the Blessed One, having set out for his almsround, entered the cave where he was lying down to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in order to favor him—"
Having entered [the meditation], he sat down. Sīha, having returned from gathering food, saw the Blessed One at the entrance of his cave;

delighted and joyful, he made an offering of water-born and land-born flowers and, with a serene mind, stood there with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, letting out lion’s roars three times a day to drive away wild beasts from the forest for the sake of the Blessed One’s protection. Just as...
He worshipped him in this manner for the first day, and likewise for seven days.

When the seven days had passed, the Blessed One emerged from cessation (*nirodha*) and, thinking, "Such will be the extent of his supporting condition (*upanissaya*)," he leapt into the air right before the king's very eyes and went back to the monastery.
Unable to endure the suffering of separation from the Buddha—just like the elephant Pālileyyaka—Sīha passed away.
Having been reborn in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī, he reached maturity and went to the monastery together with the city dwellers.
Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he offered a great almsgiving for seven days and performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived.
Wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he became, in the time of our Blessed One, the son of the royal chaplain in Kosambī during the reign of King Udena.

Having offered the sacrifice, he was reborn by the name Bhāradvāja. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and, while teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins, was abandoned by them because his conduct did not accord with their high social status.
He went to Rājagaha, and seeing the gains and honors received by the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he went forth in the Dispensation; however, he was immoderate in food.
Having offered the oblation and wandered about, he was established by the Teacher in moderation through a skillful means;
having then applied insight, before long he became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In former times I was a deer-hunter, wandering then in the forest;”
I saw the stainless Buddha, who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena.
Taking a piyāla fruit, with a heart full of faith, I gave it with my own hands to the Best of Buddhas, the Hero, that field of merit.
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, when I gave that fruit back then, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges, he uttered a lion’s roar before the Blessed One, saying, "I have attained that which is to be attained by disciples," and before the community of monks, saying, "Let whoever has doubt regarding the path or the fruit question me.
Therefore, the Blessed One declared of him: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the monks who utter the lion’s roar."
He placed Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja in the foremost position, saying, "That is to say, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja.
One day, out of compassion for a miserly brāhmaṇa of wrong views who had been his companion in lay life and had approached him, he spoke a discourse on giving.
Although the brāhmaṇa frowned, thinking, "This man wishes to ruin my wealth," [the Buddha said], "Give even a single meal to you..."
When this was said, [the brahmin] redirected it to the Saṅgha, saying, "Give that to the Saṅgha; do not give it to me.

Again, when the brahmin expressed his dissatisfaction, thinking, "This man wishes to have me give to many," on the following day the Dhamma-Senāpati, having inspired confidence in him by explaining the great fruitfulness of offerings made to the Saṅgha, said, "This brahmin..."
"He thinks, 'He is urging me toward giving out of greed for food,' yet he does not know that I have fully understood food in its entirety;
well then, let me make him know.
"This life is not sustained by this [wrong] way; food is not near to the heart."
"The compound body subsists on nutriment"—seeing this, I practice seeking alms.
"For they have known it as a mire: that which is the salutation and worship among families;
honor is a subtle arrow, difficult to extract, hard for a base man to abandon."
He spoke two verses.

Therein, "This life is not by wrong means" means that this life of mine is not sustained by wrong or improper ways, such as the seeking of alms through the giving of bamboo or the giving of flowers, because of the absence of craving for life.
And "Food does not come near the heart" refers to the food being brought [to the body].
The intention is that food does not bring peace to the heart-mind (*hadaya-citta*) like the knowledge of the path and its fruition; rather, it merely provides immediate relief from hunger.

Alternatively, the phrase "food is not near to the heart" means that food—which is the basis for craving for flavors—is not attached as something near to the heart, precisely because of the absence of craving for flavors. It may also be read as "near" (*santike*).
They recite as follows: For one who wanders greedy for food and devoted to gain and honor, that food is said to be "near to the heart" because it must be frequently brought to mind.
But for one who has fully understood food, desire and lust for it have been abandoned;
thus, food is not said to be "near to his heart," because he no longer brings it to mind with thoughts such as, "How might I obtain it? and so forth.
Because of their absence. For if there were no attachment to life and no craving for the taste of food, then why would one go on alms-round?
Reflecting on this inquiry, he said: "Seeing that this body is sustained by nutriment, I wander seeking it.
That which has nutriment as its sustenance, its support, and its condition is "sustained by nutriment" (*āhāraṭṭhitika*). It means: "one whose livelihood is dependent upon nutriment."
"Having seen that 'the body is a heap,' and having understood this matter and established it in my intellect, I wander seeking;
the meaning is that I perform the search for alms.
When approaching families for the sake of requisites, one becomes bound there by salutations, worship, and gains and honors.
Showing that one should not think in such a way regarding those like me, he spoke the verse beginning with “Mud. Its meaning is as follows:

that esteem for and honoring of virtues which will arise among families and householders toward those who have gone forth and approached the conditions [for living]—since that, for those who have not developed themselves, serves as a mire in the sense of causing them to sink and by making them defiled.

The Buddhas and others have known, understood, and proclaimed that "mud" [is the desire for honor]; therefore, it does not lead to the bondage of the virtuous, precisely because they have abandoned it.

For the wicked person, however, the desire for honor is a subtle arrow, difficult to extract, because its nature is hard to discern, because it produces affliction, because it pierces inwardly, and because it is impossible to pull out.
For that very reason, honor is difficult for such a base person to abandon and hard to relinquish, because he does not practice the way of its relinquishment;
it is abandoned only through the abandonment of the hope for honor. Having heard this, the brahmin became deeply devoted to the Elder.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Valliya.
The verses beginning with “A monkey at the five-gated [city]” belong to the Venerable Elder Valliya. What is his origin?
This venerable one also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, [lived] thirty-one aeons ago from now.
Having been reborn in a noble family and reached the age of discretion, he one day went into the forest on some business.
There, seeing the Paccekabuddha named Nārada dwelling at the foot of a tree, his heart was filled with serene faith;
he constructed a hall out of reeds, thatched it with grass, and gave it to him. Furthermore, having cleared a place for walking meditation, he scattered sand over it.
He gave [it]. Circulating among gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the son of a wealthy brahmin; his name was Valliya.
When he had reached maturity and entered the prime of youth, he wandered about under the sway of his senses, but through association with virtuous friends, he [encountered] the Blessed One.
Having approached and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and having established insight, he attained arahantship before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Hārita;”
At that time, the Self-Existent One named Nārada was dwelling at the foot of a tree.
Having constructed a hut of reeds, I covered it with grass;
and having cleared a walking path, I offered it to the Self-Existent One.
“By that well-performed kamma, and through my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. There,
a well-constructed mansion was made for me, fashioned like a reed hut.”
Sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width.
“For fourteen eons I delighted in the world of the gods;
seventy-one times I exercised sovereignty over the devas.”
“Thirty-four times I was a wheel-turning monarch;
my regional sovereignty was vast, beyond all counting.
Having ascended the Palace of Dharma, which is peerless in every excellent aspect...”
“I may dwell as I wish within the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.
Thirty-one eons ago, whatever deed I performed then, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that reed-hut.
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, he declared his realization (*aññā*) by illustrating the difference between the way his mind formerly functioned at will among sense objects such as forms during his time as a worldling, and its state now having been restrained by the Noble Path:
“A monkey, having entered a hut with five doors;”
He went around the door, knocking again and again. [The Teacher] spoke these two verses:
“Stop, monkey! Do not run! For it is no longer as it was before for you.
You are restrained by wisdom; you shall not go far.”
In this context, "shaking" means that, like a monkey seeking fruit, one repeatedly agitates the tree by abandoning one branch and seizing another due to one's own restlessness;
likewise, by abandoning one object such as a visible form and grasping another through various doors such as the eye,
one fails to make the continuum of consciousness steady through the practice of concentration.
By not granting it a place to stay, constantly striking and shaking it, he revolves around that very same object such as a visible form and wanders about at will.
Here, the present tense is used because of its proximity to the ongoing state. And while wandering thus, [the Teacher says]:
"Stop, monkey! Do not run, you mind-monkey! Stop now, do not run; from this moment forth..."
They are unable to run away; therefore, they cannot enter that abode of selfhood as they did before, because its doors have been closed.

Furthermore, you have been restrained by wisdom, and having yourself now severed the "feet"—namely, the defilements and volitional formations—through the wisdom of the Path, you have attained ultimate restraint. Therefore...
“You will not go far from this selfhood”: this shows that you will not go far from this present existence to a second or subsequent existence;
rather, your going shall extend only as far as the final consciousness (*carimakacitta*). There is also a reading, “Not far from here,” which has the same meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Valliya is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gaṅgātīriya The verses beginning with “Three palm leaves for me” are the stanzas of the venerable elder Gaṅgātīriya. What is their origin?
It is said that he was reborn in a family home during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; having reached maturity, he became deeply devoted to the Teaching.
Having offered it, he gave drinking water to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;

and having performed further merits and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha as the son of a certain householder in Sāvatthī, and his name was Datta. When he reached maturity, he entered the life of a householder.
Vasanta, not knowing that it was an improper place, committed an offense;
later, having realized it was an improper place, he became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went forth into homelessness, and, loathing that past deed, practiced an austere way of life.
Taking a rag-robe like a shroud for a corpse and an earthen bowl, he stayed on the bank of the Ganges with three palm leaves.
Having built a hut, he lived there; because of that, he became known by the name Gaṅgātīriya.
Having resolved his mind thus, "I will not converse with anyone until I have attained arahantship," he lived for the first year remaining silent, making no vocal utterance at all.
In the second year, in the village where he went for alms, a certain woman [asked], "Is he mute?"...
When she, wishing to investigate whether [the Buddha] was "no" [present], poured milk into her bowl and made hand-gestures, even though it was sprinkled, the words "Enough, sister!
issued forth. But in the third year, during the very rainy season, while striving and exerting himself, she attained *arahantship*.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“With a clear heart and joyful mind, I filled a water-jar for the peerless Saṅgha of Padumuttara Buddha.
Whether on a mountain peak, on a difficult path, in the sky, or upon the ground;”
Whenever I desire water, it appears for me instantly.
Because I gave that gift of water a hundred thousand eons ago, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving water.
“The defilements have been burnt up by me… [etc. …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having become an Arahant, he then declared his higher knowledge (*aññā*) by way of illustrating his own practice during the prior stage:
“On the bank of the Ganges, with three palm leaves, my hut was built;”
“A bowl as large as a chickpea and a robe made of rags were mine.
During two rainy seasons, I uttered but a single word;
in the third rainy season, the mass of darkness was shattered. Thus he spoke these two verses.

"In that place, with three palm leaves, a hut was built for me on the bank of the Ganges"—meaning that with three palm leaves sent from a palm tree, a small hut was constructed on the bank of the river Ganges for the purpose of protection from the rain. By this, he demonstrates his contentment with his own dwelling.
For it has been said by the General of the Dhamma:
“For one sitting cross-legged, the knees do not get wet by the rain;
this is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
There is also a reading, “tālapattīnaṃ,” which has the same meaning. “My bowl is like a vessel for a corpse” means my bowl is similar to a vessel used for a corpse.
The meaning is that it is like a pit for pouring milk for the deceased. "Rags and robes" means robes made from scraps of cloth discarded on paths between villages, in cemeteries, and so forth;

with these two terms, he demonstrates contentment with requisites. "In the interval between two rains" means during the two years following his going forth, those years in which he had not yet attained *arahantship*.
“One word was spoken by me”: only one word, namely the word rejecting the milk, “Enough, sister,” was uttered by me;
there was no other verbal expression therein. By this, he demonstrates the excellence of restraint in body and speech.
“In the third year” means within the third year, while it was still incomplete. *Tamokhandha*.
"Padālito" means that the mass of darkness has been split asunder by the supreme path; the meaning is that the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) has been utterly eradicated.
By this, he speaks of the abandonment of all defilements without remainder, since they are associated with that [ignorance].
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gaṅgātīriya is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajina The verses beginning with "Even if one is a master of the three Vedas" belong to the venerable Elder Ajina. What is his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family when the world was empty of a Buddha.
Having reached the age of discretion, he went to the forest on some business.
There, seeing the Paccekabuddha named Sucintita sitting afflicted by illness, he approached him, paid homage, and with a devout mind offered clarified butter as medicine.
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods, and having performed further acts of merit in successive lives...
Wandering only through happy realms of existence, he took rebirth in this present age of a Buddha in the house of a certain poor brahmin in Sāvatthī.
At the time of his birth, they received him wrapped in an antelope skin; therefore, they gave him the name Ajina (Antelope Skin).
Because he had not performed deeds leading to wealth, he was born into a poor family, and even upon reaching maturity...
Wandering about with no food or drink, he saw the power of the Buddha at the acceptance of the Jeta Grove.
Having gained faith, he went forth and, applying himself to insight (vipassanā), before long became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"To the Well-Considered One, the Blessed One, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men..."
Seeing the Great King seated there, afflicted by a wind ailment,
I gladdened his mind and offered him clarified butter and cream.
Because of that deed and its accumulation, this river Bhāgīrathī became the Gaṅgā.
“The four great oceans have become a single vessel for me;
and this earth, terrible, immeasurable, and incalculable, has become honey and sugar for me. Knowing my intention, it becomes so.”
These trees, growing from the earth, are found throughout the four continents.
"Knowing my intention, they become wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*);
fifty times, O Lord of Devas, I exercised sovereignty over the gods."
“Fifty-one times I was a wheel-turning monarch;
my local sovereignty was vast and beyond counting.
Whatever gift I gave back then, ninety-four eons ago...”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the *ghatamaṇḍa* offering.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Even after attaining Arahantship, however, due to the residual influence of his past karma, he remained one who received little gain and was little known. He did not even receive meals by invitation or tickets.
They attain only the inferior. And because of the very fruit of their own karma, ordinary monks and novices despise him, thinking, "He is unknown.
To stir those monks to spiritual urgency, the Elder said:
"Even if he is one who possesses the threefold knowledge, A slayer of death, free from taints..."
"Those fools, through their ignorance, despise him as one who lacks wisdom:
'Even if a person here is an obtainer of food and drink,
though he be of evil character, he is honored by them.'"

He spoke two verses. In this context, *api* is a particle used for emphasis (*sambhāvane*). *Cet* is used in the sense of supposition (*parikappane*). *Hoti* means "exists" (*bhavati*). One who possesses the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) is called a *tevijjo*.

One who abandons death (*maccuṃ pajahati*) is a *maccuhāyī*. One who is free from the taints (*anāsavo*) due to the absence of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the others is so called. This is what was said.
He possesses these three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*): the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

Because he has attained these three knowledges, he is "possessed of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjo*); and because the taints of sensual desire and the rest have been completely exhausted, he is "taintless" (*anāsavo*).

Furthermore, because he does not grasp at renewed existence in the future, he is "one who has abandoned death" (*maccuhāyī*) due to the absence of further dying. Even though this is so, fools do not recognize him as such.

Foolish and dull-witted persons despise that supreme person—even one who stands having attained his own goal for which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—saying, "He is not renowned, he is not well-known," because they lack the arising of gain, thinking, "He is a mere proclaimer of the ascetic practices, a man of much learning, a preacher of the Dhamma. Why? Because of their ignorance.
It shows that ignorance of virtues is itself the cause [of such behavior] there.

And just as fools, through ignorance of virtues, despise even one who is worthy of esteem due to gain and fame, so too, through ignorance of virtues, they esteem even one who should thus be despised because of gain and fame; showing this, he recites the second verse.
He said: In this context, "he" (*yo*) is an indefinite term. The word "and" (*ca*) implies distinction;

thus, it produces a specific quality for this person being described, as distinguished from the person previously mentioned. "Indeed" (*kho*) is used for emphasis. "Of food and drink" (*annapānassa*) is merely an illustration.
"A gainer" (*lābhī*) means one who possesses gain. "In this world" (*idha*) refers to this world. Because it fills each respective abode of beings with aging and death, [it is called *loka*].
And there is the person by way of their character. "Of evil nature" means one of base nature. This is the meaning here:

that person who obtains only the basic requisites such as robes, but not jhānas and so forth—even though they are of inferior nature due to being immoral because of evil desires—they are honored and respected in this world by fools on account of their gain and reputation.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ajina is finished.
6. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Meḷajina begins with the words, "When I heard the Dhamma... What is his origin? He too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various states of existence, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Blessed One walking for alms, he offered a sweet *āmoda* fruit with a devout heart.
By that meritorious deed, he [passed] through the realms of gods and humans...
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a kṣatriya family in Bārāṇasī.
Having attained mastery in the sciences and arts, he became known by the name Meḷajina; he was wise, proficient, and renowned in all directions.
When the Blessed One was staying at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, he went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, he acquired faith.
Having gone forth and established insight meditation, he attained arahantship on that very day. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One, the thousand-rayed, the self-become, the unconquered;
having emerged from seclusion, went out for his almsround.”
“Holding fruit in my hand, I saw the Bull among Men and approached him;
with a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave him the fruit from the tree.
Ninety-four aeons ago, that fruit which I then gave—”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving the fruit.

Having attained arahantship, on a later occasion, when asked by the bhikkhus, “Friend, what superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) have you realized? he uttered this lion’s roar: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Having thus attained arahantship, on a subsequent occasion, when asked by the bhikkhus, “Friend, what superhuman state have you attained? he roared this lion’s roar:
“When I heard the Dhamma from the Teacher as he spoke,
O All-Knowing One, Unconquered, I did not perceive any doubt.
[I place my faith] in the Great Hero, the Caravan-Leader, the most excellent among charioteers.”
“Regarding the path or the way of practice, no doubt exists for me”—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, *yadā* means at which time. *Ahaṃ* refers to himself. *Dhammaṃ* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
*Assosiṃ* means I heard. *Satthuno* means of the Teacher, in the sense of one who teaches disciples through matters pertaining to the present life and so forth.
They have doubts; they have uncertainty. He is "Omniscient" (sabbaññū) in the sense of knowing the conditioned and the unconditioned without exception.

He is "Unconquered" (aparājita) by virtue of being undefeated from any quarter. He is a "Charioteer of Men" (satthavāha) in the sense of driving those beings who are to be disciplined toward Nibbāna out of the wilderness of saṃsāra.
This is what is meant: from the time that I [heard] the Dhamma of the Teacher as he was teaching the Dhamma of the Four Truths...

I heard it by way of the door of the ear, I reflected upon it, and I apprehended it; from that time forth, because I have known all conditioned and unconditioned conventional phenomena through my self-born knowledge (*sayambhū-ñāṇa*), I am the All-Knowing One with unobstructed vision.

Because I have overcome the five Māras and am unconquered by them, and because I possess the Wheel of Dhamma that is irresistible in the world including the devas, I am "Unconquered" (*Aparājita*). [And] for those beings who are to be trained...
In the Fully Enlightened One, who is like a caravan leader in the sense of being a guide out of the wilderness of greed and so forth; who is a Great Hero by virtue of his great prowess;
