who is the most excellent and supreme among charioteers because he tames through ultimate subduing those men to be tamed who are difficult for others to tame—I do not recognize any doubt as to whether he is enlightened or not, due to my state of independence from others.

When such a Noble Path has been taught, as well as the practice consisting of virtue and so forth which constitutes its basis, there exists no doubt or perplexity as to whether it is "leading to liberation" or not; that is to say, such doubt is absent.

Furthermore, it should be understood here that by stating the absence of doubt regarding the Noble Dhamma, the absence of doubt regarding the Noble Saṅgha is likewise stated, because for one established therein, there is no possibility of it being otherwise.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Meḷajina is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Rādha:
"Just as a house with a leaky roof... and so forth. These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Rādha. What is their origin? It is said that this...

During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and having reached maturity, he went to a monastery, approached the Teacher, and paid homage.

Sitting to one side, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those who possess ready wit (*paṭibhāneyyaka*). He himself then aspired to that very position and gave a great almsgiving.
He performed a magnificent offering to the Teacher. Having thus made his aspiration, when he passed away from that life, he accumulated merit in various successive existences.
During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a noble family;
upon reaching maturity, one day seeing the Teacher going for alms, with a mind full of serene faith, [he offered] sweet mango fruits.
He gave it away. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the gods;
having performed further merits and wandering through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn at the time of our Blessed One in a brahmin family in Rājagaha.
Having received the name Rādha and reached maturity, while living the life of a householder, he was cast out by his wife and children in his old age. "What use have I..."
Thinking, "I shall go forth from the household life," he went to the monastery, approached the elder bhikkhus, and requested the going-forth.
When they refused him, saying, "This brahmin is old and cannot fulfill the duties of the observances," he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having declared his own aspiration, the Teacher, having observed the excellence of his spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), [granted it].
Having been ordained by the Dhamma-Commander at the command [of the Buddha], he established insight and before long attained Arhatship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Golden-Hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings;”
To one setting out on a journey, I gave a fruit from a tree.
Ninety-one eons ago, because I gave that fruit at that time, I have never known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained arahantship, he lived as one who frequented the presence of the Teacher and became foremost among those who possess the knowledge of *paṭibhāna* (readiness of wit), which serves as a condition for the Teacher’s inspired eloquence in preaching the Dhamma. For it was due to the Elder’s manifestation of right view that—
To the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, fresh and new teachings on the Dhamma occurred to him. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, in ready wit, namely Rādha.
On one occasion, thinking, “These beings are overcome by passion due to a lack of cultivation; if there were cultivation, that would not exist,” he praised cultivation.
With the words “Just as a house,” etc., he spoke two verses (133–134).
Therein, “house” (*agāra*) refers to any dwelling whatsoever. “Ill-thatched” (*duccchanna*) means poorly covered, with gaps here and there.

“It leaks” (*samativijjhati*) means the falling rain penetrates it. “Uncultivated” (*abhāvita*) refers to that house, just as rain [penetrates] it, so too [the mind] is not cultivated by meditation (*bhāvanā*).

Because it is devoid [of development], the mind is undeveloped. "Lust pierces through it" means that not only lust, but also hatred, delusion, conceit, and all other defilements likewise pierce through such a mind.

"Well-developed" means thoroughly developed by the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*); such a mind, like a well-roofed house, cannot be pierced by the defilements such as lust, just as rain cannot enter.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Rādha is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Surādha:
“For my birth is exhausted,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Surādha. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various births, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a mind full of faith, offered him a citron fruit.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; and by performing further merits, he continued to be reborn only in the happy realms.
Wandering through *saṃsāra*, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha as the younger brother of the Elder Rādha mentioned immediately above;

his name was Surādha. When his elder brother Rādha had gone forth, he too went forth and, applying himself to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*), attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“I saw the Leader of the World, blazing like a *kaṇikāra* flower, like the full moon on the fifteenth day, and like a flaming lamp-tree.
Taking a mātuluṅga fruit, I gave it to the Teacher.”
With my own hands, full of faith, I gave fruit to the Hero worthy of offerings.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that gift of fruit which I then gave, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc.]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, however, in order to demonstrate the liberating nature of the Dispensation, he declared his realization (aññā) with the two verses beginning, “For me, they are exhausted,” and so forth.
135–6. Therein, “exhausted” (khīṇā) means they have reached destruction or the end. “Birth” (jāti) means existence or the arising of existence. “Lived out” (vusitaṃ)...
"The teaching of the Victor" (*jinasāsana*) means the dispensation of the Victor, the Fully Enlightened One—the holy life of the Path that has been practiced and fully cultivated.

"The net-like [defilements] have been abandoned" (*pahīno jālasaṅkhāto*): because it ensnares the continuum of beings and provides no escape, that which is termed the "net"—namely, wrong view and ignorance—has been abandoned and utterly eradicated by the Path. "The conduit to existence has been uprooted" (*bhavanetti samūhatā*):...
Craving, which is designated as the "guide to existence" because it leads to and causes the continuation of existence such as that of the sense-sphere, has been eradicated.
"For the sake of which I went forth": for whatever purpose, for whatever goal, I went forth—that is, entered the homeless life—from the home, from the household.
That [goal] consists in the destruction of all fetters and bonds, classified as those pertaining to the lower realm and those pertaining to the higher realm.
The meaning is that I have reached and attained the state of destruction known as Nibbāna, the ultimate goal (paramattha), and the personal welfare known as Arahantship.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Surādha is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Gotama.
"Sleeping happily": this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Gotama. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having reached maturity, one day, upon seeing the Blessed One, his mind became filled with serene faith.
She gave him a fruit of fragrance. By that meritorious deed, having been reborn in the world of the devas and performing further merits, she wandered through the happy realms alone.
In this present dispensation of a Buddha, she was reborn in a brahmin family in Rājagaha and received the name Gotama.
At the age of seven, he underwent the initiation ceremony; he went out for alms of jewels, and having obtained a thousand [pieces of gold], he—
Having established him in such a position and practicing his vow, when he was sixteen or seventeen years old, he was led away by evil friends toward sensual pleasures;
he gave that thousand-fold sum of goods to a certain woman who lived off her beauty, and having thus brought about the ruin of his celibacy, she, upon seeing his appearance as a celibate student,
displayed an attitude of detachment, and at that very sight, through staying with her for only a single night, he became utterly disillusioned with the form of existence.
Remembering his own dwelling in the holy life and the loss of his wealth, he felt remorse, thinking, "I have done what is unseemly.
The Teacher, knowing his excellence of cause and the state of his mind, manifested himself in a place near him.
Upon seeing the Teacher, he approached with a serene mind; the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. He [listened to] the Dhamma...
Having heard this, he gained faith and, upon going forth, attained *arahantship* at the very tip of his razor. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“I gave a fruit, full of joy, to the Golden-Hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings, as he was entering the street.”
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave that fruit back then, I have never known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

However, after he had attained arahantship and was spending his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition, a certain lay friend approached him and asked, "Friend, what did you do with the precious alms-food you received when you went forth? Upon hearing this, the elder, instead of explaining exactly what he had done, spoke of the faults of women and, by virtue of his own state of being free from passion, [declared: "I have abandoned all attachment. Hearing this, the friend thought, "He has not told me anything at all," and departed. The elder then reflected: "If I were to tell him, 'I have become an arahant,' he would surely say, 'You are a liar; you have not even reached the stage of non-returning (anāgāmī), let alone arahantship. Therefore, it is better that he does not know. Having considered this, he remained silent. Subsequently, the elder passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world. When the Blessed One surveyed the world at dawn, he saw the elder there and addressed the monks: "Monks, that monk who was my attendant has been reborn in the Brahma-world. The monks then asked, "But how did he attain such a state? The Blessed One replied, "Monks, that monk was wise and discerning. While living the holy life under me, he understood the Dhamma well. However, because he was of a lustful nature, he did not speak of his attainment of arahantship to others. He only spoke of the faults of women. Because of that, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. The monks then asked, "Venerable sir, why did he speak of the faults of women? The Blessed One explained: "Monks, that monk had previously lived the holy life under another teacher. At that time, he was overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, he committed misconduct. Fearing the censure of his fellow practitioners, he left that teacher and came to me. It was because of that past incident that he spoke of the faults of women. The monks then asked, "Venerable sir, what was the name of that woman? The Blessed One replied, "Monks, she was named Sāmāvatī. The monks then asked, "Venerable sir, what kamma did she perform to be reborn in the human world and subsequently in the Brahma-world? The Blessed One replied, "Monks, in a previous birth, Sāmāvatī was the daughter of a wealthy householder. One day, while playing in the garden with her friends, she saw a Pacceka Buddha and offered him a handful of lotuses. Because of that deed, she was reborn in the heavenly realms for many hundreds of thousands of aeons. In this present age, she was reborn as the daughter of King Bimbisāra. She was so beautiful that she captivated the hearts of all who saw her. Later, she became the chief queen of King Bimbisāra. After the King had passed away, she became the chief queen of King Ajātasattu. Once, while she was staying in the palace, she saw the Elder Mahākaccāyana entering the city for alms. She felt great faith toward him and, having provided him with food, she gave him a set of robes. Because of that deed, she was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Thereafter, she passed through various celestial realms until she was reborn in the Brahma-world. Thus did the Blessed One explain the matter. This story is included in the *Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a wooden post, the person who is like a reed, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Yet, fearing the censure of his fellow practitioners, he conceals it and does not reveal it. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a wooden post? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Yet, fearing the censure of his fellow practitioners, he reveals it and does not conceal it. This, monks, is called a person like a wooden post. And how, monks, is one a person like a reed? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Then, out of shame and fear of wrongdoing, he goes to that woman and says, 'Sister, I have committed such-and-such misconduct; please forgive me. This, monks, is called a person like a reed. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Then, out of shame and fear of wrongdoing, he goes to that woman and says, 'Sister, I have committed such-and-such misconduct; please forgive me. That woman replies, 'Venerable sir, I too am subject to the same fault; we both share this same condition. Do not worry about it. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. Thus did the Blessed One speak. This passage is included in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*. Furthermore, in the *Udāna*, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a wooden post, the person who is like a reed, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Yet, fearing the censure of his fellow practitioners, he conceals it and does not reveal it. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a wooden post? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Yet, fearing the censure of his fellow practitioners, he reveals it and does not conceal it. This, monks, is called a person like a wooden post. And how, monks, is one a person like a reed? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Then, out of shame and fear of wrongdoing, he goes to that woman and says, 'Sister, I have committed such-and-such misconduct; please forgive me. This, monks, is called a person like a reed. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is overcome by lust for a woman and, unable to control himself, commits misconduct. Then, out of shame and fear of wrongdoing, he goes to that woman and says, 'Sister, I have committed such-and-such misconduct; please forgive me. That woman replies, 'Venerable sir, I too am subject to the same fault; we both share this same condition. Do not worry about it. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. Thus did the Blessed One speak. This passage is included in the *Udāna*. Furthermore, in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, it is said: "At that time, the daughter of King Bimbisāra, named Sāmāvatī, was exceedingly beautiful and possessed of great splendor. She was the chief queen of King Bimbisāra. Later, she became the chief queen of King Ajātasattu. One day, while she was staying in the palace, she saw the Elder Mahākaccāyana entering the city for alms. She felt great faith toward him and, having provided him with food, she gave him a set of robes. Because of that deed, she was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Thereafter, she passed through various celestial realms until she was reborn in the Brahma-world. Thus is the account recorded in the *Mahāvaṃsa*. Furthermore, in the *Jātaka*, it is said: "In a previous birth, Sāmāvatī was the daughter of a wealthy householder. One day, while playing in the garden with her friends, she saw a Pacceka Buddha and offered him a handful of lotuses. Because of that deed, she was reborn in the heavenly realms for many hundreds of thousands of aeons. In this present age, she was reborn as the daughter of King Bimbisāra. She was so beautiful that she captivated the hearts of all who saw her. Later, she became the chief queen of King Bimbisāra. After the King had passed away, she became the chief queen of King Ajātasattu. Once, while she was staying in the palace, she saw the Elder Mahākaccāyana entering the city for alms. She felt great faith toward him and, having provided him with
While proclaiming his own realization, he spoke these two verses beginning with “They sleep in happiness.
(137) Therein, “The sages sleep in happiness, who are not bound to women”:
those sages, ascetics with restrained faculties, who are not bound to women—whether as objects of the senses or as signs—by the bond of passion; they are the sages.
The intention is that they sleep happily and dwell happily; there is no suffering for them.
For the phrase "they sleep" is merely an illustration. Regarding the words "always indeed to be guarded," this means they must be guarded at all times, without exception.
For even if women are made to dwell on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace devoid of men, or even if they are placed within the womb—
They cannot be guarded; therefore, they must be protected at all times like cows in a threshing floor.

Alternatively, because of their fickle nature, they must be protected at all times by the husband through the provision of clothing, ornaments, and so forth, lest their minds become otherwise inclined.
Or, they are to be protected because their minds must be guarded by means of concealing the true nature of their bodies with garlands, perfumes, and the like. In them, truth...
"Extremely rare" means that in such women, true speech cannot be found;
for women will enter even fire, consume poison, take up weapons, and even die by hanging themselves, yet they are unable to abide in truth.
Therefore, it shows that the sages who remain having avoided such women are indeed happy.

138. Now, demonstrating his own thorough abandonment and absolute finality regarding that sensual desire (*kāma*) by virtue of which one might still be bound even to such women as these because it has not been abandoned, he spoke the second verse: "We have carried out your execution, O Kāma.
"Execution" means we have carried out your absolute eradication by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). It is also read as "vadhaṃ carimhase."
The meaning is: "We have practiced the holy life of the path for the sake of abandoning [them] and for their destruction. As for the phrase "Now we are no longer in debt to you":
from the moment one has attained the supreme path (*aggamagga*), because that which creates the state of debt has been abandoned, we are now free from debt to you;
we do not owe you any debt. For one who is not yet free from passion (*avītarāga*) is, by virtue of being subject to passion, as if bearing a debt to it.
[The world] exists, but one who is free from passion has transcended it and is endowed with the supreme sovereignty of mind.
"Now, being debtless, we go to Nibbāna"—the meaning is: we now go to, that is, we attain, that very Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna), having gone to which one does not grieve;
for in that Nibbāna, due to the total absence of all causes of grief, one does not grieve because of the act of going.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gotama is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vasabha:
"First he slays himself... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Vasabha. What is their origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, he was reborn in a brahmin family in a world empty of Buddhas.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained perfection in the sciences and crafts of the brahmins;
then, out of a disposition toward renunciation, he abandoned the household life, went forth as an ascetic, and dwelt in the Himalayas with a retinue of fourteen thousand ascetics.
Having established a hermitage on a mountain not far away called Samagga and dwelling there, he developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal powers.
While providing instruction and guidance to the ascetics, one day he thought:
"I am now living here honored, revered, and worshipped by these ascetics; yet, no one worthy of being worshipped by me is to be found. This life is indeed suffering."

"In this world, this is what is called 'living as a homeless one'. Having reflected thus, and because he had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he recollected the offerings and honors he himself had rendered at the stūpas of those former Buddhas.

Thinking, "What if I were now to construct a sand-stūpa in honor of the previous Buddhas and perform worship to it?", he—elated and joyful—created a golden sand-stūpa by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and [decorated it] with golden [ornaments] and so forth.

Performing daily worship with three thousand flowers and performing meritorious deeds for the duration of his life, he passed away without falling away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Remaining there for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn among the Thirty-three gods (*Tāvatiṃsa*).
Wandering successively through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he was born in Vesālī into the Licchavi royal family.
Having been reborn and received the name Vasabha, upon reaching maturity, he witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural power during the Blessed One’s journey to Vesālī.
Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, he applied himself to insight meditation (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Not far from the Himālaya is a mountain named Samagga;
my hermitage is well-constructed, with a leaf-hut beautifully arranged.
There dwells one named Nārada, a matted-hair ascetic of fierce austerities."
“Fourteen thousand disciples attend upon me.
Secluded and at peace, I then thought:
‘Everyone honors me, yet I do not honor anything at all.’”
“I have no instructor, nor is anyone found to admonish me;
without a teacher or preceptor, I have come to dwell in the forest.
While dwelling there, I shall maintain a mind of reverence toward him whom I approach.”
“Thus I have no teacher; my dwelling in the forest is in vain.
I shall seek out one worthy of offerings and likewise venerable;
with a companion I shall dwell, so that no one will find fault.”
“The river Uttānakūlā, with its beautiful banks, pleasant and delightful,
strewn with pure sand, is not far from my hermitage.
Having then approached that river named Amarikā,”
Having built up a mound of sand, he made a sand stupa (pulinacetiya), saying:
"Those who were the Fully Awakened Ones, the sages who brought an end to existence—for them such a monument as this was [erected]; let us make that a sign."
“Having made a sand mound into a stupa, I had it constructed of gold;
I worshipped it with three thousand golden *kiṅkani* flowers.
Day and night, filled with devotion, I paid homage with palms joined.”
I paid homage to the Pulina Cetiya as if it were the Fully Enlightened One himself present before me:
"Whenever defilements arise and thoughts based on worldly attachment occur,
I remember the well-constructed stupa and reflect upon it at that very moment."
“Dwelling in dependence upon the Charioteer of Sages, the Leader,
you should not dwell with the defilements, O venerable sir;
for when the stupa is brought to mind, reverence arises in me at that time.”
I diverted myself with jokes, like an elephant agitated by a goad.
While I was living in this way, the King of Death overcame me;
having passed away there, I went to the Brahma world.
“Having lived out my full lifespan, I was reborn among the Thirty-three gods;
eighty times I served as the lord of the gods, exercising divine sovereignty.
And three hundred times I became a wheel-turning monarch.”
"A sovereign rule over the land, vast and beyond counting—
such is the ripening of the *soṇṇakiṅkaṇī* flower that I now experience.
In this existence, hundreds of thousands of nurses attend upon me."
“Because of my service to the stupa, dust and dirt do not cling to me;
sweat does not break out on my limbs, and I am possessed of great radiance.
Oh, how well constructed is my stupa! How well seen is the Amarikā River!”
Having built a stupa from sand, I have attained the unshakable state.
"For a person who desires to perform wholesome deeds and seeks the essential core, there is no field that is either fertile or barren;
rather, it is practice alone that brings success."
"Just as a strong man, unable to endure the vast ocean,
might take up a small piece of wood and leap into a great lake, thinking:
'Relying on this wood, I shall cross over the great ocean.'"
“With resolve and energy, a man might cross the ocean.
In the same way, whatever deed I performed— though it was limited and small—
I relied upon that very deed and thus transcended saṃsāra.”
“When my final existence had been reached, impelled by the root of merit from the past,
I was born in the city of Sāvatthī into a very wealthy family of great sāla trees.
My mother and father were endowed with faith and had gone for refuge to the Buddha.”
Both of them, having seen the state, followed the teaching.
Having taken a slip from the Bodhi tree, they had a golden stupa built;
morning and evening they paid homage as if in the presence of the Son of the Sakyas.
“On the day of the Uposatha, they brought forth the golden stupa;
praising the virtues of the Buddha, they spent the three watches of the night there.
Upon seeing the stupa, I immediately recalled the Pulinacetiya.”
Sitting upon a single seat, I attained arahantship.
Seeking that hero, I saw the General of the Dhamma;
having gone forth from the home, I went into his presence and took ordination.
“In my seventh year from birth, I attained arahantship;
the Buddha, the Seer, ordained me after recognizing my virtues.
While still a mere child, I have brought my task to completion.”
“Today I have done what was to be done in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans.
Having transcended all enmity and fear, having gone beyond all attachments, this seer is your disciple, O Great Hero; this is the fruit of the golden stupa.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, however, he does not refuse the requisites brought by donors when seeking to benefit them;
rather, he makes use of exactly what he receives. Worldlings think of him: “This man is full of physical vigor and his mind is unguarded.”
Thinking thus, they despise him. The Elder dwells there, disregarding them.
Not far from him, however, lived a certain hypocritical monk who, being of evil desires, presented himself as one of few desires and contented, deceiving the world.
The great multitude regarded him as an Arahant. Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, [approached him].
Having learned of that occurrence, he approached the Elder and asked, "Venerable sir, what does a deceiver do?
The Elder, censuring the one of evil desires, said:
"First he strikes himself, and afterwards he strikes others."
“He destroys himself, like a bird caught in a snare.
“A brahmin is not one who is fair outwardly; for a brahmin is one who is fair within.
He in whom evil deeds reside, O Sujampati, is indeed black. Thus he spoke these two verses.

In this context, "first he destroys himself" means that the deceitful person, while deceiving the world through his own deceitful conduct, first destroys himself by means of evil qualities such as evil desires (*pāpicchatā*) and the like; he ruins his own portion of the wholesome.
"Afterwards he destroys others" means that after that deceiver has first destroyed himself in the manner described, he subsequently destroys others by means of those [qualities].
"Those who perform services for him out of respect, thinking, 'This monk is pleasant and noble,' he destroys;
having rendered their services fruitless by performing them upon himself, he destroys them by destroying the very conditions [for their merit].
Although the deceiver destroys both, the author says, 'He destroys his own self well,' to show this specific distinction regarding the destruction of the self. That deceiver, his own self—
"Killing, having made it a well-killed [slaughter], he kills and destroys. How so? "Like a bird-catcher with a decoy-bird (*vītaṃsa*).
A *vītaṃsa* is a decoy-bird; "with that"—meaning, by means of it. "A bird-catcher" (*pakkhimā*) is a fowler.

Just as that bird-catcher, deceiving other birds while killing them, kills himself even in this world through such things as being censured by the wise and being of a blameworthy nature; and furthermore, in the future life—
It only destroys him by means of the defilement of a miserable rebirth (*duggatiparikkilesa*), yet it cannot kill those birds afterwards;

likewise, the deceiver (*kuhaka*), having deceived the world through his guile (*kohañña*), destroys himself in this world through remorse, the censure of the wise, and so forth, and in the next world through the defilements of a miserable rebirth, but he does not cause those who provide him with requisites to fall into the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*). Furthermore, the deceiver...
It is said that he "kills the donor" by making the sacrificial gift (dakkhiṇā) yield no great fruit, not by making it entirely fruitless.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Having given a gift to an immoral person who has become human, a thousandfold reward for the gift is to be expected.
Therefore, he said: "He kills himself badly."

Thus, showing that persons who merely abide in external cleansing are not truly pure, but rather become pure only through internal purity, he spoke the second verse beginning with "Not a brahmin. Its meaning is as follows:
one does not become a brahmin by mere external excellence, such as the maintenance of postures and so forth;
for here the word *vaṇṇa* has the sense of "excellence. However, it is by internal excellence, such as virtue (*sīla*) and the like, [that one becomes a brahmin].
“He is a brahmin,” thinking, “a brahmin is one who has banished evil.
Therefore, Sujampati, Lord of the Devas, know this: “In whomsoever base and evil deeds are found, he is categorically a dark and inferior person.
Having heard this, Sakka rebuked the deceitful bhikkhu, exhorted him, saying, “Act according to the Dhamma,” and returned to his own place.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vasabha is finished.
The commentary on the first chapter of the Book of Twos is finished.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahācunda "Sussūsā" (Desire to Hear) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Mahācunda. What is its origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn into a potter’s family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having reached maturity and living by the work of a potter, he once saw the Teacher;
with a mind full of faith, he fashioned a clay bowl with his own hands and gave it to the Blessed One.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this current dispensation of the Buddha in the village of Nālaka in the kingdom of Magadha as the son of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī.
He was reborn as the younger brother of the Elder Sāriputta; his name was Cunda Tissa.
Upon reaching maturity, he followed the Dhammasenāpati into the religious life and, relying upon him, established insight meditation.
By striving and exerting himself, before long he became a possessor of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a potter;
I saw the stainless Buddha, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints.
I gave a well-fashioned clay bowl to the Best of Buddhas.”
Having offered a bowl to the Blessed One,
who was upright and poised, [I made this vow]: "In whatever existence I am reborn, may I receive golden plates—
made of silver, gold, and jewels— as well as platters."
“I enjoy these dishes; this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.
I am preeminent in fame and in wealth.
Just as even a small seed sown in a fertile field [yields great fruit]...”
"As the rain of the right Dhamma pours down, the fruit satisfies the farmer.
So too, this gift of a bowl, planted in the field of the Buddha,
will satisfy me as the rain of joy pours down."
“As many fields as there may be, whether they be monastic communities or assemblies, there is none equal to the field of a Buddha, which bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!”
Having given a single alms-bowl, I have attained the unshakable state.
"In the ninety-first aeon, when I gave that bowl at that time, I did not experience a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of the gift of a bowl."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then, having attained the six direct knowledges, while praising the reliance upon his teachers and his dwelling in seclusion as the causes for the excellence he had personally attained, he said:
“Desire to hear increases learning; learning increases wisdom;”
Through wisdom one knows the goal; the known goal brings happiness.
“One should frequent remote lodgings and live for the sake of liberation from the fetters;
if one does not find delight there, one should dwell in the Saṅgha, guarding oneself and mindful.”
He spoke two verses.
Therein, "desire to hear" (*sussūsā*) means the wish to listen to all that is worthy of being heard, as well as dwelling with a teacher.

For one who desires to hear the meaning—divided into that pertaining to the present life and so forth—one must approach a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), attend upon them by performing the proper duties, and [wait] when...
When their minds have been won over by such attendance, they desire to sit near someone;

then, having sat down, because they wish to hear what has been attained [by the teacher], they listen with an attentive ear. Thus, even dwelling with a teacher is called "desire to hear" (*sussūsā*) because it is a cause for that desire to hear.
Furthermore, this desire to hear consists in listening to what is connected with the Truths, Dependent Origination, and so forth.
It increases and expands for the person who possesses it; thus, it is "one who increases what has been heard" (*sutavaddhanī*), meaning one who practices great learning (*bāhusacca*).

Regarding "the increase of what has been heard through wisdom": that great learning which was described by such methods as "one who retains what has been heard, one who accumulates what has been heard," and "here, a certain person has much that has been heard—suttas, geyyas, and vyākaraṇas"—is the cause for the abandoning of the unwholesome and the attainment of the wholesome.
"He increases wisdom" means that learning is the nourishment of wisdom; for this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who is learned abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless, and maintains himself in purity.
"He knows the meaning through wisdom" means that one who is well-learned, established in knowledge consisting of what has been heard, and practicing that very path of practice...
By means of investigation according to the Sutta, by the examination of the meaning, by reflection on the Dhamma, and by meditation,
one understands and penetrates as it really is the meaning— distinguished as mundane and supramundane, divided into the categories of "seen in this life" and so forth,
and divided into suffering and so forth. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of what has been heard and mastered, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
One examines the meaning of the teachings that have been retained; as one examines the meaning, the teachings become acceptable through reflection.
When there is acceptance through reflection on the teachings, zeal arises; having developed zeal, one exerts effort; having exerted effort, one investigates.
"Having weighed [the matter], he exerts himself; being resolute, he realizes the supreme truth with his own body and, having penetrated it through wisdom, he sees it. And:

"The goal known brings happiness" means that the goal as previously described—the goal pertaining to the present life and so forth, as well as the goal consisting of the cessation of suffering and so forth—when known and attained according to reality, brings about and accomplishes happiness distinguished as mundane and supramundane. This is the meaning.
Since the wisdom of development (*bhāvanā-paññā*) established [in the mind] is not accomplished by mere hearing alone, he spoke the words "One should resort to... [and so forth]...
for liberation" in order to show the method of practicing it. Therein, "one should resort to remote lodgings" refers to physical seclusion (*kāya-viveka*).

Because the abandoning of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) will be explained later, and because one who is worthy of seclusion must dwell in seclusion, [the text mentions] the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so forth.
Here, it should be understood that [the following] is established even if not explicitly stated:

"One should practice for the sake of liberation from the fetters" means that one should practice and apply oneself to the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā*) and the cultivation of the path (*magga*) in such a way that the mind is liberated from the fetters.
"If one does not find delight therein" refers to those remote lodgings and the superior wholesome states obtained therein.
And he would not find delight because of failing to obtain further distinction between what was before and what is after;

rather, within the Saṅgha—the community of monks—he should dwell and abide mindful, having protected himself by grasping his meditation subject and having established the protection of mindfulness at the six sense-doors through guarding the mind.
The intention is that for one who dwells in this way, there may indeed come to be liberation from the fetters.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahācunda is finished.

2. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jotidāsa begins with the words "Those indeed who...": these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Jotidāsa. What is their origin? This one, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.
Accumulating merits in various states of existence, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having attained maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher going for alms, he offered a *kāsumārika* fruit with a devout heart.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was born in this present arising of a Buddha in the country of Pādiyattha.
He was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin, and his name was Jotidāsa.
Upon reaching maturity, while living as a householder, one day he saw the Elder Mahākassapa wandering for alms in his village.
With a mind full of faith, he invited the elder to eat; having heard the Dhamma from the elder’s presence, he [built] on a mountain near his own village...
Having had a great monastery built and having settled the Elder there, he served him with the four requisites.

Through the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, he became stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went forth, and while practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), before long he attained the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“I saw the Buddha, free from defilement, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, shining like a *kaṇikāra* flower as he sat amidst the mountains.
With a clear mind and joyful heart, placing my joined palms upon my head,”
“Taking a kāsumārika fruit, I gave it to the Buddha, the Best of Buddhas.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, because of that fruit I offered then, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*) and mastered the Three Pitakas—having reached a state of exceptional proficiency specifically in the Vinaya Piṭaka—and having served as an attendant for ten years, he went together with many bhikkhus to pay homage to the Blessed One.
While traveling toward Sāvatthī, he entered the park of the non-Buddhist ascetics (*tīrthika*) along the way to rest from the fatigue of the journey.

Sitting to one side, he saw a brahmin performing the "five-fire" austerity (*pañcatapa*) and said, "Brahmin, why do you perform one kind of austerity when there is another to be practiced? Upon hearing this, the brahmin became angry and said, "O shaveling!..."
"What else is there that causes burning? he asked. The Elder replied to him:
"Anger and envy, the harming of others, conceit, provocation, intoxication, and negligence;
craving, ignorance, and the fetters of existence—these are what cause burning, for it is not the aggregate of form."
He taught the Dhamma in verse. Having heard it, that brahmin and all the other members of the non-Buddhist sect in that heretical monastery went forth under the Elder.
The Elder, together with them, went to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Blessed One, stayed there for a few days, and then returned to his own birthplace to see his kinsmen who had come to visit him.
Admonishing those who held various attainments and were purified by sacrifice:
“Those people who, with harsh undertakings, obstruct others by means of diverse actions mixed with fetters— ”
"The fruits ripen right there; for indeed, karma does not perish.
Whatever action a person performs, whether it be wholesome or evil, he is the heir to each and every one, whatever deed he has done. Thus he spoke these two verses.
In this context, *ye* is an indefinite designation; *te* is an indefinite correlative reference. Both terms are connected with the word “people” (*janā*). *Khu* is a mere particle.
*Veṭhamissena* means by the wrapping of strips of leather and the like around the head and other parts of the body. There is also a reading *vedhamissena*, which has the same meaning.
*Nānattena ca kammunā* means by various kinds of actions, such as killing, slaughtering, and the cutting off of hands, feet, and so forth.
And by various kinds of harmful actions toward others, such as the giving of small stones and the like. "Human beings" is merely an illustration;
therefore, the intended meaning is "whatever beings. "Oppress" means they afflict. "With harsh undertakings" means with cruel applications;
the sense is that their deeds are brutal. "People" refers to sentient beings. "They too are crushed right there" refers to those individuals of the aforementioned type.

The meaning is that by those very same acts of violence with which they oppressed others, they themselves are likewise subjected and cast into those same conditions, experiencing exactly such suffering.

There is also the reading “tatheva kīranti,” which means that just as they themselves caused suffering to others, so too are they made to do the same by others; they are made to experience suffering. Why is this?
For karma does not perish; indeed, accumulated karma does not vanish without having given its result, for it certainly ripens when the remaining conditions come together—this is the intended meaning.
Now, having analyzed in brief the point stated as "for karma does not perish," [the text explains] the ownership of karma by sentient beings.
In order to clarify this, he spoke the verse beginning with "Whatever one does. Its meaning is as follows:

whatever action—a wholesome and skillful one, or alternatively, an evil and unwholesome one—a sentient being performs, while performing it, they fashion and accumulate that very action in such a way that it becomes capable of yielding its fruit.
They are the heir to each and every one of those respective fruits of action.
"By way of grasping" means that one becomes a partaker of the result to be given by this or that karma. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Young man, beings are owners of their karma, heirs to their karma," and so forth. Having heard these verses, the relatives of the Elder were established in the doctrine of being owners of their own karma.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Jotidāsa is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Heraññakāni The verses beginning with "Days and nights pass away" belong to the Venerable Elder Heraññakāni. What is their origin?
It is said that he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; having reached maturity, he became a servant for others.
Having offered it while still alive, one day he gave away half a cloth to a disciple of the Teacher named Sujāta who was seeking a *paṃsukūla* (rag-robe).
By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods;
passing from there to there, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he became a village headman for the King of Kosala, a scout for the thieves.
He was reborn as a son, and his name was Heraññakāni. Upon reaching maturity, after his father’s passing, he was appointed by the king to that very same position of village headman.
Having witnessed the power of the Buddha during the acceptance of the Jeta Grove, he gained faith.
He then had his younger brother appointed to that office, requested permission from the king, and went forth into homelessness. [Therein] he developed insight...
Having established [the practice], he attained *arahantship* before long. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The disciple named Sujāta of the Blessed One Padumuttara was then wandering among the refuse heaps, seeking a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*).”
“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a servant for others;
having given half a garment, I paid homage with my head bowed low.
By that well-performed deed and by my intention and aspiration, [I have attained this fruit].”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Thirty-three times I served as the Lord of the Gods, exercising divine sovereignty;
and seventy-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
“With the gift of half a cloth, I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter— enjoying a regional sovereignty vast and beyond counting.
If I so desired today, I could [rule] this earth with its forests and mountains...”
“I would cover [the earth] with cloth from Khoma; this is the fruit of that half-cloth.
“In a hundred thousand aeons past, because of the gift I gave then, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of that half-cloth.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, desiring to turn his younger brother away from that work, and seeing him still delighting in it, he exhorted him:
“Days and nights pass away; life comes to an end;”
“The life of mortals wastes away, like the water of small streams.
Yet, while performing evil deeds, the fool does not understand;
later it becomes bitter for him, for its ripening is indeed evil.”
He spoke two verses.
Therein, "passing away" (*accayanti*) means they go beyond; the sense is that they depart very quickly. "Days and nights" (*ahorattā*) refers to nights and days.
"Life is cut off" (*jīvitaṃ uparujjhati*) means the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) ceases by way of momentary cessation. For it is said: "In a moment..."
“Bhikkhu, at every moment you are born, you age, you die, you pass away, and you reappear.
Regarding the phrase “the life-span of mortals is exhausted”: because they have the inherent nature of having to die, these beings are given the name “mortals” (maccā).
Their life-span is one whose maximum duration is thus delimited: “He who lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more. This is the ultimate limit of time for their lifespan.
It wastes away and goes to exhaustion and dissolution;

how so? Just like the water of mountain streams—that is, the water of small streams flowing from the mountains does not remain for long, it wastes away more quickly, and as soon as it arrives, it vanishes—so too the lifespan of beings wastes away more quickly and goes to exhaustion.
And here, "water" (*udaka*) alone is called "the watery" (*odaka*), just as the mind (*mano*) alone is called "mental" (*mānasa*).
Now, regarding the phrase "the fool does not understand while performing evil deeds": although *saṃsāra* is likewise impermanent, the fool performs evil deeds through either greed or anger;
even while performing them, he does not understand that he is committing evil. And while committing evil...

There is no one who does not understand, thinking, “I am doing evil. However, because he does not know that “such is the painful result of this karma,” it is said that “he does not understand. Later it becomes bitter for him:
even if, at the moment of performing an evil deed, he does not understand that “such is the result of this karma,” nevertheless, later on, in the hells and so forth...
For that foolish person who has been reborn, there is only bitter, undesirable suffering. For his result is evil, because the result of an evil deed is indeed evil, base, and undesirable.
Having heard this exhortation, the Elder’s younger brother took leave of the king, went forth into homelessness, and before long accomplished his own goal.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Heraññakāni is finished.
4. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Somamitta:
"A small door," these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Somamitta. What is their origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit in various existences, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity and hearing of the Buddha’s qualities, his mind became filled with serene faith.
One day, seeing a *kiṃsuka* tree in full bloom, he gathered its flowers and, dedicating them to the Teacher, cast them into the air as an offering. By that act...
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans by means of his meritorious deeds, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī.
Having received the name Somamitta and having mastered the three Vedas, he frequently went into the presence of the elder named Vimala because of their prior acquaintance;
there, having heard the Dhamma and gained faith in the Dispensation, he became a follower of the Teaching.
Having gone forth and received full ordination, he wandered about fulfilling his duties and obligations. Vimala Thera, however, was indolent and prone to drowsiness;
he spent his days and nights in sloth. Somamitta thought, "What benefit is there in relying on one who is so indolent?
Abandoning him, he approached Mahākassapa Thera, stood by his instruction, and established insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
Before long, he was established in arhatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having seen a kiṃsuka tree in full bloom, and having raised my joined palms;
remembering the Best of Buddhas, I worshipped him in the sky.”
“By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Thirty-one eons ago, that was the deed I performed then.”
I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.”
“Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of my Buddha;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.
Having thus attained arahantship, he exhorted the Elder Vimala with this admonition:
“Just as one who has boarded a small raft might sink in the great ocean,
so too does even a person of good life sink by associating with one who is indolent.
Therefore, one should avoid that indolent person of inferior energy.”
“Dwell together with those who are secluded, noble, resolute, meditators,
always energetic, and wise”— thus he spoke these two verses. In this regard,
just as one might sink into the great ocean after climbing onto a small piece of wood, even a well-behaved son of good family [sinks] by associating with a person who is indolent and lazy.
Relying on this, one sinks and falls into *saṃsāra*; one does not go to its further shore, which is *nibbāna*.

Since this is so, therefore, one should entirely avoid that person who is "lazy" (*kusīta*)—so called because they sink due to what is base—and who is "of inferior energy" due to the absence of the exertion of vigor;
one should not follow their example. This is the meaning.

Having thus shown the disadvantage of indolence by means of this verse addressed to individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā*), the words beginning with "by those who are secluded" (*pavivittehi*) are now spoken to show the benefits of the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambha*). Its meaning is as follows:

those who are secluded through the arising of physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*), and because of that very fact are noble (*ariya*) due to being far removed from the defilements (*kilesa*), and because their minds are directed toward Nibbāna, they are "resolute" (*pahitatta*); [they are so] by way of sustained reflection upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).

"Those who meditate by means of reflection on the characteristics [of phenomena], who have initiated energy through the constant exertion of vigor at all times, and who are wise because they are endowed with wisdom—both mundane and supramundane—one who desires to accomplish his own goal should dwell together with them; he should live in their company.
Having heard this, the Elder Vimala, with a heart moved by spiritual urgency, established insight (*vipassanā*).
He attained the supreme goal. This matter will be explained further below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Somamitta is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sabbamitta.
"Man is bound to man"—this is the verse of the Venerable Sabbamitta Thera. What is its origin?

This [Thera] also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; accumulating merit in various states of existence, ninety-two aeons ago during the time of the Blessed One Tissa, he was reborn into a hunter's family.
He lived as a forest-dweller, killing deer in the woods and subsisting on their meat.
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring him, showed him three footprint-relics (*padacetiya*) near his dwelling place and departed.
Because he had cultivated familiarity with the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, upon seeing the wheel-marks, his mind became filled with serene faith;
he made an offering of *koraṇḍa* flowers and, through that meritorious deed, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and thereafter continued to be reborn only in the happy destinies.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī;

his name was Sabbamitta. Upon reaching maturity, having witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during the acceptance of the Jeta Grove, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and took up a meditation subject.
While dwelling in the forest, he entered upon the rains retreat, and having completed the rains, he approached the Blessed One.
While traveling toward Sāvatthī to pay his respects, he saw on the way a young fawn caught in a snare set by hunters.
Its mother, though not yet caught in the snare, did not go far away out of affection for her son, nor did she approach the vicinity of the snare out of fear of death;
and the young fawn, terrified, was tossing back and forth, crying piteously.
Seeing him lamenting, the Elder thought, "Alas! How great is the suffering of beings caused by affection!
As he proceeded further, he saw a large number of bandits who had captured a man alive, wrapped his body in a bundle of straw, and were burning him while he cried out with a great roar.
Witnessing both of these sights, a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose within him; and even as those bandits were listening, he said:
“People are bound to people; people depend on people alone. People are harmed by people, and people harm people.
For what purpose is there for him any use of people, or of those born as people?”
"Leaving behind the people, I go, having harmed many folk"—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "people" (*jana*) refers to ignorant, foolish folk. "Among people" (*janamhi*) means among other people. "Bound" (*sambaddha*) means bound by the fetter of craving (*taṇhā-bandhana*).
Or it is bound by such notions as "this is my son," "this is my mother," and so forth. Or rather, this is the reading: "These sustain me, I..."
The meaning is: "I live depending on these," thus having a mind bound [by craving].
"One person is dependent on another person" means that one person is dependent on, attached to, and grasping another person—such as thinking, "This is my son" or "This is my daughter.
"Person is harmed by person, and person harms person" is said because of the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*) and the realization of things as they truly are.
Without maintaining equanimity toward non-existence, just as people rely on one another out of greed,
so too does one person harm and oppress another out of hatred. And people harm one another without realizing, "This will fall back upon me as the fruit of the harm I have inflicted."
"What indeed is the use of that person to him? means: what benefit is there for that other person from another person who is supported by craving or harmed by hatred?
Or, "by one born of that person": what is the use of being born of that other person, having become his mother or father?
"Leaving that person behind and going, having harmed many people"—because for one wandering in *saṃsāra*, [this is the case].

"This is the appropriate course of conduct for people; therefore, having abandoned, completely relinquished, and cast aside both that craving which afflicts those people and that hatred which stands afflicting many people, I shall go—meaning, I shall go to and reach a place untroubled by them. Having spoken thus, the Elder...
At that very moment, having intensified his insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“In former times I was a forest-worker; I lived with my father and mother, supporting myself by tending cattle.
No wholesome merit (kusala) was found in me.”
“Near my dwelling, the Leader of the World, Tissa,
the One with Vision, out of compassion showed three footprints.
And having seen the footprints left by the Teacher named Tissa,”
Joyful with a joyful heart, I gladdened my mind at his footprints:
“Having seen the *koraṇḍa* tree in bloom, growing from the earth,
I took what was mine and worshipped that most excellent footprint.”
“By that well-performed kamma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Whichever womb I am reborn in— whether among the gods or among humans— ”
“May I have skin the color of the *koraṇḍaka* flower, may I become one of great radiance.
Because I performed that deed ninety-two aeons ago, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping his foot.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having heard the Dhamma from the Elder, those thieves were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), went forth, and practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and its discipline.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sabbamitta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākāḷa "Kāḷī the woman" refers to the verses of the Venerable Elder Mahākāḷa. What is their origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family ninety-one aeons ago.
Having reached the age of discretion, he went into the forest on some business.

There, seeing a rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*) hanging from the branch of a certain tree, he thought with a devout heart, "The banner of the Noble Ones is hanging there," and taking *kiṅkaṇī* flowers, he worshipped the rag-robe.
Through that meritorious deed, as he transmigrated among gods and humans, in this [life]...
During the time of a Buddha's appearance, having been born in the city of Setavyā into a caravan-leader’s family and having received the name Mahākāḷa,
he reached maturity and lived as a householder; then, taking merchandise with five hundred carts, he went to Sāvatthī for trade,
and having stationed his caravan on one side and dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he [addressed] his own retinue.
Seeing lay followers going to Jetavana in the evening with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, he also went to the monastery with them.

Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, and dwelling in a charnel ground by undertaking the practice of living in a cemetery, he resided there. Then one day, a certain woman named Kāḷī...
Chavaḍāhikā, for the sake of the Elder’s meditation subject, soon after death, broke both the thighs, broke both the arms, and broke the head like a bowl of curd;
having then reassembled all the limbs and members, she placed them in a position suitable for the Elder to observe and sat down to one side. Seeing this, the Elder, admonishing himself, said:—
“A dark woman, large and of terrifying form, having split one thigh and then the other,
having split one arm and then the other, and having split the head like a bowl of curd—
there she sits, having joined them all together.”
“The fool who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions, repeatedly encounters suffering.
Therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions, lest I lie again with my head shattered.
Thus he spoke these two verses.
In that context, *Kāḷī* is her name, or she is so called because of her black complexion. *Brāhatī* means one with a large body, possessing great height and girth.
*Dhaṅkarūpā* means one whose form resembles a crow precisely because of her black complexion. *Satthiñ ca bhetvā* means having broken the thigh bone of the dead body by splitting it at the knee.
*Aparañ ca satthiṃ* means having broken the other thigh as well. *Bāhañ ca*... [and the arm]...
"Having broken the upper arm" means having broken it precisely at the location of the upper arm joint. "And having broken the head like a bowl of curd" means having broken the head of the dead body;

because it was thus broken, the brain flowed out like a bowl of curd leaking from a jar when struck by a clod of earth, a staff, or the like—this is the meaning. "She sat down, having joined [the parts] together" refers to the severed and broken limbs.
Having joined her dead body together by placing each limb in its proper position,
she sits there as if displaying a meat-stall.
"He who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions" refers to one who, even upon seeing this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) presented by her, remains ignorant and unskilled.

Abandoning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), one who through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) gives rise to the substrate of defilements (*kilesa-upadhi*)—being dull and of dull wisdom—does not transcend the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and thus repeatedly undergoes suffering again and again in the hells and other realms.

Therefore, "knowing, one should not make a substrate" (*pajānaṃ upadhiṃ na kayirā*): "therefore" (*tasmā*) means because this is so; "knowing, one should not make a substrate" (*pajānaṃ upadhiṃ*) refers to whatever suffering exists here.
Understanding thus, "it arises," and attending wisely, one would not create nor produce the substrate of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*).
Why? Lest I lie with my head split, like this dead body lying with its head split;
lest I, by repeatedly arising in *saṃsāra* through the substrate of defilements, become an increaser of the funeral pyre and lie with my head split.
They will say [this]. While speaking thus, the elder intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa;
there I saw a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) hanging upon the branch of a tree.”
“Having then plucked three kiṅkaṇī flowers,
with a joyful heart, I joyfully honored the rag-robe (paṃsukūla).
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations, [I have attained this fruit].”
Having abandoned my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Ninety-one eons ago, because of the deed I performed then—
having honored the banner of the Arhat— I have not known a state of misery.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahākāḷa is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa.
"He gains many enemies" is the verse of the Venerable Tissa Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassi. Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in the various arts.
Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. Having established a hermitage in a grove of *sāla* trees in a forest region, he lived there.

For the sake of favoring him, the Blessed One entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and sat down in a *sāla* grove not far from that hermitage. As he was departing from the hermitage to go in search of various fruits, he [saw the Buddha].
Having seen the Blessed One, with a mind full of serene faith, he set up four poles and, above the Blessed One, fashioned a bower of branches from blossoming *sāla* trees.
For seven days, he stood there worshipping the Blessed One with ever-fresh *sāla* flowers, never relinquishing the rapture inspired by the Buddha as his object of focus.
At the end of those seven days, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*).
He thought of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. At that very moment, about a hundred thousand who had exhausted the taints surrounded the Teacher.
The Blessed One, explaining his future prosperity, spoke words of appreciation and departed.
Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas; wandering from one happy destination to another, during this arising of a Buddha, he [was born] in Rājagaha.
Having been reborn in a brahmin family and received the name Tissa, he reached maturity and became a master of the three Vedas.
While teaching the mantras to about five hundred young students, he attained the pinnacle of gain and fame.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s supernatural power during the Teacher’s journey to Rājagaha, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and after establishing insight (vipassanā), before long—
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having plunged into the sāla grove, my well-prepared hermitage was there;
covered with sāla blossoms, I dwelt then in that forest."
“The Blessed One Piyadassī, the self-become, the supreme person;
the Sambuddha, desiring solitude, approached the Sāla grove.
Having departed from my hermitage, I went to the forest.”
Seeking roots and fruits, I was then wandering in the forest.
There I saw the Fully Awakened One, lovely to behold and of great renown,
seated in perfect composure, shining resplendently in the great forest.
“Having set up four poles above the Buddha,
I constructed a well-made pavilion and covered it with *sāla* flowers.
Having maintained that *sāla*-covered pavilion for seven days,”
Having gladdened my mind there, I paid homage to the Best of Buddhas:
"At that time, the Blessed One, having emerged from meditative concentration,
sat down, the Supreme among Men, gazing a yoke’s length ahead."
“A disciple named Varuṇa approached the Teacher Piyadassī,
the Guide, together with one hundred thousand seers.
And the Blessed One Piyadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men— ”
Having sat down in the community of bhikkhus, the Jina manifested a smile.
Anuruddha was the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassi;
having arranged his robe over one shoulder, he questioned the Great Sage.
“What, indeed, O Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher’s smile?
Since there is a reason present, the Teacher has manifested a smile.
‘The young brahmin who bore my sāla-leaf canopy for seven days—’”
Recalling that deed, I broke into a smile:
"I see no place where merit ripens—whether in the world of the gods or among humans; there is simply no room for it."
“For one who dwells in the world of the gods, endowed with meritorious deeds,
whatever assembly he has shall be shaded by *sāla* trees.
There, amidst divine dances, songs, and instrumental music,”
The virtuous one, established in meritorious deeds, will always find delight.
As long as his assembly remains, it shall be fragrant with perfumes,
and for that duration, a rain of *sāla* flowers shall fall.
“Falling from there, this person will come back to the human world;
here too, the canopy of *sāla* trees shall endure for all time.
Here, there shall be dancing and singing, accompanied by the rhythmic beating of drums.”
“They will always attend upon me; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
And as the sun rises, a shower falls from the *sāla* tree;
joined with my meritorious deed, it rains at all times.”
“In eighteen hundred kappas from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world.
His heir to the Dhammas, his own legitimate son, fashioned by the Dhamma— ”
Having fully understood all taints, one will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
For one who penetrates the Dhamma, there will be a roof made of *sāla* trees;
for one being cremated on the funeral pyre, that shall serve as the covering there.
Having proclaimed the result of his kamma, the Great Sage Piyadassī taught the Dhamma to the assembly, gladdening them with a rain of Dhamma.
For thirty eons, he exercised sovereignty among the devas.
Sixty-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
Having come here from the world of the gods, I obtain abundant happiness;
even here is this Sāla-canopy—this is the fruit of that pavilion.
“This is my last, my final existence now proceeds;
even here, the shade of the *sāla* tree shall be mine for all time.
Having satisfied the Great Sage Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas,”
I have reached the unshakable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.
Because I worshipped the Buddha during eighteen hundred eons, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he reached the very pinnacle of gain and fame.
Thereupon, some bhikkhus who were still worldlings, seeing the elder’s gain and honor, displayed an attitude of intolerance due to their foolishness. The elder, perceiving this, [reflected:]...
Revealing the danger in gain and honor, as well as his own state of non-attachment therein, he said:
“One with shaven head, clad in the outer robe, receives many enemies:
One who gains food and drink, clothing and bedding.”
“Having understood this danger, the great peril in honors;
with few gains and free from craving, let the mindful bhikkhu wander.”—
Thus he spoke these two verses.
The meaning of this is as follows: He is "shaven" (*muṇḍa*) because he has shaved off his hair and beard without leaving even a tuft;
he is "clad in the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭipāruto*) because he wears the patched saṅghāṭi robe after having cut and sewn it.

Thus, having entered upon a change of appearance and living dependent on others, if such a renunciant (*pabbajita*) obtains food, drink, and so forth, he too gains many enemies; many who are envious of him arise. Therefore, this...

Having understood such great fear, vast terror, disadvantage, and fault in gains and honors, and having established fewness of wishes and contentment in his heart, he possesses "few gains" by avoiding even blameless gains that have arisen;
for that very reason, he is "unsullied" due to the absence of being drenched by craving for them; and because he has seen the fear in saṃsāra through the destruction of the defilements, he is...
"Or rather, a bhikkhu, by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension which are conducive to contentment, should wander, travel, and dwell being mindful.
Having heard this, those bhikkhus immediately asked the Elder for forgiveness.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tissa is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kimila The verses beginning with “In the Eastern Bamboo Grove” belong to the venerable elder Kimila. What is his origin?
His former practice, the arising of spiritual urgency, and his going forth have already been explained in the commentary on the verse “Overwhelmed” in the Ekakanipāta.
By that verse, the Elder demonstrated the cause for his own attainment of distinction.
Here, however, it should be understood that he demonstrates his own dwelling in harmony with the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Nandiya, who had likewise attained distinction.
Now, showing how they dwelt while living in such harmony:
“At the Eastern Bamboo Park, the Sakyan sons were companions;
having abandoned abundant wealth, they delighted in alms gathered in their bowls.
With energy aroused, resolute, and always firm in their exertion.”
“They delight in the joy of the Dhamma, having abandoned worldly pleasure”—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, “at Pācīnavaṃsadāya” means in the forest named Pācīnavaṃsa, which was protected, guarded, and well-defined.
For that forest, because it stood to the east of the village and was surrounded by groves of bamboo, was called “Pācīnavaṃsadāya.”
It is said that he "blows" by way of being a bamboo flute. "Sons of the Sakyans" refers to the Elder Anuruddha and others who were princes of the Sakya clan.

"Companions" means they are companions because they proceed and move together through the arising of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), the going forth, the practice of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*), and living in community.
"Having abandoned abundant wealth" means having abandoned great riches, both those acquired through the power of sublime merit and those inherited through family lineage.
"Having abandoned the mass of enjoyments. There is also a textual variant: "sahāyānappake. "Delighting in what is gathered in the alms-bowl" (*uñche pattāgate ratā*):

because it is brought by the practice of alms-gathering (*uñchācariyā*), and because it has come into the bowl, it is "gathered in the alms-bowl" (*pattāgate*). It means they delight in and are devoted to that which is contained within the bowl;
having rejected extra gains such as meals provided by the Sangha, they are content with the mixed food obtained solely through wandering for alms by the strength of their own legs.
"Exerting energy" means having already accomplished energy from the very beginning for the attainment of the supreme goal.
"Resolute" means having directed their minds toward Nibbāna by way of inclining, leaning, and tending toward it, and by entering meditative attainments from time to time.
"Always firm in effort" means at all times through the application to the practice of duties and to dwelling in happiness in this very life.

They are of unflagging exertion. Having abandoned worldly delight—so called because it is known in the world and because it is included within the world—they abandon delight in sense objects such as forms by means of path-wisdom;
they delight and take great pleasure in the delight in the supramundane Dhamma, which is the joy in the supreme fruit (aggaphala) and Nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kimila is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nanda.
"Improper attention" refers to the verses of the Venerable Elder Nanda. What is their origin? It is said that this [Elder] was [a disciple] of Padumuttara...
In the time of the Blessed One, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and having reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties,
he himself aspired to that same position and performed abundant offerings and honors to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
