Having performed a great act of giving, he made this aspiration: "In the future, may I too become such a disciple of a Buddha like you.

From that time forth, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn as a large tortoise in a river named Vinatā during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi. One day, while the Teacher was [crossing] the river...
Seeing the Blessed One standing on the bank, wishing to cross to the other side, he lay down at the Teacher’s feet, desiring to carry him across himself.
The Teacher, observing his intention, mounted upon his back. Overjoyed, he cut through the current with speed and brought him swiftly to the opposite shore.
The Blessed One, offering words of thanksgiving and speaking of the future prosperity that would come to him, departed.

Thus, wandering through successive happy rebirths by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was born into this current dispensation of a Buddha as the son of the great king Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu, in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
On the day of his naming ceremony, because he was born bringing joy to the assembly of his kinsmen, they gave him the name Nanda. When he reached maturity...
The Teacher, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma and performing an act of grace for the world, went to Kapilavatthu.
At the gathering of his kinsmen, he took the occasion of the "Lotus Rain" to relate the Vessantara Jātaka.
On the following day, having entered the city for alms, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry by means of the verse beginning, "Arise, do not be negligent!"

Having gone to the residence, he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning by means of the verse, “One should live according to the Dhamma, practicing good conduct.
On the third day, while the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s consecration, entry into the palace, and marriage were taking place, he entered for alms;
having given his bowl into Prince Nanda’s hand and pronounced an auspicious blessing, he [bestowed it] upon him.
Without taking the bowl from his hand, he went to the monastery; once the man had returned to the monastery with the bowl in hand, he ordained him even though he was unwilling.
Knowing that the man was oppressed by dissatisfaction due to having been ordained in such a manner, he dispelled that dissatisfaction through a skillful means.
By applying wise reflection and establishing insight, he attained Arahantship before long.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the self-become leader of the world,
the Tathāgata, approached the bank of the Vinatā river.”
“Having emerged from the water, I, a tortoise whose domain is the water,
approached the Buddha, the Leader of the World,
desiring to ferry him across. ‘May the Buddha, the Great Sage Atthadassī, step upon me!’”
“I shall ferry you across; you are one who brings an end to suffering.
Having understood my intention, the world-leader Atthadassī, of great renown, mounted upon my back and stood there.
“As far back as I can remember, since I attained the age of reason,
there has been no such happiness for me as that which is felt when the soles of my feet are touched [by the Buddha’s hand].
Having crossed over, the Sambuddha Atthadassī of great renown— ”
Standing on the riverbank, he spoke these verses:
“As far as my mind extends, I am crossing the current of the Ganges;
and this wise king-tortoise has ferried me across.”
“By means of this crossing over to Buddhahood and through his possession of a mind of loving-kindness,
he will delight in the world of the gods for eighteen hundred kappas.
Having come here from the world of the gods, impelled by the root of merit of his white deeds,”
Sitting upon a single seat, he shall cross over the stream of doubt:
"Just as even a small seed sown in a fertile field,
when provided with proper irrigation, satisfies the farmer with its fruit."
“Just so is this Buddha-field, taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
may the fruit of bestowing this perfect support satisfy me.
I am one whose self is intent on striving, peaceful, and free from acquisitions.”
“Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
Because of the deed I performed back in eighteen hundred eons, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of that crossing.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
Having attained Arahantship, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he thought:

“Oh, how skillful is the Teacher’s method, by which I have been lifted from the mire of existence and established upon the dry land of Nibbāna! Thus, regarding his own abandoned defilements and what he had attained—
Having reflected on this happiness and feeling joy arise within him, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Through improper attention, I devoted myself to adornment;
I was restless and fickle, tormented by sensual lust.”
“By the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, who is skilled in means,
having practiced with systematic attention, my mind was drawn out from existence”—
thus he spoke these two verses. Therein, “unsystematic attention” means attending to the foul body as beautiful due to unskillful (anupāya) attention.
"Because of attending to it as beautiful" means that one perceives the unattractive body as beautiful.

"Adornment" (*maṇḍana*) means the decorating of the personal existence with ornaments such as bracelets and so forth, as well as with garlands, perfumes, and the like. "Devoted to" (*anuyuttā*) means "I was devoted," which is to say, I was intent upon the beautification of the body.
"Excited" (*uddhata*) means having an unquiet mind, excited by pride in one's birth, clan, physical form, youth, and so on.
"Capala" means fickle due to an unsteady mind, like a monkey in a forest; or it means fickle because of being engaged in frivolity such as adorning the body and adorning oneself with clothes.
"Āsiṃ" means I was. The construction is: "I was afflicted, oppressed, and tormented by sensual lust"—that is, by the desire and passion for sense-objects (*vatthukāma*).
"By the one skilled in means" refers to the Blessed Buddha, the cause, who is expert and proficient in the means for taming those to be trained.

This instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause. For he speaks with reference to his own removal of sensual lust by means of the admonition regarding the "monkey's speech" upon seeing the celestial nymph Paluṭṭhamakkaṭī.
Indeed, the Blessed One [first addressed] the Venerable Elder Nanda...
Taking the Janapadakalyāṇī as the standard, [he said], "Just as this monkey is, so too are the women with feet like a hen's compared to the Janapadakalyāṇī.
Thus, like a scavenger who removes a small peg while driving in a large one, or like a physician who, after moistening the body with an emollient,
expels the humors through emetics and purgatives, he [described] the Janapadakalyāṇī by way of the comparison to the woman with feet like a hen's.

Having caused his mind to become dispassionate, and further causing his mind to become dispassionate even toward the "pecking hen" through the discourse on renunciation, he established him firmly upon the Noble Path by means of the proper application of serenity and insight. Therefore it is said:

"Having practiced with wise discernment, he drew out his mind from existence. By means of skillful method and the right way, [he established him] in the path of purification through serenity and insight.

"Having practiced [the path], I have rescued with my hand—by means of the Noble Path—the mind that was submerged in the mire of existence, and established it on the dry land of Nibbāna"; this is the meaning.
Having uttered this inspired utterance (udāna), on the following day the Elder approached the Blessed One and spoke thus: "That which for me..."
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One was a guarantor for the acquisition of five hundred kakuṭapāda nymphs;

Venerable sir, I release the Blessed One from that promise. The Blessed One said, “Nanda, when your mind is liberated through non-clinging from the taints, then I am released from that promise. Then the Blessed One [spoke] to him with particular emphasis.

Having understood the quality of guarding the doors of the sense faculties and cultivating that virtue, [the Buddha] placed him in the foremost position for guarding the doors of the sense faculties, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who guard the doors of the sense faculties, namely Nanda.
For the Elder had thought: "It was precisely through lack of restraint over the sense faculties that I fell into this misfortune; [therefore, I shall practice restraint]."

"I shall thoroughly subdue that very [defilement]," he thought, and filled with zeal, possessing powerful moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), and because he had performed his duties therein,
he reached the highest perfection (*ukkaṃsapārami*) in the restraint of the sense faculties.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nanda is finished.
10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirima:
“And others praise him. These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sirima. What was his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, [fulfilled] the perfections under the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having fulfilled [his perfections] while residing in the Tusita heaven, he was reborn into a brahmin family;

upon reaching maturity, he became a master of the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇṭu and Keṭubha vocabularies, the phonetics (Sakkharappabheda), and the histories as the fifth—being a scholar of grammar and etymology, and unerring in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man.
Through his inclination toward renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic.
Having gone forth and being surrounded by a company of eighty-four thousand ascetics, he dwelt in a hermitage created by a deity in the region of the Himalayas.

Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*), and because of the merit he had performed under previous Buddhas as well as the method prescribed in the *Lakkhaṇa-manta*, he recollected the qualities of the Buddha. Then, with reference to the Buddhas of the past, at a certain bend in a river—
Having constructed the Pulina Cetiya, he became devoted to making offerings and paying honor to it. Seeing this, the ascetics asked, "In whose name are these offerings and honors being performed?

He brought forth the manuals on the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) for them, analyzed the marks of a Great Man present there, and, relying on his own power in accordance with that, he extolled the virtues of the Buddha.
Having heard this, those ascetics too became clear-minded; from that time forth, they dwelt performing stupa-worship dedicated to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
At that same time, the Bodhisatta Padumuttara, having passed away from the Tusita realm, descended into his mother’s womb.
In his final existence, the thirty-two omens appeared, as did all the wondrous and marvelous phenomena.
The ascetic, having shown those [relics] to his disciples and greatly increased their faith in the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
While his own body was being honored with offerings by them, he appeared in visible form, approached, and said:
"I am your teacher, reborn in the Brahma-world; you must be diligent."

"Devote yourselves to the worship of the *pulinacetiya* (sand-stupa) and apply yourselves diligently to spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*)," he said, and having spoken thus, he departed for the Brahma-world itself.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a householder family in Sāvatthī.
Because the family’s prosperity and glory increased from the very day of his birth, he was known as Sirimāta.
They gave him a name. At the time he was traveling on foot, his younger brother was born; because he was born increasing their prosperity (*siri*), they gave him the name Sirivaḍḍha.
Both of them, having seen the power of the Buddha at the acceptance of the Jeta Grove and having gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
Among them, Sirivaḍḍha had not yet [attained] any superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
He became a recipient of the four requisites, honored and revered by both householders and those who had gone forth.
But Sirima Thera, from the time he went forth, was a recipient of little due to such a flaw in his past karma and was not esteemed by many people;
yet, while applying himself to serenity and insight, before long he attained the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"On a mountain in the Himālayas, there was an ascetic named Devala;
there I had a walking path constructed by non-human beings.
Burdened by a mass of matted hair, I always carried a water-pot."
Seeking the supreme goal, I then departed from the forest.
Eighty-four thousand students attended upon me;
devoted to their own karma, they lived in the forest at that time.
“Having departed from my hermitage, I went to the Pulinacetiya;
having gathered various flowers, I worshipped that shrine.
Having brought peace to my mind there, I entered my hermitage.”
All the students gathered together and asked me about this matter:
"O Lord, regarding this stupa made of sand which you revere—desiring to know it ourselves, we ask you; please explain it to us."
“Have those of great fame and vision indeed pointed out the words of the mantras?
It is to them, the supreme Buddhas of great renown, that I pay homage.
Of what sort were those great heroes, the omniscient leaders of the world?”
“What is their appearance? What is their conduct? Of what sort are those of great renown?
“The Buddhas possess thirty-two marks and forty minor characteristics;
their eyes have eyelashes like those of a cow, and their teeth resemble jujube fruits.”
“And as those Buddhas walk, they look only the distance of a yoke’s length;
their knees do not make a sound, nor is the sound of their joints heard.
And as the Sugatas walk, they move as if lifting their feet.”
First they place the right foot down— this is the natural law of the Buddhas.
Undaunted like a maned lion, the kings of beasts,
those Buddhas neither exalt themselves nor disparage other living beings.
“Freed from honor and dishonor, equal toward all living beings,
not exalting themselves— this is the nature of the Buddhas.
And when the Fully Awakened Ones arise, they bring forth light.”
They cause this entire earth to tremble in six ways.
These beings see the hell, and then the hell is extinguished;
a great cloud pours down rain—this is the natural law of the Buddhas.
“Such are those Great Nāgas, incomparable and of great renown;
they do not surpass [you] in beauty, for the Tathāgatas are immeasurable.
All my disciples, full of reverence, have rejoiced in my words.”
And so they practiced, according to their capacity and according to their strength.
Desiring the results of their own deeds, they honored the sandy shore,
placing faith in my words with minds devoted to the Buddha.
“Then, descending from Tusita, a son of the gods of great renown was conceived in his mother’s womb, and the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled.
Standing upon the walking-path not far from the hermitage, I— ”
All the disciples gathered together and came into my presence:
"The earth roars like a bull, it cries out like the king of beasts;
it bellows like a crocodile—what will be the result?"
“The Fully Enlightened One whom I honored near the sand-stupa—
now that Blessed One, the Teacher, has entered his mother’s womb.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to them and extolled the Great Sage,”
Having dismissed my own disciples, I sat down cross-legged.
"Indeed, my strength has been exhausted by that supreme illness;
having recollected the Best of Buddhas, I passed away right there."
“Then all my disciples gathered together and prepared a funeral pyre;
taking my body, they placed it upon the pyre.
Having surrounded the pyre and pressed their palms together in reverence at their heads,”
Overwhelmed by the dart of grief, they gathered together and wailed aloud.
As they were thus lamenting, I then went to the funeral pyre:
"I am your teacher; do not grieve, O wise ones."
“You should strive for the true goal, untiringly by day and night;
do not be heedless, for the moment has been granted to you.
Having instructed my own son, I have returned once more to the world of the gods.”
For eighteen eons, I delighted in the world of the gods.
Five hundred times, I was a wheel-turning monarch;
and many hundreds of times, I exercised sovereignty over the gods.
“In all the remaining eons, I wandered through various births;
yet I do not recall ever falling into an evil state—this is the fruit of that arising.
Just as many trees blossom in the month of Kattika, so too did my fame spread throughout the world.”
In the same way, at this time, I have been made to blossom by the Great Seer.
My energy is the yoke-bearing ox that carries me toward the attainment of security from bondage;
like an elephant that has severed its fetters, I dwell free from taints.
“For a hundred thousand aeons, because I praised the Buddha, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of praising him.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as follows] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Ordinary people— both monks and novices— who did not recognize the Venerable Sirima Thera as a Noble One (Ariya), despite his being possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña),
and who failed to honor him because he was not widely known to the world due to his lack of material gain, spoke disparagingly of him after saying whatever they pleased. However,
because the Venerable Sirivaḍḍha Thera was honored and respected by the world for being a recipient of requisites (paccaya), [the same did not occur].

Thinking thus, they praise him. The Elder, censuring the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)—thinking that "to speak praise of one who deserves blame, and to speak blame of one who deserves praise, is the fault of the state of an ordinary person"—said:
"But others praise him, while he himself is unconcentrated."
“The praise of others is in vain if one is not composed oneself.
But if one is well-composed oneself,
then the censure of others is in vain, for one is well-composed oneself.”
He spoke two verses. Regarding that:
"others" (*pare*) refers to those other than oneself; however, in this context, it is intended to mean fools who are other than the wise.
For since they speak without knowing or having thoroughly investigated, their praise—just like their censure—is likewise without measure. "Them" (*naṃ*).

That person. "They praise" means they laud or extol that person—either because of their own ignorance or because of being afflicted by craving—or else by attributing non-existent qualities, saying, "Such-and-such a monk is an attainer of jhāna, an Ariya.
Furthermore, the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of including oneself; thus, others praise that person, and [he himself does so as well].
This shows the meaning that there is merely praise for them, but no actual basis for such praise exists in them.

"If one is oneself unconcentrated" means: if the person whom others praise is themselves unconcentrated—neither concentrated by way of the concentration of the Path nor the concentration of the Fruit, nor even by way of mere access or absorption concentration—then, because of the factors that are the opposites of concentration...
The meaning is that because the defilements have not been abandoned, one is distracted and has a wandering mind.
Furthermore, by the term "unconcentrated" (*asamāhito*), he shows the absence of the qualities that are the signs of concentration.
The word "vainly" (*mogha*) is a neuter noun used adverbially, as in such expressions as "the moon and sun move unevenly. "Others praise him" refers to those who praise that unconcentrated person.
They praise [him] in vain, pointlessly, and without foundation. Why? Because his own self is unconcentrated;
that is to say, because the mind of that person is unconcentrated.

In the second verse, "they revile" means that due to their own ignorance or because of internal hatred, they revile a noble one who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and direct knowledge (*abhijñā*).

Similarly, they censure, revile, or upbraid [others] by way of exposing their failure to practice—saying, for instance, "Such-and-such a bhikkhu does not apply himself to wakefulness even for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
he dwells merely intent on physical strength, delighting in sleep, delighting in talk, and delighting in company"—or by way of proclaiming the ruin of his virtues. The rest is as in the first verse.

This is to be understood according to the manner already stated. Thus, when the Elder had declared his own state of freedom from defilement and Sirivaḍḍha’s state of being possessed of defilement through these verses, Sirivaḍḍha, having heard this, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
He established insight (*vipassanā*) and before long fulfilled his own goal. Furthermore, those who had censured him asked the Elder for forgiveness.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirima is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Third Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara "The aggregates have been fully understood by me": these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Uttara. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, ninety-four [aeons] ago from now—
In the aeon of the Blessed One Siddhattha, having been reborn in a noble family and attained maturity, he gained faith in the Dispensation and formally declared himself a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

After the Teacher had attained *parinibbāna*, he gathered his kinsmen together, prepared extensive offerings and honors, and performed a reliquary worship (*dhātupūjā*). By that meritorious deed, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Sāketa.
Having received the name Uttara and reached maturity, he went to Sāvatthī on some business. There, having witnessed the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, he gained confidence.
Furthermore, his faith increasing upon the teaching of the Kāḷaka-ārāma Sutta, he went forth as a monk under the Teacher.

Having gone together to Rājagaha and received full ordination, he dwelt right there, established insight meditation, and before long became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the Protector of the World had passed away, when Siddhattha, the Leader of the World, had attained Nibbāna;”
Having gathered my kinsmen, I performed a worship of the relics.
Because I worshipped the relic ninety-four aeons ago, I have never known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the relic.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge (chaḷabhiñña), while the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī, he arrived from Rājagaha at Sāvatthī for the purpose of attending upon the Buddha.
The monks asked him, “Friend, have you brought the duties of one gone forth to their ultimate fulfillment?”
Being questioned, he answered with another verse:
"The aggregates have been fully understood by me; craving has been thoroughly uprooted by me;
the factors of enlightenment have been cultivated by me; the destruction of the taints has been attained by me."
“Having fully understood the aggregates, having pulled out the net, and having cultivated the factors of enlightenment, I shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints”—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, “aggregates” refers to the five aggregates of clinging. “Fully understood” means: “This is suffering; there is nothing beyond this.”
"Having been delimited, known, and developed. By this, he speaks of the clear realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) of the Noble Truth of Suffering.

"Craving" (*taṇhā*): it is called craving because one trembles (*tasati*) and is terrified (*paritasati*). "Well-eradicated" (*susamūhatā*): it means completely uprooted. By this, he speaks of the clear realization through abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*) of the Truth of the Origin.

"'The factors of enlightenment have been developed by me'": [this refers] to the collection of states beginning with mindfulness that is designated as "enlightenment," and to the possessor of those [states].
Or, they are called *bojjhaṅga* because they are the factors (*aṅga*) of the noble person known as "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).

The states comprised within the path—namely mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which have been developed, generated, and increased by me, are what is meant.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the very mention of the "factors of enlightenment," all the path-factors associated with them, as well as all the qualities conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), are included.
By this very statement, he demonstrates the realization through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) of the Truth of the Path.

"The destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) has been attained by me": because the taints—such as the taint of sensual desire and the others—are destroyed therein, it is given the name "destruction of the taints"; this unconditioned state (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*) has been attained and realized by me.

By this, he speaks of the realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) of the Truth of Cessation. To this extent, he demonstrates his own attainment of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*sa-upādisesa-nibbāna*).
Now, demonstrating the attainment of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*), he spoke the second verse beginning with "So haṃ.
Its meaning is as follows: Having fully understood—that is, having thoroughly comprehended—the aggregates (*khandhā*) in the manner described;

and while thus comprehending them, [I saw] the mode of binding within my own personal existence and the existences of others, that is, within the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) divided by past and other categories.
Having pulled out craving— which has received the name "jālinī" because it possesses a net consisting of repeated occurrence—

from the continuum of my own mind, and while thus pulling it out, having cultivated the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) distinguished as previously described and brought them to the perfection of cultivation,
I have stood therefrom as one free from taints (anāsava); now, through the cessation of the final consciousness—
"Like a fire without fuel, I shall go out; I shall attain final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttara is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhaddaji.
"Panāda was that king"—this is the verse of the Venerable Bhaddajī Thera. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a brahmin family;

having reached maturity and attained mastery in the sciences and arts of the brahmins, he abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth as a forest ascetic, and lived after establishing a hermitage in a woodland region.
One day, seeing the Teacher traveling through the air, he stood with a mind full of serene faith, raising his hands in reverential salutation.
The Teacher, knowing his inner disposition, descended from the sky. When the Blessed One had descended, he offered him honey, lotus stalks, ghee, and milk;
out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted these and gave a discourse of thanksgiving.
Having spoken thus, he departed. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven;

remaining there for the full span of his life, and thereafter wandering from one happy destination to another, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he became a wealthy merchant and, having fed sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus, clothed them in the three robes.
Having performed much wholesome karma in this way, he was reborn in the world of the devas; remaining there for the full span of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn among humans.
In a world devoid of a Buddha, he served five hundred paccekabuddhas with the four requisites.
Passing away from there, he was reborn in a royal family, and while ruling the kingdom, his son attained the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha.
Having attended upon him while he was still living, and having taken the relics of him who had attained final Nibbāna, he erected a cetiya and made offerings to it.

Having thus performed those meritorious deeds in various places, in this present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn as the only son of the merchant Bhaddiya of the city of Bhaddiya, who possessed a wealth of eight hundred million; his name was Bhaddaji. It is said of him:
The perfection of sovereignty, wealth, retinue, and so forth was like that of the Bodhisattva in his final existence.
At that time, having spent the rains retreat at Sāvatthī, the Teacher went to the city of Bhaddiya with a great community of monks to win over Prince Bhaddaji;
he stayed in the Jātiyā Grove, awaiting the ripening of the prince’s wisdom. He too—

Sitting on the upper palace and opening the lion-window to look out, he saw the great multitude going into the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dhamma. Having asked, "Where is this great multitude going?
and having heard the reason, he himself went into the presence of the Teacher with a large retinue, listening to the Dhamma while still adorned with all his ornaments.
Having exhausted all defilements, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having plunged into a lotus pond frequented by various elephants, I was then pulling up lotus roots there for the sake of food."
“At that time, the Blessed One named Padumuttara,
the Buddha clad in saffron robes, was walking along the wind-swept path.
Shaking off the dust from his rag-robe, I then heard a sound.”
Looking upwards, I beheld the Leader of the World.
Standing right there, I made this request to the Leader of the World:
"Please accept honey together with lotus roots, milk, ghee, and water-lily stalks."
“May the Buddha, the One with Vision, accept my offering out of compassion.
Then the compassionate Teacher, of great renown,
descended and accepted my alms out of compassion, he who possesses vision.
Having accepted it, the Perfectly Awakened One offered me this expression of appreciation:
"May you be happy, O one of great merit; may your destiny be fulfilled.
By this gift of a lotus, may you obtain abundant happiness."
Having said this, the Fully Awakened One,
whose name is the Supreme among those born from the water— the Victorious One— taking his alms,
came through the air. Then, having taken the lotus root, he arrived at my hermitage.
Having tied a lotus root to a tree, I recollected my past gift:
"A great wind arose and then shook the forest;
the sky resounded and lightning struck then."
“Then a thunderbolt fell upon my head;
while I was sitting there, I passed away.
Bound by my meritorious karma, I was reborn in the Tusita heaven.”
“My physical body has fallen away, and I delight in the world of the gods.
Eighty-six thousand women, beautifully adorned,
attend upon me morning and evening— this is the fruit of the gift of a lotus.”
“Having come to birth among humans, I was then happy;
there was no deficiency in my wealth—this is the fruit of the gift of lotus roots.
I was shown compassion by that God of Gods, the Imperturbable One.”
All taints are utterly destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
"In a hundred thousand aeons past, because I gave that lotus root at that time, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of the gift of the lotus root."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
When he had attained Arahantship, the Teacher addressed the merchant Bhaddiya:
“Your son, while listening to the Dhamma, has become established in Arahantship; therefore, it is fitting for him to go forth this very day. If he does not go forth, [he will fall away].”
“He will attain final Nibbāna. The merchant said, “There is no need for my son’s final Nibbāna while he is still so young;

let him go forth [into the homeless life]. Having caused him to go forth and conferred full ordination upon him, the Teacher stayed there for seven days and then reached Koṭigāma, which was situated on the bank of the Ganges.
The residents of Koṭigāma [honored] the community headed by the Buddha...

They offered a great almsgiving to the community of monks. As soon as the Teacher had begun his expression of thanks, the Elder Bhaddaji went outside the village and sat down after entering a meditative attainment, thinking, "I shall emerge when the Teacher arrives at the vicinity of the path on the bank of the Ganges.
Even though the great elders were passing by, he did not emerge; rather, it was only when the Teacher arrived that he emerged.
He emerged. The bhikkhus who were ordinary worldlings complained, “This man, having only recently gone forth, stood haughtily and did not emerge when the great elders were approaching.
The inhabitants of Koṭigāma tied together many boats for the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The Teacher, thinking, “Well now, let me manifest his power,” stood upon the joined boats and asked, “Where is Bhaddaji?”
He asked. The Elder Bhaddaji approached the Teacher, saying, "It is I, Bhante," and stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Teacher said, "Come, Bhaddaji; board the same boat as us. He leapt up and stood upon the boat where the Teacher was standing.
When they had reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, during the time of King Mahāpanāda..."
“Where is the palace of Ajjhāvuṭṭha-Ratana? he asked. “It is submerged in this place,” [the Elder] replied.

“In that case, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubt of your fellow celibates. At that moment, the Elder paid homage to the Teacher, traveled by means of his psychic power, and pressed down the pinnacle of the palace with the space between his toes, [reducing] the twenty-five-league palace—
Having taken hold of it, he leaped into the air; and as he was leaping, he lifted the palace fifty *yojanas* out of the water.
Then his kinsmen from a previous existence—who, having been overcome by greed for the palace, had become fish, turtles, and frogs—turned over and fell into the water as that palace rose up.
Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, these are your kinsmen."
“...are weary,” he said. By the Teacher’s word, the Elder released the palace; the palace settled back in its original place.
When the Teacher, who had reached the further shore, was asked by the monks, “Venerable sir, when did the Elder Bhaddaji come to dwell in this palace?
he related the Mahāpanāda Jātaka and caused the great multitude to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. The Elder—
Then, having shown him the golden palace he had formerly inhabited, [the deity said]:
"That king was named Panāda, whose sacrificial post was made of gold;
it was sixteen cubits across and, they say, a thousand cubits high."
“With a thousand stalks and a hundred joints, adorned with banners and made of emerald;
there, six thousand gandhabbas danced in seven ways.
Describing it with these two verses, he answered the other’s question.

Regarding the phrase "that king was named Panāda," he refers to himself as if he were another because his individual existence (*attabhāva*) has passed away; for from the time he stood in the kingdom,
he was known as "King Mahāpanāda" because he was always endowed with great royal majesty through the perfection of his energy and the like, and possessed of great fame.
"Whose sacrificial post is golden": for that king, this sacrificial post—the palace—is made of gold.
"In width sixteen spans high": in breadth, it measures sixteen *kaṇḍapāta* units; however, it is about half a *yojana* in size. "They say it is a thousandfold in height":
they say that the height of this palace is a thousandfold, measuring a thousand *kaṇḍapāta* units; yet it is [only] one *yojana* in length.
It measures twenty-five yojanas. However, some here have lengthened the word to "āhu" for the sake of metrical ease in the verse;
they explain that "āhu" means "it was" (ahosi).
"Sahassakaṇḍo" means having a thousand tiers. "Satageṇḍu" means having many hundreds of spires. "Dhajālū" means [adorned] here and there with banners.
It was endowed with staff-flags, cloth-flags, and banner-flags set up upon the cornices, pinnacles, and other parts [of the palace].
"Made of emerald" (*haritāmayo*) means made of refined gold (*cāmīkara-suvaṇṇa*); however, some say it is "resembling an emerald-gem.
"Gandhabbas" refers to actors. "Seven thousand in six ways" means that six thousand gandhabbas [were present] at that palace in seven ways.
The meaning is that they danced for the purpose of pleasing the king in seven ways. Even though they danced in this manner, they were unable to make the king laugh.
Then Sakka, the King of the Devas, sent celestial dancers and held a festival; at that time, the king laughed.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhaddaji is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sobhita.
"Mindful and wise"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sobhita. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara...
Having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī, he reached maturity and, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma,
saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who possess knowledge of past lives.
Having made a resolution for that very station for himself and having performed meritorious deeds, he wandered through the happy destinies until the time of Sumedha.
Having been reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached maturity and attained perfection in the knowledge and arts of the brahmins.
Resolved upon renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as a forest-dwelling ascetic.
Having established a hermitage in a forest tract near the Himalayas and subsisting on roots and fruits of the woods, he heard of the appearance of a Buddha.

Staying for only a single night in every place, he approached the Teacher at the city of Bhaddavatī with a devout mind and praised him with six verses beginning with, “You are the Teacher and the Banner. The Teacher then proclaimed his future success.
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
He was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They gave him the name Sobhita.

On another occasion, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and by developing insight, became one possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
He also attained mastery over the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the south of the Himalayas, my well-prepared hermitage was located;
seeking the supreme goal, I dwelt there in the forest at that time.
Content with gain or loss, and with roots and fruits;”
Seeking a teacher, I lived all alone.
At that time, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha appeared in the world;
he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths, uplifting the great masses of people.
“I did not hear of the Fully Awakened One, nor did anyone tell me;
it was only after eight years had passed that I heard of the Leader of the World.
Having carried out firewood and having swept the hermitage,”
Having taken up a khāri-load, I departed from the forest.
Dwelling for one night in villages and market towns,
I eventually approached Candavatī.
“At that time, the Blessed One, Sumedha, the Leader of the World,
was teaching the deathless state while uplifting many beings.
Having passed beyond the multitude of people and having paid homage to the Ocean-like Conqueror,”
Arranging my deerskin robe over one shoulder, I praised the Leader of the World:
“You are the Teacher and the banner, the standard and the sacrificial post for living beings;
you are the refuge, the support, and the island—the supreme among bipeds.”
“Heroic in insight, you who are free from guile have delivered the people across;
there is no other deliverer in the world, O Sage, superior to you.
It might be possible to measure the greatest ocean with the tip of a blade of kusa grass;”
But it is not possible to measure your omniscient wisdom.
"Even if one were to place the earth on a scale, it might be possible to weigh it;
but for your wisdom, O Visionary One, there is no measure at all."
“Space can be measured with a cord or even with a finger,
but your omniscience, O All-Knowing One, cannot be measured by means of virtue.
The water in the great ocean, the sky, and the earth— ”
“These are measurable, but you, O Visionary One, are immeasurable.
Having praised the All-Knowing One of great glory with these six verses,
I then stood silent with my hands joined in reverence.
“He who is called Sumedha, the one of vast wisdom and great intelligence,
sat down in the community of monks and spoke these verses:
‘He who has proclaimed my knowledge with a mind of utter clarity— ’”
I shall proclaim this; listen as I speak.
For seventy-seven eons he will delight in the world of the gods;
a thousand times he will exercise divine sovereignty as the Lord of the Gods.
“Many hundreds of times he will become a wheel-turning monarch;
his local sovereignty will be vast, beyond counting.
Whether as a god or a human, he will be established in meritorious deeds.”
With a mind free from deficiency and resolute intention, he will possess sharp wisdom.
"In the thirty thousand kappas hence, born in the Okkāka clan,
one named Gotama by lineage will become a Teacher in the world."
“Having gone forth from the home life, this one with few possessions will go forth;
at the age of seven, he will realize arhatship.
Since I remember myself [in the past], since I have received the teaching;”
"In the interval between those times, I do not recall any unpleasant volition.
Having wandered through all states of existence, I have experienced every prosperity;
there has been no deficiency in my wealth, which is the fruit of praising knowledge."
“The three fires have been extinguished within me; all states of existence have been utterly uprooted.
All taints are completely destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
Thirty thousand eons ago, that knowledge which I attained on the earth—”
“I do not know a state of woe, through the praise of the fruit of knowledge.
‘The defilements are burnt up by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then recollected his own past lives in successive order, back as far as the non-percipient realm.”
He saw the mindless rebirth-linking; then, for five hundred eons, not seeing any occurrence of consciousness and seeing only the cessation [of it], he reflected, "What is this?
and through the method of inference reached the conclusion:

"This must be the state of non-percipient existence. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are gods called the non-percipient beings who have long life-spans; having passed away from there, Sobhita..."
“Having been reborn here, he knows that existence; Sobhita recollects it.
Seeing thus the Elder’s skill in recollection as he recollected in this manner, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives.
For this very reason, this Venerable One’s own knowledge of the recollection of past lives became especially distinguished, as well as its causal basis.
Having reflected upon his practice and filled with joy, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) that illustrates its significance:
“The mindful and wise bhikkhu, having aroused powerful energy,
I have recollected five hundred eons in a single night.”
“Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness and the seven and eight [factors],
I recalled five hundred eons in a single night”— thus he spoke these two verses.

Therein, “mindful” (*sati-mā*) means having attained the fullness of mindfulness through the perfection of the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, which has been fully accomplished by oneself.
And he is mindful. "Possessed of wisdom" means one who has attained the abundance of wisdom through the fulfillment of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

He is a "bhikkhu" because his defilements have been shattered. He is one whose strength and energy are exerted through the complete accomplishment and perfection of the powers of faith and so forth, as well as the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhāna*).
Here, although mindfulness and the other factors also possess the nature of powers, they are included by the mention of "powers" specifically referring to faith and the rest.

As it is said: "The equipment of merit and knowledge is bound to the ox. When he says, "I recollected five hundred eons as if they were a single night," he recollected them as if they were a single night.
For here, the word "like" (*viya*) is used elided; by this, he demonstrates his mastery over the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).
Now, in order to show that practice by which his state of being mindful and so forth,
as well as his knowledge of former births, was accomplished pre-eminently, he spoke the second verse beginning with "The four. Therein,

"the four foundations of mindfulness" refers to the fourfold foundations of mindfulness— consisting of both the mundane and the supramundane— which are comprised of the applications of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body, distinguished according to their respective objects.
“Seven” refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). “Eight” refers to the eight path-factors (*maggaṅga*).

For one whose mind is well-established in the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the seven factors of enlightenment indeed reach the fullness of their development, as does the noble eightfold path. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma said:
“Those whose minds are well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness [develop] the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are...”

By such phrases as “having developed,” it is shown that among the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) divided into seven groups, when one group reaches the perfection of development, there are none of the others that do not likewise reach it. They are called "development" because they cause development.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sobhita is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Valliya:
“Whatever task [is to be done] with firm energy,” etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Valliya. What is their origin? He too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various states of existence, he was reborn into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha.
Upon reaching maturity, he attained proficiency in the sciences and arts;
then, renouncing eighty million in wealth, he went forth as an ascetic and established a hermitage at the foot of a mountain in a forest region on the bank of a river.
While dwelling there after having had it constructed, he saw the Teacher approaching for the sake of favoring him;

with a mind full of faith, he spread out a deerskin and gave it to him. Having honored the Blessed One as he sat upon it with flowers and sandalwood paste, and having offered mango fruits, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration. To him, the Blessed One [spoke of] the excellence of his seat.

Having expressed his thanksgiving while making it known, he departed. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Vesālī.
Having received the name Kaṇhamitta, upon reaching maturity, he saw the majesty of the Buddha when the Teacher visited Vesālī; having gained faith, [he approached] the Elder Mahākaccāna.
He went forth into homelessness in the presence [of the Buddha]. Being of dull wit and slow progress, he lived for a long time depending entirely upon a learned fellow-celibate.

The bhikkhus said, "Just as a creeper cannot grow without depending on something such as a tree, so too this man cannot grow without depending on some wise person," and thus they called him "The Creeper" (Vallī).

They practiced accordingly. Later, however, having approached the Elder Veṇudatta and abiding by his instruction, dwelling mindful and clearly comprehending, and because his knowledge had reached maturity, he asked the Elder about the stages of practice:
"That which must be done with firm energy, that which must be done by one desiring enlightenment..."
“I shall act and I shall not fail; behold my energy and my exertion!
‘And you, tell me the path, the direct way leading to the Deathless;
through wisdom I shall realize it, as the current of the Ganges flows to the ocean’—with these words he spoke two verses.”

In this context, "the task that must be done with firm energy" means the task that ought to be performed or undertaken with firm energy— that is, with strong and steadfast exertion— or by a person of great strength (*purisadhorayha*).
"The task desired to be awakened to" refers to the task desired by one who wishes to awaken to or penetrate the Four Noble Truths, or indeed Nibbāna itself.
"Whatever task is to be done, I shall do it and not fail; now I shall do it and not neglect it;
I will practice according to the instruction. Behold the energy and exertion:

because one proceeds by way of the method in the phenomena as one practices, it receives the name "energy" (*vīriya*); and because one steps from stage to stage, it receives the name "exertion" (*parakkama*).
"Behold right effort, not faith alone"—this shows his own desire to act.

"And you"—this addresses the spiritual friend who bestows the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Tell me the path"—the meaning is: "Speak of the noble path; speak of the meditation subject on the Four Noble Truths which leads to the supramundane path. "The straight path" (*añjasam*)—

It is "straight" (*ujuka*) because, by way of the middle way, it does not approach either of the two extremes. It is "plunged into the deathless" (*amatogadha*) because it is established as that which leads to the attainment of Nibbāna, the deathless.
"By means of wisdom" (*monena*) means by means of knowledge, the path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*). "They shall know" (*monissanti*) means they shall know, penetrate, and reach Nibbāna.
"Just as the Ganges stream [reaches] the ocean": just as the stream of the Ganges reaches the great ocean.
Not failing in his resolve, he plunged in single-mindedly; thus, saying, "As I apply myself to this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), I shall attain Nibbāna through the knowledge of the Path;
therefore, explain that meditation subject to me," he requested the meditation subject from the Elder.

Having heard this, the Elder Veṇudatta gave him the meditation subject. And he, applying himself to that meditation subject, before long brought insight (*vipassanā*) to its peak and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure— those lovely and delightful forms—
and having renounced eighty crores, I went forth into the homeless life.
Having gone forth, I avoided evil deeds with my body.”
Having abandoned verbal misconduct, I was living on a riverbank.
While I was dwelling there all alone, the Supreme Buddha approached me.
Not knowing he was the Buddha, I offered him hospitality.
“Having offered me hospitality, I asked for your name and clan:
‘Are you a deva, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka, the first-born?
‘Who are you, or whose son are you? A Great Brahmā has come here.’”
He illuminates all directions like the rising sun.
"O Noble One, wheels with a thousand spokes are seen upon your feet;
who are you, whose son are you, and how may we know you?"
“Proclaim your name and clan, and dispel my doubt:
I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba; I am not Sakka, the first-born.
Nor do I possess the state of a Brahmā; I am the highest among these.”
“The past was their domain; they severed the bond of sensual desire.
Having incinerated all defilements, they attained supreme enlightenment.
Hearing his words, I spoke these words:”
“If you are the Buddha, the All-Knowing One, sit down, O Great Sage;
I shall honor you, for you are the bringer of an end to suffering.
Having spread out a deerskin, I gave it to the Teacher.
There the Blessed One sat, like a lion in a mountain cave:
“Having quickly climbed the mountain, I gathered the fruit of the mango tree,
a flower from the noble *sāla* tree, and precious sandalwood.”
“Quickly taking all of that, I approached the Leader of the World;
having offered the fruit to the Buddha, I worshipped him with a *sāla* flower.
Having anointed him with sandalwood, I paid homage to the Teacher.”
With a serene mind and a joyful heart, filled with vast rapture,
the Wise One, the Leader of the World,
sat upon a deerskin and recounted his own deeds, bringing me joy at that time.
“By this gift of fruit and both these garlands of fragrance,
he will delight in the world of the gods for twenty-five hundred kappas.
With his intentions unimpaired, he will become a master of his own power.”
In two hundred and twenty-four aeons, he will attain human birth.
He will become a Wheel-turning Monarch of great power, ruling over the four quarters;
there will be a city named Vebhāra, built by Vissakamma.
“He will shine with all-gold, adorned with various jewels;
by this very means, he will wander through existence.
Having been honored everywhere, both in the state of a deva and among humans,”
When his final existence has been reached, he will become a kinsman of Brahmā.
Having gone forth from the home to the homeless life,
having attained mastery over the higher knowledges, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
“Having said this, the Sambuddha, Sumedha, the Leader of the World,
departed through the air while I was gazing after him.
By that well-performed deed and by my volition and aspiration, [I have attained this state].”
Having abandoned my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Having passed away from Tusita, I was reborn in a mother’s womb;
there was no deficiency in the wealth within the womb where I dwelt.
"While I was in my mother's womb, food and drink—
whatever I desired— were produced for my mother according to her wish.
At the age of five, I went forth into the homeless life."
When my hair was shorn off, I attained arahantship.
While investigating my past karma, I saw nothing more recent than this;
thirty thousand eons ago, I recollected my own deed.
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
Having come to your teaching, I have attained the unshakable state.
For thirty thousand eons, I made offerings to the Buddha.”
“I do not recognize a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

Having attained arahantship and declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*), the Elder spoke these very verses: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished. Thus he spoke.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Valliya is finished. 5.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vītasoka begins with the words, “Who will shave my hair? What is his origin? He too—
Having performed services under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit throughout various existences, he was reborn into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Having attained mastery in the sciences and arts of the brahmins, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth as a seer (isi).
Dwelling in the forest surrounded by a great company of seers, he heard of the appearance of a Buddha.
Delighted and joyful, thinking, "The Blessed Buddhas are as rare to behold as the udumbara flower;
they must be approached right now," he set out with a great assembly to see the Teacher.

When one and a half yojanas remained, he fell ill and passed away while his consciousness was directed toward the Buddha. Having been reborn among the devas, he wandered on through successive births among gods and humans.
During this dispensation of the Buddha, he was born as the younger brother of King Dhammāsoka at the end of two hundred and eighteen years;

his name was Vītasoka. Having reached maturity and attained perfection in the sciences and crafts to be learned by kṣatriya princes, he entered the household life under the guidance of the Elder Giridatta and [studied] the Sutta Piṭaka.

Having become confident in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, one day while at the time for shaving, he took a mirror from the hands of his barber and, looking at his body, saw the wrinkles, grey hair, and other signs of age.

Stricken with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he applied his mind to insight (*vipassanā*) and, by intensifying his meditation, became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) on that very seat; [he then went] to the Elder Giridatta.
Having gone forth in his presence, he attained arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“A student of the scriptures, a bearer of the mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas, together with the *Lakkhaṇa*, the *Itihāsa*, the *Nighaṇḍu*, and the *Keṭubha*.”
“Then my students came to me, resembling the flow of a river;
untiringly, day and night, I taught them the mantras.
At that time, the Fully Awakened One named Siddhattha appeared in the world.”
Having destroyed that darkness, he brought forth the light of knowledge.
"One of my disciples told this to me among his own disciples;
having heard this matter from them, they then reported it to me."
“A Buddha has arisen in the world, the All-Knowing One, the Leader of the World;
people follow after him, so no gain is found for us.
Buddhas appear only occasionally—those who possess vision and great renown.”
"What if I were now to see the Best of Buddhas, the Leader of the World?
Having taken my deer-skin, my bark-cloth garment, and my water-pot,
I departed from the hermitage and addressed my disciples:
“Like the udumbarika flower, like a hare’s mark in the moon,
like milk among crows, so rare is the Leader of the World.
A Buddha has arisen in the world, yet even human birth is difficult to obtain.”
"Even when both [the Buddha and his teaching] exist, hearing [the Dharma] is very difficult to obtain.
'A Buddha has arisen in the world! We shall obtain the Eye!
Come, all of you, let us go into the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One.'"
“Carrying water-pots, all clad in rough antelope skins,
and burdened with loads of matted hair, they then departed from the forest.
Looking only a yoke’s length ahead, seeking the supreme goal,”
Free from the fault of attachment, they were like fearless lions.
Having few duties, free from greed, prudent, and living in peace,
those who lived by gleaning approached the Best of Buddhas.
“When one and a half yojanas remained [of my life], a disease arose in me.
Remembering the Best of Buddhas, I passed away there.
In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, that perception which I then obtained—”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of perceiving [all beings] as Buddhas.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge:—
“‘They will paint me,’ thought I, as the painter approached;
then, taking a mirror, I examined my body.
The body appeared empty; darkness had vanished from the gloom.”
“All tangles are severed; now there is no further becoming”—thus he spoke these two verses.

Regarding that: “The barber approached to shave my hair”—at the time of the lay life, during the occasion for grooming the beard, because one fashions (*kappati*) the hair and so forth by means of cutting and other such acts, thinking, “I shall shave and fashion my hair,” the barber (*kappaka*) was the one who washed and groomed him.

He approached him. From that point on, having had his hair and beard trimmed, while examining his body in a full-length mirror by way of observing the signs of grey hair, wrinkles on the face, and so forth, he reflected upon his own body as being overcome by old age, thinking:

"Alas, my body has indeed been overcome by old age. And as he was thus reflecting, the body appeared empty to him, being devoid of such qualities as permanence, stability, pleasure, and intrinsic nature.

The body was seen and became manifest. Why? Because in darkness, when the gloom—known as unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*)—has departed, those who were blinded regarding their own bodies do not see the existing nature of foulness and so forth, and instead grasp at the non-existent aspect of beauty and so forth;
[now], in that darkness, in that place of blinding, regarding the body, through what is known as wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*)...
Through the light of knowledge, the darkness of ignorance has vanished; consequently, all "cloths" (coḷā)— so named because they are like thieves for they steal the goods of the wholesome,
because they should not be accepted by the virtuous, because they should not be embraced,
and because they are to be loathed by noble persons and lords like a piece of rags discarded in a rubbish heap— have been utterly cut off as defilements.
And because these have been utterly eradicated by the supreme path, there is now no further existence; there is no future production of renewed existence.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vītasoka is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa.
"Having abandoned the five hindrances," and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇamāsa. What is their origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Having reached maturity, one day, while the Teacher was dwelling in the forest, [he saw] a rag-robe (*paṃsukūlacīvara*).
Having hung his bow upon a branch and entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī), he entered the thicket with his bow in hand;
seeing the Teacher’s rag-robe (paṃsukūla), his mind became serene, and setting aside his bow, he paid homage to the robe while recollecting the virtues of the Buddha.
By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this current dispensation of the Buddha into a householder family in Sāvatthī.
He was reborn. It is said that on the day of his birth, all the vessels in that house were already filled with coins made of gold and precious gems.
Therefore, they gave him the name Puṇṇamāsa.

When he reached maturity, he took a wife, and after a son was born to him, he abandoned the household life, went forth into homelessness, and while living in a village monastery, he applied himself to his practice.
Exerting himself, he became one possessing the six higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Therefore it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Blessed One named Tissa, the self-become (*sayambhū*), the supreme person (*aggapuggala*);
having set aside his rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), the Conqueror entered the monastery.”
“Taking my curved bow, I wandered about for the sake of food;
having taken up my sword, I entered the forest.
There, I then saw a rag-robe caught upon the branch of a tree.”
Having set aside my bow right there and placing my joined palms upon my head,
with a clear mind and a joyful heart, and filled with abundant rapture,
I remembered the Best of Buddhas and paid homage to the rag-robe.
“Ninety-two aeons ago, I paid homage to a rag-robe wearer;
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state—this is the fruit of that homage.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having become one possessed of the six supernormal powers, he returned to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and dwelt in the charnel ground.
Not long after his arrival, the son of the Elder’s mother died.

Hearing that the Elder had arrived, the boy’s mother—fearing that the king might confiscate this property which was now without an heir—and desiring to cause him to disrobe, set out with a great retinue.
Having approached the Elder and exchanged greetings, she began to seduce him.
To make her aware of his state of being free from passion, the Elder stood in the air and, while teaching her the Dhamma by way of praising his own practice, said:
"Having abandoned the five hindrances for the sake of attaining security from bondage..."
Having taken up the mirror of the Dhamma,
my own vision of knowledge, I reflected upon this body in its entirety,
both internally and externally; within and without, the body appeared empty.
He spoke two verses.

Therein, "having abandoned the five hindrances" means having relinquished the five hindrances beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), having destroyed them through the attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
"For the sake of attaining security from bondage" means for the sake of that which is secure and unassailed by the four bondages (*yoga*) beginning with the bondage of sensual desire.
For the attainment of Nibbāna. "The mirror of the Dhamma" means a mirror consisting of the Dhamma.

Just as a mirror reveals the beauty and blemishes of the physical body to one who gazes into it, so too the mirror of the Dhamma—which consists of knowledge and vision because it brings about the comprehension of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena through insight (vipassanā)—reveals, for one practicing insight, the distinction between the defiled and purified states of phenomena, thereby serving as the means for their abandonment.
And he specifically demonstrates the excellence within the collection of names (nāmakāya). Therefore he said:
“Having taken up the mirror of the Dhamma, I examined this body of mine— all of it, both internal and external— with the vision of knowledge.”
Taking this body— a collection of phenomena that is my own selfhood— along with all its internal and external sense bases,
both inner and outer, in their entirety without exception, as the mirror of phenomena (*dhammādāsa*),
I reflected upon it and saw it with the eye of knowledge as "impermanent," "suffering," and "non-self. And while seeing thus, within myself and externally— that is, within my own continuity— ...

And in the mental continuum of others, he saw with the eye of knowledge that the body was empty—devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth—and that the physical body, which is designated as the "five aggregates," was empty.
For indeed, the entire pentad of aggregates is called "body" (*kāya*) in such passages as:
"Bhikkhus, for the fool who is shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus come to be."

By saying, “It has been seen,” he declared his full enlightenment (*añña*), demonstrating that he had fulfilled his duty by showing that whatever was to be seen in the body had been seen and nothing further remained for him to see. Thus,
having taught the Dhamma to his former wife with these verses, the Elder established her in the Refuges and the Precepts and dismissed her.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nandaka:
"Just as a noble thoroughbred horse... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Nandaka. What is their origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties by doing meritorious deeds in various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was born in a border region;
having reached maturity and living as a forest-dweller, one day, upon seeing the Teacher’s place for walking meditation, he scattered sand with a devout heart.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, in this [existence]...
During the arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in Campā into a householder’s family, and they gave him the name Nandaka.
His elder brother, however, was named Bharata. His past connection will be revealed in the immediately following story.
When both of them reached maturity, having heard that the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa had gone forth, [they thought], "Even Soṇa, though so delicately nurtured..."

“Since even he went forth, why should we not? and so they all went forth. Among them, Bharata, after increasing his insight (vipassanā) before long, became possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña).
But Nandaka, because of the strength of his defilements (kilesa), was not yet able to exert himself in insight;
he merely continued to perform the work of insight. Then the Elder Bharata, knowing his disposition, provided him with support.
Desiring to become [an arahant], he made him his attendant, left the monastery, and sitting near the road, spoke on the subject of insight (vipassanā).
At that time, as a caravan of carts was passing by, an ox harnessed to one of the carts, being unable to pull the cart out from a muddy spot, fell down.
Thereupon, the caravan leader unyoked the ox from the cart and gave it grass and water.
Having removed the exhaustion and restored his strength, he yoked the ox once more.
Then the ox, its fatigue allayed and its strength regained, lifted that cart out from the place of mud and set it upon dry land.
Thereupon, the Elder Bharata pointed this out to Nandaka, saying, "Friend Nandaka, do you see this deed of ours? To which he replied, "I see it."
When this was said, [the teacher] replied, "Reflect thoroughly upon this matter.
The other thought, "Just as this ox, its fatigue allayed, draws the load out from the place of mud, so too must I draw myself out from the mire of saṃsāra.
Taking that very object as his focus, he applied himself to the work of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the past, I was a deer-hunter in the forest wilderness;
while searching for a wind-deer, I saw a walking path.
Taking sand in the hollow of my hand, I scattered it upon that walking path.”
With a serene mind and a joyful heart, [I offered sand] to the glorious Sugata.
"In the thirty-first aeon from now, I scattered sand;
I do not know a state of misery—this is the fruit of that sand."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his realization in the presence of his elder brother, the Venerable Bharata:
“Just as a noble thoroughbred horse, having stumbled, stands firm again;”
“Having gained even greater spiritual urgency, undaunted, he bears his burden.
Thus he spoke these two verses: “Know me as one perfected in vision, a disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, a noble steed, the legitimate son of the Buddha.”
Therein, having gained even greater spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he carries the burden undaunted:

having gained spiritual urgency, thinking, "It is unbecoming to me—given my birth, strength, and energy—that I should not carry the burden that has come to me," he is undaunted, with an undaunted mind and an unshrinking heart.
Or the reading is *alīno*; it has the same meaning. *Bhiyyo* means again and again; *bhiyyosomattāya* means to an exceeding degree.
He bears and carries his own yoke and burden. The remainder is exactly as explained in the commentary on the verse of the Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin below.
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Nandaka is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Bharata.
"Come, Nandaka, let us go"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bharata. What is its origin?

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassi, having been reborn in a noble family and having reached maturity, one day this man took a pair of sandals that were pleasant to look at and soft to the touch, and while walking along, he saw the Teacher walking up and down the path. With a mind full of faith, he [offered] the sandals...
Having presented them, he said, “May the Blessed One put on these sandals; may it be for my long-term welfare and happiness.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One put on the sandals.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through successive births among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in the city of Campā within a householder family; his name was Bharata.
When he reached the age of discretion, having heard that the Elder Soṇa had gone forth, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, "Even he has gone forth!
He himself went forth, performed the preliminary duties, and while practicing insight meditation, before long became a possessor of the six supernormal powers.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men,
having emerged from his midday rest, set out upon the road, the Visionary One.
Taking up his well-crafted sandals, he embarked upon the journey.”
There I saw the Fully Awakened One, walking on foot, beautiful to behold.
Having calmed my own mind and taken off my sandals,
I placed them at his feet and spoke these words:
“Ascend, O Great Hero, Lord of Sugatas, Guide!
From this I shall obtain the fruit; may that purpose of mine be fulfilled.
The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men...”
Having mounted his sandal, he spoke these words:
“I shall praise him who gave me this sandal with his own hands out of faith; listen as I speak.
“Having understood the Buddha’s speech, all the devas have assembled;
with uplifted hearts, joyful, filled with rapture, and with palms joined in reverence:
‘By this gift of a drink, he shall become happy.’”
And fifty-five times he will exercise sovereignty over the devas.
A thousand times he will be a universal monarch (cakkavattī),
and his local sovereignty will be vast, beyond counting.
“In an immeasurable aeon from now,
one born of the Okkāka clan, named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir in the Dhammas, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma, [will be you].”
Having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
"In the world of gods or among humans, the meritorious one will be reborn;
he will obtain a vehicle resembling a celestial chariot."
“Palaces, palanquins, and chariots; well-adorned elephants;
and chariots yoked with noble steeds were always manifest to me.
Even when departing from my home, I departed by means of a chariot.”
While my hair was being cut, I attained Arhatship.
"It is a gain for me, it is well-gained by me; my trade has been successfully conducted.
Having given a single sandal, I have reached the unshakable state."
“In an immeasurable aeon from now, because I gave a drink [to the Buddha], I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that drink.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as in the standard formula]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Having become one possessed of the six supernormal powers, when his younger brother, the Elder Nandaka, had delivered his declaration of final knowledge in the manner described above, he thought:
"Now Nandaka too has become an Arahant; come, let us both go into the presence of the Teacher and report that we have lived the holy life.
Expressing this reflection to the Elder Nandaka, he said:
“Come, Nandaka, let us go to our preceptor’s presence;
we shall let out a lion’s roar in the face of the Buddha, the Most Excellent One.
Out of compassion for us, the Sage ordained us.”
Thus, when the goal had been reached—the destruction of all fetters—he spoke these two verses:
“Nandaka,” he said, as a form of address. “Come,” he said, to bring him into his own presence. “Let us go,” he said, as a statement of the action to be performed together with him.
“Of the preceptor” means of the Perfectly Enlightened One; for the Perfectly Enlightened One...

Indeed, because he contemplates the faults and virtues of the world including its devas by means of his universal eye (*samantacakkhu*) and his Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), observing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and temperaments of beings as they truly are, he especially deserves to be called "Upajjhāya" (Preceptor).
To show the purpose for which he went, [the text says]: "We shall roar the lion's roar in the presence of the Supreme Buddha."
He said: "Because he proclaims qualities as they truly are and because he utters his roar without fear, it is the 'Lion's Roar' of the Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One;

for that very reason, [it is spoken] in the presence, before, the Best, who is the most excellent of all beings—or of the Buddhas, such as the Disciple-Buddhas and others, who are the best. This is the meaning."
Furthermore, wishing to roar the lion’s roar, he spoke the verse beginning with “yāyā” to demonstrate it. Therein, “yāyā” means for which purpose;
“for the attainment of which purpose” is the meaning. “No” means our own. “Anukampāyā” means by way of compassion, [the Blessed One] caused both of us to go forth—that is, he ordained us.
“Munī” refers to the Blessed One. “So no attho anuppatto” means that purpose, the purpose of all the fetters—[has been attained].
The fruit of arhatship, which is the state of destruction, has been attained by us; the meaning is that it has been realized.
The commentary on the verses of the elder Bharata is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the elder Bhāradvāja.
“They indeed roar thus, O wise one”—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Bhāradvāja. What is its origin?
This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a noble family thirty-one aeons ago.
Having reached the age of discretion, one day, with a mind full of serene faith upon seeing the Paccekabuddha named Sumana wandering for alms, he...

He gave a ripe vallikāra fruit. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Rājagaha; he became known by his clan name as Bhāradvāja.
When he reached maturity and lived as a householder, he obtained an only son, for whom they gave the name Kaṇhadinna.
