When he had reached the age of discretion, [his father] sent him to Takkasilā, saying, "Son, go and learn a craft in the presence of such-and-such a teacher.
While traveling, on the way, he encountered a certain great elder, a disciple of the Teacher and a spiritual friend;
having heard the Dhamma from him, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and performed the preliminary duties.
Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Sambuddha named Sumana was then dwelling in Takkarāyaṃ.
Having taken a vallikāra fruit, I gave it to the Self-Existent One.”
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, when I gave that fruit back then, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Then his father, Bhāradvāja, having approached the Blessed One while he was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove and having heard the Dhamma, went forth and before long realized arhatship.
Then the son, having come to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher, saw his father sitting in the presence of the Teacher and, with a joyful heart, thought: "My father too has gone forth."
Inquiring, "Has he indeed brought the task of going forth to its ultimate conclusion?
and perceiving that his taints were exhausted, the Blessed One, desiring to make him utter a lion’s roar, asked: "It was well done by you who went forth;
but has the task of going forth been brought to its ultimate conclusion? Thereupon, Bhāradvāja, illustrating his son's attainment, said:
“Thus do the wise roar like lions in the mountain caves—
heroes who have conquered in battle, having defeated Māra along with his mount.
The Teacher has been served by me, and the Dhamma and the Saṅgha have been honored.”
“I too am joyful and glad-minded, having seen my son free from taints”—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, *nadanti* means they roar or trumpet with a fearless cry by way of proclaiming their qualities as they truly are.
*Evaṃ* indicates the manner in which what is now to be said [is expressed]. *Sappaññā* means those who have attained all wisdom through the attainment of the supreme path-wisdom.
They have attained the full expansion of all wisdom. "Heroes" (vīrā): they are heroes because they are endowed with the energy of the fourfold right exertion;

for that very reason, by crushing the entire side of defilements without exception, they have completely conquered the Māra of defilements along with his mount, the Māra of volitional formations, and the Māra of the son of a god, and thus they roar, being possessed of wisdom—this is the connection [of the words].

Having thus demonstrated the lion’s roar by means of the conquest of what was to be conquered, he now spoke the second verse, beginning with “The Teacher has been served by me,” in order to demonstrate that same roar by means of the perfect fulfillment of what is to be fulfilled and the attainment of what is desired. Therein, “The Teacher has been served by me” means:
my Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, has been served by me through the practice of the instructions and exhortations exactly as they were taught.
The intention is that [the Dhamma] has been attended to, but the legal matters concerning the Dhamma have not been purified.

"The Dhamma and the Saṅgha have been honored" means that the ninefold supramundane Dhamma and the Noble Saṅgha—who have attained the path through practice according to the Dhamma and who have reached the commonality of virtue and view—have been honored and revered by me.
And I am gratified and joyful; having seen my son who is free from taints (*anāsava*), [I rejoice].
Having seen one whose taints were entirely exhausted, because of that vision, I too was gladdened and satisfied with spiritual joy (*nirāmisā pīti*);
for this reason, I became well-disposed through spiritual gladness (*nirāmisena somanassena*). This is the meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhāradvāja is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Kaṇhadinna "Those who have waited upon the True Men"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kaṇhadinna. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family ninety-four aeons ago from now.
Having been reborn and reached the state of discernment, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sobhita;

with a devout heart, he made an offering of *puṇṇāga* flowers. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Rājagaha, where he received the name Kaṇhadinna and reached maturity.
Urged on by the excellence of his supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), he approached the Dhamma General (*Dhammasenāpati*), and having heard the Dhamma, attained faith.
Having gone forth and developed insight (*vipassanā*), he reached Arahantship. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Fully Enlightened One named Sobhita then dwelt on Cittakūṭa;”
Having taken a mountain *punnāga* tree, I worshipped the Self-Existent One (*Svayaṃbhū*).
Because I worshipped the Buddha ninety-four eons ago, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his realization:
“I have attended upon true men; the Dhamma has been heard by me repeatedly.”
Having heard it, I shall practice the straight path that leads to the deathless:
“For one like me, who has struck down the craving for existence, craving for existence no longer exists;
it has not existed in the past, it will not exist in the future, and it does not exist in the present.”
He spoke two verses.
Therein, "upāsita" means served; served by means of the service of practice.

"Sappurisā" means persons endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth, namely noble individuals such as the Elder Sāriputta and others. By this, he [demonstrates] his own attainment of the first pair of wheels.
He shows this. For, without dwelling in a suitable locality, reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*) is not possible.
"The Dhammas heard" refers to the teachings associated with the Truths, Dependent Origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and so forth, which have been grasped by means of the ear-door.
By this, while showing his own great learning (*bāhusacca*), he demonstrates the perfection of the latter two wheels [of the Dhamma]. "Frequently" (*abhiṇhaso*) means many times, not occasionally.
The time. And this phrase should also be connected with the words “having waited upon true persons. “Having heard, I shall practice the straight path leading to the deathless”:

having heard those teachings, having discerned the aforementioned material and immaterial phenomena there according to their specific characteristics and so forth, and having gradually increased insight, [I shall follow] that straight path which leads to and establishes one in Nibbāna, the state immersed in the deathless.
I have entered upon and attained the Noble Eightfold Path.
"While I was struck by the craving for existence"— that is, while I was struck and afflicted by the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) throughout the beginningless cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*),
or else, while the craving for existence had been struck down by the supreme path— "the craving for existence no longer exists in me."
Therefore, now once again, I have no lust for existence (*bhavarāga*).

"It was not, it will not be, and it does not exist for me now"—even though previously, during the time of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and during the time of a trainee (*sekkha*), I had lust for existence, from the moment of attaining the supreme path (*aggamagga*) onwards, it has not been, it did not exist;
furthermore, it will not be for me in the future, and even now, at this very moment, it does not exist.
And it exists for me, yet it is not found; the meaning is that it has been abandoned.

By the mention of "lust for existence" (*bhavarāga*) alone, the absence of pride and the other fetters is also stated here because they are associated with it; thus, he demonstrates the complete exhaustion of the fetter of existence.
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Kaṇhadinna is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Migasira.
"Since I went forth"—this is the verse of the Venerable Migasira Thera. What is its origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a mind full of faith, offered him a bundle of *kusa* grass.
Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he took rebirth in this current dispensation of a Buddha within a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala.
Because he was born under the constellation Migasira, he received the name Migasira.
Upon reaching maturity, having attained proficiency in the sciences and crafts of the brahmins, he learned a spell called Chavasīsamanta, by reciting which—
Even for those who had died three years prior, he would strike their heads with his fingernail and know, "This being has been reborn in such-and-such a place.
Not desiring the life of a householder, he went forth into the wandering life of a paribbājaka;
and traveling about, honored, revered, and receiving gains by virtue of that knowledge, he arrived at Sāvatthī and went into the presence of the Teacher. Then, regarding himself—
Displaying his supernatural power, he said, "Sir Gotama, I know the place where the dead are reborn.

When asked, "But how do you know? he replied, "By having corpses' heads brought, reciting a mantra, and tapping the skull with my fingernail, I know their respective places of rebirth, such as hell and so forth. Then the Blessed One [said to him]:
Having had the skull of a monk who had attained final Nibbāna brought, he said, "Tell me first the destination of him whose skull this is.
After reciting a mantra over that skull and tapping it with his fingernail, he could see neither its end nor its limit.
Then, when the Teacher said, "You are not able, wanderer," he replied, "I shall investigate further."
Having said, "That much," he turned it over and over again, yet he still did not see it.
For how could he know the destination of one whose taints were exhausted by means of an outsider's manual? Then sweat broke out from his head and his armpits.
Feeling ashamed, he stood silent. The Teacher said, "Are you weary, wanderer? He replied, "Yes, I am weary; I do not know this one's destination."
“I know; you too should know. Having said, “I know this, and I know even more than this,” he replied, “He has attained Nibbāna. The wanderer said, “Give me this knowledge.

[The Master] said, “In that case, go forth,” and having ordained him, first directed him toward the meditation subject of calm (*samatha*), and then toward the super-knowledges (*abhiññā*) of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
He instructed him in the practice of insight (vipassanā). While performing the work of insight, he attained Arahatship before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Of the Blessed One Kassapa, while the brahmin was living the holy life;”
With a clear mind and a joyful heart, I gave eight blades of *kusa* grass.
In this very same eon, I gave those eight blades of *kusa*;
I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state—this is the fruit of the eight blades of *kusa*.
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [the rest as in the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he then declared his realization:
“Since I went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
“Being liberated, I rose up; I transcended the realm of sense-desire.
While Brahmā was looking on, my mind was then liberated.
“My liberation is unshakable,” he said, “through the destruction of all fetters.”—Thus he spoke these two verses.

In this context, "since I went forth into the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One" means from the time I first went forth into the dispensation of the Blessed Buddha; that is, starting from the moment of my ordination.

"Rising up while being liberated" means that, first of all, while being liberated from the side of defilement by means of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), I arose through hearing the Dhamma of purification (*vodāna*). Thus...
Rising up, I transcended the realm of sense-desire (*kāmadhātu*) by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*), and thus I completely passed beyond the realm of sense-desire.

While Brahmā was looking on, my mind was liberated from that [realm]. Because of his being the supreme and most excellent one in the world including the devas, through the application of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the Buddha, the Blessed One—the Brahmā—[thought]: "This clansman, in my teaching..."
While he was observing, "Having gone forth, how indeed does one practice?", after the attainment of the path of non-returning,
my mind was completely liberated from all defilements through the attainment of the supreme path. "Unshakable is my liberation" means that because my mind is thus liberated,
there is the destruction and total exhaustion of all fetters.
Thus, "My liberation is unshakable," he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Migasira is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Sivaka.
“Impermanent are dwellings,” this is the verse of the Venerable Sīvaka Thera. What is its origin?
This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various births, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having reached maturity, one day, upon seeing the Blessed One wandering for alms, his mind became filled with serene faith.

Taking a bowl and filling it with boiled rice, he gave it to him. By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in a brahmin family in Rājagaha; his name was Sivaka.
When he reached maturity and attained proficiency in the sciences and arts, due to his inclination toward renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth as a wandering ascetic.
Having gone forth and wandering about, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, went forth.
Performing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"While wandering in search [of alms], Of Vipassi, the Great Sage..."
Seeing an empty bowl, I filled it with boiled rice gruel.
Because I gave that alms-food ninety-one eons ago, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that rice gruel.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he then declared his final knowledge:
“Houses are impermanent, again and again in various places;”
Seeking the house-builder, one undergoes birth again and again, which is suffering.
"O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no more houses;
all your rafters are broken, and your ridgepole is shattered."
"A mind made free from boundaries will scatter right here"—
thus he spoke these two verses. Therein, "the houses are impermanent" means that in each respective birth,
the houses— the dwellings of the self (attabhāva)— arising again and again, are not eternal, unstable, temporary, and short-lived.
"Seeking the house-builder": the intention is that for so long he has wandered about searching for the builder of this house of individual existence, namely, the carpenter who is craving (*taṇhā*).
"Suffering is birth again and again": this is the statement of the reason for seeking the house-builder;
because birth—being mixed with old age, sickness, and death—is painful to undergo again and again.
And that [desire] does not cease until he is seen; therefore, the meaning is that one wanders about searching for him.
"The house-builder has been seen": now, however, by means of that eye of noble-path knowledge through which he can be seen, the house-builder has been seen.
"Again to a house": again, in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), to what is called a personal existence (attabhāva).
"You shall not build my house; you will not build it. All your rafters are broken"—all the rafters of your defilements (*kilesa*) without exception have been shattered by me.

"The ridge-pole is split asunder"—the central pillar known as ignorance (*avijjā*), which serves as the foundation for the house of your personal existence (*attabhāva*) that you would now attempt to build, has been broken.
"My mind is made free from boundaries"—my mind has been rendered devoid of limits for the future.
It has been brought to the state of non-arising. For that very reason, it will be dispersed right here; it will perish in this very existence;
the meaning is that it will cease with the cessation of the final consciousness.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sivaka is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Upavāṇa "Arahant, Sugata"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Upavāṇa. What is its origin?
It is said that he was born into a poor family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara; having reached maturity, after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, [he...]
Having taken the relic, when stupas seven *yojanas* in height and made of the seven precious gems had been constructed by humans, devas, *nāgas*, *garuḷas*, *kumbhaṇḍas*, *yakkhas*, and *gandhabbas*,
he tied his own well-washed upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) to the tip of a bamboo pole, made it into a banner, and performed an offering there. Taking that [banner],
the *yakkha* general named Abhisammataka was appointed by the devas for the purpose of guarding the worship of the cetiya.
Remaining invisible and supporting the cetiya in the air, he circumambulated it three times.

Upon seeing this, his mind became even more filled with serene faith. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; having reached maturity, he received the name Upavāṇa.

Having seen the Buddha’s majesty at the acceptance of the Jeta Grove, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight meditation, attained arahantship and became possessed of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena...”
Having blazed like a mass of fire, the Perfectly Enlightened One has attained final Nibbāna.
Great crowds of people having gathered and paid homage to the Tathāgata,
they set their minds upon the Sugata and enshrined his body.
“Having performed the funeral rites for the body, they enshrined the relics there;
all those beings, including gods and humans, erected a stupa for the Buddha.
The first was made of gold, and the second was made of jewels.”
The third was made of silver, the fourth of crystal.
There, the fifth was made of ruby,
the sixth of emerald, and everything above was made of every kind of gem.
“The base was made of jewels, the railing was made of gems;
the stupa was entirely made of gold, rising a league in height.
Then the devas, having gathered there, consulted together.”
“We too shall build a stupa for the Protector of the World,
the Tathāgata. Since there are no separate relics and his body remains as a single mass,
we shall construct a casing for this Buddha-stupa.”
“The devas increased another league with the seven jewels;
the stupa was two leagues in height, and it dispelled the darkness.
Then the nāgas, having gathered there, deliberated together as one.”
Both humans and gods built that stupa for the Buddha.
"May we not be heedless; may we, together with the world of gods, be diligent.
We too shall build a stupa for the Protector of the World, the Tathāgata."
“Having gathered together indranīla gems, great blue sapphires, and also jotirasa jewels, they covered the Buddha’s stupa.
The entire Buddha-cetiya, for as far as it extended, was made of jewels.”
At that time, it rose three yojanas high and brought forth light.
Then the garuḍas gathered together and consulted one another;
humans, devas, and nāgas all performed worship to the Buddha.
“Let us not be heedless; let us be heedful along with the world of devas.
We too shall build a stupa for the Protector of the World, the Tathāgata.
They constructed a stupa made entirely of jewels and fashioned a casing for it.
They increased the length of the Buddha-cetiya by another yojana.
“The Buddha-thūpa, four yojanas in height, shines resplendent;
it illuminates all directions like the risen sun with its hundred rays.”
Then the kumbhaṇḍas gathered together and deliberated on one side,
as did the humans, the gods, the nāgas, and likewise the garuḷas.
They constructed a supreme stūpa for the Best of Pratyekabuddhas.
“Let us not be heedless, but remain diligent along with the devas.
We too shall build a stupa for the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World;
we shall cover the long Buddha-cetiya with jewels.”
“They increased the length of the Buddha’s cetiya by one yojana;
the stupa, five yojanas in height, then shone forth.
The yakkhas, having gathered there, then deliberated together.”
Humans, devas, nāgas, garuḷas, and kumbhaṇḍas built a supreme stūpa for the most excellent Pratyekabuddha, [saying]:
"May we not be heedless; may we, together with the devas, be diligent."
“We too shall build a stupa for the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World;
we shall cover the long Buddha-cetiya with crystal.
They increased the length of that Buddha-cetiya by another yojana.
At that time, the stupa, four yojanas in height, shone with radiance.
Then the gandhabbas gathered together and deliberated in one place,
as did the humans, deities, nāgas, kumbhaṇḍas, and likewise the garuḷas.
“Everyone has built a stupa for the Buddha; we alone have not done so here.
We too shall build a stupa for the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World.
Having constructed seven altars, they fashioned a banner and a parasol.
At that time, the gandhabbas constructed a stupa made entirely of gold.
Seven yojanas in height, the stupa then shone forth;
day and night were no longer discernible, for there was light at all times.
“The moon, the sun, and the stars do not outshine its radiance;
even a lamp did not burn for a hundred leagues around it.
At that time, whatever humans there were who worshipped the stupa,”
They do not climb the stupa; they toss [the offerings] into the air.
"A yakkha appointed by the devas, named Abhisammata, offers a banner or a garland of flowers above."
“They do not see that spirit; they see only the garland as it goes by.
Seeing things thus as they go, all shall go to a happy destination.
Those who are hostile toward the Word and those who have faith in the Teaching—”
Desiring to see the miracle, humans worship the stupa.
"At that time, I was a hired laborer in the city of Haṃsavatī;
seeing the people filled with joy, I then thought thus:"
“Sublime is the Blessed One,
toward whose relic-shrine these people are so joyful that they do not tire of performing acts of merit.
I too shall perform an act of merit for the Protector of the World, the Neutral One.”
“In the future, I shall be an heir to his Dhamma.
“I had my washerman thoroughly clean my upper garment;
having fastened it to the tip of a bamboo pole, I raised it as a banner in the sky.”
“Having seized my beloved banner, it was carried away into the sky;
seeing the banner fluttering in the wind, I gave rise to even greater laughter.
Having settled my mind there in faith, I approached the ascetic.”
Having paid homage to that bhikkhu, I asked about the result of the banner.
Ānanda spoke to me, generating joy within me:
"You shall experience the result of that banner at all times."
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—a fourfold army—will always attend upon you; this is the fruit of giving a banner.
Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-adorned drums [shall likewise attend you].”
“They will always attend upon you; this is the fruit of the gift of a banner.
“Eighty-six thousand women, beautifully adorned, wearing variegated garments and ornaments, with jewels and earrings fastened upon them,”
“With long, lotus-like eyes, beautiful, well-proportioned and slender-waisted, women shall always attend upon you; this is the fruit of the gift of banners.
For thirty thousand eons, you will delight in the world of the gods.”
Eighty times you will exercise sovereignty as the Lord of Devas.
A thousand times you will be a universal monarch (cakravartin),
and your regional kingdoms will be vast beyond counting.
“In a hundred thousand aeons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a teacher in the world.
Having passed away from the deva-world, impelled by the root of his white merit,”
“Bound by your meritorious deed, you shall become a kinsman of Brahmā.
Having abandoned eighty million [pieces of gold], along with many slaves and laborers,
you will go forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Gotama.”
“Having propitiated the Perfectly Enlightened One, Gotama, the bull among the Sakyans,
you shall become a disciple of the Teacher by the name of Upavāṇa.
The karma performed during one hundred thousand [aeons] has shown its fruit here to me.”
“Like an arrow released from a bow, I have extinguished my defilements.
While I was a wheel-turning monarch, the lord of the four continents,
banners were constantly raised for three *yojanas* all around me.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons ago, whatever deed I performed then, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of the gift of a banner.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Now, the Venerable Upavāṇa was the Blessed One’s attendant. At that time, a wind ailment arose in the Blessed One.
A brahmin named Devahita, who was a lay friend of the Elder, was living in Sāvatthī;
he provided the Elder with the four requisites. Then, the Venerable Upavāṇa, having dressed himself and taken his bowl and robe, [went] to him...

He approached the brahmin’s residence. Knowing that the Elder had come for some other purpose, the brahmin said, "Venerable sir, please tell us what you require. The Elder, explaining his purpose to the brahmin, said:
"The Worthy One, the Well-Gone-One in the world, the Sage, is afflicted by a wind ailment."
“If there is warm water, O brahmin, give it to the Sage.
He then spoke these two verses: “Honored by those worthy of honor, Revered by those worthy of reverence, Worshiped by those worthy of worship— I desire that he be given [this offering].”

The meaning of this is as follows: he who is honored by the gods such as Sakka and others, and by the Brahmās such as Mahābrahmā and others—all those worthy of worship among those to be worshipped in this world;
who is honored by Bimbisāra, the Kosalan King, and others—all those worthy of respect among those to be respected;

who is honored by the Great Seers and the Arahants whose taints are destroyed—all those worthy of veneration among those to be venerated; and who is "Arahant" because of being far removed from defilements, and because of his beautiful departure [from saṃsāra], and so forth.

"The Sugata, the All-Knowing Sage, my Teacher, the God of Gods, the Sakka of Sakkas, the Brahmā of Brahmās—he has now become afflicted with a disease caused by the winds, due to the winds, on account of the disturbance of the winds.
If, Brahmin, there is warm water, I wish for it to be brought and used to pacify this wind-affliction. Having heard this, the Brahmin—
He offered the Blessed One warm water and medicine suitable for it that was resistant to wind; by this, the Teacher’s illness was allayed.
The Blessed One then expressed his appreciation for him.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Upavāna is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Isidatta "Seen by me"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Isidatta. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds in various states of existence while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having been reborn and attained the state of full maturity, he took a fan and made an offering to the Bodhi tree.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a merchant family in the Sunāparanta country.
Having received the name Isidatta, upon reaching adulthood, he witnessed the miracle performed by the Teacher when accepting the sandalwood pavilion.
With a serene mind, he approached the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, became a stream-enterer while still living at home.
A benevolent deity, out of compassion for his welfare, exhorted him:
"I have seen lay disciples who uphold the Dhamma, declaring that sensual pleasures are impermanent."
“Infatuated and passionately attached to jeweled earrings, they have expectations regarding their children and wives.
‘Surely they do not know the Dhamma here, for they say that sensual pleasures are impermanent;
yet they lack the strength to cut through their passion, and therefore they remain bound to children, wives, and wealth.’”
He spoke two verses. Regarding them:
"I have seen lay followers who uphold the Dhamma, proclaiming that sensual pleasures are impermanent"—here, I have seen certain lay followers who uphold the Dhamma of the scriptures;
because they uphold the Dhamma of the scriptures, they say, "These sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change."
While preaching the Dhamma connected with the danger in sensual pleasures, they themselves were passionately attached to jewels and earrings,
and were full of longing for their children and wives; being thus inflamed by intense passion for jewels and earrings—
or for earrings set with jewels— and having acquired affection for their sons, daughters, and wives, they spoke otherwise.
The meaning is: "I have seen them doing otherwise. "Because" (*yataḥ*) means:

since those lay followers are passionately attached to jewels and earrings, and are full of longing for their children and wives, therefore they certainly (*addhā*), that is, unilaterally (*ekamsena*), do not know the Dhamma as it truly is in this teaching of the Buddha. Thus...
And it has truly been said: "Sensual pleasures are impermanent. Furthermore, the intention is that the nature of beings (*sattapakati*) is of diverse characteristics.

And because they do not possess the power to cut off passion—since those lay followers lack such power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*) to sever or completely eradicate passion—therefore, for that reason, they are bound by craving and dependent upon their children and wives.
“‘They cling to wealth and do not relinquish it’—all this the deity spoke by way of another pretext, referring specifically to that same lay follower.
Having heard this, the lay follower was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); he went forth and before long attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
‘At the supreme tree of enlightenment of the Blessed One Vipassi...’”
Sumana took a fan and [honored] the supreme Abīji Bodhi tree.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because of this supreme Abīji Bodhi tree, I do not recall ever being born in an evil state; this is the fruit of fanning."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, he spoke these very verses while declaring his final knowledge (*aññā*).
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of the Elder Isidatta.
5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sambulakaccāna "Devo ca...
etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sambulakaccāna. What is his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds throughout various existences after having fulfilled his obligations under previous Buddhas, was born into a noble family ninety-four aeons ago.
Having been reborn and reached the age of discretion, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsi emerging from cessation and wandering for alms;

with a mind full of faith, he offered him a palm fruit. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a householder’s family in the kingdom of Magadha as "Sambula."
Having received the name Kaccāna because of his Kaccāna clan, he became known as Sambula-Kaccāna.
When he reached maturity, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and gained faith, he went forth into homelessness.
He dwelt near the Himālaya mountains, performing the work of insight meditation in a mountain cave named Bheravā. Then, one day—
A great, untimely cloud—consisting of hundreds and thousands of layers—arose, beginning to rain, thundering, flashing forth streaks of lightning, and rumbling;
thunderbolts struck. Hearing that sound, hyenas, jackals, forest buffaloes, elephants, and other creatures, terrified and trembling, let out cries of fear.
But the Elder, because he had applied himself to insight (vipassanā), was indifferent toward both body and life.
Free from horripilation and no longer reflecting on that [past event], he performed the work of insight (vipassanā) alone.

With his mind concentrated through the departure of the heat and the attainment of a favorable climate, he immediately accelerated his insight and reached Arahantship together with the higher knowledges (abhiññā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One named Sataraṃsī, the Self-Existent, the Unconquered;”
Having emerged from seclusion, I went forth to seek alms.
Seeing the Bull among Men with fruit in my hand, I approached him;
with a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave him a palm fruit.
“In ninety-four aeons ago, the fruit that I gave then— I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, he was filled with joy and, uttering an inspired exclamation as he declared his final knowledge, said:
“The sky is raining, the sky is thundering;
and I dwell alone in a fearsome cave.”
As I dwelt alone in that terrifying cave, there was no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation.
This is my natural state: that while I am alone in a terrifying cave, [there is no fear].
"While dwelling [in this state], there is no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation"—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "the god rains, the god gurgles" means that the god, the cloud, rains; "gurgles" (gaḷagaḷā) [is the sound of the rain].
And the meaning is that he roars while doing so; for this is an imitation of his roaring. "And I dwell alone in a fearsome cave" means:
"I, alone and without companion, dwell in this mountain cave which is full of terror;
for me, being in such a state, there is no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation"—that is to say, no mental agitation known as terror.
There is no fear caused by that, nor any trembling of the body, nor even the mere bristling of the hair. Why is that?

He states the reason for this: "This is my natural state. For one who has not fully understood the basis [of fear] would necessarily experience fear and so forth due to the presence of unabandoned desire and lust;
however, I have fully understood it in every respect, and desire and lust for it have been abandoned.

"Because it has been utterly cut off, there is an absence of fear and so forth; this is my nature (*dhammatā*), this is my own essential character (*dhammasabhāva*)," he thus explained his higher knowledge (*aññā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sambulakaccāna is finished.
6. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nitaka.
"Whose mind is like a rock?"—this is the verse of the Venerable Nitaka Thera. What is its origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, lived as a garden-keeper in the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
One day, seeing the Blessed One traveling through the air, he felt a heart full of serene faith.
He desired to give a coconut fruit. The Teacher, wishing to favor him, stood in mid-air and accepted it.
Having given it, he experienced a sublime sense of joy and gladness.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala, where he received the name Nitaka.
Having reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, acquired faith, went forth, and taking up a meditation subject, dwelt in the forest.
Striving diligently, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a monastery attendant;”
I saw the stainless Buddha walking along the dust-free path.
Having taken a coconut fruit, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas;
standing in the air, the one of great glory accepted it.
“Producing joy for me and bringing happiness in this very life,
having given the fruit of the Buddha with a mind of clear confidence,
I then attained rapture and vast, supreme bliss.”
A jewel indeed arises, being produced here and there.
"In the ninety-first aeon, the fruit that I gave back then—I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving that fruit."
“My divine eye is purified, I am skilled in concentration;
I have reached the perfection of direct knowledge—this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements are burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But after [the Elder] had attained arahantship and was dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna while other elders were doing likewise,
the Elder Padhānapariggāhaka went to that forest region and, for the purpose of inquiring after the monks living there,
recited the first verse beginning with "To whom is the mountain-like... and so forth.
191. Regarding the question, "Whose mind is like a rock, stable and unshakable?":
among the monks dwelling in this forest region, whose mind—having attained the supreme fruit—is like a mountain made of solid rock;
because it is free from all agitation and has reached mastery, it remains stable and is not shaken or moved by any of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
Now, in order to show its state of immovability along with the reason for it, the passage beginning with "dispassionate" (*viratta*) was stated.

Therein, "dispassionate toward things that provoke passion" means: by means of the Noble Path, which is termed dispassion (*virāga*), it is dispassionate toward those phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) that are provocative of passion and serve as causes for the arising of lust;
the meaning is that passion has been completely eradicated therein. "Toward what provokes agitation" means toward what is a basis for aversion (*paṭigha*); in all [such cases]...
Regarding the grounds for malice: "he does not become angry" means he does not feel ill will nor undergoes a transformation of mind.

"Whose mind is thus developed"—that noble person whose consciousness and mind have been developed by way of the aforementioned method through the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*)—from where shall suffering come to him?
From where shall suffering approach that person, whether from a sentient being (*satta*) or from conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)?
The meaning is that for one such as this, suffering does not exist.

(192) Thus, having resolved the matter asked about in an indefinite manner, the Elder Nītaka answered with the second verse beginning with "My mind is like a rock," applying it to himself and thereby declaring his attainment of *aññā* (full knowledge). That [verse] has already been explained in its literal sense.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nītaka is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Soṇa Poṭiriyaputta:
"It is not yet time to sleep. This verse belongs to the Venerable Soṇa Poṭiriyaputta. What is his origin?
Having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, he lived as a forest-dweller during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi; one day...
Seeing the Teacher, with a mind full of faith, he gave a *kurañjiya* fruit to the Teacher.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Kapilavatthu as the son of a village headman named Poṭiriya;
his name was Soṇa. When he reached maturity, [he entered the service] of King Bhaddiya the Sākiyan.
He became the commander-in-chief. Then, when King Bhaddiya had gone forth in the manner described above, the commander-in-chief thought, "The king himself has indeed gone forth;
what use have I for the household life? and so he went forth. Having gone forth, however, he lived delighting in sleep and did not apply himself to meditation.
While the Blessed One was staying at Anupiya in the Mango Grove, he caused his own radiance to shine forth [and summoned him].
Therefore, having aroused mindfulness, he exhorted him with this verse:
“This night, garlanded with stars, is not yet for sleep;
for one who understands, this very night is for keeping watch.”
“If an elephant were to follow me as I fell from the back of an elephant, it would be better for me to die in battle than to live defeated. He spoke these two verses.
Therein, “it is not yet time to sleep, for the night is garlanded with stars” refers to the ninth [occasion], which is free from the eight inopportune moments (*akṣaṇa*).

For a person of wise nature who has found this moment and stands firm, as long as arahantship has not come into his hands, this night adorned with constellations is not a time for sleeping or slumbering; it is not a time for sleep.
On the contrary, this very night is for watchfulness; "it is a time for the discerning"—thus, this is called "night" for both humans and animals.
"Because it is through the attainment of sleeplessness that one especially recognizes within oneself a practice characterized by silence at the proper time;
therefore, it is desired by the wise person who understands that they must apply themselves precisely to the practice of wakefulness.
Having heard this, Soṇa, his mind deeply stirred, established shame and fear of wrongdoing and resolved upon the practice of living in the open air.
While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he spoke the second verse:
"It is as if fallen from the back of an elephant. In this context, *avapatita* means fallen face-down, that is, fallen with feet upward and face downward.
*Kuñjaro ce anukkameti* means "if the elephant were to advance. This is what is meant: when I had mounted the elephant and entered the battle...

"If I had fallen from the back of the elephant and been crushed to death by that elephant in battle at that time, that death would have been better for me than to live now defeated by the defilements; that [former] death was better.
While speaking this verse, he intensified his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the past, I was a deer-hunter wandering through the forest;
there I saw the stainless Buddha, who has gone beyond all phenomena.
Taking a kurañjiya fruit, I gave it to the Supreme Buddha.”
With my own hands, full of faith toward that Tathāgata, a field of merit, I gave that fruit.
For thirty-one eons from then on, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of giving that fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, he recited both verses—those spoken by the Teacher and those spoken by himself—beginning with “Falling from the back of the elephant,” and so forth. Thus, this itself became his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Soṇa Koṭivīsaputta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Nisabha "Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Nisabha. What is its origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having been reborn and reached the state of discernment, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms and, with a devout heart, gave him a kapittha fruit.
By that meritorious deed, wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a noble family in the Koliya country;
having received the name Nisabha, upon reaching maturity, [he became the leader] of the Sākyans and Koliyans.
Having seen the power of the Buddha in battle, he gained faith, went forth, and on that very day attained arahantship.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"The Sambuddha, golden-hued, the recipient of offerings..."
As he was setting out on his journey, I gave him a wood-apple fruit.
"In the ninety-first aeon ago, because I gave that fruit, I have not known a state of misery; this is the fruit of giving fruit."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, however, seeing his companion monks spending their time in negligence, he exhorted them:
“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are lovely and delightful...”
“Having gone forth from the home out of faith, one may become an ender of suffering”—thus he spoke the first verse.
Its meaning is as follows: because of the nature of being dear to the foolish worldling, and because of the nature of being pleasant and agreeable in what is dear...
Having abandoned, relinquished, and renounced the five strands of sensual pleasure— the delightful objects of form and so forth— which are the divisions of desire,
a person of discerning nature goes forth from home into homelessness out of faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem;
and from the time of his going forth, by striving and exerting himself, he becomes one who brings an end to the suffering of saṃsāra.
"May it be so in each existence. Having thus exhorted those bhikkhus, he said, "Do not think that this one dwells merely instructing others while he himself is a non-doer";
and revealing his own state of practice, he declared:
"I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;..."
"I await my time, mindful and clearly comprehending"—with this second verse, he declared his final knowledge (*añña*). In that context, "I do not rejoice in death" means I do not long for death.
"I do not rejoice in life," however, is the statement of the reason for that; because I do not rejoice in life...

"Therefore, I do not delight in death. For whoever accumulates and amasses the formative forces of defilement for the sake of future birth, aging, and death, such a person—delighting in the production of renewed existence—by the very necessity of that cause, is said to delight even in his own death, because the cause has not been abandoned.
But one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), having utterly abandoned all phenomena leading to accumulation...

Established in the nature of things that lead to diminution and having fully understood the basis [of existence], one who does not delight in life at all is said to "not delight even in death" because the very cause [for such attachment] has been thoroughly abandoned. Therefore it was said: "I do not delight in death; I do not delight in life.
If this is so, then for one whose taints are destroyed, there is both a longing for final Nibbāna and a persistence until that final Nibbāna.

How so? He said: “I await the time, mindful and clearly comprehending. Since the parinibbāna of the defilements has been accomplished, having attained the full development of mindfulness and wisdom, being mindful and clearly comprehending, I merely await the time for the parinibbāna of the aggregates;
I dwell watching for it and awaiting it, but I have no longing for either death or life.
Because it was eradicated by the path of arahantship itself.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nisabha is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Usabha.
The verses beginning with "Resembling the young shoots of the *ambapalla* tree" belong to the Venerable Elder Usabha. What is their origin?

This [Venerable] also, having performed his duties under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds here and there in various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having attained maturity, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms, and with a mind full of serene confidence—

He gave a *kosamba* fruit. By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance within the royal Sakyan family at Kapilavatthu.
Having received the name Usabha and having reached maturity, he witnessed the majesty of the Buddha during a gathering of the Teacher’s kinsmen;
having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness. From the time of his going forth...
Without performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he spent his days delighting in social company and passed the entire night in sleep.

One day, having fallen asleep with unguarded mindfulness and a lack of clear comprehension, he dreamed that he had shaved off his hair and beard, donned a robe the color of mango shoots, and sat upon the neck of an elephant as he entered the city for alms; while he was right there among the people...
Seeing them arrive, he descended from the elephant’s back out of shame; upon seeing himself [in that state], he woke up.

With a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arising at the thought, “I have seen such a dream while sleeping heedlessly and without clear comprehension,” he applied insight (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship*. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Then, as the god of gods, the bull among men, Kakudha,
was proceeding along the highway as if in full splendor, I offered him a *kosamba* fruit.
Thirty-one eons ago, that is the fruit of the offering I gave then.”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving the fruit [of my gift].
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me… [as before] …the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then the Elder, taking the dream as he had seen it as a goad, because he had attained Arahatship, declared his own state of knowledge (Aññā) by way of praising that very dream:
“Placing my robe upon my shoulder, which was as green as an ambapalla leaf,
I sat upon the neck of an elephant and entered the village for alms.
Having descended from the elephant’s back, I then experienced a sense of spiritual urgency.”
"Thus, being elated at that time, I attained the destruction of the taints"—with these words he spoke two verses.

Therein, "having placed upon his shoulder the robe resembling the sprout of a mango" means having placed on his shoulder—that is, having made the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga)—the robe which was the color of coral and had the appearance of a mango sprout. "The village" refers to his own royal capital [placed] upon the neck of the elephant.
While seated, I entered for alms; as soon as I had entered, being gazed upon by the great multitude, I descended from the back of the elephant and stood there, whereupon I awoke.
Having awakened, I then experienced a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking: "This has arisen because I fell asleep while being unmindful and lacking clear comprehension.
Others, however, say: "Even though he was a king, during the night..."
They say that having seen this dream, when the night had turned to dawn, he mounted the back of an elephant and wandered through the city streets;
remembering that dream, he descended from the elephant’s back, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
Having attained *arahantship*, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) and spoke these verses. "Ditto" refers to that period of time during his reign as king.
The construction is: being intoxicated by pride in birth, pride in wealth, and so forth, he did not attain a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Usabha is finished.
10. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Kappaṭakura.
"This is Kappaṭa" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kappaṭakura. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having reached maturity, one day he [saw] the Blessed One on the bank of a certain river named Vinatā.
Seeing him sitting at the foot of a tree, he offered worship with *ketaka* flowers with a devout mind.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a poor family in Sāvatthī.
Until he reached maturity, knowing no other means of livelihood, he lived there clad in rags from dust-heaps, carrying an alms-bowl in his hand.
There he wandered about searching for *kura* grass, and thus he became known as Kappaṭakura.
When he reached maturity, he made his living by selling grass.

One day, having gone to the forest to cut grass, he saw a certain elder (*thera*) whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). Approaching him and paying homage, he sat down. The elder taught him the Dhamma.
He preached. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and thought, "What use have I for this difficult livelihood?
He went forth into homelessness and placed his own rag-robe (*kappaṭacoḷa*) in one spot.
Whenever dissatisfaction arose within him, by looking at that rag-robe, his dissatisfaction would vanish and he would experience a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Acting in this way—
He went forth seven times. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then one day, while the monk Kappaṭakura was sitting at the edge of the assembly in the Dhamma Hall, he fell asleep. Addressing him as a reproach, the Blessed One said:
“This is Kappaṭa, Kappaṭakura, In the deep, heavy darkness.”
In the village of Amataghaṭikā, Dhammika, who was merely a carrier of pots, attempted to take away the meditative absorptions (jhānas) [of his teacher].
[The teacher said: “Do not shake your rag, O Kappaṭa! I shall not strike you on the ear!
For you, Kappaṭa, did not realize even a mere measure [of the danger], as you were nodding off in the midst of the Saṅgha.”
He spoke two verses.
Therein, "this rag-robe" (*kappaṭa*) refers to the rag-robe wearer, the monk. "This is my rag-robe;
having put this on, I shall live however I may"—such is the unwholesome thought of desire that has arisen, while [the robe] is worn out and excessively heavy.
While my vessel of the Deathless rains the Deathless here and there from my jar of the Deathless, proclaiming with such words as, “I have attained the Deathless; I instruct,
I teach the Dhamma,” and “In this world that has become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless,” as I pour down the rain of the Dhamma-Deathless,
those who have set foot [upon it] are able to attain the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and cultivate both mundane and supramundane absorptions.
"This is my teaching (sāsana), wherein the path of meditation has been prepared and the path of cultivation has been established.
Nevertheless, addressing Kappaṭakura— who, though possessing only a mere scrap of Dhamma from my teaching, was weary of heart and devoid of mental resolve— He reproved him and,
as if catching a thief along with his stolen goods, spoke the verse beginning "Mā kho tvaṃ, kappaṭa, pacālesi" to show his state of negligence.
In this regard, "Do not nod off, Kappaṭa"—O Kappaṭakura, having sat down thinking, "I shall listen to my Dhamma," do not nod off, do not drowse, and do not fall asleep.
Lest they strike you on the ear—lest I, while you are sleeping, should strike you on the ear, that is, near the ear, with the hand of teaching. Just as...
From this point forward, I shall not advise you for the sake of abandoning the defilements; rather, the meaning is: "Practice in such a way.

"For you, Kappaṭa, do not know the measure" means that you, Kappaṭa, while nodding off in the midst of the Saṅgha, do not consider the measure or limit, [thinking] even this much: "This extremely rare opportunity has been obtained; let it not be lost."
"You do not know; see how far you have transgressed!"—thus the Blessed One rebuked him with two verses. Having been firmly rebuked by the Blessed One, he was as if pierced by eight spears;
like a fierce elephant descending from its path, he was seized by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), established insight (*vipassanā*), and before long, [attained realization].
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the Vinatā river, the Supreme Person dwelt;
I saw the stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-composed.”
“At that time, with a heart full of faith and a joyful mind, I worshipped the Best of Buddhas with a *ketaka* flower that had the fragrance of honey.
For ninety-one eons, because of that flower which I offered in worship— ”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc. ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, he recited back those very two stanzas spoken by the Teacher as the hook for his own attainment of Arahantship. Thus, that itself became his declaration of final knowledge.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kappaṭakura is finished.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Fifth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumārakassapa "O Buddha!
O Dhamma!"—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kumārakassapa. What is their origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, [served] Padumuttara...

Having been reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One, he reached the age of discretion. However, in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that he was born in a "family home" (*kulageha*).
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being the foremost among those who discourse on the mind.
Desiring that same station for himself, he made a formal aspiration and performed deeds corresponding to that goal.

While performing meritorious deeds during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he practiced the duties of a recluse and, wandering only through happy realms, took rebirth in this current appearance of a Buddha within the womb of a merchant’s daughter in Rājagaha.

It is said that even while she was still a young girl, she desired to go forth; having requested her parents but not obtaining permission for ordination, she went to her family home, yet even while she remained there pregnant—
Not knowing [her condition], she won over her husband and, with his permission, went forth among the bhikkhunīs.
When the bhikkhunīs saw that she was pregnant, they questioned Devadatta; he said, "She is not a samaṇī. They questioned the Teacher again;
the Master entrusted the matter to the Elder Upāli. The Elder [informed] the families living in the city of Sāvatthī and the female lay follower Visākhā.
Having summoned her, he adjudicated the matter before the assembly including the king and declared, "The pregnancy was conceived previously; her renunciation is blameless.
The Teacher, saying, "This legal case has been well-adjudicated," gave his approval to the Elder.
That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala raised him, and he was named Kassapa.
They gave him a name. Later, having adorned him, they led him into the presence of the Teacher, who ordained him.
Because he had gone forth while still a youth, when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa; give this fruit or hard food to Kassapa," [the monks asked], "Which Kassapa?
[The Buddha replied], "Kumārakassapa. Thus he received the name by which he was known to the King.
Because he was the son of a cattle-breeder (*posāvanika*), even in his old age he was known simply as "Little Calf" (*Kumārakassapa*).
From the time of his going forth, he applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and mastered the word of the Buddha.
Then, having practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) with him on a mountain peak, he became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heaven.

Mahābrahmā, thinking, "I shall show the way to the attainment of the paths and fruits by demonstrating the gateway to insight (vipassanā)," formulated fifteen questions and went away after instructing the Elder dwelling in the Andhavana forest, saying, "You should ask the Teacher about these questions.
The Elder asked those questions of the Blessed One, and the Blessed One answered them for him. The Elder [reported] to the Teacher...
Having mastered [the teachings] exactly according to what was explained, he brought insight to maturity and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Leader appeared;
The Hero, the benefactor of the whole world, named Padumuttara.”
“Then, having become a brahmin, renowned and a master of the Vedas,
while wandering for my midday rest, I saw the Leader of the World.
He was proclaiming the Four Truths and awakening the world together with its gods.”
While he was extolling his preeminence among those who speak with eloquence before the great assembly,
I, with a joyful heart, invited the Tathāgata and,
having adorned the pavilion with cloths of various colors, [prepared it for him].
“I fed the Buddha together with the Saṅgha there, which shone with various jewels;
having fed them for seven days with food of various excellent flavors,
I honored him along with his disciples with flowers of many colors.”
Prostrating at his feet, I made a prayer for that very place.
Then the Supreme Sage, whose heart’s abode is the single flavor of compassion, said:
"Behold this noble brahmin, whose eyes are like lotus faces!"
“Abounding in rapture and gladness, with the hair on his body bristling,
his wide eyes filled with laughter, and longing for my teaching—
he fell at my feet, his mind set solely on the one robe.”
He aspired to that state of being a teacher of diverse discourses:
"In a hundred thousand aeons from now, one born in the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world."
“He shall be a true heir to the Dhamma, a legitimate son fashioned by the Dhamma;
he will be a disciple of the Teacher known as Kumārakassapa.
By means of various flowers, garments, and precious gems,”
He will attain the preeminence among those who discourse on diverse matters.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
“Wandering through various states of existence like an actor on a stage,
having become a deer with branches, I entered the womb of a doe.
While I was thus conceived in her womb, the turn for execution arrived.”
“My mother, out of affection for her son, had gone for refuge to the banyan tree.
By that king of deer, she was delivered from death;
having sacrificed his own life, he then exhorted me in this way.”
“One should attend only to the banyan tree; one should not dwell among the branches.
Death under the banyan is better than life among the branches.
Thus instructed by the leader of the deer herd, I, my mother, and the others likewise—
Having come from the delightful abode of Tusita, he went abroad as if returning to his own home.
Later, when the teaching of the heroic Kassapa was coming to an end,
he ascended the mountain peak and dedicated himself to the dispensation of the Conqueror.
“Now, I was born in Rājagaha into a family of wealthy merchants;
while my mother was pregnant with me, she went forth into the homeless life.
Knowing that she was with child, they brought her to Devadatta.”
Thus he spoke: "Destroy this wicked nun!
Even now, my mother in the nuns' quarters has been made happy by the Lord of Sages, the Conqueror, who has shown her compassion."
“Having learned of this, the Kosalan king protected me;
I was known by the name Kassapa through my princely upbringing.
Because of Mahākassapa, I am called Kumārakassapa.”
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the body being like an anthill,
my mind was then completely liberated through non-clinging.
Having tamed Pāyāsi, I attained this foremost state.
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, and being placed by the Teacher in the foremost position among those who discourse on the mind, he reviewed his own practice and, by way of proclaiming the virtues of the Triple Gem, declared his final knowledge (aññā), saying:
“Oh, the Buddhas! Oh, the Dhammas! Oh, the excellence of our Teacher!
Wherein a disciple may realize such a Dhamma as this:
"Throughout incalculable eons, they have been subject to personal existence;
for them, this is the last one; this is the final body."
“The cycle of birth and death has ended; there is now no further becoming. Thus he spoke these two verses.
In this context, *aho* is a particle used in the sense of wonder. *Buddhā* refers to the omniscient Buddhas;

the plural is used out of reverence, meaning “O, how wonderful are the Fully Awakened Ones! *Dhammā* refers to the nine supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) together with the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*).
"Aho! Our Teacher’s accomplishments! means: "Aho! The perfections of our Teacher, the One Possessing the Ten Powers. "In whom" means:
in which Teacher, by dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Such a Dhamma as this, a disciple shall realize":

such as this, of such a kind—accompanied by perfectly purified meditative absorptions and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), bringing about the total destruction of all defilements, peaceful, sublime, and unsurpassed.
"A disciple too shall indeed realize the Dhamma; therefore, oh, how wonderful are the Blessed Buddhas, who are the cause for attaining such distinguished qualities!
How wonderful are the qualities of the Dhamma! How wonderful are the perfections of our Teacher!"—thus he proclaimed his resolute confidence (*adhimutti*) in the virtues of the Triple Gem.
For by the very praise of the perfection of the Dhamma, the excellence of the Saṅgha’s practice is also extolled.
Having thus shown the realization of the Dhamma by way of generality, he now spoke the verse beginning with “In incalculables” (*asaṅkheyyesu*) to show it as applied to himself.
Therein, “incalculables” (*asaṅkheyyesu*) refers to great eons (*mahākappa*) that have transcended the path of calculation.

“Personal existence” (*sakkāya*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*). For these, because they are a collection of phenomena existing in the ultimate sense, are called “personal existence.”
They are so called. Because the means for turning back [from existence] had not been attained, they remained without having departed.
"This is their last, this is their final heap": because this is the very last of all, it is therefore the final one;

thus, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—characterized by the succession of aggregates and so forth, accompanied by birth and death—now has no further becoming in the future, as there is no more renewed existence.
"This is my final birth" is the meaning.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kumārakassapa is finished.
2. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammapāla.
"Whosoever is a young bhikkhu"—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Dhammapāla. What is its origin?

This [Thera] also, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
Having reached maturity, he went to the edge of a forest on some business and, upon seeing the Teacher, [was inspired].

With a serene mind, he gave a pilakkha fruit as an offering. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Avantī after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna.
Having received the name Dhammapāla, he reached maturity, went to Takkasilā, mastered his craft, and while returning on the road, he...

Having seen a certain elder in a monastery and heard the Dhamma from him, he gained faith, went forth, and by developing insight became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"Having seen the Buddha Atthadassi of great renown in the midst of a forest..."
With a clear mind and a joyful heart, I gave a fruit from a pilakkha tree.
Because I gave that fruit eighteen hundred eons ago, I have never known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge (*chaḷabhiññā*), while spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-sukha*), one day the Elder saw two novices in that monastery plucking flowers from the tops of trees;
when the branch they had climbed broke, he saw them falling down. Then, by means of his supernormal power (*iddhānubhāva*), the Elder—
Taking them by the hand and setting them down on healthy ground, he taught the Dhamma to those novices:
“Indeed, that young bhikkhu who applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching,
who is vigilant while others sleep— his life is not in vain.”
“Therefore, the wise person, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas, should devote themselves to faith, virtue, confidence, and the vision of the Dhamma.”—he spoke these two verses.
Therein, *yo* is an indefinite pronoun. *Hava* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis. *Daharo* means young. *Bhikkhati* means... [begs].
"Bhikkhu": he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. "Jāgaro" means one endowed with the quality of wakefulness. "Suttesu" means among those who are sleeping.

This is what is meant: a bhikkhu who, while still young and in the prime of life, does not think, "I shall know [this] later when I am old," but instead applies himself to the practice of diligence in the teaching of the Buddhas through the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

He practices yoga; he is awake among those who are asleep due to the slumber of ignorance, and among those who are heedless, he is awake through his possession of the awakening qualities such as faith.
For that very reason, his life is not in vain nor barren, because it fulfills both his own welfare and the welfare of others.
And since this is so, therefore, "faith" refers to the faith in the fruit of karma, proceeding in the manner of: "Karma exists, the result of karma exists," and so forth.

Because virtue is bound up with faith, the wise person [cultivates] the virtue of the fourfold purification which is its necessary support, the confidence in the Triple Gem that arises as "The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened;

the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing the good way," and the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths through the knowledge of full understanding and so forth by means of path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom.

A bhikkhu endowed with the wisdom that feeds on the Dhamma, recollecting the teaching, advice, and instruction of the Buddhas, should apply himself even while regarding his own head as if it were ablaze;
the meaning is that he should exert himself and apply ardor toward that practice.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammapāla is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Brahmāli:
"Kassindriyāni samathaṅgatāni" (Whose faculties have entered into tranquility) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Brahmāli. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [attained his goal].
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī and having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms;
with a mind full of faith, he paid homage and offered him a foot-stool. After the Teacher had delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, he departed.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, at this present arising of a Buddha—
Having been reborn in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala and having received the name Brahmālī, he reached the age of discretion.
Urged on by the perfection of his causal conditions, he conceived a sense of spiritual urgency regarding *saṃsāra*.

Having gone forth in the Buddha’s dispensation through reliance upon such a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), and having taken up a suitable meditation subject (*kammatthāna*) while dwelling in the forest, he reached the full maturity of knowledge.
Before long, having increased his insight (vipassanā), he became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“To the golden-hued Sambuddha, the recipient of offerings, as he was entering the road, I gave a fruit from a tree.”
“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave that fruit back then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Having become one possessed of the six higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*), and spending his time in the bliss of the path and the bliss of the fruit, one day, while the elder who was his overseer of striving was supervising the application of striving for the sake of the monks in that forest region, [the Blessed One] spoke this verse:
“Whose faculties have reached tranquility, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer?
Of whom—free from conceit and free from taints—do even the gods envy, such a one?”
“The faculties of sense have reached tranquility, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer;
for me, who have abandoned conceit and am free from taints, even the gods envy such a one as I.
Thus he spoke these two verses.

The meaning of this is as follows: Among the bhikkhus dwelling in this forest region, which bhikkhu—whether senior, junior, or of middle standing—has brought the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, to a state of tranquility, tamed condition, and lack of turbulence, like well-trained horses by a skilled charioteer?
Who, having abandoned the ninefold conceit, stands firm because of that?
For one who has abandoned conceit and is thus "taintless" (*anāsava*) due to the absence of the four taints (*āsava*),

and who is "such-like" (*tādi*) because he has attained the characteristic of equanimity toward the desirable and so forth, even the gods envy him, and humans also aspire to him with reverence by observing his right practice and so on. In this regard,
the first half of the verse asks about the attainment of the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi*), for even in the case of a non-returner, the faculties...

Through the abandoning of sensual desire and ill will, his faculties have reached a state of tranquility and non-activity. By the other [verse], the attainment of the path of Arahantship is indicated;
for an Arahant is called "one whose conceit is abandoned, who is taintless, and such-like.
Then the Venerable Brahmāli recited the verse spoken by the Director of Exertion: "In whom do the faculties [dwell]?"
Explaining the meaning of that by way of applying it to himself, he answered with the second verse beginning with “My faculties,” and so forth;
therein, “my faculties” (*mayhindriyāni*) refers to my own faculties, such as the eye and the rest. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Brahmāli is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mogharāja "Repulsive in body, but auspicious in mind": these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Mogharāja. What is his origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, and upon reaching maturity...
One day, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu as the foremost among those who wear coarse robes.
Desiring that same position, he made a formal aspiration (paṇidhāna) and performed meritorious deeds throughout various successive existences.
During the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi, he was reborn into a brahmin family and [served] the brahmins...
Having attained proficiency in the sciences and arts, while instructing brahmin youths in those same sciences and arts,
one day he saw the Blessed One Atthadassi proceeding, surrounded by the community of monks. With a mind full of faith, he prostrated himself with the fivefold salutation,
placed his joined palms to his head, and praised him with six verses beginning with, “As far as there are beings possessed of form.”
Having filled a vessel, he offered him honey. The Teacher accepted the honey and gave a blessing of thanksgiving.
Through that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a minister to the king named Kaṭṭhavāhana.
Sent by the king with a thousand men for the purpose of bringing the Teacher, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having gone there and heard the Dhamma, he acquired faith and went forth into homelessness.

After practicing the ascetic life for twenty thousand years, he passed away from that state and, wandering through happy realms for the duration of one *buddhantara*, was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a brahmin family.
Having received the name Mogharāja and mastered the arts under the brahmin Bāvari, he became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone forth into the ascetic life, surrounded by a thousand ascetics, he was sent to the presence of the Teacher together with Ajita and the others;
being the fifteenth among them, he asked questions, and at the conclusion of the answers to those questions, he attained arahantship.
