Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the self-become, the unconquered,
set out upon the highway, surrounded by the community of monks.
Surrounded by my disciples, I went forth from home.”
Having gone forth from there, I saw the Leader of the World.
Having paid homage to the Fully Awakened One and placing my joined palms to my head,
I gladdened my own heart and praised the Leader of the World.
“Whatever beings there are, whether possessing form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient—
all of them are contained within your knowledge, submerged therein.
It is like one who casts water into a fine-meshed net.”
Whatever living beings there are in the water that remain within the net—
whether they possess volition, are material, or are immaterial—
they are all contained within your wisdom, submerged therein.
“You have rescued this world, which was overwhelmed by darkness;
having heard your Dhamma, they cross over the stream of doubt.
In a world shrouded by ignorance and enveloped in gloom...”
While your wisdom shines forth, the darknesses have been dispelled.
"You are the eye for all, the dispeller of great gloom;
having heard your Dhamma, the multitude attains Nibbāna."
“Having filled a vessel with honey, pure and unadulterated,
I took it with both hands and offered it to the Great Sage.
The Great Hero, the Great Seer, accepted it with his own hand.”
Having eaten that, the All-Knowing One rose up into the sky through the air.
Standing in the atmosphere, the Teacher Atthadassī,
the Bull among Men, spoke these verses, inspiring confidence in my mind:
“Because this knowledge has been extolled and the Best of Buddhas praised,
by that serene confidence of mind he shall not go to a state of misery.
And fourteen times he shall exercise sovereignty over the devas.”
He shall dwell upon the earth, ruling over the kingdom of the world for eight hundred years.
Furthermore, he shall become a wheel-turning monarch five hundred times,
and he shall exercise regional sovereignty over the great earth for incalculable periods.
“A reciter of the Vedas, a bearer of mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas,
will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama.
With his wisdom, he will investigate the profound and subtle meaning.”
“By the name Mogharāja, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.
Endowed with the three knowledges, having accomplished his task and being free from taints,
Gotama, the foremost leader of the caravan, will place him at the head of this foremost group.”
“Having abandoned human bondage, having severed the fetter of existence, and having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having attained arahantship, he wore rag-robes (paṃsukūla) that were specifically characterized by a threefold coarseness: coarseness of the needlework, coarseness of the thread, and coarseness of the dye.
Because of this, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes.
Later on, due to the conditions of past karma and because he did not attend to his physical needs, boils and sores appeared on the elder’s body.
Having been born, they grew. Thinking, "The lodging will become worn out," he would spread out mats of straw even during the winter months and sleep in the Magadha fields.

One day, when the man had approached the Teacher for an audience, paid his respects, and was seated to one side, the Teacher questioned him with the first verse beginning with "Chavipāpakā" as a friendly greeting.
207. In this context, "one with foul skin" (*chavipāpaka*) refers to one whose skin is broken by burns, scabs, or pustules, and thus has inferior or diseased skin.

"One with a noble mind" (*cittabhaddaka*) refers to one who possesses a noble and beautiful mind through the complete abandonment of all defilements (*kilesa*) and the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"Mogharāja" is an address to him. "Constantly concentrated" (*satataṃ samāhita*) means always and frequently [concentrated] by means of the concentration of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-samādhi*).
With a concentrated mind. "Winter-cold-night-times" means the nights of the cold season during the winter period. This is the accusative case used to express continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*).
There is also a textual reading: "hemantikā sītakālarattiyo. In that context, "hemantikā" means included in winter or comprised within winter.
"O monk, you are cold" means: "Monk, who are you?"—thus [he speaks] to others.
"Having made [this] your dwelling, while those who do not give [elsewhere] are not entering the dwellings belonging to the Saṅgha, how will you manage?
Thus the Teacher asked, "How will you sustain your person during the cold season as previously described?
When questioned in this way, the Elder explained the matter to the Teacher:
“The Magadhas have abundant crops, so I have heard;
they sleep under a thatch of straw, unlike others who live in comfort. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “abundant crops” means the harvest has been produced. “Magadhas” refers to the kingdom of Magadha. As for the name “Magadhas”:
The princes of the various provinces; their residence was even a single province, which by way of conventional usage is called "Magadha" using the plural form.
"Kevala" means without remainder. "Iti me sutaṃ" means thus heard by me. In this context, the word "heard" is used with reference to that region which was not seen [by the narrator].
By this it is meant that at such a time, I lived anywhere within Magadha.
He shows that he is capable. Regarding the phrase "a bed covered with straw, unlike those who live in comfort":

just as other monks who live in comfort, having obtained suitable lodgings, lie down in ease upon beautiful rugs and coverlets, so too do I lie down upon a mere layer of straw, my body covered above and across by a roof of straw alone.
"I shall lie down on a bed covered with straw"—this expresses his contentment with whatever he may obtain.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mogharāja is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Visākha Pañcālaputta.
"Neither lifting up nor casting down"—this is the verse of the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta.

What is its origin? This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a poor family in a frontier village fourteen aeons ago; having reached maturity...
One day, while wandering in search of fruit, he went into the forest together with some people from that village;
there, having seen a Paccekabuddha, he gave him a creeper-fruit with a devout heart.

Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha within a royal family of local chieftains in the kingdom of Magadha.
Having received the name Visākha, he later became known as Pañcālaputta because he was the son of the daughter of the King of Pañcāla.
When his father had died and he was ruling the kingdom, the Teacher arrived near his village.

He went into the presence of the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, he went forth. Accompanying the Teacher, he went to Sāvatthī and [applied himself to] insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
Having established himself [in practice], before long he became one possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Then all the people, having gathered together, went to the forest;
seeking fruit, they obtained fruit at that time.”
“Therein I beheld the Perfectly Awakened One, the Self-Existent, the Unconquered.
With a clear heart and a joyful mind, I gave him a creeper fruit.
Fourteen aeons ago from now, that fruit which I then gave—”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving alms.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge, the Elder went to his native land out of compassion for his kinsmen. There, the people—

Having approached the elder and listening to the Dhamma from time to time, one day they asked about the characteristics of a preacher of the Dhamma, saying: "Venerable sir, endowed with how many factors does one become a preacher of the Dhamma?
As the elder was explaining the characteristics of a preacher of the Dhamma to them—
“One should not lift up others, nor should one cast them down; one should not strike down those who have reached the further shore, nor should one push them away.
One should not speak disparagingly of others in assemblies; being undisturbed, measured in speech, and firm in virtue.
By one who sees the meaning that is extremely subtle and refined, who is skilled in intelligence, and whose conduct is humble—”
"By one who has served Buddhas and possesses virtuous conduct, Nibbāna is indeed not difficult to attain.
Thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "does not exalt oneself" means one should not exalt oneself through birth and so forth, or through great learning and so forth; it refers to self-praise.

One should not do so. Nor should one "cast down" others—that is, one should not cast down other persons by defining them through their birth and so forth, nor should one cast them down by way of destroying their virtues. The connection is thus: "one should not cast down others.
One should not cause others to look down upon themselves by making them feel dejected; that is, one should not cause others to be looked down upon.
The meaning is: "One should not complain. Some read "na ukkhipē" (one should not revile), which has the same meaning.

"Gone to the further shore" (*pāragata*) means one who has reached the further shore of true knowledge as if it were the further shore of *saṃsāra*—an *āsravakṣaya* (one whose taints are destroyed), a master of the three knowledges (*tevijja*), or one possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*).
One should not push, strike, or offend such a person. "One should not speak of one's own excellence in assemblies" means one's own appearance, virtues, gain, honor, and fame.
Desiring [to speak], one should not speak among assemblies of kṣatriyas and the like. "Undisturbed" means free from restlessness;
for people do not heed the words of one who is restless. "Measured in speech" means speaking properly and with moderation;
the meaning is that one is habituated to speaking words that are timely, well-founded, limited, and connected with the goal. The speech of one who speaks otherwise than this is not worth taking up.
“Subbata” means one who possesses beautiful vows, that is, one endowed with virtue (*sīla*). The word “siyā” (might there be) should be supplied and connected as a verb.

Thus the Elder, having briefly stated the characteristics of a preacher of the Dhamma and being convinced that those qualities were present in himself, perceived that the great multitude was even more deeply inspired with faith, and [said]: “Of such a preacher of the Dhamma...”

Showing that for one who relies upon the bases of liberation, Nibbāna is not difficult to attain, but rather easily attained, he spoke the second verse beginning with "By one who sees the exceedingly subtle and refined meaning.
The meaning of this has already been explained above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Visākha Pañcālaputta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cūḷaka.
"The peacocks cry out, with their beautiful crests and beautiful plumage"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Cūḷaka. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various states of existence.
Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn in a noble family.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher, he offered a *chattapanniphalam* with a devout heart.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present dispensation of the Buddha in a brahmin family in Rājagaha, receiving the name Cūḷaka.

Having reached maturity and gained confidence in the Teacher through the taming of Dhanapāla, he went forth into homelessness and, while practicing the duties of a recluse, dwelt in the Indasāla Cave.
One day, sitting at the entrance of the cave, he gazed upon the Magadha country.
At that moment, a rain-cloud of the monsoon season appeared, with a deep and sweet resonance, possessing a hundred and a thousand layers [of water] like collyrium.

Filling the sky, it rained down from near the mountain peaks; and flocks of peacocks, delighted and thrilled upon hearing the thundering of the clouds, wandered about dancing here and there while uttering their cries.

For the Elder as well, within the chamber of his dwelling, because his mind was free from defilements through the touch of the cloud-wind, his body attained a state of pliancy and tranquility by obtaining what is favorable to the season.
His mind became one-pointed and entered the path of the meditation subject. Knowing this, he encouraged himself toward development by way of praising the perfection of the time and other factors:
“The peacocks cry out, with beautiful crests, beautiful tails, beautiful blue necks, beautiful faces, and beautiful calls;”
“May this great earth be well-provided with moisture, and may the sky be filled with fine rain.
For one who meditates with a happy mind, there is the excellent practice of right conduct within the teaching of the Well-Awakened One.
May you touch that supreme, deathless state—utterly bright, subtle, and difficult to perceive.”
He spoke two verses.
Therein, regarding the phrase "the peacocks cry out—well-crested, well-feathered, with beautiful blue necks, beautiful faces, and beautiful cries":
they are called "well-crested" because they are endowed with beautiful crests rising from their heads; and they are "beautiful" because of their various, manifold, and lovely colors.

Because they possess beautiful tail-feathers, they are well-tailed (*sapekhuna*); because they possess a beautiful, dark-blue neck that resembles the color of a lotus, they are "well-dark-necked" (*sunīlagīva*);
because of their beautiful faces, they are "fair-faced" (*sumukha*); because of their charming calls, they are "well-criing" (*sugajjina*).
The peacocks (*morā*), possessing crests (*sikhā*), uttering the six notes, and emitting the *kekā* sound, cry out and roar. And they are also very resonant.
The great earth is coming into being, and this vast earth is covered with lush, beautiful green grass.
It is well-spread with water (*subyāpitambū*) because of the fresh rain, with its waters overflowing here and there; it is thus thoroughly pervaded by water, with water spread far and wide.

There is also the reading *susukkatambū*, which means "possessing very pure water. And the sky, the atmosphere, is filled with beautiful clouds, [adorned] with [clouds] resembling the petals of blue lotuses.
*Suvalāhakam*: because it stands filled on all sides with beautiful clouds (*valāhaka*), it is "well-clouded.
*Sukallarūpo sumanassa jhāyatan-ti*: now, by obtaining a season favorable to meditation, you are "very pliant" (*sukallarūpa*), meaning your nature is well-suited for work;
for one whose mind is not overcome by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and thus possesses a beautiful mind (*sumana*), that which—by way of closely contemplating the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*)—...
And it is called *jhāna* by way of reflecting upon the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).

"One of excellent conduct... [pe] ...the deathless state"—meditating thus, one becomes one of beautiful conduct within the teaching of the Well-Awakened One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; and through the state of perfectly purified virtue, one is "very bright" (*susukka*);
and through the state of a purified nature, because one does not fall into the range of any defilement whatsoever, one is "bright" (*sukka*).
"Touch that Nibbāna— the subtle state because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, extremely difficult to see because of its supreme profundity,
supreme because of its excellence and sublime nature, and the deathless state because of its eternal essence—
by making it personally manifest through right practice."

Thus, while exhorting himself, the Elder—his mind concentrated by obtaining favorable weather conditions—intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“Like a blooming *kaṇikāra* tree, like the full moon on the fifteenth day, like a blazing lamp-tree, I beheld the Leader of the World.”
“Taking a plantain fruit, I gave it to the Teacher;
with a clear mind and joyful heart, I paid homage and departed.
Thirty-one eons ago, that fruit which I then gave—”
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

Having attained arahantship, the Elder reflected upon his own practice and, filled with joy and gladness, recited those very same verses beginning with “The peacocks cry out. Thus, this itself became his declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷaka is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Anūpama:
“The mind that has come, rejoicing... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Anūpama. What is his origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, he was reborn in a noble family thirty-one aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Paccekabuddha named Paduma wandering for alms on the street, he offered *aṅkola* flowers with a devout heart. By that meritorious deed, he...
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance in a clan of hunters in the kingdom of Kosala.

Having received the name Anūpama (The Peerless) due to his incomparable physical beauty, he reached maturity; then, owing to his possession of the necessary spiritual prerequisites (*upanissaya*), he abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth into homelessness, and dwelt in the forest performing the work of insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
However, his mind wandered outward toward external objects such as forms and the like.
The meditation subject was being turned over in his mind. As the Elder was restraining the wandering mind, he said:
“The mind that has come here full of delight, Is as if being impaled upon a stake;
Thither you go, wheresoever it may be, To that very stake and that very post.”
“Therefore, I call that a corruption of the mind; I call that a betrayal of the mind.
The Teacher, so difficult to find, has been found by you; do not lead him to his ruin.
With these two verses he exhorted him.
In this context, "the mind that has come while rejoicing" means the mind that has come—meaning arisen—while rejoicing and delighting.

"Being impaled on a stake" refers to being impaled for such a long time upon various states of existence (bhava) by way of kamma and defilements; because it is a place where suffering arises, it is like a stake (sūla).
"By that very [path] you go, where the stake and the splinter are"—that is, you go to wherever the stake and the splinter lie.

"Wherever there are the 'stakes' known as states of existence (*bhava*), the 'wooden posts' known as rebirths, and the 'blows' known as the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*)—to each and every one of those places you go, O evil-minded one; you approach that very spot and do not perceive your own harm.
Therefore, I call you a 'stake of the mind' (*cittakali*); because of your state of negligence, I call you a stake of the mind, a black-spotted crow of the mind."

I shall speak. Again, I say this to him: I speak of the "deceiver of the mind" (*cittadubbhaka*), so called because it brings harm to one's own mental continuum (*santāna*), which is designated as "mind" and is of great benefit.
They also read it as "cittadubbhagā. The meaning is: those who deceive the mind, who are characterized by its lack of mindfulness, and who possess little merit.
If you ask, "What does he say? he says: "The Teacher, so difficult to find, has been found; do not lead me toward ruin."

Even for incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa), the world may indeed be empty of a Buddha. Even when a Teacher has appeared, the attainment of human birth, faith, and so forth, are themselves difficult to obtain;
and even when these have been obtained, a Teacher remains difficult to find. Thus, this Teacher who is so difficult to find has now been found by you.
Yet, even with him found, worldly success leads to what is unwholesome and harmful, and brings about future misfortune and suffering.
"Do not enjoin me to what is unwholesome. Thus, while exhorting his own mind, the Elder increased his insight and attained arahantship.
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
"The Sambuddha named Paduma then dwelt on Cittakūṭa;..."
Having seen that Buddha, the Self-Existent One, the Unconquered,
I then saw a flowering *aṅkola* tree; having gathered it,
I approached the Fully Enlightened One and honored the Victor with that lotus.
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered that flower in worship, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.’”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Anūpama is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjita:
"Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ" (Wandering through the long course of existence) is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vajjita. What is his origin? He too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, he was reborn in a frontier village fifty-six aeons ago.
Upon reaching maturity, he lived as a forest-dweller and one day saw the Paccekabuddha named Upasanta dwelling in a mountain cave. Beholding his tranquility, his mind became filled with serene faith.

He made an offering with a *campaka* flower. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current arising of a Buddha into a clan of outcasts in the kingdom of Kosala. From the day of his birth, whenever he came into the hands of a woman, he would weep.
It is said that because he had descended from the Brahma-world, he could not endure the touch of a woman.
Therefore, because he avoided contact with women, the name "Vajjita" (The Avoider) arose for him.

When he reached maturity, having seen the Teacher’s Twin Miracle and gained faith, he went forth into homelessness. Having established insight meditation, he became a possessor of the six supernormal powers on that very day.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Perfectly Awakened One, having attained peace, dwells amidst the mountain ranges;
taking a single campaka flower, I approached that Supreme among Men.
With a clear heart and a joyful mind, [I approached] the Supreme Private Buddha.”
Taking it up with both hands, I honored the Unconquered One.
Because I offered that flower during the fifty-sixth aeon, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge and recollecting his own past lives, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (dhammasaṃvega) and said:
“Through a long course of wandering, I have transmigrated through various states of existence;”
“Not seeing the Noble Truths, the worldling remains blind.
“For me, being heedful, the cycle of existence has been crushed;
all destinations have been cut off—now there is no further becoming. Thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "they wander" means wandering from one state of existence to another by way of taking up and laying down [the body] as they run on and on.
"For a long duration" means for a long time, an immeasurable period in beginningless *saṃsāra*.
"In the destinies" means in happy and miserable destinies according to the influence of well-done and ill-done kamma. "They revolve" like a waterwheel.
He wanders about, revolving from one state to another by way of passing away and being reborn. He states the cause for that revolution:

"Not seeing the Noble Truths, the worldling has become blind. Not seeing and not penetrating the four Noble Truths—suffering and so forth—with the eye of knowledge, he is therefore "blind" due to the blindness of ignorance (*avijjā*) among the many.
The interpretation is that, being a worldling (*puthujjana*) due to causes such as birth and so forth, one wanders through the various realms of existence; for this very reason the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, it is because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of the Four Noble Truths that this long course has been run and wandered through by both me and you.
Now, while I was formerly a worldling in the manner described, I have now become diligent according to the method bestowed by the Teacher.

For one who has reached the pinnacle of the cultivation of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) through the practice of heedfulness (appamāda), the "saṃsārās" have been rendered devoid of reeds.
Because beings wander by means of these, they are given the name "saṃsārās"—namely, kamma and the defilements (kilesa).

Since these have been utterly severed by the supreme path (aggamagga), they are stripped of their reeds and rendered rootless. Thus, all destinations (gati) have been cut off; in this way, the rounds of kamma and defilements—
Because his nature was rendered free from the taints (*vinaḷīkatattā*), all destinations beginning with hell were completely cut off and destroyed;
for that very reason, there is now no further becoming in the future. And this indeed was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vajjita is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Saṇḍhita "Assatthe haritobhāse" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Saṇḍhita. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, during the thirty-first aeon ago, [served] the Blessed One Sikhī...

At that time, there was a certain cowherd. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he approached a certain elder and, having heard from him the Dhamma connected with the qualities of the Buddha, his mind became filled with serene confidence. He asked, "Where is the Blessed One?
and upon hearing that the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he thought: "Even Buddhas of such great power must indeed succumb to the sway of impermanence."
"Alas! Conditioned phenomena are unstable," he thought, and thus he attained the perception of impermanence. The Elder encouraged him to honor the Bodhi tree.
From time to time, he would go to the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, establish insight meditation, and, recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, pay homage to the Bodhi tree.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
Having been reborn in a clan of merchants in the kingdom of Kosala and having received the name Sandhita, he reached maturity and heard a discourse on the Dhamma concerning impermanence.
Stricken with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he went forth into homelessness.

Having established insight (*vipassanā*) and brought his knowledge to full maturity, he soon became a possessor of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*). Recalling his own past lives, [he saw] those of Sikhī...
Recalling the worship of the Bodhi tree at the time of the Blessed One, the recollection of the Buddha, and the attainment of the perception of impermanence,
and thereby manifesting his own special achievement through that very support,
he said: “In the Assattha tree, shining with greenness, where the trees have grown thickly;”
“Mindful, I obtained a single perception directed toward the Buddha:
‘Thirty-one eons ago, I obtained that perception;
by the power of that perception, I have attained the destruction of the taints.’”
He spoke two verses.

Therein, "assatthe" means "in that which stands in the place of an assattha tree. That which is now our Blessed One’s Bodhi tree, the Assattha, was at that time the Puṇḍarīka Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Sikhi; thus, it is referred to as such because of its standing in the place of an assattha.
“Assatthe” is said. Or, it is because it produces consolation (*assāsa*) for sentient beings (*satta*). Others, however, say:
“The Elder spoke thus, ‘Assatthe,’ because he had sat at the foot of an *assattha* tree and, at that time, had cultivated the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
“Haritobhāse” means shining with green, emerald-colored luster. “Saṃvirūḷhamhi” means well-grown, firmly established.
They say it is "covered and overspread with thickly and densely packed leaves, foliage, and sprouts. *Pādapa* means a tree.

One perception directed toward the Buddha—recalling him—is obtained; because the object is of a single nature, the perception accompanied by the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), which proceeds in the manner of "Thus indeed is that Blessed One," etc., [is called] one perception regarding the qualities of the Buddha.
Having become mindful by means of successive refuge, I obtained it.
But when was that perception (saññā) obtained, and by how much [of a path] was it accomplished? To this he said: "In the thirty-first aeon from now," and so forth.
From this present Bhaddakappa, counting upwards, in the thirty-first aeon. "That perception" refers to the perception accompanied by the recollection of the Buddha.
Or, having seen the impermanence of the Buddhas and following that, I then obtained the perception of impermanence regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"By the force of that perception" means by way of the causal state of that aforementioned perception, making it a decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"The destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been attained by me" means: "Now the destruction—that is, the cessation—of the taints has been realized by me. And by this very [statement], for him...
There are also the verses of the Elder’s *Apadāna*, which say:
“In the shade of an *assattha* tree, shimmering with green... [pe] ...the destruction of my taints was attained.
Thirteen eons ago from now, there was a kshatriya named Dhaniṭṭha;”
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc. ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sandhita is finished.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Book of Twos is also finished.
3. The Book of Threes.

1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja In the *Tikanipāta*, the verse beginning with "Those who seek purity through improper means" belongs to the venerable Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja.

What is his origin? This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, cultivated the necessary conditions for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various successive existences.
Accumulating merit, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi thirty-one aeons ago.
Having reached maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher wandering for alms, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration with a devout mind and raised his joined palms in reverence.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, in this [life]...
During the time of a Buddha's appearance, he was born in a city named Ukkaṭṭha near the Himālayas into the home of a wealthy brahmin.
Having received the name Aṅgīrasa Bhāradvāja, he reached maturity and attained perfection in the sciences and arts.
Due to his inclination toward renunciation, he went forth as a wandering ascetic and practiced the austerity of immortality there.
While wandering there, he saw the Perfectly Enlightened One traveling on a journey through the countryside;
with a mind full of faith, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, abandoned that wrong asceticism, and went forth into the Dispensation.
Performing the work of insight meditation, before long he became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"With a clear heart and joyful mind, I paid homage to Vessabhū, the bull among men, the preeminent hero, the victor,
the best of Buddhas. Thirty-one aeons ago, that was the deed I performed then."
I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of my salutation.
In the twenty-fourth aeon, I was named Vikatānanda;
endowed with the seven treasures, I was a mighty wheel-turning monarch.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge (chaḷabhiññā) and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, he went to his own birthplace out of compassion for his kinsmen;
there he established many relatives in the refuges and the precepts, and having returned from there, he went to the kingdom of Kuru.
While dwelling in a forest not far from the town named Kuṇḍiya,
he went to Uggārāma on some business and met with certain brahmins who had come from the Northern Region (Uttarāpatha) and were his acquaintances. When they asked him, "O Bhāradvāja,
having seen what have you abandoned the system of the brahmins and adopted this system?", he [related] to them [the matter] from this teaching of the Buddha.
Showing that there is no purity externally, he spoke the first verse:
“Seeking purity through improper means, I tended the fire in the forest;
Not knowing the path to purity, I practiced asceticism for immortality.”
In this context, *ayoniso* means "unreasonably" or "without method. *Suddhim* refers to purification from saṃsāra, that is, liberation from existence.
*Anvesanti* means "they seek" or "they search for. *Aggiṃ paricariṃ vane*: "I served the fire in the forest.

This means that with the intention, "This is the path to purity," I established a fire-sanctuary (*agyāgāra*) within a fire-offering hall (*aggihuta-sālā*) in a forest region and, offering oblations, I served the Fire-god (*aggi-deva*), worshipping him according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas.

Not knowing the path to purity, not knowing the path to Nibbāna, I practiced and followed the pursuit of self-mortification—such as the five-fire austerity and so forth—thinking, "This is the path to purity," just as one might perform fire-worship in the hope of immortality. I performed it;
I practiced it; I pursued it.

Thus, as if going from one hermitage to another, the Elder— having demonstrated the absence of purity outside this teaching by showing that he had not attained purity through the performance of fire-worship and other rites according to the methods prescribed in the Vedas—
now shows: "In this very dispensation, purity has been attained by me."
“Having attained happiness through happiness, behold the excellence of the Dhamma!
The threefold knowledge has been achieved; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”—this he spoke as the second verse.
Therein, “that” refers to that for the sake of which, seeking purity and not knowing the path, he had tended the sacrificial fire.

"I practiced immortal asceticism; that bliss of Nibbāna was attained, reached, and realized by me through the happiness of serenity and insight, through the pleasant path, without falling into the pursuit of self-mortification.
Behold the excellence of the Dhamma!"—this means: "Behold, know, the excellence of the Teacher's dispensation, the nature of the Dhamma as a non-perverted, leading-out truth."
He speaks by way of addressing him with the Dhamma, or he addresses himself. Yet, showing that this state has been attained by him, he said:
“The three knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. This has the meaning already explained.
Thus, because purity has been achieved, he shows: “From this point on, I am a brahmin in the ultimate sense.”
“I was a mere kinsman of Brahmā in the past, but now I am a true brahmin;
I am one who knows the three Vedas, a cleansed one, a learned scholar, and a master of the Veda. Thus he spoke the third verse.
Its meaning is as follows: previously, by virtue of birth alone, he was called a “kinsman of Brahmā” (brahmabandhu) according to the common designation for brahmins.
...was my name. But now, through the attainment of Arahatship, I am truly a Brahmin in the ultimate sense.

Previously, by the mere conventional designation of having studied the three types of knowledge known as the Vedas—which produce the accumulation of existence—I was called "one possessed of the threefold knowledge" (tevijjo). Now, however, by virtue of the knowledge that brings about the destruction of existence, [I am one possessed of the threefold knowledge].* *Note: The sentence is left incomplete in the source text, but the context refers to the Buddha’s claim of being a *tevijjo* based on the three knowledges (*vijjā*) of the destruction of the taints.*
Because I have attained true knowledge (*vijjā*), I am a "knower of the threefold lore" (*tevijja*) in the ultimate sense.

Likewise, whereas previously—being attached to the gratification of existence and having achieved the status of a "bathed one" (*nhātaka*) through the mere conventional designation resulting from my lineage—I was called a "bathed one" only by name;

now, because the stains of defilement have been thoroughly washed away by the water of the Eightfold Path, I am a "bathed one" in the ultimate sense. Previously, by means of jhāna which did not release me from the gratification of existence...
Having been called a "learned one" (*sottiya*) merely by way of conventional usage, I am now, through the meditative absorption on the Dhamma that is well-liberated from existence,
a learned one in the ultimate sense. Previously, having been called a "knower of the Vedas" (*vedagū*) merely because of the study of those Vedas whose evil qualities have not yet been relinquished,
I am now— by means of the knowledge of the Path known as "Veda"— a knower of the Veda of the four truths, which is the crossing over the great flood of *saṃsāra*.
And because he had reached the further shore, attained it, and known it, he became a *vedagu* (one who has found knowledge) in the ultimate sense.
Having heard this, the brahmins proclaimed a sublime faith in the Teaching (*sāsana*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paccaya “Five days have I been gone forth”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Paccaya. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, in the ninety-first aeon ago, [encountered] Vipassī...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher walking along the bank of a river named Vinatā.
With a mind full of faith, he gathered large, beautiful-looking udumbara fruits and offered them to him.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering only through happy destinies, in this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa)...

When the Blessed One Kassapa had appeared in the world and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he went forth in his dispensation and applied himself to meditation, establishing insight while cultivating spiritual development.
One day, reflecting upon the suffering of saṃsāra, he became deeply moved by a sense of urgency;
sitting in the monastery, he resolved: "I shall not leave this place until I have attained arahantship."
Exerting himself while resolving his mind, he was unable to bring about the intensification of insight because his knowledge was not yet mature.
Having passed away, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans; now, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a kshatriya family in the city of Rohita.
Having received the name Paccaya, he reached maturity and, upon the death of his father, was established in the kingship. One day...
He began to perform the Great King’s Sacrifice (*mahārājabali*). There, a great multitude gathered.

At that assembly, in order to inspire faith in them, the Teacher sat upon a jeweled lion-throne within a jeweled gabled chamber fashioned by Vessavaṇa in the sky, even as the great multitude looked on, and taught the Dhamma.
A realization of the Dhamma occurred for the vast crowd of people. Having heard that Dhamma—
The King of Pañcāla also, urged by his previous causes, renounced his kingdom and went forth.

Having made a formal promise just as he had done in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he entered a monastery and, increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), attained Arahantship at that very moment due to the ripening of his knowledge. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“On the bank of the Vinatānadī, the Supreme Person dwelt;
there I saw the stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-composed.
With a mind full of faith toward him, who washes away the stains of the defilements...”
Having gathered an udumbara fruit, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas.
For ninety-one eons since I gave that fruit back then, I have not known an evil rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving that fruit.
“In this auspicious aeon, with a mind full of spiritual urgency,
I went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having thus gone forth, I devoted myself to meditation.”
Having made up my mind, "I shall not depart from this monastery," [I thought]:
"I have not yet attained the supreme goal, nor have I reached it thus far;
but now, through the ripening of my knowledge, I am extinguished."
“I have reached the unshakable state, having touched the deathless goal.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship, he proclaimed his own final knowledge (*aññā*) by way of praising his own practice:
“Five days have passed since I went forth; I am still a trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s goal.
As I entered my dwelling, a resolve arose in my mind:
‘I shall neither eat nor drink, and I shall not leave this dwelling.’”
“I shall not cast down my gaze as long as the dart of craving has not been pulled out.
“Behold the exertion of energy of one who dwells thus:
the three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
He spoke these three verses.
Therein, "I am five days ordained" (*pañcāhāhaṃ pabbajito*) means that I have been ordained for five days; the meaning is that the fifth day since the day of my ordination has concluded.
"A trainee who has not yet attained his mind's goal" (*sekho appattamānaso*) refers to one who is training in the higher training of virtue and so forth.
A trainee (*sekha*). One who completely cuts off conceit (*māna*) without remainder is "one whose mind is [free from] conceit" (*mānasa*); this refers to the supreme path (*aggamagga*).

That which has arisen from that [path], or that which has come from the state of being free from conceit, is "the mind free from conceit" (*mānasa*), namely, Arahantship. Alternatively, one who has not yet reached that is "one whose mind has not yet reached [freedom from conceit]" (*appattamānasa*).
"When I had entered my dwelling, there was a resolution of the mind"—thus, when I, a trainee, had entered the small room, the dwelling where I reside.
The mind’s aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) of such a kind as is now being described occurred to him while he was mindful; the meaning is: "In this way my mind was directed.

By means of the words "I will not eat," etc., he demonstrates that mental aspiration. Therein, "I will not eat" (*nāsissanti*)—whatever food, I shall not have eaten, I shall not eat—provided the arrow of craving has not been extracted, has not been removed from my heart; thus it should be applied to all the following phrases.
"I will not drink" means I will not drink anything whatsoever that is to be drunk.
"I will not go out from the dwelling" means I will not emerge from this chamber where I am now sitting.
"Nor will I cast down my side" means I will not cast down even one side of my body for the sake of dispelling physical fatigue; the meaning is that I will not lie down on even a single side.
“While I was dwelling thus”: while I was dwelling by means of the application of insight (*vipassanā*), having made such a resolve for my mind and established firm energy (*vīriya*).
“Behold the exertion and the striving” (*passa vīriyaparakkamaṃ*):
behold the effort that has become intense—termed “energy” because it must be set in motion according to the proper method, and termed “striving” because it advances toward the supreme state.
"Know this. Furthermore, "by whose power have the three knowledges been attained by me, and has the Buddha’s teaching been fulfilled?"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Paccaya is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Bākula.
"Whatever was to be done before"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bākula. What is its origin?

It is said that in the past, at the conclusion of an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeya*) plus one hundred thousand eons prior to the appearance of the Blessed One Anomadassi, he was reborn in a brahmin family.
Having reached maturity and mastered the three Vedas, he perceived therein no essence.
Not seeing [the truth], he thought, "I shall seek the welfare of the future life," and having gone forth as an ascetic, he dwelt at the foot of a mountain.
Having attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, while dwelling there, he heard of the appearance of a Buddha.
He went into the presence of the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, he was established in the refuges. When a stomach ailment arose in the Teacher, [he brought] medicines from the forest.
Having brought it and extinguished that [fire], he dedicated the merit there for the sake of health; passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Wandering among gods and humans for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya*), during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those with few ailments, he...
Desiring that very station for himself, he made a formal aspiration and, having accumulated merit throughout his life, wandered only among the happy realms.
Even before the appearance of the Blessed One Vipassi, he was reborn in the city of Bandhumatī into a brahmin family;
there, in the same manner as before, he went forth as a seer, attained the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, and dwelt at the foot of a mountain.
Vasanta, having heard of the appearance of a Buddha, went into the presence of the Teacher and, having heard the Dhamma, was established in the refuges.
When a disease caused by grass-flowers arose among the monks, he pacified it. Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, [he came] at the time of the Blessed One Kassapa...
Having been reborn in a noble family in Benares at that time and living the life of a householder,

he saw a great monastery that was old and decaying; having had all the dwellings there, such as the Uposatha hall, constructed, and having provided all medicinal requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
he performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and spent an entire interval between Buddhas among gods and humans.
While wandering in saṃsāra, even before the arising of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the house of a merchant in Kosambī.
While being bathed in the great Yamunā River for the sake of his health, he was swallowed by a fish from the hand of his nurse;
when the fish was sold and taken by the wife of a merchant in Bārāṇasī after falling into the hands of a fisherman, even as it was being cut open, [the child emerged] by the power of his merit.
Having become healthy, he was taken as a son by her and raised; when his biological parents heard of this occurrence and demanded,
"This is our son, give us our son," the King adjudicated that he should belong to both families as their common heir,
and because he was thus established, he received the name Bākula.
Having reached maturity and enjoyed great prosperity, he became eighty years old.
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, and remained an ordinary person (puthujjana) for only seven days;
on the eighth dawn, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Not far from the Himālaya is a mountain named Sobhita;
there my well-constructed hermitage stands, built by my own disciples.
There are many pavilions there, and flowering *sindhuvāraka* shrubs.”
And there were many kapittha trees in full bloom, as well as jīvajīvaka trees.
There were many nigguṇḍī trees, along with badara and āmalaka trees;
phārusaka and alābu trees, and puṇḍarīka trees in full bloom.
“Āḷaka trees and beluva trees are there, as well as plantains and mātuluṅga trees;
many mahānāma trees are there, along with ajjuna and piyaṅgu trees.
Kosamba, saḷala, and nimba trees, as well as nigrodha and kapittha trees.”
“Edisa was my hermitage, and I lived there with my disciples.
The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Self-Become One, the Leader of the World,
seeking seclusion, came to my hermitage.”
“When the Great Hero of unsurpassed glory had arrived,
a wind ailment suddenly arose in the World-Protector.
While wandering in the forest, I saw the Leader of the World.”
Having approached the Fully Awakened One, the Visionary of Great Renown,
and having observed his deportment, I then discerned:
"Without a doubt, illness has arisen in the Buddha."
“I quickly returned to the hermitage in the presence of my disciples;
desiring to prepare medicine, I then addressed my disciples.
Having respectfully assented to my words, all my disciples—”
They gathered together at once out of their reverence for me, the Teacher:
"Quickly ascending the mountain, we shall bring all the great medicinal herbs;
having prepared a mixture of water, let us give it to the Buddha, the Most Excellent."
“When the Great Hero, the omniscient leader of the world, had finished his meal,
the wind quickly subsided for the Sugata, the Great Seer.
Seeing that the distress had been stilled, the one of great fame, Anomadassi, [spoke].”
Having sat down on his own seat, he spoke these verses:
“He who gave me medicine and brought my illness to an end—him I shall praise; listen as I speak.”
“For a hundred thousand eons, he will delight in the world of the gods;
there, amidst the sounding of musical instruments, he shall always rejoice.
Having come to the world of men, impelled by the root of his wholesome merit,”
A thousand times he will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch.
In the fifty-fifth aeon, there will be a kshatriya named Anoma,
a conqueror of the four quarters, the lord of the Jambudvīpa realm.
“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power,
he shall shake even the realm of the Thirty-three and exercise sovereignty there.
Whether as a god or as a human, he will be free from illness.”
Having abandoned all possessions, he will cross over the disease of the world.
"In an immeasurable eon from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world."
“An heir to the Dhamma, a true-born son fashioned by the Dhamma,
having fully understood all taints, he will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Having incinerated the defilements, he will cross over the stream of craving.”
“One named Bākula by name will be a disciple of the Teacher.
Having directly known all this, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
while seated in the community of monks, will place him at the very head.”
“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the self-become leader of the world,
came to my hermitage while looking out from his seclusion.
When the Great Hero, the omniscient leader of the world, had arrived, I— ”
With all kinds of medicinal herbs, I satisfied him, full of faith with my own hands.
That well-performed deed of mine was like a successful sowing of seed in a fertile field;
even now, I am unable to exhaust that merit which was so well performed by me at that time.
“Profit for me, a great gain for me, that I have beheld the Leader!
By the remainder of that karma, I have attained the unshakable state.
Having directly known all this, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas—”
Having sat within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he placed me in the foremost position.
"In an immeasurable eon from now, whatever deed I performed then, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of that medicinal offering."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, one day when the Teacher was assigning his disciples to their respective positions in order, he placed him in the foremost position among those who are free from illness.
At the time of his Parinibbāna, while giving exhortation to the monks in the midst of the Saṅgha, he proclaimed his own higher knowledge, saying:
“He who wishes to do later what ought to have been done earlier, falls away from that state of happiness and later regrets it. For what one has done, that one should speak;
what one has not done, that one should not speak.”
The wise fully understand one who does not act [wrongly] while speaking.
He uttered these three verses: “Extremely blissful indeed is Nibbāna, taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One— Sorrowless, dust-free, and secure, wherein suffering ceases.”

In this context, "he who wishes to do later what should have been done before" refers to that person who, out of negligence, fails to perform those actions conducive to his own welfare and happiness—which ought to be done earlier—while he is not yet overcome by old age, disease, and so forth;
and who, having let the time for performing them pass, subsequently desires to do them. The word *so* is merely a particle. At that time, however—
Because he is overcome by old age, disease, and other such afflictions, he is unable to act; being unable to act, he falls from his state of happiness and later regrets it.

Thus, that person, falling away from his state of happiness—whether from heaven or from Nibbāna—because he has failed to produce the means thereto, later regrets it and falls into remorse, thinking, "I have not done what is wholesome," and so forth.

The syllable *ma* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). However, showing that he speaks thus to you only after having performed what was to be done, he spoke the second verse beginning with "yañhi kayirā.
Therein, "parijānanti" means they know by delimiting [it], thinking "this is just this much," and do not imagine it to be much.
For it is only one who acts exactly as they speak who shines through right practice, and not otherwise than that.
Now, in order to show the meaning stated generally by way of what is to be done, he spoke the third verse beginning with "How blissful indeed!
The meaning of this is as follows: it was taught by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), because he has awakened to all phenomena rightly and for himself.
Because it is entirely devoid of causes for sorrow, it is "sorrowless" (asoka); because it is free from the dust of passion and the like, it is "dustless" (viraja);

because it is not afflicted by the four yokes, it is "secure" (khema). Nibbāna is indeed supreme bliss! Why? Because in that Nibbāna, the entire suffering of the round of existence ceases and is utterly stilled.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bākulatthera is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhaniyatthera:
"If one wishes to live happily... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Dhaniya. What is their origin? He too, during previous Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various states of existence, he was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher, he offered worship with a reed garland with a mind full of faith.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in Rājagaha during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having been reborn in a potter’s family and receiving the name Dhaniya, he reached adulthood and lived by the work of a potter.
At that time, the Teacher, sitting in the workshop of the potter Dhaniya, taught the *Chadhātuvibhaṅga-sutta* to the young man Pukkusāti.
Having heard it, he accomplished his task. Dhaniya [learned] of his having attained final Nibbāna...

Having heard this, he gained faith, thinking, "The Buddha’s teaching is truly leading to liberation, for even by a single night's acquaintance one can be freed from the suffering of the cycle of existence.
Having gone forth, while dwelling devoted to the decoration of his hut, he was censured by the Blessed One on account of building huts.
Subsequently, dwelling in a lodging belonging to the Saṅgha, he developed insight and attained arahantship.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“I saw the World-Leader, the Sambuddha of golden hue, the recipient of offerings, walking along the edge of the forest.”
“Taking a reed garland, as I was departing at that time,
I saw there the Fully Enlightened One, who had crossed the flood and was free from taints.
With a clear heart and joyful mind, I offered that reed garland.”
"To the Great Hero, worthy of offerings, who has compassion for the entire world:
'In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered this garland, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.'"
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, however, he declared his final knowledge (*añña*) by way of giving advice to those bhikkhus who, having exalted themselves through the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), accepted communal meals and the like while looking down upon other bhikkhus:
“If you wish to live happily, Having regard for the state of a recluse;”
One who desires to live happily, looking toward the state of a recluse, should not despise what belongs to the Saṅgha— robes, food, and drink.
Like a snake in a mouse-hole, one should frequent lodgings and seats.
"If one wishes to live happily, having regard for the state of a recluse, one should be content with whatever comes and cultivate a single quality. Thus he spoke these three verses.

Therein, "if one wishes to live happily, having regard for the state of a recluse" means having regard for the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*), that is, for the condition of being a monk (*samaṇabhāva*).
If one wishes to live happily by having intense reverence for the training, the meaning is that one should abandon wrong livelihood if one desires to live by the happiness of the ascetic life.
One should not despise what belongs to the Saṅgha—namely, robes, drink, and food;
one should not look down upon robes and food brought from the Saṅgha, for the acquisitions arising for the Saṅgha are indeed of pure origin.
The intention is that for one who consumes it, the bliss of recluseship (*sāmaññasukha*) comes into the very palm of their hand through the arising of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi*).
"Like a snake in a mouse-hole" means one should resort to, or use, a lodging (*senāsana*) like a snake resorts to a hole dug by a mouse;
just as a serpent, instead of making its own dwelling, dwells in a dwelling made by a mouse or by another.
Just as one departs according to one's desire, so too a bhikkhu, having himself prepared his lodging and not fallen into defilement,
may depart after staying wherever he wishes— this is the meaning. Now,
whether the requisite conditions have been mentioned or not, the happiness of the ascetic life exists only through contentment with whatever is obtained, and not otherwise.
Showing this, he said: “One should be content with whatever. The meaning is: one should attain satisfaction with whatever requisite condition has been obtained, whether it be inferior or superior.
“A single thing” refers to the state of heedfulness (*appamāda*);
for one who devotes oneself to that, all blameless worldly happiness and supramundane happiness come into the very palm of one’s hand. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“For one who meditates with diligence, vast happiness is attained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhaniya is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Mātaṅgaputta.
"Atisītaṃ" (It is too cold) is the verse of the Venerable Mātaṅgaputta Thera. What is its origin?
It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a powerful Nāga king in a great Nāga abode beneath a vast lake near the Himalayas.
One day, having emerged from the Nāga abode and wandering about, he [saw] the Teacher.
Seeing him traveling through the air, he, with a mind full of faith, made an offering with his own crest-jewel.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in the kingdom of Kosala as the son of a householder named Mātaṅga;
thus he became known simply as Mātaṅgaputta. Having reached the age of discretion, he was by nature indolent.
Having performed some burnt offerings, he did nothing further and was censured by his relatives and others, who said, "These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, live in luxury.
Desiring such a life of ease for himself, and having become well-acquainted with the monks, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith.
Having gone forth, he saw other monks possessed of supernormal powers and, aspiring to the power of *iddhi*, [he strove for it].
Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and applying himself to its cultivation, he became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena, the Sambuddha desiring solitude, was traveling along the wind-swept path.”
“Not far from the Himālayas, there was a great lake of birth;
there my dwelling was, produced by meritorious deeds.
Having gone forth from that dwelling, I saw the Leader of the World.”
“Like a blooming blue lotus, like a blazing sacrificial fire—
I saw that flower being gathered, which they would offer to the Leader.
Having gladdened my own heart, I paid homage to the Teacher.”
“Taking a jewel from my head, I worshipped the Leader of the World.
By this worship of the jewel, may there be a fortunate ripening.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings—”
Standing in the sky, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“May that intention of yours be fulfilled; may you obtain abundant happiness.
Through this worship of the jewel, may you enjoy great glory.”
Having spoken this, the Blessed One, whose name is the Supreme Lotus,
the Best of Buddhas, went to where his mind was directed.
For sixty eons, I ruled as the Lord of Devas.
"And many hundreds of times I was a wheel-turning monarch.
As I recalled my past deeds while existing as a deity,
a jewel manifested for me that provides light for me."
“Sixty-four thousand women were my attendants;
they wore variegated garments and ornaments, and were adorned with jeweled earrings.
With arched brows and lovely smiles, they were well-proportioned, slender-waisted, and delicate.”
They constantly attend upon me; this is the fruit of my jewel-worship.
"There are vessels made of gold, made of gems, and likewise made of ruby;
they are well-crafted for me, whatever ornaments you desire."
“Delightful gabled mansions and a costly couch appear at my will,
manifesting according to my every thought.
Great is their gain, and well-acquired by those who obtain the opportunity to overhear [my discourse].”
A field of merit for humanity, a medicine for all living beings.
"For me too, well-performed is the deed, since I have seen the Leader;
I am liberated from the lower realms and have attained the unshakable state."
“Whatever womb I am reborn into— whether among the gods or among humans—
there is always light for me by day and by night.
By that very same merit from worshipping the jewel, having experienced such prosperity, [I have attained this state].”
The light of knowledge has been seen by me; I have attained the unshakable state.
"In a hundred thousand aeons past, because I worshipped that jewel, I do not know a state of misery; this is the fruit of worshipping the jewel."

“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Having attained the six supernormal powers, however, he censured indolence by way of a personal example and praised his own exertion of energy, saying: “Too cold! Too hot! This evening has become too late! ... [The verse continues: ...I am weary, my back aches; I shall sit down for a while. (Theragāthā 103) He thus rebuked those who were indolent, thinking, “It is too cold,” or “It is too hot,” or “It is too late,” or “I am weary,” or “My back aches,” and he exhorted them to strive with diligence. Then, having attained the six supernormal powers, he spoke this verse to praise his own exertion of energy: “Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu; Atijalābhitattaṃ vā, na kālo idha maddave. Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu; Atijalābhitattaṃ vā, na kālo idha yogino. Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu; Atijalābhitattaṃ vā, iti vīriyaṃ pamajjati. Evaṃ apamādena, appamattānusikkhare; Appamatto hi jhāyanto, pappoti vipulaṃ sukhaṃ. Thus do the moments pass by for the youth who has neglected his duties.
But he who considers cold and heat no more than blades of grass,
performing the tasks of a man— he is not deprived of happiness.
“Dabba grass, kuśa grass, poṭakila, usīra, muñja, and pabbaja—these I shall brush aside with my chest;
cultivate seclusion!”—thus he spoke these three verses.
Therein, “excessively cold” (*atisīta*) means extremely cold due to the falling of snow, frost, rain, and so forth; this is to be connected by supplying the word “was” (*ahū*).
*Atiuṇhaṃ* means excessively hot due to the heat of the Dhamma and so forth; by both [terms], he states a cause for laziness by way of the season.
*Atisāyaṃ* means late in the day when the day has reached its decline; by the mention of "late" (*sāya*), the morning (*pāta*) is also included here;
by both of these, he states a cause for laziness by way of time. *Iti* means in this manner. By this, [it refers to the passage]: "In this case, monks..."
This includes the basis for indolence as stated in the passage beginning, "A formal act (kamma) must be performed by a bhikkhu.
"Vissaṭṭhakammante" means those who have abandoned their efforts and duties. "Khaṇā" refers to the opportunities for living the holy life (brahmacariya), such as the arising of a Buddha.
"Accenti" means they pass away. "Māṇave" refers to sentient beings. "Tiṇā bhiyyo na maññatī" means he does not regard anything as more than grass; [he regards even] grass...
He considers [them] as if they were [insignificant]; having overcome cold and heat, he performs what must be done by himself. "Performing" means doing.

"Manly duties" (*purisakiccāni*) refers to the tasks to be performed by a heroic man for his own welfare and the welfare of others. "As happiness" (*sukhā*) means from the perspective of happiness; the intended meaning is "from the happiness of Nibbāna.
The meaning of the third verse has already been stated above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mātaṅgaputta is finished.
6. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khujjasobhita:
"Those who speak with wisdom and are well-versed in the scriptures... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Khujjasobhita. What is his origin? This—

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family and reached the age of discretion, he one day saw the Blessed One proceeding with a great community of monks; with a mind full of faith, he praised him with ten verses.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, during this current appearance of a Buddha—
He was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Pāṭaliputta, and his name was Sobhita. However, because he was slightly hunchbacked, he became known simply as Khujjasobhita.

When he reached maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he went forth under the Elder Ānanda and became possessed of the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiñña). This is stated in the Apadāna:
“Who, upon seeing the bull among men, the god of gods, shining like Mount Kakudha as he enters the highway, would not feel serene confidence?
Having destroyed that darkness and having delivered many people across [to safety],”
Who, upon seeing him shining with the light of knowledge, would not have faith? Who,
upon seeing the Leader of the World being escorted by one hundred thousand masters,
uplifting many beings, would not have faith?
“Who, upon seeing him who beats the drum of Dhamma, crushes the hosts of heretics,
and roars the lion’s roar, would not have faith?
Even from as far as the Brahma-world, having come together with the Brahmas, [they all gather].”
They ask subtle questions—who, having seen this, would not have faith?
“To him whom the world with its devas makes supplication, having joined their palms in reverence;
through that merit they experience [the results]—who, having seen this, would not have faith?”
“All people have gathered together and offer hospitality to the One with Vision;
though entreated, he does not waver—who, having seen him, would not find faith?
When he enters the city, many drums resound for him.”
The intoxicated elephants trumpet; who, upon seeing them, would not be inspired with confidence?
He who walks along the street always shines with all-encompassing light;
his elevated limbs are perfectly even— who, upon seeing him, would not be inspired with confidence?
“The speech of the Buddha is heard even across a world-system;
it makes itself understood to all beings—who, having seen this, would not have faith?
For a hundred thousand aeons, I have praised the Buddha.”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of praise.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having become one possessed of the six higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*), at the time of the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*) in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave at Rājagaha, he joined the assembly.
Commanded by the Saṅgha with the words, “Summon the Venerable Ānanda,” he sank into the earth, rose up before the Elder, and delivered the Saṅgha’s message.
Then, departing earlier than the others, he traveled through the air and arrived at the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave.
At that time, a host of deities had gathered for the purpose of warding off Māra and his followers.
A certain deity, having been sent, stood at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. As the Elder Khujjasobhita was announcing his arrival, he said:
“Those monks who dwell in Pāṭaliputta, who are eloquent in speech and deeply learned;”
"Among them, this youth Khujjasobhita stands at the gate"—thus he spoke the first verse.
Therein, "one who speaks with variety" (*cittakathī*) means one who is a preacher of the diverse Dhamma;
[one who preaches] by means of various methods such as summarizing, expanding, making profound, making plain, dispelling doubt, and establishing in the Dhamma, and so forth. For others...

The meaning is: those whose habit is to teach the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations [of others]. "Learned" means learned through the fulfillment of both the learning of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and the penetration of their meaning (*paṭivedha*).
"Ascetics" (*samaṇā*) because they have completely stilled evil. "Residents of Pāṭaliputta"—one among them—means one who is a resident of the city of Pāṭaliputta;
"one among them. This venerable one is long-lived (*āyuvā*), meaning he has a long life. "He stands at the gate" refers to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave.
"He stands at the gate" means he wishes to enter with the Sangha's permission. Having heard this, that deity, announcing the Elder’s arrival to the Sangha, spoke the second verse:
"Those who speak with wisdom... [as before] ...stands at the gate, fanned by the breeze."
In that context, "stirred by the wind" means stirred by the wind produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*); the meaning is that he had arrived through the power of *iddhi*.
Thus, having been granted leave by the Saṅgha as announced by that deity, the Elder, while going into the presence of the Saṅgha, [recited]:
“By fair fighting, by fair sacrifice, and by victory in battle;”
"By practicing the holy life, thus does this happiness increase"—
with this third verse he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*).

In that context, "by a well-fought battle" means by fighting well against the defilements in the prior stage through the abandonment [of them] by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and by way of eradication (*tadaṅga*).
"By well-bestowed [gifts]" means by the gift of suitable Dhamma given from time to time by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"And by victory in battle" means by the victory in battle obtained through the total crushing of the defilements and volitional formations by means of their complete abandonment.
"By the practice of the holy life" means by the practice of the supreme holy life of the Path (*agga-magga-brahmacariya*). "In this way, he prospers in happiness."
In the manner thus described, this Khujjasobhita nourishes—that is to say, experiences—the bliss of Nibbāna and the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Khujjasobhita is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vāraṇa.
"Whosoever among men..."—this is the verse of the Venerable Thera Vāraṇa. What is its origin?

This [Thera] too, having performed meritorious deeds throughout various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a brahmin family ninety-two aeons ago, even before the arising of the Blessed One Tissa.
Having become one who had reached the further shore of the brahmins' branches of knowledge and arts (*vijjāsippa*), he...
Having gone forth into the ascetic life, he lived teaching the mantras to fifty-four thousand disciples.
At that time, when the Blessed One Tissa—while still a bodhisatta—passed away from the Tusita heaven and descended into his mother’s womb for his final existence, a great earthquake occurred.
Seeing this, the great multitude was terrified and deeply moved.
Having approached that seer, he asked the reason for the earthquake.

He [the seer] reassured him by explaining that this earthquake was due to the Great Bodhisatta having descended into his mother’s womb, saying, "Therefore, do not be afraid," and thus described it as a precursor to the arising of a Buddha, causing him to experience rapture centered on the Buddha.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, he [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala.
Having received the name Vāraṇa, when he reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma from a certain forest-dwelling elder;
having gained faith, he went forth and practiced the duties of a recluse. One day, while going to attend upon the Buddha, on the way he [encountered] a snake's nest...
Having seen them die after quarreling with one another, he was moved with a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, "These beings have met their end through mutual conflict.
He went into the presence of the Blessed One; and the Blessed One, knowing the movement of his mind, gave him exhortation suited precisely to that state:
“Whatever person among humans harms the lives of others,
that man falls away from both this world and the next. But he who,
with a mind of loving-kindness, has compassion for all living beings...”
“For such a person produces much merit.
“Let him train in well-spoken words, in attending upon recluses,
in solitude at a single seat, and in the calming of the mind”— thus he spoke these three verses.
In this context, "whosoever here among humans" refers to anyone among humans—whether a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, a śūdra, a householder, or one who has gone forth.

It should be understood that the mention of "humans" here is intended to indicate the highest class of sentient beings. "He harms other living beings" means he kills or injures other creatures. "From this world" refers to this [present] life.

"From this world" (*lokato*). "The supreme" (*paramhā*) means from the other world (*paralokato*). "He falls away from both" (*ubhayā dhaṃseti*) means he falls away from both; the meaning is that he is deprived of the welfare and happiness included within both worlds. "A person" (*naro*) refers to a sentient being.
Having thus shown the unwholesome state characterized by the affliction of others, [the text now] shows the wholesome state characterized by the cessation of the affliction of others.
Teaching the Dhamma, he spoke the second verse beginning with “He who with a mind of loving-kindness...
and so forth. Therein, “with a mind of loving-kindness” means with a mind associated with loving-kindness, whether it has reached absorption (*appanā*) or is otherwise [access concentration].

“He has compassion for all living beings” means he treats all beings with loving-kindness as if they were his own legitimate children. For such a person generates much merit; such is the nature of that man.
Such a person dwelling in loving-kindness produces, acquires, and attains much, great, and no small amount of wholesome merit.
Now, directing [the practitioner] toward the factors of serenity and insight along with their requisites, he spoke the third verse beginning with “One should train in what is well-spoken.
Therein, “one should train in what is well-spoken” refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures, which is classified as the discourse on fewness of desires and so forth.
One should train by means of listening, retention, and inquiry. Regarding "and the attendance upon recluses":
one should train in both attending upon and associating with virtuous friends—recluses who have stilled their evil—from time to time, as well as in practicing in their presence according to the path.
And regarding "solitude, seclusion, and the calming of the mind": for one...
