Being without companions and cultivating physical seclusion, he should train in sitting on a seat by means of devotion to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Thus applying himself to the meditation subject and bringing his meditation (*bhāvanā*) to its culmination, he should train in the stilling of the mind through the total eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*).
By means of these trainings in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth, the defilements are completely...
They are calmed and abandoned; for one training in the training of the path and its fruits, the mind becomes truly and utterly calmed.
At the conclusion of the verse, having increased his insight, he attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having plunged into the Himalayas, I was then reciting the mantras.”
Fifty-four thousand disciples attended upon me.
All of them were masters of the Vedas, having reached perfection in the six branches of knowledge;
firm in their own sciences, they dwell in the Himālaya mountains.
“Having passed away from the Tusita realm, the son of the gods of great renown was conceived in his mother’s womb, fully aware and mindful.
As the Fully Enlightened One was being reborn, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.”
The blind regained their sight as the Leader was appearing.
This entire earth shook in every way;
hearing the sound of the roar, the great masses of people were terrified.
“All people gathered together came into my presence;
the earth shook—what will be the result?
Then I said to them: “Do not be afraid; there is no fear for you.”
“Be joyful, all of you; this arising is auspicious.
The earth trembles, struck by eight causes;
likewise, signs are seen: a vast and great radiance.”
“Without doubt, the Supreme Buddha, the Visionary One, will arise;
having instructed the people, he spoke to me regarding the five precepts.
Having heard of the five precepts and the rarity of a Buddha’s appearance,”
Filled with upliftment, joyful, and with hearts thrilled and exultant, they said:
“In ninety-two aeons from now, regarding the sign I prophesied, I do not know a state of misery;
this is the fruit of that prophecy.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vāraṇa is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vassika.
"Even one who is faithful and wise"—this is the verse of the Venerable Vassika Thera. What is its origin?

This venerable one, too, having performed his duties under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds here and there in various births, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi.
Having attained maturity, one day, upon seeing the Teacher, he became filled with serene faith and [offered] pilakkha fruits.

He gave [the gift]. Circulating through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha within a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kosala.
Having received the name Vassika, when he reached maturity, he saw the Teacher’s Twin Miracle and, having gained faith, went forth into homelessness.
While practicing the duties of a recluse, he became afflicted with illness. Then him—
His kinsmen attended to him with a medicinal regimen prescribed by physicians and restored him to health. Having recovered from that illness, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
he applied himself to meditation and became one possessed of the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“Having seen the Buddha Atthadassi of great glory in the midst of the forest...”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I gave a *pilakkha* fruit.
For eighteen hundred eons, because of that fruit I gave at that time, I have not known an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of giving fruit.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained the sixfold direct knowledge (chaḷabhiññā), he went through the air to the presence of his kinsmen; standing in the air, he taught them the Dhamma and established them in the Refuges and the Precepts.
Among them, some who had passed away were, because they were established in the Refuges and the Precepts, [reborn in a happy destination].
They were reborn in heaven. Then the Teacher, seeing him approach to pay homage to the Buddha, asked: "Vassika, is it well with your kinsmen?
He related to the Teacher the service he had rendered his relatives, saying:
"Even a single person who is faithful and wise, among kinsmen here who are faithless..."
Established in the Dhamma and perfected in virtue, he brings benefit to his kinsmen.
Having restrained my relatives out of compassion and exhorted them,
they have performed services for the monks out of love for their kinsmen and relatives.
“They have passed away and died; they have reached the bliss of the Thirty-three [Heavens].
My brothers and my mother rejoice there, enjoying all their desires.”—Thus he spoke these three verses.
Herein, this is the meaning of the first verse: he who is endowed with faith by way of both faith in the fruit of kamma and faith in the Triple Gem;
who is likewise wise through his application to the knowledge that one’s own actions are one’s own property (kammassakata-ñāṇa) and so forth;

who is established in the Dhamma because he stands firm in the Teacher’s instruction and in the nine supramundane states (navalokuttara-dhamma); and who is perfected in virtue by way of the virtue of conduct, the virtue of the path, and the virtue of the fruit.
Thus, even a single person, by virtue of the absence of the aforementioned faith,

comes to be for the sake and welfare of those who are faithless— those known here in this world as "relatives" (*ñātī*) in the sense that they are to be recognized as "these are ours," and likewise as "kinsmen" (*bandhū*) in the sense that they are bound by the ties of affection.
Having thus applied to oneself the meaning stated in general, the subsequent verses beginning with "niggayha" were spoken to demonstrate this.
Therein, "niggayha anukampāya, coditā ñātayo mayā" means: thinking, "Even now they are in a miserable state;
having failed to perform wholesome deeds, may they not experience further defilement in the future," I restrained them and exhorted my kinsmen out of love for my relatives and kin.
Because they were unable to transgress my instruction due to the affection that arose from thinking,
"This one is our kinsman," they performed acts of service, became devoted in heart toward the bhikkhus, and by giving the requisites such as robes and by attending upon them,
they showed honor and respect to the bhikkhus; having thus passed away and died, they have transcended this world.
*Puna te* is merely an emphatic particle. *Tidivaṃ sukhaṃ* means the happiness included within the world of the gods;
or, they have attained the desirable happiness of the three heavens (*tidiva*). "But who are they? he asks. "My brothers and my mother rejoice, desiring their desires.
The meaning is that they delight, being endowed with the objects of desire according to their own wishes.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vassika is finished.
9. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Yasojja:
“Resembling a black bamboo joint” is a verse of the venerable Elder Yasojja. What is its origin? He too, among former Buddhas...
Having performed his duties and accumulated merits in various existences, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a family of garden-keepers.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Blessed One Vipassī traveling through the air,
he offered a *labuja* fruit with a mind full of serene faith.

Thus, wandering through the realms of gods and humans by virtue of that meritorious deed, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in the village of Keṭaka at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī as the eldest son of a fisherman who was the head of five hundred families;
they gave him the name Yasodatta. When he reached maturity, together with his companions, the sons of fishermen, for the purpose of catching fish...
He cast a net in the Aciravatī River. There, a large golden-colored fish entered within the net.
They presented it to King Pasenadi. The king, thinking, "The Blessed One knows the reason for the color of this golden-colored fish," had the fish caught and showed it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "This [fish] was [the son] of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One..."
"Having gone forth while the Teaching was declining, he practiced wrongly and caused the Teaching to decline;
having been reborn in hell and cooked there for the duration of one *buddhantara*, when he passed away from there, he was reborn as a fish in the Aciravatī River.
Having said this, [the Buddha] spoke of how his sisters were reborn in hell and how that elder brother had attained final Nibbāna.
Having had this story told, the Blessed One taught the *Kapilasutta* on this occasion.
Having heard the Teacher’s teaching, Yasoja was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Together with his companions, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One;
and while dwelling in a suitable place, one day, accompanied by his followers, he went to Jetavana to pay homage to the Blessed One.
He arrived. Upon his arrival, there was a great noise and clamor in the monastery due to the preparation of lodgings and other activities. Hearing this, [the thought arose]:
"The Blessed One has dismissed Yasoja along with his retinue. All of this should be understood according to the method set forth in the Udāna.
Once dismissed, however, the Venerable Yasoja—with a mind deeply stirred like a noble thoroughbred horse struck by a whip—[departed] together with...

Dwelling on the bank of the river Vaggumudā in the assembly, he applied himself with effort, increased his insight (*vipassanā*), and while still within that very residence, became one possessed of the six higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a monastery attendant..."
I saw the stainless Buddha walking along the path of the wind.
"Taking a *labuja* fruit, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas;
standing as if suspended in mid-air, the one of great glory accepted it."
“From the moment I perceived that joy, it brought happiness to me in this very life;
having given the fruit of the Buddha with a mind full of serene confidence,
I then attained rapture, vast and supreme bliss.”
A jewel indeed arises here and there for one who has been reborn.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because I gave that fruit back then, I have not known a miserable destiny; this is the fruit of giving that fruit."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then the Teacher, having summoned the Venerable Yasoja—who possessed the six supernormal powers together with his retinue—welcomed him with the attainment of imperturbability (*āneñjasamāpatti*).
He practiced by undertaking all the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and because of that, his body became emaciated.
It became coarse and discolored; praising him for his supreme fewness of desires, the Blessed One spoke the first verse:
“Resembling a black bamboo joint, emaciated, with veins showing, A man who knows the proper measure in food and drink, and whose mind is not dejected. Thus he spoke.
In this context, "resembling the joints of a black bamboo" means that due to the loss of flesh and the emaciated, withered state of the limbs of his body, he resembles the joints of a rattan creeper;
hence it is said, "emaciated, with veins showing. "Emaciated" (kiso) means one whose body has become thin through the fulfillment of the practice of monastic austerity (moneyya-paṭipadā).
"With veins showing" (dhamanisanthato) means one whose limbs are covered with veins, whose body is stretched out with prominent sinews and arteries due to the lack of flesh and blood.
"Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññū*) means one who knows the limit regarding seeking, receiving, using, and giving away.

"With a mind that is not depressed" (*adīnamānaso*) means one whose mind is not cowed and whose conduct is not indolent, because he is not overcome by laziness and the like. "A man" (*naro*) means a person;
the intended meaning is a "bull among men" (*purisadhorayho*), one endowed with the characteristics of a man because he bears the burden of human duty.
Thus praised by the Teacher, the Elder, in a manner befitting that praise, spoke the Dhamma to the monks by way of extolling his own endurance, patience, exertion of energy, and delight in seclusion:
"Though touched by gadflies and mosquitoes in the forest,
in the great woodland, the Naga, mindful, should endure it there, as if at the head of a battle."
“As one as Brahmā, two as a deva,
three as a village; beyond that, it is a clamor.”—
he spoke these two verses.
In this context, "the elephant who frequents the battlefield" means that just as a well-bred elephant, having endured blows from swords, spears, lances, and so forth on the field of battle,
destroys the enemy army, even so should a monk, mindful and clearly comprehending, endure the dangers of gadflies and the like in the forest,
in the great woods, as one devoted to the forest; and having endured them, he should shatter the power of Māra through the power of meditation.

"Just as Brahmā": just as Brahmā dwells alone, free from mental agitation, constantly happy through the bliss of jhāna, so too does the bhikkhu dwell happily, alone and without a companion, cultivating the bliss of seclusion.
For it is said that "the happiness of one who is alone is sublime. By this, the bhikkhu who dwells alone is called "equal to Brahmā."

He gives advice. "As with a deity, so with two": just as there might be occasional agitation of the mind even among deities, so too there might be friction in the co-residence of two bhikkhus; thus, by virtue of living with a companion, a bhikkhu is called "equal to a deity.
"As with a village, so with three": in this very reading, the co-residence of three bhikkhus is like living in a village.

The intention is that there is no dwelling in seclusion (*viveka*). "Loud clamor beyond that" means that the dwelling of many people even further than that—resembling a great assembly with high-pitched noise, loud sounds, and much commotion—is like a tumult; therefore, one should live alone.
This concludes the commentary on the verses of the Elder Yasojja.
10. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Sāṭimattiya "‘In former times you had faith...’"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sāṭimattiya. What is its origin?
This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various states of existence, [served] the Blessed One Siddhattha.
Having been reborn in a noble family at the proper time and having reached maturity, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a mind full of faith, gave him a palm-leaf fan.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha. Having received the name Sāṭimattiya and having reached adulthood, because of his possession of the necessary causes—
Having gone forth in the presence of forest-dwelling bhikkhus and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he became possessed of the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiñña).
Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:
“I gave a palm-leaf fan to the Blessed One Siddhattha;”
“I wear this highly precious [robe] covered with jasmine flowers.
Ninety-four eons ago, I gave a palm-leaf fan;
I do not recall being born in an evil state—that is the fruit of that palm-leaf fan.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me…pe… the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained the six supernormal knowledges, he exhorted and instructed the bhikkhus, and after preaching the Dhamma to many beings, established them in the refuges and the precepts.
Furthermore, he converted a certain family that was faithless and lacking in confidence, making them faithful and confident.
He did so. Consequently, the people in that family became deeply devoted to the Elder.
There, a certain beautiful and lovely girl served the Elder with great care with food as he entered for alms.
Then one day, Māra, thinking, "In this way his ill repute will increase and he will be left without support," assumed the form of the Elder.
Having gone there, he took the girl by the hand. The girl realized, "This is not the touch of a human being," and she made him let go of her hand.
When the household members saw this, they conceived a lack of faith toward the Elder.
On the following day, the Elder went to that house without reflecting upon that incident; there, the people showed him disrespect. The Elder—
Reflecting on that cause and seeing Māra’s deed, he resolved: "Let a dog's carcass be fastened around his neck.
When Māra approached him for the sake of removing it and was asked to recount the actions he had performed on the previous day, the Teacher rebuked him and released him.
Seeing this, the head of the household asked for forgiveness, saying, "Venerable sir, forgive my transgression," and having obtained his pardon—
“From this day forward, Bhante, I myself shall attend upon you,” he said. As the Elder was preaching the Dhamma to him, he spoke these verses:
“You had faith before, but today it is no longer found in you.
What belongs to you, belongs to you alone; there is no misconduct of mine.”
“Faith is indeed impermanent and fickle; thus has it been seen by me.
People become attached and then dispassionate; what, O Sage, can be worn away therein?
The meal of the Sage is cooked little by little from family to family.”
“I shall go for alms from house to house; I have strength in my legs,” he said, and recited three verses.
Therein, “Previously you had faith, but today it is no longer found in you”: O lay follower, formerly you had faith in me.
“‘The venerable one is a practitioner of the Dhamma, a practitioner of equanimity’—with such words you had faith; that faith of yours is not found in you today, now.
Therefore, ‘what belongs to you, let it belong to you alone’—this gift of the four requisites: let this be yours alone; I have no need for it.
For a gift, indeed, should be given with a mind of right confidence. This is the intended meaning. Alternatively, “what belongs to you... [the rest follows as above].
"‘It belongs to you alone’: the meaning is that whatever disrespect was shown toward me by you today, that belongs to you alone;
its fruit must be experienced by you alone, not by me. ‘There is no misconduct for me’:
there is indeed no such thing as misconduct for me, because the defilements which are the causes of misconduct have been completely eradicated by the Path."
“Faith is indeed impermanent and wavering” means that because the faith of an ordinary person is impermanent and not absolute,
it is therefore wavering— unstable like a gourd placed on the back of a horse or like a post driven into a heap of chaff.
“For I have seen it as such” means that such faith has been seen by me in you, known through direct experience.

"They become attached and they become dispassionate"—because of this very instability of theirs, these beings sometimes, in certain places, become attached through intimacy with friends and develop affection, and sometimes they become dispassionate and their minds become detached.
In that regard, "what does the sage lose?"—the meaning is: when ordinary people become attached or dispassionate, what does the sage, the renunciant, lose? What loss does he suffer?
Showing that one should not think, "If you do not accept my requisites, how will you sustain yourselves?", he spoke this verse beginning with "It is cooked.
Its meaning is as follows: for a sage who has gone forth, food is cooked little by little from house to house, door to door, day after day; it is not only in your own home. I shall wander for alms.
“I have strength in my legs” means: I possess the strength of my legs; I am neither one with bowed legs, nor lame, nor afflicted by foot disease.

Therefore, he shows: “I shall wander for alms with mixed food from the village, and having wandered for alms in the manner taught by the Teacher in the verse beginning ‘Just as a bee [gathers] from the flower,’ I shall sustain myself.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāṭimattiya is finished.
11. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Upāli:
"Having gone forth through faith," these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Upāli. What is his origin? He too [was born] during the time of Padumuttara...

Having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One, one day, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Having performed a work of merit, he aspired to that very station. Having practiced wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this appearance of a Buddha, he took rebirth in the household of Kappaka; they gave him the name Upāli.

When he reached maturity, having become a devotee of the six kṣatriyas beginning with Anuruddha, he went forth together with those six kṣatriyas who were departing for the sake of the religious life while the Tathāgata was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove. Of him—
The procedure for going forth (pabbajjā) has already been recorded in the Canon.

Having gone forth and received full ordination (upasampadā), he took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the presence of the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please grant me permission to dwell in the forest.
The monk replied, "If you dwell in the forest, only one burden will increase for you; for us—"
"However, by living in his presence, he will fulfill both the task of study and the task of insight.
Having accepted the Teacher’s words, the Elder applied himself to the work of insight and before long attained Arahatship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"In the city of Haṃsavatī, there was a well-born brahmin named Sujāta..."
He possessed a hoard of eight hundred million, with abundant wealth and grain.
He was a reciter who bore the mantras, one who had mastered the three Vedas,
and had reached perfection in the science of marks, in history, and in his own sacred doctrine.
“Wanderers with a single topknot, disciples of Gotama, ascetics,
and forest-dwellers were then wandering upon the earth.
They too surrounded me, thinking, ‘This is a renowned brahmin.’”
“Many people honor me, yet I do not honor anything at all.
At that time, I did not see anyone worthy of honor, for I was stiff with pride;
the word ‘Buddha’ did not exist, as the Conqueror had not yet appeared.”
“After the passing of a day and night,
one named Padumuttara arose in the world as the Visionary One, having dispelled all darkness.
While the Teaching was widespread, well-known, and had become extensive— ”
Then the Buddha approached the city named Haṃsa.
For the sake of his father, that Buddha, the Seer, taught the Dhamma;
at that time, the assembly extended for a league all around.
“Appointed among men was that ascetic named Sunanda;
he then covered the entire assembly of the Buddha with flowers.
While the Best One was proclaiming the Four Truths in the pavilion of flowers,”
There was a realization of the Dhamma by one hundred thousand times ten million beings.
Having rained down showers of Dhamma for seven nights and days,
on the arrival of the eighth day, the Jina praised Sunanda.
“Wandering through existence in the world of the gods or among humans,
he will pass from birth to birth as the most excellent of all beings.
In a hundred thousand aeons, he will be born into the lineage of the Okkākas.”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma—
Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī— will be a disciple of that Teacher.”
“Thus did the Fully Awakened One praise the ascetic Sunanda at that time,
making all the people laugh and displaying his own power.
With palms joined in reverence, the people paid homage to the ascetic Sunanda.”
Having performed an act of service toward the Buddha, he purified his own destiny.
"At that time, having heard the words of the Sage, this resolve arose in me:
'I too shall perform an act of service, so that I may see Gotama.'"
“Having thus reflected, I thought about what action I should perform in this unsurpassed field of merit: ‘What deed shall I carry out?
And here is this reciter-monk, the foremost reciter in the teaching.”
“Placed as foremost in the Vinaya, may I aspire to that very state.
‘This immeasurable wealth of mine, unshakeable like the ocean—
by means of this wealth, may I have a monastery built for the Buddha.’”
“In the eastern part of the city, there was a beautiful park;
having purchased it for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], I had a monastic complex built there.
There were gabled halls, palaces, pavilions, open-roofed halls, and caves.”
Having constructed well-made walking paths, I had a monastic park built.
Having had a sauna, a fire hall, as well as a water pavilion,
and a bathing house constructed, I gave them to the community of monks.
“Chairs and stools, articles for use, and vessels;
monastery attendants and medicine—all this I gave away.
Having established a guard, I had a strong wall built.”
“May no one harm him—him who is peaceful in mind and steadfast.
“I had a dwelling built in the Saṅghārāma at the cost of a hundred thousand;
having constructed that Vepulla, I offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One.”
“I have completed this monastery; please accept it, O Sage.
I shall dedicate it to you, O Hero; please consent, O Visionary One.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings—”
Understanding my intention, the Leader consented.
Knowing the consent of the All-Knowing Great Sage,
I prepared the food and announced that it was time.
“When the time had been announced, the Leader Padumuttara,
together with a thousand monks whose taints were exhausted, came to my monastery.
Knowing that he was seated, I satisfied him with food and drink.”
When he had finished eating, I, knowing it was the right time, spoke these words:
"Purchased for a hundred thousand, and built at that same cost—
this beautiful monastery named Sobhana— please accept it, O Sage."
“By this gift of a monastery, and by my volition and aspiration,
may I, when reborn in existence, obtain my heart’s desire.
Having accepted this well-constructed monastic park, the Fully Enlightened One— ”
Sitting in the community of monks, he spoke these words:
"I shall praise him who gave to the Buddha a well-constructed monastery for the Saṅgha; listen as I speak."
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—a fourfold army—will constantly surround him;
this is the fruit of this monastery for the Saṅgha.
Sixty thousand lutes and drums, all beautifully adorned,”
“They shall always attend upon me; this is the fruit of that monastery.
“Sixty-eight thousand women, beautifully adorned, wearing variegated garments and ornaments, with jewels and earrings fastened upon them.”
“With long, lotus-like eyes, beautiful, well-proportioned, and slender-waisted, she shall always attend upon me; this is the fruit of this monastery.
For thirty thousand eons, she will delight in the world of the gods.”
A thousand times the Lord of Devas will exercise sovereignty over the gods.
He will obtain everything that is to be obtained by a king of the gods;
having possessed full and undiminished wealth, he will exercise sovereignty over the gods.
“One thousand times he will be a wheel-turning monarch, a king over the realm;
his sovereignty over the earth will be vast, beyond calculation.
In a hundred thousand aeons, born into the lineage of Okkāka,”
“One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
His legitimate heir to the teachings, born of the Dhamma and fashioned by the Dhamma,
will be a disciple of the Teacher known by the name Upāli.”
“Having reached perfection in the Vinaya and being skilled in what is possible and impossible,
he will dwell free from taints, upholding the teaching of the Conqueror.
Having directly known all this, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans— ”
Having sat within the community of bhikkhus, he will place me in the foremost position.
"For immeasurable eons, I have aspired to your teaching;
that goal of mine has now been attained—the destruction of all fetters."
“Just as a man impaled on a stake, tormented by the king’s punishment,
finds no pleasure in the stake and desires only release; even so,
O Great Hero, have I been tormented by the punishment of existence.”
Bound by my past actions, tormented by the sensation of thirst,
I find no pleasure in existence while being consumed by the three fires.
Like one punished by a king, I seek complete liberation.
“Just as a man overcome by poison would search for an antidote to destroy the poison and preserve his life; while searching,
he might see an antidote that destroys the poison.”
"Having drunk that, he would become happy through liberation from the poison.
In the same way, O Great Hero, just like that man afflicted by poison, I was oppressed by ignorance;
you have administered the medicine of the True Dharma."
“Seeking the medicine of the Dhamma, I beheld the teaching of the Sakyans—
the foremost of all medicines, the remover of all thorns.
Having drunk the medicine of the Dhamma, I have uprooted every poison.”
I have touched Nibbāna, the cool state that is free from aging and death.
Just as a person afflicted by a spirit-demon, established in the reality of his condition,
would seek out a physician for spirits in order to be liberated from that demon.
“Searching, he might see one skilled in the knowledge of spirits;
that man would dispel his spirit and destroy it along with its root.
In the same way, O Great Hero, I am oppressed by that [spirit] which has seized me.”
“I sought the light of knowledge for the sake of complete liberation from darkness.
Then I saw the Sakyan Sage, the cleanser of the darkness of the defilements;
he dispelled my darkness, just as a true physician treats a disease.”
“I have cut off the stream of saṃsāra and blocked the stream of craving;
I have uprooted all existence, just as a physician for living beings [extracts] it from the root.
Just as a garuḷa swoops down upon its prey, the serpent.”
He agitates the great lake for a hundred yojanas all around.
Having seized the serpent and holding it upside down, he afflicts it;
then, like a bird, he takes it and departs wherever he desires.
“Just so, O Great Hero, like a powerful Garuḍa bird,
seeking the Unconditioned, I have washed away all faults.
I have seen the excellent Dhamma, the unsurpassed state of peace.”
One should dwell taking hold of this, just as a garuḷa seizes a serpent.
There is a creeper named Āsāvatī, grown in the Cittalatāvana grove;
for it, a single fruit ripens only after a thousand years.
“The gods attend upon her when her fruit is still far off;
thus this supreme creeper, Āsāvatī, is dear to the gods.
Taking up [the practice] for a hundred thousand years, I attended upon that Sage.”
“Morning and evening I pay homage, as the gods do to Āsāvati.
‘Service is not in vain, and homage is never fruitless;
though I have come from afar, this moment has not failed me.’”
“Searching through existence, I do not perceive a rebirth-linking;
free from acquisitions and utterly liberated, I wander in peace.
Just as the lotus named Paduma blossoms by the rays of the sun,”
In the same way, O Great Hero, I have blossomed by the radiance of the Buddha:
"Just as in the womb of the crane, a male chick is never found,
yet they always conceive when the clouds thunder."
“They carry the fetus for a long time until the cloud thunders;
they are released from their burden when the cloud pours down rain.
When the Buddha Padumuttara thunders with the rain-cloud of Dhamma,”
Through the sound of the Cloud of Dhamma, I received the womb of the Dhamma.
For a hundred thousand years, I bore the womb of merit;
yet I was not released from my burden, for the Cloud of Dhamma did not thunder.
“When you, O Sakya-muni, thundered with the cloud of Dhamma in delightful Kapilavatthu, I was liberated from the burden.
Emptiness, the signless, and likewise the wishless— ”
I have thus understood all four fruits as merely states of mind.
Having taken up my practice immeasurably long ago, I have aspired to your teaching;
that goal has now been attained by me—the unsurpassed state of peace.
“Having reached perfection in the Vinaya, just like the seer Pāṭhika, there is no one equal to me; I uphold the Dispensation.
In the Vinaya, in the Khandhakas, in the Tikaccheda, and in the Pañcaka...”
In this matter I have no doubt, whether regarding the vowels or the consonants.
He is skilled in refutation and in remedial action, and in what is possible and what is impossible;
he has reached perfection in all respects, including reinstatement and formal emergence from probation.
“Having set down a word in either the Vinaya or the Khandhaka,
I would extract it from both sides and expound it according to its true flavor.
Skilled in grammar and proficient in both the meaning and the non-meaning,”
“There is nothing unknown to me; I am single-minded in the Teacher’s dispensation.
Today, I am an eyewitness to form within the dispensation of the Son of the Sakyans;
I dispel all doubt and cut through every uncertainty.”
“I am skilled in every respect—in the words, the following words, the syllables, and the phonemes; in the introduction and in the conclusion.
Just as a powerful king, having subdued his enemies...”
Having won the battle, he should establish a city there.
He should cause to be built a rampart and a moat, as well as watchtowers, gatehouses,
and many various kinds of watch-stations within the city.
“One should have a crossroads and a marketplace built, with well-laid-out shops;
and there, one should establish a hall for the adjudication of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
This is for the purpose of suppressing enemies and for knowing the vulnerabilities and strengths [of others].”
For the protection of his body, he appoints a commander of the army.
Thinking, "May my goods not be lost," he appoints a man skilled in storage for the sake of guarding his merchandise.
He appoints a guardian of the goods.
“He gives a legal case to one who is devoted to him, whom the king desires to promote,
and who acts as a friend. [He gives it] to one skilled in portents, omens, and bodily marks.”
He appoints a reciter who has mastered the mantras as his domestic chaplain.
Endowed with these qualities, one is called a kshatriya;
they always protect the king, just as the cakravāka bird protects its mate when she is distressed.
“In the same way, O Great Hero, you are like a Kṣatriya who has slain his enemies;
you are called the Dharma King of the world together with its devas.
Having utterly defeated the heretics and even Māra along with his host,”
Having dispelled that darkness, he caused the City of Dhamma to be built.
“Therein, virtue is the rampart, wisdom is the gateway-tower;
faith is your pillar, O Hero, and restraint is the gatekeeper.”
“The watchtower is the foundations of mindfulness, O Sage; wisdom is your crossroads;
the bases of psychic power are the junctions, and the streets of the Dhamma are well-laid out.
The Suttantas, the Abhidhamma, and the entirety of the Vinaya—”
The word of the Buddha in its nine divisions—
this is your chamber of Dhamma. Emptiness, the signless,
the dwelling free from desire, the imperturbable, and cessation— this is your hut of Dhamma.
“Placed at the pinnacle of wisdom, skilled in inspired eloquence,
he who is known by the name Sāriputta is your Dhamma-general.
He is expert in passing away and reappearing, having reached the perfection of psychic power.”
“O Sage, you were known by the name Kolita, the royal chaplain.
You were a bearer of the ancient lineage, of fierce energy and difficult to approach;
you were foremost in the virtue of those who preach the ascetic practices (dhuta), O Sage, a seer among the wise.”
“Learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and one who has mastered all the scriptures within the Teaching—
Ānanda by name, you are the guardian of the Dhamma,
O Sage. Having surpassed all these, the Blessed One has sent me here.”
“You have granted me the *Vinicchaya*, which was taught by those learned in the *Vinaya*.
Whatever question regarding the *Vinaya* any disciple of the Buddha asks, I have no need for reflection thereupon; I shall explain that very matter.”
“Within the entire field of a Buddha, except for that Great Sage himself, there is no one like me in the Vinaya; how could there be anyone superior?
Seated within the Saṅgha of monks, Gotama thunders thus.”
There is no one equal to Upāli in the Vinaya and the Khandhakas.
"To whatever extent there is that which was spoken by the Buddha, the ninefold teaching of the Teacher—
all of that has its depth in the Vinaya for one who perceives the root of the Vinaya."
“Remembering my deed, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
sat amidst the community of bhikkhus and placed me at the very foremost.
Having made offerings for a hundred thousand years, I aspired for this state.”
Thus my goal has been attained, having reached perfection in the Vinaya.
Formerly, I was a barber, bringing joy to the Sakyans;
having abandoned that birth, I am now born as the son of the Great Sage.
“In this second aeon, there was a kshatriya named Añjaso;
he was a protector of the earth of great wealth, possessing infinite splendor and immeasurable fame.
I was the son of that king, a kshatriya named Candana.”
"Arrogant with my birth, and with the pride of fame and wealth:
'Hundreds of thousands of nāgas, adorned with every ornament—
elephants with temples split in three ways— always surround me.'"
“Surrounded by my attendants and desiring to go to the park,
I then mounted the elephant Sirika and departed from the city.
Endowed with noble conduct, guarding my senses, and well-restrained;”
The Fully Enlightened One named Devala came before me.
Having sent forth the nāga Sirika, I then provoked the Buddha;
thereupon, that nāga, having become enraged, did not lift his foot.
“Seeing the Naga with a grieving mind, I directed anger toward the Buddha;
having harassed the Perfectly Enlightened One, I went back to my garden.
There, I found no pleasure, as if my head were ablaze.”
“I am burning with fever, like a fish caught on a hook.
The earth, as far as the ocean’s edge, seems to me as if it were ablaze.
Having approached my father, I spoke these words.”
“As if approaching an angry venomous snake, as if approaching a mass of fire,
or as if approaching an elephant in rut with tusks—
I have encountered the Self-Existent One. The Buddha, the terrible Conqueror of fierce asceticism, has been encountered by me.”
"Otherwise we shall all perish; we must ask that sage for forgiveness.
If we do not appease him—who is self-tamed and composed—within seven days my kingdom will be destroyed."
“Sumekhalo, Kosiya, Siggava, and Sattaka—
having harmed these seers, those men of Soraṭṭha fell into a miserable state.
When seers who are self-restrained and lead lives of celibacy become enraged, [they bring great destruction].”
They are destroying the world with its gods, its oceans, and its mountains.
Having assembled men from three thousand yojanas,
I approached the Self-Existent One (the Buddha) in order to confess my transgression.
“With all their limbs and all their heads [bowed], everyone with palms joined together, having fallen at the feet of the Buddha, spoke these words:
‘Forgive us, O Great Hero; this people implores you.’”
“Dispel this fever; do not destroy our kingdom.
Even if all beings—gods, humans, asuras, and rakkhasas—were to constantly split my head with an iron mallet, [I would still endure].”
“Fire does not remain in water, nor does a seed grow on a rock;
a worm does not remain in an antidote, and anger does not arise toward a Buddha.
And just as the earth is immovable, and the ocean is immeasurable;”
And space is infinite; thus are the Buddhas unshakable.
“The great heroes are always patient, and the ascetics are forgiving;
for those who are patient and forgiving, no going forth [into rebirth] exists.”
“Having spoken thus, the Fully Awakened One, dispelling the fever [of my mind],
then rose up into the sky before the great multitude.
‘By that deed, O Hero, I have fallen into a state of inferiority.’”
Having transcended that birth, I entered the city of fearlessness.
Then too, O Great Hero, while I was burning yet well-composed,
you dispelled my fever, and I, the Self-Existent One, offered my apology.
“Even now, O Great Hero, though I am burning with three fires,
you have extinguished those three fires for me and brought me to a state of coolness.
Those who have the capacity to listen, listen as I speak.”
I shall declare the matter to you, just as I have seen my own state:
"Having shown contempt for that Self-Existent One, whose mind was peaceful and composed,
because of that kamma I am today born into a low womb."
"Do not let the opportune moment pass you by, for those who have missed the moment grieve;
strive for your own true welfare, for the moment has been prepared for you.
For some there is emesis, and for others purgation."
To some it is the deadly halāhala poison, and to others it is medicine.
For those practicing emesis it is the fruit, for those established in the fruits it is the purgative;
for those who have attained the fruits it is medicine, and for those seeking the field of merit it is the field itself.
“Like the deadly poison *halāhala*,
so does the venomous snake whose bite is seen consume that man who opposes the Teaching.
Once drunk, the *halāhala* poison brings an end to life.”
Having violated the Teaching, one burns for ten million eons.
But by means of patience, non-violence, and a mind of loving-kindness, one delivers the world together with its devas; therefore, do not fail in these.
“They do not cling to gain or loss, nor to honor or dishonor;
Buddhas are like the earth, therefore they are not offended.
Even toward Devadatta, the murderer, and the thief Aṅgulimāla,”
Toward Rāhula and toward Dhanapāla, the Sage was equal toward all.
"In these there is no aversion, and passion is not found in them;
the Buddha is equal toward all, toward the executioner and toward his own son."
“Seeing a discarded yellow robe, though smeared with filth,
one should place one’s hands in añjali upon the head and pay homage to that banner of the sages.
And those Buddhas who have passed away, those who are present now, and those yet to come— ”
By this banner they are purified; therefore, these are worthy of homage.
“I bear within my heart the Teacher’s well-disciplined Vinaya;
paying homage to the Vinaya, I shall dwell at all times.”
“The Vinaya is my dwelling place; the Vinaya is my standing and walking.
I make my abode in the Vinaya; the Vinaya is my field of activity.
Having reached perfection in the Vinaya, I am also skilled in the methods of calming.”
Upāli, O Great Hero, pays homage at the feet of the Teacher:
“Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town,
paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Therein, the Teacher himself had him learn the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. Later on, he adjudicated these three cases:
the Bhārukacchaka case, the Ajjukā case, and the Kumārakassapa case. In each one of them, the Teacher—

Having adjudicated the case and given his approval, he made that very decision the occasion for a formal discourse (*aṭṭuppatti*) and established the Elder in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Later, on a certain Uposatha day, while instructing the monks at the time of reciting the Pātimokkha, he said:
“Having gone forth out of faith, a newly ordained novice;”
One should associate with the virtuous, those of pure livelihood who are untiring.
Having gone forth out of faith, a newly ordained novice,
a wise bhikkhu dwelling within the Saṅgha, should train in the Vinaya.
“Having gone forth out of faith, a newly ordained novice, skilled in what is proper and improper, should wander without being led by others”—thus he spoke these three verses.
Therein, "out of faith" means for the sake of faith, not for the sake of a livelihood. Or, "out of faith" means [confidence] in the fruits of kamma.
"And having placed faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem. "Having gone forth" means having departed from the household life.
"A newly ordained one" means one who has gone forth as a novice; that is, one who has gone forth in the very first stage of life. "New" means fresh in the training of the Dispensation, being young.
"One should associate with virtuous friends who live pure lives and are untiring" refers to those described by such phrases as "dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem," and so forth.

One should associate with and approach spiritual friends who possess the characteristics already described, who are pure in livelihood by avoiding wrong livelihood, and who are untiring due to their exertion of energy;
one should serve them by receiving their advice and instructions.
Dwell in the Saṅgha—meaning, dwelling within the community of monks by fulfilling the duties and counter-duties—one should train in the Vinaya.
"Buddha" means that having become well-skilled in the knowledge of awakening (*bodhañāṇa*), one should train in the study of the Vinaya.
For the Vinaya is the life-span of the Dispensation; when it stands, the Dispensation stands. They also read "Buddho," which has the same meaning.

"Skilled in what is allowable and what is unallowable" means being expert and clever according to the Suttas and in accordance with the Suttas regarding what is permissible and what is impermissible. "Not neglectful" means...
One should dwell not being honored by craving and the like, without expecting honor from anyone.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Upāli is finished.
12. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttarapāla.
"Truly, I am wise"—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Uttarapāla. What is its origin?

This [Elder] as well had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; accumulating merit in various states of existence, he caused a bridge to be built on the path taken by the Blessed One Vipassī.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, in this [present life]...
Having been born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī at the time of a Buddha's appearance and having received the name Uttarapāla, he attained maturity.
Upon witnessing the Twin Miracle, he gained faith, went forth, and practiced the duties of a recluse.
One day, due to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), sensual desire arose in him as he recollected an object previously experienced. At that very moment—

Like one seizing a thief caught in the act, he restrained his own mind; filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he suppressed the defilements through the mental application of their opposites.
Performing the work of insight (*vipassanā*) and intensifying his meditation, he attained Arhatship.
Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, while he was walking back and forth,
with a clear mind and a joyful heart,
I had a bridge constructed. For ninety-one eons, because I had that bridge built, [the fruit has ripened].”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving a bridge.
Having attained arahantship, he reviewed his own practice and uttered this lion’s roar: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Then, having reached arahantship and reflecting upon his own conduct, he let out a lion’s roar:
“Though I am indeed wise and capable of reflecting on what is beneficial,
the five strands of sensual pleasure in this world have cast me down through delusion.
Having leaped into the domain of Māra, I am pierced by a firm arrow.”
“I have been able to escape from the snares of the King of Death.
All sensual pleasures have been abandoned by me; all states of existence have been shattered.
The wandering through births is exhausted; there is now no further becoming.”
He recited three verses.
Therein, "I am indeed wise" refers to being endowed with wisdom by way of the wisdom consisting of what is heard and reflection;
"one who considers the welfare"—that is, one capable of considering the benefit and welfare of both oneself and others.
"Capable," "sufficient," or "adequate" refers to one who is able to contemplate the meaning (*attha*) or one who sees the meaning capable of destroying the defilements (*kilesa*);
the Elder says all this because he is in his final existence. "The five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) refers to the five divisions of sensual desire, beginning with visible forms.
"In the world" (*loke*) indicates the sphere where they occur. "From delusion" (*sammohā*) means from the cause of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), which is the sign of delusion.

"Delusion" (sammoha) means deluding or causing delusion. "They cast down" (pātayiṃsu) means they caused me to fall from my state of steadfastness; or the meaning is that they cast me down into the world when I desired to transcend it. "Having entered" (pakkhando) means having gone within.
"Into the realm of Māra" (māravisaye) means into the realm of the defilements, the place where the Māra of defilements operates. Of him—
The intended meaning is "having come under [his] power. Or, having entered and remained in the place of sovereignty belonging to the Māra who is a son of the devas;
"pierced by a firm dart" means firmly or steadily, or pierced by a firm dart—the heart being struck and pierced by the dart of passion (*rāga*).
"I was able to escape from the snares of King Death"—by means of the tongs of the supreme path, [he removed] the dart of passion and the other [defilements].
While extracting [the thorns] without remainder, I was able to be liberated from the snares of King Māra known as the bonds of lust;
from that, I freed myself.

And for that very reason, all sensual desires have been abandoned by me, and all states of existence (bhava) have been shattered—[desires] which are divided into many varieties according to their bases, objects, and so forth.
All defilement-desires (*kilesakāma*) have been abandoned by me through their total eradication by means of the Noble Path.

For when the defilement-desires are abandoned, the object-desires (*vatthukāma*) are likewise abandoned. Similarly, all states of existence (*bhava*), such as sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), have been shattered and destroyed by the sword of path-knowledge.
For when kamma-existences are shattered, the rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*) are necessarily shattered as well.
Thus, because the states of kamma-existence have been shattered, the cycle of birth has been exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
The meaning of this has already been explained above. And this very statement was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Uttarapāla is finished.
13. Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Abhibhūta.
"Listen, all you kinsmen," etc., are the verses of the Venerable Elder Abhibhūta. What is his origin?

This [Elder] also, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit in various states of existence, was born into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū.
Having been reborn and attained the state of maturity, he became deeply devoted to the Teaching through his reliance on such a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).

When the Teacher had passed into *parinibbāna*, while the great multitude was making efforts to take his relics, he himself extinguished the funeral pyre with scented water first of all. By that meritorious deed, among gods and humans...
Wandering through the cycle of existence, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a royal family in the city of Veṭhadīpa, where he received the name Abhibhū.
Upon his father’s passing, he ruled the kingdom. At that time, while the Blessed One was traveling on a journey through the countryside, he eventually arrived at that city.
Then, having heard that "the Blessed One has indeed arrived at my city," the king [approached] the Teacher...
Having gone into his presence and heard the Dhamma, he offered a great almsgiving on the following day.
After the Blessed One had finished eating, he gave a blessing in accordance with the king’s disposition and taught the Dhamma in detail.
Having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, the king renounced his kingdom, went forth, and realized arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“When the body of Vessabhu, the Great Seer, was burning,
I took scented water and extinguished the funeral pyre.
Thirty-one eons ago, I extinguished the funeral pyre.”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of scented water.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, while he was thus [living], his kinsmen, ministers, and courtiers—”
The citizens and the people of the countryside all gathered together and lamented, saying, "Venerable sir, why have you gone forth into homelessness, leaving us behind as if we were helpless?
Seeing those people, led by his kinsmen, thus lamenting, the Elder preached the Dhamma to them by way of explaining the reason for his own going forth:
"Listen, all you kinsmen, as many as are assembled here!..."
“I shall teach you the Dhamma: birth is suffering again and again.
‘Exert yourselves! Strive on! Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.’”
“He who, in this Dhamma and Discipline, shall dwell with diligence;
having abandoned the cycle of birth, he will make an end of suffering”—thus he spoke these three verses.
Therein, "listen" means pay close attention; now, with ears pricked and following the gateway of the ear, attend to what is being said by me.
The meaning is as follows. "Kinsmen" (ñātayo) refers to addressing all of them by placing their kinsmen at the head; thus he said, "All you who have gathered here.
The sense is: however many there are in this assembly, or those who have gathered for this going-forth of mine.
Now, that which was intended when the command to listen was given with the words "Listen," is expressed by the statement, "I shall teach the Dhamma to you."
Having made this declaration, he began to teach by means of the passage beginning, "Birth is suffering again and again.

In this context, "birth is suffering again and again" means that birth is indeed suffering because it serves as the basis for manifold kinds of suffering, such as the various types rooted in conception in the womb and the various types beginning with aging.
When it occurs repeatedly, it is exceedingly painful.
Showing that effort must be made for the sake of transcending that birth, he said, "Exert yourselves," and so forth.
Therein, "exert yourselves" means: perform the energy known as the element of exertion (*ārambhadhātu*). "Strive" means:

because it has emerged from the side of indolence, perform the further energy known as the element of striving (*nikkamadhātu*). "Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching" means: apply yourselves to the practice of the Dhamma.
Because for those established in these qualities— namely, restraint by virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension—
the elements of initiative and exertion come to fruition through devotion to wakefulness;
therefore, being thus constituted, within the Blessed One’s dispensation known as serenity and insight, or as the training in higher virtue and so forth—
"Be diligent and apply yourselves with effort. Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.

Practicing in this way, one destroys the weak and frail army of the King of Death—who leads beings under his power—just as a powerful elephant endowed with great strength instantly demolishes a hut made of reeds; even so, [one destroys it].
"Shake off the mass of defilements; scatter them, destroy them"—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, showing that for one who exerts such effort in the Buddha’s teaching, the transcendence of the suffering of birth is certain, he spoke the third verse beginning with "He who in this... That is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Abhibhūta is finished.
14. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gotama.
These verses belong to the Venerable Elder Gotama. What is his origin?

It is said that this [Elder], having performed meritorious deeds in various existences while fulfilling his obligations under previous Buddhas, [built] a funeral pyre for the Blessed One Sikhī when He had attained final Nibbāna.
While gods and humans were making offerings, he honored the funeral pyre with eight *campaka* flowers.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance within the Sakyan royal family.

Having attained a name distinguished by his clan as Gotama, and having reached maturity, he gained faith upon meeting the Teacher’s kinsmen; he then went forth and applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
While performing that deed, he became one possessed of the six supernormal powers. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"While the Blessed One Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World, was meditating, I offered eight campaka flowers upon his funeral pyre."
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered that flower, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worship with a heap of flowers.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
But having become one possessed of the six direct knowledges and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one day, when asked by his kinsmen, "Venerable sir,
why did you go forth, abandoning us? he explained both the suffering he had experienced within saṃsāra and the bliss of Nibbāna now attained:
“Indeed, wandering in saṃsāra, I went to hell; again and again I went to the world of the hungry ghosts (petas).
Even in the animal womb, suffering was endured by me for a long time in many ways.
And even human existence was craved; I went to the heavenly body again and again.”
“In the realms of form and the formless realms, established in the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
having well understood that these conditioned things are hollow, unstable, and subject to decay,
and having realized their origin from the great mass [of ignorance], the mindful one has attained peace alone.”
He taught the Dhamma to them with three verses.

In that context, "they wander" means that while wandering through beginningless *saṃsāra*, they pass from one state to another by way of death and rebirth among the five destinations due to the defilements of karma.
The word "hi" is a mere particle. They will go to hell, such as Sañjīva and the others.
I entered, by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the eightfold Great Hell and the sixteenfold Ussada Hells, such as Kukkuḷa and the rest.

The word "again and again" (*punappunaṃ*) should also be supplied here. "The world of ghosts" (*petalokaṃ*) means the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), that is, the state of existence as a ghost characterized by hunger, thirst, and so forth.
"I went" (*agamaṃ*) means I approached and was reborn there by way of rebirth-linking. "Again and again" (*punappunaṃ*).

"Successively" (*aparāparam*). "Even in suffering" (*dukkhamamhipi*): this is stated with a change of gender as "even in suffering," meaning that it is difficult to endure even amidst various sufferings such as the piercing of sharp thorns and the striking of goads against one another.

"In the animal womb" (*tiracchānayoniyam*) means in the animal realm divided into species such as beasts and birds. "In many ways" (*nekadhā hi*) refers to [birth] as a camel, ox, donkey, and so forth, as well as a crow, crane, hawk, and so forth.
And for many varieties of beings and on many occasions, throughout a long and extended period, I have lived and experienced suffering constantly through such states as a mind in perpetual terror.
Here, the word "long" (*cira*) is used to show that a being reborn in the animal realm,
due to extreme delusion, revolves back and forth in that very state for an even longer duration.

"And a human existence was attained" means that even this human state (*manussattabhāva*) was attained, accomplished, and achieved by me through such wholesome karma (*kusalakamma*) and its convergence. Here, the *Kāṇakacchapa-sutta* (The Simile of the Blind Tortoise) should be cited.

"I went to the heavenly host once upon a time" means that, by way of being reborn from time to time—that is, occasionally—I went to the heavenly host reckoned as the celestial realm of the sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-devakāya*).

"I went. Regarding "in the form realm" (*rūpadhātu*): this refers to existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*) up to the limit of the peak of existence for worldlings (*puthujjana-bhavagga-pariyosāna*). Regarding "in the formless realm" (*arūpadhātu*):

this refers to existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*). "Established among those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception and among the non-percipient" should be connected by supplying the words:

"I was reborn and established not only among those with perception, but also among those with neither-perception-nor-non-perception and among the non-percipient, within both the form and formless realms."

Here, by the mention of "neither-perception," the state of "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" is included. Although these two states of existence are already included by the mention of the form and formless realms,
it should be understood that they are mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the falsity of that perception for those outsiders who regard them as permanent and as liberation from existence.

Thus, having shown his own experience of the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*) within beginningless *saṃsāra* because the root of existence (*bhavamūla*) has not been severed by means of these two verses, he now speaks the third verse beginning with "Sambhavā" to show his experience of the bliss of the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭasukha*) through its severance.
Therein, "Sambhavā" means existences (*bhavā*). For it is precisely the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*) and so forth that come into being through the convergence of causes and conditions.
"Arising here" is what is said. "Well-known" means well-known by means of the wisdom of the path accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
The passage beginning with "insubstantial" is a demonstration of the manner in which they are known. Therein, "insubstantial" means devoid of any essence such as permanence.
"Conditioned" means made by conditions having come together and combined. "Shaking" means, precisely because they are conditioned, [shaken] in various ways by arising, aging, and so forth.
“Moving” means unstable. “Constantly shaken” (*saderitā*) means always, at all times, shaken by dissolution;

the meaning is that they are transient, subject to dissolution, and perishable. Having understood that—the aforementioned conditioned nature which arises from a self (*attasambhava*), produced within the self, belonging to the self, and not dependent on another such as a Lord (*issara*)—by means of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*).

"Having understood this, I—being mindful through the mindfulness of the wisdom of the path—attained, reached, and realized Nibbāna itself, which is peace and the very opposite of that [suffering], by means of the cultivation of the Noble Path.
In this way, the Elder declared his final knowledge (*aññā*) by means of a Dhamma teaching for his kinsmen.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Gotama is finished.
15. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hārita "Those things which ought to be done previously... These are the verses of the Venerable Elder Hārita. What is their origin?

He too, having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and having attained maturity, performed the funeral pyre worship for the Teacher after he had attained final Nibbāna.

While it was being performed, he made an offering with perfume. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.

Having received the name Hārita, when he reached maturity, relying on his pride in birth, he addressed others with the word "outcaste" (vasala). He went into the presence of the bhikkhus and [listened to] the Dhamma...
Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth as a monk; yet, because of his long-standing habituation, he did not abandon his conduct toward outcasts.
Then one day, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.
Establishing insight (*vipassanā*) and examining the movement of his own mind, he saw that it was obstructed by pride and restlessness. Abandoning those, he applied himself to insight.
Having exerted himself with diligence, he attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“While the funeral pyres were being prepared and various perfumes were being gathered, with a serene heart and a joyful mind, I offered a handful of fragrant powder.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons past, I honored a funeral pyre;
I do not know a state of misery—this is the fruit of honoring the pyre.
‘The defilements have been incinerated by me... [the rest as in the standard verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Having become an arahant and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he declared his final knowledge (*aññā*) by means of giving exhortation to the bhikkhus through three verses beginning with, "Those duties which were to be done before... The meaning of these has already been explained above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Hārita is concluded.
16. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vimala.
"Evil friends"—this is a verse by the Venerable Elder Vimala. What is its origin?

This venerable one, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Upon reaching maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, on the days of the festival of joyful games...
When the lay followers had passed by and were taking the Teacher’s body toward the cremation site, he reflected upon the Teacher’s virtues and,
with a devout mind, made an offering of *sumana* flowers. Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans,
he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī, receiving the name Vimala.
Having reached maturity, he went forth into the Teaching under the guidance of the Elder Somamitta.
Encouraged by him, he established insight meditation and before long attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
"While the body was being carried out, as the drums were being beaten..."
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I offered a *paṭṭi* flower.
"Because I offered that flower a hundred thousand aeons ago, I have not known a state of misery;
this is the fruit of worshipping the physical body."
“The defilements have been burnt up by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, he gave this exhortation to his companion bhikkhu:
“Having avoided evil friends, one should associate with the supreme person;”
One should abide by his instruction, aspiring for unshakable happiness:
"Just as one who has boarded a small wooden raft might sink in the great ocean,
so too, by relying on a person who is lazy, even one who lives rightly sinks."
Therefore, one should avoid that person who is indolent and of inferior energy.
One should dwell together with wise ones— noble ones who live in seclusion,
who are resolute, who meditate, and who have constantly applied their energy.
He spoke three verses.
Therein, "evil friends" refers to unwholesome companions, ignoble persons, and those of inferior energy. "Having avoided" means having shunned them from afar by not associating with them.
"One should associate with the supreme person" means [associating with] a noble person, a wise one, and a virtuous friend by way of receiving their advice and instructions.
“He should serve”: he should abide by the advice and instruction of that good friend, practicing in accordance with what has been instructed.
“Aspiring”: desiring. “Unshakable happiness”: the happiness of Nibbāna and the happiness of the fruit (phalasukha).
For that too is called “unshakable” because its state is unshakeable. The rest has already been explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vimala is finished.
The commentary on the Triads (Tikanipāta) is finished.
The first volume is finished.
